title: Establish sequential convergence of Lloyd’s algorithms without globally subanalytic densities
background_latex:
Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with compact support \(\mathrm{Supp}(\mu)\) and density \(f\) with respect to Lebesgue measure (so \(d\mu(x)=f(x)\,dx\)). Fix \(N\in\mathbb{N}^*\) and write \(Y=(y_1,\dots,y_N)\in (\mathbb{R}^d)^N\) for the support points of a discrete measure. Let \(\Delta_N:=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}^N_+:\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i=1\}\) be the probability simplex and let \(\delta_y\) denote a Dirac mass at \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

For optimal quantization, define the objective
\[
G_N(Y):=\min_{\pi\in\Delta_N}\frac12\,W_2^2\Bigl(\mu,\sum_{i=1}^N \pi_i\,\delta_{y_i}\Bigr)=\frac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\min_{1\le i\le N}\|x-y_i\|^2\,f(x)\,dx,
\]
where \(W_2\) is the 2-Wasserstein distance for the squared Euclidean cost. When \(Y\) has distinct points, the Voronoi cells are
\[
V_i(Y):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\ \|x-y_i\|^2<\|x-y_j\|^2\ \forall j\ne i\},\qquad i=1,\dots,N.
\]
The Lloyd update for optimal quantization maps \(Y\) to the vector of Voronoi barycenters
\[
T_N(Y):=\Bigl(\frac{\int_{V_i(Y)} x\,d\mu(x)}{\mu(V_i(Y))}\Bigr)_{i=1}^N,
\]
and generates iterates \(Y_{n+1}=T_N(Y_n)\) (under suitable conditions ensuring \(\mu(V_i(Y_n))>0\)).

For uniform quantization, define
\[
F_N(Y):=\frac12\,W_2^2\Bigl(\mu,\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \delta_{y_i}\Bigr).
\]
The corresponding Lloyd-type update for uniform quantization can be written (via semi-discrete optimal transport duality) as a Laguerre/power-cell barycentric map \(B_N\), producing iterates \(Y_{n+1}=B_N(Y_n)\).

Sequential convergence means that the entire iterate sequence \((Y_n)_{n\ge 0}\) converges to a single limit point (equivalently, has a unique accumulation point), typically a critical point of the relevant objective \(G_N\) or \(F_N\).

The paper proves sequential convergence of these Lloyd iterates under the additional hypothesis that the density \(f\) is globally subanalytic (hence definable in an o-minimal structure), which yields the Kurdyka-\L{}ojasiewicz inequality for \(G_N\) and \(F_N\).

open_problem_quote: Beyond existing results, a general sequential convergence guaranty for Lloyd’s methods in the semi-discrete setting remains open.
counterexample_suitability_rationale: The statement asks for general sufficient conditions guaranteeing convergence for all instances in a broad continuous-measure setting, so there is no finite or easily parameterized instance family whose exhaustive search would decisively refute a candidate theorem. While one can simulate Lloyd iterates for specific densities to look for nonconvergence, such experiments are not definitive for an unconditional mathematical guarantee.
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: One can code Lloyd iterations and search over parametrized families of densities/initializations to discover empirical nonconvergence phenomena or to conjecture weaker sufficient conditions (e.g., smoothness, log-concavity) by fitting to observed behavior. However, translating such computational findings into a correct general theorem (or a rigorous counterexample) would still require substantial human-driven analysis beyond the fitness signal.

literature_review.synthesis:
The 2025 paper of Portales–Cazelles–Pauwels establishes sequential convergence of Lloyd-type fixed-point iterations for both optimal quantization \(Y_{n+1}=T_N(Y_n)\) and uniform quantization \(Y_{n+1}=B_N(Y_n)\) under the rigidity hypothesis that the target density \(f\) is globally subanalytic (hence definable), which implies the Kurdyka–\L{}ojasiewicz (KL) property for the semi-discrete objectives \(G_N\) and \(F_N\). The proof combines (i) the classical identities \(\nabla G_N(Y)=M(V(Y))(Y-T_N(Y))\) and \(\nabla F_N(Y)=\tfrac1N(Y-B_N(Y))\), (ii) a strong descent condition along Lloyd iterates, and (iii) KL-based convergence theorems for gradient-like methods.

Beyond this definability framework, the open problem asks for alternative conditions on \(\mu\) ensuring sequential convergence. The only forward-citing work provided here ("Weighted quantization using MMD") does not advance this question for \(W_2\)-quantization; it studies different objectives (MMD) and dynamics, though it reinforces the general strategy of viewing fixed-point quantization schemes as (preconditioned) gradient methods where KL-type inequalities can yield convergence.

Given the current forward-citation evidence supplied, there is no identified solution removing global subanalyticity/definability assumptions. Promising directions suggested by the source paper include: finding other verifiable KL mechanisms for \(G_N\) and \(F_N\) (e.g., analyticity of parameterized integrals under alternative geometric hypotheses on \(\mathrm{Supp}(\mu)\)), or proving isolation/stratification properties of critical sets (which would imply convergence once accumulation points are known to be critical).

sources.title: Weighted quantization using MMD: From mean field to mean shift via gradient flows
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces MMD-optimal weighted quantization algorithms based on Wasserstein–Fisher–Rao (WFR) gradient flows and a fixed-point scheme (MSIP). Key statements include: (i) an interacting particle ODE system discretizing the WFR gradient flow for the MMD functional (Proposition 3.1), with global existence/uniqueness and monotone decrease of the MMD functional along the ODE trajectory under mild kernel assumptions (Proposition 3.2); (ii) a characterization of stationary points via kernel moment conditions (19)–(20) and a resulting fixed-point iteration (24)–(25); (iii) an identity showing MSIP is a preconditioned gradient descent for the finite-particle objective \(F_M(Y)=\inf_{w\in\mathbb R^M}\tfrac12\mathrm{MMD}^2(\pi,\sum_i w_i\delta_{y_i})\), namely \(\nabla F_M(Y)=P(Y)(Y-\Psi_{\mathrm{MSIP}}(Y))\) (Theorem 3.4), and an existence result of step sizes ensuring descent of \(F_M\) for squared-exponential kernels (Proposition 3.5).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for sequential convergence of Lloyd iterates for semi-discrete \(W_2\)-quantization (optimal and uniform) under conditions on \(\mu\) beyond global subanalyticity/definability of the density. This citing paper does not address sequential convergence of Lloyd’s algorithm for \(W_2\) quantization; it only recalls the classical identity \(\nabla G_M(Y)=D(Y)(Y-\Psi_{\mathrm{Lloyd}}(Y))\) from Du et al. (1999) as an analogy. Its new convergence/descent results concern different objectives (MMD-based quantization) and different dynamics (WFR gradient flow, MSIP fixed-point/preconditioned gradient descent). It therefore does not solve or partially solve the stated open problem, but it is tangentially related by importing the ‘Lloyd as preconditioned gradient descent’ viewpoint and by suggesting future use of Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz ideas (citing Portales et al. 2025) for their own algorithms.

title: Establish a central limit theorem for stochastic mirror descent risk budgeting portfolios
background_latex:
Let \(d\in\mathbb{N}\) be the number of assets and \(X\) an \(\mathbb{R}^d\)-valued random vector of asset returns on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\). For portfolio weights \(u\in\Delta_d:=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^d_+:\sum_{i=1}^d u_i=1\}\), the portfolio loss is \(-\langle u,X\rangle\).

Fix a risk-budget vector \(b\in\Delta^{>0}_d:=\{b\in(0,\infty)^d:\sum_{i=1}^d b_i=1\}\). Let \(\rho\) be an RB-compatible risk measure (positive homogeneous and subadditive) such that the map
\[r_\rho(y):=\rho(-\langle y,X\rangle),\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^d_+\]
is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}^d_+\) and continuously differentiable on \((0,\infty)^d\). Let \(g:\mathbb{R}_+\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, convex, and increasing, and define the strictly convex objective
\[\Gamma_g(y):= g(r_\rho(y)) - \sum_{i=1}^d b_i\log y_i,\qquad y\in(0,\infty)^d.\]
Let \(y^\star\in(0,\infty)^d\) denote the unique minimizer of \(\Gamma_g\), and \(u^\star:=y^\star/\|y^\star\|_1\) the corresponding (unique) risk budgeting portfolio.

Assume a stochastic representation of \(g\circ r_\rho\): there exists a convex loss function \(L:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) such that for all \(y\in(0,\infty)^d\),
\[g(r_\rho(y)) = \min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{E}[L(\xi,-\langle y,X\rangle)] = \mathbb{E}[L(\xi^\star(y),-\langle y,X\rangle)],\]
where \(\xi^\star(y)\) is uniquely defined. Define the joint variable \(z=(\xi,y)\in\mathbb{R}\times(0,\infty)^d\), and the population objective
\[h(z):=\mathbb{E}[H(z,X)],\qquad H(z,X):=L(\xi,-\langle y,X\rangle) - \sum_{i=1}^d b_i\log y_i.\]
Let \(z^\star=(\xi^\star,y^\star)\) be the unique minimizer of \(h\).

Because \(\nabla_y H\) is singular as some \(y_i\downarrow 0\), the paper introduces a tamed factor \(\kappa(y):= (\min_{1\le i\le d} y_i)\wedge 1\). Using i.i.d. samples \((X_k)_{k\ge 1}\), a stochastic mirror descent (SMD) recursion is defined for a chosen radius \(m>0\) (assumed \(m\ge \|y^\star\|_1\)) and step sizes \((\gamma_k)\):
1) \(\xi_{k+1} = \xi_k - \gamma_{k+1}\,\partial_\xi H(z_k,X_{k+1})\).
2) \(y_{k+1} = P^{m}_{y_k}\bigl(\gamma_{k+1}\,\kappa(y_k)\,\nabla_y H(z_k,X_{k+1})\bigr)\),
where \(P^{m}_{y}(v)\) is the negative-entropy mirror (KL) proximal map onto \((0,\infty)^d\cap\{\|y\|_1\le m\}\) (explicitly \(y\mapsto y\odot e^{-v}\) followed by \(\ell_1\)-rescaling if needed).
The paper proves almost sure convergence \(z_k\to z^\star\) and provides an almost sure non-asymptotic bound for the weighted averaged iterates \(\bar z_n := (\sum_{k=1}^n \gamma_k z_{k-1})/(\sum_{k=1}^n \gamma_k)\).
problem_definition_latex:
Under suitable regularity and moment assumptions ensuring the SMD recursion \((z_k)_{k\ge 0}\) is well-defined and converges to \(z^\star\), derive an asymptotic distributional error characterization for the stochastic mirror descent risk-budgeting estimator.

Concretely, establish a central limit theorem (CLT) for an appropriately normalized error of either the raw iterates \(z_n\) or the averaged iterates \(\bar z_n\), i.e. prove convergence in distribution of the form
\[a_n\,(\bar z_n - z^\star) \;\Rightarrow\; \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma),\]
for a deterministic scaling \(a_n\to\infty\) and a covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), and characterize \(a_n\) and \(\Sigma\) in terms of the model primitives \((L,X,b,g,\rho)\) and the mirror map/taming mechanism \((\kappa, P_y^m)\).

title: Characterize the exact worst-case approximation ratio for i.i.d. k-selection prophet inequalities
background_latex:
Fix integers \(n\ge k\ge 1\). In the i.i.d. \(k\)-selection prophet inequality problem, a decision-maker observes a sequence of nonnegative random values \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) revealed sequentially, where \(X_t\) are independent and identically distributed from a known distribution \(F\) supported on \(\mathbb{R}_+\). After observing \(X_t\), the decision-maker must irrevocably either accept it (and then it contributes \(X_t\) to the payoff) or reject it. The policy may accept at most \(k\) values in total.

Let \(\pi\) denote any (possibly randomized) online policy for this problem. Its expected reward is \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t\in S_\pi} X_t]\), where \(S_\pi\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\) is the (random) set of accepted indices with \(|S_\pi|\le k\).

The offline (prophet) benchmark is the expected sum of the \(k\) largest values among \(X_1,\dots,X_n\). Writing the order statistics as \(X_{(1)}\le \cdots \le X_{(n)}\), the benchmark is
\[
\mathrm{OPT}_{n,k}(F)=\sum_{i=n-k+1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_{(i)}].
\]
The approximation ratio of a policy \(\pi\) on distribution \(F\) is
\[
\mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t\in S_\pi} X_t]}{\mathrm{OPT}_{n,k}(F)}.
\]
Define the optimal worst-case approximation ratio for \((k,n)\) as
\[
\gamma_{n,k}=\sup_{\pi}\;\inf_{F}\; \mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F),
\]
where the infimum is over i.i.d. nonnegative distributions \(F\) (the paper works with continuous \(F\), but the precise regularity is not essential for stating the ratio).

For \(k=1\), \(\gamma_{n,1}\) has a known tight value in the limit \(n\to\infty\), obtained via the Hill--Kertz differential equation; for \(k\ge 2\), no comparable closed-form characterization is known. The paper introduces a coupled nonlinear system of differential equations, parameterized by constants \(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_k\), whose solvability yields provable lower bounds of the form \(\gamma_{n,k}\gtrsim \sum_{j=1}^k \theta_j\) for large \(n\), but it does not give an exact analytical formula for \(\gamma_{n,k}\) or for its worst-case limit over \(n\).
problem_definition_latex: Determine an analytical (closed-form) characterization of the worst-case optimal approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for the i.i.d. \((k,n)\)-selection prophet inequality problem, for general \(k\ge 2\) (and/or of the worst-case limit \(\inf_{n\ge 1}\gamma_{n,k}\)), rather than only bounds derived from the nonlinear differential-equation system.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem from Brustle--Perez-Salazar--Verdugo ("Splitting Guarantees for Prophet Inequalities via Nonlinear Systems") asks for an analytic closed-form characterization of the minimax i.i.d. \((k,n)\)-selection prophet ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}=\sup_\pi\inf_F \mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F)\) for \(k\ge 2\), analogous to the Hill--Kertz ODE characterization for \(k=1\). The source paper itself makes two key structural advances: it gives an exact infinite-dimensional quantile-space LP \([P]_{n,k}\) for \(\gamma_{n,k}\) (with the worst-case distribution encoded by a nonincreasing quantile function \(h(u)=F^{-1}(1-u)\)), and it derives a coupled nonlinear ODE system (involving upper incomplete gamma functions \(\Gamma_\ell\)) whose solvability at parameters \(\theta_1^*,\dots,\theta_k^*\) yields asymptotic lower bounds \(\gamma_{n,k}\gtrsim \sum_{j=1}^k \theta_j^*\) for large \(n\). Numerically, this gives strong constants (e.g. \(\sum_{j=1}^2\theta_j^*\approx 0.829\)), but the paper explicitly leaves open whether \(\inf_n\gamma_{n,k}=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_j^*\) or any closed-form expression exists.

Subsequent work provides complementary partial progress toward “exactness,” but not a closed-form minimax constant for general \(k\ge 2\). "Tightness without counterexamples: A new approach and new results for prophet inequalities" gives an exact minimax characterization of \(\gamma_{k,n}\) for each fixed \((k,n)\) as a semi-infinite LP over quantiles, together with a provably convergent discretization scheme that computes \(\gamma_{k,n}\) to arbitrary accuracy; it also recovers the Hill--Kertz characterization when \(k=1\). This essentially resolves the *variational* characterization and computation of \(\gamma_{n,k}\), but it still does not yield an analytic closed form for \(k\ge 2\) or identify the worst-case limiting constant as \(n\to\infty\).

Other cited papers obtain analytic formulas in restricted regimes that inform the open problem’s landscape. "Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities" gives a genuine closed form for the best *single-threshold* policy (and a competition-complexity variant), yielding the explicit ratio \(Q_{n,k}(k/n)/k\approx 1-1/\sqrt{2\pi k}\) when \(m=n\); this is a lower bound on \(\gamma_{n,k}\) but not tight for optimal adaptive policies. "Multiunit IID Prophet Inequalities via Extreme Value Asymptotics" and "Posted Pricing and Competition in Large Markets" use extreme-value asymptotics to derive explicit \(n\to\infty\) ratios for fixed \(F\) (and often restricted policies), showing how performance depends on tail index and giving large-\(k\) expansions such as \(1-\Theta((\log k)/k)\) or \(1-\Theta(1/\sqrt{k})\) in certain classes; however, these do not perform the full minimax \(\inf_F\) over all i.i.d. distributions. Overall, the problem remains open: we now have exact LP characterizations and strong asymptotic lower bounds via nonlinear systems, plus analytic results for restricted policy classes or distribution classes, but no Hill--Kertz-style closed-form solution for the minimax \(\gamma_{n,k}\) when \(k\ge 2\).

sources.title: Tightness without counterexamples: A new approach and new results for prophet inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result: In the IID k-selection prophet inequality with n agents, the paper formulates the tight worst-case guarantee of the optimal adaptive online policy (DP) versus the prophet as a semi-infinite linear program: \(\gamma_{k,n}=\mathrm{iidLP}^{\mathrm{DP/Proph}}_{k,n}=\max\{\theta: \theta\,\mathbb{E}[\min\{\mathrm{Bin}(n,q),k\}]\le \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{\ell=1}^k \min\{y_i^\ell,q x_i^\ell\}\ \forall q\in(0,1],\ (x,y)\in\mathcal P_n^k\}\), where \(\mathcal P_n^k\) encodes the slot-remaining state dynamics. It also gives an \(\varepsilon\)-discretization scheme (Prop. 5) to compute \(\gamma_{k,n}\) numerically to any desired accuracy, and for \(k=1\) recovers the Hill–Kertz characterization and the tight constant \(\inf_n \gamma_{1,n}=\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{1,n}=\theta^*\approx 0.745\) via an ODE \(\tfrac1{\theta^*}-1=H(x)(\ln H(x)-1)-H'(x)\) with \(H(0)=1,H(1)=0\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an analytical closed-form characterization of the worst-case optimal approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for IID \((k,n)\)-selection prophet inequalities for general \(k\ge2\), beyond bounds from nonlinear differential-equation systems. This paper makes substantial progress by (i) giving an exact minimax/duality-based characterization of \(\gamma_{k,n}\) for every fixed \((k,n)\) as a single semi-infinite LP over quantiles \(q\in(0,1]\), eliminating the outer infimum over IID distributions; and (ii) providing a provably accurate discretization method to compute \(\gamma_{k,n}\) numerically. However, it explicitly states it does not analytically determine \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}\) or \(\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}\) for general \(k>1\). Thus it does not solve the open problem, but supplies a tight variational characterization and computational procedure that narrows the remaining analytic gap. The paper also notes subsequent work (Brustle et al. 2024) that reportedly derives an analytic \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}\) using a variant framework, but that result is not contained/proved here.

sources.title: Multiunit IID Prophet Inequalities via Extreme Value Asymptotics
sources.theorem_or_result:
For distributions F on \(\mathbb{R}_+\) satisfying the extreme value condition with extreme value index \(\gamma\), the paper gives an explicit asymptotic (\(n\to\infty\)) characterization of the optimal online-to-prophet ratio for fixed \(k\):
- Define \(\mu_{n,k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\mathbb{E}[X_{n-j:n}]\) and \(V_{dp}(n,k)\) the optimal online value.
- Theorem 3.1: \(\mathrm{ACR}_k(F):=\lim_{n\to\infty} V_{dp}(n,k)/\mu_{n,k}\) equals
\[\mathrm{ACR}_k(F)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(1-\gamma)^{1-\gamma} v_k\,\Gamma(k)}{\Gamma(k+1-\gamma)}, & \gamma\in(0,1),\\ 1, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\]
where \(v_1=1\) and for \(k>1\), \(v_k-v_{k-1}\) is the unique positive solution \(x\) of \(x^{1/\gamma}+v_{k-1}x^{1/\gamma-1}-1=0\).
- Proposition 3.2: for \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(\mathrm{ACR}_k(F)=1-\frac{\gamma(1-\gamma)}{2}\frac{\log k}{k}+O(1/k)\), uniformly in \(k\).
- Corollary 3.3: uniformly over all such \(F\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) and large enough \(k\), \(\mathrm{ACR}_k(F)\ge 1-\frac{\log k}{8k}(1+\varepsilon)\), and this worst case is attained at \(\gamma=1/2\) at leading order.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a closed-form characterization of the worst-case optimal approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}=\sup_\pi\inf_F \mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F)\) (or its worst-case limit over \(n\)) for i.i.d. \(k\)-selection, beyond implicit ODE-based bounds.

This paper does not characterize \(\inf_F\) over all i.i.d. distributions in the original (finite-\(n\)) minimax sense. Instead it fixes \(F\) and studies the instance-dependent limit \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \mathrm{CR}_{k,n}(F)\), obtaining an explicit formula in terms of the extreme value index \(\gamma\) (Theorem 3.1), and then derives an explicit large-\(k\) worst-case bound \(1-\frac{\log k}{8k}(1+\varepsilon)\) over the subclass of distributions satisfying the extreme value condition.

Thus it provides partial progress toward an analytic understanding of how the asymptotic ratio depends on \(k\), and identifies the (EVT-class) worst-case tail index \(\gamma=1/2\) at leading order, but it does not resolve the full worst-case minimax ratio \(\inf_F\) over all distributions nor give an exact closed-form for \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for general \(k\ge2\).

sources.title: The iid prophet inequality with limited flexibility
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies the i.i.d. single-selection prophet inequality (choose at most one value) under the restriction that the stopping rule uses at most \(k\) distinct thresholds over time (“\(k\)-dynamic” policies). It gives an exact infinite-dimensional LP characterization of the optimal worst-case ratio \(\gamma^*_{n,k}\) for this restricted policy class, proves \(\gamma^*_{n,1}=1-(1-1/n)^n\) and numerically \(\gamma^*_{n,2}\approx 0.70804\) as \(n\to\infty\). For general \(k\), via a relaxation it proves asymptotic bounds \[\gamma^*_{n,k}\ge \bar\gamma\Bigl(1-c_1(\tfrac{\log k}{k}+\tfrac{k^2}{n})\Bigr),\qquad \lim_{n\to\infty} v^*_{n,k}=v^*_{\infty,k}\le \bar\gamma\Bigl(1-c_2\tfrac{\log k}{k}\Bigr),\] where \(\bar\gamma\approx 0.745\) is the optimal fully-dynamic i.i.d. single-choice ratio (Hill–Kertz/Kertz constant).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a closed-form characterization of the optimal worst-case approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for the i.i.d. \(k\)-selection prophet inequality (can accept up to \(k\) items), for \(k\ge 2\). This citing paper does not study \(k\)-selection; it studies single-selection (accept at most one) but with limited flexibility in the time-varying threshold schedule (at most \(k\) distinct thresholds). Thus it does not resolve the \(k\)-selection characterization problem. Indirectly, it contributes related methodology (infinite-dimensional LP/duality, asymptotic ODE analysis) that could be relevant as tools for analyzing worst-case ratios in other i.i.d. prophet settings, but it provides neither the exact \(k\)-selection ratio nor a closed-form limit for \(\gamma_{n,k}\) in that model.

sources.title: Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives an exact closed-form characterization of the worst-case competitive ratio of the best single-threshold (static) algorithm when the online player sees a length-m i.i.d. sequence but is benchmarked against a prophet on length-n, selecting up to k items. Writing Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(m,k/n)\u0000 and Q_{m,k}(q)=\mathbb{E}[\min\{k,\mathrm{Binomial}(m,q)\}]\u0000, they prove (Theorem 1) that
\[
\gamma_{m,n,k}=\inf_F\sup_{q\in[0,1]}\frac{\mathrm{ALG}_{m,k}(F,q)}{\mathrm{OPT}_{n,k}(F)}=\frac{Q_{m,k}(k/n)}{k}=\frac{1}{k}\Bigl(k-\mathbb{E}[(k-Y)^+]\Bigr).
\]
They also characterize the resulting \((1-\varepsilon)\)-competition complexity for single-thresholds: \(\beta_1(\varepsilon)=\ln(1/\varepsilon)\) and for \(k>1\),
\[
\frac{\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{k}\le \beta_k(\varepsilon)\le 1+\frac{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{k-1}+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{k-1}}.
\]
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a closed-form characterization of the optimal worst-case approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}=\sup_\pi\inf_F \mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F)\) for the full i.i.d. \(k\)-selection prophet inequality (allowing optimal multi-threshold/dynamic policies) for general \(k\ge2\). This paper does not resolve that: it restricts attention to the subclass of single-threshold policies and, moreover, studies a competition-complexity variant where the online algorithm may observe \(m\ge n\) samples while the prophet sees only \(n\). Within that restricted model it *does* provide an exact analytical formula for the worst-case ratio \(\gamma_{m,n,k}\) and shows the optimal quantile is \(q=k/n\). For the original setting \(m=n\), their formula recovers the known single-threshold guarantee \(\gamma_{n,n,k}=Q_{n,k}(k/n)/k\approx 1-1/\sqrt{2\pi k}\), which is a lower bound on the true \(\gamma_{n,k}\) but not a characterization of it. Thus the contribution is partial progress: an exact characterization for a prominent restricted policy class, not for the optimal policy over all online algorithms.

sources.title: Posted Pricing and Competition in Large Markets
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper studies large-market (fixed distribution, \(n\to\infty\)) welfare guarantees of fixed-price (single-threshold) posted pricing for selling up to \(k\) identical units. For i.i.d. values from \(F\) satisfying an extreme-value condition, it defines \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sup_T \mathbb{E}[R^{n}_{k,T}]/\sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb{E}[M_n^j]\), where \(M_n^1\ge\cdots\ge M_n^n\) are order statistics and \(R^{n}_{k,T}\) is the welfare of the fixed-price policy. Main theorem (Thm. 1):
- If \(F\) has Fr\'echet extreme type with parameter \(\alpha>1\), then for every \(k\), \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)\ge \varphi_k(\alpha)\), where
\[\varphi_k(\alpha)=\frac{\Gamma(k)}{\Gamma(k+1-1/\alpha)}\max_{x>0} x e^{-x^{-\alpha}}\sum_{j=1}^k\sum_{s=j}^\infty \frac{x^{-s\alpha}}{s!}.\]
In particular \(\mathrm{apx}_1(F)\ge 0.712\) and \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)\ge 1-1/\sqrt{2\pi k}\).
- If \(F\) has Gumbel or reversed-Weibull extreme type, then \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)=1\) for all \(k\).
Tightness (Thm. 2): for Pareto(\(\alpha=2\)), \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)\le 1-(1-\varepsilon)/\sqrt{2\pi k}\) for all large \(k\).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for an exact (closed-form) characterization of the worst-case optimal approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}=\sup_\pi\inf_F \mathrm{AR}_{n,k}(\pi,F)\) for i.i.d. \(k\)-selection prophet inequalities (general online policies), especially for \(k\ge2\). This paper does not characterize \(\gamma_{n,k}\) nor the worst-case over all i.i.d. \(F\); instead it analyzes a different regime and a restricted policy class:
- Regime: fixed \(F\), \(n\to\infty\) (“large market”), with \(F\) assumed to satisfy an extreme-value condition.
- Policies: fixed-price (single-threshold) mechanisms, not the optimal dynamic \(k\)-selection stopping rule.
Thus it does not solve the stated open problem. It is partially related because (i) it explicitly cites Br\"ustle et al. (the open-problem source) and discusses the same i.i.d. \(k\)-unit selection benchmark \(\sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb{E}[M_n^j]\), and (ii) it provides closed-form asymptotics for a restricted class of policies and distributions, showing \(\approx 1-1/\sqrt{2\pi k}\) behavior and tightness in \(k\) for Pareto tails. These results do not pin down \(\gamma_{n,k}\) but inform what can be achieved by simple thresholds in large markets and how guarantees scale with \(k\).

sources.title: Online Selection with Uncertain Disruption
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies a different online selection model (OS-UD) with i.i.d. values and disruption risk. It proves: - For non-adaptive single-threshold policies, the optimal worst-case competitive ratio is exactly \(1-1/e\) (Theorem 1.1). - For adaptive nonincreasing-threshold policies, \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma^{AD}_{n,p,\zeta}=\theta^*\approx 0.745\) for any fixed disruption probability \(p\in(0,1)\) and recovery \(\zeta\in[0,1]\) (Theorems 1.2–1.3), where \(\theta^*\) is the Hill–Kertz constant characterized by an integral equation / ODE.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an exact analytical characterization of the worst-case optimal approximation ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for i.i.d. \(k\)-selection prophet inequalities for general \(k\ge 2\). This paper does not analyze the \(k\)-selection prophet inequality benchmark (sum of top \(k\) order statistics) nor derive \(\gamma_{n,k}\). It only references Brustle et al. (2025) as prior work introducing a nonlinear ODE system for \(k\)-prophet inequalities, and it uses the \(k=1\) Hill–Kertz equation/constant \(\theta^*\) in its own OS-UD model. Thus it provides context and a related technique (quantile/ODE methods) but no new characterization for \(\gamma_{n,k}\) when \(k\ge 2\).

title: Global convergence theory for Anderson mixing methods for Euclidean fixed-point problems
background_latex:
Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a (possibly nonlinear) mapping and consider the fixed-point problem
\[
\text{find }x^\star\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ such that }g(x^\star)=x^\star.
\]
Define the residual \(r(x):=g(x)-x\). A basic fixed-point iteration is \(x_{k+1}=g(x_k)\).

Given a memory parameter \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), Anderson mixing (also called Anderson acceleration) constructs iterates \(x_k\) by combining current and past residual information. In a common form (depth \(m\)), define differences \(\Delta x_j := x_{j+1}-x_j\) and \(\Delta r_j := r(x_{j+1})-r(x_j)\). Form matrices
\[
X_k := [\Delta x_{k-m},\ldots,\Delta x_{k-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m},\qquad
R_k := [\Delta r_{k-m},\ldots,\Delta r_{k-1}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}.
\]
Compute coefficients \(\Gamma_k\in\mathbb{R}^m\) as a least-squares solution
\[
\Gamma_k \in \arg\min_{\Gamma\in\mathbb{R}^m}\ \|r(x_k)-R_k\Gamma\|_2,
\]
and then update, for some mixing parameter \(\beta_k>0\),
\[
\bar x_k := x_k - X_k\Gamma_k,\qquad \bar r_k := r(x_k)-R_k\Gamma_k,\qquad
x_{k+1} := \bar x_k + \beta_k \bar r_k.
\]
(Equivalent one-step forms exist, but the above captures the standard Anderson mixing scheme.)

An algorithm is said to be globally convergent (for a specified class of maps \(g\), possibly under additional conditions and parameter choices) if, for any initial point \(x_0\) (or at least for all \(x_0\) in a specified region), the generated sequence \(\{x_k\}\) is well-defined and converges to a fixed point \(x^\star\) (or has a subsequence converging to a fixed point), typically without requiring the initial point to be sufficiently close to \(x^\star\).

counterexample_suitability_rationale: One can search computationally for maps (e.g., low-dimensional polynomial or piecewise-smooth contractions/noncontractions) and initial points where Anderson mixing cycles or diverges, because iterates are easy to simulate. However, the space of admissible nonlinear maps is vast, and failures/successes may be sensitive to parameterization, so automated search is only partially informative.
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: Candidate representations such as parametric families of mappings \(g\), or algorithmic safeguards/parameter rules \(\beta_k\) and regularizations, can be evolved with a fitness signal based on empirical convergence across test suites. This can generate plausible conjectures or counterexamples, but does not directly yield a proof of global convergence in full generality.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem asks for a general global convergence theory for Euclidean Anderson mixing (Anderson acceleration) for fixed-point problems from arbitrary initial points. The provided forward-citation evidence contains only one partially relevant work, which studies a Riemannian analogue on the Bures–Wasserstein manifold of Gaussian measures. That work establishes local linear convergence under assumptions closely paralleling the classical Euclidean local theory: a (local) contraction of the fixed-point map and an a priori uniform bound on the Anderson coefficients, plus geometric regularity and boundedness of vector transport.

In particular, the cited paper reinforces that current convergence theory for Anderson mixing remains predominantly local and hinges on conditions that are difficult to verify or enforce globally (notably boundedness of the least-squares coefficients and staying within a region where the map is contractive and smooth). It does not provide a Euclidean global convergence result, nor a general mechanism ensuring convergence from arbitrary initial points. Consequently, based on the supplied citation set, the Euclidean global convergence theory remains open; promising directions include adding globalization safeguards (regularization, damping, line search, trust-region-like acceptance) that can guarantee descent or residual decrease while retaining the acceleration effect locally, and developing coefficient-control conditions that are verifiable from iterates.

sources.title: Anderson Mixing in Bures Wasserstein Space of Gaussian Measures
sources.theorem_or_result:
For fixed-point maps on the Bures–Wasserstein manifold of zero-mean Gaussians of the form \(G(\Sigma)=\mathrm{Exp}_{\Sigma}(-F(\Sigma))\), assuming (i) local bi-Lipschitz bounds on \(F\) and its Jacobian under parallel transport on a ball \(B_r(\Sigma^*)\), (ii) local contraction \(W_2(G(\Sigma_1),G(\Sigma_2))\le \kappa W_2(\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2)\) with \(\kappa<1\), (iii) a bounded vector transport \(\|T^{\Sigma_2}_{\Sigma_1}V\|_{\Sigma_2}\le M\|V\|_{\Sigma_1}\), and (iv) uniform boundedness of Anderson coefficients \(\|\Gamma_k\|_\infty\le M_\Gamma\), Theorem 3 proves local convergence of Riemannian Anderson mixing: if \(\Sigma_0\) is sufficiently close to \(\Sigma^*\), then all iterates stay in \(B_r(\Sigma^*)\) and the residuals satisfy
\[\|r_{k+1}\| \le \theta_k(1-\beta_k+\kappa\beta_k)\|r_k\| + \sum_{i=0}^{m_k} O(\|r_{k-i}\|^2),\qquad \theta_k=\|\bar r_k\|/\|r_k\|\le 1.\]
They also establish geometric regularity of small balls around nondegenerate \(\Sigma^*\) (compactness, bounded sectional curvature, local injectivity of \(\mathrm{Exp}\); Theorem 2) and show contractivity on such balls for specific operators (OU flow map (29) and KL-gradient explicit step (32); Theorem 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a general global convergence theory for Euclidean Anderson mixing for fixed-point problems \(g(x)=x\) from arbitrary initial points. This paper does not address Euclidean global convergence. Instead it develops a local convergence analysis for a Riemannian Anderson mixing variant on the Bures–Wasserstein manifold of Gaussian measures, requiring (local) contraction and a priori bounded Anderson coefficients, and only guarantees convergence when the initial point lies in a sufficiently small neighborhood of the fixed point. Thus it provides partial progress only in the sense of extending/validating convergence assumptions in a non-Euclidean setting and proving local convergence under contraction—conditions reminiscent of (but weaker than) a global theory.

title: Analytically prove equality of asymptotic and worst-case IID k-unit prophet ratios
background_latex:
Consider the IID multi-unit prophet inequality with a uniform matroid (capacity) constraint. There are integers \(k\ge 2\) (number of selection slots) and \(n\ge 1\) (number of sequentially arriving agents). Each arriving agent \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\) reveals a nonnegative random value \(R_i\) upon arrival; the \(R_i\) are independent and identically distributed (IID) according to a known distribution. An online policy must irrevocably accept or reject each agent upon arrival, may accept at most \(k\) agents in total, and aims to maximize expected total accepted value \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_{i\in S} R_i]\), where \(|S|\le k\) is the (random) accepted set.

Let \(\mathrm{DP}(I)\) denote the expected value of an optimal adaptive online policy (equivalently, the optimal dynamic program) on instance \(I\). Let \(\mathrm{Proph}(I)\) denote the prophet benchmark, defined as the expected sum of the \(k\) largest realized values among \(R_1,\dots,R_n\), i.e.
\[\mathrm{Proph}(I)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{S\subseteq \{1,\dots,n\},\ |S|\le k}\ \sum_{i\in S} R_i\Big].\]
For fixed \(k\) and \(n\), define the tight IID prophet-inequality guarantee
\[\gamma_{k,n} := \inf_{I\in \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{IID}}_{k,n}} \frac{\mathrm{DP}(I)}{\mathrm{Proph}(I)},\]
where \(\mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{IID}}_{k,n}\) denotes the class of all IID instances with \(k\) slots and \(n\) agents (over all nonnegative value distributions).

Two natural aggregations over \(n\) are:
1) the asymptotic-in-\(n\) limit \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \gamma_{k,n}\) (when it exists), and
2) the worst case over all horizons \(\inf_{n\ge 1} \gamma_{k,n}\).

\[\gamma_{k,n} := \inf_{I\in \mathcal{I}^{\mathrm{IID}}_{k,n}} \frac{\mathrm{DP}(I)}{\mathrm{Proph}(I)},\]

literature_review.synthesis:
In the notation of Jiang–Ma–Zhang (2025), the IID capacity-\(k\) tight ratio \(\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_{I\in\mathcal I^{\mathrm{IID}}_{k,n}} \mathrm{DP}(I)/\mathrm{Proph}(I)\) admits an exact minimax reformulation as a semi-infinite “type coverage” LP (their \(\mathrm{iidLP}^{\mathrm{DP/Proph}}_{k,n}\)), obtained by dualizing an inner LP over value gaps \(\Delta_j\) after fixing the quantile-type distribution. This framework yields numerical evidence (e.g. Table 1 for small \(k\)) and motivates the open question whether the horizon-worst case \(\inf_{n\ge 1}\gamma_{k,n}\) is attained asymptotically, i.e. equals \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}\), for every fixed \(k>1\).

The strongest forward progress is the nonlinear-systems approach of “Splitting guarantees for prophet inequalities via nonlinear systems”, which (i) gives an infinite-dimensional LP \([P]_{n,k}\) that exactly characterizes \(\gamma_{k,n}\) for each finite \(n,k\), and (ii) derives a coupled ODE system producing explicit asymptotic lower bounds of the form \(\gamma_{k,n}\ge (1-O(k\log^2 n/n))\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_j^\star\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). This substantially advances analytic control of the \(n\to\infty\) regime, but it does not establish any horizon monotonicity or an identity between \(\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}\) and the asymptotic constant; indeed it leaves open whether \(\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_j^\star\).

Related works provide partial templates and tools rather than a solution. “Prophet Inequalities: Competing with the Top \(\ell\) Items is Easy” proves a clean horizon-monotonicity phenomenon \(CR_\ell(2n)\le CR_\ell(n)\) in a \(k=1\) setting (with a different benchmark), suggesting that proving a suitable monotonicity/subadditivity property in \(n\) could be the key missing step for \(k>1\). Several papers on static pricing/thresholds and OCRS (e.g. “Static pricing for multi-unit prophet inequalities” and “Tight Guarantees for Multi-unit Prophet Inequalities and Online Stochastic Knapsack*”) rigorously identify Poisson or infinitesimal-splitting limits as worst cases in their respective models, reinforcing the conjecture that the minimax over horizons should be governed by an asymptotic (often Poisson-like) limit. However, none currently bridge these Poisson-limit extremality principles to the full-information optimal DP vs prophet benchmark in the IID \(k\)-unit setting, so the equality \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_{n\ge1}\gamma_{k,n}\) remains open for \(k>1\).

sources.title: Splitting guarantees for prophet inequalities via nonlinear systems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces an infinite-dimensional LP [P]_{n,k} that exactly characterizes the worst-case i.i.d. k-selection prophet ratio \(\gamma_{n,k}\) for each finite \(n,k\) (Theorem 1), and a coupled nonlinear ODE system (1)–(3) with parameters \(\theta_1^\star,\dots,\theta_k^\star\) such that for each fixed \(k\) there exists \(n_0(k)\) with \[\gamma_{n,k}\ge \Bigl(1-\tfrac{24k\ln^2 n}{n}\Bigr)\sum_{j=1}^k \theta_j^\star\quad\text{for all }n\ge n_0(k).\] (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to prove analytically that for each \(k>1\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_{n\ge1}\gamma_{k,n}\). This paper develops asymptotic lower bounds on \(\gamma_{n,k}\) via an ODE system and shows these bounds hold for all sufficiently large \(n\), but it does not establish that the worst-case over \(n\) is attained asymptotically, nor any monotonicity/limit-equality statement relating \(\inf_n\gamma_{n,k}\) to \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{n,k}\). In fact, it explicitly states that obtaining tight analytic formulas and extending results to all \(n\) remain open, and it leaves open whether \(\inf_{n\ge1}\gamma_{n,k}=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_j^\star\). sources.title: Prophet Inequalities: Competing with the Top ℓ Items is Easy
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves for the single-selection case (decision maker selects 1 item) and benchmark equal to the average of the top \(\ell\) order statistics that the worst-case i.i.d. competitive ratio \(CR_\ell:=\inf_{n\ge \ell}\inf_F \sup_\tau \mathbb E[X_\tau]/\mathbb E[\frac1\ell\sum_{i=1}^\ell X_{(i)}]\) equals the unique solution in \([0,1)\) of an integral equation (Theorem 1.1), and shows a horizon-monotonicity property \(CR_\ell(2n)\le CR_\ell(n)\) implying \(CR_\ell=\liminf_{n\to\infty} CR_\ell(n)\) (Lemma 3.1 and Eq. (3.1)). For the multi-selection extension (select \(k\) items) with the same top-\(\ell\)-average benchmark, it gives an asymptotic lower bound \(\liminf_{n\to\infty} CR_{k,\ell}(n)\ge \frac{CR_\ell}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k \prod_{t=1}^j \theta_{t,\ell}^{-1}\) where \(\theta_{t,\ell}\) are defined via a boundary-value ODE system (Theorem 1.3), but states it does not prove asymptotic tightness nor that the worst case is attained as \(n\to\infty\) for \(k>1\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks, for the standard i.i.d. \(k\)-unit prophet inequality with prophet benchmark equal to the sum of the top \(k\) values, to prove analytically that the worst-case ratio over horizons equals the asymptotic-in-\(n\) limit: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}\). This paper proves an analogous ‘worst case at large \(n\)’ statement only in the \(k=1\) selection setting (Lemma 3.1 gives \(CR_\ell(2n)\le CR_\ell(n)\), hence \(\inf_n CR_\ell(n)=\liminf_{n\to\infty} CR_\ell(n)\)). However, it does not establish the corresponding horizon equality for the true \(k\)-unit benchmark (top \(k\) sum) nor even for its own \(k\)-selection generalization \(CR_{k,\ell}(n)\); it explicitly notes the lack of a proof that \(CR_{k,\ell}=\liminf_{n\to\infty} CR_{k,\ell}(n)\) for \(k>1\). Thus it provides partial progress/related evidence and techniques (ODE limits, boundary-value formulations) but does not solve the stated open problem for \(k>1\).

sources.title: Posted Pricing and Competition in Large Markets
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper studies large-market (fixed distribution, \(n\to\infty\)) welfare guarantees for fixed posted prices and competition complexity. For the \(k\)-unit i.i.d. setting it defines \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sup_T \mathbb{E}(R^n_{k,T})/\sum_{j=1}^k \mathbb{E}(M_n^j)\). Under an extreme-value condition on \(F\):
- If \(F\) is Fr\'echet with parameter \(\alpha\), then \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)\ge \varphi_k(\alpha)\) where \(\varphi_k\) is an explicit optimization expression (Eq. (3)); in particular \(\mathrm{apx}_1(F)\ge 0.712\) and \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)\ge 1-1/\sqrt{2\pi k}\).
- If \(F\) is Gumbel or reversed Weibull, then \(\mathrm{apx}_k(F)=1\).
It also characterizes large-market competition complexity \(C(F)\) for the optimal dynamic pricing/prophet policy as \(C(F)=(1-\gamma)(\Gamma(1-\gamma))^{1/\gamma}\) where \(\gamma\) is the extreme-value index (Theorem 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an analytic proof that for the i.i.d. \(k\)-unit prophet ratio \(\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_I \mathrm{DP}(I)/\mathrm{Proph}(I)\), the worst case over horizons equals the asymptotic limit: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_{n\ge1}\gamma_{k,n}\). This paper does not address \(\gamma_{k,n}\) for the optimal dynamic program versus the prophet benchmark across all i.i.d. distributions and finite \(n\). Instead it analyzes a different ratio: fixed-price (single-threshold) welfare versus the prophet/optimal-offline benchmark, and it does so in a large-market regime with additional assumptions (extreme value condition) on \(F\). While it cites work on i.i.d. \(k\)-unit prophet inequalities and discusses large-\(n\) behavior, it neither proves monotonicity/tightness of \(\gamma_{k,n}\) in \(n\) nor identifies the finite-\(n\) worst case for the optimal adaptive policy. Thus it does not solve the stated equality, but it provides related asymptotic analysis tools (extreme-value/regular-variation methods) that could be relevant for studying \(n\to\infty\) limits.

sources.title: Competition Versus Complexity in Multiple-Selection Prophet Inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper studies competition complexity for the i.i.d. multi-unit prophet setting within single-threshold policies. It gives an exact closed form for the worst-case (over distributions) competitive ratio of the best single-threshold algorithm when the online algorithm sees a length-
m sequence but is benchmarked against a prophet with length-
n sequence: 
\[\gamma_{m,n,k}=\inf_F\sup_{q\in[0,1]} \frac{\mathrm{ALG}_{m,k}(F,q)}{\mathrm{OPT}_{n,k}(F)}=\frac{Q_{m,k}(k/n)}{k},\]
where \(Q_{m,k}(q)=\mathbb{E}[\min\{k,Y\}]\) for \(Y\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(m,q)\). In particular, the optimal quantile is \(q=k/n\), independent of \(m\). It also derives bounds on the (1-
\(\varepsilon\))-competition complexity \(\beta_k(\varepsilon)\): for \(k=1\), \(\beta_1(\varepsilon)=\ln(1/\varepsilon)\); for \(k>1\), \(\ln(1/\varepsilon)/k\le \beta_k(\varepsilon)\le 1+\frac{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{k-1}+\sqrt{\frac{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{k-1}}\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to analytically prove that for the optimal adaptive online policy (dynamic program) in the i.i.d. k-unit prophet inequality, the worst-case ratio over horizons equals the asymptotic-in-n limit: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_{n\ge1}\gamma_{k,n}\), where \(\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_I \mathrm{DP}(I)/\mathrm{Proph}(I)\). This paper does not analyze \(\mathrm{DP}(I)\) vs \(\mathrm{Proph}(I)\) as a function of \(n\); instead it analyzes a different ratio \(\gamma_{m,n,k}\) for the restricted class of single-threshold algorithms with an enlarged sample size \(m\) benchmarked against a prophet with horizon \(n\). Thus it does not resolve the equality of asymptotic and worst-case horizons for \(\gamma_{k,n}\) (optimal DP). However, its infinite-dimensional LP/duality framework and explicit extremal constructions in quantile space may be adaptable as analytic tools for horizon-monotonicity/tightness questions in the full DP setting.

sources.title: Static pricing for multi-unit prophet inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies worst-case competitive ratios of a particular class of online policies (anonymous, non-adaptive, order-oblivious static threshold pricing) for the multi-unit prophet inequality with capacity k. It proves that choosing a price \(\pi\) that equalizes \(\delta_k(X_\pi)=\mu_k(X_\pi)\), where \(\delta_k(X)=\Pr[X\le k-1]\) and \(\mu_k(X)=\tfrac1k\mathbb{E}[\min\{X,k\}]\), guarantees welfare at least \(\varphi_k\) times the prophet benchmark, where \(\varphi_k\) is characterized by a Poisson worst case: letting \(X_\lambda\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and choosing \(\lambda_k\) such that \(\delta_k(X_{\lambda_k})=\mu_k(X_{\lambda_k})\), the competitive ratio is at least \(\varphi_k:=\delta_k(X_{\lambda_k})=\mu_k(X_{\lambda_k})\).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the *optimal adaptive* IID k-unit prophet ratio \(\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_I \mathrm{DP}(I)/\mathrm{Proph}(I)\) and asks to prove that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}=\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}\). This paper does not analyze \(\gamma_{k,n}\) as a function of horizon \(n\) for the optimal adaptive policy, nor does it compare asymptotic vs worst-case-in-n behavior. Instead it gives a horizon-independent worst-case guarantee for a restricted policy class (static prices) in the general (not necessarily IID) setting, and characterizes worst-case instances via Poisson limits. The Poisson-limit/worst-case characterization may be conceptually related to asymptotic-in-n phenomena, but it does not establish the equality of \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_{k,n}\) and \(\inf_n\gamma_{k,n}\) for optimal adaptive policies.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper characterizes the tight LP-relative guarantee \(\gamma_k^*\) for the adversarial-order \(k\)-unit prophet inequality / \(k\)-unit OCRS problem: \(\gamma_k^* = \inf_{p: \sum_t p_t = k} \mathrm{LPOCRS}_k(p)\), and the infimum is attained in the limit by splitting arrivals into infinitesimal probabilities, yielding a Poisson-rate-\(k\) limit characterized by an ODE (Theorem 2). This citing paper studies a different model: adversarial (possibly heterogeneous) arrivals and compares online algorithms to an LP relaxation (via OCRS), not to the prophet benchmark, and not restricted to IID. It does show a related “worst case is Poisson/infinitesimal splitting” phenomenon for the OCRS/LP benchmark (Lemma 2, Theorem 2), but it does not address the IID prophet-benchmark ratios \(\gamma_{k,n}\) nor the equality between \(\inf_n\) and \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\) in that IID setting.

sources.title: The iid prophet inequality with limited flexibility
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies the single-choice IID prophet inequality under the restriction that the stopping rule uses at most \(k\) distinct thresholds over \(n\) arrivals (a \(k\)-dynamic policy). It gives an infinite-dimensional LP characterization of the optimal approximation \(\gamma^*_{n,k}\) achievable by such policies and derives bounds such as \(\gamma^*_{n,1}=1-(1-1/n)^n\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma^*_{n,2}\approx 0.70804\), and for large \(k\ll n\), \(\gamma^*_{n,k}\ge \bar\gamma\bigl(1-c\,(\log k/k + k^2/n)\bigr)\) where \(\bar\gamma\approx 0.745\) is the optimal fully-dynamic IID prophet ratio.

This citing paper instead considers the single-unit (choose at most one) IID prophet problem, but restricts the policy class to use at most \(k\) thresholds (a different parameter \(k\) measuring pricing flexibility, not selection capacity). It does not analyze the multi-unit/top-\(k\) prophet benchmark nor the equality between asymptotic-in-\(n\) and worst-case-in-\(n\) ratios for capacity \(k\). At most, its infinite-dimensional LP/ODE methodology could be a tool inspiration for analyzing horizon dependence in other prophet-inequality variants.

title: Define and justify competitive fairness under lower congestion bounds setting
background_latex:
Let there be a finite set of posts (items) \(A\) with \(|A|=m\) and a finite set of agents \(N\) with \(|N|=n\). A (deterministic) assignment is a family \(P=(S_a)_{a\in A}\) of pairwise disjoint subsets of \(N\) whose union is \(N\), where \(S_a\) is the set of agents assigned to post \(a\). Under anonymous congestion, the congestion at post \(a\) in assignment \(P\) is \(s_a:=|S_a|\), and agent \(i\)'s realized allocation is the pair \((a,s_a)\) when \(i\in S_a\). Each agent \(i\in N\) has an ordinal preference relation \(\preceq_i\) over all feasible allocations \(A\times \{1,2,\dots,n\}\), assumed to be strictly decreasing in the congestion coordinate at each fixed post (i.e., for each \(a\), \((a,s+1)\prec_i (a,s)\) for all \(s\)).

Now introduce post-specific congestion bounds: for each \(a\in A\), a lower bound \(\underline s_a\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}\) and an upper bound \(\overline s_a\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}\) with \(\underline s_a\le \overline s_a\). Feasible assignments are those with \(\underline s_a\le s_a\le \overline s_a\) for all \(a\in A\), and \(\sum_{a\in A} s_a=n\). In a setting with bounds, a central fairness notion of the paper (without bounds) is a competitive assignment: an assignment \(P\) with congestion profile \(s\) is competitive if for every agent \(i\in S_a\) and every post \(x\in A\), agent \(i\) weakly prefers \((a,s_a)\) to the hypothetical move \((x,\max\{s_x,1\})\) (interpreting an empty post as having a minimal effective congestion of 1).

With lower bounds \(\underline s_a>0\), some posts must be populated even if all agents dislike them, creating tension with the usual interpretation of competitiveness (envy-freeness-like conditions using congestion as a price).
problem_definition_latex:
Give a mathematically well-defined notion of \emph{competitiveness} (a competitive-fairness concept) for congested assignment problems with anonymous congestion and post-specific lower bounds \((\underline s_a)_{a\in A}\) and upper bounds \((\overline s_a)_{a\in A}\) on the congestion levels, and provide a principled justification that this notion appropriately accounts for forced population of posts when \(\underline s_a>0\), i.e., when some posts must host at least \(\underline s_a\) agents even if agents would prefer to avoid them.

In particular, specify how the competitive comparison \((a,s_a)\) versus \((x,\cdot)\) should be defined when feasibility requires \(s_x\ge \underline s_x\) for all \(x\), and address how to treat situations where a lower bound forces assignment to a unanimously disliked post.

literature_review.synthesis:
The forward-citation evidence provided contains only one citing work, which develops and analyzes the competitiveness concept for congested assignments without post-specific lower bounds. In that baseline model, competitiveness is defined by a no-envy/no-profitable-virtual-move condition comparing an agent’s realized allocation \((a,s_a)\) to \((x,\max\{s_x,1\})\), thereby assigning an effective congestion of 1 to empty posts. This device is central to ruling out degenerate envy-free outcomes where everyone piles onto a single post while leaving others empty.

However, once feasibility imposes lower bounds \(\underline s_a>0\), the interpretation of \(\max\{s_x,1\}\) breaks: posts cannot be left empty, and agents may be forced into unanimously disliked posts to meet \(\underline s_a\). The citing paper explicitly flags this as an open question and does not propose a replacement competitive comparison or equilibrium-like condition that internalizes the mandatory minimum occupancies. Therefore, based on the provided forward-citation analysis, the problem of defining and justifying competitive fairness under lower congestion bounds remains open.

title: Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz analog for universal-quantifier-defined polynomial positivity sets
background_latex:
Let \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\) and \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_m)\) be real variables. Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a closed set, and let \(g=(g_1,\dots,g_s)\) be polynomials \(g_j\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]\). Define the feasible set
\[
K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: g_1(x,y)\ge 0,\dots,g_s(x,y)\ge 0\ \forall y\in Q\}.
\]
Fix a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\nu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) with \(\mathrm{supp}(\nu)=Q\) that satisfies the multivariate Carleman condition
\[
\sum_{d=0}^\infty \Big(\int y_j^{2d}\,d\nu(y)\Big)^{-\frac{1}{2d}}=\infty,\qquad j=1,\dots,m.
\]
For \(g_0:=1\), define the associated quadratic module (a convex cone in \(\mathbb{R}[x]\))
\[
\mathrm{QM}[g,\nu]:=\left\{\sum_{j=0}^s \int \tau_j(x,y)\, g_j(x,y)\, d\nu(y):\ \tau_j\in\Sigma^2[x,y]\right\},
\]
where \(\Sigma^2[x,y]\) denotes the cone of sum-of-squares polynomials in \((x,y)\).
A classical (quantifier-free) Krivine--Stengle Positivstellensatz gives algebraic certificates for polynomial inequalities on semialgebraic sets, including non-compact and empty-set certificates, typically using preorderings and denominators.
In the present setting, the constraint description uses a universal quantifier \(\forall y\in Q\), and \(Q\) may be non-semialgebraic, so \(K\) may be non-semialgebraic as well.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Hu–Klep–Nie, 2024) establishes a Putinar/Jacobi-type Positivstellensatz for universally quantified constraint sets \(K=\{x: g_j(x,y)\ge0\  orall y\in Q\}\) using the integral quadratic module \(\mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\) built from SOS multipliers \(	au_j(x,y)\) integrated against a Carleman-determinate measure \(
u\) with \(\mathrm{supp}(
u)=Q\). In the Archimedean case, strict positivity \(f>0\) on \(K\) implies \(f\in \mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\), and emptiness is characterized by \(-1\in \mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\). In the non-Archimedean case they obtain a perturbation result: \(f\ge0\) on \(K\) iff for all \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(r\) with \(f+\varepsilon\Omega_r\in \mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\), where \(\Omega_r\) is an explicit high-degree positive polynomial.

The open problem asks for a genuine Krivine–Stengle analogue in this quantified setting, i.e., a denominator/preordering-style certificate for nonnegativity and especially an algebraic infeasibility certificate for \(K=\emptyset\) without Archimedean assumptions. Among the forward citations provided, the closest partial progress is "Positivstellens" atze for polynomial matrices with universal quantifiers", which extends the \(\mathrm{QM}[\cdot,
u]\) methodology to polynomial matrix inequalities and proves several non-Archimedean positivity certificates with explicit multipliers/denominators (e.g., \(\|x\|^{2N}\), \((e^	op x)^N\), or \(	heta^{N_\varepsilon}\)) under additional structural hypotheses such as homogeneity or restriction to \(\mathbb R_+^n\). The remaining citing works are primarily algorithmic or complexity-oriented: they develop KKT-based or Moment–SOS methods for semi-infinite/robust problems with structured parameter sets (polyhedral or semialgebraic) or provide degree bounds for matrix Putinar-type certificates. None supplies a full Krivine–Stengle-type Positivstellensatz (with denominators and an emptiness certificate) for general universally quantified scalar constraints over possibly non-semialgebraic \(Q\).

Thus, based on the provided forward-citation set, the problem remains open. Promising directions suggested by partial results include: (i) importing homogenization/Putinar–Vasilescu and P'olya-type multiplier techniques to the integral quadratic module \(\mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\); (ii) identifying structural conditions on \(g\) and \(Q\) under which a denominator certificate \(p(x)f\in \mathrm{QM}[g,
u]\) (or a preordering analogue) holds; and (iii) developing a quantified analogue of Krivine–Stengle infeasibility certificates, potentially via moment-duality and determinacy (Carleman) combined with homogenization for unbounded \(K\).

sources.theorem_or_result:
They prove several Positivstellensätze for universally quantified polynomial matrix inequality sets. In particular, for 
\[X:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n: G(x,y)\succeq 0\ \forall y\in Y\},\]
with a Borel measure \(\nu\) supported on \(Y\) satisfying Carleman, they show:
- (Archimedean case) If \(Q_p(G,\nu)\) is Archimedean and \(F(x)\in S[x]_p\) is positive definite on \(X\), then
\[F(x)=S_0(x)+\int_Y \langle S(x,y),G(x,y)\rangle_p\,d\nu(y)\in Q_p(G,\nu),\]
for SOS matrices \(S_0\in S[x]_p\), \(S\in S[x,y]_{pq}\) (Theorem 3.1).
- (Non-Archimedean generalizations) Under homogeneity/orthant hypotheses they obtain denominator-type certificates such as
\[\|x\|^{2N}F(x)=S_0(x)+\int_Y\langle S(x,y),G(x,y)\rangle_p\,d\nu(y)\]
(Theorem 4.1) and a Pólya-type \((e^\top x)^N\) certificate on \(\mathbb R_+^n\cap X\) (Theorem 4.2), plus inhomogeneous \(\theta^{N_\varepsilon}(F+\varepsilon\theta^{d_F}I_p)\) variants (Corollary 4.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a Krivine–Stengle-type Positivstellensatz (including infeasibility/emptiness certificates) for sets \(K=\{x: g_j(x,y)\ge 0\ \forall y\in Q\}\) without Archimedean assumptions. This paper extends Hu–Klep–Nie’s Archimedean, measure-based quadratic-module certificate to the matrix/PMI setting and, importantly, provides some non-Archimedean Positivstellensätze with denominators/multipliers (\(\|x\|^{2N}\), \((e^\top x)^N\), or \(\theta^{N_\varepsilon}\)) under additional structural assumptions (homogeneity in \(x\), or restriction to \(\mathbb R_+^n\)). However, it does not establish a full Krivine–Stengle analogue for general (inhomogeneous) universally quantified scalar constraints, nor does it give a general algebraic emptiness certificate for \(K=\emptyset\) in this quantified, potentially non-semialgebraic setting. Thus it is partial progress: it supplies non-Archimedean positivity certificates in special regimes and develops techniques likely relevant to a future Krivine–Stengle-type theorem.

sources.title: A Global Approach for Generalized Semi-Infinite Programs with Polyhedral Parameter Sets: X. Hu, J. Nie, S. Zhong
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops a disjunctive KKT-based semidefinite (Moment–SOS) algorithm for polynomial generalized semi-infinite programs (GSIPs) with polyhedral parameter sets. A central structural result is the decomposition of the KKT parameter set for the inner minimization 
\[v(x)=\inf\{g(x,u): Au\ge b(x)\}\]
into finitely many semi-algebraic pieces indexed by rank-
\(r=\mathrm{rank}(A)\) subsets \(J\) of active constraints: for \(K(x)=\{u:\exists\lambda\ge0,\ \nabla_u g(x,u)-A^T\lambda=0,\ 0\le Au-b(x)\perp\lambda\ge0\}\),
\[K(x)=\bigcup_{J\in\mathcal P} K_J(x),\]
where each \(K_J(x)\) admits an explicit description using the partial Lagrange multiplier expression
\(\lambda_J(x,u)=(A_JA_J^T)^{-1}A_J\nabla_u g(x,u)\) and complementarity constraints (Theorem 3.4 and Proposition 3.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a Krivine–Stengle-type Positivstellensatz (including emptiness certificates) for sets \(K=\{x: g_j(x,y)\ge0\ \forall y\in Q\}\) without archimedeanity, potentially with non-semi-algebraic \(Q\), using measure-based quadratic modules \(\mathrm{QM}[g,\nu]\). This citing paper does not provide such a Positivstellensatz or an algebraic infeasibility certificate for universally quantified constraints in that generality. Instead, it treats a different (more structured) universal quantifier setting arising from GSIPs where the quantified set is polyhedral (and may depend on \(x\)): \(U(x)=\{u: Au\ge b(x)\}\). The paper’s contribution is algorithmic: it replaces the universal constraint by solving/relaxing an inner polynomial optimization over a polyhedron via KKT conditions, then solves resulting polynomial programs by Moment–SOS. The KKT-set decomposition and partial Lagrange multiplier expressions are potentially useful tools for handling universal quantifiers over polyhedra, but they do not yield a Krivine–Stengle-style representation of \(\{f\ge0\text{ on }K\}\) nor a measure-based certificate for \(K=\emptyset\) in the non-archimedean, non-semi-algebraic \(Q\) setting of the open problem.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops Algorithm 3.3: a hierarchy of polynomial optimization relaxations for polynomial generalized semi-infinite programs (GSIPs) of the form \(\min f(x)\) s.t. \(g(x,u)\ge 0\ \forall u\in U(x)\), using “polynomial extensions” \(q(x)\) with \(q(\hat x)=\hat u\) and \(q(x)\in U(x)\ \forall x\in X\) to generate finitely many polynomial constraints \(g(x,q(x))\ge 0\). It also shows that when the inner minimization in \(u\) is convex and KKT-attained, the universal constraint can be reformulated via KKT conditions into a single (polynomial/rational) optimization problem (Theorems 5.1–5.2).

sources.title: On the complexity of matrix Putinar's Positivstellensätz
sources.theorem_or_result:
Main results are effective (degree/complexity) bounds for matrix Putinar-type Positivstellensätze on semialgebraic sets defined by polynomial matrix inequalities. In particular, if the quadratic module 
\(\mathrm{QM}[G]_\ell\) is Archimedean (e.g. \((1-\|x\|_2^2)I_\ell\in \mathrm{QM}[G]_\ell\)) and \(F(x)\succeq F_{\min}I_\ell\succ 0\) on \(K=\{x: G(x)\succeq 0\}\), then for an explicit polynomially-bounded degree \(k\) (Theorem 1.1 / 5.1) one has a certificate
\[F = S + \sum_{i=1}^t P_i(x)^T G(x) P_i(x),\]
with \(S\in \Sigma[x]_\ell\) and \(\deg(S),\deg(P_i^TGP_i)\le k\). For unbounded \(K\), a Putinar–Vasilescu-type certificate is proved: if additionally the leading homogeneous part \(F_{\mathrm{hom}}\succ 0\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), then for explicit \(k\), \((1+\|x\|_2^2)^k F\in \mathrm{QM}[G]_\ell\) with controlled degree (Theorem 1.2 / 5.3).

Huang’s paper does not address this quantifier/integration setting, nor Krivine–Stengle-style certificates with denominators or emptiness certificates for such \(K\). It instead gives effective degree bounds for (matrix) Putinar and Putinar–Vasilescu certificates on semialgebraic sets \(\{x: G(x)\succeq 0\}\), and briefly notes that a matrix inequality can be rewritten as a universal quantifier \(y^T G(x) y\ge 0\ \forall \|y\|=1\), suggesting future work on universal-quantifier Positivstellensätze. Thus it is only tangentially relevant as a complexity/technique reference, not a solution to the Krivine–Stengle analogue sought.

title: Convergence of exact Nash equilibria to mean field equilibria in ergodic Markovian games
background_latex:
Consider a symmetric continuous-time $n$-player stochastic game on a finite state space $[d]=\{1,\dots,d\}$. Each player $i\in[n]$ has a controlled jump process $X^{i}_t\in[d]$ with transition rates chosen by a (possibly time-dependent) Markovian strategy. The control of player $i$ at time $t$ is a rate vector $\alpha^i(t,x)=(\alpha^i_y(t,x))_{y\in[d]}$ depending on the current full configuration $x\in[d]^n$, where for $y\neq x_i$ one has $\alpha^i_y(t,x)\in[\underline a,\overline a]$ and $\alpha^i_{x_i}(t,x)=-\sum_{y\neq x_i}\alpha^i_y(t,x)$, so that $\alpha^i(t,x)$ is a valid row of a rate matrix.

Let $f:[d]\times A_{[d]}^d\to\mathbb R$ be a running cost depending on the player’s state and her chosen rate vector, and let $F:[d]\times\mathcal P([d])\to\mathbb R$ be a mean-field interaction cost depending on the player’s state and the empirical distribution of the other players. For a Markovian strategy profile $\alpha=(\alpha^1,\dots,\alpha^n)$, define the empirical distribution of players other than $i$ by
\[\mu_t^{\alpha,i}:=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq i}\delta_{X_t^{\alpha,j}}\in\mathcal P([d]).\]
The (ergodic) cost for player $i$ under profile $\alpha$ is
\[J^{n,i}_0(\alpha):=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\Big[\int_0^T \big(f(X_t^{\alpha,i},\alpha^i(t,X_t^{\alpha})) + F(X_t^{\alpha,i},\mu_t^{\alpha,i})\big)\,dt\Big].\]
An exact (Markovian) Nash equilibrium for the $n$-player game is a profile $\alpha^{(n)}$ such that for every $i$ and every alternative Markovian strategy $\beta^i$,
\[J^{n,i}_0(\alpha^{(n)})\le J^{n,i}_0(\alpha^{(n),-i};\beta^i),\]
where $(\alpha^{(n),-i};\beta^i)$ denotes the profile obtained by replacing player $i$’s strategy with $\beta^i$.

The associated mean field game (MFG) considers a representative player with state $X_t\in[d]$ controlled by rates $\alpha(t,x)$, facing a flow of measures $\mu(t)\in\mathcal P([d])$. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the MFG is characterized by an ergodic master equation for a potential $U_0:[d]\times\mathcal P([d])\to\mathbb R$ and a scalar value $\varrho\in\mathbb R$, of the form
\[\varrho = H(x,\Delta_x U_0(\cdot,\eta)) + F(x,\eta) + \sum_{y,z\in[d]} \eta_y\, D_\eta^{yz}U_0(x,\eta)\,\gamma^*_z\big(y,\Delta_y U_0(\cdot,\eta)\big),\]
where $H$ is the Hamiltonian defined by minimizing $f(x,a)+a\cdot p$ over admissible rates, $\gamma^*$ is the minimizing selector (optimal feedback rate), $\Delta_x$ is the finite-difference operator $\Delta_x b=(b_y-b_x)_{y\in[d]}$, and $D_\eta^{yz}$ denotes directional derivatives on the simplex.

In the ergodic Markovian setting (infinite-horizon average cost), a central conceptual question is whether exact Nash equilibria of the finite-$n$ games converge, as $n\to\infty$, to the MFG equilibrium (or to the solution of the master equation / MFG system), in an appropriate sense (e.g., convergence of equilibrium empirical measures and/or value functions).
problem_definition_latex:
Establish a rigorous convergence result for exact Nash equilibria of the finite-state, infinite-horizon ergodic $n$-player game with Markovian (closed-loop) strategies to the corresponding mean field equilibrium as $n\to\infty$.

Concretely, given a sequence of exact Markovian Nash equilibria $\alpha^{(n)}$ for the $n$-player ergodic game, determine conditions under which one can prove that the associated empirical measure process (or its stationary distribution) converges to the MFG equilibrium measure (e.g., the stationary mean field equilibrium $\bar\mu$ or the MFG flow $\mu(t)$), and/or that the equilibrium values $\varrho_n$ converge to the MFG value $\varrho$.

\[J^{n,i}_0(\alpha):=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\mathbb E\Big[\int_0^T \big(f(X_t^{\alpha,i},\alpha^i(t,X_t^{\alpha})) + F(X_t^{\alpha,i},\mu_t^{\alpha,i})\big)\,dt\Big].\]
An exact (Markovian) Nash equilibrium for the $n$-player game is a profile $\alpha^{(n)}$ such that for every $i$ and every alternative Markovian strategy $\beta^i$,
\[J^{n,i}_0(\alpha^{(n)})\le J^{n,i}_0(\alpha^{(n),-i};\beta^i),\]
where $(\alpha^{(n),-i};\beta^i)$ denotes the profile obtained by replacing player $i$’s strategy with $\beta^i$.

The associated mean field game (MFG) considers a representative player with state $X_t\in[d]$ controlled by rates $\alpha(t,x)$, facing a flow of measures $\mu(t)\in\mathcal P([d])$. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the MFG is characterized by an ergodic master equation for a potential $U_0:[d]\times\mathcal P([d])\to\mathbb R$ and a scalar value $\varrho\in\mathbb R$, of the form
\[\varrho = H(x,\Delta_x U_0(\cdot,\eta)) + F(x,\eta) + \sum_{y,z\in[d]} \eta_y\, D_\eta^{yz}U_0(x,\eta)\,\gamma^*_z\big(y,\Delta_y U_0(\cdot,\eta)\big),\]
where $H$ is the Hamiltonian defined by minimizing $f(x,a)+a\cdot p$ over admissible rates, $\gamma^*$ is the minimizing selector (optimal feedback rate), $\Delta_x$ is the finite-difference operator $\Delta_x b=(b_y-b_x)_{y\in[d]}$, and $D_\eta^{yz}$ denotes directional derivatives on the simplex.

In the ergodic Markovian setting (infinite-horizon average cost), a central conceptual question is whether exact Nash equilibria of the finite-$n$ games converge, as $n\to\infty$, to the MFG equilibrium (or to the solution of the master equation / MFG system), in an appropriate sense (e.g., convergence of equilibrium empirical measures and/or value functions).

Establish a rigorous convergence result for exact Nash equilibria of the finite-state, infinite-horizon ergodic $n$-player game with Markovian (closed-loop) strategies to the corresponding mean field equilibrium as $n\to\infty$.

Concretely, given a sequence of exact Markovian Nash equilibria $\alpha^{(n)}$ for the $n$-player ergodic game, determine conditions under which one can prove that the associated empirical measure process (or its stationary distribution) converges to the MFG equilibrium measure (e.g., the stationary mean field equilibrium $\bar\mu$ or the MFG flow $\mu(t)$), and/or that the equilibrium values $\varrho_n$ converge to the MFG value $\varrho$.
open_problem_quote: This paper does not address the convergence of exact Nash equilibria to mean field equilibria. Our method relies on the Lipschitz continuity of \(U_0\), the solution to the master equation. While the structure of the Nash system resembles that of the master equation, connecting the two falls outside the scope of this work. The first author is actively working on this problem, which remains open (see [8]).
counterexample_suitability_rationale: The problem is about proving convergence for all games satisfying structural assumptions, rather than refuting a concrete conjectured bound on a finite instance family. Failures of convergence may depend on subtle equilibrium-selection and closed-loop feedback effects that are not easily certified by finite brute-force search.
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: One can programmatically generate finite-state ergodic games, compute (approximate) Markovian Nash equilibria numerically for increasing $n$, and compare empirical measures to MFG predictions to search for phenomena (e.g., multiple limits) or to test hypotheses about sufficient conditions. However, exact equilibrium computation and reliable limit inference are computationally heavy, and numerical evidence may not directly translate into proofs.

literature_review.synthesis:
In the finite-state ergodic Markovian setting of Cohen--Zell, the paper itself constructs asymptotic Nash equilibria (of order \(C/\sqrt n\)) from solutions of the ergodic MFG system and from the ergodic master equation, and proves propagation of chaos for the induced \(n\)-player dynamics. However, it explicitly leaves open the harder question of whether *exact* Markovian Nash equilibria \(\alpha^{(n)}\) of the \(n\)-player ergodic game must converge, as \(n\to\infty\), to the MFG equilibrium (e.g. convergence of invariant empirical measures and values \(\varrho_n\to\varrho\)).

The most directly relevant forward-citing progress is the development of uniform-in-time quantitative propagation-of-chaos estimates for mean-field interacting jump processes under exponential stability of the limiting nonlinear Kolmogorov equation. Applied to the master-equation-derived feedback controls, these results strengthen the approximation theory by giving \(O(1/n)\) weak error bounds uniformly over \(t\ge 0\) for test functionals of the empirical measure. This provides a key ingredient one would likely need in any attempt to upgrade approximate equilibria results to statements about exact equilibria, but it does not yet control the selection/structure of exact Nash equilibria.

Other cited work (e.g. turnpike results in LQG \(N\)-player games) addresses different asymptotic regimes (long horizon rather than many players) and different information structures (open-loop rather than Markovian closed-loop). Overall, the convergence of exact Markovian Nash equilibria to the ergodic MFG equilibrium in finite-state jump games remains open, with the main obstacles tied to feedback effects and potential non-uniqueness/multiple mean-field limits in ergodic closed-loop settings.

sources.theorem_or_result:
Main quantitative limit theorem (Theorem 2.7): for an N-particle mean-field interacting continuous-time jump process on a finite state space with rates \(\alpha(\mu)\), assuming \(\alpha\) is Lipschitz with Lipschitz functional derivative (\(\alpha\in\) (D-Lip)) and the limiting nonlinear Kolmogorov equation \(\dot m(t;\mu)=m(t;\mu)\alpha(m(t;\mu))\) is exponentially stable with suitable Lipschitz regularity of \(\delta m/\delta m\) (assumption (Erg)), then for any test function \(\Phi\in\) (D-Lip) and i.i.d. initial data with law \(\mu_0\),
\[\sup_{t\ge 0}\big|\mathbb E[\Phi(\mu_t^N)]-\Phi(m(t;\mu_0))\big|\le \frac{C}{N}.\]
Moreover, they give checkable sufficient conditions for (Erg) via a linearized stability condition (Lin-Erg) and apply the result to N-player ergodic finite-state MFG dynamics under master-equation-derived feedback controls, yielding uniform-in-time weak convergence of the empirical measure to the mean-field law at rate \(1/N\) (Theorem 5.2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence of exact Markovian Nash equilibria of the finite-n ergodic game to the mean field equilibrium (e.g., convergence of equilibrium empirical measures and values). This paper does not analyze sequences of exact Nash equilibria \(\alpha^{(n)}\) nor prove that every exact equilibrium converges to the MFG equilibrium. Instead it proves a strong, uniform-in-time propagation-of-chaos/mean-field limit with rate \(1/N\) for interacting jump processes whose rates depend on the empirical measure, under exponential ergodicity of the limiting nonlinear Markov chain. In Section 5.2 it applies this to the specific closed-loop dynamics induced when players use feedback controls constructed from the ergodic MFG master equation (as in Cohen–Zell), thereby strengthening prior results for these approximate equilibria by giving uniform-in-time convergence of the induced empirical measure process to the mean-field law. Thus it provides a key tool/partial progress toward the convergence question, but only for MFG-derived (approximate) equilibrium controls, not for arbitrary exact Nash equilibria.

sources.title: Turnpike properties in linear quadratic Gaussian N-player differential games
sources.theorem_or_result:
In an open-loop linear–quadratic–Gaussian (LQG) N-player stochastic differential game, the paper proves a turnpike estimate comparing the finite-horizon Nash equilibrium \((X_T^i,\alpha_T^i)\) to the ergodic-game Nash equilibrium \((X^i,\alpha^i)\): there exist constants \(K_e(N),\lambda_e(N)>0\) (independent of \(t,T\)) such that for all \(t\in[0,T]\),
\[\sup_{i\in[N]}\mathbb E\big[\|X_T^i(t)-X^i(t)\|^2+\|\alpha_T^i(t)-\alpha^i(t)\|^2\big]\le K_e(N)\big(e^{-\lambda_e(N)t}+e^{-\lambda_e(N)(T-t)}\big).\]
Under additional uniform-in-\(N\) structural assumptions, there exist \(K_e,\lambda_e>0\) independent of \(t,T,N\) such that
\[\sup_N\frac1N\mathbb E\big[\|X_T(t)-X(t)\|^2+\|\alpha_T(t)-\alpha(t)\|^2\big]\le K_e\big(e^{-\lambda_e t}+e^{-\lambda_e (T-t)}\big).\]
It also proves exponential convergence of the finite-horizon Riccati/FBS-ODE system to the associated algebraic (ergodic) system and convergence of time-averaged values: \(\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T V_T^i(0,x)=c_i\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence, as \(n\to\infty\), of exact Nash equilibria in finite-state ergodic Markovian (closed-loop) games to the mean field game (MFG) equilibrium/master-equation solution. This paper does not study the mean-field limit \(N\to\infty\) nor finite-state Markov jump dynamics, and it works with continuous-state LQG diffusions and open-loop (private-filtration) equilibria. Its main convergence is a long-horizon turnpike: finite-horizon equilibria converge to the ergodic \(N\)-player equilibrium as \(T\to\infty\), with some estimates uniform in \(N\). Thus it does not resolve convergence of exact \(n\)-player ergodic equilibria to an MFG equilibrium as \(n\to\infty\). Indirectly, the uniform-in-\(N\) stability/turnpike estimates and techniques for coupled HJB–FP systems may be useful tools toward controlling large-\(n\) behavior, but they address a different asymptotic regime (\(T\to\infty\) rather than \(n\to\infty\)).
