\max_{(x_0,f):\ \|x_0-x^\star\|\le D} \|\nabla f(x_\sigma)\| 
< \frac{LD}{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i + 1}.
\]

Equivalently, prove that (C1) holds if and only if averaging cannot improve the worst-case objective-gap guarantee over returning \(x_N\), and (C2) holds if and only if averaging cannot improve the worst-case gradient-norm guarantee over returning \(x_N\).
open_problem_quote:
That is, numerical results suggest that the converses of Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 are true, i.e., (C1)/(C2) hold if and only if averaging is not beneficial. We state this formally in the following conjecture.

Conjecture 3.3. Consider gradient descent with stepsizes \(h = (h_0, \dots, h_{N-1}) > 0\). For any \(L, D > 0\), if the worst-case final iterate objective gap is not characterized by (C1), then there exists nondegenerate \(\sigma\) such that
\[\max_{(x_0,f)\in \mathcal{F}_{L,D}} f\Bigl(\sum_{j=0}^N \sigma_j x_j\Bigr) - \inf f < \frac{LD^2}{4\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i + 2}.\]
Similarly, if the worst-case final iterate gradient norm is not characterized by (C2), then there exists nondegenerate \(\sigma\) such that
\[\max_{(x_0,f)\in \mathcal{F}_{L,D}} \|\nabla f\bigl(\sum_{j=0}^N \sigma_j x_j\bigr)\| < \frac{LD}{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i + 1}.\]
counterexample_suitability_rationale: The conjecture can be tested for fixed small \(N\) and stepsize sequences by solving the associated PEP semidefinite programs for both the last iterate and the best averaged iterate, and checking whether an improving nondegenerate \(\sigma\) exists whenever (C1)/(C2) fail. This makes automated search over stepsize patterns and averaging weights feasible.
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: Candidate objects (stepsize sequences \(h\) and averaging weights \(\sigma\)) admit a direct computational fitness signal via PEP SDPs approximating the worst-case gaps/gradient norms. An evolutionary loop could search for counterexamples (instances where (C1)/(C2) fail but averaging still does not help, or vice versa) or discover structural patterns suggesting a proof strategy.

literature_review.synthesis:
The conjectured converse (Conjecture 3.3 in Luner--Grimmer) asks for a tight equivalence between two phenomena for fixed-step gradient descent on the smooth convex class \(\mathcal F_{L,D}\): (i) the last-iterate worst-case objective gap and gradient norm are exactly the Huber-attained expressions (C1)/(C2), and (ii) no nondegenerate averaging \(x_\sigma\) can strictly improve the corresponding minimax guarantee. Luner--Grimmer prove the forward direction: if (C1) (resp. (C2)) holds, then \(\sigma^{\mathrm{last}}\) uniquely minimizes the worst-case objective gap (resp. gradient norm) over all \(\sigma\in\Delta_{N+1}\), using the fact that the Huber function is affine over the convex hull of iterates and makes any nontrivial convex combination strictly worse.

Forward-citing work to date does not resolve the converse in general, but it expands the catalog of stepsize schedules for which (C1)/(C2)-type equalities are now known to hold tightly, thereby strengthening the empirical alignment observed in Luner--Grimmer’s Figure 1. In particular, "Relaxed proximal point algorithm: Tight complexity bounds and acceleration without momentum" proves tight last-iterate bounds for gradient descent under the silver stepsize schedule, establishing the exact (C1)/(C2) forms (depending only on \(\sum h_i\)) for that family. "Accelerated objective gap and gradient norm convergence for gradient descent via long steps" similarly provides tight last-iterate guarantees for certain recursively defined long-step schedules and exhibits explicit extremal quadratic/Huber-type instances; it also notes that averaging can be strictly worse for those schedules, consistent with the ‘no averaging benefit’ side when last-iterate bounds are tight. "Composing optimized stepsize schedules for gradient descent" develops compositional machinery to build stepsize schedules with certifiable tight last-iterate guarantees, offering a pathway to systematically generate further instances where (C1)/(C2) hold.

The main gap remains: a general proof (or counterexample) that whenever the last-iterate worst-case deviates from (C1) or (C2), there must exist a nondegenerate \(\sigma\) with strictly smaller minimax objective gap or gradient norm than the Huber-based expressions. Promising directions suggested by the existing PEP-based framework include: (a) analyzing the joint minimax problem \(\min_{\sigma\in\Delta_{N+1}}\max_{f\in\mathcal F_{L,D}}\) via SDP duality to relate optimal \(\sigma\) to slackness of the last-iterate dual certificate; and (b) leveraging the composability/inductive constructions for stepsizes to reduce the converse to verifying a finite set of extremal patterns. At present, however, no forward citation provides a full converse characterization, so the problem remains open.

sources.title: Relaxed proximal point algorithm: Tight complexity bounds and acceleration without momentum
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves tight worst-case convergence bounds for the relaxed proximal point algorithm (RPPA), and as a byproduct proves [LG24, Conjecture 3.2] for gradient descent (GD) with the silver stepsize schedule \(\pi^{(m)}\) (with \(N=2^m-1\)): for any convex \(L\)-smooth \(h\), \[h(x_N)-h(x^\star)\le \frac{L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2}{4\rho^m-2}=\frac{L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2}{2(2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\alpha_i+1)},\qquad \|\nabla h(x_N)\|\le \frac{L\|x_0-x^\star\|}{\rho^m}=\frac{L\|x_0-x^\star\|}{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\alpha_i+1},\] and both bounds are tight (Theorem 5.2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a converse characterization: for fixed GD stepsizes \(h\), the last iterate is worst-case optimal among all averages iff the last-iterate worst-case equals the explicit formulas (C1)/(C2). This paper does not study averaging schemes \(x_\sigma\) at all, nor does it prove any ‘if and only if’ link between tight last-iterate bounds and impossibility of improvement by averaging. However, it is relevant because it establishes additional instances where the last-iterate worst-case bounds take the exact (C1)/(C2)-type form (depending only on \(\sum h_i\)), notably proving tightness for the silver stepsize schedule conjectured in [LG24]. These results support the ‘only if’ direction’s plausibility by expanding the class of stepsizes for which (C1)/(C2)-style equalities hold, but they do not address the converse implication about existence of improving nondegenerate averages when (C1)/(C2) fail.

sources.title: Accelerated objective gap and gradient norm convergence for gradient descent via long steps
sources.theorem_or_result:
For specific long-stepsize schedules \,\(h^{(k)}_{\mathrm{left}}\) and \,\(h^{(k)}_{\mathrm{right}}\) (and their concatenation), the paper proves tight last-iterate worst-case guarantees for L-smooth convex minimization after \,\(N=2^k-1\) (or \,\(2^{k+1}-2\)) steps:
- (Gradient-norm from function gap) With \,\(h=h^{(k)}_{\mathrm{left}}\): \(\tfrac12\|\nabla f(x_N)\|^2 \le \tfrac{L(f(x_0)-f(x^\star))}{r_k}\).
- (Objective gap from distance) With \,\(h=h^{(k)}_{\mathrm{right}}\): \(f(x_N)-f(x^\star) \le \tfrac{L}{2}\,\tfrac{\|x_0-x^\star\|^2}{r_k}\).
Here \(r_k = 2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} h_i + 1 = \prod_{i=0}^{N-1}(1-h_i)^{-2}\) and \(r_k \asymp N^{\log_2(\varrho)}\) with \(\varrho=1+\sqrt2\). The bounds are claimed tight (attained) on a quadratic and on a Huber-type function.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a converse characterization: if the last-iterate worst-case is not exactly the (C1)/(C2) expressions \(LD^2/(4\sum h_i+2)\) and \(LD/(\sum h_i+1)\), then some nontrivial averaging \(x_\sigma\) should strictly improve the worst-case guarantee. This paper does not prove that converse in general. However, it provides evidence in a particular direction for certain long-stepsize schedules: it constructs explicit worst-case functions (quadratic and Huber) that attain the paper’s last-iterate bounds, and it states (Remark 2) that for these stepsizes, reporting an average \(\sum \sigma_i x_i\) instead of \(x_N\) strictly worsens worst-case performance. That is consistent with the ‘no averaging benefit’ side of the conjectured equivalence, but only for these specific schedules and without establishing the (C1)/(C2) exact worst-case characterizations for arbitrary \(h\) or the full converse implication.

sources.title: Composing optimized stepsize schedules for gradient descent
sources.theorem_or_result: Develops a theory of “composable” fixed stepsize schedules for gradient descent on smooth convex functions. In particular, it defines f-composable schedules (tight final objective-gap guarantee) and g-composable schedules (tight final gradient-norm guarantee) characterized by the equalities \(\eta=\frac{1}{1+2\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}h_i}=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(h_i-1)^2\), and proves inductive composition theorems (Theorems 1–3) showing that certain join operations on schedules preserve f-/g-/s-composability with explicitly computable new rates. It then constructs optimized basic schedules (OBS-F/OBS-G) conjectured minimax-optimal for minimizing \(f(x_n)-f(x^\star)\) or \(\|\nabla f(x_n)\|\) at the last iterate.
sources.connection: The open problem concerns when averaging \(x_\sigma=\sum_j\sigma_j x_j\) can strictly improve the worst-case guarantee over the last iterate \(x_N\), and conjectures an equivalence with whether the last-iterate worst-case equals the closed forms (C1)/(C2). This citing paper does not study averaging over iterates at all; it studies how to choose fixed stepsizes \(h\) to optimize last-iterate performance and gives tight certificates/worst-case instances (quadratic/Huber) for certain structured schedules. Indirectly, it provides tools to identify stepsize schedules for which last-iterate bounds are tight and witnessed by specific extremal functions, which is adjacent to verifying conditions like (C1)/(C2), but it does not address the converse ‘if not (C1)/(C2) then averaging helps’ characterization.

title: Extend uniform subdifferential convergence rates to max-of-smooth weakly convex models
background_latex:
Let \(\Xi\) be a measurable space with probability measure \(P\), and let \(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_m\) be i.i.d. samples from \(P\). Consider a stochastic optimization objective of the form
\[
\phi(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim P}[f(x,\xi)]+R(x)+\iota_X(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^d,
\]
with empirical (sample-average) counterpart
\[
\phi_S(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f(x,\xi_i)+R(x)+\iota_X(x).
\]
Here \(R:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is a proper closed convex function, \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty closed convex, and \(\iota_X\) is the indicator of \(X\). Let \(\partial\) denote the Fr\'echet (regular) subdifferential, and let \(H(A,B)\) denote the Hausdorff distance between nonempty compact subsets \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\).

A (locally) weakly convex function on an open set \(O\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a function \(g:O\to\mathbb{R}\) such that for each \(x\in O\) there exists \(\lambda<\infty\) and a neighborhood on which \(y\mapsto g(y)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|y\|^2\) is convex.

The paper establishes, for a specific subclass of stochastic weakly convex objectives called stochastic convex-composite models (with one-dimensional convex outer function), high-probability bounds on
\[
\sup_{x\in X\cap B(x_0;r)} H(\partial\phi(x),\partial\phi_S(x)),
\]
in terms of dimension and a VC-dimension complexity measure of threshold sets induced by the model.

A commonly studied different weakly convex model class is the class of max-of-smooth functions, i.e., objectives representable (at least pointwise) as a maximum over a family of smooth functions; such functions are typically nonsmooth and can be weakly convex under suitable regularity.
problem_definition_latex:
Develop an analogue of the paper's uniform Hausdorff-distance bound for subdifferential mappings,
\[
\sup_{x\in X\cap B(x_0;r)} H(\partial\phi(x),\partial\phi_S(x)),
\]
with explicit (high-probability) convergence rates in \(m\), for stochastic weakly convex objectives in the max-of-smooth model class (rather than the stochastic convex-composite class treated in the paper).

literature_review.synthesis:
Ruan (2025) develops a deterministic reduction (Theorem 1) for locally weakly convex functions on an open set \(O\): uniform Hausdorff control of \(x\mapsto \partial f(x)\) reduces to uniform control of any subgradient selections \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\). This enables sharp high-probability rates for stochastic convex-composite models \(f(x,\xi)=h(c(x;\xi))\) with one-dimensional convex outer \(h\), by choosing a selection built from indicator thresholds \(\mathbf 1\{c(x,\xi)\ge t\}\) and controlling it via VC dimension of the induced threshold class. The resulting bound (Theorem 5) yields essentially \(m^{-1/2}\) rates (up to logs) for \(\sup_{x\in X\cap B(x_0;r)} H(\partial\phi(x),\partial\phi_S(x))\) in that model class.

For the max-of-smooth weakly convex class, the lone forward-citing work provided here gives a complementary, negative message: “Failure of uniform laws of large numbers for subdifferentials and beyond” constructs structured max-type objectives (even convex, in \(d=2\), with only two smooth pieces combined by \(\max\{\cdot,0\}\)) where uniform LLNs for subdifferentials fail, and hence uniform Hausdorff convergence \(\sup_x H(\partial f(x),\partial f_S(x))\to 0\) cannot hold in full generality. This indicates the open problem remains unsolved as stated: an analogue of Ruan’s uniform rate bound for general max-of-smooth models is impossible without strengthening assumptions.

Promising directions therefore shift from a blanket extension to identifying verifiable additional conditions under which a Ruan-style reduction plus learning-theoretic control can succeed for max-of-smooth models. Natural candidates include: (i) restricting the index set of maximizers to a class with finite complexity (e.g., finite max, parametric families with bounded VC/pseudodimension), (ii) imposing margin or nondegeneracy conditions ensuring stability of the active set \(\arg\max\) under sampling, or (iii) weakening the target metric (graphical distance, fixed \(\varepsilon\)-enlarged subdifferentials, or local-in-probability notions) to bypass the demonstrated obstructions.

title: Determine tight PTAS running times for q-norm load balancing with intermediate machines
background_latex:
We consider scheduling on $m$ identical parallel machines with $n$ jobs, each job $j$ having processing time $p_j>0$. A schedule is an assignment of jobs to machines. For a schedule, let the load on machine $i$ be
\[C_i=\sum_{j\to i} p_j.\]
Fix a constant $q>1$. The optimization objective is the $q$-power sum (equivalently the $\ell_q$-norm) of loads:
\[\min \sum_{i=1}^m C_i^q \qquad \text{(equivalently minimize }(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i^q)^{1/q}\text{).}\]
This problem is denoted $P\|\|\sum_i C_i^q$ in three-field scheduling notation.

An algorithm is a PTAS if for every $\varepsilon>0$ it outputs a schedule of objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times optimal in time $T(n,m,\varepsilon)$ that is polynomial in $n$ for each fixed $\varepsilon$.

We are interested in the fine-grained dependence of the best possible PTAS running time on $\varepsilon$ and on $m$ when $m$ grows as a power of $1/\varepsilon$. In particular, let
\[m = \Theta\bigl((1/\varepsilon)^\theta\bigr)\]
for a fixed exponent $\theta\in(1/2,1].\]
The paper establishes (under ETH) a nearly tight running time $2^{\tilde O(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon})}+n^{O(1)}$ for the regime $m=\Theta(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon})$, and shows that for sufficiently large $m$ (e.g. $m=\Omega((1/\varepsilon)\log^2(1/\varepsilon))$) there are algorithms with running time polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$; it also gives a PTAS with running time $(1/\varepsilon)^{O(m)}+n^{O(1)}$ for $m=O(\sqrt{1/\varepsilon})$. The remaining regime $m=\Theta((1/\varepsilon)^\theta)$ for $\theta\in(1/2,1]$ is left unresolved.
problem_definition_latex:
For the scheduling problem $P\|\|\sum_{i=1}^m C_i^q$ with fixed constant $q>1$, determine the tight asymptotic running time (as a function of $\varepsilon$ and $n$) of the fastest PTAS in the parameter regime
\[m = \Theta\bigl((1/\varepsilon)^\theta\bigr)\quad\text{for a fixed }\theta\in(1/2,1].\]
In particular, either:
1) prove a matching (ETH-based) lower bound on the PTAS running time in this regime (a subexponential lower bound in $1/\varepsilon$), or
2) design a PTAS whose running time improves over the known bounds in this regime,
so as to characterize the optimal dependence on $1/\varepsilon$ for these values of $m$.

title: Prove existence of a simpler all-norms approximation clustering for correlation clustering
background_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an unweighted complete graph on \(n=|V|\) vertices whose edges are labeled \(+\) (similar) or \(-\) (dissimilar). Write \(E^+\) and \(E^-\) for the sets of positive and negative edges, respectively.

A clustering \(\mathcal C\) is a partition of \(V\) into clusters. For a vertex \(u\in V\), let \(\mathcal C(u)\) denote the cluster containing \(u\), and let \(V\setminus \mathcal C(u)\) be the vertices in other clusters.

An edge \(\{u,v\}\in E^+\) is a disagreement under \(\mathcal C\) if \(u\) and \(v\) lie in different clusters; an edge \(\{u,v\}\in E^-\) is a disagreement if \(u\) and \(v\) lie in the same cluster.

Define the disagreement count (disagreement degree) of \(u\) under \(\mathcal C\) by
\[

title: Resolve smoothed complexity of pure Nash equilibria in unrestricted congestion games
background_latex:
A congestion game consists of a finite set of players \(N=[n]\) and resources \(R\). Each player \(i\in N\) has a strategy set \(\Sigma_i\subseteq 2^R\). Each resource \(r\in R\) has a latency function \(\kappa_r:[n]\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). For a pure strategy profile \(\boldsymbol\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)\in \Sigma:=\Sigma_1\times\cdots\times\Sigma_n\), the load on resource \(r\) is \(\ell_r(\boldsymbol\sigma):=|\{i\in N: r\in\sigma_i\}|\). Player \(i\)'s cost is \(C_i(\boldsymbol\sigma):=\sum_{r\in\sigma_i}\kappa_r(\ell_r(\boldsymbol\sigma))\).

A pure Nash equilibrium (PNE) is a profile \(\boldsymbol\sigma^*\in\Sigma\) such that for every player \(i\in N\) and every deviation \(\sigma_i'\in\Sigma_i\), \(C_i(\boldsymbol\sigma^*)\le C_i(\sigma_i',\boldsymbol\sigma^*_{-i})\). Congestion games are exact potential games with Rosenthal potential
\[\Phi(\boldsymbol\sigma)=\sum_{r\in R}\sum_{\ell=1}^{\ell_r(\boldsymbol\sigma)}\kappa_r(\ell),\]
which strictly decreases along any better-response move.

In smoothed analysis for congestion games, the numerical parameters of the latency functions are independently perturbed from continuous distributions with densities bounded above by a parameter \(\phi\). The paper considers several standard representations:
1) General latencies: each value \(\kappa_r(\ell)\) is independently drawn from a distribution on \([0,1]\) with density in \([0,\phi]\).
2) Polynomial latencies of degree at most \(d\): each coefficient \(\alpha_{r,j}\) in \(\kappa_r(\ell)=\sum_{j=0}^{d_r}\alpha_{r,j}\ell^j\) is independently drawn from a distribution on \([0,1]\) with density in \([0,\phi]\).
3) Step-function latencies with at most \(d\) breakpoints: each jump size parameter \(\alpha_{r,j}\) is independently drawn from a distribution on \([0,1]\) with density in \([0,\phi]\), while breakpoints are adversarially fixed.

A standard algorithmic process to find a PNE is better-response dynamics: starting from an arbitrary profile, repeatedly choose some player with an improving deviation and update her strategy (according to any pivoting rule). The running time is the number of improving moves until reaching a PNE. Smoothed complexity asks for bounds on the expected number of improving moves (and thus expected running time, since each move is efficiently computable under the representation).
problem_definition_latex: Determine whether, for (not necessarily restrained/compact) congestion games under the smoothed perturbation models above (general, polynomial, or step-function latencies with independent noise of density bounded by \(\phi\)), the expected number of iterations of better-response dynamics needed to reach a pure Nash equilibrium is bounded by a polynomial in the input size and \(\phi\); if not, characterize the correct smoothed complexity (e.g., give superpolynomial lower bounds or identify the precise structural conditions separating polynomial from superpolynomial smoothed running time).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Giannakopoulos--Grosz--Melissourgos, 2025) develops a general black-box theorem (via \((\lambda,\beta,\mu)\)-separability) that yields polynomial expected convergence of exact local search under \(\phi\)-smooth independent perturbations, and it instantiates this for exact PNE computation in congestion games only under structural restrictions (notably \(B\)-restrained games and certain compact network congestion games). The open problem asks whether such polynomial smoothed convergence extends to unrestricted congestion games under the same perturbation models (general explicit latencies, bounded-degree polynomials, and step functions with perturbed jump sizes).

Forward-citation evidence currently provides strong progress only for approximate equilibria: Giannakopoulos (EC 2024) proves a smoothed FPTAS in which \((1+\varepsilon)\)-improving dynamics reach a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate PNE in expected strongly polynomially many steps, with bounds polynomial in \(\phi\), the input size, and \(1/\varepsilon\), and covering precisely the three latency representations considered in the open problem. However, the dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) leaves open the exact case \(\varepsilon=0\), where arbitrarily small potential drops could in principle lead to superpolynomial paths.

A separate line of work on smoothed local search lower bounds (e.g., superpolynomial smoothed complexity for 3-FLIP Max-Cut) indicates that even under i.i.d. continuous perturbations, improvement dynamics for some PLS problems can admit superpolynomial-length improving sequences. While not directly transferable to Rosenthal-potential better responses in congestion games, it motivates investigating whether unrestricted congestion games admit analogous constructions, or whether additional structure (like bounded \(B\) in the source paper) is necessary and essentially tight for polynomial smoothed convergence of exact better-response dynamics.

sources.title: A smoothed FPTAS for equilibria in congestion games
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves smoothed strongly polynomial convergence of approximate better-response dynamics: in a \(\phi\)-smooth congestion game (independent perturbations with densities \(\le \phi\)), any sequence of \((1+\varepsilon)\)-improving moves reaches a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate pure Nash equilibrium after an expected number of steps polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\), \(\phi\), and the input size. Concretely, for general congestion games with costs \(c_r(\ell)\in[0,1]\) i.i.d. \(\phi\)-smooth, \(\mathbb{E}[T]=\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-1}\phi n^2 m^3)\); for step-function costs with total \(d\) breakpoints, \(\mathbb{E}[T]=\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-1}\phi n m d^2)\); for polynomial costs of constant degree \(d\) with perturbed nonzero coefficients, \(\mathbb{E}[T]=\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-1}\phi n^{d+1} m^3)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the smoothed complexity of reaching an exact PNE via (exact) better-response dynamics in unrestricted congestion games under several perturbation models (general, polynomial, step-function). This paper does not settle the exact-PNE question, but gives strong partial progress: it establishes polynomial (in \(\phi\) and input size) expected convergence time for \((1+\varepsilon)\)-better-response dynamics to a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-approximate PNE, and it covers the same three perturbation/representation models (general costs perturbed per load, step-function jump sizes perturbed with adversarial breakpoints, and polynomial costs with perturbed coefficients). Thus it resolves the smoothed complexity for approximate equilibria, showing that the exponential worst-case behavior is fragile under smoothing, but leaves open whether \(\varepsilon=0\) (exact improvements / exact PNE) also yields smoothed polynomial convergence or whether a superpolynomial lower bound persists.

sources.title: Superpolynomial smoothed complexity of 3-FLIP in Local Max-Cut
sources.theorem_or_result: They prove a superpolynomial smoothed lower bound for local search in Max-Cut with 3-vertex moves. In particular (Theorem 1.1), for all n there exist graphs G with O(n) vertices such that if edge weights are drawn i.i.d. uniformly from an interval [a,b] and the initial cut is uniform random, then with high probability there exist executions of the 3-FLIP algorithm from this initial cut that take \(2^{\Omega(\sqrt n)}\) improving steps. They also give a worst-case (non-smoothed) exponential lower bound for 1-FLIP (Theorem 1.2): graphs of max degree 4 with an initial cut from which the unique improving 1-FLIP execution to a local optimum has length \(\Omega(2^n)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether better-response dynamics in (unrestricted) congestion games has polynomial smoothed complexity under standard perturbation models, or whether superpolynomial lower bounds occur. This paper does not study congestion games or Rosenthal potential directly; it studies local search for Max-Cut (a different PLS problem) under smoothed edge-weight perturbations. However, Max-Cut local optima correspond to pure Nash equilibria of party-affiliation / cut games (a special class of potential games), so the paper provides evidence that smoothed analysis can still allow superpolynomial improvement paths for certain local-search neighborhoods (3-FLIP). It suggests that, analogously, in potential games one may need structural restrictions (e.g., neighborhood/pivot rules) to obtain polynomial smoothed convergence, but it neither proves nor refutes polynomial smoothed convergence for better responses in general congestion games under the latency-perturbation models stated.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for exact matching in bipartite graphs
background_latex:
Let \(G=(A,B;E)\) be a bipartite graph in which every edge is colored either red or blue, and let \(|A|=|B|\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is perfect if every vertex in \(A\cup B\) is incident to exactly one edge of \(M\). For a perfect matching \(M\), let \(r(M)\) denote the number of red edges in \(M\).

The \(\textit{exact matching problem}\) asks, given \((G,k)\) with integer \(k\), whether there exists a perfect matching \(M\) with \(r(M)=k\). The paper studies a different class of problems (popular near-maximum-weight matchings) and proves that if one could solve a certain popularity-constrained matching problem deterministically in polynomial time, then one could solve the exact matching problem deterministically in polynomial time. The paper notes that no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is known for exact matching.

literature_review.synthesis:
The exact matching problem of Papadimitriou–Yannakakis asks for a perfect matching with exactly \(k\) red edges in a red/blue-colored bipartite graph \(G=(A,B;E)\). As emphasized in Csáji–Király–Takazawa–Yokoi (2024), this problem remains a central derandomization challenge: randomized polynomial-time algorithms are known (via the isolation lemma/Tutte matrix style techniques), but a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm is still not known in general.

The 2024 paper uses exact matching as a hardness yardstick for “popular near-maximum(-weight)” matching: Theorem 4 shows that a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the one-sided popular near-maximum-weight matching problem (even with weights in \(\{0,1\}\) and weak orders) would imply a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for exact matching. Thus, their tractability results for popular maximum-weight/maximum-utility solutions (Theorems 1–3) are complemented by evidence that moving from “optimal” to “near-optimal” popularity constraints runs into the same barrier as exact matching.

Among the forward citations provided, “Max-Utility Matchings with Popularity via Critical Vertices” develops deterministic polynomial-time algorithms and polyhedral formulations for several popularity-with-utility variants (popular critical matchings, popular max-utility matchings). While methodologically adjacent (it also leverages structure of popular matchings and criticality), it does not address the red/blue exact-count constraint and does not yield a deterministic algorithm for exact matching. Consequently, based on the available forward-citation evidence, the exact matching problem remains open, and progress continues to be indirect—either by reductions showing that new deterministic algorithms would derandomize exact matching, or by developing deterministic algorithms for neighboring constrained-popularity problems that carefully avoid exact-count constraints.

sources.title: Max-Utility Matchings with Popularity via Critical Vertices
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves existence and gives polynomial-time algorithms for popularity notions in bipartite matching with strict preferences and edge utilities. In particular: (i) for any critical set \(C\subseteq A\cup B\), a popular critical matching exists and a max-size (and min-size) popular critical matching can be computed in \(O(m+|C|m)\) time (Theorem 1); (ii) for any utility function \(f:E\to\mathbb{Q}\), a popular max-utility matching exists and can be computed in polynomial time (Theorem 2); (iii) the popular max-critical matching polytope admits a compact extended formulation (Theorem 3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the exact matching problem: given a red/blue-colored bipartite graph and \(k\), decide if there is a perfect matching with exactly \(k\) red edges. This paper studies a different framework (popular matchings under preferences, critical vertices, and utilities) and provides deterministic polytime algorithms there. However, nothing in the provided excerpt indicates a reduction that would yield a deterministic polytime algorithm for exact matching, nor does it address counting red edges in perfect matchings. At best, the paper supplies algorithmic/LP machinery for certain constrained popularity/utility matching problems, which is conceptually adjacent to the original paper’s theme but does not resolve exact matching.

title: Existence of equilibrium with rich firm using control and poor firm using strategy
background_latex:
Consider the two-player continuous-time stochastic game of dividend distribution described as follows.

1) Probability space and noise: Let \((B_t)_{t\ge 0}\) be a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge 0},\mathbb P)\).

2) Parameters: drifts \(\mu_0>0\) (duopoly) and \(\hat\mu>\mu_0\) (monopoly), volatility \(\sigma>0\), discount rate \(r>0\).

3) Controls (dividends): Each player chooses a cumulative dividend process, modeled as a singular control: a right-continuous, nondecreasing, \((\mathcal F_t)\)-adapted process with \(L_{0-}=0\) for Player 1 and \(D_{0-}=0\) for Player 2. Admissibility requires that jumps cannot exceed current cash reserves.

4) Cash-reserve dynamics (duopoly phase): Starting from initial endowments \((x,y)\in[0,\infty)^2\), the controlled reserves are
\[
X_t = x + \mu_0 t + \sigma B_t - L_t,\qquad Y_t = y + \mu_0 t + \sigma B_t - D_t.
\]
Default times are \(\gamma_X=\inf\{t\ge 0: X_t\le 0\}\) and \(\gamma_Y=\inf\{t\ge 0: Y_t\le 0\}\).

5) Monopoly continuation value: If one firm defaults first, the survivor becomes a monopolist with drift \(\hat\mu\) and continuation value \(\hat v\), where for initial reserve \(z\ge 0\)
\[
\hat v(z) := \sup_{\xi}\,\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_C]} e^{-rt}\,d\xi_t\Big],\qquad C_t = z + \hat\mu t + \sigma B_t - \xi_t,\ \gamma_C=\inf\{t\ge 0: C_t\le 0\}.
\]

6) Payoffs: For a control pair \((L,D)\), Player 1 and 2 payoffs are
\[
J^1_{x,y}(L,D)=\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_X\wedge\gamma_Y]} e^{-rt}\,dL_t + \mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_Y<\gamma_X\}}e^{-r\gamma_Y}\,\hat v(X_{\gamma_Y})\Big],
\]
\[
J^2_{x,y}(D,L)=\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_X\wedge\gamma_Y]} e^{-rt}\,dD_t + \mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_X<\gamma_Y\}}e^{-r\gamma_X}\,\hat v(Y_{\gamma_X})\Big].
\]

7) Strategies: A (pure) feedback strategy for a player is a non-anticipative mapping that assigns a dividend path as a functional of the observed Brownian path and the opponent’s past dividend path. The paper also allows randomised strategies (Aumann-style) by adding an independent randomisation variable \(u\in[0,1]\). A strategy profile must be control-inducing (i.e., the induced fixed point defining the pair of controls exists and is unique on every finite horizon).

8) Nash equilibrium: A pair of (possibly randomised) strategies is a Nash equilibrium if neither player can improve their payoff by unilateral deviation within the admissible class of randomised strategies.

The paper constructs equilibria where (in the asymmetric initial-endowment case \(y>x\)) the poorer firm uses a pure control and the richer firm uses a pure strategy. It explicitly leaves open the existence of equilibria with the roles reversed (richer firm using a control; poorer firm using a strategy).

1) Player 1: \(\Xi_1\) is an admissible strategy mapping that may depend on the opponent’s dividend path (and possibly on a randomisation variable), and
2) Player 2: \(\Xi_2\) is an admissible control viewed as a strategy that does not depend on the opponent’s dividend path,
with \((\Xi_1,\Xi_2)\) being control-inducing and satisfying the Nash inequalities against all unilateral deviations in the full class of admissible randomised strategies.

If such equilibria exist, characterize conditions/structure ensuring existence (e.g., for all parameter choices and initial states as in the model).

2) Parameters: drifts \(\mu_0>0\) (duopoly) and \(\hat\mu>\mu_0\) (monopoly), volatility \(\sigma>0\), discount rate \(r>0\).

3) Controls (dividends): Each player chooses a cumulative dividend process, modeled as a singular control: a right-continuous, nondecreasing, \((\mathcal F_t)\)-adapted process with \(L_{0-}=0\) for Player 1 and \(D_{0-}=0\) for Player 2. Admissibility requires that jumps cannot exceed current cash reserves.

4) Cash-reserve dynamics (duopoly phase): Starting from initial endowments \((x,y)\in[0,\infty)^2\), the controlled reserves are
\[
X_t = x + \mu_0 t + \sigma B_t - L_t,\qquad Y_t = y + \mu_0 t + \sigma B_t - D_t.
\]
Default times are \(\gamma_X=\inf\{t\ge 0: X_t\le 0\}\) and \(\gamma_Y=\inf\{t\ge 0: Y_t\le 0\}\).

5) Monopoly continuation value: If one firm defaults first, the survivor becomes a monopolist with drift \(\hat\mu\) and continuation value \(\hat v\), where for initial reserve \(z\ge 0\)
\[
\hat v(z) := \sup_{\xi}\,\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_C]} e^{-rt}\,d\xi_t\Big],\qquad C_t = z + \hat\mu t + \sigma B_t - \xi_t,\ \gamma_C=\inf\{t\ge 0: C_t\le 0\}.
\]

6) Payoffs: For a control pair \((L,D)\), Player 1 and 2 payoffs are
\[
J^1_{x,y}(L,D)=\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_X\wedge\gamma_Y]} e^{-rt}\,dL_t + \mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_Y<\gamma_X\}}e^{-r\gamma_Y}\,\hat v(X_{\gamma_Y})\Big],
\]
\[
J^2_{x,y}(D,L)=\mathbb E\Big[\int_{[0,\gamma_X\wedge\gamma_Y]} e^{-rt}\,dD_t + \mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_X<\gamma_Y\}}e^{-r\gamma_X}\,\hat v(Y_{\gamma_X})\Big].
\]

7) Strategies: A (pure) feedback strategy for a player is a non-anticipative mapping that assigns a dividend path as a functional of the observed Brownian path and the opponent’s past dividend path. The paper also allows randomised strategies (Aumann-style) by adding an independent randomisation variable \(u\in[0,1]\). A strategy profile must be control-inducing (i.e., the induced fixed point defining the pair of controls exists and is unique on every finite horizon).

8) Nash equilibrium: A pair of (possibly randomised) strategies is a Nash equilibrium if neither player can improve their payoff by unilateral deviation within the admissible class of randomised strategies.

The paper constructs equilibria where (in the asymmetric initial-endowment case \(y>x\)) the poorer firm uses a pure control and the richer firm uses a pure strategy. It explicitly leaves open the existence of equilibria with the roles reversed (richer firm using a control; poorer firm using a strategy).

Assume asymmetric initial endowments with \(y>x\ge 0\). Determine whether there exists a Nash equilibrium (in the sense of admissible randomised strategies described above) for which Player 1 (the poorer firm with initial reserve \(x\)) uses a strategy (pure or randomised) and Player 2 (the richer firm with initial reserve \(y\)) uses a control (pure or randomised), i.e., an equilibrium whose action profile is of the form
1) Player 1: \(\Xi_1\) is an admissible strategy mapping that may depend on the opponent’s dividend path (and possibly on a randomisation variable), and
2) Player 2: \(\Xi_2\) is an admissible control viewed as a strategy that does not depend on the opponent’s dividend path,
with \((\Xi_1,\Xi_2)\) being control-inducing and satisfying the Nash inequalities against all unilateral deviations in the full class of admissible randomised strategies.

If such equilibria exist, characterize conditions/structure ensuring existence (e.g., for all parameter choices and initial states as in the model).

The question as to whether an equilibrium exists in which Player 1 uses a strategy and Player 2 uses a control (both either pure or randomised) is open when \(y > x\), especially if we seek an equilibrium valid for all parameter choices and initial states.

literature_review.synthesis:
In De Angelis–Gensbittel–Villeneuve (2025), the asymmetric-endowment equilibrium for 

a) poorer firm using a pure control (the classical reflection-at-\(a_0\) dividend policy \(\xi^0\)) and 

b) richer firm using a pure feedback strategy \(\Psi^*\) that depends on the opponent’s dividend path via the induced state \(X^*\),

is constructed by solving a coupled free-boundary/variational system in \((x,z)\)-coordinates with \(z=y-x\). The paper explicitly leaves open the reversed-role configuration: an equilibrium in which the richer firm commits to a control (i.e., a strategy independent of the opponent’s dividend path) while the poorer firm uses a (possibly randomized) strategy reacting to the richer firm’s dividends.

The only forward-citing work provided, “Splitting infinity: a de Finetti game with state-dependent profit rates and singular control for diffusions,” develops verification and construction methods for Markovian Nash equilibria in a different class of de Finetti-type games where both players exert singular control on a single common diffusion. While its techniques (verification for singular-control equilibria, handling reflection/local-time type controls) are conceptually adjacent, it does not engage with the two-dimensional asymmetric dividend-competition structure, the duopoly-to-monopoly switching payoff \(\hat v\), or the strategy/control asymmetry central to the open problem.

Given the current forward-citation evidence, there is no published resolution of the role-reversal equilibrium question. Progress likely requires either (i) a new fixed-point/verification framework for equilibria mixing open-loop singular controls with feedback strategies in two-dimensional state spaces with absorption and regime-switching continuation values, or (ii) a counterexample showing nonexistence under the paper’s admissibility/control-inducing requirements. At present, the problem should be regarded as open.

sources.title: Splitting infinity: a de Finetti game with state-dependent profit rates and singular control for diffusions
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves existence and verification of symmetric global Markovian Nash equilibria for a two-player de Finetti-type extraction game where both players apply singular control to a common one-dimensional diffusion absorbed at 0. In particular, under Assumptions 1–2 it constructs threshold-type equilibria where each player uses the same state-dependent extraction rate \(\lambda_b^*(x)\) (and possibly skew-point local-time control at finitely many discontinuities of a profit rate \(g\)), yielding an equilibrium value \(V_b\) given by (11) for \(g\equiv 1\) and by (19) for general \(g\). It also exhibits a bang-bang equilibrium with reflection at \(\ell\) and initial jumps to \(\ell\) in a special profit-rate case (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns an asymmetric two-firm dividend competition model with separate reserve processes \((X_t,Y_t)\) driven by a common Brownian motion, with duopoly-to-monopoly switching at default, and an equilibrium concept based on (possibly randomized) feedback strategies where one player may use a strategy depending on the opponent’s past dividends while the other uses an open-loop control. The citing paper studies a different game: both players control a single common state process \(X_t\) (resource level) via Markov (state-feedback) singular controls (rates, jumps, local-time/skew points). It does not address asymmetric initial endowments, separate states, default-triggered regime switching, or the mixed control/strategy role reversal in the sense of De Angelis–Gensbittel–Villeneuve. Thus it neither proves nor disproves existence of an equilibrium where the richer firm uses a control and the poorer firm uses a strategy in the dividend-competition model. At most, it provides techniques (verification for singular-control Nash equilibria; handling simultaneous jumps/local time; Markov perfect equilibrium construction) that could be conceptually relevant.

title: Polynomial-time approximation of justified envy-free Pareto-optimal lotteries in two-sided markets
background_latex:
Consider a bipartite two-sided cardinal-utility matching market with two sets of agents \(A\) and \(B\), with \(|A|=|B|=n\). Each \(i\in A\) has nonnegative rational utilities \(u_{ij}\) for being matched to \(j\in B\), and each \(j\in B\) has nonnegative rational utilities \(w_{ji}\) for being matched to \(i\in A\).

A (fractional) allocation is a matrix \(x=(x_{ij})_{i\in A, j\in B}\) with \(x_{ij}\ge 0\) satisfying the fractional perfect matching constraints
\[
\sum_{j\in B} x_{ij}=1 \ \forall i\in A, \qquad \sum_{i\in A} x_{ij}=1 \ \forall j\in B.
\]
This corresponds to a lottery over integral perfect matchings via Birkhoff--von Neumann decomposition, and agents evaluate allocations by expected utility.

Utilities induced by \(x\) are
\[
U_i(x)=\sum_{j\in B} u_{ij}x_{ij}\quad (i\in A), \qquad W_j(x)=\sum_{i\in A} w_{ji}x_{ij}\quad (j\in B).
\]

Justified envy-freeness (JEF) is a two-sided fairness notion. For \(i,i'\in A\), agent \(i\) has justified envy toward \(i'\) under allocation \(x\) if
\[
U_i(x) < \sum_{j\in B: \ w_{ji}\ge w_{ji'}} u_{ij} x_{i'j}.
\]
(The definition is symmetric for pairs \(j,j'\in B\).) An allocation \(x\) is JEF if it has no justified envy on either side.

Pareto-optimality (PO) in two-sided markets means there is no other feasible allocation \(y\) such that \(U_i(y)\ge U_i(x)\) for all \(i\in A\), \(W_j(y)\ge W_j(x)\) for all \(j\in B\), and at least one of these inequalities is strict.

For \(\alpha\ge 1\), an \(\alpha\)-approximately JEF allocation informally means justified envy is bounded within a multiplicative factor \(\alpha\) (the paper asks for an \(\alpha\)-approximation analogue of JEF, without fixing a particular formalization beyond the constant-factor approximation goal).
problem_definition_latex:
Design a polynomial-time algorithm that, given any bipartite two-sided cardinal-utility matching market \((A,B,u,w)\), outputs a feasible lottery/allocation \(x\) that is Pareto-optimal and \(\alpha\)-approximately justified envy-free for some constant \(\alpha\ge 1\) (independent of \(n\)).

Equivalently: determine whether there exists a constant \(\alpha\) for which such an allocation can always be computed in time polynomial in \(n\) and the input encoding size, and if so, give such an algorithm (including the achieved constant \(\alpha\)).

counterexample_suitability_rationale: If one fixes a concrete definition of \(\alpha\)-approximate JEF, small instances can be searched computationally (e.g., via LPs over the Birkhoff polytope) to test whether a candidate algorithm achieves a target \(\alpha\). literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Tr{"o}bst--Vazirani, 2025) motivates the two-sided question by showing that exact EF+PO lotteries can fail to exist even for very small extensions beyond symmetric \(\{0,1\}\) utilities, and proposes justified envy-freeness (JEF) as a stability-like replacement. It proves unconditional existence of JEF allocations that are weakly Pareto-optimal (no allocation strictly improves everyone), via a limiting argument based on Manjunath’s double-indexed-price (DIP) equilibrium and a subsequent polyhedral extreme-point argument to obtain rationality. However, weak PO is strictly weaker than the strong Pareto-optimality required in the open problem, and the paper leaves open whether one can always compute (or even guarantee existence of) a strongly PO allocation that is constant-factor approximately JEF.

Subsequent work on two-sided cardinal matching has so far not closed this gap. The most directly relevant follow-up ("Cardinal-Utility Matching Markets and Online Matching") reinforces the landscape: it highlights the existence of JEF+weak-PO allocations and provides a strong obstruction for a natural polynomial-time candidate, Nash bargaining, by exhibiting instances with \(\Theta(n)\)-factor justified envy. On the algorithmic side, "Time-efficient algorithms for Nash-bargaining-based matching market models" supplies fast polynomial-time methods for computing approximate Nash-bargaining outcomes on the Birkhoff polytope; these outcomes are Pareto-optimal but can be far from JEF, so the algorithms do not yield constant-\(\alpha\) approximate JEF.

More broadly, recent convex-optimization-based fairness relaxations (e.g., proportional fairness / Nash welfare and harm-ratio criteria) show that one can compute Pareto-optimal outcomes with certain constant-factor envy-type guarantees in related divisible-goods models, but the guarantees either do not match the two-sided JEF definition (which depends on the \(w\)-threshold sets \(\{j: w_{ji}\ge w_{ji'}\}\)) or degrade with \(n\). Overall, the existence of JEF+weak-PO suggests that JEF is structurally compatible with feasibility, but obtaining strong PO together with any constant-factor approximation to JEF in polynomial time remains open; promising directions include identifying a convex program whose KKT/dual structure directly enforces approximate JEF constraints, or proving impossibility (e.g., that any strongly PO allocation must incur \(\Omega(n)\) justified envy in the worst case).

sources.title: Cardinal-Utility Matching Markets and Online Matching
sources.theorem_or_result: For two-sided cardinal-utility bipartite matching markets, the paper proves existence (and rationality) of allocations that are justified envy-free (JEF) and weakly Pareto-optimal: there always exists a rational fractional perfect matching \(x\) with no justified envy (Definition 39) and such that there is no feasible allocation \(y\) that strictly improves every agent’s expected utility (weak PO). It also shows Nash-bargaining solutions can have \(\Theta(n)\)-factor justified envy (Theorem 46), and poses as an open question whether one can compute constant-\(\alpha\) approximately JEF + (strong) PO in polynomial time.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm that always outputs an allocation that is (strong) Pareto-optimal and constant-factor approximately JEF in two-sided markets. This paper does not give such an algorithm nor establish existence of JEF+PO, but it makes progress by: (i) introducing the specific JEF notion used in the open problem and proving unconditional existence of JEF + weak PO allocations (Theorem 40), including a rational extreme-point argument; (ii) giving negative evidence for a natural candidate mechanism (Nash bargaining), showing it can violate JEF by a factor \(\Theta(n)\) (Theorem 46), so it cannot yield constant-\(\alpha\) approximate JEF in general; and (iii) explicitly listing the constant-\(\alpha\) approx-JEF+PO computability question as open in its conclusion. Thus it advances the structural landscape (existence/obstructions) but does not resolve the algorithmic constant-factor approximation question.

sources.title: Time-efficient algorithms for Nash-bargaining-based matching market models
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives polynomial-time, provably fast first-order algorithms (MWU and conditional gradient/Frank–Wolfe) to compute an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate Nash-bargaining solution for several cardinal-utility matching-market convex programs, including the two-sided linear Arrow–Debreu model
\[
\max_x \sum_{i\in A}\log(U_i(x)-c_i)+\sum_{j\in B}\log(W_j(x)-d_j)\quad\text{s.t. }x\text{ is a fractional perfect matching}
\]
(Program (7)), and its SPLC generalization (Program (8)/(35)). In particular, for one-sided linear Arrow–Debreu (Program (5)) they prove MWU computes an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate Nash bargaining solution in \(O(n\log n/\varepsilon^2)\) iterations with \(O(n^2)\) work per iteration (Theorem 7), and for conditional gradient they obtain \(O(\mathrm{poly}(n,\kappa,1/\delta)/\varepsilon)\) iteration bounds (e.g., Theorem 25 for two-sided SPLC with endowments).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a Pareto-optimal (PO) lottery that is constant-factor \(\alpha\)-approximately justified envy-free (JEF) in general two-sided cardinal-utility matching markets.

This paper does not study JEF as defined in the open problem, nor does it provide a constant-factor approximation guarantee for JEF. Instead it focuses on computing Nash-bargaining (NB) allocations efficiently for one- and two-sided matching markets. NB solutions are Pareto-optimal by construction, and the paper proves certain approximate fairness properties (approximate equal-share/proportionality) for these NB models (e.g., Lemma 4 and related lemmas), but these are different from two-sided JEF.

Thus the paper contributes relevant algorithmic machinery (fast polynomial-time computation of PO convex-program solutions on the matching polytope) and an alternative approximate-fairness notion, but it does not resolve whether there exists a constant \(\alpha\) for PO + \(\alpha\)-approximate JEF, nor does it give such an algorithm.

sources.title: Harm ratio: A novel and versatile fairness criterion
sources.theorem_or_result: Defines new fairness notions for the public outcomes model: individual harm ratio (IHR) and group harm ratio (GHR). Shows that proportional fairness (PF) implies 1-GHR, hence PO and 1-IHR (Proposition 2). Under compactness and upper convexity of the feasible utility set \(U\), every maximum Nash welfare (MNW) outcome is PF (Theorem 2), hence 1-GHR and PO. Computationally, when \(U\) is convex and given by polynomially many linear constraints, a \((1+\varepsilon)\)-PF outcome can be computed in time polynomial in input size and \(1/\varepsilon\), and \((1+\varepsilon)\)-PF implies \((1+n\varepsilon)\)-GHR (Proposition 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a Pareto-optimal lottery in a two-sided matching market that is constant-factor approximately justified envy-free (JEF). This paper does not study two-sided matching or JEF; instead it introduces IHR/GHR as alternative fairness criteria and relates them to PF/MNW. Its computational result yields approximate PF (hence approximate GHR) via convex programming when the feasible utility region is convex/linearly described. In the two-sided fractional matching market, the feasible set is a Birkhoff polytope (convex, linear constraints), so their framework could in principle compute \((1+\varepsilon)\)-PF and thus \((1+n\varepsilon)\)-GHR, which is not a constant-factor guarantee independent of \(n\), and it is for GHR/IHR rather than JEF. Therefore it does not resolve the stated open problem, but provides potentially relevant convex-optimization machinery and an alternative fairness relaxation that implies PO.

sources.title: Approximating competitive equilibrium by Nash welfare
sources.theorem_or_result: In Fisher markets with divisible goods and concave utilities, any Nash-welfare-maximizing allocation (y_i) together with its dual (Gale) prices (q) forms a 2-demand-approximate competitive equilibrium; in the equal-budget case this implies 2-approximate envy-freeness: u_i(y_i)\ge \tfrac12\max_{\langle q,x\rangle\le b_i}u_i(x) and hence u_i(y_i)\ge \tfrac12 u_i(y_k) for all agents i,k (Theorem 1.2). For \(\Sigma\)-Gale-substitutes utilities, the Nash-welfare-maximizing allocation guarantees each agent at least half of their utility in any (thrifty) competitive equilibrium: u_i(y_i)\ge \tfrac12 u_i(x_i) (Theorems 1.3 and 1.6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm in two-sided bipartite matching markets that outputs a Pareto-optimal lottery that is constant-factor approximately justified-envy-free (JEF). This paper is in a different model (Fisher markets with divisible goods) and studies approximate competitive equilibrium / approximate envy-freeness via Nash welfare maximization. It does not address two-sided matching constraints, nor the specific two-sided JEF notion based on mutual acceptability thresholds \(w_{ji}\ge w_{ji'}\). However, it provides a relevant technique: maximizing (weighted) Nash welfare via the EisenbergGale convex program yields Pareto optimality and a constant-factor (2) approximate envy-freeness guarantee, and the paper explicitly notes that a matching-utilities result of TrbstVazirani (2024) giving PO + 2-envy-free can be viewed as a special case. Thus it offers conceptual/algorithmic tools (NSW convex programming, dual-price analysis) that might be adapted, but it does not solve the stated JEF+PO approximation problem in two-sided matching markets.

sources.title: Tight Efficiency Bounds for the Probabilistic Serial Mechanism under Cardinal Preferences
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves tight efficiency guarantees for the Probabilistic Serial (PS) mechanism in the one-sided random assignment problem (agents vs. items). In particular, PS achieves an \,\(H_n\)-approximation to maximum Nash welfare and hence is \,\(H_n\)-approximately Pareto efficient under cardinal utilities, where \,\(H_n=\sum_{k=1}^n 1/k\in[\ln n,\ln n+1]\) (Theorem 2.6 / Theorem 1.1). It also gives a polynomial-time algorithm that computes an envy-free allocation that is \,\((e^{1/e}-\varepsilon)\)-approximately Pareto efficient (equivalently \,\((1/e)^{1/e}\)-approximate Nash welfare) for random assignment and a submodular generalization (Theorem 3.4 / Theorem 1.3).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns two-sided bipartite matching markets with utilities on both sides and asks for a polynomial-time algorithm outputting an allocation that is Pareto-optimal (exact PO) and constant-factor approximately justified envy-free (two-sided JEF). This paper studies a different model: one-sided random assignment (agents vs. items) with standard envy-freeness among agents, not two-sided JEF, and it relaxes efficiency to approximate Pareto efficiency (or approximating Nash welfare) rather than exact Pareto-optimality. Thus it does not solve the stated two-sided JEF+PO approximation problem. However, it is methodologically related: it uses Nash-welfare/market-equilibrium ideas and convex programming to obtain envy-free allocations with constant-factor approximate efficiency, which could be relevant as tools or inspiration for the two-sided setting.

title: Improve Wasserstein convergence rate for vector martingale central limit theorem
background_latex:
Let \(\{m_k\}_{k\ge 1}\) be a \(d\)-dimensional martingale difference sequence with respect to a filtration \(\{\mathcal F_k\}_{k\ge 0}\), meaning \(m_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, \(\mathbb E\|m_k\|<\infty\), and \(\mathbb E[m_k\mid \mathcal F_{k-1}]=0\) for all \(k\ge 1\). Define partial sums \(S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n m_k\) and the normalized sum \(W_n=S_n/\sqrt n\).

Assume there exists \(\beta\in(0,1)\) such that \(\mathbb E\|m_k\|^{2+\beta}<\infty\) for all \(k\), and the conditional covariance matrices \(\Sigma_k:=\mathbb E[m_k m_k^\top\mid \mathcal F_{k-1}]\) exist. Let \(\Sigma_\infty\succ 0\) be a positive definite matrix intended to represent the limiting (asymptotic) covariance of \(W_n\) in a martingale central limit theorem.

Let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). For random vectors \(X,Y\in\mathbb R^d\), the \(1\)-Wasserstein distance is
\[
 d_W(X,Y)=\sup_{h\in\mathrm{Lip}_1} \mathbb E[h(X)-h(Y)],
\]
where \(\mathrm{Lip}_1\) is the set of real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R^d\) with Lipschitz constant at most 1 w.r.t. the Euclidean norm.

A non-asymptotic martingale CLT bound in Wasserstein distance can have the form
\[
 d_W\bigl(W_n,\, \Sigma_\infty^{1/2} Z\bigr) \le \text{(explicit bound depending on moments, }\Sigma_k,\Sigma_\infty\text{)}.
\]
In the paper, a general bound is proved that (in typical applications) yields the rate \(O(\log n/\sqrt n)\) in \(d_W\).
problem_definition_latex:
Find additional, verifiable conditions on the martingale difference sequence \(\{m_k\}\) (beyond the finite-\((2+\beta)\) moment and conditional covariance assumptions stated above) under which the Wasserstein error
\[
 d_W\bigl(W_n,\, \Sigma_\infty^{1/2} Z\bigr)
\]
admits an improved rate of convergence \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) (i.e., with the \(\log n\) factor removed) as \(n\to\infty\), while keeping a vector-valued martingale setting and a Gaussian limit with covariance \(\Sigma_\infty\).

literature_review.synthesis:
Srikant’s 2026 paper proves a non-asymptotic vector martingale CLT in 1-Wasserstein distance via a Lindeberg decomposition combined with multivariate Stein regularity estimates (Gallou\"et–Mijoule–Swan; Fang–Shao–Xu). The resulting bound (Theorem 1) has a typical \(O((\log n)/\sqrt n)\) rate when one pushes the Hölder parameter \(\beta\uparrow 1\) to approach the i.i.d.-optimal \(n^{-1/2}\) scaling; the \(\log n\) arises from the blow-up of Stein-solution Hölder constants like \((1-\beta)^{-1}\). In the Markov-chain application, Poisson’s equation yields a martingale difference sequence with bounded moments and geometrically decaying covariance mismatch \(\|\mathbb E\Sigma_k-\Sigma_\infty\|\), but the same Stein-regularity mechanism still produces \(O((\log n)/\sqrt n)\) in Wasserstein-1.

Among forward citations, the most direct evidence that the \(\log n\) factor is not intrinsic comes from “Wasserstein-p Central Limit Theorem Rates: From Local Dependence to Markov Chains”, which attains the optimal \(O(n^{-1/2})\) Wasserstein-1 rate for additive functionals of geometrically ergodic Markov chains under drift/minorization and \((2+\delta)\)-moment domination (with \(\delta>1\)), and in the homogeneous case transfers this to \(\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\infty)\) when the covariance stabilizes at \(O(1/n)\). This suggests that log-free \(n^{-1/2}\) rates are achievable in dependent settings when one avoids the particular Stein-equation regularity step that forces \(\beta\uparrow 1\), for example via local-dependence/regeneration couplings or alternative Stein couplings tailored to Markov chains.

However, none of the citing works provides a general theorem for arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional martingale differences \(m_k\) in terms of predictable covariances \(\Sigma_k=\mathbb E[m_km_k^\top\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\) that removes the \(\log n\) while keeping only verifiable structural assumptions. Several papers in stochastic approximation and RL (two-time-scale SA, Q-learning, nonlinear SA) explicitly rely on martingale Wasserstein CLTs with \(\log n\) losses and identify improved martingale Wasserstein bounds as a key missing ingredient. Overall, the problem remains open at the level of a general vector martingale CLT, though optimal \(O(n^{-1/2})\) rates are known in important subclasses (notably geometrically ergodic Markov-chain additive functionals) under stronger dependence/moment and covariance-stabilization conditions.

sources.title: Wasserstein-p Central Limit Theorem Rates: From Local Dependence to Markov Chains
sources.theorem_or_result:
For additive functionals of a geometrically ergodic Markov chain 
\[S_n=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h_i(x_i),\qquad \Sigma_n:=\tfrac1n\mathrm{Var}(S_n),\]
under a drift/minorization (geometric ergodicity) condition and a moment domination \(\|h_i\|_{2+\delta}\le V\) for some \(\delta>1\), the paper proves an optimal Wasserstein-1 CLT rate
\[W_1\bigl(\mathcal L(S_n/\sqrt n),\,\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_n)\bigr)=O(n^{-1/2}).\]
In the homogeneous case \(h_i\equiv h\), with \(\Sigma_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Sigma_n\) and \(\|\Sigma_n-\Sigma_\infty\|=O(1/n)\), this yields
\[W_1\bigl(\mathcal L(S_n/\sqrt n),\,\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\infty)\bigr)=O(n^{-1/2}).\]
(Their Theorem 3 plus a Gaussian covariance-mismatch bound.)

The open problem asks for additional verifiable conditions on a vector-valued martingale difference array \(m_k\) ensuring an improved Wasserstein-1 martingale CLT rate \(O(n^{-1/2})\) (removing a \(\log n\) factor) for \(W_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n m_k\) versus \(\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\infty)\).

This paper does not treat general martingale difference sequences directly, nor does it give a general martingale CLT bound in terms of conditional covariances \(\Sigma_k=\mathbb E[m_km_k^\top\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\). Instead it proves an \(O(n^{-1/2})\) \(W_1\) CLT rate for dependent partial sums arising from geometrically ergodic Markov chains (and also for locally dependent sequences), by bypassing Stein-equation regularity estimates that cause \(\log n\) losses.

Nevertheless, it provides concrete *additional conditions* (geometric ergodicity + a Lyapunov domination \(\|h_i\|_{2+\delta}\le V\) with \(\delta>1\), plus nondegenerate covariance) under which one gets the desired \(O(n^{-1/2})\) Wasserstein-1 rate for a broad dependent-data class. Via standard martingale decompositions of additive functionals, their techniques are conceptually relevant to martingale CLTs, but they do not resolve the open problem in the full generality of arbitrary vector martingale differences with only moment and conditional covariance assumptions.

sources.title: Nonasymptotic clt and error bounds for two-time-scale stochastic approximation
sources.theorem_or_result:
For linear two-time-scale stochastic approximation with Polyak–Ruppert averaging driven by martingale-difference noise \,\(N_t=(W_t,V_t)\) with bounded \((2+\beta)\)-moments and constant conditional covariance \(\mathbb E[N_tN_t^\top\mid H_{t-1}]=\Gamma\), and step sizes \(\alpha_t=\alpha_1 t^{-a},\ \gamma_t=\gamma_1 t^{-b}\) with \(1/2<a<b<1\), the paper proves a non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 CLT for the scaled averaged errors. In particular (Theorem 1), for \((a,b)\) in a specified region \(\Theta\),
\[
 d_1\bigl(\sqrt n\,G(\bar x_n-x^*),\ \pi_{\bar x}\bigr),\ d_1\bigl(\sqrt n\,\Delta(\bar y_n-y^*),\ \pi_{\bar y}\bigr)
 = O\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt n}\bigl(n^{a-1/2}/(a-1/2)+1/(b-a)+n^{b/2}+n^{2a-b-1/2}/(2a-b-1/2)\bigr)\Bigr),
\]
where \(\pi_{\bar x},\pi_{\bar y}\) are centered Gaussians with covariances characterized by limits of \(n^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\sum_{t\le n}(W_t-A_{fs}A_{ss}^{-1}V_t))\) and \(n^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\sum_{t\le n}(V_t-A_{sf}A_{ff}^{-1}W_t))\). Corollary 1 further yields \(\mathbb E\|\bar x_n-x^*\|,\mathbb E\|\bar y_n-y^*\| = (1/\sqrt n)\,\mathbb E\|Z\| + o(n^{-1/2})\) for the corresponding Gaussian \(Z\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for verifiable conditions on a vector martingale difference array \(m_k\) under which the Wasserstein-1 CLT error for \(W_n=S_n/\sqrt n\) improves from \(O((\log n)/\sqrt n)\) to \(O(1/\sqrt n)\). This citing paper is directly about non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 CLTs for martingale-driven recursions and explicitly uses a martingale Wasserstein-1 CLT from prior work ([19] in their bibliography). However, it does not provide a general martingale CLT with \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) for \(S_n/\sqrt n\); instead it derives a problem-specific bound for Polyak–Ruppert averaged two-time-scale SA, where the Wasserstein-1 distance to a Gaussian limit decays at rates that are generally slower than \(1/\sqrt n\) (e.g. optimized to about \(O(n^{-1/4})\) for their step-size choices). The paper does, nonetheless, highlight additional structural assumptions beyond mere \((2+\beta)\)-moments—most notably: (i) the noise is a martingale difference sequence independent of the iterates, (ii) the conditional covariance is constant \(\Gamma\) (no time variation), and (iii) linear dynamics allow explicit control of remainder terms. These are the kinds of extra conditions that, in principle, can remove logarithmic factors in martingale CLT bounds, but the paper does not establish the desired \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) Wasserstein rate for the normalized martingale sum itself.

sources.title: Finite-Sample Wasserstein Error Bounds and Concentration Inequalities for Nonlinear Stochastic Approximation
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops finite-sample Wasserstein bounds for stochastic approximation by assuming a quantitative martingale/Markov-noise CLT for the driving noise. In particular, for a martingale difference sequence \(\{M_k\}\) satisfying a non-asymptotic \(W_1\)-CLT with third moments (Lemma 2, based on [Srikant 2025]), it obtains for the normalized last iterate \(y_n=\gamma_n^{-1/2}(x_n-x^*)\) the rate
- \(W_1(y_n,U_\infty)=O\bigl(\gamma_n^{1/6}(\log \gamma_n)^{1/3}+E_n^a/\gamma_n\bigr)\) (Theorem 1(1)),
and for Polyak–Ruppert averaging \(\bar y_n=\sqrt n(\bar x_n-x^*)\) a bound reducing to \(W_p(\bar y_n,\bar\Sigma^{1/2}Z)=O(n^{-1/6})\) when \(\gamma_n\asymp n^{-2/3}\) and the martingale sum \(n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n M_k\) satisfies a \(W_p\)-CLT (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for additional conditions on a vector-valued martingale difference array \(m_k\) under which the Wasserstein-1 martingale CLT error improves from the typical \(O(\log n/\sqrt n)\) to \(O(1/\sqrt n)\). This paper does not remove the \(\log\) factor; instead it explicitly uses an existing \(W_1\) martingale CLT bound that contains \(d\log n/\sqrt n\) (Lemma 2) and notes that sharper CLTs (e.g., for independent noise or under Poincaré/spectral gap assumptions) could be plugged in. Section 5.1 highlights as an open direction the lack of quantitative martingale CLTs in \(W_p\) for \(p\ge2\), reinforcing that improved martingale Wasserstein rates are not obtained here. Thus, it provides a framework that would immediately yield \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) for SA iterates if one had an \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) martingale \(W_1\)-CLT for \(\sum m_k\), but it does not itself establish new verifiable martingale conditions achieving that improvement.

sources.title: Quantifying Normality: Convergence Rate to Gaussian Limit for Stochastic Approximation and Unadjusted OU Algorithm
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves non-asymptotic Wasserstein-1 bounds for rescaled stochastic approximation (SA) iterates and for a related discrete Ornstein–Uhlenbeck recursion (DOUG). In particular, for DOUG
\[z_{k+1}=(I+\alpha_k J_k^{(\alpha,\xi)})z_k+\sqrt{\alpha_k}\,b(w_k),\]
with i.i.d. mean-zero noise having finite third moment, Theorem 4.2 gives
- for \(\alpha_k=\alpha/(k+K)^\xi\), \(\xi\in(0,1)\): \(d_W(z_k,\Sigma_1^{1/2}Z)\le O\bigl(\tfrac{\log(k+K)}{(k+K)^{\xi/2}}\bigr)+O((k+K)^{-\xi})+\text{transient}\);
- for \(\xi=1\): \(d_W(z_k,\Sigma_2^{1/2}Z)\le O\bigl(\tfrac{\log(k+K)}{\sqrt{k+K}}\bigr)+O((k+K)^{-1})+\text{transient}\).
For SA, Theorem 4.1 yields analogous bounds for \(y_k=(x_k-x^*)/\sqrt{\alpha_k}\), with an additional bias term \(O((k+K)^{-\xi\delta/2})\) from nonlinear drift; when \(\delta=1\) the DOUG term \(O(\log(k)/\sqrt{k})\) is rate-limiting.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for verifiable conditions on a vector martingale difference array \(m_k\) under which the Wasserstein-1 CLT error for \(W_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{k\le n} m_k\) improves from \(O(\log n/\sqrt n)\) to \(O(1/\sqrt n)\). This paper studies a different but closely related setting: weighted sums of i.i.d. noise (DOUG) and SA iterates, and it explicitly identifies the \(\log\) factor as coming from their Stein-method bound for weighted sums with only a finite third moment assumption. They do not remove the \(\log\) factor; in fact they state improving DOUG’s rate (and hence removing the \(\log\)) as an open question. However, the analysis clarifies which additional structure might help: (i) Gaussian noise yields \(O(\alpha_k)\) rates in related Langevin/ULA work; (ii) symmetric negative definite drift allows sharper norm control; (iii) stronger smoothness/regularity of Stein solutions or stronger moment/tail assumptions could potentially eliminate the \(\log\). Thus the paper provides partial progress/tools but not the desired \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) martingale CLT rate.

sources.title: Central Limit Theorems for Asynchronous Averaged Q-Learning
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a non-asymptotic 1-Wasserstein CLT for Polyak–Ruppert averaged asynchronous Q-learning iterates. In particular, for stepsizes \(\alpha_k=\alpha(k+b)^{-\beta}\) with \(\beta\in(1/2,1)\), under Assumptions 1–2 it establishes
\[
W_1\Bigl(K^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^K \Delta_k,\; \widetilde N\Bigr) \le \frac{\sqrt{|S||A|}}{\rho(1-\gamma)^2\sqrt K}\,\widetilde O\Bigl((\rho(1-\gamma))^{\frac{\beta-2}{1-\beta}} + K^{\beta/2}\rho^{-1}(1-\gamma)^{-1} + K^{1-\beta} + K^{(1-\beta)/2}\rho^{-1-\beta}(1-\gamma)^{-\beta}\Bigr),
\]
where \(\Delta_k=Q_k-Q^*\), \(\widetilde N=(A^{-1}\Sigma A^{-\top})^{1/2}N(0,I)\), \(A=D-\gamma D P_{\pi^*}\), and \(\Sigma\) is defined via the Poisson equation for the underlying finite-state Markov chain. For \(\beta=2/3\) this simplifies to \(W_1( K^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^K\Delta_k,\widetilde N)\le \widetilde O(\sqrt{|S||A|}\,K^{-1/6}\rho^{-2}(1-\gamma)^{-3})\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for additional conditions under which a vector martingale CLT in \(W_1\) improves from a typical \(O(\log n/\sqrt n)\) rate to \(O(1/\sqrt n)\). This paper does not remove a \(\log n\) factor in a general martingale CLT; instead it applies an existing non-asymptotic martingale CLT bound (Srikant 2024) to a specific martingale difference sequence obtained from Markovian noise via a Poisson-equation decomposition. The resulting overall \(W_1\) rate for the averaged Q-learning error is slower than \(1/\sqrt K\) (e.g. \(K^{-1/6}\) in the displayed corollary), and some intermediate bounds still involve harmonic sums (\(\sum 1/i\)) that are controlled by \(\widetilde O(\log K)\). Nevertheless, the paper is relevant because it identifies a concrete martingale difference sequence arising from Markovian noise, verifies the moment/covariance conditions needed for the martingale CLT, and shows how Poisson-equation/mixing assumptions yield explicit non-asymptotic \(W_1\) bounds—suggesting that stronger mixing/uniformity conditions might be leveraged to sharpen the summation terms that produce logarithms in general bounds.

sources.title: Gaussian Approximation for Asynchronous Q-learning
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a high-dimensional Gaussian approximation for sums of -dimensional martingale differences over hyper-rectangles. In particular, under (i) finite third moments \(\mathbb E\|X_k\|_\infty^3<\infty\) and (ii) (in Theorem 1) almost surely deterministic predictable quadratic variation \(\sum_{k=1}^n V_k=\Sigma_n\) with \(V_k=\mathbb E[X_kX_k^\top\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\), it bounds the Kolmogorov distance
- \(d_K(S_n,\,\mathcal N(0,\Sigma))\)
by a term of order \(\log^{5/4}(d)\,\sigma(\Sigma_n)^{-1/2}\bigl(\sigma(\Sigma)+\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb E[\|X_k\|_\infty^3/\lambda_{\min}(P_k+\Sigma)]\bigr)^{1/2}\), where \(P_k=\sum_{i=k}^n V_i\).
It also extends to random predictable variation (Theorem 6) assuming a concentration inequality for \(\sum_{k=1}^n \mathbb E[X_kX_k^\top\mid\mathcal F_{k-1}]\) around \(\Sigma_n\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions yielding an \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) Wasserstein rate for vector martingale CLTs (removing a \(\log n\) factor). This paper does not provide Wasserstein \(d_W\) bounds; instead it gives high-dimensional Kolmogorov bounds over hyper-rectangles for martingale sums, with rates typically \(n^{-1/4}\) (plus polylog factors) and with a key term involving \(\sum_k \lambda_{\min}(P_k+\Sigma)^{-1}\) that is controlled only up to \(n\log n\), producing logarithmic factors. Thus it does not resolve the Wasserstein \(O(1/\sqrt n)\) question, but it develops Stein+Lindeberg techniques and identifies that improving rates would require stronger lower bounds on \(\lambda_{\min}(P_k)\) (or related non-degeneracy/uniform variance growth), which is conceptually related to removing log factors in martingale CLTs.

title: Achieve quota, population monotonicity, and ex-ante proportionality without varying house size
background_latex:
An apportionment instance is a pair \((p,H)\) with \(p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n\) (state populations) and \(H\in\mathbb{N}\) (house size). Let \(P=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\) and define the quota of state \(i\) as \(q_i=\frac{p_i}{P}H\).

An (integer) apportionment vector is \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{N}_0^n\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=H\). A (possibly randomized) apportionment method outputs such a vector for each instance.

Quota compliance means that for every instance and every state \(i\), the realized allocation satisfies \(x_i\in\{\lfloor q_i\rfloor,\lceil q_i\rceil\}\).

Population monotonicity is the standard strong monotonicity requirement: when populations change so that the ratio \(p_i/p_j\) weakly increases in favor of state \(i\) (relative to state \(j\)), then it must not happen that \(i\) loses a seat while \(j\) gains a seat (formally, the method must avoid such pairwise monotonicity violations across any two instances \((p,H)\) and \((p',H')\)).

A randomized method is ex-ante proportional if for every instance and every state \(i\), the expectation equals quota: \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]=q_i\), where \(X\) is the random apportionment vector.

The paper constructs randomized methods that satisfy quota compliance, population monotonicity, and ex-ante proportionality by allowing the realized total number of seats \(\sum_i X_i\) to deviate from \(H\) (variable house size), while still meeting \(H\) in expectation.
problem_definition_latex:
Design (or characterize the existence of) a randomized apportionment method that, for every instance \((p,H)\), outputs an integer apportionment vector \(X\in\mathbb{N}_0^n\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i=H\) almost surely, and simultaneously satisfies:

1) Quota compliance: for all \(i\in[n]\), \(X_i\in\{\lfloor q_i\rfloor,\lceil q_i\rceil\}\) almost surely.

2) Population monotonicity (in the strong pairwise-ratio sense described above).

3) Ex-ante proportionality: for all \(i\in[n]\), \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]=q_i\).

Equivalently, determine whether such a method exists without allowing ex-post deviation from the house size \(H\), and if it does, provide a construction/characterization.
