literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Cembrano et al., 2024) isolates a central tension in apportionment: deterministic population-monotone rules are essentially divisor methods (Balinski--Young), but divisor methods can violate quota; randomization over stationary divisor methods still leaves worst-case expected quota deviation linear in \(H\) (Proposition 4). The paper then shows that if one relaxes the fixed-house constraint ex post (allowing \(\sum_i X_i\neq H\) but keeping \(\mathbb E[\sum_i X_i]=H\)), one can simultaneously achieve quota compliance, strong population monotonicity, and ex-ante proportionality via randomized fixed-divisor methods (Theorem 2), with deviation from \(H\) controlled by concentration bounds.

The open problem asks whether the same triple of properties can be achieved while keeping \(\sum_i X_i=H\) almost surely. The only forward-citing work provided here, "Online Proportional Apportionment", does not resolve the static question, but it establishes a sharp impossibility threshold in an online model: for \(n\ge 4\), no randomized online method can simultaneously keep the per-step house size fixed, satisfy an ex-post quota-type guarantee at all times, and be ex-ante proportional at each step. Although online constraints are stronger than the one-shot setting and the paper does not incorporate the strong population-monotonicity axiom, its flow-based characterizations and impossibility constructions suggest that enforcing exact house size together with both ex-post quota and exact ex-ante proportionality may face fundamental obstructions beyond the variable-house approach.

At present, based on the supplied citation analysis, there is no known construction or impossibility theorem that settles the fixed-house, quota-compliant, population-monotone, ex-ante proportional randomized method in the classic one-shot model. Promising directions include adapting the network-flow/polyhedral characterizations used for house-monotone quota methods (as in the source paper’s Section 5) to incorporate population monotonicity constraints, or extracting static impossibility instances by compressing the online impossibility gadgets into two-instance comparisons that witness population-monotonicity violations.

sources.title: Online Proportional Apportionment
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies an online (sequential) apportionment model. Its main randomized result (Theorem 2) states: an online apportionment method that (i) allocates exactly the prescribed number of seats each step, (ii) satisfies global quota ex post at every time (i.e., for all parties and all times, cumulative seats satisfy \(A_i^t\in\{\lfloor V_i^t\rfloor,\lceil V_i^t\rceil\}\)), and (iii) is ex-ante proportional at every step (\(\Pr[i\in X^t]=v_i^t\)) exists for all instances if and only if \(n\le 3\). For \(n\ge 4\), impossibility follows from their deterministic lower bound (Corollary 1) that global quota online is achievable for all instances iff \(n\le 3\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a randomized apportionment method in the classic one-shot setting with fixed house size \(H\) almost surely, satisfying (1) quota compliance, (2) strong population monotonicity, and (3) ex-ante proportionality \(\mathbb E[X_i]=q_i\). This paper does not address that exact static problem or the strong population-monotonicity axiom. Instead it treats a different, online/sequential model and proves a sharp feasibility threshold (\(n\le 3\)) for simultaneously achieving an ex-post quota-type guarantee (global quota over time) and ex-ante proportionality while keeping the per-step house size fixed. Methodologically, it provides a constructive network-flow characterization of all such online methods (Proposition 2). These flow/rounding ideas are related to the original paper’s use of flows/lotteries to reconcile quota and expectation constraints, but they neither construct nor rule out the desired static, population-monotone, fixed-house method in general. At best, it offers related tools and an impossibility phenomenon in a stricter online setting, suggesting potential barriers but not resolving the open problem.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of knapsack facet recognition by distinct coefficients parameter
background_latex:
Let 
\[Q:=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n: a^\top x\le b\}\]
be a (0--1) knapsack set with \(a\in\mathbb{N}^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\max_i a_i\le b\), and let \(P:=\mathrm{conv}(Q)\) be the associated knapsack polytope, which is then full-dimensional.

Consider a linear inequality
\[\alpha^\top x \le \beta\]
with \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}_+\) (componentwise nonnegative integers). Let
\[K := |\alpha|_+ := \bigl|\{\alpha_i : \alpha_i>0,\ i\in[n]\}\bigr|\]
be the number of distinct positive coefficient values appearing among \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\).

Define the decision problem \(\text{KNAPSACK\_FACETS}\): given \((a,b,\alpha,\beta)\) as above, decide whether \(\alpha^\top x\le \beta\) defines a facet of \(P\) (i.e., it is valid for \(P\) and the face \(\{x\in P: \alpha^\top x=\beta\}\) has dimension \(\dim(P)-1\)).

The paper shows that \(\text{KNAPSACK\_FACETS}\) is \(\mathrm{D}^p\)-complete in general, and gives an XP-time algorithm parameterized by \(K\) that runs in time \(n^{K+O(1)}\) (assuming unit-cost arithmetic).

Settling the computational complexity of the min-cost popular maximum matching problem in a many-to-one instance with strict and incomplete preferences is an interesting problem.
title: Settle complexity of min-cost popular maximum matchings in many-to-one settings
background_latex:
Let \(G=(R\cup H,E)\) be a bipartite hospitals/residents instance. Each resident \(r\in R\) has capacity \(1\) and a strict preference order over its neighbors in \(H\); each hospital \(h\in H\) has an integer capacity \(\mathrm{cap}(h)\ge 1\) and a strict preference order over its neighbors in \(R\). Preferences may be incomplete, i.e., \(E\) need not be complete bipartite.

A (many-to-one) matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) such that \(|M(r)|\le 1\) for all \(r\in R\) and \(|M(h)|\le \mathrm{cap}(h)\) for all \(h\in H\), where \(M(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in M\}\).

Define the voting-based comparison between matchings \(M\) and \(N\) as follows.

1) For a resident \(r\), let \(\mathrm{vote}_r(M,N)\in\{-1,0,1\}\) be \(1\) if \(r\) prefers its assignment in \(M\) to its assignment in \(N\), \(-1\) if it prefers its assignment in \(N\), and \(0\) if the assignments are the same. Being unmatched is the worst outcome.

2) For a hospital \(h\), to compare two assigned sets \(M(h)\) and \(N(h)\), remove common residents and compare the symmetric differences \(S'=M(h)\setminus N(h)\) and \(T'=N(h)\setminus M(h)\) by choosing a bijection \(\psi:S'\to T'\) (adding dummy residents if needed to equalize sizes, each dummy ranked below all real residents). The hospital's vote is defined adversarially as the minimum, over bijections \(\psi\), of the sum of pairwise votes induced by comparing each \(r\in S'\) with \(\psi(r)\in T'\):
\[
\mathrm{vote}_h(M,N) := \min_{\psi:S'\to T'} \sum_{r\in S'} \mathrm{vote}_h\bigl(r,\psi(r)\bigr),
\]
where \(\mathrm{vote}_h(r,r')=1\) if \(h\) prefers \(r\) to \(r'\), \(-1\) if it prefers \(r'\) to \(r\), and \(0\) otherwise.

3) The net margin is
\[
\Delta(M,N):=\sum_{v\in R\cup H} \mathrm{vote}_v(M,N).
\]
A matching \(M\) is popular (within a specified feasible family) if \(\Delta(M,N)\ge 0\) for all \(N\) in that family.

Let \(\mathrm{cost}:E\to\mathbb{R}\) be an edge-cost function and \(\mathrm{cost}(M)=\sum_{e\in M}\mathrm{cost}(e)\).

A matching \(M\) is a maximum matching if it has maximum cardinality among all matchings in \(G\). Define a \emph{popular maximum matching} to mean a maximum-cardinality matching \(M\) such that \(\Delta(M,N)\ge 0\) for every maximum matching \(N\) in \(G\).
problem_definition_latex:
Given a hospitals/residents instance \(G=(R\cup H,E)\) with strict (possibly incomplete) preferences and an edge-cost function \(\mathrm{cost}:E\to\mathbb{R}\), determine the computational complexity of computing a minimum-cost popular maximum matching.

Equivalently, decide whether there is a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs
\[
M^*\in\arg\min\{\mathrm{cost}(M): \; M \text{ is a maximum matching in }G \text{ and } \Delta(M,N)\ge 0 \;\forall N\text{ maximum in }G\},
\]
or prove that this optimization problem is NP-hard.

literature_review.synthesis:
The min-cost popular maximum matching problem in the hospitals/residents (many-to-one) model with strict, possibly incomplete preferences remains open in the sense highlighted by Kavitha and Makino: while min-cost popular matchings with complete preferences are now polynomial-time solvable in many-to-one, the restriction of popularity to the family of maximum-cardinality matchings in the incomplete-preference case does not admit a known polynomial-time algorithm nor a hardness proof.

The closest forward-cited progress in the provided analysis is the work on popular perfect matchings in the many-to-many setting, which develops structural characterizations of popularity via the nonexistence of positive-weight alternating cycles and leverages a reduction to min-cost stable matching in a carefully constructed colorful auxiliary instance. These techniques mirror the cycle/certificate viewpoints used in the many-to-one complete-preference setting and suggest that an eventual resolution for popular maximum matchings may require a refined decomposition of maximum-matchings’ symmetric differences (cycles and alternating paths) together with a way to encode the adversarial hospital vote within an optimization framework.

A key remaining gap is that, unlike the perfect-matching case where cloning/projection arguments can be made surjective (and dual certificates can be strengthened), popular maximum matchings in many-to-one can be strictly richer than those induced by popular maximum matchings in the cloned one-to-one instance. This obstruction blocks straightforward reductions to known polynomial-time algorithms for one-to-one popular maximum matchings, leaving open whether the many-to-one problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-hard.

sources.title: Perfect matchings and popularity in the many-to-many setting
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves that in a bipartite many-to-many instance with strict (possibly incomplete) preferences and edge costs, assuming the instance admits a perfect matching, a minimum-cost popular perfect matching can be computed in polynomial time (Theorem 4). The algorithm reduces min-cost popular perfect perfect matching to a min-cost stable matching problem in a constructed colorful auxiliary many-to-many multigraph, using a characterization of popular perfect matchings via absence of positive-weight alternating cycles (Theorem 5) and a surjective projection from stable matchings in the auxiliary instance to popular perfect matchings in the original instance.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the complexity of computing a minimum-cost popular maximum matching in the hospitals/residents (many-to-one) setting with possibly incomplete preferences, where popularity is defined only among maximum-cardinality matchings. This paper does not resolve that: it studies popular perfect matchings (popularity restricted to perfect matchings) in the more general many-to-many setting, and gives a polynomial-time algorithm for min-cost popular perfect matchings under the assumption that a perfect matching exists.

Nevertheless, its techniques are closely related: it uses the same adversarial-bijection voting rule for capacitated vertices and develops a reduction from min-cost popular perfect matchings to min-cost stable matchings in a colorful auxiliary instance. The paper explicitly states as an open problem the min-cost popular maximum matching problem in hospitals/residents and notes why the one-to-one reduction does not extend. Thus it provides partial progress/tools but not the sought complexity classification for popular maximum matchings.

title: Efficiently update density-based decompositions under single-element insertions and deletions
background_latex:
Let $M=(V,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid with rank function $\operatorname{rank}_M:2^V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$. For any nonempty $U\subseteq V$ with $\operatorname{rank}_M(U)>0$, define its density by
\[\rho_M(U)=\frac{|U|}{\operatorname{rank}_M(U)}.\]
(With the conventions: $\rho_M(\emptyset)=0$ and $\rho_M(U)=+\infty$ if $U\neq\emptyset$ and $\operatorname{rank}_M(U)=0$.)

For a subset $V'\subseteq V$, let $M|_{V'}$ denote the restriction of $M$ to $V'$. Consider the greedy procedure that, starting from $M|_{V'}$, iteratively selects a densest subset of maximum cardinality and then contracts it, producing a partition (allowing empty parts)
\[V'=U_1\cup U_2\cup\cdots\cup U_k,\]
where $k=\operatorname{rank}_M(V)$ and $U_j$ is a maximum-cardinality densest subset in the contracted matroid $(M|_{V'})/(U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_{j-1})$.
This partition is called the density-based decomposition of $V'$ in $M$.

Suppose we maintain such a decomposition while $V'$ is dynamically updated by single-element operations: insertion of an element $u\in V\setminus V'$ (replacing $V'$ by $V'\cup\{u\}$) or deletion of an element $u\in V'$ (replacing $V'$ by $V'\setminus\{u\}$). A naive update recomputes the entire density-based decomposition from scratch after each operation, using (in general) submodular function minimization to find densest sets.
problem_definition_latex: Design an algorithm that maintains the density-based decomposition $U_1,\dots,U_k$ of $V'$ in a matroid $M$ under a sequence of single-element insertions and deletions to $V'$, and does so more efficiently than recomputing the whole decomposition from scratch after every update.

literature_review.synthesis:
The density-based decomposition in Huang–Sellier is a greedy rephrasing of the principal sequence/principal partition of a matroid restriction \(M|_{V'}\): it repeatedly selects a maximum-cardinality densest set \(U_j\) in the current contraction and contracts it, yielding parts \(U_1,\dots,U_k\) with strictly decreasing densities. The paper’s key structural contribution toward dynamic maintenance is the pair of modification lemmas (Lemmas 20–21), which show a strong Lipschitz/sensitivity phenomenon under single-element updates of \(V'\): insertion makes all associated densities \(\tilde\rho_M(v)\) monotone nondecreasing and confines changes to elements whose old density lies in an interval of length 1 around the inserted element’s old density (and symmetrically for deletions). These statements suggest that the decomposition changes “locally in density space,” a property reminiscent of stability results for principal partitions.

Subsequent/related work on submodular water-filling (e.g., in the online submodular assignment problem and online matroid intersection via submodular water-filling) studies essentially the same densest-set contraction chain for polymatroids/submodular functions, providing minimax and submodular-minimization characterizations of the level sets and proving monotonicity/locality properties under changes in weights. While these frameworks do not address fully dynamic insert/delete updates of the ground set \(V'\), they offer alternative viewpoints (unique maximal minimizers, market/convex duality) that could be leveraged to design incremental algorithms.

At present, none of the forward-citing analyses provided contains an explicit data structure or algorithm with provably improved update time for maintaining the full decomposition \(U_1,\dots,U_k\) under single-element insertions/deletions, beyond recomputation via repeated submodular minimization. Thus the problem remains open. Promising directions include exploiting Lemmas 20–21 to update only a small contiguous block of levels, and specializing to structured matroids (laminar, transversal) where densest-set computations admit faster primitives, potentially enabling polylogarithmic or near-linear-in-affected-region update times.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper introduces the density-based decomposition (a greedy/principal-sequence decomposition by iteratively taking a maximum-cardinality densest set and contracting) and proves two “modification lemmas” describing how the associated densities \,\(\tilde\rho_M(v)\) change under a single-element insertion/deletion in the maintained subset \(V'\):
- (Insertion, Lemma 20) For all \(v\in V\), \(\tilde\rho^{new}_M(v)\ge \tilde\rho^{old}_M(v)\); for the inserted element \(u\), \(\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)\le \tilde\rho^{new}_M(u)\le \tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)+1\); and elements with \(\tilde\rho^{old}_M(v)\notin [\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u),\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)+1]\) keep the same associated density.
- (Deletion, Lemma 21) Symmetric monotonicity: \(\tilde\rho^{new}_M(v)\le \tilde\rho^{old}_M(v)\); for the deleted element \(u\), \(\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)\ge \tilde\rho^{new}_M(u)\ge \tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)-1\); and elements with \(\tilde\rho^{old}_M(v)\notin [\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)-1,\tilde\rho^{old}_M(u)]\) keep the same associated density.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an algorithm that maintains the full density-based decomposition \(U_1,\dots,U_k\) of \(V'\) under single-element insertions/deletions faster than recomputation (which may require submodular minimization each time). This paper does not give such a dynamic maintenance algorithm or improved update-time bounds. However, it develops structural sensitivity results (Lemmas 20–21) precisely about how the decomposition’s induced associated densities change under one-element updates. These lemmas are a key prerequisite for designing efficient dynamic update algorithms (the authors explicitly note this as an open direction), and they are used to implement a local-search construction of a sparsifier (DCS) via repeated insert/delete operations.

sources.connection: The open problem asks for a dynamic algorithm to maintain the density-based decomposition of a matroid restriction \(V'\) under single-element insertions/deletions, more efficiently than recomputing via submodular minimization. This paper is not about dynamic updates, but it directly studies essentially the same densest-set contraction/principal-partition-type decomposition (Algorithm 1) for a polymatroid defined by a submodular function \(f\), and relates it to principal partition sequences of matroids. Thus it provides a clean characterization of the decomposition and strong structural properties (monotonicity, locality, Lipschitz under small-bids) that could be leveraged to design incremental update rules. However, it does not present data structures or update-time guarantees for maintaining the decomposition under element insertions/deletions in \(V'\) (or changes in \(x\)/ground set), so it does not resolve the dynamic maintenance problem.

sources.title: Sparsification for graph and matroid optimization problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis develops and analyzes a greedy density-based decomposition of a matroid (Chapter 5.2) and uses it to construct a sparsifier for matroid intersection called a Density-Constrained Subset (DCS). In particular, it proves existence/constructibility of a DCS of size \(O(|S_{opt}|/\varepsilon)\) that contains a \((3/2+\varepsilon)\)-approximate maximum common independent set for matroid intersection (Theorem 5.2, as summarized in the thesis abstract/intro), with applications to one-way communication (Theorem 5.5) and random-order streaming (Theorem 5.6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an efficient dynamic (single-element insertion/deletion) maintenance algorithm for the density-based decomposition \(U_1,\dots,U_k\) of a changing subset \(V'\subseteq V\) in a fixed matroid \(M\), improving over recomputation via submodular minimization. This thesis uses essentially the same density notion \(\rho_M(U)=|U|/\operatorname{rank}_M(U)\) and explicitly introduces/uses a greedy “density-based decomposition” (Chapter 5.2) as a structural tool to build sparsifiers for matroid intersection. However, the provided excerpted material does not present any algorithm for dynamically updating the decomposition under insertions/deletions of elements of \(V'\); the algorithms discussed are for streaming/random-order and for constructing sparsifiers (DCS/DBS), not for fully dynamic maintenance of the decomposition itself. Thus it contributes relevant structural understanding and motivation but does not resolve the dynamic-update problem.

sources.title: Online Matroid Intersection: Submodular Water-Filling and Matroidal Welfare Maximization
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper defines a “water level” vector for poly-matroids (monotone submodular functions) via an iterative densest-set-and-contract procedure (Algorithm 1), equivalent to level sets given by submodular minimization 
\[S_f^*(y)=\text{unique maximal minimizer of }\min_{S\subseteq E}(f(S)-y(S))\]
and to an SUA-market convex program; it proves key properties (monotonicity, feasibility indication, duality, locality) and uses them to obtain a deterministic polynomial-time \((1-1/e)\)-competitive algorithm for fractional online poly-matroid intersection (Theorem 1.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a dynamic (single-element insert/delete) algorithm to maintain the density-based decomposition of a matroid restriction, where each step selects a maximum-cardinality densest set and contracts it. This paper is not about dynamic updates, but it develops essentially the same kind of densest-set contraction chain (principal partition / density-based decomposition) as a central object: Algorithm 1 repeatedly finds a (unique maximal) densest set with respect to a weight vector \(x\) and contracts it, producing nested sets/levels. It also characterizes level sets via submodular minimization \(\min_S\{t\,f(S)-x(S)\}\), which is the same primitive used in naive recomputation in the open problem. These structural characterizations and locality/monotonicity properties describe how the decomposition changes as \(x\) changes, and could plausibly be leveraged toward efficient incremental maintenance under updates, but the paper does not provide an algorithm or complexity bounds for maintaining the decomposition under insertions/deletions of elements of \(V'\).

title: Solvability conditions for asymmetric indefinite Riccati equation in mean-field game feedback
background_latex:
Consider a continuous-time linear-quadratic (LQ) mean-field game with common noise and partial observation, in which the decentralized optimal control is expressed in linear state-feedback form once certain matrix-valued Riccati equations are solvable.

Let the state dimension be 
\(n\) and the control dimension be \(m\). Let \(A_t,\bar A_t,D_t,\bar D_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(B_t,\bar B_t,F_t,\bar F_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(Q_t\in\mathbb{S}^n\), \(R_t\in\mathbb{S}^m\), \(S_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), and \(L_T\in\mathbb{S}^n\) be given deterministic coefficient functions/matrices on \([0,T]\) (bounded/measurable as needed so the equations below are well-defined). The scalar constants \(\alpha_1,\alpha_3,\beta_1\) (and other constants appearing in the model) are given.

In the paper’s feedback derivation, two Riccati-type ordinary differential equations appear. One is a (symmetric) stochastic-LQ Riccati equation for a symmetric matrix \(\Pi_t\in\mathbb{S}^n\). The other is a generally \emph{asymmetric} (not necessarily symmetric) Riccati equation for a matrix \(\Sigma_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) of the form
\[
\dot\Sigma_t + \Sigma_t(A_t+\bar A_t) + A_t^\top \Sigma_t + D_t^\top \Sigma_t(D_t+\bar D_t)
- \Sigma_{e,t} R_{e,t}^{-1} \bar\Sigma_t^\top + (1-\alpha_1)Q_t = 0,
\qquad \Sigma_T = (1-\alpha_3)L_T.
\]
Here the auxiliary matrices \(R_{e,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\), \(\Sigma_{e,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), and \(\bar\Sigma_t\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\) are (as defined in the paper) affine functions of \(R_t,S_t,F_t,\bar F_t,B_t,\bar B_t\) and \(\Sigma_t\); in particular \(R_{e,t}\) depends on \(\Sigma_t\) and must be (uniformly) invertible for the equation to make sense.

This Riccati equation is called in the paper an “asymmetric indefinite equation with complex structure,” reflecting that neither \(Q_t\) nor \(R_t\) is assumed positive semidefinite/definite, and \(\Sigma_t\) is not restricted to be symmetric.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine general verifiable conditions on the coefficient data \(A_t,\bar A_t,D_t,\bar D_t,B_t,\bar B_t,F_t,\bar F_t,Q_t,R_t,S_t,L_T\) and constants \(\alpha_1,\alpha_3,\beta_1\) that guarantee existence and uniqueness of a (sufficiently regular) solution \(\Sigma:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) to the (generally asymmetric) indefinite Riccati equation
\[
\dot\Sigma_t + \Sigma_t(A_t+\bar A_t) + A_t^\top \Sigma_t + D_t^\top \Sigma_t(D_t+\bar D_t)
- \Sigma_{e,t} R_{e,t}^{-1} \bar\Sigma_t^\top + (1-\alpha_1)Q_t = 0,
\qquad \Sigma_T = (1-\alpha_3)L_T,
\]
in a way that ensures \(R_{e,t}\) is (uniformly) invertible on \([0,T]\) (so that \(R_{e,t}^{-1}\) is well-defined) and the resulting feedback representation for decentralized strategies is well-posed.

title: Characterize the optimal equilibrium stopping region under general aggregation preferences
background_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) support a one-dimensional time-homogeneous diffusion \(X=(X_t)_{t\ge 0}\) with continuous paths and the strong Markov property, started from \(X_0=x\in\mathbb R\). Let \(\mathbb F=(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge 0}\) be the filtration generated by \(X\), and let \(\mathcal T\) be the set of all \(\mathbb F\)-stopping times.

Let \(\rho\) be a nonnegative random discount rate with distribution function \(F_\rho\) on \([0,\infty)\), independent of \(X\). Let \(g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be a measurable payoff function. Let \(\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be a strictly increasing “attitude” (aggregation) function.

For a Borel set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R\) interpreted as a stopping region, define the hitting time (given current state \(x\))
\[\tau(x,R):=\inf\{t>0: X_t^x\in R\},\]
where \(X^x\) denotes the process started at \(x\).

Define the aggregated continuation payoff under policy \(R\) by
\[J(x,R):=\int_0^\infty \varphi\Big(\mathbb E\big[e^{-r\tau(x,R)}\, g(X^x_{\tau(x,R)})\big]\Big)\,dF_\rho(r).\]
Define the induced value when today’s self can either stop immediately or continue assuming future selves follow \(R\):
\[V(x,R):=\varphi(g(x))\vee J(x,R).\]

A (mild) equilibrium is a Borel set \(R\) such that it is a fixed point of the policy-improvement operator \(\Theta\) constructed from the comparison between \(\varphi(g(x))\) and \(J(x,R)\) (equivalently, a time-consistent stopping region in the sense of consistent planning). Let \(\mathcal E\) denote the collection of all such equilibria.

An optimal equilibrium is an equilibrium \(R^*\in\mathcal E\) such that \(V(x,R^*)\ge V(x,R)\) for all \(x\) and all \(R\in\mathcal E\).
problem_definition_latex:
Find general conditions and/or an explicit characterization of an optimal equilibrium \(R^*\in\mathcal E\) (when it exists) for the time-inconsistent aggregated optimal stopping problem with payoff aggregator \(J\) above, i.e., determine \(R^*\in\mathcal E\) such that
\[V(x,R^*)\ge V(x,R)\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb R\text{ and all }R\in\mathcal E,\]
without restricting \(\varphi\) to satisfy the structural condition that \(x\mapsto \varphi'(x)x\) is increasing (and beyond the special cases analyzed in the paper).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Deng–Yu–Zhang’s aggregation model, the planner evaluates a stopping region \(R\) through \(J(x,R)=\int_0^\infty \varphi(\mathbb E[e^{-r\tau(x,R)}g(X_{\tau(x,R)})])\,dF_\rho(r)\), which generally destroys the reduction to a single discount function and hence breaks the decreasing-impatience machinery used in earlier time-inconsistent stopping. The paper nevertheless shows (for one-dimensional diffusions) that mild equilibria are fixed points of the policy-improvement operator \(\Theta\), and provides sufficient conditions (notably \(x\mapsto \varphi'(x)x\) increasing) under which the smallest one-barrier equilibrium \([0,a^*]\) is optimal for the put payoff. Their Section 5 examples demonstrate that once this structural condition fails, the smallest equilibrium can cease to be optimal and an optimal equilibrium may not exist.

Among forward citations, the closest progress toward a general selection principle is “Almost strong equilibria for time‐inconsistent stopping problems under finite horizon in continuous time,” which proves—under log sub-additivity of a (single) discount function and 1D regularity—that the optimal equilibrium is the minimal closed equilibrium given by the intersection of all closed equilibria. While it does not cover heterogeneous exponential-rate aggregation or nonlinear \(\varphi\), it offers a template: if one can establish an analogue of equilibrium monotonicity/dominance (smaller equilibria yield larger continuation values) and show closure under intersections for the aggregated functional \(J\), then an intersection-type characterization of an optimal equilibrium may follow.

A different direction is suggested by “Time-inconsistent mean-field stopping problems: a regularised equilibrium approach,” which develops entropy-regularized fixed-point methods to obtain stationary relaxed equilibria without monotonicity assumptions. This is relevant to the aggregation setting precisely because Deng–Yu–Zhang exhibit parameter regimes where no pure optimal equilibrium exists; regularization/relaxation may provide a well-posed substitute notion of optimality or selection among multiple equilibria when \(\varphi\) is general. Overall, the open problem remains unresolved: beyond special cases (e.g., put payoff with \(x\mapsto \varphi'(x)x\) increasing), there is no general characterization of an optimal equilibrium for the aggregated preference, and existence/selection can fail without additional structure.

sources.title: Almost strong equilibria for time‐inconsistent stopping problems under finite horizon in continuous time
sources.theorem_or_result:
Assuming a one-dimensional continuous strong Markov process and a non-exponential discount function \(\delta\) that is log sub-additive \(\delta(s)\delta(t)\le \delta(s+t)\), plus a diffusion/regularity condition (Assumption 4.1) and integrability/limit conditions (4.2)–(4.3), the paper constructs an optimal equilibrium stopping region
\[R^*:=\bigcap_{R\in\mathcal E,\,R\ \text{closed}} R\]
and proves \(R^*\in\mathcal E\) and \(V(x,R^*)\ge V(x,R)\) for all \(x\) and all equilibria \(R\in\mathcal E\) (Theorem 4.1). It also gives a sufficient condition for uniqueness among closed optimal equilibria: if \((R^*)^c=C_{R^*}\) (no indifference outside \(R^*\)), then \(R^*\) is the unique closed optimal equilibrium (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for general conditions/explicit characterization of an optimal equilibrium for an aggregated stopping payoff \(J(x,R)=\int \varphi(\mathbb E[e^{-r\tau(x,R)}g(X_{\tau})])\,dF_\rho(r)\), without imposing the structural monotonicity condition on \(x\mapsto \varphi'(x)x\). This citing paper does not study random discount-rate aggregation nor a nonlinear attitude/aggregation \(\varphi\); instead it treats the classical (linear) expected payoff \(J(x,R)=\mathbb E[\delta(\rho(x,R))f(X_{\rho})]\) with a single discount function \(\delta\). Nevertheless, it provides a closely related ‘Phase II’ selection result: under log sub-additivity (a decreasing-impatience condition) and 1D diffusion regularity, the optimal equilibrium is the minimal (intersection) closed equilibrium. This suggests an approach for the aggregation model if one can establish an analogue of Lemma 3.1/Corollary 3.1 (smaller equilibria dominate larger ones) and closure/intersection stability for equilibria under the nonlinear aggregated functional. The paper therefore gives partial progress and a template of conditions (subadditivity-type inequality + intersection-closedness) that could be adapted, but it does not resolve the open problem in the general \(\varphi,F_\rho\) setting.

sources.title: Time-inconsistent mean-field stopping problems: a regularised equilibrium approach
sources.theorem_or_result:
Main results (discrete-time mean-field MDP with stopping, non-exponential discount):
- Theorem 3.2/Cor. 3.3: for each entropy/discount regularization parameter \(\lambda>0\), there exists a stationary Lipschitz regularized equilibrium \(\phi_\lambda\in F_S^{\mathrm{Lip}}\) characterized as a fixed point \(\phi_\lambda=T_1^\lambda\circ T_2^\lambda(\phi_\lambda)\), where \(T_1^\lambda\) is the Gibbs/logit map \(\phi(\mu)=\frac{\exp(r(\mu)/\lambda)}{\exp(r(\mu)/\lambda)+\exp(\mathbb E_0 v(T_0(\mu,Z_0))/\lambda)}\) and \(T_2^\lambda(\phi)=\tilde J_\lambda^\phi\).
- Theorem 3.5: under additional absolute-continuity assumptions on the one-step transition kernel (Assumption 4), there exists a stationary relaxed (mixed) equilibrium \(\phi_0\) for the unregularized problem, obtained as a \(\lambda\to0\) limit of \(\phi_\lambda\).
- Theorem 3.4: \(\phi_\lambda\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium for the unregularized problem for \(\lambda\) small.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a characterization of an optimal equilibrium stopping region \(R^*\) for a 1D diffusion under an aggregation functional \(J(x,R)=\int \varphi(\mathbb E[e^{-r\tau}g(X_\tau)])\,dF_\rho(r)\), without structural monotonicity assumptions on \(\varphi\). The citing paper does not study this continuous-time diffusion/region equilibrium nor the same aggregator \(\varphi\circ\mathbb E[\cdot]\) integrated over discount rates. Instead it treats a discrete-time mean-field MDP stopping problem with a general (non-exponential) discount sequence \(\delta(k)\), and proves existence of stationary mixed (relaxed) equilibria via entropy regularization and fixed-point arguments, without assuming decreasing impatience.
Thus it provides related methodological progress: (i) existence of mixed equilibria under very general discounting without monotonicity assumptions, (ii) a regularization/limit scheme \(\lambda\to0\) to obtain equilibria when pure strategies may fail. However it does not characterize an optimal equilibrium among all equilibria, nor identify a stopping region \(R^*\) in a 1D diffusion, nor address the specific aggregation over heterogeneous exponential rates and attitude function \(\varphi\).

title: Characterize Nash product rule under strategyproofness and core fairness conditions
background_latex:
Let there be a set of agents \(N=[n]\) and alternatives \(M=[m]\). Outcomes are distributions \(q\in\Delta^m:=\{q\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}:\sum_{j\in M} q_j=1\}\).

Each agent \(i\in N\) has a unique ideal distribution (peak) \(p_i\in\Delta^m\) and evaluates an outcome \(q\) using Leontief utility
\[
 u_i(q)=\min_{j\in M_i}\frac{q_j}{p_{i,j}},\qquad M_i:=\{j\in M: p_{i,j}>0\}.
\]
An aggregation mechanism is a function \(f:(\Delta^m)^n\to\Delta^m\) mapping the profile of peaks \(P=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\) to an outcome \(f(P)\).

Continuity of \(f\) means: for every \(P\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(\|P-P'\|_1<\delta\) implies \(\|f(P)-f(P')\|_1<\varepsilon\), where \(\|\cdot\|_1\) denotes the \(\ell_1\) norm on the finite-dimensional vector space.

Strategyproofness means that no single agent can benefit by misreporting her peak, holding others fixed, where preferences are induced by \(u_i\) with true peak \(p_i\). Group-strategyproofness is the analogous condition for coalitions.

Core-fair-share (a core-based fairness notion) for an outcome \(q\) at profile \(P\) means there is no coalition \(N'\subseteq N\) and distribution \(q'\in\Delta^m\) such that for every \(q''\in\Delta^m\), every agent \(i\in N'\) strictly prefers \((|N'|/n)q' + (1-|N'|/n)q''\) to \(q\) (preferences again induced by \(u_i\)). A mechanism satisfies core fair share if \(f(P)\) has no blocking coalition for every \(P\).

The Nash product rule (Nash welfare maximizer) for Leontief utilities is
\[
\mathrm{NASH}(P)\in\arg\max_{q\in\Delta^m}\prod_{i\in N} u_i(q),
\]
which is known (in the paper) to be single-valued for these utilities.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether the following implication holds for Leontief utilities on \(\Delta^m\):

If a mechanism \(f:(\Delta^m)^n\to\Delta^m\) is continuous, satisfies strategyproofness (for the Leontief-induced preferences), and satisfies core fair share, must it coincide with the Nash product rule \(\mathrm{NASH}\) on all profiles \(P\in(\Delta^m)^n\), i.e., must \(f(P)=\mathrm{NASH}(P)\) for every \(P\)?

Equivalently, is group-strategyproofness dispensable in the characterization stating that \(\mathrm{NASH}\) is the unique continuous mechanism satisfying group-strategyproofness and core fair share?

An aggregation mechanism is a function \(f:(\Delta^m)^n\to\Delta^m\) mapping the profile of peaks \(P=(p_1,\dots,p_n)\) to an outcome \(f(P)\).

Continuity of \(f\) means: for every \(P\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(\|P-P'\|_1<\delta\) implies \(\|f(P)-f(P')\|_1<\varepsilon\), where \(\|\cdot\|_1\) denotes the \(\ell_1\) norm on the finite-dimensional vector space.

Strategyproofness means that no single agent can benefit by misreporting her peak, holding others fixed, where preferences are induced by \(u_i\) with true peak \(p_i\). Group-strategyproofness is the analogous condition for coalitions.

Core-fair-share (a core-based fairness notion) for an outcome \(q\) at profile \(P\) means there is no coalition \(N'\subseteq N\) and distribution \(q'\in\Delta^m\) such that for every \(q''\in\Delta^m\), every agent \(i\in N'\) strictly prefers \((|N'|/n)q' + (1-|N'|/n)q''\) to \(q\) (preferences again induced by \(u_i\)). A mechanism satisfies core fair share if \(f(P)\) has no blocking coalition for every \(P\).

The Nash product rule (Nash welfare maximizer) for Leontief utilities is
\[
\mathrm{NASH}(P)\in\arg\max_{q\in\Delta^m}\prod_{i\in N} u_i(q),
\]
which is known (in the paper) to be single-valued for these utilities.

Determine whether the following implication holds for Leontief utilities on \(\Delta^m\):

If a mechanism \(f:(\Delta^m)^n\to\Delta^m\) is continuous, satisfies strategyproofness (for the Leontief-induced preferences), and satisfies core fair share, must it coincide with the Nash product rule \(\mathrm{NASH}\) on all profiles \(P\in(\Delta^m)^n\), i.e., must \(f(P)=\mathrm{NASH}(P)\) for every \(P\)?

Equivalently, is group-strategyproofness dispensable in the characterization stating that \(\mathrm{NASH}\) is the unique continuous mechanism satisfying group-strategyproofness and core fair share?
open_problem_quote:
We conjecture that continuity is required for the characterization as well.

Some concrete open questions are:

counterexample_suitability_rationale: A counterexample would be an explicit continuous, strategyproof, core-fair-share mechanism distinct from Nash, or a profile witnessing necessity of group-strategyproofness; verifying the axioms is nontrivial but mechanizable for small \(n,m\) by discretizing peaks and checking incentive constraints approximately. Exact verification over the continuous simplex is harder, so brute-force search is only a proxy.

However, enforcing global continuity and exact (not sampled) incentive/core conditions is difficult, so the loop would mainly help discover plausible counterexamples or conjecture refinements rather than certify them.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Brandt, Greger, Segal-Halevi, and Suksompong (2025), the Nash product rule \(\mathrm{NASH}\) for Leontief utilities on the simplex \(\Delta^m\) is shown to satisfy continuity, group-strategyproofness, and a core-based fairness notion (core fair share). Moreover, their Theorem 3 provides a sharp characterization: \(\mathrm{NASH}\) is the unique continuous mechanism satisfying group-strategyproofness and core fair share. The open problem asks whether group-strategyproofness is actually necessary in this characterization, i.e., whether continuity + (individual) strategyproofness + core fair share already force \(\mathrm{NASH}\).

The paper itself indicates that the proof of Theorem 3 uses group-strategyproofness only at a specific step (Lemma 9), suggesting the axiom might be weakenable, but it remains unresolved for plain Leontief utilities. A closely related positive result is established for the refined Leximin-Leontief preference extension: Theorem 4 shows that for Leximin-Leontief preferences, continuity + strategyproofness + core fair share do characterize \(\mathrm{NASH}\). This strengthens the plausibility that the Leontief case might also admit such a weakening, but the refinement changes the incentive constraints, so it does not settle the original question.

The only forward-citing item provided here is a general survey on divisible voting, which (based on the limited information available) does not contribute a proof or counterexample. Thus, with the current citation set, the problem remains open: no known paper among the provided forward citations resolves whether individual strategyproofness suffices for the Leontief-utility characterization under core fair share and continuity.

An immediate open question for future research is whether one or more of these problems admit fully polynomial time approximation schemes (FPTAS). That is, for any constant \(\epsilon > 0\), can we obtain a \((1 + \epsilon)\)-approximation in \(\mathrm{poly}(n, 1/\epsilon)\) time? We note that an FPTAS is impossible for our Multi-Dimensional Santa Claus problem, since even with 3 machines, it already captures the strongly NP-hard 3-Partition problem [GJ02]. title: Designing fully polynomial approximation schemes for stochastic probing and stopping problems
background_latex:
This paper studies several stochastic combinatorial optimization problems defined on independent nonnegative random variables \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) whose distributions are known.

An algorithmic approximation scheme for a maximization problem with optimal value \(\mathrm{OPT}\) is:
1) An EPTAS: for every \(\epsilon>0\), it outputs a solution of value at least \((1-\epsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) in time \(t(\epsilon)\cdot \mathrm{poly}(|I|)\), where \(t\) depends only on \(\epsilon\) and \(|I|\) is the input length.
2) An FPTAS: for every \(\epsilon>0\), it outputs a solution of value at least \((1-\epsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\) (sometimes written \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation depending on minimization/maximization convention) in time \(\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\epsilon)\).

The paper provides EPTASes for several stochastic problems (e.g., Free-Order Prophets, non-adaptive and adaptive ProbeMax, and Pandora's Box with Commitment) via reductions to a multi-dimensional Santa Claus feasibility problem. It is noted that an FPTAS for the paper's multi-dimensional Santa Claus subroutine is impossible in general because the problem captures strongly NP-hard instances (via 3-Partition) even for a constant number of machines, so any FPTAS for the stochastic problems (if possible) would require different techniques than those used here.

literature_review.synthesis:
Segev–Singla (2025) give EPTASes for several stochastic probing and selection-stopping problems (Free-Order Prophets, Pandora’s Box with Commitment, non-adaptive and adaptive ProbeMax) by reducing them to a constant-machine, constant-dimension Multi-Dimensional Santa Claus feasibility problem and then applying an EPTAS for that subroutine. Their paper explicitly notes that an FPTAS for the Santa Claus subroutine is impossible in general (via strong NP-hardness from 3-Partition), so any FPTAS for the stochastic problems would require techniques that avoid this reduction or exploit additional structure in the stochastic objectives.

The only forward-citing work provided here, "Approximation Schemes for Sequential Hiring Problems", makes partial progress in the broader direction of approximation schemes for stochastic dynamic decision problems by proving a PTAS based on structural simplifications (block-responsive policies) and dynamic programming. However, its dependence on \(1/\epsilon\) is super-polynomial, so it does not resolve whether any of the Segev–Singla problems admit an FPTAS. At present, based on the supplied citation data, the FPTAS question remains open; promising directions include identifying special cases where the stochastic objectives admit pseudo-polynomial dynamic programs (enabling scaling-based FPTASes) or proving hardness of FPTAS for specific stochastic probing/stopping problems under standard complexity assumptions.

sources.title: Approximation Schemes for Sequential Hiring Problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the sequential hiring problem: for any fixed \(\epsilon>0\), there is an algorithm running in \(O(n^{O(1)}\cdot T^{2^{\tilde O(1/\epsilon^2)}})\) time that outputs an (efficiently representable) adaptive hiring policy with expected reward at least \((1-\epsilon)\) times optimal (Theorem 1.1). It also shows existence of near-optimal block-responsive policies of size \((1/\epsilon)^{O(k)}\) (Theorem 4.3) and uses this to obtain a truly polynomial-time PTAS in the few-positions regime and an approximation scheme via prior work when \(k\ge 1/\epsilon^2\).

This citing paper studies a different stochastic optimization model (sequential hiring) and provides a PTAS whose running time is polynomial in \(n\) but has super-polynomial dependence on \(1/\epsilon\) (and also depends on \(T\) as \(T^{2^{\tilde O(1/\epsilon^2)}}\)). Therefore it does not give an FPTAS for the Segev–Singla problems, nor does it resolve the barrier about FPTAS impossibility for their multi-dimensional Santa Claus subroutine. Its relevance is that it develops structural/rounding and block(-responsive) policy techniques in stochastic dynamic optimization/probing that could be conceptually related to designing faster schemes, but it does not establish fully polynomial dependence on \(1/\epsilon\) for the target problems.

title: Compute Lipschitz modulus of regularized least-squares solution mapping under stability
background_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(A\in \mathcal{L}(X,Y)\) a linear operator with adjoint \(A^*\), \(b\in Y\), and \(\mu>0\). Let \(g:X\to \mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed, proper, and convex. Consider the regularized least-squares problem
\[
\min_{x\in X}\; F_{A,b,\mu}(x):=\frac{1}{2\mu}\|Ax-b\|^2+g(x),
\]
with solution mapping
\[
S(A,b,\mu):=\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in X} F_{A,b,\mu}(x).
\]
Assume that around a reference parameter triple \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\) the mapping \(S\) is single-valued and locally Lipschitz, i.e., there exist neighborhoods \(\mathcal{U}\) of \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\) and a constant \(L\ge 0\) such that
\[
\|S(A_1,b_1,\mu_1)-S(A_2,b_2,\mu_2)\|\le L\,\|(A_1,b_1,\mu_1)-(A_2,b_2,\mu_2)\|\quad \forall (A_i,b_i,\mu_i)\in \mathcal{U}.
\]
The infimum of all such \(L\) (for a fixed choice of local neighborhoods) is called the (local) Lipschitz modulus of \(S\) at \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\); informally, it is the smallest constant governing the local Lipschitz bound.

The paper establishes first-order characterizations for when this Lipschitz stability holds, but notes that computing the Lipschitz modulus in general can be approached via coderivatives (which typically require second-order-type variational information about \(g\)).
problem_definition_latex: Determine (or provide computable formulas/estimates for) the local Lipschitz modulus of the solution mapping \(S\) at a reference triple \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\) in the regime where \(S\) is single-valued and locally Lipschitz around \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\), using an approach that does not rely on involved second-order variational structures of the regularizer \(g\) (e.g., avoiding explicit computation of second-order objects such as coderivatives of \(\partial g\) that are difficult beyond polyhedral cases).

literature_review.synthesis:
The 2024 source paper (Cui–Hoheisel–Nghia–Sun) reframes the regularized least-squares KKT system through the Fenchel–Rockafellar dual and applies Robinson strong regularity to obtain a purely first-order characterization of when the solution mapping \(S(A,b,\mu)\) is locally single-valued and Lipschitz: under \(C^2\)-cone reducibility of \(g^*\) at \(\bar z=-\tfrac{1}{\bar\mu}\bar A^*(\bar A\bar x-\bar b)\), Lipschitz stability is equivalent to the subspace qualification \(\ker \bar A\cap \operatorname{par}\partial g^*(\bar z)=\{0\}\). The paper explicitly flags as open the quantitative step of computing the local Lipschitz modulus (the smallest Lipschitz constant) without resorting to coderivatives/second-order variational objects for \(g\).

Forward-citing work so far provides partial progress mainly in polyhedral settings. The survey/talk “Stability of nonsmooth optimization problems” retains coderivative-based criteria in general but, for LASSO, derives an explicit computable upper bound on the Lipschitz modulus in terms of singular values of an active submatrix \(A_J\) and the scaled residual \(A\bar x-\bar b\). “Lipschitz continuity of solution multifunctions of extended regularization problems” gives polyhedral-geometry characterizations (global Lipschitzness in \((\lambda,b)\) for fixed \(A\), and local Lipschitzness under an active-set linear independence condition) but does not provide an explicit modulus. “Isolated Calmness in Regularized Convex Optimization” supplies geometric necessary/sufficient conditions for isolated calmness in broader composite least-squares models, which supports existence of some local Lipschitz bound but again stops short of a computable minimal constant.

Overall, the problem of determining the exact local Lipschitz modulus of \(S\) at \((\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu)\) in the general \(C^2\)-cone reducible-conjugate regime, using only first-order information about \(g\), remains open. Current promising directions include: (i) exploiting active-manifold/effective-subspace reductions (as in Newton methods for polyhedral regularizers) to express the modulus via restricted linear systems; and (ii) extending such reductions beyond polyhedral \(g\) to broader \(C^2\)-cone reducible \(g^*\) by identifying computable representations of \(\operatorname{par}\partial g^*(\bar z)\) and deriving tight norm bounds for the implicit map induced by the dual strong-regularity linearization.

sources.title: Stability of nonsmooth optimization problems
sources.theorem_or_result:
For the regularized least-squares problem \(\min_x \tfrac12\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda g(x)\) with \(g\) closed proper convex, the talk derives a Mordukhovich-type sufficient condition for local single-valued Lipschitz stability of the solution map \((A,b,\lambda)\mapsto \arg\min_x \tfrac12\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda g(x)\): if \(\bar x\) solves the problem and \(\bar u:=\tfrac1\lambda A^*(b-A\bar x)\in\partial g(\bar x)\), then the Mordukhovich criterion holds provided \[\ker A\cap D^*(\partial g^*)(\bar u\mid \bar x)(0)=\{0\}.\]
In the polyhedral-support case \(g=\sigma_P\), this reduces to the computable qualification \(\operatorname{par}\partial g^*(\bar u)\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) (denoted (R)). For unconstrained LASSO \(g(x)=\|x\|_1\), under the intermediate condition \(\ker A_J=\{0\}\) (equivalent to (R)), the solution map \(S(b,\lambda)\) is semismooth and locally Lipschitz at \((\bar b,\bar\lambda)\) with an explicit upper bound on the Lipschitz modulus:
\[L\le \frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}(A_J)^2}\Big(\sigma_{\max}(A_J)+\big\|A_J^T(A\bar x-\bar b)/\bar\lambda\big\|\Big).\]
sources.connection: The open problem asks for computable formulas/estimates of the local Lipschitz modulus of the solution mapping \(S(A,b,\mu)\) for regularized least squares, preferably avoiding heavy second-order objects (coderivatives of \(\partial g\)). This citing work does not give a general formula for the exact Lipschitz modulus for arbitrary convex \(g\); it still uses the Mordukhovich criterion and coderivative expressions to certify Lipschitz stability. However, it provides (i) a reduction of the stability condition to a more tangible qualification \(\operatorname{par}\partial g^*(\bar u)\cap\ker A=\{0\}\) in polyhedral-support/PLQ settings, and (ii) an explicit, easily computable upper bound on the Lipschitz modulus for the LASSO solution map in terms of singular values of a submatrix \(A_J\) and the residual \(A\bar x-\bar b\). Thus it constitutes partial progress toward computable modulus estimates in important special cases (\(\ell_1\), PLQ, \(C^2\)-cone reducible conjugates), but does not resolve the general-modulus computation problem posed in the original paper.

sources.title: Lipschitz continuity of solution multifunctions of extended regularization problems
sources.theorem_or_result: For the extended \(\ell_1\) regularization/Lasso solution multifunction \(S(\lambda,b,A)\), the paper proves: (a) for fixed \(A\), \(S(\cdot,\cdot,A)\) is globally Lipschitz continuous on its convex domain \(\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R^m\) (Theorem 3.1) via a polyhedral decomposition of \(\operatorname{gph}S\); (b) for \(\lambda>0\), local Lipschitz continuity of \(S\) around \((\bar\lambda,\bar b,\bar A)\) is equivalent to Condition 1.2 (linear independence of active columns) (Proposition 4.1); and (c) on compact \(U\subset \mathbb R_{++}\times\mathbb R^m\), \(S\) is Lipschitz on \(U\times V\) for some neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar A\) iff Condition 1.2 holds at \((\lambda,b,\bar A)\) for all \((\lambda,b)\in U\) (Theorem 4.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for computable formulas/estimates of the local Lipschitz modulus of the solution mapping for general convex regularizers \(g\), avoiding coderivatives/second-order variational objects. This paper addresses a special polyhedral regularizer \(g(x)=\|x\|_1\) (Lasso/extended \(\ell_1\) model) and establishes Lipschitz continuity characterizations using polyhedral theory rather than coderivatives. However, it does not compute the Lipschitz modulus (minimal constant) at a reference triple, nor does it treat general \(g\) beyond \(\ell_1\). The results provide structural decompositions and equivalences that could help bound a modulus in the \(\ell_1\) case, but no explicit modulus formula is given.

sources.title: Isolated Calmness in Regularized Convex Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For the least-squares regularized composite problem \(\min_x \tfrac{1}{2\mu}\|\Phi x-b\|^2+g(Kx)\), the paper gives geometric necessary/sufficient conditions for isolated calmness (local single-valued Lipschitz behavior at an isolated solution) of the solution mapping \(S_{LS}(b,\mu)\). In particular, if \(x\bar\in S_{LS}(\bar b,\bar\mu)\), \(\bar y\in \partial g(K\bar x)\) with \(K^*\bar y=-\tfrac{1}{\bar\mu}\Phi^*(\Phi\bar x-\bar b)\), and \(g\) satisfies quadratic growth at \(K\bar x\) for \(\bar y\), then \(S_{LS}\) is isolated calm at \((\bar b,\bar\mu)\) for \(\bar x\) provided \(\operatorname{Ker}\Phi\cap K^{-1}(T_{\partial g^*(\bar y)}(K\bar x))=\{0\}\); moreover this condition is also necessary under mild qualification assumptions (e.g. \(\partial g^*(\bar y)\) polyhedral or \(\operatorname{Im}K\cap \operatorname{ri}(\partial g^*(\bar y))\neq\emptyset\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for computable formulas/estimates of the local Lipschitz modulus of the solution mapping \(S(A,b,\mu)\) in the regime where it is single-valued and locally Lipschitz, preferably avoiding heavy second-order objects (coderivatives/second-order variational structures of \(g\)). This paper does not compute the Lipschitz modulus. Instead it studies the weaker/related property of isolated calmness (a local Lipschitz bound around an isolated solution) and provides geometric characterizations in terms of tangent cones to \(\partial g^*(\bar y)\) and kernels of \(\Phi\) and \(K^*\). While these conditions can help verify Lipschitz stability and imply existence of some modulus \(\kappa\), the paper does not provide an explicit minimal constant (modulus) nor a computable bound in terms of \(\bar A,\bar b,\bar\mu\) without second-order information; it still uses second-order-related structures (graphical derivatives/second subderivatives) but packages them into tangent-cone conditions under quadratic growth.

However, it develops a first-order-computable object \(\operatorname{par}\partial g^*(z)\) (effective subspace) and uses tilt-stability/metric regularity to obtain quadratic local convergence of Newton-type methods for least-squares-type models with polyhedral regularizers (including Lasso/TV/OSCAR). Tilt-stability is closely tied to strong metric regularity and hence to Lipschitz behavior of solution mappings, so the paper provides algorithmic tools and explicit subspace formulas that could help estimate sensitivity in polyhedral cases, but it does not provide an explicit Lipschitz-modulus formula for \(S(A,b,\mu)\) under general convex \(g\) or even for polyhedral \(g\).

sources.title: Tilt Stability of Ky-Fan -Norm Composite Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper derives point-based necessary and sufficient conditions for tilt stability (single-valued Lipschitz behavior under tilt perturbations) of composite problems of the form \(\min_X\; \nu\,\vartheta(X)+\Psi_\kappa(X)\), where \(\vartheta\) is \(C^2\) and locally convex and \(\Psi_\kappa\) is the Ky-Fan \(\kappa\)-norm. In particular, it provides an explicit formula for the second subderivative \(d^2\Psi_\kappa(X\mid\Gamma)(G)\) (Propositions 3.1–3.2) and a verifiable characterization of tilt stability: a local minimizer \(X\) is tilt-stable iff \(\operatorname{Ker}\nabla^2\vartheta(X)\cap \Upsilon=\{0\}\), where \(\Upsilon\) is an explicitly described set of directions determined by the SVD structure of \((X,\Gamma)\) (Theorem 4.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for computable formulas/estimates of the local Lipschitz modulus of the solution mapping \(S(A,b,\mu)\) for regularized least squares, preferably avoiding heavy second-order variational objects (coderivatives of \(\partial g\)). This paper does not address the parameterized least-squares mapping \(S(A,b,\mu)\) nor compute its Lipschitz modulus. Instead, it studies tilt stability of minimizers for matrix composite problems with Ky-Fan \(\kappa\)-norm regularizers, using explicit second subderivative calculations. Tilt stability implies a single-valued Lipschitz localization of \((\partial f)^{-1}\), so the results provide second-order tools/criteria that are conceptually related to Lipschitz stability, but they rely heavily on second subderivatives and are specialized to spectral regularizers rather than giving modulus formulas for \(S(A,b,\mu)\) in the least-squares setting.

title: Scaling limit of dynamic risk measures with Wasserstein-type one-step penalties
background_latex:
Let \(\Omega:=C([0,1];\mathbb{R})\) be the canonical continuous-path space with canonical process \(X_t(\omega)=\omega_t\). Fix \(p>0\) and a reference law \(P\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\) (typically a martingale law).

For each \(N\in\mathbb{N}\), let \((Q)^N\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^N)\) denote the law of \((X_{1/N},\dots,X_{N/N})\) under \(Q\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\), and similarly for \((P)^N\).

For probability measures \(Q,P\in\mathcal{P}_1(\mathbb{R}^N)\) with suitable regular conditional distributions, define the time-consistent multistep discrepancy (additive chain construction)
\[
D^{W}_{1,p}(Q\|\|P):=W_1(Q,P)^p,
\]
\[
D^{W}_{N,p}(Q\|\|P):=D^{W}_{N-1,p}(Q_{1:N-1}\|\|P_{1:N-1})+\int W_1\bigl(Q^{x_{1:N-1}}_N,\,P^{x_{1:N-1}}_N\bigr)^p\,dQ_{1:N-1}(x_{1:N-1}),
\]
where \(W_1\) is the 1-Wasserstein distance on \(\mathbb{R}\), \(Q_{1:N-1}\) is the projection onto the first \(N-1\) coordinates, and \(Q^{x_{1:N-1}}_N\) denotes the conditional law of the \(N\)th coordinate given \(x_{1:N-1}\) (and similarly for \(P\)).

Let \(\rho_N\) be the dynamic (multi-period) risk measure with penalty function built from a one-step penalty \(\alpha_1\) via additive decomposition: \(\alpha_N(Q)=\int \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_1(Q_i^{x_{1:i-1}})\,dQ\). The paper considers in particular the one-step penalty \(\alpha_1(\cdot)=\pm W_1(\cdot,P_1)^{p}\), yielding an objective of the general form
\[
\inf_{H\ \text{predictable}} \rho_N\bigl(F_N(X)-(H\cdot X)_N\bigr)
\]
whose formal minimax dual involves \(D^{W}_{N,p}((Q)^N\|\|(P)^N)\) (up to sign/convention).

The paper identifies the scaling \(N^{p/2-1}D^{W}_{N,p}((Q)^N\|\|(P)^N)\) as the correct continuous-time order for martingale laws, and proves existence/identification of the corresponding limit for a specific divergence functional, but does not analyze the scaling limit of the associated dynamic risk measure/pricing functional \(\inf_H\rho_N(\cdot)\) itself when \(\alpha_1(\cdot)=\pm W_1(\cdot,P)^{p}\).
problem_definition_latex:

\[
\inf_{H\ \mathrm{predictable}}\ \rho_N\bigl(F_N(X)-(H\cdot X)_N\bigr)
\]
when the one-step penalty of \(\rho_N\) is given by \(\alpha_1(q)=\pm W_1(q, P_1)^p\), i.e., when the induced \(N\)-step penalty is the additive functional corresponding to \(D^{W}_{N,p}\), and identify the correct normalization in \(N\) (if any) and the resulting continuous-time limit functional on laws \(Q\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega)\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper introduces the chain-constructed multistep discrepancy \(D^{W}_{N,p}\) built from one-step \(W_1^p\) costs and identifies the correct normalization \(N^{p/2-1}\) for continuous-time limits under martingale laws. It proves that for continuous martingales with absolutely continuous quadratic variation, \(N^{p/2-1}D^{W}_{N,p}((Q)^N\|\|(P)^N)\) converges to an explicit integral functional of the volatility mismatch, e.g. \(\mathrm{SW}^p(Q\|P)=(2/\pi)^{p/2}\,\mathbb E^Q[\int_0^1||\sigma_t|-|\eta_t||^p\,dt]\) for diffusion-martingale reference \(P\).

However, the open problem concerns the scaling limit of the associated time-consistent dynamic risk measure / robust hedging functional \(\inf_H\rho_N(F_N-(H\cdot X)_N)\) when the one-step penalty is \(\alpha_1(q)=\pm W_1(q,P_1)^p\). The forward citations provided do not resolve this: the reciprocal specific relative entropy paper develops a related continuous-time control problem and links entropy to the \(p\downarrow2\) derivative of the specific \(p\)-Wasserstein divergence, while the multidimensional specific relative entropy paper provides an entropy analogue of the scaling-limit-to-quadratic-variation paradigm. Thus, based on the available forward-citation evidence, the discrete-to-continuous scaling limit for the full dynamic risk measure/pricing functional remains open.

sources.title: Reciprocal Specific Relative Entropy between Continuous Martingales
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper introduces the reciprocal specific relative entropy between a continuous martingale law \(Q\) and Wiener measure \(W\),
\[h(Q\|W)=\tfrac12\,\mathbb E^Q\Big[\int_0^1 \big(\Sigma_t\log\Sigma_t+1-\Sigma_t\big)\,dt\Big],\]
where \(\Sigma_t=d\langle X\rangle_t/dt\). It proves (Theorem 3.1) that, over the class \(\mathcal M^{\mathrm{win}}_{t,x}\) of win-martingales on \([t,1]\) starting at \(x\in(0,1)\) and ending in \(\{0,1\}\) at time 1, the unique minimizer of \(\inf_{Q\in\mathcal M^{\mathrm{win}}_{t,x}} \tfrac12\mathbb E^Q[\int_t^1 \Sigma_u\log\Sigma_u\,du]\) is the scaled neutral Wright–Fisher diffusion \(dM_s=\sqrt{\frac{M_s(1-M_s)}{1-s}}\,dB_s\), and the value function is explicit. It also shows this objective equals the derivative at \(p=2\) of the specific \(p\)-Wasserstein divergence objective \(\inf_{Q\in\mathcal M^{\mathrm{win}}_{0,x}}\mathbb E^Q[\int_0^1 \Sigma_t^{p/2}\,dt]\) under an integrability condition.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the scaling limit of a discrete-time dynamic risk measure/hedging functional whose penalty is built from one-step \(\pm W_1(\cdot,P_1)^p\), i.e. the additive multistep Wasserstein-type discrepancy \(D^W_{N,p}\), including the correct normalization \(N^{p/2-1}\), and identification of the limiting continuous-time functional on path laws \(Q\in\mathcal P(\Omega)\).

This citing paper does not analyze the discrete-time dynamic risk measure \(\inf_H\rho_N(F_N-(H\cdot X)_N)\) nor the chain-constructed \(D^W_{N,p}((Q)^N\|\|(P)^N)\) scaling limit. Instead it studies a different continuous-time divergence functional \(h(Q\|W)\) (an entropy in quadratic variation) and shows it arises as the \(p\downarrow2\) derivative of the *specific* \(p\)-Wasserstein divergence from [10], which itself is a continuous-time scaling limit object. Thus the paper is relevant mainly as a related tool/insight: it identifies a canonical second-order (critical \(p=2\)) refinement/selection criterion for the specific Wasserstein divergence, and provides PDE/control methods and explicit optimizers in a calibration problem.

So it does not solve the stated scaling-limit problem for the dynamic risk measure with one-step Wasserstein penalties, but it may inform what the limiting penalty could look like near \(p=2\) (entropy-type correction) and suggests techniques (HJB/viscosity) for continuous-time limits of discrete-time robust pricing problems.

sources.title: Multidimensional specific relative entropy between continuous martingales
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper defines the multidimensional specific relative entropy between continuous martingale laws by the scaling limit 
\[h_l(Q\mid P):=\liminf_{n\to\infty}2^{-n}H(Q\mid P)\big|_{\mathcal F_{2^n}},\]
and proves (multidimensional Gantert inequality) that for a square-integrable \(\mathbb R^l\)-valued \(Q\)-martingale with absolutely continuous quadratic covariation \(d\langle X\rangle_t/dt=\Sigma_t^Q\),
\[h_l(Q\mid B^l)\ge \mathbb E^Q\Big[\int_0^1 F_l(\Sigma_t^Q)\,dt\Big],\qquad F_l(\Sigma)=\tfrac12(\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma)-l-\log\det\Sigma).\]
It further shows this lower bound is tight in the convex-analytic sense: the functional \(Q\mapsto \mathbb E^Q[\int_0^1 F_l(\Sigma_t^Q)dt]\) is the convex lower semicontinuous envelope of \(Q\mapsto h_l(Q\mid B^l)\).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns scaling limits of dynamic risk measures whose discrete-time penalty is an additive chain of one-step \(W_1^p\) costs, i.e. a specific Wasserstein-type divergence \(D^W_{N,p}\) with normalization \(N^{p/2-1}\), and asks for the limiting continuous-time risk/pricing functional \(\inf_H\rho_N(\cdot)\). This citing paper instead studies a different divergence (relative entropy) and its scaling limit \(2^{-n}H(\cdot\mid\cdot)\) for continuous martingales, proving inequalities and convex envelopes in terms of quadratic variation. It does not analyze Wasserstein penalties, the chain-constructed \(D^W_{N,p}\), nor any dynamic risk measure optimization \(\inf_H\rho_N\). Thus it does not solve the stated open problem, but provides background/analogous results for another divergence where the scaling limit yields an integral functional of quadratic variation.

Remark 5. One limitation of our analysis is the assumption that the exact distribution of uncertainties is known. In practice, the true distribution of these uncertainties may remain unknown, highlighting the importance of incorporating distributional robustness into the control policy. Recent work in a different context has demonstrated stability in expectation within the stochastic MPC framework when the Wasserstein distance between the true and nominal distributions is bounded [45]. Nevertheless, the dynamic regret analysis regarding the distributional robustness property remains an open question.

Analyzing dynamic regret under inexact knowledge of the distribution presents an intriguing avenue for future research.
title: Dynamic regret bounds for distributionally robust stochastic model predictive control policies
background_latex:
Consider the finite-horizon stochastic control problem over stages \(t=0,1,\dots,T\) with random disturbances \(\xi:=\{\xi_t\}_{t=0}^T\). The system evolves according to linear dynamics with additive and multiplicative uncertainty
\[
 x_t = A(\xi_t)x_{t-1}+B(\xi_t)u_{t-1}+d(\xi_t),
\]
and incurs a (possibly random) quadratic stage cost
\[
\ell(x_t,u_t;\xi_t)=\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}x_t\\u_t\end{bmatrix}^\top
\begin{bmatrix}Q(\xi_t)&0\\0&R(\xi_t)\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x_t\\u_t\end{bmatrix}-
\begin{bmatrix}q(\xi_t)\\r(\xi_t)\end{bmatrix}^\top\begin{bmatrix}x_t\\u_t\end{bmatrix}.
\]
A (nonanticipative) control policy chooses \(u_t\) after observing the history \(\xi_{0:t}\). Let \(J^\star(\xi_0;w_{-1})\) denote the optimal expected total cost over \(t=0,\dots,T\) under the true distribution of \(\xi\), given initial augmented state-control \(w_{-1}=(x_{-1},u_{-1})\) and initial uncertainty \(\xi_0\).

Stochastic model predictive control (SMPC) with prediction horizon \(W\) constructs a closed-loop policy by repeatedly solving, at each stage \(\tau\), a truncated-horizon stochastic optimal control problem over the next \(W\) stages using a (nominal) conditional distribution of future disturbances given \(\xi_{0:\tau}\), then applying only the first control action and re-optimizing at the next stage. Let \(J^{(W)}(\xi_0;w_{-1})\) denote the expected total cost incurred by the resulting SMPC closed-loop policy.

The dynamic regret of the SMPC policy is
\[
\mathrm{Regret}(W):=J^{(W)}(\xi_0;w_{-1})-J^\star(\xi_0;w_{-1}).
\]
In the paper's main results, dynamic regret bounds are proved under the assumption that the distribution of \(\xi\) is exactly known (and, for the main analysis, has finite support so that a scenario tree representation is available).

In practice the true distribution of \(\xi\) may be unknown. A distributionally robust variant of SMPC would design the truncated problems using a nominal distribution \(\widehat{\mathbb P}\) but aim to guarantee performance under an unknown true distribution \(\mathbb P\) belonging to some ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) (for example, a Wasserstein ball around \(\widehat{\mathbb P}\)). Let \(J_{\mathbb P}^\star\) and \(J_{\mathbb P}^{(W)}\) denote the optimal and SMPC expected costs when expectations are taken under \(\mathbb P\).

\[
J_{\mathbb P}^{(W)}(\xi_0;w_{-1})-J_{\mathbb P}^\star(\xi_0;w_{-1})
\]
under inexact knowledge of the distribution of \(\xi\) (for instance, in a distributionally robust setting where \(\mathbb P\) is only known to belong to an ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\)).

A related question is: how well can one approximate an \(n\)-dimensional symmetric convex body with a finite intersection of \(m\) (co-centered) ellipsoids, with \(m\) growing potentially with \(n\)? Since we have shown that a GE-\(d\), with \(d = 2m-3\), can exactly represent an intersection of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids (see Corollary 5.6 and Theorem 5.1), progress on this question can potentially improve our approximation factor in Theorem 5.7.
title: Approximate symmetric convex bodies by intersections of co-centered ellipsoids in high dimensions
background_latex:
Let \(C\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) be a symmetric convex body, i.e., a compact convex set with nonempty interior such that \(x\in C\Rightarrow -x\in C\). An ellipsoid (centered at the origin) is a set of the form
\[E(Q):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQx\le 1\},\]
where \(Q\in \mathbb{S}^n_{++}\) is symmetric positive definite. (Equivalently, an ellipsoid is the unit ball of a quadratic norm.)

For an integer \(m\ge 1\), an intersection of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids means a set of the form
\[\bigcap_{i=1}^m E(Q_i)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQ_i x\le 1\ \text{for all } i=1,\dots,m\},\]
with all ellipsoids centered at the origin.

Given two symmetric convex bodies \(K,L\subset \mathbb{R}^n\), a standard multiplicative (sandwich) approximation notion is: \(K\) \(\varepsilon\)-approximates \(L\) if
\[K\subseteq L\subseteq (1+\varepsilon)K,\]
where \((1+\varepsilon)K:=\{(1+\varepsilon)x: x\in K\}\) is a uniform radial scaling.

The paper introduces generalized ellipsoids (GEs) and shows (i) any intersection of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids can be represented exactly as a generalized ellipsoid of degree \(d\le 2m-3\), and (ii) every symmetric convex body can be approximated by a GE with a quantitative degree bound obtained via known results on polytopic approximation. The question below asks directly about approximation by intersections of ellipsoids, which would in turn sharpen the degree-vs-accuracy bounds for GE approximation.
problem_definition_latex:
For fixed dimension \(n\) and approximation parameter \(\varepsilon>0\), determine (or tightly bound) the smallest integer \(m=m(n,\varepsilon)\) such that for every symmetric convex body \(C\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) there exist positive definite matrices \(Q_1,\dots,Q_m\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}\) with
\[\bigcap_{i=1}^m \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQ_i x\le 1\}\ \subseteq\ C\ \subseteq\ (1+\varepsilon)\,\bigcap_{i=1}^m \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQ_i x\le 1\}.
\]
Equivalently, characterize the best possible approximation quality achievable by intersections of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids as a function of \(m\) and \(n\).

Given two symmetric convex bodies \(K,L\subset \mathbb{R}^n\), a standard multiplicative (sandwich) approximation notion is: \(K\) \(\varepsilon\)-approximates \(L\) if
\[K\subseteq L\subseteq (1+\varepsilon)K,\]
where \((1+\varepsilon)K:=\{(1+\varepsilon)x: x\in K\}\) is a uniform radial scaling.

The paper introduces generalized ellipsoids (GEs) and shows (i) any intersection of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids can be represented exactly as a generalized ellipsoid of degree \(d\le 2m-3\), and (ii) every symmetric convex body can be approximated by a GE with a quantitative degree bound obtained via known results on polytopic approximation. The question below asks directly about approximation by intersections of ellipsoids, which would in turn sharpen the degree-vs-accuracy bounds for GE approximation.

For fixed dimension \(n\) and approximation parameter \(\varepsilon>0\), determine (or tightly bound) the smallest integer \(m=m(n,\varepsilon)\) such that for every symmetric convex body \(C\subset \mathbb{R}^n\) there exist positive definite matrices \(Q_1,\dots,Q_m\in\mathbb{S}^n_{++}\) with
\[\bigcap_{i=1}^m \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQ_i x\le 1\}\ \subseteq\ C\ \subseteq\ (1+\varepsilon)\,\bigcap_{i=1}^m \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: x^TQ_i x\le 1\}.
\]
Equivalently, characterize the best possible approximation quality achievable by intersections of \(m\) co-centered ellipsoids as a function of \(m\) and \(n\).

title: Existence of non-deterministic equilibrium portfolio strategies under rank-dependent utility
background_latex:
Fix a finite time horizon \(T>0\). Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\{\mathcal F_t\}_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb P)\) support a \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion \(W\). The market has one risk-free asset with constant rate \(r\) and \(n\le d\) risky assets with constant excess-return vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^n\) and volatility matrix \(\sigma\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) such that \(\sigma\sigma^{\top}\) is positive definite. A (possibly stochastic) trading strategy is an \(\mathbb R^n\)-valued progressively measurable process \(\pi(t)\) with \(\int_0^T |\pi(t)^{\top}\mu|\,dt+\int_0^T \|\pi(t)^{\top}\sigma\|^2\,dt<\infty\) a.s., interpreted as the proportions of current wealth invested in the \(n\) stocks. The associated self-financing wealth process \(X^{\pi}\) with initial wealth \(X^{\pi}(t)=x>0\) satisfies
\[
\frac{dX^{\pi}(s)}{X^{\pi}(s)}=\bigl(r+\pi(s)^{\top}\mu\bigr)\,ds+\pi(s)^{\top}\sigma\,dW(s),\qquad s\in[t,T].
\]
The agent has CRRA outcome utility
\[
U(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\gamma}x^{\gamma},&\gamma\ne 0,\\ \log x,&\gamma=0,\end{cases}\qquad x>0,
\]
for some \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\). Preferences are rank-dependent: for each time \(t\), terminal wealth \(X\) is evaluated by a (possibly time-dependent) probability weighting function \(w(t,\cdot):[0,1]\to[0,1]\), strictly increasing with \(w(t,0)=0\), \(w(t,1)=1\), and sufficiently regular so the rank-dependent utility functional is well-defined. Writing \(Q_X^t(p)\) for the conditional quantile of \(X\) given \(\mathcal F_t\), the time-\(t\) rank-dependent utility is
\[
J(t,x;\pi)=\int_0^1 U\bigl(Q_{X^{\pi}(T)}^t(p)\bigr)\,w(t,dp),
\]
where integration is with respect to the Lebesgue--Stieltjes measure induced by \(w(t,\cdot)\).

A strict equilibrium strategy (SES) \(\pi\) is an admissible strategy such that, for every \(t\in[0,T)\) and every bounded \(\mathcal F_t\)-measurable direction \(\kappa\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal F_t;\mathbb R^n)\setminus\{0\}\) for which the spike-perturbed strategy \(\pi^{t,\varepsilon,\kappa}\) (equal to \(\pi+\kappa\) on \([t,t+\varepsilon)\) and to \(\pi\) otherwise) is admissible for small \(\varepsilon>0\), one has the strict first-order inequality
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\varepsilon'\in(0,\varepsilon)}\frac{J(t,x;\pi^{t,\varepsilon',\kappa})-J(t,x;\pi)}{\varepsilon'}<0\quad\text{a.s. for all }x>0.
\]
The paper focuses on deterministic SES (DSES), i.e., \(\pi(t)\) deterministic, and derives characterizations via singular ODEs for these DSES under various assumptions on \(w\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists an SES \(\pi\) that is \emph{not} deterministic (i.e., \(\pi\) is not a deterministic function of time) for the continuous-time portfolio selection problem with rank-dependent utility \(J(t,x;\pi)\) in the above incomplete Brownian market.

Equivalently: establish existence (or nonexistence) of progressively measurable, non-deterministic strategies \(\pi\) satisfying the strict equilibrium condition
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow 0}\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\varepsilon'\in(0,\varepsilon)}\frac{J(t,x;\pi^{t,\varepsilon',\kappa})-J(t,x;\pi)}{\varepsilon'}<0\quad\text{a.s. for all }t\in[0,T),\ x>0,\ \kappa\in L^{\infty}(\mathcal F_t;\mathbb R^n)\setminus\{0\}.
\]
