literature_review.synthesis:
In the NeurIPS 2019 SPO generalization paper, the margin-based bounds for strongly convex feasible regions hinge on showing that the \(\gamma\)-margin SPO loss is Lipschitz in the dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) (Theorem 3), and then converting this Lipschitz property into a Rademacher complexity bound via Maurer’s vector-contraction inequality. The authors explicitly restrict the final contraction step to the \(\ell_2\) setting (Theorem 4) because the most general available vector contraction tool they cite (Maurer 2016) is Euclidean; they note only partial analogues for \(\ell_\infty\) and leave general norms (including \(\ell_q\)) open.

The forward-citing literature provided here does not resolve this contraction question. Instead, multiple subsequent predict-then-optimize and learning-to-optimize works (e.g., Integrated conditional estimation-optimization; Decision-focused learning with directional gradients; End-to-end learning to warm-start for real-time quadratic optimization; Risk bounds and calibration for a smart predict-then-optimize method) continue to formulate Lipschitzness and stability in \(\ell_2\) precisely so that Maurer’s \(\ell_2\) vector contraction can be applied. This pattern reinforces that a norm-dependent contraction inequality \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n(\phi\circ\mathcal H)\le C(\|\cdot\|)L\,\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n(\mathcal H)\) would have immediate impact by allowing analyses to align with the natural geometry of the decision/parameter spaces.

On the tools side, work on uniform convexity/smoothness of norm balls (Local and global uniform convexity conditions) suggests a plausible route: in Banach-space language, contraction constants typically depend on type/cotype or uniform smoothness parameters of \((\mathbb R^d,\|\cdot\|)\) and its dual. However, none of the cited papers actually prove a Maurer-style vector contraction inequality for general norms or provide explicit constants for \(\ell_q\) beyond the known special cases. Thus, based on the provided forward citations, the problem remains open; promising directions include leveraging Banach-space type/smoothness (especially for \(\ell_q\), Schatten-\(q\), and group norms) to obtain explicit \(C(\|\cdot\|)\) and identifying the right multivariate complexity notion that matches \(\|\cdot\|\) and \(\|\cdot\|_*\).

sources.title: Integrated conditional estimation-optimization
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a finite-sample generalization bound for its integrated conditional estimation-optimization (ICEO) method by combining (a) Lipschitzness of a regularized optimization oracle and (b) Maurer’s (2016) 
vector contraction inequality
 for 
\(\ell_2\)-Lipschitz maps. Concretely, under Assumption 3 (\(c(\cdot)\) is \(L_c\)-Lipschitz in \(w\) and \(\phi\) is 1-strongly convex), Proposition 2 shows \(w_\rho\) is \((L_c/\rho)\)-Lipschitz in \(p\) (in \(\ell_2\)), implying \(c\circ w_\rho\) is \((L_c^2/\rho)\)-Lipschitz. Then Theorem 3 states that for any \(\delta\in(0,1]\) and \(\rho_n>0\), with prob. \(\ge 1-\delta\), for all \(f\in\mathcal H\):
\[
R(w_{\rho_n}\circ f)\le \widehat R_n(w_{\rho_n}\circ f)+\sqrt{2}\,\frac{L_c^2}{\rho_n}\,R_n(\mathcal H)+\bar c\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}.
\]
The step bounding \(R_n(c\circ w_{\rho_n}\circ\mathcal H)\) by \(\sqrt{2}(L_c^2/\rho_n)R_n(\mathcal H)\) explicitly invokes Maurer (2016), which is an \(\ell_2\)-based vector contraction result.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a vector-contraction inequality for empirical Rademacher complexity when \(\phi\) is Lipschitz w.r.t. a general norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), extending Maurer (2016) beyond \(\ell_2\) (and some \(\ell_\infty\) cases). This paper does not develop such a general-norm contraction inequality; instead it stays within the \(\ell_2\) framework precisely to apply Maurer (2016). It even notes (Assumption 3.A) that \(c(\cdot)\) is Lipschitz in output measured by \(\|\cdot\|_2\), and then applies Maurer’s \(\ell_2\)-based contraction to relate the scalar Rademacher complexity of the composed loss class \(c\circ w_\rho\circ\mathcal H\) to the multivariate Rademacher complexity of \(\mathcal H\). Thus the paper provides additional motivation and an application context where a general-norm contraction would be useful (since decisions are measured in a generic norm \(\|\cdot\|\) but outputs are forced into \(\ell_2\) to use existing tools), but it does not resolve the open problem nor extend the inequality to general norms \(\ell_q\), etc.

sources.title: Decision-focused learning with directional gradients
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves uniform approximation/generalization bounds for its perturbation-gradient surrogate losses in predict-then-optimize. In particular (Theorem 3.4), under boundedness and a Lipschitz log-conditional density assumption, for any step size h with 0<h<1/L, with probability at least 1-\delta\),
\[
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Big|\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \hat\ell_h^b(f(X_i),Y_i)-\mathbb E[\ell(f(X),Y)]\Big| \lesssim BLh + \frac{B^2}{h}\,\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal F) + B\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}},
\]
where \(\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal F)=\mathbb E[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i^\top f(X_i)]\) is the multivariate Rademacher complexity. They obtain excess-regret bounds (Theorem 3.8) such as \(\mathrm{ERegret}(\hat f_h)\lesssim \sqrt{B^3L\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal F)}+\sqrt{B/n}\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a vector-contraction inequality for empirical Rademacher complexity under general norms \(\|\cdot\|\) (beyond \(\ell_2\), \(\ell_\infty\)). This paper explicitly uses Maurer (2016) vector contraction to control the Rademacher complexity of a composed class arising from a Lipschitz surrogate loss (see proof of Theorem 3.4), but it does so with the Euclidean norm \(\|\cdot\|_2\): Assumption 1.1 bounds \(\|z\|_2\), Lemma 2.1 gives Lipschitzness in \(\|\cdot\|_2\), and the contraction step yields a factor \(\propto (B/h)\mathfrak R_n(\mathcal F)\). The paper does not develop a contraction inequality for a general norm \(\|\cdot\|\) nor identify an explicit constant \(C(\|\cdot\|)\) for \(\ell_q\) norms. Still, it provides a concrete application context where such a general-norm contraction would immediately extend their bounds (e.g., if decisions are bounded in a non-Euclidean norm or if one wants Lipschitzness w.r.t. \(\|\cdot\|_q\)).

sources.title: Local and global uniform convexity conditions
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops quantitative equivalences between uniform convexity/smoothness of norm balls (and their gauges/support functions) and scaling inequalities. In particular, for a centrally symmetric convex body (norm ball) \(C\subset\mathbb R^m\) and \(p\ge2\), \(q\in(1,2]\) with \(1/p+1/q=1\), Theorem 4.1 shows equivalence between: (i) \((\alpha,p)\)-uniform convexity of \(C\) (modulus \(\delta_{\|\cdot\|_C}(\varepsilon)\ge \alpha\varepsilon^p\)); (ii) a global scaling inequality \(\langle d, y-x\rangle\ge \alpha\|d\|_{C^\circ}\,\|y-x\|_C^p\) for \(y\in\partial C\), \(d\in N_C(y)\); and (iii) uniform smoothness of the power of the support function \(\sigma_C^q\): there exists \(c\) such that \(\sigma_C^q\) is \((c,q)\)-uniformly smooth w.r.t. \(\|\cdot\|_{C^\circ}\). Theorem 5.1 gives local analogues at a boundary point/direction. Section 6.2 uses these to bound Rademacher complexity of low-norm linear predictors when the regularizer ball is uniformly convex.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a vector-contraction inequality for empirical Rademacher complexity under a general norm \(\|\cdot\|\) for \(L\)-Lipschitz \(\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). This paper does not prove such a contraction inequality. Instead it studies geometric/functional properties of general norm balls (uniform convexity/smoothness, duality, scaling inequalities) and derives a (scalar) Rademacher complexity bound for low-norm linear classes (Theorem 6.5) via Banach-space type. These results are potentially relevant tools because vector-contraction constants for general norms often depend on type/cotype or smoothness of the underlying Banach space; the paper supplies quantitative links between uniform convexity/smoothness and Rademacher type, but it does not address contraction for composing \(\phi\) with vector-valued classes \(\mathcal H\) nor provide a bound of the form \(\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n(\phi\circ\mathcal H)\le C(\|\cdot\|)L\widehat{\mathfrak R}_n(\mathcal H)\).

sources.title: Risk bounds and calibration for a smart predict-then-optimize method
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper’s main theoretical results are calibration/risk bounds for the SPO+ surrogate loss in predict-then-optimize. For a bounded polyhedral feasible set \(S\), it proves a uniform lower bound on the SPO+ calibration function of the form \(\hat\delta_{\ell_{\mathrm{SPO}+}}(\epsilon) \ge c\,\min\{\epsilon^2,\epsilon\}\) over a restricted distribution class (Theorem 3.1), yielding an excess SPO risk rate \(O(n^{-1/4})\) when combined with a generalization bound (Corollary 3.1). For \(S\) a level set of a \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth function with respect to a norm \(\|\cdot\|_A\), it proves linear calibration \(\hat\delta_{\ell_{\mathrm{SPO}+}}(\epsilon)\ge c'\,\epsilon\) (Theorem 4.1), yielding an excess SPO risk rate \(O(n^{-1/2})\) (Corollary 4.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a vector-contraction inequality for empirical Rademacher complexity under general norms \(\|\cdot\|\), extending Maurer (2016) beyond \(\ell_2\). This paper does not develop new vector-contraction inequalities. It explicitly relies on Maurer’s \(\ell_2\)-based vector contraction to derive generalization/sample-complexity bounds for SPO+ (see discussion before Corollary 3.1 and Appendix A). While the paper uses generic norms and dual norms in its optimization/calibration analysis (e.g., Assumption 4.1 with a norm \(\|\cdot\|_A\)), it does not translate Lipschitzness under a general norm into Rademacher complexity bounds via a new contraction tool. Thus it provides motivation and an application context where such a general-norm contraction inequality would be useful, but it does not resolve the open problem.

sources.title: End-to-end learning to warm-start for real-time quadratic optimization
sources.theorem_or_result:
Assuming the Douglas–Rachford (DR) operator family \(T_\theta\) is contractive in \(\ell_2\), i.e. \(\|T_\theta(z)-T_\theta(w)\|_2\le \beta_\theta\|z-w\|_2\) with \(\beta:=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}\beta_\theta\in(0,1)\), they prove a generalization bound for end-to-end learned warm-starts: with probability \(\ge 1-\delta\), for all networks \(h_W\in\mathcal H\) satisfying \(\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{fix}\,T_\theta}(h_W(\theta))\le B\),
\[
R^k(h_W)\le \widehat R^k(h_W)+2\beta^k\Big(2\sqrt2\,\mathrm{erad}(\mathcal H)+\frac{3B\log(2/\delta)}{2N}\Big),
\]
where \(R^k\) is expected fixed-point residual after \(k\) DR iterations and \(\mathrm{erad}(\mathcal H)\) is multivariate empirical Rademacher complexity of the warm-start network class. The proof uses Maurer (2016, Cor. 4) vector-contraction in \(\ell_2\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for vector-contraction inequalities for empirical Rademacher complexity under general norms \(\|\cdot\|\) (e.g. \(\ell_q\)), extending Maurer’s \(\ell_2\) result. This paper does not extend contraction to other norms; instead it applies Maurer (2016) in \(\ell_2\) to bound a Rademacher term arising in a learning-to-warm-start analysis. The only Lipschitz/contraction property used is \(2\beta^k\)-Lipschitzness of \(\ell_\theta\circ T_\theta^k\) in \(\|\cdot\|_2\), followed by Maurer’s \(\ell_2\) vector contraction. Thus it provides motivation and an application context where a general-norm contraction inequality would be useful, but it does not develop such an inequality.

sources.title: On learning latent models with multi-instance weak supervision
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves Rademacher-style generalization/error bounds for multi-instance partial-label learning under semantic loss and its top-k approximation. In particular, for a single classifier and known transition \(\sigma\) that is 1- and \(M\)-unambiguous, with probability \(\ge 1-\delta\):
\[
R_{01}(f) \le \Phi\Big((k+1)\big(\widehat R^k_P(f;\sigma;T_P) + 2\sqrt{k}M^{3/2} R_{Mm_P}(F) + \sqrt{\tfrac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m_P}}\big)\Big),
\]
where \(R_{Mm_P}(F)\) is a (vector-valued) Rademacher complexity of the scoring class \(F\) (Def. 8) and \(\Phi\) is increasing with \(\lim_{t\to 0}\Phi(t)/t=1\) (Theorem 2). Analogous bounds are given for multiple classifiers (Theorem 4) and for unknown transitions under an unambiguous transition space (Theorem 5).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a vector-contraction inequality for empirical Rademacher complexity for Lipschitz maps \(\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) under general norms \(\|\cdot\|\), extending known \(\ell_2\) vector contraction results. This paper does use a contraction lemma (citing Cortes et al. 2016) to bound the Rademacher complexity of a composed loss class arising from semantic loss/top-\(k\) WMC, but:
- the contraction lemma employed is explicitly \(\ell_2\)-based (Lipschitz w.r.t. \(\|\cdot\|_2\)) and yields bounds in terms of an \(\ell_2\)-type vector Rademacher complexity;
- there is no development of contraction inequalities for general norms (e.g., \(\ell_q\) with \(q\ne 2,\infty\)), nor an explicit constant \(C(\|\cdot\|)\) depending on an arbitrary norm.
Thus it does not solve the stated open problem. At best, it is tangentially relevant as an application context where such generalized vector-contraction tools could tighten or generalize their Rademacher bounds for semantic loss under alternative norm/Lipschitz structures.

title: Compute a competitive equilibrium utility profile for divisible chores with variable size
background_latex:
There are \(n\) agents and \(m\) divisible chores, with one unit of each chore to be allocated. Agent \(i\in[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\) receives a bundle \(z_i=(z_{i,1},\dots,z_{i,m})\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}\), where \(z_{i,j}\) is the fraction of chore \(j\in[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}\) assigned to agent \(i\). Feasibility requires \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_{i,j}=1\) for every chore \(j\).

Preferences are additive and strictly negative (chores): values are given by a matrix \(v\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}_{<0}\), where \(v_{i,j}<0\) is agent \(i\)'s value for performing one unit of chore \(j\). The utility of agent \(i\) for bundle \(z_i\) is
\[u_i(z_i)=\sum_{j=1}^m v_{i,j} z_{i,j},\]
and the utility profile of an allocation \(z\) is \(u(z)=(u_1(z_1),\dots,u_n(z_n))\in\mathbb{R}^n_{<0}\).

Agents have (virtual) strictly negative budgets \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n_{<0}\). A price vector is \(p\in\mathbb{R}^m_{<0}\), and the price of a bundle \(x\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}\) is \(p(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j x_j\).

A feasible allocation \(z\) is a competitive allocation (competitive equilibrium with budgets \(b\)) if there exists \(p\in\mathbb{R}^m_{<0}\) such that each agent \(i\) maximizes \(u_i(x)\) over all bundles \(x\in\mathbb{R}^m_{\ge 0}\) satisfying \(p(x)\le b_i\). A competitive utility profile is any \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for which there exists a competitive allocation \(z\) with \(u=u(z)\).

In the paper, when either \(n\) or \(m\) is fixed, there is a strongly polynomial-time algorithm that enumerates all competitive utility profiles for additive chores; however, the complexity when both \(n\) and \(m\) are variable is unresolved.
problem_definition_latex: Design an algorithm that, given arbitrary \(n,m\), a valuation matrix \(v\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}_{<0}\) and budgets \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n_{<0}\), computes at least one competitive utility profile \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n_{<0}\) (equivalently, one competitive allocation) in time polynomial in \(n+m\).

title: Deciding existence of equilibria in Fisher markets with earning and utility limits
background_latex:
A (linear) Fisher market with satiation consists of:
1) A set of buyers \(B\) and a set of divisible goods \(G\), each good \(j\in G\) having unit supply.
2) For each buyer \(i\in B\): a budget \(m_i\ge 0\), a utility cap \(c_i>0\), and per-unit values \(u_{ij}\ge 0\) for goods \(j\in G\).
3) For each good \(j\in G\): an earning (income) cap \(d_j>0\).

An allocation is a matrix \(x=(x_{ij})_{i\in B, j\in G}\) with \(x_{ij}\in[0,1]\) and \(\sum_{i\in B} x_{ij}=x_j\le 1\) for each good \(j\). Buyer \(i\)'s budget-additive utility is
\[
U_i(x_i)=\min\Bigl(c_i,\;\sum_{j\in G} u_{ij}x_{ij}\Bigr),\qquad x_i=(x_{ij})_{j\in G}.
\]
Let \(p=(p_j)_{j\in G}\) be nonnegative prices. Given prices \(p\), define buyer \(i\)'s maximum bang-per-buck (MBB) ratio as
\[
\alpha_i=\max_{j\in G: p_j>0}\frac{u_{ij}}{p_j},
\]
(with the convention that goods with \(p_j=0\) are treated separately). A bundle is MBB (also called thrifty) for buyer \(i\) if it assigns positive amount only to goods attaining the maximum ratio \(u_{ij}/p_j=\alpha_i\).

A demand bundle for buyer \(i\) at prices \(p\) is any \(x_i\) that maximizes \(U_i(x_i)\) subject to the budget constraint \(\sum_j p_j x_{ij}\le m_i\). A demand bundle is called modest if it does not overshoot the cap, i.e., \(\sum_j u_{ij}x_{ij}\le c_i\) (equivalently, if capped then it hits \(c_i\) exactly).

For each good \(j\), a seller chooses an effective supply \(e_j\le 1\) to maximize revenue up to its earning cap, i.e., earns \(\min(d_j, p_j e_j)\). A modest supply at prices \(p\) is
\[
e_j=\min\Bigl(1,\frac{d_j}{p_j}\Bigr)
\]
(with \(e_j=1\) if \(p_j=0\) by continuity).

A thrifty and modest equilibrium is a pair \((x,p)\) such that:
1) \(p_j\ge 0\) for all \(j\).
2) Each buyer \(i\) receives a thrifty (MBB) and modest demand bundle at prices \(p\).
3) Each good \(j\) uses a modest supply \(e_j\) and is not overallocated: \(x_j\le e_j\).
4) Walras' law holds: \(p_j(e_j-x_j)=0\) for all \(j\) (so if a good is not fully sold under its modest supply, its price is zero).

The computational decision problem asks, given integer input data \((u_{ij},m_i,c_i,d_j)\), whether at least one thrifty and modest equilibrium exists.

Given a Fisher market instance specified by \(B,G\) and nonnegative parameters \((u_{ij})\), \((m_i)\), \((c_i)\), and \((d_j)\), determine whether there exists a thrifty and modest equilibrium \((x,p)\) satisfying:
\[
\text{(i) } p\ge 0;\qquad \text{(ii) each }x_i\text{ is an MBB and modest demand bundle at }p;\qquad \text{(iii) }x_j\le \min\Bigl(1,\frac{d_j}{p_j}\Bigr);\qquad \text{(iv) } p_j\Bigl(\min\Bigl(1,\frac{d_j}{p_j}\Bigr)-x_j\Bigr)=0\ \forall j.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem from Garg–Hoefer–Mehlhorn asks for a decision procedure for existence of a thrifty and modest equilibrium in linear Fisher markets with both buyer utility caps \(c_i\) (budget-additive satiation) and seller earning caps \(d_j\). The source paper establishes that equilibrium existence is not guaranteed in general, and identifies the money-clearing condition \(\sum_{i\in \hat B} m_i \le \sum_{j\in N(\hat B)} d_j\) as a sufficient (but not necessary) condition for existence. It further shows nonconvexity of the equilibrium set, provides an FPTAS for approximate equilibria in money-clearing markets via perturbation and a descending-price method, and places exact equilibrium computation (under money clearing) in \(\mathrm{PPAD}\cap\mathrm{PLS}\), with polynomial-time solvability when the number of buyers or goods is constant.

Among the forward citations provided, the thesis “Nash Welfare, Valuated Matroids, and Gross Substitues” contributes related algorithmic tools (auction algorithms for approximate equilibria under weak gross substitutes and spending-restricted variants, including capped utilities in budget-SPLC form). However, it does not resolve the core existence/decidability question for the combined earning+utility cap Fisher model with the specific thrifty/modest equilibrium notion. Consequently, based on the available citation set, the decision problem remains open beyond the sufficient money-clearing regime, and no complete characterization or hardness result is identified here.

Promising directions suggested by the source paper’s techniques include: (i) seeking a necessary-and-sufficient combinatorial condition generalizing money clearing to incorporate utility caps, (ii) proving hardness (e.g., NP-hardness) of existence when money clearing fails, potentially via reductions that exploit nonconvexity and zero-price components, and (iii) leveraging the LCP/Lemke framework to derive certificates of nonexistence or to separate equilibrium from spurious LCP solutions without assuming money clearing.

sources.title: Nash Welfare, Valuated Matroids, and Gross Substitues
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis develops auction algorithms for computing approximate equilibria in exchange/Fisher markets under weak gross substitutes (WGS) demands, and applies them to spending-restricted equilibria and Nash social welfare approximations. In particular, it gives an auction algorithm that computes a 4\varepsilon\)-approximate market equilibrium for exchange markets with WGS demand oracles (Theorem 2.3.1), and a modified auction algorithm that computes a \(4\varepsilon\)-approximate spending-restricted (SR) equilibrium for Fisher markets with WGS demands (Theorem 3.1.3), with implementations for budget-SPLC (capped) utilities (Theorem 3.2.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for deciding existence of a thrifty and modest equilibrium in a linear Fisher market with both buyer utility caps \(c_i\) (satiation) and seller earning caps \(d_j\), i.e., a Fisher market with both utility limits and earning limits. This thesis does not study that equilibrium concept or the decision problem. It treats (i) exchange markets and Fisher markets under WGS demands, (ii) spending-restricted equilibria (a different model: caps on spending per good of the form \(\min\{1,1/p_j\}\)), and (iii) capped utilities in the budget-SPLC setting but without seller earning caps \(d_j\) and without the specific "modest supply"/Walras-law conditions of earning-limited markets. Thus it does not resolve existence/decidability for the earning+utility limited Fisher model; at best it provides algorithmic techniques (auction-style price adjustment, handling of utility caps in SR/Gale-demand formulations) that might be adaptable.

title: Characterize when constant expected unvisited vertices requires duration at least hitting time
background_latex:
Consider a growing graph process in discrete time in which, for each integer 
\(i\ge 1\), there is a connected simple undirected graph \(G^{(i)}=(V^{(i)},E^{(i)})\) with \(V^{(i)}=\{v_1,\dots,v_i\}\) and \(G^{(i+1)}\) is obtained from \(G^{(i)}\) by adding one new vertex \(v_{i+1}\) and connecting it to at least one existing vertex (so \(V^{(i)}\subseteq V^{(i+1)}\)).

Let \(d:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) be a duration (growth-rate) function: the system stays on \(G^{(i)}\) for exactly \(d(i)\) consecutive random-walk steps before the next vertex is added. Define the change times \(T_1:=0\) and \(T_{i}:=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} d(j)\) for \(i\ge 2\), so that the vertex set size equals \(i\) during times \(t\in[T_i,T_{i+1})\).

A random walk on this growing graph is specified by transition matrices \(P^{(i)}\in[0,1]^{V^{(i)}\times V^{(i)}}\), where during the period when the current graph is \(G^{(i)}\), the walker evolves as the time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition matrix \(P^{(i)}\). Assume each \(P^{(i)}\) is irreducible (so the walk on \(G^{(i)}\) is well-defined) and define its hitting time
\[
 t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i) \, := \, \max_{u,v\in V^{(i)}} \mathbb{E}\big[\min\{t\ge 0: X_0=u,\ X_t=v\}\big],
\]
where \((X_t)_{t\ge 0}\) denotes a Markov chain with transition matrix \(P^{(i)}\).

Let \((Z_t)_{t\ge 0}\) denote the overall walk on the growing graph (so \(Z_t\in V_t\), and in fact \(Z_t\in V_{t-1}\) for \(t\ge 1\)). Define the number of unvisited vertices just before the \((n+1)\)-st vertex is added by
\[
U(n) \, := \, \left|\, V^{(n)} \setminus \bigcup_{t=0}^{T_{n+1}} \{Z_t\}\,\right|,
\]
and write \(\mathbb{E}[U(n)]\) for its expectation under the law of the walk determined by \((d,(G^{(i)}),(P^{(i)}))\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether the following implication holds uniformly over all random walks on growing graphs as defined above:

If \(\mathbb{E}[U(n)] = O(1)\) as \(n\to\infty\), must it be the case that
\[
 d(i) = \Omega\big(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\big) \quad \text{as } i\to\infty?
\]
Equivalently, decide whether there exists a family \((d,(G^{(i)}),(P^{(i)}))\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[U(n)]\) stays bounded while \(d(i)/t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\to 0\), or prove that no such family exists.

literature_review.synthesis:
In the RWoGG model of Kijima–Shimizu–Shiraga (arXiv:2008.10837), the central sufficient condition for bounded expected unvisited vertices is Theorem 1.2: if there exists \(C>1\) with \(d(i)\ge C\,t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\) for all large \(i\), then \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\), and if \(d(i)/t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\to\infty\) then \(\mathbb E[U(n)]\to 0\). The paper also shows that for specific families (complete graphs and paths/Metropolis walks) the scale \(d(i)\asymp t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\) is essentially tight for achieving \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\), but it leaves open whether such a lower bound must hold uniformly over all growing-graph processes.

Forward-citing work so far does not resolve this necessity question. The most conceptually adjacent tool is the theory of reversible time-inhomogeneous chains on a fixed vertex set with common stationary distribution, where one can bound the probability of avoiding a vertex over \(T\) steps by \(\exp(-T/t_{\mathrm{HIT}})\) and obtain cover-time bounds in terms of worst static hitting time; however, the fixed-vertex-set and common-\(\pi\) assumptions do not directly apply to vertex growth. Other forward citations develop coupling/monotonicity frameworks (LHaGG/weakly-LHaGG, pausing couplings) and sharp recurrence/transience thresholds for RWoGG on growing trees, hypercubes, and increasing-dimension grids; these results indicate that some global properties (recurrence to a root/origin) can occur with \(d(i)\) far smaller than typical cover times, but they do not control the number of distinct vertices visited.

At present, the implication \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\Rightarrow d(i)=\Omega(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i))\) remains open. Promising directions include: (i) attempting to adapt dynamic-graph hitting-time avoidance bounds to the growing-vertex setting by proving that each round begins sufficiently close to stationarity (or by controlling the \(\ell_2(\pi)\) distance as in the original paper’s Theorem 3.6 machinery), and (ii) searching for counterexamples where new vertices attach in a way that makes them easy to hit quickly even though worst-case \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\) is large (e.g., graphs with a small “gateway” set that the walk visits frequently, while worst-case pairs are separated by bottlenecks).

sources.title: Reversible random walks on dynamic graphs
sources.theorem_or_result: For a time-inhomogeneous random walk on a fixed vertex set with transition matrices \((P_t)_{t\ge1}\) that are irreducible, reversible (often lazy), and share a common stationary distribution \(\pi\), the paper proves uniform bounds on dynamic hitting/cover/coalescing times in terms of the worst static hitting time: in particular, for one walk, \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}((P_t)) = O(\max_t t_{\mathrm{hit}}(P_t))\) (Theorem 1.4(i), with laziness), and \(t_{\mathrm{cov}}((P_t)) = O(\max_t t_{\mathrm{hit}}(P_t)\,\log n)\) (Theorem 1.4(ii)). A key lemma is that if \(X_0\sim\pi\), then for any vertex \(w\) and \(T\ge0\), \(\Pr[\wedge_{t=0}^T\{X_t\neq w\}]\le \prod_{t=1}^T(1-1/t_{\mathrm{hit}}(P_t))\le \exp(-T/t_{\mathrm{HIT}})\) where \(t_{\mathrm{HIT}}:=\max_t t_{\mathrm{hit}}(P_t)\) (Lemma 1.11/4.3).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns a *growing-vertex* graph process with dwell times \(d(i)\) on \(G^{(i)}\), and asks whether bounded expected number of unvisited vertices \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\) forces \(d(i)=\Omega(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i))\). This paper studies a different model: dynamic graphs/Markov chains on a *fixed* vertex set, with time-inhomogeneous \(P_t\) but (crucially) a common stationary distribution. It does not analyze vertex growth, the quantity \(U(n)\), nor provide lower bounds relating a dwell time schedule to hitting times. However, its techniques (spectral-radius bounds for killed chains and exponential tail bounds for avoiding a vertex when started from stationarity) could be useful tools when analyzing periods on each \(G^{(i)}\) in the growing-graph setting, especially if one can couple each stage to a chain started near stationarity. Still, it neither proves nor disproves the implication \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\Rightarrow d(i)=\Omega(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i))\).

sources.title: An analysis of the recurrence/transience of random walks on growing trees and hypercubes
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves phase transitions for recurrence/transience of random walks on specific growing graphs (complete \(k\)-ary trees, boxes in \(\mathbb Z^d\), and hypercubes \(\{0,1\}^n\)) in the RWoGG model with duration \(d(n)\). For the growing complete \(k\)-ary tree with biased walk parameter \(\lambda\) (simple RW when \(\lambda=1\)), it shows (Theorem 4.2) that the root is recurrent iff \(\sum_{n\ge1} d(n)(\lambda/k)^n=\infty\) (and always recurrent if \(\lambda\ge k\)). For the growing hypercube it shows (Theorem 5.9) that the origin is recurrent iff \(\sum_{n\ge1} d(n)/2^n=\infty\). It introduces the monotonicity/coupling property “less-homesick as graph growing” (LHaGG) and general sufficient conditions for recurrence/transience (Lemmas 3.2–3.5) in terms of stationary mass \(p(n)=\pi_n(v)\) (or even-time stationary mass) and mixing times.
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether bounded expected number of unvisited vertices \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\) forces phase durations \(d(i)\) to be at least on the order of the worst-case hitting time \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\) for each static graph \(G^{(i)}\). This citing paper does not study \(\mathbb E[U(n)]\), cover/unvisited vertices, or relate \(d(i)\) to \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\). Instead it studies recurrence/transience (return probabilities) on growing graphs and provides coupling-based monotonicity (LHaGG) plus criteria involving stationary probabilities and mixing times. These techniques may be relevant background/tools for analyzing time-inhomogeneous walks on growing graphs, but they do not resolve (or directly address) the implication about unvisited vertices vs hitting time. In particular, their thresholds (e.g., \(d(n)\asymp k^n/(n\log n)\) for recurrence on growing trees) are far smaller than typical hitting/cover times on those graphs, suggesting that recurrence phenomena can occur with \(d(n)\ll t_{\mathrm{hit}}(n)\); however this is about returning to a fixed vertex, not visiting all vertices, so it does not provide a counterexample or proof for the open problem.

sources.title: The Recurrence/Transience of Random Walks on a Bounded Grid in an Increasing Dimension
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves a phase transition for recurrence/transience of a lazy simple random walk on growing boxes \(\{0,\dots,N\}^{n_0+n-1}\) under the RWoGG model: the origin \(o\) is recurrent iff \(\sum_{k\ge1} d(k)/(2N)^k=\infty\), and transient otherwise (Theorem 6). More generally, it gives sufficient conditions for recurrence (Theorem 2: if \(\sum_k d(k)\,\pi^{(k)}(o)=\infty\) under a mild mixing-time summability condition) and for transience (Theorem 4: if \(\sum_{k\ge2} d(k)\,\pi^{(k-1)}(o)<\infty\) assuming a monotonicity property ‘weakly LHaGG’ plus the same mixing condition).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether bounded expected number of unvisited vertices \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\) forces durations \(d(i)\) to be at least on the order of the worst-case hitting time \(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\) uniformly over all growing-graph random walks. This paper does not study \(U(n)\) or cover/miss counts, nor does it relate bounded unvisited vertices to hitting times. Its results concern recurrence/transience (return probabilities to the origin) in the RWoGG framework and introduce coupling/monotonicity tools (weakly LHaGG, pausing coupling) and mixing-time-based criteria. These techniques could be tangentially relevant for analyzing time-inhomogeneous walks, but they do not address whether \(d(i)=\Omega(t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i))\) is necessary for \(\mathbb E[U(n)]=O(1)\), nor provide a counterexample with \(d(i)/t_{\mathrm{hit}}(i)\to0\).

title: Characterize limiting competitive ratio of p-sample matroid secretary via i.i.d. analogues
background_latex:
Let \((S,\mathcal I)\) be a matroid (or more generally an independence system) on a finite ground set \(S\). In a sampling-based online selection problem parameterized by \(p\in[0,1)\), each element \(e\in S\) is independently placed into an information set \(H\) with probability \(p\) and otherwise into an online set \(S\setminus H\). An adversary assigns nonnegative weights \(Y(e)\ge 0\) to all elements. The algorithm observes the elements in \(H\) (and their relative ranking by weight), then the online elements arrive in uniformly random order; upon each arrival, the algorithm must irrevocably decide whether to accept the element, maintaining that the accepted set remains independent in \((S,\mathcal I)\).

Let \(S[q]\) denote the random subset obtained by including each element of \(S\) independently with probability \(q\). The online set has the same distribution as \(S[1-p]\). For a fixed weight function \(Y\), define
\[\mathrm{OPT}(\mathcal I,q,Y) := \mathbb E\big[\max\{\sum_{e\in I} Y(e): I\in\mathcal I,\ I\subseteq S[q]\}\big],\]
where the expectation is over the randomness of \(S[q]\).

For a class \(\mathcal C\) of independence systems, define \(\beta_{\mathcal C}(p)\) as the infimum, over \((S,\mathcal I)\in \mathcal C\), of the best competitive ratio achievable by any online algorithm in the above \(p\)-sampling model, where competitiveness is measured against \(\mathrm{OPT}(\mathcal I,1-p,Y)\).

Let \(\mathcal M\) denote the class of all matroids. The matroid secretary conjecture asks whether \(\beta_{\mathcal M}(0)>0\), i.e., whether there exists a constant-competitive algorithm for the matroid secretary problem (the case \(p=0\)). The paper observes that understanding the limit \(L:=\lim_{p\to 1} \beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) and identifying an appropriate full-information/i.i.d.-type analogue whose optimal competitive ratio equals \(L\) would have major consequences.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists a natural matroid-valued analogue of the single-choice i.i.d. prophet inequality whose optimal competitive ratio equals
\[L := \lim_{p\to 1} \beta_{\mathcal M}(p),\]
where \(\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) is the optimal worst-case competitive ratio for the \(p\)-sample-driven online selection problem on the class \(\mathcal M\) of all matroids (with adversarial nonnegative weights and random arrival order), benchmarked against \(\mathrm{OPT}(\mathcal I,1-p,Y)\).

In particular, decide whether one can prove an equality of the form
\[\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p) = \rho,\]
where \(\rho\) is the optimal competitive ratio of a specified i.i.d.-type matroid online-selection model with known distributions (or another clearly defined probabilistic matroid model), analogous to how \(\lim_{p\to 1}\alpha(p)=\alpha^*\) holds in the rank-1 (single selection) case.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Correa--Cristi--Epstein--Soto (2021), the rank-1 (single-choice) \(p\)-sample-driven optimal stopping problem is solved exactly via a limit LP and an optimal-transport structural theorem, yielding an optimal threshold policy and a competitive ratio \(\alpha(p)\) that satisfies \(\lim_{p\to 1}\alpha(p)=\alpha^*\approx 0.745\), matching the classical i.i.d. prophet inequality constant. In Section 5.3 they pose the matroid generalization: define \(\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) for the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model benchmarked against \(\mathrm{OPT}(\mathcal I,1-p,Y)\), and ask whether \(L=\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) equals the optimal competitive ratio of some natural i.i.d./full-information matroid analogue. They observe that proving such an identification with any known constant-competitive matroid prophet/prophet-secretary/random-assignment model would imply \(L>0\) and, by monotonicity in \(p\), would yield \(\beta_{\mathcal M}(0)>0\), resolving the matroid secretary conjecture.

The forward-citing literature provided does not resolve this limiting-characterization question. The closest conceptual progress is the development of bridges between secretary-type random-order models and prophet-type distributional models under matroid constraints. "Secretary Problems, Prophet Inequalities, and Contention Resolution Schemes" shows that constant-competitive matroid secretary is equivalent (up to constants) to the existence of universal random-order contention resolution schemes, reframing the difficulty in terms of online CRS that work for broad (even correlated) priors. On the prophet-from-samples side, "Single-sample prophet inequalities via greedy-ordered selection" gives constant-factor single-sample prophet inequalities for several matroid families (e.g., transversal matroids) and proves that certain strong single-sample prophet guarantees would imply constant-competitive order-oblivious secretary algorithms, suggesting that extending such results to all matroids may be as hard as matroid secretary.

Other cited works contribute tools on the i.i.d./prophet side (posted-price implementations; equivalences between prophet benchmarks) and sharpen rank-1 sampling limits, but none identifies a matroid-valued i.i.d. analogue whose optimal ratio provably equals \(\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\). Thus the problem remains open; a promising direction is to formulate an i.i.d.-type matroid model that captures the information revealed by a \(p\to 1\) sample (nearly full ordinal information on most elements) and then relate its optimal ratio to universal RO contention resolution or to prophet-secretary/pricing frameworks, while avoiding implications that would immediately settle the matroid secretary conjecture.

sources.title: Secretary Problems, Prophet Inequalities, and Contention Resolution Schemes
sources.theorem_or_result: Main theorem (Theorem 3.1): the matroid secretary conjecture is equivalent (up to constant factors) to the existence of universal online random-order contention resolution schemes for matroids. Concretely, the following are equivalent: (i) there exists a constant-competitive algorithm for matroid secretary; (ii) there exist constants \(0<\beta\le \alpha<1\) such that every matroid admits a \((\beta,\alpha)\)-universal random-order contention resolution scheme (RO-CRS), i.e. \(\beta\)-balanced for all \(\alpha\)-uncontentious distributions; (iii) there exists \(c>0\) such that every matroid admits an RO-CRS that is \((c\alpha,\alpha)\)-universal simultaneously for all \(\alpha\in[0,1]\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize \(L=\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) for the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model and relate it to a natural i.i.d./full-information analogue (as in rank-1 prophet inequalities). This paper does not analyze \(\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) as a function of \(p\) nor identify \(L\) or an i.i.d.-type matroid model whose optimal ratio equals \(L\). Instead it provides a different equivalence: constant-competitiveness of the (standard, \(p=0\)) matroid secretary problem is equivalent to existence of universal random-order contention resolution for correlated priors. The techniques (reductions through correlated prophet secretary and labeled contention resolution) are conceptually adjacent to the ‘i.i.d./stochastic analogue’ theme, but they do not yield the requested limiting characterization as \(p\to 1\).

sources.title: Single-sample prophet inequalities via greedy-ordered selection
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops a greedy-threshold framework for single-sample prophet inequalities (SSPI) and proves improved constant competitive ratios for several combinatorial constraints, including: - General (non-bipartite) matching with adversarial edge arrivals: a 16-competitive SSPI (Theorem 2.1). - Bipartite matching with adversarial vertex arrivals: an 8-competitive SSPI (Theorem 3.1) and a truthful 16-competitive mechanism (Theorem 3.2). - Transversal matroids: an 8-competitive SSPI (Theorem 3.3). - Budget-additive combinatorial auctions: a 24-competitive SSPI (Theorem 4.1). - Matroids with the \(\alpha\)-partition property: a \(2\alpha\)-competitive SSPI (Theorem 5.1). It also proves a partial converse between SSPIs and order-oblivious secretary algorithms: any \(\alpha\)-competitive pointwise-SSPI (P-SSPI) implies a \(2\alpha\)-competitive order-oblivious secretary (OOS) algorithm (Theorem 6.2).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks to characterize \(L=\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) for the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model and identify a natural i.i.d./full-information analogue whose optimal competitive ratio equals \(L\). This paper does not analyze the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model nor the limit \(p\to 1\), and it does not propose or prove an equality \(\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)=\rho\) for a matroid i.i.d.-type model.

However, it is relevant in two ways:
- It advances the ‘i.i.d./sample-based’ side by giving constant-factor SSPIs for certain matroid classes (transversal matroids; more generally matroids with an \(\alpha\)-partition property), which are probabilistic analogues of prophet inequalities with limited information.
- It clarifies limitations: for a broad class of SSPI policies (P-SSPIs), constant-factor SSPI would imply constant-factor order-oblivious secretary (Theorem 6.2). This suggests that proving strong SSPI results for general matroids (and thus potentially relating to \(L\)) may be as hard as the matroid secretary conjecture unless one uses non-P-SSPI techniques.

So the paper provides partial progress/insight toward the landscape connecting sampling-based online selection and prophet/secretary models, but it does not resolve the specific limiting-ratio characterization problem posed.

sources.title: Power of posted-price mechanisms for prophet inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result: Main result (Theorem 1 / Theorem 4): for any prophet-inequality (Bayesian online optimization) algorithm \(A_{\mathrm{inp}}\) under an arbitrary feasibility constraint \(F\subseteq X_1\times\cdots\times X_n\), there exists a posted-price (pricing-based) algorithm \(A_{\mathrm{out}}\) such that (i) \(A_{\mathrm{out}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{inp}}\) induce the same joint distribution over assigned outcomes \((A_1,\dots,A_n)\), and (ii) \(\mathbb E[v(A_{\mathrm{out}})]\ge \mathbb E[v(A_{\mathrm{inp}})]\) (indeed agent-wise), while maintaining feasibility. An efficient sampling-based implementation (Theorem 19) achieves approximate preservation and welfare up to \((1-\varepsilon)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize \(L=\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) for the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model with adversarial weights, and to identify a natural i.i.d./full-information matroid analogue whose optimal competitive ratio equals \(L\). This paper is about prophet inequalities (Bayesian/i.i.d. values with known distributions) and shows any such algorithm can be implemented via posted prices, extending also to prophet secretary. It does not analyze the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model, does not define or identify an i.i.d. matroid model matching \(\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\), and provides no results about the limit \(p\to 1\) or about adversarial weights. Its relevance is indirect: it strengthens the toolkit on the i.i.d./prophet side (pricing implementations), which could be useful if one first establishes an equivalence between the \(p\to 1\) sampling model and a prophet-type matroid model.

sources.title: Prophet inequalities via the expected competitive ratio
sources.theorem_or_result: For any downward-closed feasibility family \(\mathcal F\) (including matroids), the worst-case optimal guarantees under the two prophet-inequality objectives RoE and EoR are within constant factors: \(\mathrm{EoR}(\mathcal F)\ge \mathrm{RoE}(\mathcal F)/12\) (Theorem 2) and for every product distribution \(\mathcal D\), \(\mathrm{RoE}(\mathcal F,\mathcal D)\ge \mathrm{EoR}(\mathcal F,\mathcal D)/68\) (Theorem 3), hence \(\mathrm{RoE}(\mathcal F)/\mathrm{EoR}(\mathcal F)\in \Theta(1)\) (Corollary 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize \(L=\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\) for the \(p\)-sample matroid secretary model and to identify a natural i.i.d.-type matroid analogue whose optimal competitive ratio equals \(L\). This paper does not study the \(p\)-sample secretary model nor the \(p\to 1\) limit, and it does not propose an i.i.d. matroid model intended to match \(\lim_{p\to 1}\beta_{\mathcal M}(p)\). Instead it develops constant-factor reductions between two performance measures (ratio of expectations vs expected ratio) for prophet inequalities under downward-closed constraints (including matroids). These techniques (tail/core split; concentration via self-bounding of the offline optimum) could be useful if one tries to relate different benchmarks in any candidate i.i.d.-matroid analogue, but they do not identify \(\rho\) or prove an equality with \(L\).

sources.title: Secretary problems: The power of a single sample
sources.theorem_or_result:
Studies the rank-1 (single-choice) single-sample secretary / two-sided Game of Googol model. Main quantitative results:
- Random-order: a comparison-based “block-rank” algorithm selects the maximum with probability at least 
\[0.5009,\]
and no comparison-based algorithm can exceed 
\[\gamma\approx 0.5024.\]
- Under a no-\(\varepsilon\)-superstars condition, achieves \(\gamma-O(1/\log(1/\varepsilon))\).

sources.title: Prophet Inequality from Samples: Is the More the Merrier?
sources.theorem_or_result: In the single-choice prophet inequality from samples with unknown independent distributions and an identity-blind pool of samples (k samples per distribution), the paper proves: - Hardness: there exist k0 and c<1/2 such that for all k≥k0 and any online algorithm, the worst-case competitive ratio \(\alpha_k\le c\) (Theorem 3.1, with an explicit constant \(c\approx 0.4997\)). - For ordinal static-threshold algorithms that pick the \(\ell\)-th highest sample as a threshold and accept the first online value exceeding it, the asymptotically optimal competitive ratio as \(k\to\infty\) is \(1-\rho\approx 0.433\), where \(\rho\in(0,1)\) solves \(\rho e^{\rho}=1\) (Theorems 4.1–4.2).

This citing paper does not study matroid secretary or matroid feasibility constraints; it studies rank-1 (single-choice) prophet inequality from samples with unknown distributions and identity-blind samples. title: Respecting improvement for best core allotments in unbounded Shapley-Scarf markets
background_latex:
A (Shapley--Scarf) housing market consists of a finite set of agents/objects \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\). Agent \(i\in N\) is initially endowed with object \(e_i=i\) and has complete and transitive (weak) preferences \(R_i\) over \(N\). Write \(P_i\) for the strict part and \(I_i\) for indifference.

An allocation is a permutation \(x=(x_i)_{i\in N}\in N^N\) such that each agent receives exactly one object and each object is assigned to exactly one agent. An allocation \(x\) is individually rational if \(x_i R_i i\) for all \(i\).

A nonempty coalition \(S\subseteq N\) blocks an allocation \(x\) if there exists an allocation \(z\) using only objects of \(S\) (i.e., \(\{z_i:i\in S\}=S\)) such that \(z_i P_i x_i\) for all \(i\in S\). The (weak) core \(C(R)\) is the set of allocations that are not blocked by any coalition.

An "improvement for agent \(i\)" is a change of preferences from \(R\) to \(\widetilde R\) such that: (1) \(\widetilde R_i=R_i\); (2) for each other agent \(j\neq i\), object \(i\) can only move weakly up in \(j\)'s ranking among acceptable objects (relative orderings among objects \(\neq i\) are unchanged).

For a set of allocations \(X\) and agent \(i\), define the set of objects \(X_i:=\{x_i: x\in X\}\). Define \(\mathrm{best}_i(X)\) as an \(R_i\)-maximal element of \(X_i\) (i.e., an agent \(i\)'s most preferred allotment attainable within \(X\); if there are ties, \(\mathrm{best}_i(X)\) may be non-unique).

The paper proves that the unique competitive/strong-core allocation respects improvement under strict preferences, and gives related setwise results for competitive allocations under weak preferences, but leaves open a question for the (weak) core under unbounded exchanges.
problem_definition_latex:
Given a housing market \((N,R)\) with unbounded exchange cycles and its core \(C(R)\), and an agent \(i\in N\), consider a preference change to \((N,\widetilde R)\) where \(\widetilde R\) is an improvement for \(i\) with respect to \(R\).

Determine whether the following property holds: for every choice of \(x\in C(R)\) with \(x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) and every choice of \(\widetilde x\in C(\widetilde R)\) with \(\widetilde x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(\widetilde R))\), one has
\[
\widetilde x_i\; R_i\; x_i.
\]
Equivalently, decide whether agent \(i\)'s most preferred allotment among core allocations can ever become strictly worse after \(i\)'s object becomes (weakly) more desirable to other agents (with \(i\)'s own preferences fixed).

literature_review.synthesis:
Biró–Klijn–Klimentova–Viana (2021) introduced “respecting improvement” for Shapley–Scarf housing markets and proved it for the unique competitive/strong-core allocation under strict preferences (via TTC), and obtained setwise monotonicity for competitive allocations under weak preferences. They also showed that once exchanges are bounded (e.g., cycle length \(\le 3\)), even strict-preference cores can fail to respect improvement for an agent’s best attainable allotment, leaving open the unbounded-cycle question for the (weak) core: can \(\mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) become worse after a \(p\)-improvement (others rank \(i\)’s endowment weakly higher, \(R_i\) fixed)?

This open problem has been solved affirmatively by Schlotter–Biró–Fleiner in “The core of housing markets from an agent's perspective: Is it worth sprucing up your home?”. Their Theorem 2 gives a strong monotonicity: starting from any core allocation \(X\in C(H)\), after a \(p\)-improvement \(H'\) there exists \(X'\in C(H')\) with \(X'(p)=X(p)\) or \(X'(p)\,P_p\,X(p)\). Taking \(X\) to be a \(p\)-best core allocation in \(H\) implies that \(p\)’s best attainable core object in \(H'\) is weakly better, yielding the exact quantified statement posed in the source paper: for any \(x\in C(R)\) with \(x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) and any \(\widetilde x\in C(\widetilde R)\) with \(\widetilde x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(\widetilde R))\), one has \(\widetilde x_i\,R_i\,x_i\). The result holds in full generality of unbounded exchange cycles and is constructive (linear time).

Related subsequent work develops broader “respecting improvement” frameworks for mechanisms (single-valued rules) and for stronger stability notions (e.g., strong core under partial orders), but these do not substitute for the above core-correspondence comparative statics. A remaining direction, suggested already by Biró et al. (2021), is to understand analogous RI-best statements in other stability models (e.g., stable roommates) and to delineate precisely which bounded-exchange restrictions reintroduce failures of monotonicity, as seen in their bounded-cycle counterexamples.

sources.title: The core of housing markets from an agent's perspective: Is it worth sprucing up your home?
sources.theorem_or_result: Theorem 2 (Schlotter–Biró–Fleiner, 2024): For any housing market \(H\), any agent \(p\), any \(p\)-improvement \(H'\) of \(H\), and any core allocation \(X\in C(H)\), there exists a core allocation \(X'\in C(H')\) such that either \(X'(p)=X(p)\) or \(X'(p)\,P_p\,X(p)\). Moreover, such an \(X'\) can be found in \(O(|H|)\) time. Corollary 1: the core strongly satisfies the RI-best property, i.e., for any \(p\)-improvement \(H'\) of \(H\), every \(a\in \Phi_p^+(H)\) and \(a'\in \Phi_p^+(H')\) satisfy \(a\preceq_p a'\) (equivalently \(a'\,R_p\,a\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether, under an improvement for agent \(i\) (others rank object \(i\) weakly higher, \(i\)'s own preferences fixed), agent \(i\)'s best attainable core allotment can become worse: for any \(x\in C(R)\) with \(x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) and any \(\tilde x\in C(\tilde R)\) with \(\tilde x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(\tilde R))\), must \(\tilde x_i\,R_i\,x_i\) hold? This paper proves exactly this monotonicity for the core (their RI-best property) in full generality, even allowing partial orders and unbounded exchange cycles. Corollary 1 gives the setwise statement about best core outcomes across markets \(H\) and its \(p\)-improvement \(H'\), which matches the quantification over all best-core selections in the open problem. Thus the answer is ‘yes’: best core allotments cannot deteriorate after such an improvement.

sources.title: The core of housing markets from an agent's perspective: Is it worth sprucing up your home?
sources.theorem_or_result: Theorem 2 (Schlotter–Biró–Fleiner, 2024): For any housing market \(H\), any agent \(p\), any \(p\)-improvement \(H'\) of \(H\) (i.e., only \(p\)'s house moves weakly up in other agents’ rankings, with all other relative comparisons unchanged), and any core allocation \(X\in C(H)\), there exists a core allocation \(X'\in C(H')\) such that either \(X'(p)=X(p)\) or \(X'(p)\succ_p X(p)\). Moreover, such an \(X'\) can be found in \(O(|H|)\) time.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether, after an improvement for agent \(i\), the agent’s best attainable core allotment can become worse: for any \(x\in C(R)\) with \(x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) and any \(\tilde x\in C(\tilde R)\) with \(\tilde x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(\tilde R))\), must \(\tilde x_i\,R_i\,x_i\) hold?
- Theorem 2 implies the RI-best property for the core: for any \(x\in C(R)\) there exists some \(\tilde x\in C(\tilde R)\) with \(\tilde x_i\,R_i\,x_i\). Applying this with \(x\) chosen so that \(x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\) shows that \(\mathrm{best}_i(C(\tilde R))\) contains an object weakly preferred to \(x_i\).
- Therefore it is impossible for every best core allotment after the improvement to be strictly worse than a best core allotment before the improvement; equivalently, the agent’s best achievable core object cannot deteriorate.
- In fact, this yields the stronger quantifier pattern in the open problem: if there exists \(\tilde x\in C(\tilde R)\) with \(\tilde x_i\succeq_i x_i\), then any \(\tilde x\) with \(\tilde x_i\in \mathrm{best}_i(C(\tilde R))\) must satisfy \(\tilde x_i\succeq_i x_i\) (since it is at least as good as that witness). Hence the stated property holds.

sources.title: Respecting improvement in markets with indivisible goods
sources.theorem_or_result:
Main strict-domain implication: for generalized matching problems, any rule 
\(\phi: P^N\to M^f\) that satisfies individual rationality, strategy-proofness, and non-bossiness also satisfies respecting improvement (Theorem 1): for any agent \(k\) whose endowment improves in some other agent’s ranking (a \(k\)-improvement), \(\phi_k(R'_i,R_{-i})\,R_k\,\phi_k(R)\). Corollary: extending such a strict-domain rule to weak preferences via fixed tie-breaking preserves respecting improvement on \(R^N\).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the weak core correspondence \(C(R)\) in (possibly unbounded-cycle) Shapley–Scarf markets and asks whether agent \(i\)’s best attainable core object (i.e., \(\mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\)) is monotone under an improvement of object \(i\) in others’ rankings. This paper does not analyze the core correspondence’s comparative statics, nor does it prove monotonicity for \(\mathrm{best}_i(C(R))\). Instead it studies respecting improvement for single-valued mechanisms/rules (not correspondences) and shows a general sufficient condition (IR+SP+NB) on the strict domain, with extensions to weak preferences via tie-breaking. It also discusses competitive allocations and (strong/weak) core sets in housing markets, but only derives ‘optimistic’ setwise statements for competitive allocations (and notes impossibility of satisfying such best-type properties simultaneously for multiple agents). Thus it provides tools and context but does not resolve the best-core-allotment question.

sources.title: The strong core of housing markets with partial order preferences
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper’s main result on improvements is Theorem 5.4: if \(H=(N,\{\succ_i\})\) has partial-order preferences and \(H'\) is a \(p\)-improvement of \(H\) (i.e., only other agents’ rankings of \(p\)’s house move weakly upward, with all other comparisons unchanged), then for any \(X\in SC(H)\) and \(X'\in SC(H')\) we have \(X'(p)\succeq_p X(p)\). It also gives a structural characterization (Theorem 3.5) and a polynomial-time algorithm (Theorem 4.4) for finding a strong-core allocation under partial orders (with forbidden/forced arcs).
sources.connection: The open problem asks about the (weak) core \(C(R)\) under weak preferences and unbounded exchange cycles: whether agent \(i\)’s best attainable core object can become worse after an improvement for \(i\) (others value \(i\)’s object more). This paper does not address the weak core; it studies the strong core \(SC\) (no weakly blocking cycle) under partial orders and proves a respecting-improvement property for \(SC\) (Theorem 5.4). While conceptually related (same monotonicity question under ‘improvement’), the result does not imply the desired statement for \(C(R)\), because \(SC\subseteq C\) and the best-in-core comparison in the open problem is specific to \(C\) and to selecting \(R_i\)-maximal elements of \(C\). Thus it provides supporting techniques/insight but not a solution to the open problem.

sources.title: Novel integer programming models for the stable kidney exchange problem
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives integer programming formulations to compute maximum-cardinality stable and strongly stable exchanges in kidney exchange graphs with bounded cycle/chain length. In particular, it encodes stability via constraints equivalent to: for every cycle \(c\) there exists an arc \((i,j)\in A(c)\) such that \(j\) is matched in the solution to some \(k\) with \(k\) weakly preferred to \(i\) (Proposition 1), and analogous constraints for strong stability under strict/weak preferences (Propositions 2–3).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns a monotonicity/respecting-improvement property for an agent’s best (weak) core allotment in an unbounded Shapley–Scarf housing market under an ‘improvement’ change (others rank object \(i\) weakly higher). This paper does not study that monotonicity question, nor best-core selections, nor unbounded exchange cycles in the Shapley–Scarf model. It instead focuses on computational IP models for finding maximum-cardinality stable/strongly stable exchanges in kidney exchange with typically bounded cycle/chain lengths, and discusses trade-offs between stability and cardinality. While it cites the respecting-improvement property for the TTC outcome in the unbounded case as motivation, it provides no theorem about how core outcomes change under improvements, and no counterexample or proof for the best-core respecting-improvement question.

title: Compute interim envy-free lotteries maximizing expected average Nash welfare in matching instances
background_latex:
Consider a matching allocation instance with a set of agents \(N\) and a set of indivisible items \(I\) such that \(|N|=|I|=n\). Each agent \(i\in N\) has a nonnegative additive valuation \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)\) over bundles \(S\subseteq I\). A (deterministic) matching \(\mu\) assigns each agent \(i\) exactly one item \(\mu(i)\in I\), with each item assigned to exactly one agent.

A lottery \(Q\) is a probability distribution over matchings. If a matching \(\mu\sim Q\) is drawn, agent \(i\) receives the random item \(\mu(i)\). The lottery \(Q\) is interim envy-free (iEF) if for every ordered pair of agents \(i,j\in N\) and every item \(g\in I\) that agent \(i\) receives with positive probability under \(Q\) (i.e., \(\Pr_{\mu\sim Q}[\mu(i)=g]>0\)),
\[
v_i(g) \ge \mathbb{E}_{\mu\sim Q}\bigl[v_i(\mu(j))\mid \mu(i)=g\bigr].
\]

For a deterministic matching \(\mu\), the (average) Nash social welfare is the geometric mean of agents' utilities:
\[
\mathrm{avN}(\mu)=\Bigl(\prod_{i\in N} v_i(\mu(i))\Bigr)^{1/n}.
\]
For a lottery \(Q\), the objective of interest is the expected average Nash welfare \(\mathbb{E}_{\mu\sim Q}[\mathrm{avN}(\mu)]\).
problem_definition_latex:
Given a matching allocation instance \((N,I,(v_i)_{i\in N})\) with \(|N|=|I|\), determine how to compute an interim envy-free lottery \(Q\) that maximizes the expected average Nash social welfare
\[
\max_{Q\ \text{iEF}}\ \mathbb{E}_{\mu\sim Q}[\mathrm{avN}(\mu)].
\]
In particular, design an algorithm for this optimization problem (or determine its computational complexity).

literature_review.synthesis:
The EC’21 paper of Caragiannis, Kanellopoulos, and Kyropoulou introduces interim envy-freeness (iEF) for lotteries over allocations and gives polynomial-time algorithms for matching instances to compute iEF lotteries maximizing expected utilitarian welfare, egalitarian welfare, and expected log-Nash welfare (equivalently, expected \(\sum_i \ln v_i(\mu(i))\)). Their approach formulates iEF as a linear program over matchings and solves it via the ellipsoid method on the dual, using a separation oracle reducible to a novel combinatorial problem (maximum edge-pair-weighted bipartite perfect matching, 2EBM) solvable in polynomial time via Cruse’s decomposition of centrosymmetric doubly stochastic matrices.

However, the paper explicitly notes that maximizing expected average Nash welfare \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{avN}(\mu)]\), where \(\mathrm{avN}(\mu)=(\prod_i v_i(\mu(i)))^{1/n}\), is not equivalent to maximizing expected log-Nash welfare for lotteries, and leaves the former as an open problem. The only forward citation provided here (“Optimally interpolating between ex-ante fairness and welfare”) offers a generic distribution-mixing framework under total-variation constraints to a fair prior, but does not address iEF feasibility or the nonlinearity of \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{avN}(\mu)]\) under iEF constraints. Thus, with the current evidence, the computational status of iEF-constrained maximization of expected average Nash welfare in matching instances remains open.

sources.title: Optimally interpolating between ex-ante fairness and welfare
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper defines a general “fair-to-welfare interpolation” (FWI) problem: given a solution space \(S\), welfare function \(V:S\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), a “fair prior” distribution \(p^f\in\Delta(S)\) (sample access), and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), maximize expected welfare subject to total-variation proximity to the fair prior: \[\max_{p\in\Delta(S)} V(p) \ \text{s.t.}\ \mathrm{TV}(p,p^f)\le \alpha.\] They give two algorithms. (1) \(\varepsilon\)-MIX (Theorem 3.1): with \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) samples from \(p^f\) and a welfare mechanism \(M_\lambda\) producing \(A\) with \(V(A)\ge \lambda V(\mathrm{OPT})\), the output distribution \(p^\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\mathrm{TV}(p^\varepsilon,p^f)\le \alpha\) and \(V(p^\varepsilon)\ge \lambda(1-\varepsilon) V(p^{\mathrm{OPT}})\), where \(p^{\mathrm{OPT}}\) is the optimal solution to the TV-constrained problem. (2) SIMPLE-MIX (Theorem 4.1): the mixture \(p^s=\alpha\delta_A+(1-\alpha)p^f\) satisfies \(\mathrm{TV}(p^s,p^f)\le \alpha\) and \(V(p^s)\ge \min\{\lambda,\alpha\lambda+(1-\alpha)^2\}V(p^{\mathrm{OPT}}).\)
sources.connection: The open problem asks to compute an interim envy-free (iEF) lottery over perfect matchings that maximizes \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{avN}(\mu)]\). This paper does not study interim envy-freeness, nor does it optimize over the iEF-feasible region. Instead it optimizes welfare subject to a total-variation-distance constraint to a given ex-ante fair prior distribution. Thus it does not provide an algorithm or complexity result for maximizing expected average Nash welfare under iEF constraints. At best, it offers a generic mixing/sampling framework that could be used if one had (i) a prior distribution that is already iEF and (ii) a way to ensure the output remains iEF under mixing—something not addressed here (mixing with a welfare-maximizing matching will generally break iEF).

title: Determine optimal approximation constant for AnyPrice share allocations with additive valuations
background_latex:
There are \(n\) agents \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\) and a set \(M\) of \(m\) indivisible goods. Each agent \(i\) has an additive valuation \(v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) of the form \(v_i(S)=\sum_{j\in S} v_i(j)\). Agents have entitlements (budgets) \(b_i>0\) with \(\sum_{i\in N} b_i = 1\).

For a fixed agent \(i\), define the set of nonnegative price vectors with total price 1 as
\[P=\{(p_1,\dots,p_m)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^m: \sum_{j\in M} p_j = 1\}.\]
The AnyPrice share (APS) of agent \(i\) is
\[\mathrm{APS}_i \;=\; \min_{p\in P}\; \max_{S\subseteq M\, :\, \sum_{j\in S} p_j\le b_i} v_i(S).\]
(Equivalently, \(\mathrm{APS}_i\) is the largest \(z\) for which there exists a distribution over bundles \(T\subseteq M\) each of value at least \(z\), such that each item \(j\in M\) appears with total probability at most \(b_i\).)

An allocation is a partition \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)\) of \(M\) into disjoint bundles. For \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), an \(\alpha\)-APS allocation is an allocation \(A\) such that \(v_i(A_i)\ge \alpha\,\mathrm{APS}_i\) for every agent \(i\in N\).

For additive valuations and arbitrary entitlements, the paper proves existence and polynomial-time computability of \(\alpha\)-APS allocations for \(\alpha=3/5\) (and stronger entitlement-dependent bounds), and notes that exact \(\alpha=1\) is impossible in general when \(n\ge 3\), even under equal entitlements.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine the largest constant \(\alpha^\star\in(0,1)\) such that, for every instance with additive valuations \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\) and entitlements \((b_1,\dots,b_n)\) with \(\sum_i b_i=1\), there exists an allocation \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)\) satisfying
\[\forall i\in N:\quad v_i(A_i)\ge \alpha^\star\,\mathrm{APS}_i,\]
where \(\mathrm{APS}_i\) is defined by
\[\mathrm{APS}_i \;=\; \min_{p\in P}\; \max_{S\subseteq M\, :\, \sum_{j\in S} p_j\le b_i} v_i(S).\]
Equivalently, determine the optimal worst-case approximation factor for simultaneously guaranteeing each agent a fixed constant fraction of her AnyPrice share (for additive valuations), and provide matching upper and lower bounds (and, if possible, a polynomial-time algorithm achieving \(\alpha^\star\)).

literature_review.synthesis:
The AnyPrice Share (APS) benchmark of Babaioff–Ezra–Feige is defined for each agent \(i\) with entitlement \(b_i\) as \(\mathrm{APS}_i=\min_{p\in P}\max\{v_i(S):\sum_{j\in S}p_j\le b_i\}\), equivalently as the largest \(z\) for which there exists a distribution over bundles of value at least \(z\) where each item appears with total probability at most \(b_i\). For additive valuations, the source paper proves a universal constant guarantee: there is always a polynomial-time computable allocation giving every agent at least \(3/5\) of her APS (and in fact \(\max\{3/5,1/(2-b_i)\}\) depending on entitlement). It also shows exact \(\alpha=1\) is impossible for \(n\ge 3\) even under equal entitlements, so the central question is to pin down the optimal universal constant \(\alpha^\star\in(0,1)\) for additive valuations and arbitrary entitlements.

Subsequent work in the provided forward citations does not close this gap. "Weighted fairness notions for indivisible items revisited" consolidates the state of the art: it reiterates the \(3/5\) lower bound and points to an impossibility barrier inherited from maximin-share (MMS) lower bounds, namely that no \(\alpha\)-APS allocation exists for any \(\alpha>39/40\) (via instances where no allocation gives everyone more than \(39/40\) of MMS, and \(\mathrm{APS}\ge \mathrm{MMS}\)). Its main new APS-related contribution is restricted-domain: for binary additive valuations, the weighted egalitarian (WEG) rule is APS-fair (achieves \(\alpha=1\) for APS). A separate line, "Almost (Weighted) Proportional Allocations for Indivisible Chores**", studies chores and shows WPROPX implies a factor-2 approximation to a chore-analog of APS; while not directly improving goods-APS constants, it suggests that price-based and proportionality-up-to-one-item techniques can yield APS-type guarantees in other manna models.

Overall, based on the cited literature here, the optimal constant \(\alpha^\star\) for additive valuations and arbitrary entitlements remains open: the best universal lower bound is \(3/5\) (with better entitlement-dependent guarantees), and the best stated universal upper bound is \(39/40\) (inherited from MMS impossibility for equal entitlements, hence applying to APS as well). Narrowing the gap likely requires either (i) new impossibility constructions tailored to APS (not just MMS), or (ii) improved algorithms/rounding arguments that exploit the APS dual (distributional) characterization beyond the current bidding-game analysis.

title: Optimal rank among simplex-isomorphic binarizations for bounded integer variables
background_latex:
Let \(x\) be an integer variable taking values in \(\{0,1,\dots,k\}\). A (polyhedral) binarization of \(x\) is a polytope \(B\subseteq \mathbb{R}\times[0,1]^d\) in variables \((x,y)\), where \(y\in[0,1]^d\) are intended to be binary, such that
\[
\pi_x\bigl(\{(x,y)\in B: y\in\{0,1\}^d\}\bigr)=\{0,1,\dots,k\},
\]
where \(\pi_x\) denotes projection onto the \(x\)-coordinate.
A binarization \(B\) is called natural if for every vertex \((\bar x,\bar y)\in V(B)\) one has \(\bar x\in\mathbb{Z}\) (equivalently \(\pi_x(V(B))=\{0,1,\dots,k\}\)).

Given a mixed-integer polytope reformulated with binary variables, one can apply sequential convexification: for a polytope \(Q\subseteq[0,1]^h\times\mathbb{R}^{n-h}\) and a binary variable \(y_j\), define
\[
Q^{y_j}:=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{q\in Q: y_j=0\}\cup\{q\in Q: y_j=1\}\bigr).
\]
Iterating this operation over selected binary variables removes vertices fractional in those variables.

Fix a natural binarization \(B\subseteq \mathbb{R}\times[0,1]^d\) of \(x\) with range \(\{0,1,\dots,d\}\) and view it as part of some binary extended formulation. For \(\alpha\in\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}\), consider the integrality-separation property for \(x\): no vertex of the current relaxation has \(\alpha< x < \alpha+1\). The paper defines a rank parameter \(\mathrm{rk}_B(\alpha)\) measuring the minimum number of sequential convexifications on the \(d\) binary variables \(y_1,\dots,y_d\) needed to enforce this property.

For the unary binarization \(B_U(d)\) (a \(d\)-simplex with \(d+1\) vertices) and the full binarization \(B_F(d)\) (also a \(d\)-simplex), the paper derives closed-form expressions showing that \(B_U(d)\) has smaller rank than \(B_F(d)\) under this criterion.

A binarization is said to be isomorphic to a \(d\)-simplex if, as a polytope, it is combinatorially equivalent to a simplex (equivalently, it has \(d+1\) vertices and complete graph skeleton).
problem_definition_latex:
Among all natural binarizations \(B\subseteq \mathbb{R}\times[0,1]^d\) of an integer variable \(x\in\{0,1,\dots,d\}\) whose polytope \(B\) is isomorphic (combinatorially equivalent) to a \(d\)-dimensional simplex, determine whether the unary binarization \(B_U(d)\) minimizes the rank parameter among this class.

Equivalently: decide whether, for every natural simplex-isomorphic binarization \(B\) of \(x\in\{0,1,\dots,d\}\) and for every \(\alpha\in\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}\), one has
\[
\mathrm{rk}_B(\alpha)\ge \mathrm{rk}_{B_U(d)}(\alpha),
\]
or otherwise provide a counterexample binarization \(B\) (simplex-isomorphic and natural) with strictly smaller rank for at least one such \(\alpha\).

title: Random-order contention resolution for rank-1 matroids with negative correlation
background_latex:
A rank-1 matroid can be represented by a ground set of elements (here, edges) \(E\) with the feasibility constraint that at most one element may be selected. Equivalently, in a star graph with center vertex \(v\), the feasible matchings choose at most one edge incident to \(v\).

An ordered (or random-order) contention resolution scheme (CRS) for this rank-1 constraint operates as follows. Each element \(e\in E\) has an initially unknown activeness indicator \(Z_e\in\{0,1\}\). The algorithm observes elements one-by-one in some order; when an element \(e\) is revealed to be active (\(Z_e=1\)) and no previously accepted element has been chosen, the algorithm may either accept \(e\) (and then must reject all later elements) or irrevocably discard \(e\).

A random-order CRS means the observation order is a uniformly random permutation of \(E\).

Let \(z_e := \Pr[Z_e=1]\) denote the marginal activeness probability of element \(e\). The rank-1 feasibility region corresponding to these marginals is \(\sum_{e\in E} z_e \le 1\) (and \(0\le z_e\le 1\)).

A CRS is called \(c\)-selectable if for every instance and every element \(e\), the ex ante probability that the algorithm accepts \(e\) is at least \(c\, z_e\).

In the setting of this paper, the activeness indicators \((Z_e)_{e\in E}\) need not be independent; they satisfy a (pairwise-to-setwise) negative correlation property: for every subset \(S\subseteq E\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}\),
\[\Pr\big[\bigwedge_{e\in S}(Z_e=b)\big] \le \prod_{e\in S} \Pr[Z_e=b].\]
In particular, the case \(b=0\) asserts that joint inactivity events are no more likely than under independence.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order contention resolution scheme for a rank-1 matroid when the activeness indicators \((Z_e)_{e\in E}\) satisfy the negative correlation property
\[\Pr\big[\bigwedge_{e\in S}(Z_e=b)\big] \le \prod_{e\in S} \Pr[Z_e=b]\quad \forall S\subseteq E,\ b\in\{0,1\},\]
with given marginals \(z_e=\Pr[Z_e=1]\) obeying \(\sum_{e\in E} z_e \le 1\). That is, decide whether one can guarantee for all such instances that each element \(e\) is accepted with probability at least \((1-1/e) z_e\) when elements are revealed in a uniformly random order and decisions are irrevocable.
