literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Brubach–Grammel–Ma–Srinivasan) isolates a sharp gap between ordered and random-order contention resolution for the rank-1 (star) constraint when the activeness indicators \((Z_e)\) are not independent but satisfy the strong setwise negative-correlation property \(\Pr[\wedge_{e\in S}(Z_e=b)]\le\prod_{e\in S}\Pr[Z_e=b]\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). In their unit-patience bipartite matching application, dependent rounding (GKPS) produces exactly this kind of negative correlation among the \(Z_e\) incident to a vertex. They prove that if the algorithm may choose the processing order (e.g., sort by weights), then the expected value on a star is minimized by the independent case, yielding a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced ordered CRS under negative correlation. However, they explicitly leave open whether the same \((1-1/e)\) factor is achievable when the order is a uniformly random permutation.

Subsequent and related works largely continue to use \((1-1/e)\)-selectable rank-1 random-order CRSs as a black box in the independent-activation model (e.g., in probe-commit/probing variants of online stochastic matching), without extending the analysis to negatively correlated \(Z\). At the same time, work on alternative negative-dependence models for online contention resolution (e.g., random-element/batch models in revenue management) shows that negative dependence can fundamentally change achievable selectability constants, suggesting that the open problem may require either new robust analyses (showing independence is worst-case under the stated negative correlation) or explicit counterexamples tailored to random order.

A different line on two-stage stochastic matching develops star contention resolution under negative dependence (negative cylinder dependence/negative association) but typically under additional structure on marginals or without the random-order requirement. Overall, as of the cited forward literature, there is no paper establishing a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for rank-1 matroids under the full strong negative-correlation property for arbitrary marginals with \(\sum_e z_e\le 1\); the best-known \((1-1/e)\) guarantee under negative correlation remains in the ordered (chosen-order) model, while random-order \((1-1/e)\) is only proved under independence.

sources.title: Improved guarantees for offline stochastic matching via new ordered contention resolution schemes
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves existence of a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced ordered contention resolution scheme for rank-1 matroids under the negative correlation property \(\Pr[\wedge_{e\in S}(Z_e=b)]\le \prod_{e\in S}\Pr[Z_e=b]\) (for \(b\in\{0,1\}\)), but only when the algorithm may choose the processing order (not uniformly random). Concretely, for a star (rank-1) with marginals \(z_e\) satisfying \(\sum_e z_e\le 1\) and negatively correlated \((Z_e)\), probing/accepting edges in decreasing weight order achieves expected value at least \((1-1/e)\sum_e w_e z_e\) (Lemmas 7–9 / Theorem 2 specialized to a star), which via the Lee–Singla equivalence implies a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced ordered CRS under negative correlation with chosen order.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for rank-1 matroids under the stated negative correlation. This paper explicitly notes this remains open (Subsection 1.2: “To our knowledge, it remains open whether a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced Random-order Contention Resolution Scheme is possible under property (2)”). What it does provide is: (i) a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced ordered (not random-order) CRS under negative correlation, relying on the ability to choose the order (e.g., sort by weights), and (ii) a \((1-1/e)\)-balanced random-order CRS for rank-1 only in the independent-activity setting (Corollary 6), not under negative correlation. Thus it makes strong partial progress but does not resolve the random-order/negative-correlation combination.

sources.title: Online contention resolution schemes for network revenue management and combinatorial auctions
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves tight bounds for “random-element” online contention resolution under L-bounded products: (i) for adversarial order (OCRS), no random-element OCRS can be better than \(1/(1+L)\)-selectable when \(L\) is a prime power (Theorem 2.3 / Corollary 2.4), and it gives a \(1/(1+L)\)-selectable random-element OCRS (Theorem 3.3). (ii) For random-order arrivals (RCRS), it gives an \(\alpha\)-selectable random-element RCRS with \(\alpha>1/(1+L)\) for all \(L\ge2\) (Theorem 4.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether there exists a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for a rank-1 matroid (choose at most one element) when activeness indicators satisfy a strong negative-correlation condition for both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\). This paper studies a different negative-dependence model (“random-element”: elements partitioned into batches and at most one element per batch becomes active) and focuses on online/secretary-style feasibility structures such as L-bounded hypergraph matching. It does not analyze rank-1 matroids under the paper’s negative-correlation assumption, nor does it establish a \(1-1/e\) guarantee in that setting. However, it is relevant because it highlights that certain forms of negative correlation (random-element/batching) can strictly worsen achievable selectability guarantees compared to the independent case, and it provides techniques (exact selection, inclusion–exclusion improvements, Schur-concavity) that might inform attempts on the rank-1 negatively correlated random-order CRS question.

sources.title: Optimal Rounding for Two-Stage Bipartite Matching
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves tight rounding/approximation factors for two-stage bipartite matching using negative dependence from dependent rounding. In particular, it establishes a monotone star-graph contention resolution scheme (Lemma 5.3): for a star (rank-1 constraint) with fractional weights \(y_i\) (\(\sum_i y_i\le 1\)) and NCD Bernoulli activeness \(A_i\) satisfying \(\Pr[A_i=1]\ge 1-c(1-y_i)\) for \(c=2\sqrt2-2\), there exists a monotone CRS selecting at most one active index with \(\Pr[i\text{ selected}]=c\,y_i\). It also shows dependent rounding induces negative association of offline-node availabilities (Lemma 3.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether there is a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for a rank-1 matroid under a strong negative correlation condition on activeness \((Z_e)\) (negative cylinder-type bounds for both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\)), with only marginals \(z_e\) and \(\sum z_e\le 1\). This paper does not analyze random-order CRSs for rank-1 matroids with those marginals; instead it constructs (existentially, via LP duality) a monotone CRS for stars under a different set of assumptions: (i) the activeness variables satisfy negative cylinder dependence (a consequence of NA), and (ii) their marginals are lower bounded by \(1-c(1-y_i)\), which is much stronger/structured than arbitrary given marginals \(z_i\). The achieved selectability constant in Lemma 5.3 is \(c=2\sqrt2-2\approx0.828\), which is larger than \(1-1/e\approx0.632\), but it applies to this restricted marginal regime and does not address random-order arrival. Thus it provides partial progress/related techniques (negative dependence + star CRS existence) but does not resolve the open problem as stated.

sources.title: Prophet matching meets probing with commitment
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves a (1-1/e)-competitive algorithm for online stochastic bipartite matching with probing and commitment under random-order arrivals (Theorem 2.3 / Algorithm 10). The analysis uses a (1-1/e)-selectable random-order contention resolution scheme for a rank-1 matroid due to Lee and Singla (Theorem 4.3), applied to each offline vertex u with independent activations of incident edges: each edge e=(u,v) is committed independently with probability \(z_e=p_e x_e\) and then accepted with probability at least \((1-1/e)z_e\) under random order.
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether there exists a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for a rank-1 matroid when the activeness indicators \((Z_e)\) are only assumed to satisfy a strong negative-correlation condition (for both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\)). This paper does not address negatively correlated activeness; throughout, edge states/commitment events are independent Bernoulli. The \((1-1/e)\)-selectable RCRS it uses (Lee–Singla) is analyzed for the standard independent model \(R(z)\) where each element is included independently with probability \(z_i\). Thus it provides evidence/technique in the independent case but does not resolve whether the same guarantee holds under the stated negative correlation model.

sources.title: Approximation Algorithms for Action-Reward Query-Commit Matching
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper designs random-order contention-resolution–type rounding tools for stochastic query-commit matching with patience constraints. In particular, it defines a patience random-order contention resolution scheme (P-RCRS) for a star (rank-1) constraint with independent Bernoulli “suggestions” 
\(X_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(x_i)\) and independent Bernoulli “states” \(P_i\sim\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)\), under feasibility \(\sum_i x_i\le \ell\), \(\sum_i p_i x_i\le 1\), and proves (Theorem 3.4) existence of an \(\alpha\)-selectable P-RCRS with \(\alpha=1-1/e\) when \(\ell\in\{1,\infty\}\), and \(\alpha=\tfrac1{27}(19-67/e^3)\approx 0.5801\) for any finite \(2\le \ell<\infty\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether there is a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order contention resolution scheme for a rank-1 matroid when activeness indicators \((Z_e)\) satisfy a strong negative-correlation condition for both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\). This paper’s star-graph rounding subroutine (P-RCRS) is a rank-1 random-order CRS variant, but it assumes the relevant randomness is generated from independent Bernoulli variables (suggestions and states) and then uses attenuation to guarantee selectability. It does not analyze or guarantee \((1-1/e)\)-selectability under the paper’s negative-correlation model for \((Z_e)\); in fact, its reduction to \(|A|=1\) and its proofs rely on independence/product structure (e.g., Poisson regime arguments, Bennett’s inequality). Thus it provides related techniques and partial progress for independent inputs, but does not resolve the negatively correlated-activeness open problem.

sources.title: An Improved Mechanism for Pricing Ride-Hailing Fares
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper designs random-order rounding/CRS procedures for matchings and transversal matroids under independent activeness. In particular, for the rank-1 (single-item) case with independent activeness indicators 

a) Algorithm 1 (random order via i.i.d. Exp(1) arrival times plus a time- and marginal-dependent coin flip) selects each element 

- with unconditional probability 

\[\Pr[\text{select }u]=(1-1/e)\,p_u\]\nprovided \(\sum_u p_u\le 1\), and hence with conditional probability \(1-1/e\) given \(u\) is active.

b) For bipartite matchings, Algorithm 2 rounds a fractional matching \((p_{u,v})\) to a matching such that for every edge \(e=\{u,v\}\),
\[\Pr[e\in M]=(1-1/e)\,p_{u,v}.\]
They further claim a \((1-e^{-k})/k\)-balanced CRS for the intersection of \(k\) transversal matroids (Theorem 1.2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether there exists a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for a rank-1 matroid when activeness indicators are negatively correlated in the strong sense \(\Pr[\wedge_{e\in S}(Z_e=b)]\le\prod_{e\in S}\Pr[Z_e=b]\) for \(b\in\{0,1\}\). This paper achieves the \((1-1/e)\) factor for the rank-1 case (and more general matching/transversal settings) only under an independence model for activeness: it explicitly uses that each element is active independently with probability \(p_u\) in the analysis of Lemma 4.1/Theorem 4.3 (and similarly for edges in Lemma 4.4/Theorem 4.6). The negative-correlation setting is not analyzed, and the proof relies on product-form probabilities and memorylessness that do not directly extend to merely negatively correlated \(Z\). Thus it does not resolve the open problem, but it provides a candidate algorithmic template (random order + marginal-dependent dumping/coin flips) that might be adaptable if one can reprove the key blocking probability bounds under negative correlation.

sources.title: Online bipartite matching in the probe-commit model
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves that in the probe-commit model for online stochastic bipartite matching with known independently distributed (known i.d.) arrivals and random-order arrivals, there exists a 
\((1-1/e)\)-competitive algorithm against the offline adaptive benchmark (Corollary 5.6). The algorithm reduces to applying an existing \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order contention resolution scheme (RCRS) for a 1-uniform matroid (Lee–Singla 2018) to independent proposal indicators \(Z_{u,i}\) with marginals \(z_{u,i}\) satisfying \(\sum_i z_{u,i}\le 1\) for each offline vertex \(u\).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether there is a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order CRS for a rank-1 matroid when the activeness indicators \((Z_e)\) satisfy a strong negative-correlation condition (for both \(b=0\) and \(b=1\)). This paper does not study negatively correlated activeness; throughout, edge/activeness variables are independent Bernoulli, and the CRS reduction in §5 relies on independence of the proposal indicators \((Z_{u,i})\) for fixed \(u\). Thus it does not resolve existence under negative correlation.

However, it is related in that it explicitly reduces a random-order online probing/matching algorithm to the need for a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable RCRS for a 1-uniform matroid, and it uses the known Lee–Singla RCRS (which is designed for independent activations). This clarifies where such a CRS is needed and why independence matters, but it does not extend the guarantee to negatively correlated activations.

title: Convergence guarantees when stochastic gradient estimates diverge in vanishing-merit regime
background_latex:
Consider the stochastic equality-constrained optimization problem
\[
\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(x) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad c(x)=0,
\]
where \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\iota)]\) for a random variable \(\iota\) and smooth functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). Let \(J(x):=\nabla c(x)^T\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be the constraint Jacobian.

Define the constraint-violation measure
\[
\varphi(x):=\|c(x)\|_2.
\]
(Equivalently, one may consider \(\|c(x)\|_2^2\); stationarity conditions scale accordingly.) A point \(x\) is stationary for \(\varphi\) if either \(c(x)=0\) or \(c(x)\neq 0\) and
\[
\nabla \varphi(x)= J(x)^T\frac{c(x)}{\|c(x)\|_2}=0.
\]

An iterative stochastic SQP-type method generates iterates \(\{x_k\}_{k\ge 0}\) and uses stochastic gradient estimates \(g_k\) for \(\nabla f(x_k)\), e.g., unbiased with finite second moment,
\[
\mathbb{E}_k[g_k]=\nabla f(x_k),\qquad \mathbb{E}_k[\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2]\le M,
\]
where \(\mathbb{E}_k[\cdot]\) is conditional expectation given the algorithm has reached \(x_k\).

The method employs an exact-penalty merit function
\[
\phi(x,\tau)= \tau f(x)+\|c(x)\|_2,
\]
with an adaptively updated merit parameter \(\tau_k\ge 0\). One regime of interest is when \(\tau_k\to 0\) (the algorithm places vanishing weight on the objective term). In analyses where \(\tau_k\to 0\), a key additional assumption that enables convergence is that the stochastic gradient errors remain uniformly bounded along the run, i.e., \(\sup_k \|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|_2<\infty\).

Define the problematic event
\[
E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}:=\{\tau_k\to 0\ \text{and}\ \sup_{k\ge 0}\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|_2=\infty\},
\]
i.e., the merit parameter vanishes while a subsequence of stochastic gradient estimates diverges away from the true gradients.
problem_definition_latex:
Develop convergence guarantees for stochastic SQP-type methods for equality-constrained problems in the event
\[
E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}:=\{\tau_k\to 0\ \text{and}\ \sup_{k\ge 0}\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|_2=\infty\}.
\]
In particular, establish conditions under which one can still guarantee that the iterates satisfy an asymptotic stationarity property for the constraint-violation measure \(\varphi(x)=\|c(x)\|_2\) (e.g., \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\|_2=0\), or another appropriate stationarity measure), despite the divergence of the stochastic gradient estimation errors while \(\tau_k\to 0\).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Berahas--Curtis--O’Neill--Robinson’s stochastic SQP framework for equality constraints with potentially rank-deficient Jacobians, the exact-penalty merit \(\phi(x,\tau)=\tau f(x)+\|c(x)\|_2\) is paired with a normal/tangential step decomposition. Their convergence theory splits into regimes depending on the merit parameter sequence \(\{\tau_k\}\): when \(\tau_k\) stabilizes at a small positive value, one can obtain expected stationarity for the original constrained problem; when \(\tau_k\to 0\), the algorithm is meant to transition to minimizing the feasibility measure \(\varphi(x)=\|c(x)\|_2\), and they prove \(\liminf_k\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\|=0\) under an additional assumption that stochastic gradient errors remain bounded. The open gap is precisely the adverse event \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}\) where \(\tau_k\to 0\) while \(\sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\), which disrupts the intended decoupling between feasibility progress (normal step) and objective information (tangential step).

Forward work closest to the vanishing-merit setting is the “Optimistic noise-aware sequential quadratic programming…” paper, which proves liminf infeasible-stationarity bounds for \(\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\|\) in the \(\tau_k\to 0\) regime even with rank-deficient Jacobians, but only under uniformly bounded noise assumptions, so it still excludes \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}\). Several stochastic SQP/trust-region lines of work (e.g., “Fully stochastic trust-region SQP…”, “High probability complexity bounds… with heavy-tailed noise”, and “A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic SQP Method”) relax almost-sure boundedness by using probabilistic accuracy events tied to a shrinking trust-region radius; these frameworks can accommodate realized runs with \(\sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\) while still proving almost-sure or high-probability KKT-type stationarity, but they do not analyze the exact-penalty vanishing-\(\tau_k\) mechanism nor directly target stationarity of \(\varphi(x)=\|c(x)\|\) conditioned on the bad event.

Overall, the problem remains open: existing analyses either (i) rule out \(\tau_k\to 0\) by proving merit-parameter stabilization under bounded errors, (ii) analyze \(\tau_k\to 0\) but require uniform boundedness of gradient/Jacobian noise, or (iii) allow heavy-tailed/unbounded errors via probabilistic accuracy conditions but do not couple this with a vanishing-objective-weight exact-penalty regime. A promising direction is to blend the Berahas et al. normal/tangential decomposition and feasibility-stationarity target \(\liminf\|J^T c\|=0\) with probabilistic-oracle or robust-estimation machinery (e.g., truncation, median-of-means, or accuracy-forcing) that ensures sufficiently many iterations have controlled tangential noise even if \(\sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\), thereby recovering a supermartingale-type descent for \(\|c(x)\|\) on a subsequence without assuming uniform boundedness.

sources.title: Optimistic noise-aware sequential quadratic programming for equality constrained optimization with rank-deficient jacobians
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper analyzes an SQP method for equality-constrained optimization with bounded noise in objective/constraints and possibly rank-deficient Jacobians, using an exact \(\ell_2\) merit function \(\bar\phi(x,\bar\tau)=\bar\tau\,\bar f(x)+\|\bar c(x)\|\) with nonincreasing \(\bar\tau_k\). In the regime \(\bar\tau_k\to 0\), it proves (Theorem 3.38) that the iterates satisfy a liminf infeasible-stationarity guarantee for the true constraint-violation measure \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\):
\[
\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\| \le \max\Big\{\epsilon_c(\epsilon_J+\kappa_J)+\kappa_c\epsilon_J + \sqrt{\tfrac{(1+\sigma_\gamma)(\kappa_c+\epsilon_c)E_c^i}{\eta\,\alpha_{l0}^i\,\sigma_c\sigma_v}},\; 2\kappa_J\epsilon_c\Big\},
\]
where \(E_c^i\) depends on the constraint/Jacobian noise and step-size option. In the complementary regime \(\bar\tau_k\ge \bar\tau_{\min}>0\), it proves averaged bounds (Theorem 3.36) implying \(\frac1{k+1}\sum_{j=0}^k\|J(x_j)^T c(x_j)\|^2\) is \(O(1/(k+1))+O(\epsilon_f+\epsilon_g+\epsilon_c+\epsilon_J)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence guarantees for stochastic SQP when the merit parameter vanishes (\(\tau_k\to 0\)) while stochastic gradient errors can be unbounded (event \(\sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\)). This paper directly studies the \(\tau_k\to 0\) (rank-deficient) regime and proves that, even then, one can guarantee asymptotic (liminf) stationarity for the constraint-violation objective \(\|c(x)\|\) (equivalently \(\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\)) via bounds on \(\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\|\) (Theorem 3.38). However, its noise model assumes uniformly bounded errors in gradients/Jacobians (Assumption 2.2: \(\|\bar g(x)-\nabla f(x)\|\le \epsilon_g\) for all iterates), which excludes the open-problem event where gradient errors diverge. Thus it provides partial progress: it establishes the desired type of infeasible-stationarity guarantee in the vanishing-merit regime, but not under unbounded stochastic-gradient deviations.

sources.title: Inexact sequential quadratic optimization for minimizing a stochastic objective function subject to deterministic nonlinear equality constraints
sources.theorem_or_result:
They propose SISQO (stochastic inexact SQO) for 
\(\min f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x,\omega)]\) s.t. \(c(x)=0\) with deterministic smooth constraints and stochastic objective gradients \(g_k\). Under Assumptions 1–6 and on the event \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{low}}\) that the merit parameter becomes constant at a sufficiently small positive value \(\tau_k\equiv \tau_{k_{\tau,\xi}}>0\) (and \(\xi_k\) stabilizes), Theorem 1 proves an expected stationarity guarantee in terms of the “true-step” model reduction:
- If \(\beta_k\equiv\beta\in(0, A/((1-\eta)(A+\theta)))\), then
\[\mathbb E_{\tau,\mathrm{low}}\Big[\tfrac1K\sum_{j=k_{\tau,\xi}+1}^{k_{\tau,\xi}+K} \Delta l(x_j,\tau_{k_{\tau,\xi}},\nabla f_j,d^{\mathrm{true}}_j)\Big]\le \frac{\beta M}{A-(1-\eta)(A+\theta)\beta}+o(1).\]
- If \(\sum \beta_k=\infty\) and \(\sum \beta_k^2<\infty\), then
\[\lim_{K\to\infty}\mathbb E_{\tau,\mathrm{low}}\Big[\frac{\sum_{j} \beta_j\,\Delta l(x_j,\tau_{k_{\tau,\xi}},\nabla f_j,d^{\mathrm{true}}_j)}{\sum_j \beta_j}\Big]=0.\]
Moreover \(\Delta l(x_k,\tau,\nabla f_k,d^{\mathrm{true}}_k)\ge \kappa_l\tau(\|u^{\mathrm{true}}_k\|^2+\|c_k\|)\), so vanishing averages imply feasibility and first-order KKT stationarity along subsequences.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence/stationarity guarantees specifically on the adverse event \(\{\tau_k\to 0\ \text{and}\ \sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\}\), i.e., a vanishing-merit regime with potentially unbounded stochastic-gradient errors. This paper explicitly does not analyze that regime: in Section 3.3 it states there are three possibilities for \(\{\tau_k\}\) (eventually constant small, vanishing, or constant too large) and then restricts the convergence theory to the first case (Event \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{low}}\)), where \(\tau_k\) becomes constant at a sufficiently small positive value. It cites prior discussion ([3]) that \(\tau_k\to 0\) can be ruled out if gradient errors are uniformly bounded, but it provides no guarantees when errors are unbounded and \(\tau_k\to 0\). Thus it does not solve the open problem; it provides related convergence analysis conditional on avoiding the vanishing-\(\tau\) regime, and clarifies that the problematic event remains untreated.

sources.title: High probability complexity bounds of trust-region stochastic sequential quadratic programming with heavy-tailed noise
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes a trust-region stochastic SQP (TR-SSQP) method for 
\(\min_x f(x)\) s.t. \(c(x)=0\) with stochastic (possibly biased) and heavy-tailed oracle noise, and proves high-probability iteration complexity bounds: it finds a first-order \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point (in KKT residual) in \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) iterations and a second-order \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point in \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) iterations, under probabilistic oracle conditions allowing irreducible noise and heavy-tailed objective-value noise with bounded \((1+\delta)\)-moment (Theorem 4.17, Corollaries 4.18–4.19).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence guarantees in the regime where an exact-penalty merit parameter \(\tau_k\to 0\) while stochastic gradient errors \(\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|\) are unbounded (event \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}\)). This paper is related in that it studies stochastic SQP with merit/trust-region acceptance under heavy-tailed noise and does not require bounded gradient errors in the usual almost-sure sense; instead it assumes a per-iteration high-probability accuracy event for gradient estimates: \(\|\bar g_k-g_k\|\le g+\kappa_g\Delta_k^{\alpha+1}\) with probability \(\ge 1-p_g\) (Definition 3.2). This rules out the specific ‘diverging gradient estimates’ event along the realized run, because the analysis conditions on having sufficiently many accurate iterations and controls the number of inaccurate ones probabilistically. Moreover, the algorithm/analysis is trust-region based and targets KKT stationarity for the constrained problem, not stationarity of the pure feasibility measure \(\varphi(x)=\|c(x)\|\) in a vanishing-merit (\(\tau_k\to 0\)) penalty regime. Hence it does not directly provide guarantees on \(\liminf\|J(x_k)^T c(x_k)\|\) under \(E_{\tau,\mathrm{zero,bad}}\), but it offers techniques (martingale inequalities for heavy-tailed noise; handling irreducible bias) that could be relevant for developing such guarantees.

sources.title: A Trust-Region Interior-Point Stochastic Sequential Quadratic Programming Method
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes TR-IP-SSQP, a trust-region interior-point stochastic SQP method for 
\(\min_x \mathbb{E}[F(x;\xi)]\) subject to deterministic nonlinear equalities \(c(x)=0\) and inequalities \(h(x)\le 0\). Under Assumptions 4.1 (smoothness, bounded iterates, full row rank of the combined Jacobian matrix \(A_k\)) and 4.2 (eventual stabilization of the merit parameter \(\bar\mu_k\)), and probabilistic oracle conditions (Definitions 3.1–3.2) allowing heavy-tailed noise, Theorem 4.11 proves almost-sure first-order stationarity for the barrier subproblems:
- \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla L_{\theta_k}(x_k,s_k,\lambda_k,\tau_k)\|=0\) a.s., where \(\theta_k\downarrow 0\) is a prescribed barrier sequence.
Moreover, any limit point \(x^*\) of a subsequence with \(\|\nabla L_{\theta_{k_\ell}}\|\to 0\) that satisfies LICQ for the original problem is a KKT point of the original constrained problem.

This paper is closely related in that it studies fully stochastic SQP with an \(\ell_2\) exact-penalty merit function and explicitly discusses merit-parameter stability. sources.title: A sequential quadratic programming method for optimization with stochastic objective functions, deterministic inequality constraints and robust subproblems
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes a stochastic SQP method (Algorithm 2) for 
\[\min_x f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\ \text{s.t. } h(x)=0,\ c(x)\le 0\]
using a stochastic line search and an exact-penalty merit function \(\Psi(x;\rho)=f(x)+\rho\,\mathrm{dist}((h(x),c(x))\mid K)\). Under Assumptions 2.2 (smoothness/bounded iterates), 3.3 (probabilistically accurate gradient/function estimates), and 3.13 (extended MFCQ at accumulation points), it proves almost sure asymptotic stationarity:
\[\liminf_{k\to\infty}\big(\varphi(\hat x_k)^2+\chi(\hat x_k)^2\big)=0\ \text{a.s.}\]
(Corollary 3.28), where \(\varphi\) measures constraint violation and \(\chi\) measures first-order optimality for the constrained problem. It also proves \(\Pr(\lim_{k\to\infty}\hat\rho_k=+\infty)=0\) (Theorem 3.30) via a sampling/accuracy-forcing scheme.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for convergence guarantees in the regime where the merit parameter on the objective vanishes (\(\tau_k\to 0\)) while stochastic gradient errors can become unbounded (\(\sup_k\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|=\infty\)), and still to guarantee asymptotic stationarity for the constraint-violation measure \(\|c(x)\|\).

This paper is closely related but addresses a different penalty-parameter pathology: it uses an exact penalty \(f+\rho\varphi\) with \(\rho_k\) potentially \emph{blowing up} due to noisy gradients, and designs a sampling/accuracy-forcing mechanism to ensure \(\rho_k\not\to\infty\) almost surely (Theorem 3.30). Its convergence results (Corollary 3.28) are proved under a probabilistic accuracy condition of the form \(\|g_k-\nabla f(x_k)\|\le \varepsilon_g\alpha_k\|d_k\|\) with high conditional probability, which effectively prevents arbitrarily bad gradients from occurring too often.

Thus, it does not analyze the event \(\tau_k\to 0\) with unbounded gradient errors; instead it enforces sampling so that the bad-gradient events are summable (Borel–Cantelli) and rules out the analogous “bad” event for its own penalty parameter. The techniques (accuracy tied to step size, Borel–Cantelli control of rare large errors, and stationarity in terms of constraint violation \(\varphi\)) are potentially useful tools toward the open problem, but the paper does not provide guarantees \emph{conditioned on} the bad event occurring, nor does it treat a vanishing objective-weight parameter.

title: Prove existence of complete EFX allocations for general valuations setting
background_latex:
Let there be a finite set of indivisible items \(M\) and a finite set of agents \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\). Each agent \(i\in N\) has a valuation function \(v_i:2^M\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) satisfying:
1) Normalization: \(v_i(\varnothing)=0\).
2) Monotonicity: if \(S\subseteq T\subseteq M\), then \(v_i(S)\le v_i(T)\).
An allocation is an \(n\)-tuple \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) of pairwise-disjoint bundles \(X_i\subseteq M\). It is complete if \(\bigcup_{i\in N} X_i=M\).
For agents \(i,j\in N\), agent \(i\) \emph{envies} agent \(j\) under allocation \(X\) if \(v_i(X_i) < v_i(X_j)\).
An allocation \(X\) is \emph{envy-free up to any item (EFX)} if for every pair \(i,j\in N\) and every item \(g\in X_j\),
\[
 v_i(X_i) \ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\}).
\]
Equivalently, after removing any single item from \(j\)'s bundle, agent \(i\) does not prefer the remainder to her own bundle.
The central general-valuation setting imposes no further structure such as additivity, submodularity, or identical valuations beyond normalization and monotonicity.
problem_definition_latex:
Given any numbers of agents \(n\ge 1\), any finite item set \(M\), and any collection of normalized, monotone valuation functions \(\{v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\}_{i\in N}\), determine whether there must exist a complete allocation \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) of \(M\) that is EFX, i.e., satisfies
\[
\forall i,j\in N,\ \forall g\in X_j:\quad v_i(X_i) \ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\}).
\]
In particular, resolve the existence question for general valuations when all goods must be allocated.

literature_review.synthesis:
Mahara (2021) framed the central question for general (normalized, monotone) valuations: whether a complete EFX allocation must always exist. Building on the champion-graph framework of Chaudhury–Garg–Mehlhorn and the “EFX with charity” line, Mahara extended several additive-valuation existence results to general valuations via potential-function arguments (lexicographic and a new partition-leximin potential). In particular, Mahara proved complete EFX existence for two-valuation-type profiles and for the small-excess regime \(m\le n+3\), and improved bounded-charity guarantees to \(|U|\le n-2\) unallocated goods while maintaining that no agent envies the unallocated set.

The universal existence conjecture for complete EFX under general monotone valuations has since been resolved negatively by the paper titled “A Counterexample to EFX; Agents, Items, Monotone Valuations; via SAT-Solving”, which constructs an explicit instance with \(n=3\) agents and \(m=8\) goods admitting no complete EFX allocation, and further shows broad families of counterexamples for all \(n\ge 3\) once \(m\) is sufficiently larger than \(n\) (even for submodular valuations). This pins down the sharpness of Mahara’s positive results in the small-\(m\) regime and clarifies that any general-valuation existence theorem must impose additional structure (on valuations, on item-agent incidence, or by allowing charity/approximation).

Subsequent work has therefore focused on delineating maximal domains where complete EFX remains guaranteed and on principled relaxations. On the positive side, complete EFX is shown to exist for substantial structured subclasses of monotone valuations, notably multigraph/bipartite-multigraph valuation models where each good is relevant to at most two agents, and for leveled valuations where value strictly increases with bundle size. Complementarily, relaxations such as epistemic EFX (EEFX) restore unconditional existence for arbitrary monotone valuations, while other lines (e.g., rainbow-cycle-number methods) yield near-optimal \((1-\varepsilon)\)-EFX with bounded charity and additional welfare guarantees. Together, these results map a post-counterexample landscape: exact complete EFX fails in full generality, but remains attainable in rich structured settings and via carefully designed relaxations.

sources.title: A Counterexample to EFX; Agents, Items, Monotone Valuations; via SAT-Solving
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves non-existence of complete EFX allocations in the general monotone-valuation setting by exhibiting an explicit counterexample with 3 agents and 8 goods (monotone valuations) for which no allocation 
\(X=(X_1,X_2,X_3)\) satisfies EFX, and extends this to show: for every \(n\ge 3\) and \(m\ge n+5\), there exists an instance with submodular (hence monotone) valuations with no EFX allocation (Theorem 2). It also proves universal existence for the boundary case of 3 agents and 7 goods (Theorem 1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether for arbitrary normalized, monotone valuations there must always exist a complete EFX allocation. This paper answers the existence question in the negative by constructing monotone valuations (already for \(n=3, m=8\)) with no EFX allocation, and further shows such counterexamples exist broadly (\(n\ge 3, m\ge n+5\)), even within submodular valuations. Thus it refutes the conjectured universal existence in the general-valuation setting (and a fortiori in the monotone setting).

sources.title: EFX: a simpler approach and an (almost) optimal guarantee via rainbow cycle number
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves two main results about EFX. (1) For exact EFX with complete allocation: with three agents, a complete EFX allocation exists provided at least one agent’s valuation is MMS-feasible (in particular, additive); the other agents may have arbitrary normalized monotone valuations (Theorems 1–2). (2) For approximate EFX with charity: the rainbow cycle number satisfies \(R(d)=O(d\log d)\) (Theorem 3/10), implying a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a partial \((1-\varepsilon)\)-EFX allocation leaving \(\tilde O((n/\varepsilon)^{1/2})\) goods unallocated and with Nash-welfare guarantee (Theorem 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of complete EFX allocations for arbitrary numbers of agents under general (normalized, monotone) valuations. This paper does not resolve that: it gives an exact-existence theorem only for \(n=3\) under a restriction (one agent MMS-feasible), leaving the fully general \(n=3\) monotone case open, and it does not address \(n\ge 4\) exact EFX existence. It also advances a different relaxation—\((1-\varepsilon)\)-EFX with bounded charity—by nearly tight bounds on rainbow cycle number, but this does not yield complete EFX for general valuations.

sources.title: EFX allocations and orientations on bipartite multi-graphs: A complete picture
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves existence (and algorithms) of complete EFX allocations for a restricted general-valuation model where each item is valued by at most two agents (a multi-graph instance). In particular:
- Theorem 4.11: For any fair-division instance whose valuation profile is representable by a bipartite multi-graph and where each agent’s valuation is normalized and monotone (with value depending only on incident edges), a complete EFX allocation always exists; it can be computed in pseudo-polynomial time (and in polynomial time for cancelable valuations).
- Theorem 5.1 / Corollary 5.2: For multi-cycles, EFX allocations exist for MMS-feasible valuations; for cycles with at least four agents, existence holds for monotone valuations as well (pseudo-polynomial time; polynomial for cancelable).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of complete EFX allocations for arbitrary normalized, monotone valuations on all subsets of goods (no structural restrictions). This paper does not resolve that general question. Instead it establishes existence in a significant special case: valuations induced by (bi)partite multi-graphs, i.e., each good has positive marginal value for at most two agents and each agent’s value for a bundle depends only on the subset of incident goods. Within that restricted domain, it gives unconditional existence and constructive algorithms (Theorem 4.11), and extends to multi-cycles (Theorem 5.1). Thus it is partial progress: it expands the largest known valuation classes guaranteeing EFX, but leaves the unrestricted general-valuation setting open (indeed it ends with a conjecture for general multi-graphs, still far from arbitrary valuations).

sources.title: On the existence of EFX allocations in multigraphs
sources.theorem_or_result: In the multigraph valuation model (goods are edges; each agent/vertex values only incident edges; valuations are normalized and monotone), the paper proves existence of complete EFX allocations under any of the following structural conditions on the multigraph: (a) the multigraph is bipartite (Theorem 1), or (b) every vertex has at most \(\lceil n/4\rceil-1\) neighbors (Theorem 2), or (c) the shortest cycle consisting of non-parallel edges has length at least 6 (Theorem 3). In each case, all edges are allocated and the resulting allocation \(X\) satisfies \(\forall i,j\ \forall g\in X_j: v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\})\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether complete EFX allocations always exist for completely general monotone valuations over an arbitrary item set (no structural restrictions). This paper does not resolve that question. Instead it proves existence in a restricted but nontrivial subclass of general monotone valuations: the (2,\(\infty\))-bounded/multigraph setting where each good is relevant to at most two agents (incident endpoints), and additionally requires one of three graph-structural conditions (bipartite, bounded neighborhood size, or large girth in the underlying simple graph of non-parallel edges). Thus it is partial progress toward the general-valuation existence question by expanding the known positive territory beyond simple graphs and beyond additive valuations in multigraphs.

sources.title: Fair and truthful allocations under leveled valuations
sources.theorem_or_result:
Theorem 4: For any number of agents and indivisible goods, if all agents have leveled valuation functions (normalized, monotone, and strictly increasing with bundle cardinality: 
- if \(|S|>|T|\) then \(v(S)>v(T)\)), then a complete EFX allocation exists. In particular, Algorithm 1 (a serial dictatorship with quotas \(\lfloor m/n\rfloor\) for \(n-r\) agents and \(\lfloor m/n\rfloor+1\) for \(r\) agents, where \(m=kn+r\)) outputs an allocation \(A\) such that \(\forall i,j\,\forall g\in A_j: v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether complete EFX allocations always exist for completely general monotone valuations (no structure beyond normalization and monotonicity). This paper proves existence of complete EFX allocations only for the restricted class of leveled valuations, which is a strict subclass of monotone valuations (it imposes strict preference for larger cardinality bundles regardless of item identities). Thus it does not resolve the general-valuation existence question, but provides a positive existence theorem in a non-additive, non-submodular setting that still allows arbitrary rankings among equal-size bundles. The proof/algorithm (quota-based serial dictatorship) leverages the cardinality-driven structure; it does not extend to arbitrary monotone valuations where bundle size alone does not determine strict preference.

sources.title: Epistemic EFX allocations exist for monotone valuations
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves existence of epistemic EFX (EEFX) allocations for any number of agents with normalized, monotone (general) valuations: for every instance 
I=([n],M,(v_1,\dots,v_n))
 there exists a complete allocation \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) such that for each agent \(i\) there exists a partition of \(M\setminus X_i\) into \(n-1\) bundles \(C_1,\dots,C_{n-1}\) with \(v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(C_j\setminus\{g\})\) for all \(j\) and all \(g\in C_j\) (Theorem 3.5). It also shows computing EEFX is hard: exponential value-query lower bound and PLS-hardness even for identical submodular valuations (Theorems 4.7, 4.8).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of complete EFX allocations under general monotone valuations. This paper does not prove EFX existence; instead it proves existence of a relaxation, EEFX, for the full generality of monotone valuations. Thus it provides progress only in the sense of identifying a fairness notion close to EFX with unconditional existence, and it highlights that computational hardness for EEFX parallels known hardness for EFX. It does not resolve whether EFX itself always exists when all goods must be allocated.

title: Finite-sample bounds for multivariate shortfall risk estimators with streaming samples
background_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space. Fix an integer dimension \(d\ge 2\). Let \(X\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) be a bounded \(d\)-dimensional random vector representing (componentwise) losses or positions.

Let \(\ell:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be a convex loss/utility-penalty function (sometimes called an aggregation loss), and let \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\) be a fixed risk-level parameter (assumed to be in the interior of the range of \(\ell\) under the law of the argument in question).

Define the acceptance set
\[
\mathcal A := \bigl\{Y\in L^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^d): \ \mathbb E[\,\ell(-Y)\,] \le \lambda\bigr\}.
\]

A multivariate shortfall risk measure (MSRM) is a multivariate analogue of utility-based shortfall risk, defined via the cash-additivity/translation of the acceptance set: for a given position \(X\), one seeks a deterministic capital allocation vector \(m\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \(X+m\in\mathcal A\); one may consider the set of admissible allocations
\[
\mathcal R_\lambda(X) := \{m\in\mathbb R^d : \mathbb E[\ell(-(X+m))]\le \lambda\},
\]
and/or a scalarized risk value derived from \(\mathcal R_\lambda(X)\) (the precise scalarization depends on the MSRM definition).

Assume an online/streaming observation model: samples \(\{X_i\}_{i\ge 1}\) are revealed one-at-a-time, where \(X_i\) are i.i.d. copies of \(X\). An estimator for an MSRM is any measurable mapping \(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{\lambda,n}\) (or \(\widehat m_n\)) computed from \(X_1,\dots,X_n\). “Finite-sample bounds” refers to non-asymptotic guarantees (e.g., mean-squared error or concentration inequalities) as explicit functions of \(n\).
problem_definition_latex:
Develop non-asymptotic (finite-sample) performance guarantees for an online/streaming estimator of a multivariate shortfall risk measure (MSRM) based on i.i.d. samples \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) of a bounded random vector \(X\in\mathbb R^d\).

Concretely, provide explicit bounds (in \(n\)) on the estimation error of an MSRM estimator \(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{\lambda,n}\) (or an estimated capital allocation \(\widehat m_n\in\mathbb R^d\)) relative to the target MSRM determined by \(\ell\) and \(\lambda\), analogous in spirit to finite-sample bounds available for the univariate utility-based shortfall risk estimator.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Hegde et al., 2023) develops a stochastic-approximation (SA) root-finding view of univariate utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR), where \(\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(X)\) is the unique root of \(g(t)=\mathbb E[\ell(-X-t)]-\lambda\). Under boundedness and a monotonicity condition on \(g\) (via bounds on \(-\ell'\)), it proves non-asymptotic mean-squared error rates \(\mathbb E[(t_n-\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(X))^2]=O(1/n)\) for stepsize \(a_n=c/n\) when the monotonicity parameter is known, and \(O(1/n^\alpha)\) for universal stepsizes \(a_n=c/n^\alpha\), together with high-probability concentration. It also analyzes biased ratio-form gradient estimators for UBSR optimization, again with explicit finite-sample rates.

Forward-citing work to date does not resolve the multivariate extension requested in the open problem: finite-sample bounds for streaming estimators of multivariate shortfall risk measures (MSRM) defined by \(\mathcal R_\lambda(X)=\{m\in\mathbb R^d: \mathbb E[\ell(-(X+m))]\le\lambda\}\) with \(d\ge2\) and convex aggregation loss \(\ell:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). The most relevant partial progress remains in the univariate/scalar setting: (i) learning/regression work provides concentration for SAA estimators of scalar shortfall risk under tail/margin conditions; (ii) risk-sensitive RL work provides \(O(1/m)\) MSE bounds for shortfall-risk policy-gradient estimators using double sampling; and (iii) optimization papers develop efficient solvers (e.g., ADMM and semismooth Newton projections) for finite-sample SAA programs. These contributions suggest tools—uniform concentration over \(m\in\mathbb R^d\), stability of feasible-set estimators, and SA/SGD analyses with biased or ratio estimators—but a complete non-asymptotic streaming theory for MSRM set/allocator estimation appears to remain open.

sources.title: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning using expectiles, shortfall risk and optimized certainty equivalent risk
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper derives non-asymptotic mean-squared error bounds of order \(O(1/m)\) for trajectory-based estimators of policy gradients for several scalar risk objectives, including utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR) \(\mathrm{SR}_{l,\lambda}(X)=\inf\{k\in\mathbb R: \mathbb E[l(X-k)]\le \lambda\}\). In particular, for a finite-horizon MDP with bounded cumulative cost \(F\), it proves a policy-gradient formula
\[\nabla \mathrm{SR}(\theta)=\frac{\mathbb E_\theta\big[l(F-\mathrm{SR}(\theta))\,G(\theta)\big]}{\mathbb E_\theta\big[l'(F-\mathrm{SR}(\theta))\big]}\]
(Theorem 6) and, using a double-sampling estimator \(Q^m_\theta(\hat Z,Z)\), establishes an MSE bound
\[\mathbb E\big[\|\nabla \mathrm{SR}(\theta)-Q^m_\theta(\hat Z,Z)\|_2^2\big]\le \frac{C}{m}\]
(Lemma 3), with explicit constants under boundedness/regularity assumptions. Analogous \(O(1/m)\) MSE bounds are shown for expectile and OCE gradient estimators (Theorem 5, Lemma 6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for finite-sample (non-asymptotic) bounds for *multivariate* shortfall risk estimators \(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{\lambda,n}\) or capital allocations \(\hat m_n\in\mathbb R^d\) in a streaming i.i.d. setting for \(X\in\mathbb R^d\) and convex \(\ell:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). This paper provides finite-sample \(O(1/m)\) MSE bounds, but for *scalar* (univariate) UBSR/OCE/expectile objectives applied to the cumulative cost random variable \(F\) in RL, and for *gradient estimators* (policy optimization), not for estimating the multivariate allocation set \(\mathcal R_\lambda(X)\) or a multivariate MSRM from streaming samples. Thus it does not solve the multivariate streaming-estimation problem; it is partially relevant as it develops non-asymptotic analysis techniques for shortfall-type risk functionals and their sample-based root/ratio estimators, which could inform analogous bounds in the multivariate case.

sources.title: Optimizing Shortfall Risk Metric for Learning Regression Models
sources.theorem_or_result:
For univariate utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR) 
\(\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(Z)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R: \mathbb E[\ell(Z-t)]\le \lambda\}\) with \(\ell\) convex, strictly increasing and \(G\)-Lipschitz, and assuming a bracketing condition (A1) giving \(t_L\le \mathrm{SR}_\lambda(Z)\le t_U\) with margin \(\eta>0\), the sample-average approximation estimator \(\mathrm{SR}_n\) defined by \(\min_t\{t: \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(Z_i-t)\le \lambda\}\) satisfies concentration bounds:
- If \(Z\) is sub-Gaussian with parameter \(\sigma\), then with probability \(\ge 1-2\delta\),
\[|\mathrm{SR}_n-\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(Z)|\le \frac{2G\sigma (t_U-t_L)}{\eta}\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}.\]
- If \(Z\) is sub-exponential with parameter \(K\), then with probability \(\ge 1-2\delta\),
\[|\mathrm{SR}_n-\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(Z)|\le \frac{4eGK (t_U-t_L)}{\eta}\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}.\]
Additionally, for regression with squared loss \(Z=(Y-\hat Y(X))^2\), their bisection Algorithm 1 returns \(h_T\) with excess UBSR bounded as
\[\mathrm{SR}_\lambda((Y-h_T(X))^2)\le \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\mathrm{SR}_\lambda((Y-h(X))^2)+C_1\rho+C_2\rho'+C_3 2^{-T},\]
where \(\rho\) is the optimization (ERM) suboptimality in each iteration and \(\rho'\) is the UBSR estimation error.

The open problem asks for non-asymptotic finite-sample bounds for *multivariate* shortfall risk estimators (MSRM) with streaming samples \(X_i\in\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\), and aggregation loss \(\ell:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\). This paper provides finite-sample concentration bounds for the *univariate* UBSR estimator \(\mathrm{SR}_n\) (scalar \(Z\)) under sub-Gaussian/sub-exponential tails, and uses these bounds inside an algorithmic excess-risk guarantee for UBSR optimization in regression.

Thus it contributes techniques and explicit \(n\)-rates for shortfall-risk estimation, but it does not treat multivariate shortfall risk sets \(\mathcal R_\lambda(X)\subset\mathbb R^d\), capital allocation vectors \(m\in\mathbb R^d\), or online/streaming estimators for MSRM. Any extension to MSRM would require new arguments (e.g., uniform concentration for \(m\mapsto \mathbb E[\ell(-(X+m))]\) over \(m\in\mathbb R^d\), set estimation error metrics, and handling \(\ell\) on \(\mathbb R^d\)).

sources.title: An Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers for Utility-based Shortfall Risk Portfolio Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops an ADMM algorithm for sample-average-approximation (SAA) utility-based shortfall risk (UBSR) portfolio optimization and proves convergence of the ADMM iterates for the finite-sample SAA problem. In particular, for the convex program
\[
\min_{w\in\mathbb R^n,t\in\mathbb R} (1-\alpha)t-\alpha\mu^\top w\ \text{s.t. } w\in W,\ \mu^\top w\ge R_0,\ \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m l(-\xi_i^\top w-t)\le \lambda,
\]
Theorem 3.1 shows that the ADMM iterates \((w^k,t^k,z^k,s^k,\nu_1^k,\nu_2^k)\) satisfy objective residual and constraint violations decaying as \(O(1/(k+1))\):
- \((1-\alpha)(t^k-t^*)-\alpha\mu^\top(w^k-w^*)\to 0\)
- \(Rw^k+t^k\mathbf 1_m+z^k\to 0\), \(\mu^\top w^k-s^k-R_0\to 0\)
with explicit bounds \(\|Rw^k+t^k\mathbf 1_m+z^k\|^2+(\mu^\top w^k-s^k-R_0)^2\le C/(\sigma(k+1))\).
A key subroutine is fast projection onto \(Z=\{z\in\mathbb R^m: \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m l(z_i)\le\lambda\}\), solved via semismooth Newton methods (Algorithms 2–4) with local Q-superlinear (and sometimes global) convergence guarantees for the projection KKT system / equivalent univariate root-finding formulation.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for non-asymptotic finite-sample error bounds for *multivariate* shortfall risk estimators in a streaming/i.i.d. setting, i.e., bounds in sample size \(n\) comparing an online estimator \(\widehat{\mathcal R}_{\lambda,n}\) (or \(\hat m_n\)) to the population MSRM defined by \(\mathbb E[\ell(-(X+m))]\le\lambda\) for \(X\in\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\).

This paper instead treats *univariate* UBSR \(\mathrm{SR}_\lambda(X)=\inf\{t: \mathbb E[l(-X-t)]\le\lambda\}\) and focuses on computational optimization for the *SAA* approximation with \(m\) scenarios. Its guarantees are iteration-complexity bounds in ADMM iteration count \(k\) for solving the finite-sample convex program, not statistical estimation error bounds in \(m\) (or streaming regret/MSE) relative to the population risk measure. It also does not address multivariate shortfall risk (vector allocations \(m\in\mathbb R^d\) with multivariate aggregation loss \(\ell:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\)).

Nevertheless, the projection subproblem \(P_Z\) and semismooth-Newton/ADMM machinery are potentially useful tools if one designs online/SAA estimators for (multi)variate shortfall constraints, since MSRM estimation often reduces to solving convex feasibility/root-finding problems involving sample averages of convex losses.

sources.title: Some Studies on Stochastic Optimization based Quantitative Risk Management
sources.theorem_or_result: This article is primarily a survey/tutorial on stochastic-optimization-based quantitative risk management. It does not present new non-asymptotic finite-sample bounds for multivariate shortfall risk estimators. The main technical statements included are asymptotic central limit theorems for sample-average-approximation (SAA) estimators of (univariate) optimized certainty equivalent (OCE) risk and (univariate) utility-based shortfall risk (SR), e.g. for SR: if \,t_n\, solves the SAA constraint problem \(\min_{t\in T} t\) s.t. \(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\xi_i-t)\le \lambda\), then \(\sqrt n (t_n-t^*)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(\ell(\xi-t^*))/\bigl(\mathbb E[\ell'(\xi-t^*)]\bigr)^2\) under differentiability/Lipschitz conditions (Theorem 1, attributed to Hu–Zhang 2018).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for non-asymptotic (finite-sample) error bounds for online/streaming estimators of multivariate shortfall risk measures (MSRM) for bounded \(X\in\mathbb R^d\), \(d\ge2\). This paper discusses (i) univariate OCE and univariate SR estimation/optimization mainly via SAA and stochastic approximation, providing asymptotic CLTs and consistency, and (ii) it explicitly points to Hegde et al. (2024) as providing finite-sample bounds for online SR (still univariate). title: Prove convexity and monotonicity of the optimal robust ratio in acceptance probability
background_latex:
Consider the secretary problem with uncertain acceptance (SP-UA) with a known horizon length \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and acceptance probability \(p\in(0,1]\). There are \(n\) candidates with distinct absolute ranks \(1\prec 2\prec\cdots\prec n\) (rank \(1\) is best). Candidates arrive in a uniformly random permutation \(\pi=(R_1,\dots,R_n)\) of \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\), where \(R_t\) is the absolute rank of the \(t\)-th arrival.

At time \(t\), the decision maker observes only the partial rank \(r_t\in[t]\) of the current candidate among the first \(t\) arrivals. The decision maker chooses either \(\text{offer}\) or \(\text{pass}\). If \(\text{offer}\) is chosen at time \(t\), the current candidate accepts independently with probability \(p\), in which case the process stops and that candidate is selected; if the offer is rejected (probability \(1-p\)), the process continues to \(t+1\). If \(\text{pass}\) is chosen, the process continues to \(t+1\). A policy \(P\) is any (possibly randomized) Markovian rule mapping \((t,r_t)\) to a distribution over \(\{\text{offer},\text{pass}\}\).

For \(k\in[n]\), a \"top \(k\)\" candidate means absolute rank in \([k]\). Define the robust ratio of a policy \(P\) at acceptance probability \(p\) as
\[
\gamma_P(p)=\min_{k\in[n]}\frac{\Pr(\text{policy }P\text{ selects a top-}k\text{ candidate and the offer is accepted})}{\Pr(\text{at least one of the top-}k\text{ candidates would accept an offer})}.
\]
Since each candidate would accept an offer with probability \(p\) independently of everything else, \(\Pr(\text{at least one top-}k\text{ candidate accepts})=1-(1-p)^k\). The optimal robust ratio is
\[
\gamma_n^*(p)=\sup_P\gamma_P(p),
\]
and the asymptotic optimal robust ratio is \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\gamma_n^*(p)\), which exists because \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) is nonincreasing in \(n\) for fixed \(p\).
problem_definition_latex: Establish (or refute) that the optimal robust ratio \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) is a convex and decreasing function of \(p\in(0,1]\) (for fixed \(n\)), and correspondingly that \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)\) is convex and decreasing in \(p\in(0,1]\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem from Perez-Salazar, Singh, and Toriello asks for structural properties of the optimal robust ratio \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) (and its limit \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)\)) as a function of the homogeneous acceptance probability \(p\): specifically, whether it is decreasing and convex on \((0,1]\). In the source paper, \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) is characterized exactly by a linear program derived from an MDP polyhedral description of all Markovian policies, and \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)\) is approximated by a continuous LP. The paper proves several sharp bounds and identifies an exact optimal policy for \(p\ge p^*\approx 0.594\), where \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)=p^{p/(1-p)}\), but it only reports empirical evidence (via solving \((LP)_{n,p}\) numerically) that \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) appears convex and decreasing; no proof is given.

Among the forward citations provided, only “Prophets Inequalities with Uncertain Acceptance” is available and it is not directly about the robust-ratio secretary objective. It develops structural reductions for prophet inequalities with uncertain acceptance by absorbing acceptance into realized values \(Z_i=X_iA_i\), and it discusses that some uncertain-acceptance performance measures can exhibit non-monotone behavior as acceptance probabilities vary. While this does not resolve convexity/monotonicity of \(\gamma_n^*(p)\), it suggests that proving monotonicity may require exploiting the specific normalization by \(1-(1-p)^k\) and the LP structure in the secretary setting, rather than relying on generic “more acceptance helps” intuition.

Given the current citation set, there is no known solving paper establishing convexity and monotonicity of \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) or \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)\). The problem therefore remains open. Promising directions include sensitivity/parametric analysis of \((LP)_{n,p}\) and \((CLP)_p\) with respect to \(p\), potentially via dual formulations (where \(p\) enters both feasibility and objective normalization) and envelope theorems for piecewise-linear concave value functions; another direction is to attempt to prove monotonicity/convexity first for the continuous relaxation \(\gamma_\infty^*(p)\) and then transfer to finite \(n\) using the quantitative approximation bound \(|\gamma_n^* - \gamma_\infty^*|\le O((\log n)^2/(p\sqrt n))\) from the source paper.

sources.title: Prophets Inequalities with Uncertain Acceptance
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies prophet inequalities with uncertain acceptance (PI-UA), where each option has value \(X_i\) and acceptance indicator \(A_i\). Key structural result (Theorem 3.1): for \(Z_i:=X_iA_i\), the optimal online value in PI-UA equals the optimal online value in the classical prophet inequality instance \((Z_1,\dots,Z_n)\), i.e. \(DP(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)=ON(Z_1,\dots,Z_n)\). It also proves a bound for scaled Bernoulli prophet instances (Theorem 4.2): if \(X_i=\lambda_i\mathrm{Ber}(p_i)\) with fixed \(\lambda_i\ge 0\), \(p_i\in(0,1)\), then \(ON(\mathcal I)/OPT(\mathcal I)\ge \tfrac12-\min_i p_i\), tight and achievable by a single-threshold algorithm.
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the secretary problem with uncertain acceptance (SP-UA) and asks whether the optimal robust ratio \(\gamma_n^*(p)\) (a worst-case-over-\(k\) probability ratio normalized by \(1-(1-p)^k\)) is convex and decreasing in the homogeneous acceptance probability \(p\). This paper instead analyzes expected-value competitive ratios in a prophet-inequality model with uncertain acceptance, with generally heterogeneous \(p_i\) and distributional values. It does not define or study \(\gamma_n^*(p)\), nor does it prove convexity/monotonicity in \(p\) for the secretary robust-ratio objective. The only tangential link is conceptual: it highlights that some performance measures in uncertain-acceptance online selection can exhibit non-monotonic behavior in acceptance likelihood (Section 6.2), which suggests monotonicity/convexity questions can be subtle, but it provides no direct result for \(\gamma_n^*(p)\).

title: Uniqueness in law criteria for weak solutions of multidimensional Ito SDEs
background_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge 0},\mathbb P)\) be a filtered probability space supporting a standard \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion \(W\). Consider the It\^o stochastic differential equation (SDE)
\[
 dX_t = b(t,X_t)\,dt + \sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=x\in\mathbb R^d,
\]
where \(b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d\) and \(\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) are Borel measurable coefficients. A \emph{weak solution} is a tuple \((\Omega',\mathcal F',(\mathcal F'_t)_{t\ge 0},\mathbb P',W',X')\) such that \(W'\) is a Brownian motion and \(X'\) is an adapted continuous process satisfying the SDE in the It\^o sense under \(\mathbb P'\). 

The SDE is said to have \emph{uniqueness in law} (also called \emph{weak uniqueness}) if for any two weak solutions with the same initial condition \(x\), the laws of the solution processes \((X_t)_{t\in[0,T]}\) on path space coincide. One often assumes some form of (uniform) nondegeneracy/ellipticity of \(\sigma\), e.g. \(\sigma\sigma^\top\ge \lambda I\) for some \(\lambda>0\), but coefficients may still be merely measurable or discontinuous.

In the attached paper, the finite-player game dynamics lead to an \(n\)-dimensional SDE of the form
\[
 dX_t = D(t,X_t)\,dW_t,
\]
with diagonal diffusion matrix \(D(t,x)\) whose diagonal entries are bounded between two positive constants \(\sigma_1<\sigma_2\) (uniform ellipticity), but can be discontinuous as functions of \(x\) because they arise from feedback controls. The paper notes that, in dimensions greater than 2, general necessary-and-sufficient conditions for uniqueness in law of such weak solutions are not known.
problem_definition_latex:
For dimensions \(d>2\), characterize (with conditions that are simultaneously sufficient and necessary) when the It\^o SDE
\[
 dX_t = b(t,X_t)\,dt + \sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=x\in\mathbb R^d,
\]
admits uniqueness in law of weak solutions.

In particular, determine such a sharp characterization for the driftless, uniformly elliptic case
\[
 dX_t = \sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t,
\]
including the case where \(\sigma(t,\cdot)\) may be discontinuous (e.g. piecewise constant) and may be restricted to be diagonal-valued.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem highlighted in the source paper concerns sharp (simultaneously necessary and sufficient) criteria for uniqueness in law of weak solutions to multidimensional It\^o SDEs with merely measurable, potentially discontinuous coefficients, even under uniform ellipticity. In the game-motivated setting, the diffusion matrix is diagonal with entries in \([\sigma_1,\sigma_2]\) but discontinuous in the state due to feedback (rank/threshold-type) controls; the paper stresses that while weak existence follows from classical uniformly elliptic theory (e.g. Krylov), weak uniqueness can fail in dimensions \(d>2\), and no general characterization is known.

The other citing works are either methodological (PDE well-posedness for smooth controlled diffusions) or expository background, and do not address the multidimensional weak uniqueness characterization.

Overall, based on the provided forward citations, the problem remains open: there is still no known necessary-and-sufficient criterion for weak uniqueness for general uniformly elliptic, merely measurable (possibly diagonal/piecewise constant) diffusion coefficients in dimensions \(d>2\). Promising directions suggested by the source context include identifying structural subclasses (e.g. diagonal coefficients with special discontinuity geometry, or coefficients of bounded variation in each coordinate) where the martingale problem is well posed, and clarifying the boundary between well-posedness and counterexamples in higher dimensions.

sources.title: Mean-field ranking games with diffusion control
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves existence and uniqueness of a mean field equilibrium for a 1-dimensional diffusion-control ranking game, where the equilibrium control is a threshold (bang-bang) diffusion coefficient. Concretely, for 
\[dX_t = m_b(X_t)\,dB_t,\qquad m_b(x)=\sigma_2\mathbf 1_{x\le b}+\sigma_1\mathbf 1_{x>b},\]
with an independent random horizon \(\tau\), there exists a unique \(b^*\in\mathbb R\) such that \(q(X^{b^*}_\tau,1-p)=b^*\), and \((\mathrm{Law}(X^{b^*}_\tau),m_{b^*})\) is a mean field equilibrium (Theorem 3.7). They also show the corresponding \(n\)-tuple of threshold controls is an \(\varepsilon_n\)-Nash equilibrium with \(\varepsilon_n\in O(n^{-1/2})\) (Theorem 4.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for sharp necessary-and-sufficient conditions for uniqueness in law of weak solutions to multidimensional (\(d>2\)) uniformly elliptic Itô SDEs with merely measurable/discontinuous diffusion (including diagonal/piecewise constant cases). This paper does not provide such a characterization. It only (i) notes that in \(n\ge 3\) uniqueness in law can fail even under uniform ellipticity (citing Nadirashvili), and (ii) works in a special 1-dimensional driftless setting where the diffusion is a discontinuous threshold function of bounded variation; in that case they rely on known 1D results (e.g. Nakao-type pathwise uniqueness) to assert existence of a unique strong solution for the oscillating Brownian motion SDE. Thus it provides a relevant special case and motivation, but no multidimensional uniqueness criteria.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The talk identifies equilibrium/approximate equilibrium controls in a rank-based diffusion-control game where each player controls only the diffusion coefficient. In the two-player case with dynamics 
\[dX_t=a_1(X_t,Y_t)\,dW_t^1,\quad dY_t=a_2(X_t,Y_t)\,dW_t^2,\]
with measurable controls taking values in \([\sigma_1,\sigma_2]\), a saddle point is given by the discontinuous feedback 
\[a_1^*(x,y)=\sigma_2\mathbf 1_{\{x\le y\}}+\sigma_1\mathbf 1_{\{x>y\}},\quad a_2^*(x,y)=a_1^*(y,x).\]
In the mean-field limit, the best response to a threshold \(b\) for the objective \(\sup_\beta \mathbb P(X_T^\beta>b)\) is the threshold diffusion control \(m_b(x)=\sigma_2\mathbf 1_{\{x\le b\}}+\sigma_1\mathbf 1_{\{x>b\}}\), yielding an oscillating Brownian motion (OBM), and an equilibrium threshold \(b^*\) is given in closed form by solving \(\mathbb P(X_T^{m_{b^*}}>b^*)=\alpha\). The resulting profile in the \(n\)-player game is an \(\varepsilon_n\)-Nash equilibrium with \(\varepsilon_n=O(n^{-1/2})\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for sharp necessary-and-sufficient conditions for uniqueness in law of weak solutions to multidimensional Itô SDEs with merely measurable/discontinuous (uniformly elliptic) diffusion, especially diagonal diffusion in dimensions \(d>2\). This citing item is a short talk/preprint summary about ranking games; it uses discontinuous, uniformly elliptic diffusion coefficients (piecewise constant threshold controls) and explicitly references oscillating Brownian motion in 1D and a 2D two-player system. However, it does not propose or prove any general uniqueness-in-law characterization in dimensions \(d>2\), nor does it establish new uniqueness results for the \(n\)-dimensional diagonal, discontinuous diffusion matrices arising in the game. At most, it provides motivating examples where weak solutions are considered under discontinuous diffusion controls and where well-posedness/uniqueness issues are relevant.

title: Polynomial bound on degenerate simplex pivots for 0/1 polytope linear programs
background_latex:
Consider a linear program over a fixed feasible region that is a 0/1 polytope:
\[
\max\{c^\top x : x \in P\},\qquad P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: Ax=b,\; Dx\le d\},
\]
where all extreme points (vertices) of \(P\) have coordinates in \(\{0,1\}\), and the input data \(A,b,D,d,c\) are integral.

To run the Simplex method, one may convert the LP to standard equality form by introducing slack variables (without requiring those slack variables to be 0/1 at vertices):
\[
\max\{(c')^\top x' : A' x' = b',\; x'\ge 0\},
\]
with \(A'\in\mathbb{Z}^{m'\times n'}\), \(b'\in\mathbb{Z}^{m'}\), \(c'\in\mathbb{Z}^{n'}\). A feasible basis \(B\subseteq [n']\) of size \(m'\) determines a basic feasible solution (BFS) \(x'\). A simplex pivot exchanges one entering nonbasic variable with one leaving basic variable, producing a new basis (and a new BFS).

A pivot is called non-degenerate if it changes the current vertex (equivalently, the step length in the pivot direction is positive), and degenerate if the basis changes but the BFS remains at the same vertex (step length zero). Degeneracy can cause cycling or long sequences of degenerate pivots (stalling).

The paper introduces specific pivot rules for 0/1-LPs (variants of steepest-edge and shadow rules) and proves polynomial bounds on the number of non-degenerate pivots; however, the number of degenerate pivots (basis exchanges that do not move to a different vertex) may still be large and is not bounded in their analysis.
problem_definition_latex:
For at least one of the pivot rules introduced for 0/1-LPs (e.g., the paper's modified steepest-edge or modified shadow pivot rules), determine whether there exists a polynomial upper bound (in the input size, or at least in \(n,m'\)) on the total number of degenerate pivots (degenerate basis exchanges) that the Simplex method can perform when solving
\[
\max\{c^\top x : x \in P\},\qquad P\text{ a 0/1 polytope as above}.
\]
Equivalently, bound by a polynomial the number of iterations in which the basis changes but the current BFS (and hence the current vertex of \(P\)) does not change, when the Simplex method is run with one of these pivot rules on arbitrary 0/1-LPs.
