literature_review.synthesis:
Black–De Loera–Kafer–Sanità (2021) introduce pivot rules tailored to 0/1 polytopes—True Steepest-Edge and two Shadow variants (Slim/Ordered)—and prove strongly polynomial bounds on the number of non-degenerate pivots: steepest-edge paths are strongly polynomial (via circuit-augmentation results), Slim Shadow uses at most \(n\) non-degenerate pivots, and Ordered Shadow uses at most the dimension \(d\). Their analysis explicitly avoids perturbations because 0/1 polytopes are typically highly degenerate, and they isolate degeneracy as the remaining obstacle: a simplex implementation may still perform many degenerate basis exchanges while staying at the same vertex of the original polytope.

The most directly relevant forward-citing progress is the work “On the number of degenerate simplex pivots” and its journal version “On the number of degenerate simplex pivots: K. Kukharenko and L. Sanità”. These papers do not analyze the specific 0/1-polytope pivot rules of Black–De Loera–Kafer–Sanità, nor do they bound the total number of degenerate pivots over an entire run. Instead, they design an anti-stalling pivot rule for general standard-form LPs that guarantees at any non-optimal BFS the number of consecutive degenerate pivots is at most \(n-m-1\) (or \(\min\{n-m-1,m-1\}\) under stronger directional information). This shows that degeneracy can be controlled locally (stalling cannot persist too long) even without 0/1 structure, but it leaves open whether the original True Steepest-Edge / Slim Shadow / Ordered Shadow pivot rules admit polynomial bounds on total degenerate pivots on arbitrary 0/1-LPs.

Related work on smoothed analysis (e.g., “Optimal smoothed analysis of the simplex method”) largely sidesteps degeneracy by random perturbations that make degenerate pivots occur with probability 0, and work on monotone path polytopes (e.g., “Monotone Paths on Polytopes: Combinatorics and Optimization”) clarifies the combinatorics of coherent (typically nondegenerate) shadow paths. Neither yields worst-case polynomial bounds on degenerate basis exchanges in the deterministic 0/1 setting. Consequently, the specific open question posed as Question 2 in the 0/1-polytope simplex paper remains open: proving a polynomial upper bound on the total number of degenerate pivots for their pivot rules, or constructing superpolynomial lower bounds, remains a key gap.

sources.title: On the number of degenerate simplex pivots
sources.theorem_or_result: They prove existence of an “antistalling” simplex pivot rule for any LP in standard form \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) that bounds the number of consecutive degenerate simplex pivots at any non-optimal BFS by \(n-m-1\) (and in a strengthened version by \(\min\{n-m-1,\ m-1\}\)), where \(n\) is the number of variables and \(m\) the number of equality constraints (Theorems 1–2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial upper bound on the total number of degenerate pivots when solving 0/1-polytope LPs under specific pivot rules (modified steepest-edge/shadow rules). This paper does not analyze those specific 0/1-polytope pivot rules, nor does it bound the total number of degenerate pivots over the whole run. Instead it gives a general technique/pivot rule that guarantees a polynomial bound on stalling: at any non-optimal vertex, the number of consecutive degenerate pivots before a non-degenerate move is at most \(O(n)\). This is directly relevant as it shows degeneracy can be controlled (in the sense of consecutive degenerate pivots) even for general LPs, hence also for 0/1 polytopes. However, it does not by itself yield a polynomial bound on the total number of degenerate pivots for the pivot rules in the original 0/1-polytope paper; total degenerate pivots could still be large if many vertices are visited, and their rule requires access to an improving feasible direction (potentially as hard as solving the LP).

sources.title: On the number of degenerate simplex pivots: K. Kukharenko and L. Sanità
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves that for any LP in standard equality form \(\min\{c^\top x: Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), there exists an (anti-stalling) simplex pivot rule such that at any non-optimal extreme point the number of consecutive degenerate simplex pivots is at most \(n-m-1\) (Theorem 1), and in fact at most \(\min\{n-m-1,\ m-1\}\) when an improving feasible direction of the form \(\tilde x-x\) between vertices is available (Theorem 2). It also bounds the number of degenerate pivots needed at an optimal vertex to reach an optimal basis by \(n-m\) (Lemma 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial upper bound on the total number of degenerate pivots when solving LPs over 0/1 polytopes using one of the specific pivot rules from Black–De Loera–Kafer–Sanit\`a (modified steepest-edge/shadow rules). This paper does not analyze those specific 0/1-polytope pivot rules. Instead, it introduces a different pivot rule (Algorithm 1) that, given access to an improving feasible direction at the current vertex, guarantees a polynomial bound on degeneracy: it prevents long stalling by bounding the length of any run of degenerate pivots by \(O(n)\), independent of integrality/0-1 structure. Thus it provides strong partial progress toward the spirit of the open problem (controlling degeneracy), but it does not resolve whether the original 0/1-specific pivot rules themselves admit polynomial bounds on degenerate pivots, nor does it yield a polynomial bound on the total number of degenerate pivots without additional assumptions (e.g., availability of improving feasible directions, and bounds on the number of visited vertices).

sources.title: Optimal smoothed analysis of the simplex method
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves improved smoothed-analysis bounds for a (semi-random) shadow-vertex simplex method: there exists a simplex method with smoothed complexity (number of pivot steps) at most \(O(\sigma^{-1/2} d^{11/4} \log(n)^{7/4})\) (up to additional \(d^3\log(n)^2\) terms), and it gives a nearly matching lower bound \(\Omega(\sigma^{-1/2} d^{1/2} \ln(4/\sigma)^{-1/4})\) on the (semi-random) shadow size / diameter after smoothing for instances with \(n=\lfloor(4/\sigma)^d\rfloor\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a worst-case polynomial upper bound on the number of degenerate simplex pivots when solving integral 0/1-polytope LPs under specific pivot rules (modified steepest-edge or modified shadow rules) after converting to standard form with slack variables. This citing paper studies a different setting: smoothed analysis of a shadow-vertex-type simplex method for general real LPs under Gaussian perturbations, and it assumes (with probability 1) non-degeneracy of the shadow path due to random perturbations/objectives, so degenerate pivots essentially do not occur in its model. It does not analyze degeneracy in the worst case, does not specialize to 0/1 polytopes, and does not bound the number of degenerate basis exchanges for the pivot rules from the 0/1-polytope paper. At best, it provides techniques suggesting that random perturbations remove degeneracy and yield polynomial expected pivot counts, but this is not a polynomial bound on degenerate pivots in the original deterministic 0/1 setting.

sources.title: Monotone Paths on Polytopes: Combinatorics and Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives a combinatorial description of the vertices of the monotone path polytope \(M_c(\Delta(n,2))\) (for any generic direction \(c\)), yielding an explicit formula for the number of coherent monotone paths on the hypersimplex \(\Delta(n,2)\), and refines this by counting coherent monotone paths by their length \(\ell\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial upper bound on the number of degenerate simplex pivots under certain pivot rules for LPs over 0/1 polytopes. This paper studies monotone path polytopes, which encode the combinatorics of the shadow-vertex (shadow) pivot rule: vertices of \(M_c(P)\) correspond to coherent monotone paths that can occur as shadow-vertex pivot paths on \(P\) for some secondary direction \(\omega\). The results here are about enumerating coherent monotone paths on a specific 0/1 polytope family (hypersimplices), not about degeneracy or the number of degenerate basis exchanges in simplex on a standard-form formulation. Thus it provides structural/background information about possible (nondegenerate) shadow-vertex paths, but does not bound (or even model) degenerate pivots/stalling sequences.

title: Uniqueness of Sobolev solutions to min-max variational inequality with obstacle and gradient constraints
background_latex:
Fix a finite horizon \(T\in(0,\infty)\) and dimension \(d\in\mathbb{N}\). Let \(b:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\sigma:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d'}\) be continuously differentiable, locally Lipschitz, with at most linear growth, and let \(a(x):=\sigma(x)\sigma(x)^\top\). Assume local ellipticity: for every bounded \(B\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) there exists \(\theta_B>0\) such that \(\langle \zeta, a(x)\zeta\rangle\ge \theta_B\|\zeta\|_d^2\) for all \(x\in B\), \(\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^d\).

Define the second-order operator acting on sufficiently regular \(\varphi\) by
\[
(L\varphi)(x)=\tfrac12\mathrm{tr}\big(a(x)D^2\varphi(x)\big)+\langle b(x),\nabla \varphi(x)\rangle.
\]
Let \(r\ge 0\) be a constant. Let \(f,g,h:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous, with the regularity and growth conditions ensuring the expressions below are well-defined almost everywhere for Sobolev functions: specifically assume \(g\) and \(f^2\) are locally \(C^{1,2,\alpha}\) and \(h\) is locally \(C^{0,1,\alpha}\) for some \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and \(g(t,x)+h(t,x)\) has at most quadratic growth in \(x\). Assume also the compatibility condition
\[
\|\nabla g(t,x)\|_d\le f(t,x),\qquad (t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d.
\]

For \(p>d+2\), consider functions \(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d)\). By Sobolev embedding, such \(u\) have a locally H\"older-continuous spatial gradient, so the pointwise constraints \(u\ge g\) and \(\|\nabla u\|_d\le f\) are meaningful.

Define the (parabolic) min-max variational inequality on \([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d\) with terminal condition \(u(T,x)=g(T,x)\):
\[
\min\Big\{\,\max\big\{\partial_t u + Lu - r u + h,\; g-u\big\},\; f-\|\nabla u\|_d\,\Big\}=0\quad \text{a.e. on }[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d.
\]
A solution is understood in the strong (Sobolev) sense, i.e. the PDE terms hold almost everywhere, with \(u\) satisfying the obstacle and gradient constraints and the terminal condition.

Equivalently, prove or disprove: if \(u_1,u_2\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d)\) both satisfy

2) \(u_i\ge g\) and \(\|\nabla u_i\|_d\le f\) pointwise on \([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d\),

4) \(|u_i(t,x)|\le c(1+\|x\|_d^2)\),

literature_review.synthesis:
In the source paper (Bovo–De Angelis–Issoglio, arXiv:2203.06247v3) the value \(v\) of a finite-horizon zero-sum singular-controller vs. stopper game on \([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\) is identified as the maximal strong Sobolev solution \(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) (\(p>d+2\)) of the min–max variational inequality \(\min\{\max\{\partial_t u+Lu-ru+h,\ g-u\},\ f-\|\nabla u\|\}=0\) with terminal condition \(u(T,\cdot)=g(T,\cdot)\) and quadratic growth. The paper explicitly leaves open whether such a Sobolev solution is unique (Remark 3.5), noting that standard approaches (e.g. those used for singular control without an obstacle, or obstacle problems without gradient constraints) do not directly yield a comparison principle in the presence of both hard constraints and the min–max structure.

Forward-citing work to date provides substantial partial progress but no definitive uniqueness theorem for the original locally elliptic problem on \(\mathbb R^d\). Two strands are prominent. First, several papers establish uniqueness/maximality for approximating or regularised problems where uniform ellipticity is restored or the gradient constraint is modified: for example, “Stopper vs. Singular controller games with degenerate diffusions” proves that for each uniformly elliptic perturbation \(a_\varepsilon=a+\varepsilon^2I\) there is a (unique/maximal) strong Sobolev solution to the corresponding regularised VI, and then studies the \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) limit, but stops short of proving that the limit satisfies the original VI in strong Sobolev sense or that uniqueness holds in the locally elliptic/degenerate setting. Similarly, “Zero-Sum Stopper Versus Singular-Controller Games with Constrained Control Directions” develops an approximation \(\gamma\downarrow0\) for direction-constrained controls, obtaining maximal strong solutions for approximating VIs and convergence of values, but again without a limiting strong-Sobolev VI characterisation or uniqueness.

Second, a set of one-dimensional works on the half-line or time-homogeneous models (“Finite-time horizon, stopper vs. singular-controller games on the half-line”, “On the saddle point of a zero-sum stopper vs. singular-controller game”, and “Global regularity of the value function in a stopper vs. singular-controller game”) provide refined regularity and free-boundary structure (e.g. global \(C^1\) regularity, smooth-fit at the control boundary, and probabilistic representations for \(v_x\)). These results strengthen the analytical toolbox in special 1D settings and show that maximality can coincide with strong regularity and explicit boundary characterisations, but they still do not deliver a general comparison principle for the multi-dimensional Sobolev VI with variable \(f(t,x)\) and obstacle \(g(t,x)\). Overall, the uniqueness problem remains open; the most promising directions appear to be (i) developing a comparison principle tailored to the coupled obstacle/gradient-constraint min–max operator under quadratic growth on \(\mathbb R^d\), or (ii) proving that the maximal Sobolev solution coincides with the game value and is stable under penalisation/regularisation in a way that forces uniqueness (e.g. via monotone approximation and tightness/compactness arguments that rule out multiple strong solutions).

The open problem asks for uniqueness of strong Sobolev solutions \(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) to the stated min–max variational inequality on \([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d\) under local ellipticity and quadratic growth. This paper does not prove such a uniqueness theorem. Instead it:
- Uses the earlier uniformly elliptic theory (their Theorem 6, citing [1]) to obtain, for each \(\u00c03>0\), a unique/maximal Sobolev solution \(u_\u00c03\) to a *regularized* VI with \(a_\u00c03=a+\u00c03^2 I\).
- Lets \(\u00c03\downarrow0\) to construct a value function \(v\) for the degenerate game, but explicitly states they do not obtain a variational-inequality characterization of \(v\) in the degenerate case.
Thus, relative to the open problem, the paper provides partial progress/related evidence: it confirms well-posedness (existence and a maximal Sobolev characterization) in the uniformly elliptic approximations and develops approximation/compactness-free probabilistic techniques, but it does not establish uniqueness for the original locally elliptic Sobolev VI on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with obstacle and gradient constraint.

sources.title: Finite-time horizon, stopper vs. singular-controller games on the half-line
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves (Theorem 2.4) existence of a value for a 1D finite-horizon zero-sum stopper vs. singular-controller game on the half-line 

- state space 
\(O=[0,T)\times(0,\infty)\) with absorption at \(x=0\),
- payoff with running cost \(h\), terminal payoff \(g\), and singular-control cost \(\bar\alpha\,d|\nu|\),
- controlled diffusion \(dX_t=\mu(X_t)dt+\sigma(X_t)dW_t+d\nu_t\).

It shows the value \(v\) is the maximal Sobolev solution \(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(O)\cap C(\bar O)\) (for \(p>3\)) of the variational inequality with obstacle and gradient constraint plus boundary/terminal conditions:
\[\min\{\max\{\partial_t u+Lu-ru+h,\ g-u\},\ \bar\alpha-|\partial_x u|\}=0\ \text{a.e. on }O,\quad u(T,x)=g(T,x),\ u(t,0)=g(t,0).\]
Uniqueness is established for the penalised semilinear PDE approximations (Corollary 3.3) and for the penalised problem on the unbounded domain (via probabilistic representation, Proposition 4.7), but the limiting variational inequality is characterised as having a maximal solution rather than being proved unique.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for uniqueness of strong (Sobolev) solutions on \([0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\) to a min-max variational inequality with both an obstacle \(u\ge g\) and a gradient constraint \(\|\nabla u\|\le f\), under local ellipticity and quadratic growth.

This citing paper treats a closely related min-max variational inequality but only in the 1D half-line setting \([0,T]\times[0,\infty)\) with an additional Dirichlet boundary condition at \(x=0\) and with constant gradient bound \(|u_x|\le \bar\alpha\) (so \(f\) is constant). It proves existence of a value and identifies it with the maximal Sobolev solution of that VI. However, it does not prove that the Sobolev solution is unique: the main PDE statement is maximality, and the uniqueness results shown are for penalised approximating PDEs, not for the limiting VI itself. Therefore it provides partial progress (existence/characterisation and new estimates) but does not resolve the uniqueness question posed in full generality (nor even in this 1D domain case).

sources.title: Zero-Sum Stopper Versus Singular-Controller Games with Constrained Control Directions
sources.theorem_or_result:
For each approximation parameter \(\gamma\in(0,1]\), the associated unconstrained-direction game admits a value \(u^\gamma\) which is the maximal strong Sobolev solution \(u^\gamma\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^d)\) (for all \(p\)) of the min–max variational inequality
\[
\min\{\max\{\partial_t u+Lu-ru+h,\ g-u\},\ f^\gamma-|\nabla u|_\gamma\}=0,\qquad u(T,\cdot)=g(T,\cdot),
\]
with linear growth; moreover \(u^\gamma\to v\) as \(\gamma\downarrow0\) uniformly on compacts, where \(v\) is the value of the constrained-direction game, and \(v\) satisfies the partial gradient bound \(|\nabla_0 v(t,x)|\le f(t)\) a.e. and admits an optimal stopping rule \(\theta^*=\tau^*\wedge\sigma^*\).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for uniqueness of strong (Sobolev) solutions \(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) with quadratic growth for the original min–max variational inequality with obstacle \(u\ge g\) and full gradient constraint \(|\nabla u|\le f(t,x)\) on \([0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^d\). This paper does not prove such a uniqueness theorem. Instead it:
- Uses the earlier paper [4] (the source of the open problem) to obtain existence/characterisation and maximality for *approximating* VIs with a modified norm \(|\cdot|_\gamma\) and smoother/bounded data.
- Passes \(\gamma\downarrow0\) to obtain existence of a game value \(v\) in the constrained-control-direction setting, but explicitly notes they cannot guarantee solvability of the limiting VI in strong Sobolev sense.
- Provides convergence and stability estimates and an optimal stopping time, which are relevant tools/insight for future PDE/VI analysis, but do not establish comparison/uniqueness for the Sobolev VI in the open problem’s generality (notably: their main assumptions include sublinear growth and \(f=f(t)\), and the limiting object is not shown to be a Sobolev solution of the original VI).
Hence it is partial progress/related, not a solution.

sources.title: On the saddle point of a zero-sum stopper vs. singular-controller game
sources.theorem_or_result:
In a 1D, time-homogeneous zero-sum stopper vs. singular-controller game on  or [0,\infty), the value function \(v\) belongs to \(W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,T]\times O)\) for all \(p\in[1,\infty)\), satisfies the associated obstacle/gradient-constrained variational inequalities (as in (2.6)) with quadratic growth, and admits a saddle point \((\tau^*,\nu^*)\). The saddle point is characterised by two monotone moving boundaries \(a(t)\) (stopping) and \(b(t)\) (control), with \(\tau^*=\inf\{s\ge0: X^{\nu}_s\le a(t+s)\}\wedge(T-t)\) and \(\nu^*\) given by Skorokhod reflection at \(b\). A key auxiliary result is a probabilistic representation of the spatial derivative \(v_x\) as the value of an optimal stopping problem with absorption:
\[
v_x(t,y)=\inf_{\tau}\,\mathbb E\Big[e^{-\int_0^\tau \lambda(Y_u)du}\,\alpha_0\mathbf 1_{\{\tau<\tau_a\}}+\int_0^{\tau\wedge\tau_a} e^{-\int_0^s \lambda(Y_u)du}\,h_x(t+s,Y_s)\,ds\Big],
\]
with \(\tau_a\) the hitting time of the stopping boundary \(a\) by an auxiliary diffusion \(Y\), and \(\lambda=r-\mu_x\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for uniqueness of strong (Sobolev) solutions to a parabolic min-max variational inequality with obstacle \(u\ge g\) and gradient constraint \(\|\nabla u\|\le f\) on \([0,T)\times\mathbb R^d\), under local ellipticity and quadratic growth. This paper does not address uniqueness in that general PDE setting. It works in a specialised 1D, time-homogeneous game with constant gradient bound \(f\equiv\alpha_0\) and obstacle depending only on time \(g(t)\), and focuses on constructing a saddle point and free-boundary structure assuming existence/characterisation results from earlier work ([6,7]). While it derives additional regularity/structure (monotone boundaries, representation of \(v_x\)), it does not prove a comparison principle or uniqueness for Sobolev solutions of the min-max variational inequality, neither in multi-D nor even explicitly in the 1D PDE class. Thus it provides partial progress/related structural tools rather than solving the uniqueness question.

sources.title: Global regularity of the value function in a stopper vs. singular-controller game
sources.theorem_or_result: In the one-dimensional finite-horizon stopper vs. singular-controller game with constant gradient constraint \,\(v_x\le \alpha_0\) and obstacle \,\(v\ge g(t)\), the value function \,\(v\) satisfies the associated min–max variational inequality and enjoys global \,\(C^1\)-regularity: \,\(v\in C([0,T]\times O)\cap C^1([0,T)\times O)\). Moreover, \,\(v_x\in C^1(C\cup \mathrm{int}(S))\), and the second spatial derivative \,\(v_{xx}\) and mixed derivative \,\(v_{tx}\) are continuous across the control boundary \,\(b(t)\) (inaction/action boundary), with smooth-fit \,\(v_{xx}(t,b(t)-)=0\), while \,\(v_{xx}\) may jump across the stopping boundary \,\(a(t)\) (Theorem 3.8, Theorems 6.2–6.4, Proposition 5.2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for uniqueness of strong (Sobolev) solutions \,\(u\in W^{1,2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}\) to a parabolic min–max variational inequality on \([0,T)\times\mathbb R^d\) with obstacle \,\(u\ge g\) and gradient constraint \,\(\|\nabla u\|\le f\), under quadratic growth. This paper does not prove such a uniqueness theorem. Instead it studies a specific 1D game (\(d=1\)) with a constant gradient cap \,\(f\equiv \alpha_0\) and an obstacle depending only on time \,\(g=g(t)\), and establishes higher regularity (global \(C^1\)) of the value function and fine boundary regularity (smooth-fit at the control boundary). These results are compatible with, and could be useful for, uniqueness arguments in that special 1D setting (e.g., enabling verification/Itô formulas), but they do not address uniqueness of Sobolev solutions in the general \(d\)-dimensional, variable \(f(t,x)\), variable obstacle \(g(t,x)\) framework posed in the open problem.

title: Determine whether Golden Parachutes arise with an impatient agent setting
background_latex:
Consider Sannikov’s continuous-time principal–agent model with moral hazard over an endogenous retirement time.

1) Output and effort. The output process \(X\) is observed and evolves under the agent’s effort process \(\alpha=(\alpha_t)_{t\ge0}\) as
\[dX_t=\alpha_t\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t,\qquad \sigma>0,\]
where \(W\) is a Brownian motion under the measure induced by \(\alpha\). The effort \(\alpha_t\) takes values in a compact set \(A\subset[0,\infty)\) containing \(0\). The agent incurs instantaneous cost \(h(\alpha_t)\), where \(h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is increasing, strictly convex, \(C^1\), and \(h(0)=0\). Denote \(\beta:=h'(0)\).

2) Contract. A contract \(C=(\tau,\pi,\xi)\) consists of a stopping time \(\tau\) (retirement time), a nonnegative predictable payment rate \(\pi_t\) paid up to \(\tau\), and a nonnegative lump-sum payment \(\xi\) at time \(\tau\).

3) Preferences and discounting. The agent has discount rate \(r>0\) and flow utility \(u(\pi_t)\) from consumption, where \(u:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) is increasing, strictly concave, \(C^2\) on \((0,\infty)\), with \(u(0)=0\) and Inada tail condition \(\lim_{x\to\infty}u'(x)=0\). The principal is risk-neutral with discount rate \(\rho>0\). Let \(\delta:=r/\rho\).

4) Agent’s value for a contract \(C\). For a given effort \(\alpha\), the agent’s expected utility is
\[J_A(C,\alpha)=\mathbb E\Big[e^{-r\tau}u(\xi)+\int_0^{\tau} r e^{-rs}\big(u(\pi_s)-h(\alpha_s)\big)\,ds\Big].\]
The agent chooses \(\alpha\) to maximize \(J_A(C,\alpha)\), and the contract must satisfy a participation constraint \(V_A(C)\ge u(R)\) for some reservation level \(R\ge0\).

5) Principal’s value. Anticipating the agent’s optimal response, the principal chooses \(C\) to maximize her discounted expected payoff.

6) “Golden Parachute” (as defined in the paper). A Golden Parachute exists if there is an optimal contract \((\tau^*,\pi^*,\xi^*)\) such that \(\tau^*>0\) and \(\mathbb P(\xi^*>0)>0\), i.e., the agent is retired at a strictly positive time and receives a positive post-retirement payment (lump-sum and/or equivalent lifetime stream).

7) Regime of interest. The paper distinguishes regimes by \(\delta\). The open issue below concerns the case \(\delta>1\), i.e., the agent is strictly more impatient than the principal.
problem_definition_latex:
In the above model, focus on the regime \(\delta=r/\rho>1\) (agent strictly more impatient than the principal). Let \(V(y)\) denote the principal’s value when the agent’s continuation utility is held at level \(y\ge0\), and let \(F\) denote the (face-lifted) retirement reward function against which retirement is compared.

Determine whether the associated optimal stopping threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\in[0,\infty]\) at which the principal retires the agent is finite or infinite, i.e. decide whether the stopping region \(\{y: V(y)=F(y)\}\) takes the form \(\{0\}\cup[y_{\mathrm{gp}},\infty)\) with \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}<\infty\) (existence of a Golden Parachute), or whether in general \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}=\infty\) (no Golden Parachute), in the regime \(\delta>1\).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Possamaï–Touzi’s reformulation of Sannikov’s model with endogenous retirement, the principal’s second-best value as a function of the agent’s continuation utility \(y\) solves an infinite-horizon 1D obstacle problem \(\min\{V(y)-F(y),\;LV(y)\}=0\), where the obstacle \(F\) is a face-lifted retirement reward capturing the principal’s ability (when discount rates differ) to postpone retirement while keeping the agent indifferent via a deterministic post-retirement consumption plan. The open issue is precisely whether, in the impatient-agent regime \(\delta=r/\rho>1\), the stopping set \(\{V=F\}\) has a finite upper boundary \([y_{\mathrm{gp}},\infty)\) (Golden Parachute) or whether the boundary is at infinity (no Golden Parachute). The source paper proves structural results (e.g., \(\{V=F\}=\{0\}\cup[y_{\mathrm{gp}},\infty)\) under concavity assumptions) but explicitly leaves open whether \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}<\infty\) can be guaranteed for \(\delta>1\); their numerics suggest that \(V\) may stay strictly above \(F\) for all \(y>0\) in some \(\delta>1\) parameterizations.

Forward citations largely develop tools and adjacent models rather than resolving this free-boundary question. Lin–Ren–Touzi–Yang’s “Random horizon principal-agent problems” provides a general reduction of random-horizon principal–agent Stackelberg games to control/optimal stopping problems in the continuation-utility state, thereby supplying a rigorous pathway to derive the relevant HJB/obstacle equation in broad settings, but it does not analyze the \(\delta>1\) boundary behavior. “Golden parachutes under the threat of accidents” extends the face-lifting/termination-reward analysis to models with jump accidents and derives explicit variational inequalities for the face-lifted reward under \(\delta>1\), yet it still does not characterize the stopping region \(\{v^{SB}=\bar F\}\) (hence does not decide finiteness of a retirement threshold). Several works in PPP or ambiguity extensions (e.g., “Optimal stopping contract for public private partnerships under moral hazard” and “Moral Hazard, Dynamic Incentives, and Ambiguous Perceptions”) similarly reduce to 1D variational inequalities/HJBI equations and often exhibit finite stopping thresholds in numerics or assume such a structure for verification, but they do not prove the finiteness/infinity dichotomy in the original Sannikov/Possamaï–Touzi \(\delta>1\) regime.

Overall, based on the provided forward-citation set, there is no paper that proves \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}<\infty\) or \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}=\infty\) in general for \(\delta>1\) in the Brownian drift-control model with face-lifted obstacle \(F\). The problem therefore remains open. Promising directions suggested by the literature include: (i) exploiting the dual formulation in terms of \(p=V'(y)\) (as in the source paper’s dual ODE heuristics for \(\delta>1\)) to obtain sharp asymptotics of \(V-F\) as \(y\to\infty\); (ii) establishing comparison/monotonicity properties that would force eventual contact with the obstacle or preclude it; and (iii) combining the general random-horizon reduction and viscosity/regularity techniques with parameter-restricted explicit examples to delineate regions of \(\delta>1\) where contact must (or cannot) occur.

sources.title: Random horizon principal-agent problems
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a general reduction theorem for random-horizon principal–agent problems with continuous payments and a terminal lump-sum: under suitable integrability and existence of Hamiltonian maximizers, the Stackelberg game (European case: principal chooses termination \,\(\tau^P\) and payments \,\((\pi,\xi)\)) is equivalent to a stochastic control problem over the agent’s continuation utility process \,\(Y\) represented by 
\[Y_t=Y_0+\int_0^t \Big(Z_s\cdot dX_s+\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}(\Gamma_s d\langle X\rangle_s)-H_s(Y_s,Z_s,\Gamma_s)\,ds-U_A(\pi_s)\,ds\Big),\]
with terminal transfer \,\(\xi=U_A^{-1}(Y_{\tau^P})\). In the American case (agent can quit), the principal’s problem reduces similarly with endogenous termination time \,\(h_0:=\inf\{t\ge0: Y_t\le U_A(\rho)\}\). (Theorem 4.2, plus density Proposition 4.4 via random-horizon 2BSDEs.)
sources.connection: The open problem asks, in Sannikov’s model with endogenous retirement and discount-rate ratio \(\delta=r/\rho>1\), whether the optimal stopping threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) for principal-initiated retirement is finite (golden parachute) or infinite. This paper does not analyze that specific obstacle/free-boundary problem or the \(\delta>1\) regime. Instead it provides a general framework reducing random-horizon principal–agent problems (including Sannikov’s) to stochastic control/optimal stopping problems in the agent’s continuation utility state \(Y\), and derives the corresponding HJB/obstacle equations in examples (Section 5.1). It therefore supplies tools and a reduction that can be used to study the threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\), but it does not determine whether \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}<\infty\) or \(=\infty\) when \(\delta>1\).

sources.title: Golden parachutes under the threat of accidents
sources.theorem_or_result:
In a Sannikov-type principal–agent model with accidents (compound Poisson losses) and possibly different discount rates 
\(\delta=r/\rho\), the paper derives an explicit characterization of the face-lifted retirement/termination reward \(\bar F\) via the variational inequality
\[\min\{\bar F(y)-F(y),\; F^\star(\delta \bar F'(y)) - \delta y\bar F'(y) + \bar F(y) + m\}=0,\ y>0,\ \bar F(0)=0.\]
For \(\delta>1\):
- If \(m\le -F^\star(\delta F'(0))\), then \(\bar F=(w^\star)^\star\) and \(\bar F>F\) on \((0,\infty)\).
- If \(m> -F^\star(\delta F'(0))\), then \(\bar F(y)=F(y)\) on \([0,\bar y]\) where \(\bar y:=\inf\{y\ge0: F^\star(\delta F'(y)) -\delta yF'(y)+F(y)+m\le0\}\), and \(\bar F=(w^\star)^\star\) on \((\bar y,\infty)\).
For the second-best problem, the principal’s value \(v^{SB}\) is characterized as the unique continuous viscosity solution of an integro-differential obstacle problem
\[\min\{v^{SB}(y)-\bar F(y),\; F^\star(\delta (v^{SB})'(y)) -\delta y (v^{SB})'(y) + v^{SB}(y) - \mathcal J^{SB}(y,(v^{SB})'(y),(v^{SB})''(y),v^{SB})\}=0,\ y>0,\ v^{SB}(0)=0,\]
but the paper does not characterize the stopping set \(\{y: v^{SB}(y)=\bar F(y)\}\) (hence no explicit finiteness/infinity of a retirement threshold is proved).

sources.title: Optimal stopping contract for public private partnerships under moral hazard
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper formulates and (numerically) solves a continuous-time principal–agent problem with moral hazard and endogenous stopping (PPP contract termination) by reducing it to a 1D HJB variational inequality for the principal’s value function \(v(x)\) where \(x\) is the agent’s continuation utility. The value function satisfies
\[\min\Big(\delta v(x)-\sup_{(r,a)\in\mathbb R_+^2}\{\mathcal L^{a,r}v(x)+\varphi(a)-r\},\ v(x)+U^{-1}(x)\Big)=0,\quad x>0,\]
with boundary \(v(0)=0\) and stopping region \(\{x: v(x)\le -U^{-1}(x)\}\). Under smoothness/verification assumptions, the optimal stopping time is the first hitting time of the boundary of the continuation region \((0,\hat b)\), i.e. \(\tau^*=\inf\{t\ge0: J^C_t\in\{0,\hat b\}\}\), and the optimal rent is \(r^*(x)=(U')^{-1}(-1/v'(x))\mathbf 1_{v'(x)<0}\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks, in Sannikov’s model with endogenous retirement, whether in the impatient-agent regime \(\delta=r/\rho>1\) the optimal retirement threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) is finite (Golden Parachute) or infinite. This paper cites Possamaï–Touzi on golden parachutes and studies a related principal–agent-with-stopping model, deriving an HJB variational inequality and exhibiting a finite stopping threshold \(\hat b\) in numerical examples. However: (i) its model differs materially (PPP setting, bounded concave drift impact \(\varphi\), different discount notation \(\delta,\lambda\), and terminal payoff \(-U^{-1}(x)\) rather than the face-lifted retirement reward \(F\) in the golden-parachute paper); (ii) it does not analyze the regime corresponding to \(r/\rho>1\) in the original question nor prove finiteness/infiniteness of the stopping boundary in general; (iii) results are primarily verification + numerics for chosen parameters. Thus it provides partial, indirect evidence/tools but not a resolution of \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) in the stated model/regime.

sources.title: Moral Hazard, Dynamic Incentives, and Ambiguous Perceptions
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper formulates a Sannikov-style continuous-time moral hazard model with drift ambiguity and endogenous retirement/termination (finite random horizon), derives a recursive HJBI equation for the principal’s value as a function of the agent’s continuation value, and (Theorem 1) proves a verification result: if the HJBI admits a unique smooth solution and the stopping region is of the form \(S=\{0\}\cup[W_{gp},\infty)\) with finite \(W_{gp}<\infty\), then the associated feedback controls \((c(W),a(W),Y(W))\) implement an optimal contract with retirement time \(\tau=\inf\{t:W_t\in S\}\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks, in the standard Sannikov model with different discount rates and endogenous retirement, whether the golden-parachute stopping threshold \(y_{gp}\) is finite or infinite in the impatient-agent regime \(\delta=r/\rho>1\). This citing paper does not analyze that regime: it assumes a common discount rate \(r\) for principal and agent and adds drift ambiguity. It explicitly assumes (rather than proves) that the stopping region has a finite threshold \(W_{gp}<\infty\) to state its verification theorem, and it notes that ambiguity has an ambiguous effect on duration/retirement. Thus it does not resolve whether \(y_{gp}\) is finite/infinite for \(\delta>1\), but it provides related methodology (HJBI/verification with stopping) and discusses golden-parachute clauses in an extended model.

sources.title: Contracting with discretionary bonuses
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper formulates a finite-horizon principal–agent model with up to \(N\) discretionary lump-sum bonuses and proves (Theorem 2) that the principal’s value \(V_{p,n}(t,y)\) is the unique continuous viscosity solution of the recursive parabolic HJB variational inequalities
\[
\min\{-\partial_t v_{p,n}+Gv_{p,n},\ v_{p,n}-Mv_{p,n-1},\ -\partial_{yy}v_{p,n}\}=0,\quad n=1,\dots,N,
\]
with terminal condition \(v_{p,n}(T-,y)=g_n(y)=M^nF(y)\) and boundary \(v_{p,n}(t,0)=0\), where \(M\) is the impulse (bonus) operator \(MV(t,y)=\sup_{0\le \eta\le y}\{V(t,y-\eta)-(1+k)\eta^\gamma\}\). It also gives a feedback characterization of the optimal bonus size \(\eta^*_{n}(t,y)\) on the intervention region \(\{v_{p,n}=Mv_{p,n-1}\}\) via a first-order condition on \(\partial_y V_{p,n-1}\) (equation (20)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks, in Sannikov’s infinite-horizon endogenous-retirement model, whether for \(\delta=r/\rho>1\) the optimal retirement (stopping) threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) is finite (golden parachute) or infinite (no golden parachute). This paper does not study endogenous retirement/termination as an optimal stopping boundary against a retirement reward \(F\); instead it fixes a finite horizon \(T\) and models discretionary bonus payments as impulses at stopping times, with a terminal payment at \(T\). Theorem 2 provides a rigorous viscosity-solution characterization for the principal’s value with impulses, and the numerics (Figures 8 and 11) explore the regime \(\delta>1\), showing regions where an initial bonus (“golden hello”) may occur and how intervention regions change with \(N\). However, it does not establish analytically whether an infinite-horizon retirement stopping region \(\{V=F\}\) has a finite threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) when \(\delta>1\), nor does it prove existence/nonexistence of golden parachutes in that setting. At best it offers related methods (mixed control/stopping/impulse HJB-VIs) and numerical evidence in a different finite-horizon, multi-bonus model.

sources.title: Contrat optimal pour les partenariats public-privé avec aléa moral: une approche de contrôle stochastique
sources.theorem_or_result:
The thesis develops a continuous-time principal–agent model with moral hazard and endogenous stopping (termination) and derives the principal’s value as the solution of a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman variational inequality. In Chapter 3, with agent discount rate \(\lambda\) and principal discount rate \(\delta\), the principal’s value \(v(x)\) (state \(x\)=agent continuation value) satisfies
\[
\min\Big(\delta v(x)-\sup_{(r,a)\in\mathbb R_+^2}\{\mathcal L_{a,r}v(x)+\varphi(a)-r\},\ v(x)+x\Big)=0,\quad x>0,
\]
with boundary \(v(0)=0\), where \(\mathcal L_{a,r}v(x)=\tfrac12(\sigma h'(a)/\varphi'(a))^2\mathbf 1_{a>0}v''(x)+[\lambda x-U(r)+h(a)]v'(x)\). The optimal stopping time is \(\tau^*=\inf\{t\ge0: v(J_t^C)\le -J_t^C\}\) for the optimally controlled continuation value process \(J_t^C\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks, in Sannikov’s model with endogenous retirement and differing discount rates \(\delta=r/\rho>1\), whether the optimal retirement (golden-parachute) threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) is finite or infinite. This thesis treats a closely related class of continuous-time moral-hazard contracts with endogenous stopping and allows different discount rates between principal and agent (Chapter 3 uses \(\lambda\) for the agent and \(\delta\) for the principal). It sets up and verifies the HJB variational inequality and characterizes the stopping region via \(v(x)\le -x\). However, the thesis does not (in the provided text) analyze the qualitative dichotomy ‘finite vs infinite stopping threshold’ as a function of impatience ratio, nor does it match the exact Sannikov/Possamaï–Touzi golden-parachute face-lifting formulation \(V=F\) and the threshold \(y_{\mathrm{gp}}\) for \(\delta>1\). Thus it provides methodology and a related stopping characterization, but not a resolution of the specific golden-parachute threshold question.

title: Prove consecutive-service-rate optimality for sojourn-time partitioning under moment monotonicity
background_latex:
Consider a multi-type FCFS queueing system with a divisible total service capacity normalized to 1 that can be partitioned into \(k\ge 2\) parallel FCFS sub-queues with capacities \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_k)\) satisfying \(\alpha_j\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{j=1}^k \alpha_j=1\). There are \(n\) customer types indexed by \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\). Type \(i\) arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda_i>0\). Under unit capacity, type \(i\) has service time random variable \(S_i\) with first moment \(\mathbb E[S_i]=1/\mu_i\) (so \(\mu_i>0\) is the service rate) and second moment \(\mathbb E[S_i^2]=\nu_i\). When served at capacity \(\alpha_j\), service times scale as \(S_i/\alpha_j\). Routing is by type information only: an assignment matrix \(X=(x_{ij})\in[0,1]^{n\times k}\) specifies \(x_{ij}\) = probability that a type \(i\) arrival joins queue \(j\), with \(\sum_{j=1}^k x_{ij}=1\) for each \(i\). For stability/feasibility, each queue \(j\) must satisfy the load constraint \(\alpha_j>\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_{ij}/\mu_i\) whenever \(\alpha_j>0\).

The performance objective here is the expected total sojourn time (waiting time plus service time), averaged over arrivals. Using the Pollaczek–Khinchine formula for each FCFS sub-queue and the scaling of moments under capacity \(\alpha_j\), the expected total sojourn time under \((\alpha,X)\) is
\[
\tilde W(\alpha,X)=\frac{1}{2\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i}\sum_{j: \alpha_j>0}\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_{ij}\,\nu_i}{\alpha_j^2\left(\alpha_j-\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_{ij}/\mu_i\right)}\right)\; +\; \frac{1}{\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i}\sum_{j: \alpha_j>0}\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_{ij}\,\frac{1}{\alpha_j\mu_i}.
\]
(Any equivalent expression for expected sojourn time derived from Pollaczek–Khinchine and the model’s scaling is acceptable.)

Assume customer types are indexed so that service rates are strictly decreasing: \(\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots>\mu_n\). Assume also the following monotonicity property of the first two moments (the paper’s moment condition): for any two types with \(\mathbb E[S_i]\ge \mathbb E[S_{i'}]\) (equivalently \(\mu_i\le \mu_{i'}\)),
\[
\frac{\mathbb E[S_i^2]}{\mathbb E[S_i]}\ge \frac{\mathbb E[S_{i'}^2]}{\mathbb E[S_{i'}]}.
\]
This condition informally requires that types with larger mean service time have larger adjusted variability (second moment divided by mean).
problem_definition_latex:
In the joint partition-and-assignment optimization problem
\[
\min_{\alpha,X}\; \tilde W(\alpha,X)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \alpha_j\ge 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^k \alpha_j=1,\ x_{ij}\in[0,1],\ \sum_{j=1}^k x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ \alpha_j>\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i x_{ij}/\mu_i\ \forall j\text{ with }\alpha_j>0,
\]
prove (or disprove) that under the moment monotonicity condition \(\mathbb E[S_i^2]/\mathbb E[S_i]\) nondecreasing in \(\mathbb E[S_i]\) and with \(\mu_1>\cdots>\mu_n\), there exists an optimal solution \((\alpha^*,X^*)\) in which customers are assigned to queues in consecutive blocks by service rate, i.e., there exist indices
\[
1=i_0\le i_1\le \cdots\le i_{k-1}\le i_k=n+1
\]
such that for each queue \(j\in\{1,\dots,k\}\), \(X^*\) assigns every type \(i\in\{i_{j-1},\dots,i_j-1\}\) to queue \(j\) with probability 1 (and assigns types outside this block to queue \(j\) with probability 0).

title: Prove generic convergence of stochastic subgradient descent without weak convexity
background_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be a locally Lipschitz function, and let \(\partial f(x)\) denote its Clarke subdifferential. Consider stochastic subgradient descent (SGD)
\[
 x_{n+1}=x_n-\gamma_n v_n+\gamma_n\eta_{n+1},\qquad v_n\in \partial f(x_n),
\]
where \((\gamma_n)\) is a deterministic step-size sequence with \(\gamma_n\downarrow 0\), \(\sum_n\gamma_n=\infty\), and typically \(\sum_n\gamma_n^2<\infty\). The noise \((\eta_{n})\) is adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal{F}_n)\), satisfies the martingale difference property \(\mathbb{E}[\eta_{n+1}\mid \mathcal{F}_n]=0\), and has bounded conditional moments (e.g., bounded conditional fourth moments).

A point \(x^\star\) is Clarke critical if \(0\in \partial f(x^\star)\). In the definable (o-minimal) setting, Clarke critical points admit additional geometric structure via stratifications, and one can define an \(C^p\) active manifold \(M\) around \(x^\star\) on which \(f\) is smooth and off which the subgradients have norm bounded away from \(0\). An \(\emph{active strict saddle}\) is a Clarke critical point \(x^\star\) lying on such a manifold \(M\) for which the Riemannian Hessian of the restriction \(f\vert_M\) has a negative curvature direction at \(x^\star\). A \(\emph{sharply repulsive critical point}\) (as described in the cited manuscript [37] referenced by the paper) is, generically in the non-weakly convex definable case, a Clarke critical point \(x^\star\) lying on an active manifold \(M\) such that \(x^\star\) is a local minimizer of \(f\vert_M\) while nearby subgradients point toward \(M\) (intuitively attracting iterates toward \(M\) rather than repelling them).

For definable weakly convex functions, generic perturbations yield that every Clarke critical point is either a local minimizer or an active strict saddle, and the paper proves SGD avoids active strict saddles under suitable noise conditions, implying generic convergence to local minimizers in that setting.
problem_definition_latex:
Establish, for \(f\) definable and locally Lipschitz but \(\emph{not assumed weakly convex}\), a generic convergence guarantee for SGD of the form above: namely, prove that under standard Robbins--Monro-type conditions on \((\gamma_n)\) and suitable nondegenerate noise conditions on \((\eta_n)\), the iterates \((x_n)\) converge (when bounded) to a local minimizer of \(f\) with probability one.

Equivalently (as suggested by the paper's generic critical-point classification), show that in the non-weakly convex definable setting SGD \(\emph{avoids}\) with probability one both:
1) active strict saddles, and
2) sharply repulsive critical points,
so that the only possible limiting Clarke critical points are local minimizers.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Bianchi--Hachem--Schechtman, 2024) establishes that for definable weakly convex locally Lipschitz objectives, SGD with Robbins--Monro stepsizes and sufficiently nondegenerate martingale noise avoids convergence to any active strict saddle. The proof hinges on two geometric ingredients around an active manifold \(M\): (i) a Verdier-stratification-based strengthened projection formula controlling how Clarke subgradients project onto tangent spaces of adjacent strata, and (ii) an angle (proximal aiming) condition ensuring iterates contract toward \(M\). Once iterates are shown to track the projected dynamics \(y_n=P_M(x_n)\), the method reduces to a smooth stochastic approximation on \(M\) and invokes a Brandi\`ere--Duflo/Pemantle-type trap-avoidance argument in the negative-curvature directions of the Riemannian Hessian of \(f|_M\).

Beyond weak convexity, the same paper explains why the generic landscape changes: in addition to local minimizers and active strict saddles, one generically encounters "sharply repulsive critical points" (local minimizers of \(f|_M\) for which nearby subgradients point toward \(M\)), and it explicitly states that generic convergence of SGD to local minimizers remains open in this regime (Section 5.2 and Remark 4). The most directly relevant forward-citing work is the thesis "Saddle Avoidance, Asymptotic Normality, and Exponential Acceleration in Nonsmooth Optimization", which appears to remove weak convexity in the saddle-avoidance part by developing generic regularity conditions for definable/semi-algebraic objectives with active manifolds and proving almost-sure avoidance of active strict saddles for stochastic subgradient-type methods. However, based on the provided citation analysis, it is not confirmed that this thesis fully resolves the additional obstruction posed by sharply repulsive critical points in the non-weakly convex definable setting; it may instead work in a generic Clarke-regular class where such points are excluded or controlled.

Several other forward citations contribute tools toward a full resolution. "On the diameter of subgradient sequences in o-minimal structures" gives deterministic sequential convergence of bounded Clarke-subgradient iterates with \(\alpha_k\asymp 1/k\) to a Clarke critical point in the non-weakly-convex definable setting, which could serve as a key compactness/oscillation-control component in a stochastic approximation proof. "Sufficient conditions for instability of the subgradient method with constant step size" provides geometric instability criteria near semi-algebraic critical manifolds, conceptually aligned with sharply repulsive behavior, suggesting a route to show such points are not attractors for (stochastic) subgradient dynamics. Finally, works on stratification-based shadowing/rates and on Lyapunov stability for Euler discretizations of differential inclusions offer complementary frameworks for analyzing attraction/repulsion near strata, potentially enabling a unified argument that stochastic perturbations prevent convergence to both negative-curvature saddles on \(M\) and to sharply repulsive Clarke critical points when weak convexity is absent.

sources.title: Saddle Avoidance, Asymptotic Normality, and Exponential Acceleration in Nonsmooth Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis develops regularity conditions (notably strong-(a) and (b≤) regularity) for locally Lipschitz, Clarke-regular semialgebraic/definable functions with active manifolds, and uses them to prove saddle avoidance for stochastic or randomly perturbed subgradient methods: under Robbins–Monro stepsizes and nondegenerate perturbations/noise, the stochastic subgradient method (and projected/proximal variants) almost surely does not converge to an active strict saddle of a generic semialgebraic objective; consequently, any almost sure limit point (when the iterates converge/bounded) must be a local minimizer for generic Clarke-regular semialgebraic problems satisfying the strict-saddle-type classification (local minimizers vs active strict saddles).
sources.connection:
This is directly aimed at the open problem: it studies SGD/subgradient methods on definable (semialgebraic) locally Lipschitz functions without assuming weak convexity, using active-manifold geometry. It proves almost-sure avoidance of active strict saddles for stochastic subgradient-type algorithms under noise/perturbations, and establishes generic regularity along active manifolds that yields an “aiming toward the manifold” property and a shadow-iteration argument.

However, the open problem also asks to rule out convergence to sharply repulsive critical points (a phenomenon specific to non-weakly convex definable functions). From the provided excerpt, the thesis claims convergence only to minimizers for “generic, Clarke regular semialgebraic problems,” but it is unclear whether it explicitly defines/shows avoidance of sharply repulsive critical points in the sense of the cited manuscript [37] or whether it restricts to a generic class where such points do not occur (e.g., via Clarke regularity/strict-saddle classification). Thus, based on the available pages, the thesis appears to give substantial partial progress—removing weak convexity for saddle avoidance and giving generic convergence-to-minimizers statements under additional regularity/genericity hypotheses—but I cannot confirm it fully resolves the sharply-repulsive-critical-point obstruction in complete generality for all definable locally Lipschitz functions.

sources.title: On the diameter of subgradient sequences in o-minimal structures
sources.theorem_or_result:
For a locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) definable in a polynomially bounded o-minimal structure, the paper proves a quantitative diameter bound for any (deterministic) Clarke-subgradient sequence \(x_{k+1}\in x_k-\alpha_k\partial f(x_k)\) staying in a compact set and near a level set: there exist \(\alpha,\beta,\epsilon,\varsigma_1,\varsigma_2>0\) and \(\theta\in(0,1)\) such that if \(0<\alpha_{K-1}\le\cdots\le\alpha_0\le\bar\alpha\) and \(x_{0:K}\subset X\cap\{|f|\le\epsilon\}\), then
\[
\operatorname{diam}(\{x_0,\dots,x_K\})\le \varsigma_1\big(\operatorname{sgn}(f(x_0))|f(x_0)|^{1-\theta}-\operatorname{sgn}(f(x_K))|f(x_K)|^{1-\theta}\big)+\varsigma_2\Big(\alpha_0^\beta+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k^{1+\beta}+\big(\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k^{1+\beta}\big)^{1-\theta}+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\alpha_k\big(\sum_{j=k}^{K-1}\alpha_j^{1+\beta}\big)^\theta\Big).
\]
In particular, any bounded subgradient sequence with decreasing stepsizes \(\alpha_k\asymp 1/(k+1)\) converges to a Clarke critical point (Corollary 1.2).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a generic almost-sure convergence guarantee for *stochastic* subgradient descent on definable locally Lipschitz functions without weak convexity, i.e., to show (when bounded) convergence to local minimizers by avoiding both active strict saddles and sharply repulsive critical points.

This paper does not study stochastic noise, saddle avoidance, or genericity of limiting points. Instead it establishes deterministic convergence of bounded subgradient sequences under stepsizes \(\alpha_k\asymp 1/k\) (and more generally provides a diameter estimate controlled by function-value variation plus higher-order stepsize sums). This is relevant because it supplies a strong *convergence-to-a-critical-point* mechanism in the non-weakly-convex definable setting, potentially usable as a building block in a stochastic approximation analysis (e.g., to show that once the stochastic iterates track a deterministic subgradient sequence, oscillations are ruled out). However, it does not address the key missing piece of the open problem: ruling out convergence to non-minimizing critical points (active strict saddles or sharply repulsive points) under nondegenerate noise.

sources.title: Sufficient conditions for instability of the subgradient method with constant step size
sources.theorem_or_result: Theorem 1 (Josz–Lai, 2023): For a locally Lipschitz semi-algebraic function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) with critical set \(S:=\{x:0\in\partial f(x)\}\), assume \(S\) is a \(C^2\) manifold at \(x^*\in S\) of dimension \(<n\). Assume there exist \(\theta_1\ge 0\), a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^*\), and a continuous function \(C\) such that for any constant stepsize \(\alpha>0\) there is \(c_1>0\) with \(C(x_{k+1})-C(x_k)\ge c_1 d(x_k,S)^{\theta_1}\) for every subgradient-method trajectory \((x_k)\subset U\setminus S\) with stepsize \(\alpha\). Then \(x^*\) is strongly unstable for the constant-stepsize subgradient method if either (i) \(\theta_1=0\), or (ii) \(\partial f\) is metrically \(\theta_2\)-subregular at \((x^*,0)\) with \(\theta_2>1\) and \(f\) satisfies the Verdier condition at \(x^*\) along \(S\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for almost-sure convergence of diminishing-stepsize stochastic subgradient descent on definable locally Lipschitz (not weakly convex) functions, equivalently avoidance of active strict saddles and sharply repulsive critical points. This paper does not analyze diminishing-stepsize SGD or almost-sure convergence; instead it gives deterministic instability criteria for the constant-stepsize (set-valued) subgradient method near certain (non-strict) local minima of semi-algebraic functions. Conceptually, it is relevant because it identifies geometric conditions (metric \(\theta\)-subregularity with exponent \(>1\), Verdier condition, and existence of a Chetaev function) under which a local minimum is repelling for subgradient iterations—phenomena akin to “sharply repulsive” critical points in the non-weakly convex definable setting. However, the result is local, deterministic, and for constant stepsize, so it does not establish the requested generic convergence/avoidance for Robbins–Monro stepsizes with martingale noise.

sources.title: On convergence rates of subgradient descent on semialgebraic functions
sources.theorem_or_result:
Under geometric assumptions implied by Lipschitz stratifications (hence holding for semialgebraic functions and more generally definable functions in polynomially bounded o-minimal structures), constant-step subgradient descent iterates locally shadow a Riemannian gradient descent on an appropriately selected active stratum, and one can assemble descent inequalities across successive strata to obtain explicit finite-time convergence rates to a stationarity measure based on 
- the Riemannian gradient norms \(\|\nabla_{X} f(x_k)\|\) on active strata, and 
- a global projection formula relating Clarke subgradients to these Riemannian gradients.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for almost-sure convergence of stochastic subgradient descent (RobbinsMonro steps, martingale noise) to local minimizers for definable locally Lipschitz functions without weak convexity, equivalently showing avoidance of both active strict saddles and sharply repulsive critical points.

This paper studies (primarily deterministic) subgradient descent, focusing on finite-time complexity/rates under stratification-based geometric conditions (global projection formula, curvature bounds, tubular neighborhood estimates) that hold for semialgebraic/definable functions. These results provide structural tools (shadowing of Riemannian gradient descent on strata; mechanism to handle stratum switching) that could be useful in analyzing stochastic dynamics near active manifolds, including near sharply repulsive points. However, from the provided excerpt it does not establish the required stochastic avoidance results or almost-sure convergence to local minimizers in the non-weakly convex definable setting.

sources.title: Riemannian stochastic optimization methods avoid strict saddle points
sources.theorem_or_result: For a smooth objective function \(f\in C^2\) on a geodesically complete Riemannian manifold \(M\), consider the Riemannian Robbins–Monro (RRM) scheme \(X_{n+1}=\exp_{X_n}(\gamma_n \hat v_n)\) with surrogate gradients \(\hat v_n=v(X_n)+U_n+b_n\), where \(v=-\mathrm{grad}\,f\). Under: (i) \(v\) geodesically \(L\)-Lipschitz; (ii) stepsizes \(\sum_n\gamma_n=\infty\) and \(\sum_n \lambda^{1/\gamma_n}<\infty\) for all \(\lambda\in(0,1)\); (iii) bias \(\|b_n\|\le C\gamma_n\), bounded noise \(\|U_n\|\le \sigma\), and a uniform excitability condition \(\mathbb E[[\langle U_n,z\rangle]^+\mid \mathcal F_n]\ge \zeta\) for all unit \(z\in T_{X_n}M\); and (iv) injectivity radius bounded below; then for any strict saddle manifold \(S\) of \(f\), \[\mathbb P(\mathrm{dist}(X_n,S)\to 0)=0.\] (Theorem 1).
sources.connection:
The open problem concerns Euclidean stochastic subgradient descent for locally Lipschitz, definable (o-minimal) functions without weak convexity, and asks for generic convergence to local minimizers by avoiding both active strict saddles and sharply repulsive Clarke critical points. This paper proves an avoidance result, but in a different regime: \(f\) is \(C^2\) (smooth), gradients (not Clarke subgradients) are used, and the dynamics live on a Riemannian manifold with exponential/retraction updates. It establishes that Riemannian stochastic approximation avoids strict saddles (including saddle submanifolds) under nondegenerate noise.

Thus, it does not address nonsmooth Clarke-critical phenomena (active manifolds, sharp repulsion) nor the non-weakly-convex definable setting. However, its methodology—APT coupling to gradient flow, stable/center manifold arguments, and noise “excitability” conditions—could be conceptually relevant if one could extend it to differential inclusions / nonsmooth stratified dynamics arising from Clarke subgradients on definable sets.

sources.title: Lyapunov stability of the Euler method
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops Lyapunov-type criteria for stability of Euler discretizations of differential inclusions. In particular, Theorem 1.2: if (a) a set-valued map \(F\) is upper semicontinuous with nonempty compact values, (b) there exists a locally Lipschitz potential \(f\) of a conservative field \(D\) such that locally \(\max_{u\in \operatorname{co}F(x)}\min_{v\in D(x)}\langle u,v\rangle\le -\min_{w\in D(x)}\kappa(w)\) for some positive definite \(\kappa\), and \(f(x)\) is an isolated \(D\)-critical value, (c) there is a continuous function \(g\) that is d-Lyapunov near \(x\), and (d) \(x\) is a strict local minimizer of \(f+g\), then \(x\) is d-stable for the Euler scheme \(x_{k+1}\in x_k+\alpha_k F(x_k)\) with sufficiently small variable stepsizes. Extensions (Theorems 3.13, 3.15) give asymptotic \(p\)-d-stability/attractor results under \(\sum \alpha_k^p=\infty\), \(\alpha_k\to 0\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a generic almost-sure convergence guarantee for stochastic subgradient descent on definable locally Lipschitz functions without weak convexity, i.e., show SGD avoids both active strict saddles and sharply repulsive critical points. This paper does not analyze stochastic iterates, definability/genericity, or avoidance of unstable critical points. Instead it provides deterministic stability and (under additional \(p\)-d-Lyapunov decrease) asymptotic attraction results for Euler discretizations of differential inclusions, with an application to the Bouligand subgradient method for semi-algebraic \(f\). These Lyapunov/d-Lyapunov techniques could be a tool for proving stability/attraction of certain sets of minima (including nonisolated/flat minima) for deterministic subgradient-like methods, but they do not address the key stochastic avoidance mechanisms needed to rule out sharply repulsive critical points or strict saddles in the non-weakly convex definable setting.

sources.title: Contributions to non-convex stochastic optimization and reinforcement learning
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis establishes (for continuously differentiable nonconvex objectives) almost sure convergence of several stochastic momentum/adaptive-gradient algorithms with Robbins–Monro stepsizes to the set of critical points, and proves an avoidance-of-traps theorem for non-autonomous stochastic approximation schemes: for recursions \(z_{n+1}=z_n+\gamma_{n+1} b(z_n,\tau_n)+\gamma_{n+1}\eta_{n+1}+\gamma_{n+1}\rho_{n+1}\) with \(\sum\gamma_n=\infty\), \(\sum\gamma_n^2<\infty\), martingale-difference noise \(\eta_{n+1}\), and a linearization \(b(z,t)=D(z-z^\star)+e(z,t)\) near an equilibrium \(z^\star\) where \(D\) has an eigenvalue with positive real part, the event \(\{z_n\to z^\star\}\) has probability 0 under a nondegeneracy (“exciting noise”) condition in the unstable directions. Applied to smooth \(F\), this yields nonconvergence to strict saddles/local maxima for the considered algorithms.
sources.connection: The open problem concerns stochastic subgradient descent for locally Lipschitz definable (possibly non-weakly convex) functions and asks for generic convergence to local minimizers by avoiding both active strict saddles and sharply repulsive critical points (a nonsmooth phenomenon tied to active manifolds/Clarke subdifferentials). This thesis works almost entirely in the \(C^1\) setting (stochastic gradients, Hessians) and its trap-avoidance result targets unstable equilibria of an underlying (non-autonomous) ODE, corresponding to smooth strict saddles/maxima. It does not address Clarke criticality, active manifolds, definability stratifications, or sharply repulsive critical points, nor does it treat nonsmooth subgradient dynamics without weak convexity. At best, it provides a methodological template (non-autonomous avoidance-of-traps via invariant manifolds) that might be adaptable to the smooth dynamics on an active manifold, but the key missing piece is handling attraction to manifolds and nonsmooth normal dynamics that create sharply repulsive points.

title: Determine minimax regret rate for contextual dynamic pricing with unknown noise distribution
background_latex:
A seller repeatedly interacts with customers over periods \(t=1,\dots,T\). At time \(t\), a covariate (context) \(x_t\in\mathcal X\subset\mathbb R^{d_0}\) is observed, with \(\|x_t\|_\infty\le 1\). The customer's valuation is
\[
v_t = x_t^\top \theta_0 + z_t,
\]
where \(\theta_0\in\mathbb R^{d_0}\) is an unknown parameter (often assumed to satisfy \(\|\theta_0\|_1\le W\) for a known constant \(W\)), and \(\{z_t\}\) are i.i.d. draws from an unknown distribution with CDF \(F\). After the seller posts a price \(p_t>0\), the seller observes only the binary purchase indicator
\[
y_t = \mathbf 1\{v_t\ge p_t\}.
\]
The expected revenue from posting price \(p\) in context \(x\) is
\[
R(p;x) = p\,\mathbb P(v\ge p\mid x)= p\bigl(1-F(p-x^\top\theta_0)\bigr).
\]
Define the context-dependent optimal price
\[
p^*(x)\in \arg\max_{p>0} p\bigl(1-F(p-x^\top\theta_0)\bigr).
\]
The (pseudo-)regret over horizon \(T\) for a policy producing prices \(p_t\) is
\[
\mathcal R_T = \sum_{t=1}^T \Bigl( p^*(x_t)\bigl(1-F(p^*(x_t)-x_t^\top\theta_0)\bigr) - p_t\bigl(1-F(p_t-x_t^\top\theta_0)\bigr) \Bigr),
\]
and performance is measured by \(\mathbb E[\mathcal R_T]\) over the randomness in the data and any policy randomization. The model is "distribution-free" in the sense that \(F\) is unknown and not restricted to a known parametric/log-concave family; the paper assumes regularity such as Lipschitz continuity of \(F\) in some analyses.
problem_definition_latex: Characterize the minimax-optimal regret rate in \(T\) for contextual dynamic pricing under the linear valuation model \(v_t=x_t^\top\theta_0+z_t\) with unknown \(\theta_0\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\), given only binary purchase feedback \(y_t=\mathbf 1\{v_t\ge p_t\}\). In particular, determine whether there exists a policy with expected cumulative regret \(\mathbb E[\mathcal R_T]=\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) (up to logarithmic factors), or prove a matching lower bound (up to logs) showing \(\inf_{\pi}\sup_{\theta_0,F}\mathbb E_\pi[\mathcal R_T]=\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) (or the correct exponent), over an appropriate class of admissible \(F\) consistent with the paper's assumptions.
