literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Luo–Sun–Liu, 2023) framed contextual dynamic pricing with linear valuations \(v_t=x_t^\top\theta_0+z_t\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\) as a distribution-free problem under binary feedback \(y_t=\mathbf 1\{v_t\ge p_t\}\). Its DIP policy uses episodic estimation of \(\theta_0\) via a classification reduction and then reduces within-episode pricing to a perturbed linear bandit over a discretization of the residual \(p-x_t^\top\hat\theta\). Under Lipschitz \(F\) and a local quadratic revenue geometry (Assumptions 1–2), DIP yields a leading \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) term plus an additional term scaling with \(\sum_k \ell_k\,\mathbb E\|\hat\theta_{k-1}-\theta_0\|_1\), leaving open whether \(\tilde\Theta(T^{2/3})\) is the minimax rate when both \(\theta_0\) and \(F\) are unknown.

Subsequent work has essentially settled the minimax exponent under the natural “distribution-free but regular” class where \(F\) (equivalently demand \(1-F\)) is Lipschitz. In particular, "Minimax optimality in contextual dynamic pricing with general valuation models" proves a \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) regret upper bound for broad valuation classes (specializing to \(\tilde O(d_0^{1/3}T^{2/3})\) for linear valuations) and pairs it with a matching \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound (up to logarithmic factors), thereby establishing minimax optimality in \(T\) for Lipschitz \(F\). Complementarily, "Improved algorithms for contextual dynamic pricing" provides an explicit algorithmic route (VAPE) achieving \(\tilde O(d^{2/3}T^{2/3})\) regret under adversarial contexts and Lipschitz \(F\), and points to the \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound (e.g., via Xu–Wang-style constructions) showing the rate is unimprovable in this regime.

On the lower-bound side, "Towards agnostic feature-based dynamic pricing: Linear policies vs linear valuation with unknown noise" supplies a clean \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) minimax lower bound for the linear-valuation, unknown-noise, binary-feedback model, even under additional benign assumptions, clarifying that the \(2/3\) exponent is information-theoretic rather than an artifact of particular algorithms. Other partial-progress papers chart the landscape of assumptions: Explore-then-UCB achieves \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) only with extra second-order curvature, while smoothness-based semiparametric methods obtain rates depending on differentiability of \(F\). Finally, results such as "Optimal Contextual Pricing under Agnostic Non-Lipschitz Demand" indicate that \(T^{2/3}\) can remain the right rate even without Lipschitzness when one assumes stochastic, well-conditioned contexts and bounded noise, suggesting robustness of the \(2/3\) barrier beyond the original Lipschitz class.

Overall, for the core setting emphasized by the source paper—linear valuations, adversarial contexts, binary feedback, and unknown Lipschitz noise CDF—the minimax regret rate is now characterized (up to logarithmic factors) as \(\tilde\Theta(T^{2/3})\), with "Minimax optimality in contextual dynamic pricing with general valuation models" providing the definitive minimax statement.

sources.title: Minimax optimality in contextual dynamic pricing with general valuation models
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives matching (up to logarithmic factors) minimax upper and lower bounds for distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing with binary feedback when the noise CDF is only assumed Lipschitz and valuations are bounded. In particular, under realizability and boundedness and Lipschitz continuity of the unknown noise CDF \(F\), Algorithm 1 achieves regret \(\mathrm{Reg}(T)=\tilde O\big(\rho_V(\delta)^{1/3} T^{2/3}\big)\) with high probability (Theorem 1), where \(\rho_V(\delta)\) is the statistical complexity of the valuation class via an offline regression oracle. For linear valuations \(v^*(x)=x^\top\theta_0\) in \(\mathbb R^{d_0}\), this yields \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{Reg}(T)]=\tilde O(d_0^{1/3}T^{2/3})\) (Corollary 1). They also cite/extend known lower bounds showing \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) minimax regret in the Lipschitz, non-contextual case (and provide a general \(\Omega(T^{(m+1)/(2m+1)})\) lower bound for \(m\)-times differentiable \(F\); Theorem 2), thereby establishing \(T^{2/3}\) minimax optimality (up to logs) under Lipschitz \(F\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize the minimax regret rate for contextual dynamic pricing with linear valuations \(v_t=x_t^\top\theta_0+z_t\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\), given only binary purchase feedback, and in particular whether \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) is achievable and/or necessary. This paper directly targets that setting (and more general valuation classes): it proposes a distribution-free explore-then-UCB algorithm that does not require knowing the Lipschitz constant and proves a \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) regret upper bound (Theorem 1). For linear valuations it specializes to \(\tilde O(d_0^{1/3}T^{2/3})\) (Corollary 1). On the lower-bound side, it combines the known \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound for Lipschitz \(F\) in the non-contextual case (Xu and Wang 2022) with its upper bound to claim minimax optimality in \(T\) (up to logs) under Lipschitz noise; thus it resolves the exponent question posed in the open problem (the correct \(T\)-rate is \(T^{2/3}\) under Lipschitz \(F\)).

sources.title: Improved algorithms for contextual dynamic pricing
sources.theorem_or_result:
For contextual dynamic pricing with binary feedback and linear valuations with additive i.i.d. noise, the paper gives an algorithm (VAPE for Linear Valuations, Algorithm 2) that, under bounded contexts \(\|x_t\|\le B_x\), bounded parameter \(\|\theta\|\le B_\theta\), bounded noise \(|\xi_t|\le B_\xi\) and Lipschitz noise CDF \(F\) (equivalently Lipschitz demand \(D=1-F\)), achieves with probability \(1-T^{-1}\) regret
- \(R_T \le C\, d^{2/3} T^{2/3} \log(T)^{2/3}\)
for a constant \(C\) polynomial in \(B_\xi,B_x,B_\theta,L_\xi\) (Theorem 1). The paper also states this matches the known lower bound \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) for this setting (from Xu & Wang 2022).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the minimax regret rate in distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing with unknown \(\theta_0\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\), under binary purchase feedback, and in particular whether \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) is achievable and/or whether a matching \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound holds over an admissible class of \(F\) (e.g., Lipschitz). This paper directly addresses that question in the linear valuation model \(v_t=x_t^\top\theta+\xi_t\) with unknown \(\theta\) and unknown (only Lipschitz) \(F\): it provides an explicit policy with \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) regret (Theorem 1) under adversarial contexts, and it explicitly points to an existing \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound for Lipschitz demand/noise (Xu & Wang 2022), concluding minimax optimality (up to logs and dimension factors). Thus, for the natural Lipschitz-CDF distribution-free class highlighted in the open problem, it essentially settles the minimax exponent at \(2/3\).

sources.title: Towards agnostic feature-based dynamic pricing: Linear policies vs linear valuation with unknown noise
sources.theorem_or_result: For contextual dynamic pricing with linear noisy valuations (LV) where valuations satisfy \(y_t=x_t^\top\theta^*+N_t\) with \(\|x_t\|_2\le B\), \(\|\theta^*\|_2\le 1\), and i.i.d. bounded noise \(N_t\in[-1,1]\) from an unknown distribution, the paper proposes algorithm D2-EXP4 achieving expected regret \(\tilde O(T^{3/4}+d^{1/2}T^{5/8})\) (Theorem 6). It also proves a minimax lower bound \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) for LV (Corollary 9), even under stronger conditions such as stochastic contexts, Lipschitz valuation/noise distribution, and unimodal revenue curve (via Theorem 7).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks to characterize the minimax regret rate for distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing with unknown \(\theta_0\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\) under binary purchase feedback, and in particular whether \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) is achievable or whether a matching \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound holds.
- This paper directly studies essentially the same LV model (linear valuation plus i.i.d. unknown noise, binary feedback) in an adversarial-context setting, and provides a \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound, supporting \(T^{2/3}\) as an information-theoretic barrier from below.
- However, its best upper bound for the LV model is \(\tilde O(T^{3/4}+d^{1/2}T^{5/8})\), not \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\). Thus it does not close the minimax rate; it narrows the gap by improving the lower bound to \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) and giving a sublinear algorithm without distributional assumptions beyond bounded noise.
- The paper also treats a different benchmark model (LP) where one competes with the best linear pricing policy and proves tight \(\tilde\Theta(d^{1/3}T^{2/3})\) regret; this is related but not the same as the LV minimax question in the open problem.

sources.title: Contextual dynamic pricing with unknown noise: Explore-then-ucb strategy and improved regrets
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes an Explore-then-UCB (ExUCB) policy for contextual dynamic pricing with linear valuations and unknown noise CDF \(F\). Under Assumptions 1–5 (bounded \(\|x_t\|_\infty\le 1\), \(\|\theta_0\|_1\le W\), bounded valuations, \(F\) Lipschitz, and a local quadratic/2nd-order smoothness condition on the revenue around \(p^*(x)\)), Theorem 1 proves \(\mathbb E[R_T]=\tilde O(d_0^2 T^{2/3})\). Under only Lipschitz \(F\) (Assumptions 1–4), Theorem 2 proves \(\mathbb E[R_T]=\tilde O(d_0 T^{3/4})\). For lower bounds under Assumptions 1–5, Theorem 3 shows that for any \(\delta>0\), no policy can achieve \(O(T^{3/5-\delta})\) regret (i.e., minimax regret is \(\tilde\Omega(T^{3/5})\) up to logs).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks to characterize the minimax-optimal regret rate for distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing with unknown \(\theta_0\) and unknown \(F\) from binary feedback, and in particular whether \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) is achievable and/or whether a matching \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound holds over an admissible class of \(F\).
- Achievability: This paper gives the first \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) upper bound, but only under an additional 2nd-order smoothness (local quadratic curvature) assumption (Assumption 5) beyond Lipschitz continuity. Under Lipschitz-only, it attains \(\tilde O(T^{3/4})\), not \(T^{2/3}\).
- Lower bounds/minimax: It provides a new lower bound \(\tilde\Omega(T^{3/5})\) under Lipschitz+2nd-order smoothness, leaving a gap to the \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) upper bound; thus it does not establish minimax optimality nor a matching \(T^{2/3}\) lower bound in that class. The paper also notes prior \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bounds (Xu & Wang 2022) apply to Lipschitz-only but not to the 2nd-order smoothness class.
Therefore, it makes substantial partial progress: it achieves the conjectured \(T^{2/3}\) rate under stronger regularity and advances lower bounds in that smoother class, but does not fully resolve the minimax rate in the general distribution-free setting posed in the open problem.

sources.title: Optimal Contextual Pricing under Agnostic Non-Lipschitz Demand
sources.theorem_or_result:
Theorem 1 (Xu–Wang 2026): Under (i) linear valuations 
\(y_t=\langle x_t,\theta^\star\rangle+\xi_t\), (ii) i.i.d. bounded-support noise \(\xi_t\in[-c,c]\) with unknown distribution (allowing arbitrary atoms/jumps; no Lipschitz/smoothness), (iii) i.i.d. stochastic contexts with \(\lambda_{\min}(\mathbb E[x_tx_t^\top])\ge \lambda_0>0\), and (iv) an interior “price buffer” condition, Algorithm 1 (CMRUP) achieves expected cumulative pseudo-regret \(\mathbb E[R_T]\le \tilde O(T^{2/3})\), with polylog\((T)\) and polynomial dependence on problem parameters hidden in \(\tilde O(\cdot)\).
sources.connection: Directly addresses the open problem of minimax regret rates for distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing with binary purchase feedback and unknown noise CDF. The paper provides an \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) upper bound even when the induced demand/survival function is non-Lipschitz and discontinuous (atoms/jumps), improving prior agnostic contextual bounds (\(\tilde O(T^{3/4})\)). It also argues tightness in \(T\) by embedding the classical non-contextual lower bound \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) (Kleinberg–Leighton 2003) into its stochastic-context model (Appendix C.9), yielding a matching minimax lower bound in that restricted setting. However, it does not fully resolve the original open problem in the most general formulation because its main theorem assumes i.i.d. well-conditioned contexts (not adversarial contexts) and bounded-support noise plus an interior price-buffer condition; thus it characterizes the minimax rate only for that admissible subclass rather than all context sequences/classes of \(F\) contemplated in the original paper.

sources.title: Policy optimization using semiparametric models for dynamic pricing
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes an episodic explore-then-exploit policy for contextual dynamic pricing with linear valuations and unknown noise CDF \(F\) (binary purchase feedback). Under regularity/identifiability conditions (notably Assumption 2.1 ensuring a unique optimal price and smoothness of \(F\)), it proves regret upper bounds:
- If \(F\in C^{(m)}\) with \(m\ge 2\), then \(\mathrm{Regret}(T)\le \tilde O\big((Td)^{\frac{2m+1}{4m-1}}\big)\) (Theorem 4.1; logs and some \(d\)-dependence explicit in the statement).
- If \(F\) is “super-smooth” (Fourier transform decays exponentially; Assumption 4.7), then \(\mathrm{Regret}(T)\le \tilde O\big((Td)^{1/2}\big)\) (Theorem 4.3).
It also extends the \(C^{(m)}\) bound to \(\beta\)-mixing (dependent) contexts (Theorem 4.2).
sources.connection: Directly addresses the same distribution-free contextual dynamic pricing model with linear signal \(x_t^\top\theta_0\) and unknown noise CDF \(F\), with only binary purchase feedback. It provides explicit regret upper bounds as a function of the smoothness of \(F\): \(\tilde O(T^{(2m+1)/(4m-1)})\) (up to dimension/log factors) and \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) for super-smooth \(F\). This is progress toward characterizing minimax rates, but it does not establish matching minimax lower bounds for the nonparametric \(F\) class; the paper itself notes that tight lower bounds beyond the generic \(\Omega(\sqrt T)\) parametric-style lower bound remain open for finite \(m\). In particular, it does not prove a \(\tilde\Omega(T^{2/3})\) lower bound nor show \(\tilde O(T^{2/3})\) is minimax-optimal; instead it achieves exponents \(\frac{2m+1}{4m-1}\) (e.g. \(5/7\) for \(m=2\)) which are generally different from \(2/3\).

title: Bound the integrality gap of time-indexed LP for bipartite AND/OR scheduling
background_latex:
Consider the single-machine scheduling problem with AND/OR precedence constraints. There is a set of jobs partitioned as \(N=A\uplus B\). Each job \(j\in N\) has a processing time \(p_j\ge 0\) and a weight \(w_j\ge 0\). A schedule is a non-preemptive ordering of the jobs on one machine with no overlap; \(C_j\) denotes the completion time of job \(j\). AND-precedence constraints are given by a directed arc set \(E_{\wedge}\subseteq (A\times A)\cup (B\times B)\); an arc \((i,j)\in E_{\wedge}\) requires that \(i\) completes before \(j\) starts. OR-precedence constraints are given by an arc set \(E_{\vee}\subseteq A\times B\). For each \(b\in B\), its set of OR-predecessors is \(P(b):=\{a\in A:(a,b)\in E_{\vee}\}\); feasibility requires that each \(b\in B\) with \(P(b)\neq\emptyset\) starts only after at least one job in \(P(b)\) has completed. Let \(\Delta:=\max_{b\in B}|P(b)|\).

A standard approach uses a time-indexed linear programming relaxation over a discrete time horizon \(T:=\sum_{j\in N} p_j\) (for instance in the unit-processing-time case \(p_j\in\{0,1\}\), one has \(T\le n\)). Introduce variables \(x_{jt}\) indicating (fractionally) that job \(j\) completes at integer time \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\). The relaxation includes: (i) assignment constraints \(\sum_{t=1}^T x_{jt}=1\) for all \(j\); (ii) single-machine capacity constraints ensuring at most one unit-processing job executes at any time; (iii) AND-precedence constraints coupling cumulative completions so that successors cannot complete too early; and (iv) OR-precedence constraints coupling cumulative completions so that a job \(b\in B\) cannot complete by time \(t+p_b\) unless at least one predecessor \(a\in P(b)\) has completed by time \(t\). The LP objective is the fractional lower bound \(\min \sum_{j\in N} w_j\sum_{t=1}^T t\,x_{jt}\), corresponding to \(\sum_j w_j C_j\) in integer schedules.

The paper analyzes rounding algorithms based on random \(\alpha\)-points for this relaxation and notes that the tightness of these analyses (equivalently, the true worst-case integrality gap of the underlying time-indexed formulation for this AND/OR structure) is not established.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine the best (smallest) constant \(g\ge 1\) such that, for every instance of \(1\mid ao\text{-}prec=A\uplus B\mid \sum_{j\in N} w_j C_j\) and for the corresponding time-indexed linear programming relaxation described above, the ratio
\[
\frac{\text{optimal objective value of an optimal integer schedule}}{\text{optimal objective value of the time-indexed LP relaxation}}
\]
is at most \(g\). Equivalently, bound the integrality gap of the time-indexed LP relaxation for this problem class (as a function of parameters such as \(\Delta\), or by a universal constant if possible), and in particular decide whether the approximation-factor analyses obtained via random \(\alpha\)-point rounding are tight in the worst case.

title: Design accelerated proximal bundle methods for hybrid convex composite optimization problems
background_latex:
Let \(f,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper lower semicontinuous convex functions with \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\subseteq \mathrm{dom}\,f\). Consider the hybrid convex composite optimization problem
\[
\phi^*:=\min\{\phi(x):=f(x)+h(x): x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}.
\]
Assume \(h\) is \(\mu\)-convex for some \(\mu\ge 0\), meaning that \(h(x)-\frac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2\) is convex. Assume a first-order oracle \(f'\) is available with \(f'(x)\in \partial f(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathrm{dom}\,h\), and there exist parameters \(M_f\ge 0\) and \(L_f\ge 0\) such that for all \(u,v\in\mathrm{dom}\,h\),
\[
\|f'(u)-f'(v)\|\le 2M_f + L_f\|u-v\|.
\]
Let \(D\) denote the diameter of \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\) when it is finite:
\[
D:=\sup\{\|x-y\|: x,y\in \mathrm{dom}\,h\}<\infty.
\]
An \(\bar\varepsilon\)-solution is a point \(\bar x\in\mathrm{dom}\,h\) with \(\phi(\bar x)-\phi^*\le \bar\varepsilon\).

A proximal bundle (PB) method is a first-order method that iteratively solves proximalized subproblems based on a piecewise-linear (bundle) lower model of \(f\) plus \(h\), typically producing serious/null steps; the paper analyzes a generic PB framework (GPB) and obtains iteration-complexity bounds of order
\[
O\!\left(\min\left\{\frac{(M_f^2+\bar\varepsilon L_f)d_0^2}{\bar\varepsilon^2},\;\left(\frac{M_f^2+\bar\varepsilon L_f}{\mu\bar\varepsilon}+1\right)\log\left(\frac{\mu d_0^2}{\bar\varepsilon}+1\right)\right\}+1\right)
\]
(up to logarithmic factors), where \(d_0\) is the distance from the initial point to the solution set.

For the same HCCO class with finite \(D\), known lower bounds (cited in the paper) imply that an optimal (accelerated) rate in terms of \((L_f,M_f,D,\bar\varepsilon)\) is
\[
O\!\left( \frac{\sqrt{L_f}\,D}{\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}} + \frac{M_f^2 D^2}{\bar\varepsilon^2}\right)
\]
(in the sense described in the cited reference).
problem_definition_latex:
Assume \(D:=\sup\{\|x-y\|:x,y\in\mathrm{dom}\,h\}<\infty\). Develop a (proximal) bundle-type method for minimizing \(\phi(x)=f(x)+h(x)\) under the hybrid subgradient condition \(\|f'(u)-f'(v)\|\le 2M_f+L_f\|u-v\|\) whose iteration complexity to obtain an \(\bar\varepsilon\)-solution matches (up to universal constants and allowable logarithmic factors) the optimal bound
\[
O\!\left( \frac{\sqrt{L_f}\,D}{\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}} + \frac{M_f^2 D^2}{\bar\varepsilon^2}\right).
\]
Equivalently, design an accelerated variant of the generic proximal bundle framework achieving the above complexity for the HCCO problem class parameterized by \((L_f,M_f,D)\).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Liang--Monteiro's HCCO model, the oracle condition \(\|f'(u)-f'(v)\|\le 2M_f+L_f\|u-v\|\) interpolates between Lipschitz nonsmoothness (\(L_f=0\)) and smoothness (\(M_f=0\)). Their GPB framework (with serious/null steps and bundle models \(\Gamma\le \phi\)) yields a unified complexity of order \(O((M_f^2+\bar\varepsilon L_f)d_0^2/\bar\varepsilon^2)\) in the convex case \(\mu=0\), and a logarithmic dependence in \(1/\bar\varepsilon\) when \(\mu>0\). The paper explicitly notes that, when \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\) has finite diameter \(D\), the optimal worst-case bound should be \(O(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}+M_f^2D^2/\bar\varepsilon^2)\), matching accelerated composite subgradient methods, and poses the open problem of designing an accelerated bundle-type analogue.

Forward citations show partial progress but no full resolution. The closest acceleration result is "On the Acceleration of Proximal Bundle Methods", which develops accelerated PB variants and proves \(\tilde O(\sqrt{L_f}\,\|x_0-x^*\|/\sqrt{\varepsilon})\) iteration complexity (up to \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\)) in the smooth regime \(M_f=0\), aligning with the \(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) term when \(D\) controls distances. However, it does not cover the hybrid regime \(M_f>0\) nor establish the mixed bound combining \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\) and \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) terms for general HCCO with prox-friendly \(h\). Other works (e.g., universal/adaptive GPB variants and primal-dual PB analyses) strengthen universality, adaptivity, and primal-dual certification, and sharpen strongly convex rates, but their convex-case dependence on \(L_f\) remains non-accelerated (typically \(L_f/\varepsilon\) rather than \(\sqrt{L_f/\varepsilon}\)).

Overall, the evidence suggests the specific open problem remains open: there is not yet a proximal bundle-type method for general convex HCCO with bounded \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\) that provably matches \(O(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}+M_f^2D^2/\bar\varepsilon^2)\) (up to logs). Promising directions indicated by the citations include combining Nesterov-style acceleration of inexact proximal point/bundle subproblem solves with hybrid-model-aware step selection, and leveraging primal-dual viewpoints (e.g., PDCP--conditional-gradient duality) to control null steps without introducing geometry-dependent constants.

sources.title: On the Acceleration of Proximal Bundle Methods
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes accelerated proximal bundle variants and proves accelerated iteration complexity in two settings. For unconstrained smooth convex minimization \(\min_x f(x)\) with \(\nabla f\) \(L_f\)-Lipschitz, Algorithm 3 (a-PBM) reaches an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal point in \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{\rho\,\|x_0-x^*\|^2}{\varepsilon}}\,\log\tfrac1\varepsilon\right)\) iterations (Theorem 26; e.g. choosing \(\rho=L_f\) gives \(O(\sqrt{L_f}\,\|x_0-x^*\|/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon))\)). For composite objectives \(h(x)=g(x)+f(x)\) with \(g\) smooth and \(f\) convex piecewise-linear, Algorithm 5 attains \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}}\,\log\tfrac1\varepsilon\right)\) serious-step complexity and an overall bound of the form \(O\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}}\,\log\tfrac1\varepsilon\right)\) times a dimension/geometric factor controlling null steps (Theorem 37).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an accelerated proximal bundle-type method for the hybrid convex composite problem \(\min_x f(x)+h(x)\) under the hybrid subgradient condition \(\|f'(u)-f'(v)\|\le 2M_f+L_f\|u-v\|\) with finite domain diameter \(D\), achieving the optimal complexity \(O(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}+M_f^2D^2/\bar\varepsilon^2)\) (up to logs). This paper makes clear progress on the \(M_f=0\) (smooth) regime by giving the first accelerated PBM variant with \(O(\sqrt{L_f}/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\cdot\log(1/\varepsilon))\) dependence (matching the \(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) term up to replacing \(D\) by \(\|x_0-x^*\|\) and a log factor). However, it does not address the full hybrid condition with \(M_f>0\) nor provide the mixed-rate bound \(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\varepsilon}+M_f^2D^2/\varepsilon^2\) for general HCCO with a general nonsmooth \(h\) (prox-friendly) and bounded \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\). The composite result treated here is different (smooth + piecewise-linear) and its complexity depends on additional geometric quantities (e.g., pyramidal width) rather than the \((M_f,L_f,D)\) parameters of the open problem.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes a parameter-free (universal) proximal bundle method U-PB and proves functional iteration complexity bounds for hybrid composite optimization \(\min_x\,\phi(x)=f(x)+h(x)\) under the hybrid subgradient condition \(\|f'(x)-f'(y)\|\le 2M_f+L_f\|x-y\|\). Under bounded \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\) with diameter \(D\), Theorem 2.3 bounds the total number of inner (bundle) iterations by
- \(\min\{\min[\tfrac1\chi(N+U(\bar\varepsilon)/(\bar\varepsilon\mu_\phi)),\; N+U(\bar\varepsilon)/(\bar\varepsilon\mu_h)]\,\log(1+\mu_\phi d_0^2/\bar\varepsilon),\; d_0^2 U(\bar\varepsilon)/(\bar\varepsilon^2 N)\}+ N\lceil 2\log(\lambda_0 U(\bar\varepsilon)/(N\bar\varepsilon))\rceil,\)
where \(U(\bar\varepsilon)=\tfrac{4(M_f^2+\bar\varepsilon L_f)B}{(1-\chi)^2}+\tfrac{N\bar\varepsilon}{\lambda_0}\) and \(B=8+12\log(1+L_f^2D^2N/(16M_f^2))\). In particular, in the strongly convex regime \(\mu_\phi>0\) and with \(\chi\) bounded away from \(0,1\), this yields \(\tilde O(M_f^2/(\bar\varepsilon\mu_\phi)+L_f/\mu_\phi)\) dependence (up to logs).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an accelerated bundle-type method for the same HCCO class (bounded \(D\)) achieving the optimal convex (\(\mu=0\)) rate \(O(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}+M_f^2D^2/\bar\varepsilon^2)\). This paper develops a universal proximal bundle method (U-PB) and sharpens GPB-type complexity in terms of strong convexity \(\mu_\phi\), without restarts or knowing parameters. However, its main bounds are either (i) strongly convex/\(\mu_\phi\)-universal rates of order \(\tilde O(M_f^2/(\bar\varepsilon\mu_\phi)+L_f/\mu_\phi)\), or (ii) a non-strongly-convex fallback term \(O(d_0^2(M_f^2+\bar\varepsilon L_f)/\bar\varepsilon^2)\). It does not provide an accelerated \(\mu=0\) bundle method matching the optimal \(\sqrt{L_f}D/\sqrt{\bar\varepsilon}\) term; the authors explicitly note acceleration as future work. Thus it is relevant progress on universal PB design and analysis, but it does not solve the stated acceleration open problem.

sources.title: Parameter-free proximal bundle methods with adaptive stepsizes for hybrid convex composite optimization problems
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes Ad-GPB, a parameter-free adaptive modern proximal bundle framework for HCCO with bounded \,\(\mathrm{dom}\,h\) (diameter \(D\)) and hybrid subgradient condition \(\|f'(u)-f'(v)\|\le 2M+L\|u-v\|\). Its main guarantee (Theorem 2.1) is that Ad-GPB outputs \(\hat y_k\in\mathrm{dom}\,h\) with \(\phi(\hat y_k)-\phi^*\le \phi(\hat y_k)-\hat n_k\le \varepsilon\) within at most \(4\bar K(\varepsilon)\) cycles and at most
\[4\bar K(\varepsilon)\Big(1+\tfrac{\tau}{1-\tau}\log_+\tfrac{8\bar t}{\varepsilon}+2\Big)+\log_+^2\Big(\bar Q\lambda_1\big(\tfrac{M^2}{\varepsilon}+\tfrac{L}{16}\big)\Big)\]
iterations, where \(\bar t=2MD+\tfrac{L}{2}D^2\), \(\bar Q=128(1-\tau)/\tau\), and \(\bar K(\varepsilon)=2\left\lceil \tfrac{2D^2\bar Q}{\varepsilon}\left(\tfrac{M^2}{\varepsilon}+\tfrac{L}{16}+\tfrac{1}{\lambda_1\bar Q}\right)+\log_+\tfrac{\beta_0(\phi(\hat x_0)-\hat n_0)}{\varepsilon}+1\right\rceil\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an accelerated (optimal-rate) proximal bundle-type method for HCCO with bounded \(D\) achieving complexity \(\tilde O(\sqrt{L}\,D/\sqrt{\varepsilon}+M^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\). This paper studies adaptive/parameter-free step-size and cycle-termination rules for modern PB methods under the same hybrid condition and bounded \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\). However, its proven iteration complexity remains essentially \(\tilde O\big(D^2(M^2/\varepsilon^2+L/\varepsilon)\big)\) (plus logs and dependence on \(\lambda_1\)), i.e., it does not achieve the accelerated \(\sqrt{L}/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) dependence. Thus it does not solve the open problem, but provides partial progress in the direction of practical adaptivity and parameter-free tuning within the proximal bundle framework for the same problem class.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops a primal-dual proximal bundle framework (PDPB) for convex nonsmooth composite optimization 
\(\min_x\,\phi(x)=f(x)+h(x)\) under the bounded-subgradient assumption \(\|f'(x)\|\le M\) on \(\mathrm{dom}\,h\). For the PDCP inner cutting-plane scheme with \(\tau_j=j/(j+2)\), it proves a cycle complexity bound: PDCP reaches primal-dual gap \(t_j\le\varepsilon\) in 
- \(O\big(\sqrt{t_1/\varepsilon}+\lambda M^2/\varepsilon+1\big)\) inner iterations (Proposition 2.3),
and the outer PDPB method achieves total oracle complexity 
\[O\big(M^2 d_0^2/\bar\varepsilon^2+1\big)\]

It then proposes an adaptive proximal bundle method (APBM) based on proximal point iterations with this inner solver and proves a total complexity bound for minimizing \(\min_x f(x)\) under Hölder smoothness (Theorem 4.2), which is optimal only in the Lipschitz case \(\alpha=0\).

title: Compute the exact competitive ratio for minimization fractional prophet inequalities without in-house production
background_latex:
Fix integers \(n\ge 2\) and a real exponent \(p>1\). Let \(C_1,\dots,C_n\) be independent nonnegative random variables, where each \(C_i\) has a distribution \(D_i\) supported on a known interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(0<\ell\le u<\infty\). A (causal) online procurement policy \(\pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n)\) is a sequence of measurable functions \(\pi_i:[\ell,u]^i\to[0,1]\). Given a realized cost vector \(c=(c_1,\dots,c_n)\), the policy selects purchase quantities \(x_i=\pi_i(c_1,\dots,c_i)\) satisfying the feasibility constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\) (interpreted as procuring one unit of a divisible commodity).

The incurred cost under monomial cost functions is
\[\mathrm{ALG}_\pi(c,p):=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i^p.\]
The (offline) clairvoyant benchmark ("prophet") cost for realization \(c\) is the optimal value
\[\mathrm{OPT}(c,p):=\min_{x\in[0,1]^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i^p\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1.\]
The competitive ratio for the family of all independent distributions supported on \([\ell,u]\) (and with no deterministic in-house option) is
\[\mathrm{CR}(F,n):=\inf_{\pi}\ \sup_{(D_1,\dots,D_n)}\ \frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}_\pi(C,p)]}{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}(C,p)]},\]
where the supremum ranges over all choices of independent \(C_i\sim D_i\) supported on \([\ell,u]\), and expectations are with respect to \(C=(C_1,\dots,C_n)\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine (in closed form, as a function of the parameters \(p,n,\ell,u\)) the value of
\[\mathrm{CR}(F,n)=\inf_{\pi}\ \sup_{(D_1,\dots,D_n)}\ \frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}_\pi(C,p)]}{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}(C,p)]}\]
for the minimization fractional prophet inequality described above in the setting without in-house production capabilities (i.e., when all \(n\) costs \(C_1,\dots,C_n\) are random and only constrained by support \([\ell,u]\)).

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem asks for a closed-form expression for the worst-case competitive ratio \(\mathrm{CR}(F,n)\) in the minimization fractional prophet inequality for sequential procurement with convex monomial costs \(\sum_i c_i x_i^p\) (\(p>1\)), feasibility \(\sum_i x_i=1\), and independent costs supported on \([\ell,u]\), in the regime without an in-house deterministic option. The source paper establishes several anchor points: (i) for “well-behaved” distributions (invertible CDF with Lipschitz inverse) the ratio approaches 1 at rate \(1+O(1/\log n)\) via a multi-threshold interval policy; (ii) with in-house production and only a lower support bound \([\ell,\infty)\), the exact ratio is \(\bigl(1+(n-1)\ell^{-1/(p-1)}\bigr)^{p-1}\); and (iii) without in-house production, an exact formula is derived only for \(n=p=2\): \(\tfrac14(\sqrt{u/\ell}+\sqrt{\ell/u})+\tfrac12\). The paper also shows that, unlike the classical maximization prophet inequality, the worst case is not attained at \(n=2\) and the ratio can be non-monotone in \(n\), complicating attempts to generalize the \(n=2\) analysis.

Among the forward citations provided, the only analyzed citing work studies a different minimization prophet model (single-choice stopping with i.i.d. observations) and focuses on asymptotics as \(n\to\infty\), using extreme value theory to obtain closed-form asymptotic constants and to analyze multi-threshold versus single-threshold policies. Although this does not resolve the fractional procurement problem, it suggests that asymptotic characterizations (in \(n\)) may be tractable in restricted distributional regimes, and that multi-threshold structures can be optimal in minimization settings.

Overall, based on the available forward-citation evidence, the exact closed-form \(\mathrm{CR}(F,n)\) for general \((p,n,\ell,u)\) without in-house production remains open beyond the special case \(n=p=2\) and the asymptotic \(\mathrm{CR}(F,n)\to 1\) result under regularity assumptions. Key gaps include identifying the worst-case independent distributions on \([\ell,u]\) for finite \(n\) and understanding how the dynamic-program structure (e.g., the power-mean form of \(\mathrm{OPT}\) and the induced recursion for optimal online policies) interacts with distributional extremizers when both numerator and denominator depend on the distributions.

sources.theorem_or_result: For the classical single-choice I.I.D. minimization prophet inequality (choose one realized value, forced to stop by time n), for any continuous distribution F in the EVT domain of attraction D_\gamma with \(\gamma\le 0\), the asymptotic competitive ratio of the optimal (multi-threshold) stopping rule as \(n\to\infty\) equals \(\lambda_m=\max\{\Lambda(\gamma),1\}\), where \(\Lambda(\gamma)=(1-\gamma)^{-\gamma}\Gamma(1-\gamma)\). They also show for \(\gamma<0\) there exist single-threshold rules with competitive ratio \(\Theta((\log n)^{-\gamma})\), and this dependence is tight for single-threshold rules.

The citing paper instead studies the single-item stopping version (pick one observation) in the i.i.d. setting, mainly asymptotically as \(n\to\infty\), and does not treat fractional allocations, monomial power costs, or worst-case over all independent distributions on \([\ell,u]\). Thus it does not resolve the stated procurement/fractional open problem. At best, it provides EVT-based techniques and asymptotic characterizations for a related minimization prophet model.

title: Prove convergence of iterative KKT-point exclusion for nonconvex polynomial Nash equilibria
background_latex:
Consider a Nash equilibrium problem with \(N\) players. Player \(i\) chooses a strategy vector \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\) and faces an optimization problem parameterized by the other players' strategies \(x_{-i}\):
\[
\min_{x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}} f_i(x_i,x_{-i}) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad g_{i,j}(x_i)=0\ (j\in E_i),\quad g_{i,j}(x_i)\ge 0\ (j\in I_i),
\]
where \(f_i\) is a polynomial in \(x=(x_1,\dots,x_N)\) and each constraint polynomial \(g_{i,j}\) depends only on \(x_i\). The feasible set of player \(i\) is
\[
X_i := \{x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}: g_{i,j}(x_i)=0\ (j\in E_i),\ g_{i,j}(x_i)\ge 0\ (j\in I_i)\},
\]
and the joint feasible set is \(X:=X_1\times\cdots\times X_N\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(n:=\sum_i n_i\).

A (pure-strategy) Nash equilibrium is a point \(x^*\in X\) such that for every \(i\), \(x_i^*\) is a global minimizer of player \(i\)'s problem at \(x_{-i}^*\).

Assume each constraint tuple \(g_i:=(g_{i,1},\dots,g_{i,m_i})\) is \"nonsingular\" in the sense that a certain associated polynomial matrix has full column rank over \(\mathbb{C}^{n_i}\); under this assumption, the Lagrange multipliers for the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions can be expressed as polynomial functions \(\lambda_{i,j}(x)\). Then every Nash equilibrium satisfies a polynomial system encoding the KKT equalities together with complementarity and sign conditions:
1) stationarity \(\nabla_{x_i} f_i(x) - \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \lambda_{i,j}(x)\nabla_{x_i} g_{i,j}(x_i)=0\),
2) primal feasibility \(g_{i,j}(x_i)=0\) for \(j\in E_i\), \(g_{i,j}(x_i)\ge 0\) for \(j\in I_i\),
3) complementarity \(\lambda_{i,j}(x) g_{i,j}(x_i)=0\) for \(j\in I_i\),
4) dual feasibility \(\lambda_{i,j}(x)\ge 0\) for \(j\in I_i\).

The paper proposes an iterative algorithm (Algorithm 3.1) that repeatedly solves a polynomial optimization problem over the KKT-feasible set (using a generic strictly convex quadratic objective \([x]_1^\top\Theta [x]_1\) to pick a unique candidate) and then checks whether the candidate is a Nash equilibrium by solving each player's best-response problem. If the candidate \(u\) is not an equilibrium, the algorithm adds finitely many additional polynomial inequalities of the form
\[
f_i(v,x_{-i})-f_i(x_i,x_{-i})\ge 0
\]
for selected best-response points \(v\) (collected in sets \(K_i\)) to exclude the found non-equilibrium KKT point(s) and repeats.
problem_definition_latex:
Assume the nonsingularity condition holds so that polynomial Lagrange multiplier expressions \(\lambda_{i,j}(x)\) exist, and suppose a Nash equilibrium exists.

Analyze Algorithm 3.1 described above in the case where there are infinitely many KKT points that are not Nash equilibria. Determine whether, under such circumstances, the iterative procedure of repeatedly:
1) solving the current polynomial optimization problem over the KKT-feasible set augmented with the accumulated inequalities indexed by \(K_i\),
2) checking the resulting optimizer \(u\) for the Nash equilibrium property via each player's global best-response computation,
3) enlarging \(K_i\) by adding some best-response optimizer(s) when \(u\) fails the Nash equilibrium check,
necessarily converges (in finitely or infinitely many iterations) to a Nash equilibrium.

Equivalently: give conditions under which Algorithm 3.1 is guaranteed to find a Nash equilibrium (or certify nonexistence) even when the set of non-equilibrium KKT points is infinite, or provide an explicit example showing failure of convergence.

literature_review.synthesis:
In the NEPP framework of Nie–Tang, nonsingularity of each player’s constraint tuple yields polynomial Lagrange-multiplier expressions \(\lambda_{i,j}(x)\), so every Nash equilibrium lies in the semialgebraic KKT-feasible set \(G\) of (3.7). Algorithm 3.1 then runs a select–verify–cut loop: select a unique KKT point by minimizing a generic strictly convex quadratic \([x]_1^\top\Theta[x]_1\) over the current relaxation (3.10), verify equilibrium by solving each best-response global problem (3.8), and cut off the current non-equilibrium KKT point by adding inequalities \(f_i(v,x_{-i})-f_i(x_i,x_{-i})\ge 0\) for best-response witnesses \(v\in K_i\). The original paper proves finite termination when \(|G\setminus G^*|<\infty\) (Theorem 3.2) and shows that this finiteness holds generically because the complex KKT system is zero-dimensional (Theorem A.1), but explicitly leaves open the nongeneric regime where \(G\setminus G^*\) is infinite (Section 6).

Forward-citation work provides partial progress by establishing asymptotic convergence of analogous exclusion loops under additional regularity assumptions. For rational generalized Nash equilibrium problems, the rational analogue proves that if spurious KKT points are infinite, then any accumulation point of the selected iterates is a (generalized) Nash equilibrium provided certain strict-feasibility and continuity hypotheses hold (notably continuity of each player’s value function and uniform continuity of the feasible-extension maps). For polynomial variational inequalities, an essentially identical KKT-exclusion scheme yields that, in the infinite-spurious-KKT regime, any accumulation point is a true VI solution under continuity of an appropriate gap function at the limit and boundedness of selected auxiliary minimizers. These results suggest that unconditional convergence of Algorithm 3.1 is unlikely without extra assumptions; rather, one should expect convergence of accumulation points under continuity/compactness-type conditions ensuring that the separating inequalities do not “chase” a positive-dimensional set of spurious KKT points without approaching \(G^*\).

Other related papers mainly reinforce the generic-finiteness escape hatch or provide alternative computational routes. Algebraic-degree results for (generalized) Nash problems quantify generic finiteness of complex Fritz–John/KKT points, while polyhedral homotopy methods exploit this to enumerate all KKT tuples in the zero-dimensional (generic) case and then verify equilibria. SOS-based select–verify–cut methods in structured polynomial game classes (e.g., imperfect-recall games) prove asymptotic exactness of the overall loop, again pointing toward asymptotic (rather than finite) guarantees when the KKT set is not finite. Overall, the specific open question for nonconvex polynomial NEPPs with infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points remains open: existing progress indicates that convergence can be proved for accumulation points under additional continuity/feasibility assumptions, but no general theorem (or definitive counterexample) is currently established for Algorithm 3.1 in full generality.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes Algorithm 3.3 (a rational-function analogue of the KKT-point exclusion scheme) and proves: - Finite termination if the set of non-equilibrium KKT points is finite (Theorem 3.6). - If non-equilibrium KKT points are infinite, any accumulation point of the iterates is a GNE provided (i) strict-inequality constraints stay strictly feasible at the limit, (ii) each player’s value function \(\nu_i(x_{-i})=\inf_{x_i\in X_i(x_{-i})} f_i(x_i,x_{-i})\) is continuous at the limit, and (iii) the sequence of feasible extensions \(p_i^{(k)}\) is uniformly continuous at the limit (Theorem 3.7).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence guarantees (or counterexamples) for the iterative KKT-point exclusion Algorithm 3.1 for nonconvex polynomial NEPs when \(K\setminus S\) is infinite. This citing paper directly addresses the analogous difficulty (in a more general rGNEP setting) and gives an asymptotic convergence theorem (Theorem 3.7) precisely for the case \(|K\setminus S|=\infty\), under additional regularity assumptions (continuity of value functions and uniform continuity of the exclusion maps/feasible extensions). It also provides examples where \(K\setminus S\) is infinite yet the algorithm terminates finitely (Example 6.1(i),(ii)), showing that infinitude alone does not preclude convergence. However, it does not prove unconditional convergence for arbitrary nonconvex polynomial NEPs with infinite non-equilibrium KKT points; the result depends on assumptions (notably existence of feasible extensions and continuity conditions) and is formulated for generalized Nash problems with coupling constraints and rational LMEs.

sources.title: Solving polynomial variational inequality problems via Lagrange multiplier expressions and Moment-SOS relaxations
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes Algorithm 3.2 for polynomial variational inequalities VI\((X,F)\) with polynomial feasible set \(X=\{g_i\ge0, g_i=0\}\) under a nonsingularity assumption ensuring polynomial Lagrange multiplier expressions \(\lambda(x)\). Let \(K\) be the semialgebraic set of KKT points expressed purely in \(x\) via LMEs (system (2.8)), and let \(s:=|K\setminus \mathrm{SOL}(X,F)|\). Theorem 3.4 proves: (i) if \(\mathrm{SOL}(X,F)=\emptyset\) and \(s<\infty\), Algorithm 3.2 detects nonexistence in at most \(s+1\) loops; (ii) if \(\mathrm{SOL}(X,F)\neq\emptyset\) and \(s<\infty\), it finds a solution in at most \(s+1\) loops; (iii) if \(s=\infty\) and the algorithm does not finitely terminate, then any accumulation point \(u^*\) of iterates \(u^{(k)}\) is a solution provided the gap function \(\nu(u)=\inf_{y\in X}(y-u)^T F(u)\) is continuous at \(u^*\) and \(\limsup_{k\to\infty}T^{(k)}\) (minimizers of the gap subproblem) is bounded. Additionally, Theorem 3.5 shows that for generic polynomial data \(F,g\), the KKT set \(K\) is finite, implying finite termination generically.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence guarantees of an iterative KKT-point exclusion scheme (Algorithm 3.1 in the Nash equilibrium paper) in the difficult case where there are infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points. This citing paper studies an essentially identical exclusion scheme for nonconvex polynomial VIPs: it repeatedly optimizes a generic strictly convex quadratic over the KKT-feasible set \(K\), checks true VI feasibility via a global gap minimization, and adds separating inequalities \((v-x)^T F(x)\ge0\) to exclude the current non-solution KKT point. Theorem 3.4(iii) directly addresses the infinite-KKT-points regime: it does not prove finite termination, but gives asymptotic convergence of accumulation points to true solutions under extra assumptions (gap-function continuity at the limit point and boundedness of selected minimizers). It also proves finite termination when the number of spurious KKT points is finite, and shows this finiteness holds generically. While the paper is for VIPs rather than Nash equilibria, polynomial Nash equilibria can be formulated as polynomial VIPs (e.g., via Nikaido–Isoda/VI formulations under suitable conditions), so the results provide partial progress and a template of conditions for convergence in the infinite-spurious-KKT setting, but do not fully resolve the Nash-equilibrium-specific open problem in full generality.

sources.title: Solving Imperfect-Recall Games via Sum-of-Squares Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes SOS-based algorithms (following Nie & Tang, 2024) for behavioral Nash equilibria in imperfect-recall extensive-form games by reducing to polynomial games over products of simplices and applying a Select–Verify–Cut (SVC) loop over the joint KKT system. Main guarantee (Theorem 5.1): (i) SVC is asymptotically exact—if a behavioral NE exists, then as the Moment/SOS relaxation order and number of SVC iterations grow, the method returns an NE; otherwise it certifies nonexistence. (ii) Under generic utility coefficients, each SOS subproblem has finite convergence and the SVC loop terminates in finitely many iterations. (iii) In non-absentminded games, a single vertex-restricted selector program suffices; its SOS hierarchy is asymptotically exact and generically finitely convergent.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence of an iterative KKT-point exclusion algorithm (Algorithm 3.1 in Nie–Tang’s polynomial Nash equilibrium paper) in the difficult case where there are infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points. This citing paper studies essentially the same SVC/select-verify-cut paradigm specialized to imperfect-recall extensive-form games (a subclass of polynomial games over products of simplices) and proves asymptotic convergence without requiring finiteness of the non-NE KKT set (Theorem 5.1(i)). It also proves finite termination under a genericity assumption implying the joint KKT system has finitely many solutions (Theorem 5.1(ii)), which excludes the ‘infinitely many KKT points’ regime. Thus it gives partial progress: it provides conditions (generic utilities; or structural NAM case with vertex restrictions) guaranteeing finite termination, and it asserts asymptotic exactness more generally, but it does not resolve the open question of whether the original Algorithm 3.1 necessarily converges when the set of non-equilibrium KKT points is infinite, nor does it provide a counterexample of failure in that regime.

sources.title: Algebraic degrees of generalized Nash equilibrium problems
sources.theorem_or_result: Under genericity assumptions on the defining polynomials of a (generalized) Nash equilibrium problem, the paper proves the Fritz–John system has finitely many complex solutions and, generically, every Fritz–John point is a KKT point (Theorem 3.1). It further gives explicit algebraic-degree formulae counting these complex Fritz–John/KKT points for given active sets and summed over all active sets (Theorems 5.1–5.3), and upper bounds for nongeneric cases (Theorem 5.4).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns convergence/termination of an iterative algorithm that excludes non-equilibrium KKT points when there may be infinitely many such KKT points. This paper does not analyze Algorithm 3.1 or exclusion-based convergence. However, it establishes that for generic polynomial data the set of complex Fritz–John points (hence KKT points) is finite. In such generic regimes, the problematic scenario of infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points cannot occur, and one can bound the number of candidate KKT points that any exclusion-based enumeration method would ever need to consider. For nongeneric data, the paper provides only degree upper bounds when the Fritz–John set is finite, but does not give conditions ensuring finiteness of real KKT points or guarantee that iterative exclusion will reach a Nash equilibrium when infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points exist.

sources.title: On the polyhedral homotopy method for solving generalized Nash equilibrium problems of polynomials
sources.theorem_or_result: Under genericity assumptions (dense generic polynomial data), the complex KKT system for a polynomial GNEP is Bernstein generic, so its mixed volume equals its algebraic degree; consequently polyhedral homotopy continuation can compute all complex KKT tuples, and Algorithm 3.1 then returns all generalized Nash equilibria (or certifies none exist) provided all complex KKT tuples are found (e.g., when the number found equals the mixed volume).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for convergence guarantees of an iterative KKT-point exclusion scheme (Algorithm 3.1 in Nie–Tang’s NEP paper) in the difficult regime where there are infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points. This citing paper proposes a different framework: compute (generically finitely many) complex KKT tuples via polyhedral homotopy, then filter true equilibria by solving best-response polynomial optimizations via Moment-SOS. Their correctness/termination relies on finiteness of the KKT solution set (zero-dimensional KKT system) under genericity; they explicitly note that if there are infinitely many complex KKT points, their method ‘may still find one or more GNEs’ but they do not prove completeness or convergence in that case. Thus it does not resolve the open question about guaranteed convergence/exclusion when the non-equilibrium KKT set is infinite; rather, it provides tools and generic conditions that avoid the infinite-KKT regime.

sources.title: Convex generalized Nash equilibrium problems and polynomial optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For convex generalized Nash equilibrium problems with polynomial data (GNEPPs), the paper gives a polynomial-optimization reformulation of the GNE conditions using rational or parametric expressions for KKT multipliers, and proves convergence/correctness of a Moment-SOS based algorithm: under standard constraint qualifications ensuring every GNE is a KKT point and under positivity of the multiplier-expression denominators (or using parametric expressions), solving the resulting polynomial optimization (via the Moment-SOS hierarchy) returns a generalized Nash equilibrium if one exists, or certifies nonexistence when the KKT-feasible set is empty (Theorems 5.2, 5.4, 5.6).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns a nonconvex polynomial NEP algorithm (Algorithm 3.1 in Nie–Tang’s NEP paper) that iteratively excludes non-equilibrium KKT points by adding best-response inequalities, and asks for convergence guarantees or counterexamples when there are infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points. The citing paper does not analyze that nonconvex exclusion scheme. Instead it treats convex polynomial GNEPs, where KKT points are already equilibria, so the ‘infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points’ pathology cannot occur in the same way. It does, however, develop closely related machinery (rational/parametric multiplier expressions; Moment-SOS solution of KKT polynomial systems; uniqueness via generic quadratic objective) and explicitly states that extending the exclusion idea to nonconvex GNEPs/NEPs and detecting nonexistence when the KKT system is feasible are open (Section 7). Thus it provides tools and partial conceptual guidance but not a convergence proof for the nonconvex iterative KKT-point exclusion algorithm.

sources.title: Nash Equilibrium Problems of Polynomials
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes Algorithm 3.1 for computing Nash equilibria of polynomial Nash equilibrium problems (NEPPs) via Moment-SOS relaxations and iterative exclusion of non-equilibrium KKT points, and proves finite termination when the set of non-equilibrium KKT points is finite: if \(G\) is the KKT-feasible set of (3.7) and \(G^*\) the set of Nash equilibria, then if \(|G\setminus G^*|<\infty\), Algorithm 3.1 terminates in at most \(|G\setminus G^*|\) loops (Theorem 3.2). Under genericity assumptions on the polynomial data, the KKT system has finitely many complex solutions (Theorem A.1), hence Algorithm 3.1 terminates finitely and either finds an NE or detects nonexistence (Theorem 3.3). The paper explicitly states that convergence of Algorithm 3.1 is not understood when there are infinitely many non-equilibrium KKT points (Section 6).
sources.connection: This citing paper is the source of the open problem: it proves convergence/finite termination only under finiteness of \(G\setminus G^*\) (or genericity implying finitely many KKT points), and it explicitly leaves open the case where there are infinitely many KKT points that are not Nash equilibria. It provides an example (Example 5.2(ii)) where infinitely many non-NE KKT points exist yet Algorithm 3.1 still finds an NE quickly, but it does not give general conditions guaranteeing convergence nor a counterexample showing failure. title: Determine the asymptotically tight constant for traveling repairman latency under i.i.d. sampling
background_latex:
Let \(K\subset \mathbb{R}^2\) be a compact set, and let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. random points drawn from a distribution on \(K\) whose absolutely continuous part has density \(f\) (with respect to Lebesgue measure).

Given a realization \(V=\{X_1,\dots,X_n\}\), a (repairman) tour is an ordering \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) of the points, interpreted as the sequence in which they are visited, together with travel at unit speed along straight-line (Euclidean) segments.

For an ordering \(x_1,\dots,x_n\), define the latency (waiting time) of the \(i\)-th visited point \(x_i\) as
\[
\ell_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \|x_{j+1}-x_j\|,
\]
with the convention \(\ell_1=0\). The traveling repairman problem (TRP), also called the minimum latency problem, minimizes the total latency
\[
L_{\mathrm{TRP}}(x_1,\dots,x_n) := \sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i 
= \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} (n-i)\,\|x_{i+1}-x_i\|.
\]
Let \(l_{\mathrm{TRP}}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) denote the optimal value (minimum) of \(L_{\mathrm{TRP}}\) over all orderings.

For comparison, the Euclidean traveling salesman problem (TSP) tour length on \(V\), denoted \(l_{\mathrm{TSP}}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), is the minimum over cyclic tours of the total Euclidean length. Under i.i.d. sampling, the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley (BHH) theorem implies
\[
\frac{l_{\mathrm{TSP}}(X_1,\dots,X_n)}{\sqrt{n}} \to \beta_{\mathrm{TSP}} \int_K \sqrt{f(x)}\,dx
\quad \text{a.s.}
\]
for a universal constant \(\beta_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether the constant \(\beta_{\mathrm{TSP}}\) is the asymptotically tight constant governing the leading-order growth of the expected optimal TRP total latency.

Concretely, decide whether one has an asymptotic equivalence of the form
\[
\mathbb{E}\bigl[l_{\mathrm{TRP}}(X_1,\dots,X_n)\bigr] \sim \beta_{\mathrm{TSP}}\, n\sqrt{n}\, \iint_{K\times K} g_f(x,y)\,dx\,dy
\quad \text{as } n\to\infty,
\]
(or an equivalent characterization with leading constant \(\beta_{\mathrm{TSP}}\)), where \(g_f\) is the distribution-dependent integrand used to express the TRP scaling in constant-factor bounds.

Equivalently, determine the exact leading universal constant in the \(\Theta(n\sqrt{n})\) asymptotics for \(\mathbb{E}[l_{\mathrm{TRP}}]\), and whether it matches the TSP constant \(\beta_{\mathrm{TSP}}\).

title: Existence of epsilon-equilibria in multiplayer stochastic games with Borel payoffs
background_latex:
A (multiplayer) stochastic game is a tuple \(\Gamma=(I,S,(A_i)_{i\in I},p,(f_i)_{i\in I})\) where:
1) \(I\) is a finite nonempty set of players.
2) \(S\) is a finite or countably infinite set of states.
3) For each \(i\in I\), \(A_i\) is a finite nonempty action set; write \(A:=\prod_{i\in I} A_i\).
4) \(p:S\times A\to \Delta(S)\) is a transition kernel; when the current state is \(s\in S\) and action profile \(a\in A\) is played, the next state \(s'\in S\) is drawn according to \(p(\cdot\mid s,a)\).
5) A run (infinite play) is an infinite sequence \(r=(s_1,a_1,s_2,a_2,\dots)\in (S\times A)^\infty\) consistent with \(p\); let \(R\) denote the set of all runs. Each \(f_i:R\to\mathbb{R}\) is bounded and Borel-measurable (with respect to the product topology on \((S\times A)^\infty\) and the induced Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(R\)).

A (behavior) strategy for player \(i\) is a mapping \(\sigma_i:H\to\Delta(A_i)\), where \(H\) is the set of all finite histories \((s_1,a_1,\dots,s_n)\) consistent with \(p\). A strategy profile is \(\sigma=(\sigma_i)_{i\in I}\). For each initial state \(s\in S\) and strategy profile \(\sigma\), the induced probability measure on runs is denoted \(\mathbb{P}_{s,\sigma}\) and expectation \(\mathbb{E}_{s,\sigma}\).

For \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), a strategy profile \(\sigma^*\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium (Nash equilibrium with additive \(\varepsilon\)-slack) if for every initial state \(s\in S\), every player \(i\in I\), and every alternative strategy \(\sigma_i\),
\[\mathbb{E}_{s,\sigma^*}[f_i]\ge \mathbb{E}_{s,(\sigma_i,\sigma^*_{-i})}[f_i]-\varepsilon.\]
Equivalently, no player can improve expected payoff by more than \(\varepsilon\) via a unilateral deviation, from any specified initial state.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem in Flesch--Solan (2024) asks whether every multiplayer stochastic game with finite actions, finite or countable state space, and bounded Borel payoff functions admits an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium that works for every initial state. The paper itself highlights that while Martin/Maitra--Sudderth style “Martin functions” can be generalized to the multiplayer setting, the resulting existence theorems stop short of full Nash existence: they yield (i) subgame \(\varepsilon\)-maxmin strategies for each player, (ii) minmax \(\varepsilon\)-acceptable profiles (individual rationality in every subgame), (iii) extensive-form correlated \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria, and (iv) existence of an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium in some subgame (an \(\varepsilon\)-solvable subgame), but not an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium simultaneously for all initial states.

Forward-citing work provides partial progress in restricted models. “Equilibrium in two-player stochastic games with shift-invariant payoffs” extends the Martin-function approach to obtain \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria for all initial states in two-player finite-state games under the additional structural assumption of shift-invariant (prefix-independent) Borel payoffs, adapting Vieille-style reductions and using determinacy and deviation-detection ideas. On the multiplayer side, “Regularity of the minmax value and equilibria in multiplayer Blackwell games” develops regularity/approximation results for minmax values with Borel (or upper semi-analytic) payoffs and proves \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium existence in multiplayer Blackwell games under strong hypotheses such as history-independent minmax values; these results suggest that controlling the history dependence of \(v_i(h)\) is a key obstruction.

Several papers contribute tools rather than full existence theorems. “Identifying the deviator” supplies a general Borel-measurable deviation-identification mechanism that underpins detection-and-punishment constructions, which are needed in Flesch--Solan’s \(\varepsilon\)-solvable subgame result and in related equilibrium proofs for tail/shift-invariant objectives. Classical determinacy results (“Borel games” and determinacy for constrained Blackwell games) remain foundational for the zero-sum components and approximation arguments but do not by themselves resolve multiplayer Nash existence with Nature. Overall, the general statement remains open; current techniques either require two players, additional payoff structure (tail/shift invariance), or extra regularity assumptions ensuring stable minmax behavior across subgames.

sources.title: Equilibrium in two-player stochastic games with shift-invariant payoffs
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves: every two-player stochastic game with finite state and action sets and bounded, Borel-measurable, shift-invariant payoff functions admits an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium for every \(\varepsilon>0\) (Theorem 2.20).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in multiplayer stochastic games with bounded Borel payoffs (finite actions; finite or countable states), uniformly for all initial states. This paper addresses a significant special case: it establishes existence for two-player (nonzero-sum) stochastic games with finite state/action sets under the additional structural assumption that payoffs are shift-invariant (prefix-independent). It does not treat (i) more than two players, (ii) general Borel payoffs without shift-invariance, or (iii) countably infinite state spaces; the authors explicitly note the countable-state extension is open and discuss obstacles. Thus it provides partial progress and new techniques (e.g., deviation detection using inner regularity and Lévy’s zero-one law) that may be relevant for broader cases.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves existence of \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria for certain classes of multiplayer Blackwell games (simultaneous-move, no Nature) with general measurable payoffs. In particular (Theorem 4.3): if each player has finite action sets at every history, payoffs \(f_i\) are bounded and upper semi-analytic, and each player’s minmax value \(v_i(f_i)\) is history-independent across subgames, then for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the game admits an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium. It also proves (Theorem 3.1) regularity of the minmax for Borel winning sets: \(v_i(W)=\sup\{v_i(C): C\subseteq W\text{ closed}\}=\inf\{v_i(O): O\supseteq W\text{ open}\}\), and (Theorem 3.3) approximation of \(v_i(f)\) for bounded Borel \(f\) by bounded limsup functions from below/above.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in *multiplayer stochastic games with Nature* (state space finite/countable, finite actions) for *arbitrary bounded Borel payoffs*, uniformly for every initial state. This paper works in the Blackwell-game model (simultaneous moves on a game tree) without an explicit stochastic transition kernel; it proves \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria only under additional structural assumptions—most notably history-independence of each player’s minmax value (Theorem 4.3), or a strong condition on analytic winning sets plus \(\sum_i v_i(W_i)>n-1\) (Theorem 4.1). Thus it does not resolve the general existence question for all Borel payoffs in stochastic games. However, it contributes relevant tools (regularity/approximation of minmax) and yields existence for important subclasses (e.g., tail-measurable payoffs imply history-independent minmax, giving \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in that subclass). The authors explicitly list extending these methods to stochastic games with Nature as an open direction.

sources.theorem_or_result: Main general result: For any finite player set with finite action sets, any prescribed behavior-strategy profile \(\sigma^*\) and any Borel target set \(D\subseteq A^{\mathbb N}\) with \(\mathbb P_{\sigma^*}(D)=1\), there exists a Borel blame function \(f:D^c\to I\) such that for every player \(i\) and every unilateral deviation strategy \(\sigma_i\), \(\mathbb P_{\sigma_i,\sigma^*_{-i}}(D^c\cap\{f\neq i\})=0\) (Theorem 2.9). More generally, if \(\mathbb P_{\sigma^*}(D)>1-\varepsilon\), then \((\sigma^*,D)\) is \(\delta\)-testable with \(\delta\le 2\sqrt{(|I|-1)\varepsilon}\) (Theorem 2.6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in multiplayer stochastic games with countable states and bounded Borel payoffs, uniformly for every initial state. This paper does not construct equilibria or prove existence in that generality. Instead it proves a deviation-identification ("blame") theorem for repeated-action processes: whenever a prescribed strategy profile \(\sigma^*\) achieves a Borel target event \(D\) with probability 1 (or high probability), there is a Borel rule that, upon observing failure of \(D\), identifies a unique deviator with zero (or small) error probability against any unilateral deviation. Such identification is a key ingredient in equilibrium constructions based on detection-and-punishment. The authors explicitly note applications: an alternative proof of \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium existence in repeated games with tail-measurable payoffs, and (citing Flesch–Solan 2023b) existence of an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium in some subgame for finite-state stochastic games with bounded Borel payoffs. However, the paper itself does not resolve the full open problem (notably it does not address countably infinite state spaces, nor guarantee an \(\varepsilon\)-equilibrium for every initial state in the original game).

sources.title: Borel games
sources.theorem_or_result: Main theorem (Martin 1975): every two-player perfect-information infinite game with a Borel winning set is determined; i.e., for any Borel set \(A\subseteq \mathbb{N}^\omega\) (equivalently Borel subset of the play space), one of the two players has a winning strategy in the corresponding Gale–Stewart game \(G(A)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of \(\varepsilon\)-Nash equilibria in multiplayer stochastic games with bounded Borel-measurable payoffs. Martin’s Borel determinacy concerns zero-sum, two-player, perfect-information win/lose games (no stochastic transitions, no simultaneous moves, no multi-player Nash equilibrium). It does not directly imply \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in general stochastic games, but it is a foundational descriptive-set-theoretic result often used to justify measurability/selection and value/determinacy statements for Borel objectives in certain two-player (especially turn-based) game models, which can be ingredients in equilibrium-existence proofs for restricted classes (e.g., zero-sum or perfect-information settings).

sources.title: The Determinacy of Blackwell Games with a Constraint Function
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves determinacy for a class of two-player zero-sum Blackwell games (simultaneous moves, perfect monitoring) with Borel payoff of restricted complexity: if the payoff is the indicator of a \,\(G_{\delta\sigma}\) set \(S\subseteq (X\times Y)^\mathbb{N}\) (with \(X,Y\) finite), then the Blackwell game \(\Gamma(S)\) is determined (Theorem 3.10). It also proves determinacy for open sets (Corollary 3.2), \(G_\delta\) sets (Corollary 3.9), and continuous payoff functions (Corollary 3.4), and develops a truncation/approximation method via nested equivalent truncated subgames (Section 2.3, Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.7).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for existence of \(\varepsilon\)-Nash equilibria in general multiplayer stochastic games with countable states and bounded Borel payoffs. This paper addresses a different but adjacent existence question: \(\varepsilon\)-determinacy (value existence) in two-player zero-sum simultaneous-move infinite games (Blackwell games) for certain Borel payoff classes (up to \(G_{\delta\sigma}\), plus continuous). Determinacy in such zero-sum games is related in spirit to equilibrium existence, and the truncation/nested-subgame approximation techniques could be relevant tools for proving \(\varepsilon\)-equilibria in stochastic games. However, it does not treat multiplayer nonzero-sum Nash equilibria, does not handle general Borel payoffs (explicitly states that case remains open for Blackwell games), and does not incorporate a state-based stochastic transition kernel as in stochastic games.

title: Verify sharp growth constant for max-linear regression with absolute loss setting
background_latex:
Let \(a_1,\dots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be given measurement vectors and let \(\bar y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) be given observations. For an integer \(r\ge 1\), define parameters \(\beta=(\beta_1,\dots,\beta_r)\) with \(\beta_j\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Define the max-linear predictor
\[
\hat y_i(\beta):=\max_{j\in\{1,\dots,r\}}\langle \beta_j,a_i\rangle,\qquad i=1,\dots,m.
\]
Consider the nonsmooth objective
\[
f(\beta):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m \bigl|\bar y_i-\hat y_i(\beta)\bigr|.
\]
Let \(f^*:=\inf_{\beta} f(\beta)\) and \(X^*:=\operatorname{argmin} f\) denote the optimal value and set of minimizers (assumed nonempty). For \(x\) in a Euclidean space, \(\mathrm{dist}(x,X^*):=\inf_{z\in X^*}\|x-z\|\).

\[
f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\qquad\text{for all }\beta\in U
\]
holds for the max-linear regression objective \(f\) defined above.

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem from Charisopoulos--Davis asks for verifiable conditions ensuring local sharp growth \(f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\) for max-linear regression with absolute loss. In the source paper, sharp growth (Assumption (A1)) is the key regularity enabling linear convergence of Polyak-type subgradient steps and, when combined with (b)-regularity/semismoothness (Assumption (A2)), yields the superlinear improvement mechanism of PolyakBundle and the SuperPolyak scheme. The max-linear absolute-loss objective is semialgebraic and piecewise linear (hence semismooth/(b)-regular is plausible), but the missing ingredient is precisely (A1): a data/model-dependent error bound constant \(\mu\) near \(X^*\).

Forward-citing work largely develops algorithmic and variational-analytic frameworks that take growth/error bounds as assumptions rather than proving them for the max-linear regression model. Gebken's Goldstein-subdifferential analyses provide quantitative consequences of sharp (\(p=1\)) or higher-order growth combined with semismoothness-type properties, translating approximate criticality into distance-to-solution bounds; these results would become directly applicable once sharp growth is established for the regression objective. Trust-region and higher-order cutting-plane/bundle papers similarly show that sharp growth (or quadratic growth under nondegeneracy) implies strong local decrease properties and superlinear convergence of serious steps for finite max-type functions, again emphasizing the value of proving \(\mu>0\) for the target model.

Overall, none of the analyzed forward citations appears to settle the model-specific sharp growth verification for max-linear regression with \(\ell_1\) loss; the problem therefore remains open in the sense posed by the source paper. Promising directions suggested by the surrounding literature are to (i) exploit the piecewise-linear structure to reduce sharp growth to a polyhedral error bound (e.g., via metric subregularity of a KKT/normal-map system), and (ii) identify nondegeneracy conditions on the active max-indices and residual signs at \(\bar\beta\) that rule out flat directions (ensuring a positive linear growth modulus).

sources.title: Analyzing the speed of convergence in nonsmooth optimization via the Goldstein subdifferential with application to descent methods
sources.theorem_or_result: Main result (Theorem 1, as described in the provided excerpt): Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz and let \(x^*\) be a minimizer at which \(f\) satisfies a \(p\)-order growth condition (i.e., \(f(x)-f(x^*)\ge c\|x-x^*\|^p\) locally for some \(c>0\)) and a corresponding \(p\)-order semismoothness property at \(x^*\). If \(x_j\to x^*\), \(\varepsilon_j\to 0\), \(\delta_j\to 0\), and \(\min\|\partial_{\varepsilon_j} f(x_j)\|\le \delta_j\) (\((\varepsilon_j,\delta_j)\)-criticality), then there exists \(M>0\) such that \(\|x_j-x^*\|\le \max\{M\varepsilon_j^{1/p},\, M\delta_j^{1/(p-1)}\}\) (with the \(p=1\) “sharp minimum” case treated separately, where standard semismoothness suffices).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to verify a local sharp growth/error bound \(f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\) for a specific max-linear regression objective with absolute loss. Gebken (2025) does not analyze this statistical model or prove such an error bound for max-linear regression. Instead, it develops abstract relationships between \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-criticality (via the Goldstein \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential) and distance to a minimizer under assumed \(p\)-order growth (including the sharp \(p=1\) case) plus semismoothness-type conditions. Thus, the paper is relevant as a framework: if one can establish the desired sharp growth (\(p=1\)) for the max-linear absolute-loss objective (and verify semismoothness/piecewise differentiability, which is plausible for max/abs compositions), then the paper’s results can be used to quantify how quickly approximate Goldstein-critical points approach \(X^*\). But it does not provide the missing verification of \(\mu>0\) for that model.
