sources.theorem_or_result: Main abstract result (Theorem 5.1): Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz and let \(x_j\to x^*\), \(\varepsilon_j\to0\), with \(\|g_{\varepsilon_j}(x_j)\|\le \delta_j\), where \(g_{\varepsilon}(x)\) is the minimum-norm element of the Goldstein \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential \(\partial_{\varepsilon} f(x)\). Assume \(x^*\) is a local minimizer of order \(p\in\mathbb N\): \(f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\beta\|x-x^*\|^p\) locally, and a higher-order semismoothness-type condition (7): \[\liminf_{\xi\in\partial f(x^*+t d'),\ t\downarrow0,\ d'\to d}\ \frac{\langle \xi,d'\rangle}{t^{p-1}}\ge \beta\|d\|^p\quad\forall d\ne0.\] Then for \(p\ge2\) there exist \(M,N\) with \(\|x_j-x^*\|\le M\max(\varepsilon_j^{1/p},\delta_j^{1/(p-1)})\) for all \(j>N\); for \(p=1\) and \(\delta_j\to\bar\delta<\beta\), \(\|x_j-x^*\|\le M\varepsilon_j\) eventually. The paper also gives sufficient conditions for (7) for piecewise \(p\)-times \(C^p\) functions under a higher-order convexity condition (Lemma 4.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring a local sharp growth/error bound \(f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\) for the max-linear absolute-loss objective. This paper does not analyze that specific statistical model or objective, and it does not prove such an error bound for max-linear regression. However, it develops general theory linking (i) a linear growth/sharp minimum condition (the case \(p=1\) in Definition 3.1) and (ii) a semismoothness-type property to quantitative bounds on proximity to the minimizer from approximate criticality in the Goldstein \(\varepsilon\)-subdifferential. If one can establish the desired sharp growth for the max-linear absolute-loss objective (i.e., show it has a sharp minimum / order-1 growth around \(X^*\)), then the paper’s framework becomes applicable for analyzing convergence of Goldstein/gradient-sampling-type methods on that objective. The paper also provides verification tools for (7)/(8) for piecewise smooth max-type functions, which is structurally related to max-linear predictors, but it does not carry out the verification for the absolute-loss composition \(\sum_i |\bar y_i-\max_j\langle\beta_j,a_i\rangle|\).

sources.title: Enclosing minima in nonsmooth optimization via trust regions of higher-order cutting-plane models
sources.theorem_or_result:
For finite max-type functions \(f(x)=\max_{s\in S} f_s(x)\) (with \(S\) finite and \(f_s\in C^{q+1}\)), the paper proves that a trust-region decrease property (P) holds near a minimizer \(x^*\) under sharp growth (order \(p=1\)) or, under additional nondegeneracy assumptions, quadratic growth (order \(p=2\)). In particular:
- Theorem 4.1: If \(f\) has sharp growth around \(x^*\), i.e. \(f(x)\ge f(x^*)+\beta\|x-x^*\|\) locally, then (P) holds for \(p=1\).
- Theorem 4.2: If \(f\) has quadratic growth around \(x^*\) and satisfies Assumption (B2) (finite \(S\), full activity \(A(x^*)=S\) with strictly positive multiplier, affine independence of \(\nabla f_s(x^*)\)), then (P) holds for \(p=2\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring a local sharp growth/error bound \(f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\) for the max-linear regression objective with absolute loss. This paper does not analyze that statistical model or this specific objective. However, it develops general theory for finite max-type objectives: it shows that if one can establish sharp growth (order-1 growth) for a finite max-type function, then a related trust-region decrease property (P) follows (Thm. 4.1). Thus it provides a methodological bridge: proving sharp growth for the regression objective (or a reformulation as finite max-type) would imply (P), which their algorithm uses to generate shrinking trust regions containing the minimizer. The paper does not provide conditions on \(a_i,\bar y\) or on the max-linear absolute-loss structure that guarantee sharp growth, nor does it verify an explicit \(\mu\) for that problem.

sources.title: Superlinear convergence in nonsmooth optimization via higher-order cutting-plane models
sources.theorem_or_result: For a lower-C\(^2\) function \(f\) with a fixed global max-representation \(f(x)=\max_{s\in S} f_s(x)\) (Assumption (A1)) and a polynomial growth condition near a minimizer \(x^*\), the authors define the \(q\)-th order cutting-plane model \(T_{q,W}(z)=\max_{y\in W} T_q f_{s(y)}(z,y)\) and prove a Taylor-type uniform error bound on a trust region: for bounded \(V\subset U\) and \(\bar B_{\varepsilon}(x)\subset U\), there exists \(K\ge 0\) such that \(\max_{z\in \bar B_{\varepsilon}(x)} |f_W(z)-T_{q,W}(z)|\le K\varepsilon^{q+1}\) (Lemma 3.1). Using these higher-order max-models in a trust-region bundle framework yields local R-superlinear convergence of serious steps (and, for certain finite max-type functions, superlinear convergence of the overall sequence).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring a local sharp growth/error bound \(f(\beta)-f^*\ge \mu\,\mathrm{dist}(\beta,X^*)\) for the specific max-linear regression objective with absolute loss. This paper does not analyze that statistical objective or establish sharp growth for it. Instead, it develops higher-order cutting-plane (max-of-Taylor) models and proves superlinear convergence of a trust-region bundle method under an assumed growth condition (polynomial growth) for general lower-\u0002C\(^2\) max-type functions. Thus it is relevant mainly as methodology: if one could verify a sharp (linear) growth/error bound for the max-linear absolute-loss regression objective, then the papers framework suggests how to exploit such growth to obtain fast local convergence with appropriate bundle/trust-region methods.

The paper develops a globalized semismooth Newton framework for composite problems \(\min_x F(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) with \(f\in C^{2}\) having Lipschitz \(
abla f,

Using this, they define the proximal-gradient residual \(R_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}(x-P_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma

Under an additional metric subregularity (error bound) assumption on \(R_*\) at a local minimizer \(x^*\), they prove local superlinear convergence of \(\mathrm{dist}(y_k,X^*)\) (Theorem 5.1).

Our algorithm, as well as all prior work on (RO-)OCRS for matching constraints, works with the degree-bounded relaxation for matchings, which is integral for bipartite graphs, but not for general ones. A natural question is whether better (RO-)OCRS can be achieved for points in the matching polytope, i.e., points which also satisfy Edmonds’ odd-set constraints [Edm65]. Can better bounds be achieved for this polytope, perhaps via a different algorithmic approach?
title: Improve contention resolution for points in the exact matching polytope setting
background_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an (undirected) graph. A (fractional) vector \(x\in[0,1]^E\) assigns a value \(x_e\) to each edge \(e\in E\). The (degree-bounded) matching relaxation is
\[P(G):=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^E: \sum_{e\ni v} x_e\le 1\ \forall v\in V\Bigr\}.
\]
The (integral) matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^E\) is the convex hull of incidence vectors of matchings in \(G\). Edmonds' characterization gives
\[\mathrm{MP}(G)=\Bigl\{x\in P(G): \sum_{e\subseteq S} x_e \le \frac{|S|-1}{2}\ \forall S\subseteq V\ \text{with }|S|\text{ odd}\Bigr\},
\]
where \(\sum_{e\subseteq S}\) denotes the sum over edges with both endpoints in \(S\) (the odd-set constraints).

A random-order online contention resolution scheme (RO-OCRS) for matchings takes as input a fractional point \(x\) (typically in some polytope such as \(P(G)\) or \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\)). Then edges arrive online in a uniformly random order. Each edge \(e\) is independently declared active with probability \(x_e\). Upon seeing an active edge \(e\), the scheme must irrevocably accept it into the output set \(I\) or reject it, while maintaining that \(I\) is a matching.

A RO-OCRS is called \(c\)-balanced if for every graph \(G\), every feasible input point \(x\), and every edge \(e\in E\), the output matching \(I\) satisfies
\[\Pr[e\in I]\ge c\,x_e.
\]
Here probability is over the scheme’s internal randomness, the random arrival order, and the independent activations.

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an (undirected) graph. A (fractional) vector \(x\in[0,1]^E\) assigns a value \(x_e\) to each edge \(e\in E\). The (degree-bounded) matching relaxation is
\[P(G):=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^E: \sum_{e\ni v} x_e\le 1\ \forall v\in V\Bigr\}.
\]
The (integral) matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^E\) is the convex hull of incidence vectors of matchings in \(G\). Edmonds' characterization gives
\[\mathrm{MP}(G)=\Bigl\{x\in P(G): \sum_{e\subseteq S} x_e \le \frac{|S|-1}{2}\ \forall S\subseteq V\ \text{with }|S|\text{ odd}\Bigr\},
\]
where \(\sum_{e\subseteq S}\) denotes the sum over edges with both endpoints in \(S\) (the odd-set constraints).

A random-order online contention resolution scheme (RO-OCRS) for matchings takes as input a fractional point \(x\) (typically in some polytope such as \(P(G)\) or \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\)). Then edges arrive online in a uniformly random order. Each edge \(e\) is independently declared active with probability \(x_e\). Upon seeing an active edge \(e\), the scheme must irrevocably accept it into the output set \(I\) or reject it, while maintaining that \(I\) is a matching.

A RO-OCRS is called \(c\)-balanced if for every graph \(G\), every feasible input point \(x\), and every edge \(e\in E\), the output matching \(I\) satisfies
\[\Pr[e\in I]\ge c\,x_e.
\]
Here probability is over the scheme’s internal randomness, the random arrival order, and the independent activations.

Determine whether there exists a constant \(c>0.456\) and a (polynomial-time) RO-OCRS for matchings that is \(c\)-balanced when the input fractional point \(x\) is restricted to lie in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) (i.e., satisfies both degree constraints and Edmonds' odd-set constraints). More generally, determine the best achievable balance factor
\[c^*:=\sup\{c: \exists\ \text{a (polytime) RO-OCRS that is }c\text{-balanced for all }G\text{ and all }x\in \mathrm{MP}(G)\}.
\]
open_problem_quote: Our algorithm, as well as all prior work on (RO-)OCRS for matching constraints, works with the degree-bounded relaxation for matchings, which is integral for bipartite graphs, but not for general ones. A natural question is whether better (RO-)OCRS can be achieved for points in the matching polytope, i.e., points which also satisfy Edmonds’ odd-set constraints [Edm65]. Can better bounds be achieved for this polytope, perhaps via a different algorithmic approach?
counterexample_suitability_rationale: One can computationally search for small graphs and fractional points in the matching polytope that appear hard for candidate RO-OCRS policies, but the space of online policies is large and proving optimal lower bounds is difficult. Still, testing specific algorithms and generating adversarial instances is feasible via simulation and optimization over small graphs.
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: Candidate RO-OCRS policies (e.g., parametric attenuation/priority rules) can be represented as code with tunable parameters, and their worst-case (or empirically minimized) balancedness can be estimated by Monte Carlo over random orders and by adversarial search over small graphs and fractional inputs. This provides an automatic fitness signal (estimated minimum \(\Pr[e\in I]/x_e\)) enabling iterative improvement or discovery of counterexamples to proposed designs.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Pollner–Roghani–Saberi–Wajc (2022), the state of the art for random-order online contention resolution for matchings under independent edge activations is a \(0.45\)-balanced RO-OCRS for general graphs and \(0.456\)-balanced for bipartite graphs, analyzed for inputs \(x\in P(G)\) (degree constraints only). The paper explicitly raises the stronger question of whether restricting inputs to the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\)—i.e., additionally enforcing Edmonds’ odd-set constraints—permits a better balance factor, asking in particular whether one can beat \(0.456\) in this more structured setting.

The forward-citing literature summarized here does not resolve that question. The most directly relevant progress is indirect: “Towards an Optimal Contention” improves constants for offline CRSs for matchings (exceeding \(0.5\) in bipartite graphs and approaching the Karp–Sipser barrier \(\approx 0.544\) in a sparse regime for general graphs), but it neither operates online in random order nor leverages odd-set constraints. “Stationary Online Contention Resolution Schemes” develops a principled framework for permutation-invariant (stationary) OCRSs and proves constants \(1/3\) (general graphs) and \(\approx 0.382\) (bipartite) within that restricted class, suggesting that any improvement beyond \(0.456\) will require non-stationary behavior and/or new uses of polyhedral structure.

Several related-tool papers (on online dependent rounding, SOCS, and probe-commit/configuration-LP approaches) demonstrate that stronger per-edge guarantees are achievable in other online matching models by combining richer rounding primitives (negative dependence, type decompositions, configuration LPs) with local contention resolution. However, none of these works provides a random-order edge-arrival OCRS with \(\Pr[e\in I]\ge c x_e\) for all \(x\in\mathrm{MP}(G)\), nor do they quantify how odd-set constraints might be exploited to surpass the \(0.456\) barrier. Thus, based on the provided forward citations, the problem remains open; a promising direction is to design RO-OCRSs whose acceptance/attenuation decisions depend on odd-set structure (e.g., via laminar odd-cut decompositions or blossom-based online certificates) rather than only local degree slack, potentially bridging the gap between online constants (\(\approx 0.456\)) and offline benchmarks (\(>0.5\)).

sources.title: Towards an Optimal Contention
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives improved contention resolution schemes (CRSs) for matchings under independent edge sampling from a fractional matching. In particular:
- For bipartite graphs and any fractional matching satisfying only vertex constraints \(\sum_{e\ni v} x_e\le 1\), it constructs an offline (non-monotone) CRS with \(\Pr[e\in M\mid e\in R(x)]\ge 0.509\) for all edges \(e\) (Theorem 2 / Theorem 5).
- For general graphs, assuming \(\|x\|_\infty\le \varepsilon\) and \(\sum_{e\ni v}x_e=1\) for all \(v\), it gives a CRS with balance \(\gamma-f(\varepsilon)\) where \(\gamma=2(1-\lambda)-\lambda^2\approx 0.544\) and \(\lambda=e^{-\lambda}\) (Theorem 1 / Theorem 3).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a random-order online OCRS with balance \(c>0.456\) when the input \(x\) lies in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) (i.e., includes odd-set constraints), and more generally the best achievable \(c^*\) in that setting.

This paper is primarily about offline CRSs (not online, not random-order online), and it does not exploit the odd-set constraints of \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\); in fact it states its results assuming only the degree constraints \(\sum_{e\ni v}x_e\le 1\), which is a superset of \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\). Therefore it does not resolve the online question nor determine \(c^*\) for RO-OCRS on \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\).

However, it is strongly relevant as partial progress/upper-envelope context: it shows that offline balancedness can exceed 0.5 (0.509 for bipartite) and can approach the Karp–Sipser barrier \(\approx 0.544\) for general graphs under \(\|x\|_\infty\to 0\). These results sharpen the landscape in which the RO-OCRS-for-\(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) problem sits, and they suggest that any online scheme is inherently weaker (they emphasize separations between offline and random-order online factors for bipartite matchings).

sources.title: Online dependent rounding schemes for bipartite matchings, with applications
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces online dependent rounding schemes (ODRSes) for online bipartite matchings/b-matchings with per-edge guarantee \(\Pr[e\in M]\ge \alpha x_e\). Main theorem (Theorem 1.2 / 3.9–3.10): there exists a (polytime, up to \(\gamma\)) bipartite matching ODRS with rounding ratio \(\alpha\approx 0.652\) (and \(0.646\) for b-matchings), breaking the \(1-1/e\) barrier for unrestricted fractional matchings \(x\in P(G)\) in the one-sided online-vertex-arrival model.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a random-order online contention resolution scheme (RO-OCRS) for general (not necessarily bipartite) matchings with balance factor \(c>0.456\) when the input \(x\) lies in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) (i.e., includes odd-set constraints). This paper studies a different online rounding model (ODRS) for bipartite graphs under adversarial one-sided vertex arrivals, and it targets unrestricted fractional matchings \(x\in P(G)\) (degree constraints only). It achieves a much larger constant (0.652) but does not address random-order edge arrivals, does not handle general graphs/nonbipartite matchings, and does not exploit/require \(x\in \mathrm{MP}(G)\) with odd-set constraints. Thus it does not solve the stated RO-OCRS-for-\(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) problem, but it provides partial progress in the broader landscape of online rounding/CRS for matchings by introducing new techniques (grouping + offline CRS, negative dependence) that might inspire improved RO-OCRS analyses.

sources.title: Stationary Online Contention Resolution Schemes
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces stationary OCRSs (S-OCRSs) and gives explicit selectability guarantees for several feasibility systems. For matchings in general graphs (i.e., the degree-bounded relaxation), it proves existence of a \(1/3\)-selectable S-OCRS (Theorem 1). For bipartite matchings (where \(P(G)=\mathrm{MP}(G)\)), it proves an \(\alpha^*\)-selectable S-OCRS with \(\alpha^*=(3-\sqrt5)/2\approx0.382\), and shows this is optimal within the stationary class (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether one can beat \(0.456\) for random-order OCRSs when the input \(x\) lies in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) (non-bipartite, with odd-set constraints). This paper does not analyze the \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) setting for general graphs; its matching results for non-bipartite graphs assume only the degree constraints \(x\in P(G)\) and achieve \(1/3\), far below \(0.456\). It does obtain \(\approx0.382\) for bipartite matchings, but bipartite graphs already satisfy \(\mathrm{MP}(G)=P(G)\) and the constant is still below \(0.456\). Thus it does not resolve the question of improving beyond \(0.456\) for \(x\in\mathrm{MP}(G)\) in general graphs; it provides related techniques (stationary/maximum-entropy/Gibbs) and partial progress in special environments.

sources.title: Prophet matching in the probe-commit model
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives online algorithms for bipartite stochastic matching in the probe-commit model with downward-closed probing constraints, achieving competitive ratios against the offline adaptive benchmark: (i) 
\[\mathbb{E}[w(M(\pi))] \ge \tfrac12\,\mathrm{OPT}(H_{\mathrm{typ}},(D_i)_{i=1}^n)\]
for adversarial arrival order \(\pi\) (Theorem 1), and (ii)
\[\mathbb{E}[w(M)] \ge (1-1/e)\,\mathrm{OPT}(H_{\mathrm{typ}},(D_i)_{i=1}^n)\]
for uniformly random arrival order (Theorem 3). The analysis uses a configuration LP (LP-config / LP-config-id) and applies rank-1 matroid online/random-order contention resolution schemes to resolve conflicts at each offline vertex.

The open problem asks for a random-order online contention resolution scheme (RO-OCRS) for matchings that is \(c\)-balanced for all graphs when the fractional input \(x\) lies in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\), and in particular whether one can beat \(0.456\).

This paper does not study OCRS for the matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) nor does it give a \(c\)-balanced RO-OCRS guarantee of the form \(\Pr[e\in I]\ge c x_e\) for arbitrary fractional \(x\in\mathrm{MP}(G)\). Instead it studies stochastic probing/prophet matching with commitment, where the algorithm first solves a different LP (a configuration LP capturing probing strategies) and then uses contention resolution only as a subroutine to choose among multiple edges that “commit” to the same offline vertex. The contention resolution used is essentially rank-1 matroid RCRS/OCRS (yielding factors \(1-1/e\) in random order and \(1/2\) in adversarial order) applied per offline vertex, not a global OCRS for matchings with input \(x\in\mathrm{MP}(G)\).

Thus the paper is at most indirectly relevant: it leverages random-order contention resolution ideas and achieves a \(1-1/e\) factor in a different stochastic matching model, but it does not improve the balance factor for RO-OCRS on \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) beyond \(0.456\) or address that question.

sources.title: Stochastic online correlated selection
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces Stochastic Online Correlated Selection (SOCS) and a type-decomposition reduction from general fractional allocations to one-way/two-way surrogate types, and designs improved two-way SOCS/OCS algorithms for several online matching/allocation problems. For unweighted/vertex-weighted online stochastic matching it proves an optimal two-way SOCS convergence rate \(g(y)=(1+y)e^{-2y}\) (Theorem 5) and derives improved competitive ratios (e.g. 0.69 non-IID, 0.705 random-order). sources.title: Limitations of stochastic selection problems with pairwise independent priors
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves tight bounds for contention resolution and prophet inequalities on matroids under pairwise-independent (not fully independent) stochastic inputs. In particular:
- (Theorem 5.4) For any matroid of rank \(r\), there exists a \(\tfrac{1}{4r}\)-balanced online contention resolution scheme against the almighty adversary for any pairwise-independent active-set distribution with marginals in the matroid polytope.
- (Theorem 5.1) For the full linear matroid \(\mathbb{F}_q^d\times[d]\), no pairwise-independent offline CRS can be \((c+1)/d\)-balanced when \(q^{c-1}\ge d\); in particular no \(3/d\)-balanced scheme for \(q\ge d\).
- (Theorem 6.2) No \(\omega(1/\log r)\)-competitive prophet inequality exists for pairwise-independent priors on certain binary matroids (even vs oblivious adversary), while (Theorem 6.9) an \(\Omega(1/\log r)\)-competitive algorithm exists for all matroids vs almighty adversary.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for improving the balance factor of random-order online contention resolution schemes for matchings when the fractional point \(x\) lies in the exact matching polytope \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) (i.e., under independent activations with probabilities \(x_e\) and random arrival order). This paper does not study matchings under independent Bernoulli activations; instead it studies matroids under pairwise-independent (correlated) priors, and its positive/negative results are about how much balance/competitiveness is possible under that weaker independence assumption.

Thus it neither provides a RO-OCRS for matchings with \(c>0.456\) on \(\mathrm{MP}(G)\) nor addresses the effect of adding Edmonds' odd-set constraints. At most, it is tangentially relevant as it develops CRS/OCRS techniques and impossibility constructions in a different stochastic model, which could inform proof techniques but does not advance the specific constant \(0.456\) barrier for matchings in the independent-activation, random-order model.

sources.title: Online bipartite matching in the probe-commit model
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies online bipartite matching in the probe-commit model and proves optimal competitive ratios against an offline adaptive probing benchmark in several settings. In particular, for known independently distributed (i.d.) instances with random-order arrivals, it gives a polynomial-time algorithm with competitive ratio \(1-1/e\) (Corollary 5.6), using a new configuration LP (LP-config) and a reduction to a \((1-1/e)\)-selectable random-order contention resolution scheme (RCRS) for a 1-uniform matroid. It also proves a \(1/e\) ratio for edge-weighted worst-case instances with random-order arrivals (Theorem 6.3) and \((1-1/e)\) for certain vertex-weighted worst-case instances under rankability (Theorem 7.7).

title: Polynomial-time solvability of integer programs with bounded subdeterminants setting
background_latex:
An integer linear program (ILP) is
\[\min\{c^\top x: Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Z^{k\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^k\), and \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\). For \(\Delta\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), a matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{k\times n}\) is called \(\Delta\)-modular if:
1) \(A\) has full column rank \(n\); and
2) every \(n\times n\) submatrix \(B\) of \(A\) satisfies \(|\det(B)|\le \Delta\).
Equivalently, the maximum absolute value of an \(n\times n\) subdeterminant of \(A\) is at most \(\Delta\).

A special and classical case is \(\Delta=1\), where \(A\) is totally unimodular (TU): every square submatrix has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). In that case, linear optimization over \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n: Ax\le b\}\) yields an integral optimal solution whenever \(b\) is integral.

The paper studies an important subclass of bounded-subdeterminant ILPs: congruency-constrained TU problems, i.e., TU systems plus one congruency constraint \(\gamma^\top x\equiv r\pmod m\). It proves feasibility can be decided in strongly polynomial randomized time for modulus \(m=3\), and more generally for prime \(m\) when all but at most two residues are allowed.

Despite this progress, the broad question for general \(\Delta\)-modular matrices remains unresolved.

under the promise that \(A\in\mathbb Z^{k\times n}\) is \(\Delta\)-modular (i.e., has full column rank and all \(n\times n\) subdeterminants have absolute value at most \(\Delta\)).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Nägele–Santiago–Zenklusen) frames the fixed-\(\Delta\) bounded-subdeterminant ILP question as a major open frontier beyond total unimodularity, and develops new machinery in the congruency-constrained TU setting (CCTU/CCTUF and the relaxed-residue variant R-CCTUF). Its decomposition lemma for TU systems, together with flatness and proximity bounds of size \(m-|R|\), enables a strongly polynomial randomized feasibility algorithm for modulus \(m=3\), and more generally for prime \(m\) when all but at most two residues are allowed. This highlights a plausible route to bounded-minor ILPs via reductions to TU plus modular constraints, but such reductions are only known for \(\Delta=2\) (bimodular) and remain unavailable for general \(\Delta>2\).

Forward-citing work has expanded the tractable landscape mainly by adding structural assumptions. The strongest algorithmic progress toward the open problem comes from results on totally \(\Delta\)-modular matrices that are ‘nearly TU’ in matroidal/graphical senses: the cographic nearly-network case admits strongly polynomial optimization, and related work handles matrices that are two-nonzeros-per-row except for a constant-size perturbation. In parallel, a separate line advances the strictly \(\Delta\)-modular regime (full-size minors in \(\{0,\pm\Delta\}\)) via reductions to group-constrained TU feasibility and propagation through Seymour decomposition, yielding strongly polynomial randomized feasibility for \(\Delta\le 4\) (including the first composite case \(\Delta=4\)). Extended-formulation constructions further give polynomial-time optimization for strictly \(\Delta\)-modular cographic translated cones. These results collectively suggest that combining TU decomposition with modular/group constraints is powerful, but current techniques still require either strict minor structure, cographic/network structure, or cone/translation assumptions.

On the tools side, improved proximity and flatness bounds in terms of \(\Delta_{n-1}(A)\) and \(\Delta_n(A)\) sharpen the geometric control needed for enumeration or augmentation algorithms, and become dimension-independent in certain restricted minor-value regimes (including some strictly \(\Delta\)-modular factorizations \(A=TB\)). However, for general \(\Delta\)-modular matrices these bounds still typically scale with dimension, and no known method turns them into a polynomial-time (or strongly polynomial) algorithm for optimization. Overall, the general fixed-\(\Delta\) \(\Delta\)-modular ILP solvability problem remains open; progress continues through (i) identifying reductions from bounded-minor ILPs to TU plus a bounded number of modular/extra constraints, and (ii) extending group-constrained TU methods from feasibility to optimization and from strictly \(\Delta\)-modular to general \(\Delta\)-modular matrices.

sources.title: Integer programs with nearly totally unimodular matrices: the cographic case
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves (Theorem 1) that for every fixed constant \(\Delta\), the integer program \(\max\{p^\top x: Mx\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) can be solved in strongly polynomial time for the class of totally \(\Delta\)-modular matrices \(M\) that become the transpose of a network matrix after deleting a constant number of rows and columns. Equivalently, after reductions it solves Problem 1/3: optimize over a TU system \(Ax\le b\) plus \(k\) extra constraints \(Wx\le d\) (or \(Wx=d\)) with \(k\) constant, under the promise that \([A;W]\) is totally \(\Delta\)-modular, in the cographic (transpose-network) nearly-TU case.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for ILPs with \(\Delta\)-modular constraint matrix \(A\) (full column rank; all \(n\times n\) subdeterminants bounded by \(\Delta\)), for each fixed \(\Delta\), with no further structural assumptions. This paper does not resolve that general question. Instead it gives a strong positive result for a substantial subclass: totally \(\Delta\)-modular matrices that are ‘nearly TU’ in a specific sense—after deleting \(O(1)\) rows/columns one obtains the transpose of a network matrix (cographic regular-matroid building block). It develops (i) a proximity/augmentation theorem for TU+\(O(1)\) extra constraints and (ii) a graph-minor-based decomposition excluding rooted \(K_{2,t}\) minors to enable dynamic programming. Thus it provides partial progress/evidence toward the general bounded-subdeterminant ILP conjecture, but leaves the full \(\Delta\)-modular case open.

sources.title: Advances on strictly Δ -modular IPs
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves that strictly \(\Delta\)-modular IP feasibility is decidable in strongly polynomial randomized time for \(\Delta\le 4\). Concretely, it establishes: there exists a strongly polynomial-time randomized algorithm that, given a strictly 4-modular IP \(\{x\in\mathbb Z^n: Ax\le b\}\), either finds a feasible integer solution or certifies infeasibility (Theorem 4). Equivalently, it gives a strongly polynomial randomized algorithm for group-constrained TU feasibility (GCTUF) when the finite abelian group \(G\) has \(|G|\le 4\) (Theorem 5), via a strongly polynomial reduction from strictly \(\Delta\)-modular feasibility to multi-congruency-constrained TU feasibility with \(\prod_i m_i=\Delta\) (Lemma 8).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm (for each fixed constant \(\Delta\)) to solve general \(\Delta\)-modular ILPs (optimization) with full-rank \(A\) and all \(n\times n\) subdeterminants bounded by \(\Delta\). This paper does not resolve that conjecture. Instead it advances a related, weaker conjecture (Conjecture 2) for the subclass of strictly \(\Delta\)-modular matrices (all \(n\times n\) minors in \(\{-\Delta,0,\Delta\}\)) and only for the feasibility problem, not optimization. It extends prior prime-\(\Delta\) techniques by introducing group-constrained TU feasibility and proving feasibility for strictly \(\Delta\)-modular IPs when \(\Delta\le 4\), including the first non-prime case \(\Delta=4\). These techniques (reductions to MCCTU/GCTUF, Seymour decomposition, pattern/averaging arguments) are relevant tools toward the broader \(\Delta\)-modular conjecture, but they do not cover general \(\Delta\)-modular matrices nor provide an optimization algorithm.

sources.title: Totally -Modular IPs with Two Non-zeros in Most Rows
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for a structured subclass of totally \(\Delta\)-modular integer programs. Concretely (Theorem 4), for fixed constants \(\Delta,k\), it solves IPs with constraint matrix \(M=\begin{bmatrix}A & B\\ W & D\end{bmatrix}\) that is totally \(\Delta\)-modular, where after removing at most \(k\) rows and \(k\) columns (the \(W,D,B\) blocks), the remaining block \(A\) has at most two nonzeros per row. Equivalently, it solves Problem 2 (and via reduction, Problem 3):
\[\min\{c^\top x: Ax\le b,\; Wx=d,\; \ell\le x\le u,\; x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\]
when \(\begin{bmatrix}A\\ W\end{bmatrix}\) is totally \(\Delta\)-modular, \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) has exactly two nonzeros per row, and \(k\) is constant.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for general \(\Delta\)-modular ILPs (bounded \(n\times n\) subdeterminants, full column rank) for each fixed \(\Delta\). This paper does not solve that general case; instead it proves polynomial/strongly-polynomial solvability under an additional strong sparsity/structure condition: all but a constant number of rows/columns have at most two nonzeros per row (graph-incidence structure), plus a constant number \(k\) of extra constraints/variables. This is genuine progress toward the conjecture for bounded-subdeterminant IPs, extending Fiorini et al. (two nonzeros per row) to allow a constant number of additional “unifying” constraints/variables, but it leaves the unrestricted \(\Delta\)-modular case open.

sources.title: Extended formulations for the integer hull of strictly Δ-modular cographic polyhedral cones
sources.theorem_or_result: Main result (Theorem 1): For fixed \(\Delta\in\mathbb N\), if \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) has rank \(n\), is strictly \(\Delta\)-modular (every \(n\times n\) subdeterminant is in \(\{0,\pm\Delta\}\)), the row matroid \(M(A^\top)\) is cographic, and \(b\in\mathrm{span}(A)\) (so \(P(A,b)=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is a translated cone), then the integer hull \(\mathrm{conv}(P(A,b)\cap\mathbb Z^n)\) admits a polynomial-size extended formulation of size \(O(n^{\Delta})\) constructible in polynomial time. Consequently, feasibility/optimization over \(P(A,b)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) is solvable in polynomial time for this class via LP in the extension.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for ILPs with \(\Delta\)-modular constraint matrix \(A\) for every fixed \(\Delta\), with no additional structure assumptions. This paper does not resolve that conjecture, but proves polynomial-time solvability (via constructible compact extended formulations) for a structured subclass: strictly \(\Delta\)-modular matrices whose row matroid is cographic and with right-hand side \(b\) in \(\mathrm{span}(A)\) (translated cones). The proof reduces the integer hull (in slack space) to a congruency-constrained circulation problem and gives a generalized extended formulation for circulations with congruency constraints (Lemma 6). The paper also shows conditions (cographic matroid and \(b\in\mathrm{span}(A)\)) are necessary for their EF approach by citing counterexamples where compact EFs fail even for strictly bimodular matrices.

sources.title: Advances on strictly -modular IPs
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves feasibility of strictly \(\Delta\)-modular IPs for \(\Delta\le 4\) can be decided in strongly polynomial randomized time. Concretely: Theorem 4 states there is a strongly polynomial-time randomized algorithm that either finds \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(Ax\le b\) for a strictly 4-modular matrix \(A\) (i.e., all \(n\times n\) minors in \(\{-4,0,4\}\)) or certifies infeasibility. Equivalently (Theorem 5/12), for any finite abelian group \(G\) with \(|G|\le 4\) (more generally \(|G|-|R|\le 3\)), group-constrained TU feasibility \(Tx\le b,\ \gamma x\in R,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\) is solvable in strongly polynomial randomized time, and strictly 4-modular feasibility reduces to this via a strongly polynomial reduction (Lemma 8).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm (for each fixed constant \(\Delta\)) to solve general \(\Delta\)-modular ILPs \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax\le b, x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) (optimization), assuming only bounded \(n\times n\) subdeterminants \(|\det(B)|\le \Delta\). This paper does not resolve that: it addresses a narrower subclass (strictly \(\Delta\)-modular, where full-size minors are restricted to \(\{-\Delta,0,\Delta\}\)) and only the feasibility problem (not optimization). It extends prior prime-modulus techniques by introducing group-constrained TU feasibility (GCTUF) and new decomposition/averaging arguments that avoid prime-number tools, yielding the first non-prime progress (\(\Delta=4\)). These techniques are relevant as strictly \(\Delta\)-modular feasibility is a key ingredient in known approaches to bounded-subdeterminant IPs, but the result falls short of solving general \(\Delta\)-modular optimization for arbitrary fixed \(\Delta\).

sources.title: Improving the Cook et al. proximity bound given integral valued constraints
sources.theorem_or_result: Improves the classical Cook–Gerards–Schrijver–Tardos proximity bound for ILPs with integral right-hand side: for integral full-column-rank \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and an optimal LP vertex \(x^*\) of \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\), if an optimal integer solution exists then there is an optimal integer solution \(z^*\) with \(\|x^*-z^*\|_\infty < \tfrac n2\,\Delta_{n-1}(A)\). In the strictly \(\Delta\)-modular case \(A=TB\) (\(T\) TU, \(|\det B|=\Delta\)), they show \(\|x^*-z^*\|_\infty \le \max\{\Delta_{n-1}(A),\Delta_n(A)\}-1\), and provide near-matching lower bounds.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for optimizing ILPs when \(A\) is \(\Delta\)-modular for fixed \(\Delta\). This paper does not give such an algorithm. Instead it strengthens proximity bounds (distance between an optimal LP vertex and an optimal integer solution) under the additional assumption that \(b\) is integral, with bounds expressed in terms of subdeterminants (notably \(\Delta_{n-1}(A)\)). Such proximity results are a standard ingredient for algorithm design (e.g., enumeration around an LP optimum, augmentation, or dynamic programming), and are particularly relevant in bounded-subdeterminant settings; however, the bound here still scales with \(n\) in general (\(\tfrac n2\Delta_{n-1}(A)\)), so it does not by itself yield a polynomial-time algorithm for fixed \(\Delta\) independent of dimension. The strictly \(\Delta\)-modular subclass result removes the \(n\) factor, but only for that special structure \(A=TB\), not for all \(\Delta\)-modular matrices.

sources.title: Proximity and flatness bounds for linear integer optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For integral right-hand side \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), they prove improved proximity/flatness bounds in terms of subdeterminants. In particular, if \(x^*\) is an optimal LP vertex of \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\) and the IP is feasible, then there exists an optimal integer solution \(z^*\) with \(\|x^*-z^*\|_\infty < \frac{4n+2}{9}\,\Delta_{n-1}(A)\) (Theorem 2). More generally, for any \(\alpha\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\), \(|\alpha^\top(x^*-z^*)|<\frac{4n+2}{9}\,\Delta_\alpha(A)\) where \(\Delta_\alpha(A)=\max\{|\det(\alpha^\top;B)|:B\text{ is an }(n-1)\times n\text{ submatrix of }A\}\) (Theorem 5). They also show a facet-direction flatness bound: if \(P(A,b)\) is full-dimensional lattice-free with facet-defining rows, then some row \(a\) of \(A\) satisfies \(w_a(P(A,b))<\frac{4n+2}{9}\,\Delta_n(A)-1\) (Theorem 4). In the special case that all \(n\times n\) minors lie in \(\{0,\pm k,\pm 2k\}\), they obtain dimension-independent bounds (Theorem 6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm to solve ILPs when \(A\) is \(\Delta\)-modular (bounded \(n\times n\) subdeterminants) for fixed constant \(\Delta\). This paper does not give such an algorithm. Instead it develops structural bounds (proximity between LP and IP optima; flatness/lattice width bounds) in terms of \(\Delta_{n-1}(A)\) and \(\Delta_n(A)\) under the crucial assumption \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). Such bounds are often key ingredients in algorithm design (e.g., bounding search neighborhoods around an LP optimum, or bounding widths used in Lenstra-type branching). Theorem 6 treats a restricted bounded-minor regime (minors in \(\{0,\pm k,\pm 2k\}\), including strictly \(\Delta\)-modular matrices \(A=TB\) with TU \(T\)), giving stronger, dimension-independent proximity/flatness bounds; this is closer in spirit to the bounded-subdeterminant algorithmic agenda but still falls short of solving general \(\Delta\)-modular ILPs.

title: Lower bound on oracle complexity for near-stationary max-structured nonconvex optimization
background_latex:
Let \((X,\|\cdot\|_X)\) and \((Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)\) be finite-dimensional real normed spaces. Let \(r:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be closed and convex with domain \(\mathrm{dom}r\subseteq X\), and write \(\mathcal{X}:=\mathrm{dom}r\) (assumed nonempty, closed, convex). Let \(\mathcal{Y}\subseteq Y\) be nonempty, closed, convex, and bounded. Let \(g:\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and continuous.

Let \(\Phi:\mathcal{X}'\times\mathcal{Y}'\to\mathbb{R}\) be jointly continuous on open sets \(\mathcal{X}'\supseteq \mathcal{X}\), \(\mathcal{Y}'\supseteq \mathcal{Y}\), with \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) concave on \(\mathcal{Y}\) for each \(x\in\mathcal{X}\). Assume \(\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is Frchet differentiable and has Lipschitz gradient in \(x\): there is \(L_{xx}<\infty\) such that for all \(x,x'\in\mathcal{X}\), \(y\in\mathcal{Y}\),
\[\|\nabla_x\Phi(x,y)-\nabla_x\Phi(x',y)\|_{X^*}\le L_{xx}\|x-x'\|_X.\]
Assume also a cross-Lipschitz bound: there is \(L_{xy}<\infty\) such that for all \(x\in\mathcal{X}\), \(y,y'\in\mathcal{Y}\),
\[\|\nabla_x\Phi(x,y)-\nabla_x\Phi(x,y')\|_{X^*}\le L_{xy}\|y-y'\|_Y.\]
Assume weak convexity in \(x\): there exists \(\gamma\in(0,L_{xx}]\) such that for all \(x,x'\in\mathcal{X}\), \(y\in\mathcal{Y}\),
\[\Phi(x',y)\ge \Phi(x,y)+\langle \nabla_x\Phi(x,y),x'-x\rangle-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\|x'-x\|_X^2.\]
Assume \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is Frchet differentiable with Lipschitz gradient in \(y\): there exist \(L_{yy}<\infty\) and the same \(L_{xy}\) such that for all \(x,x'\in\mathcal{X}\), \(y,y'\in\mathcal{Y}\),
\[\|\nabla_y\Phi(x,y)-\nabla_y\Phi(x',y)\|_{Y^*}\le L_{xy}\|x-x'\|_X,\qquad \|\nabla_y\Phi(x,y)-\nabla_y\Phi(x,y')\|_{Y^*}\le L_{yy}\|y-y'\|_Y.\]

Define the max-structured nonconvex objective
\[q(x):=f(x)+r(x),\qquad f(x):=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\ \Phi(x,y)-g(y),\qquad q^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathcal{X}} q(x)>-\infty.\]

Fix a distance generating function (DGF) \(\omega_X:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}\) that is 1-strongly convex on \(\mathcal{X}\) and differentiable on a neighborhood of \(\mathcal{X}\), and assume \(\nabla \omega_X\) is \(\beta_X\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathcal{X}\) for some \(\beta_X\ge1\). Let the induced Bregman divergence be
\[D_{\omega_X}(x',x):=\omega_X(x')-\omega_X(x)-\langle \nabla\omega_X(x),x'-x\rangle.\]
For any \(\lambda\in(0,\gamma^{-1})\), define the proximal point mapping
\[\mathrm{prox}(q,x,\lambda):=\arg\min_{x'\in\mathcal{X}}\ q(x')+\lambda^{-1}D_{\omega_X}(x',x).\]
An \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point is a point \(x\in\mathcal{X}\) for which there exists \(\lambda\in(0,\gamma^{-1})\) such that
\[\|\lambda^{-1}(x-\mathrm{prox}(q,x,\lambda))\|_X\le \varepsilon/\beta_X.\]

The paper studies first-order methods whose cost is measured by the number of evaluations of \(\nabla_x\Phi(x,y)\) and \(\nabla_y\Phi(x,y)\) (and associated simple Bregman proximal projections for \(r\) and \(g\)), yielding upper bounds on the oracle complexities to obtain an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point. The open question concerns matching information-theoretic (worst-case) lower bounds as functions of \(\varepsilon\) and the parameters \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine a worst-case lower bound (in terms of \(\varepsilon\) and the problem parameters \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma\), and any necessary dependence on \(\beta_X\)) on the number of first-order oracle calls required by any algorithm to output an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of
\[\min_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\ q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\ \Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x),\]
over the class of instances satisfying the smoothness, cross-Lipschitz, and weak-convexity conditions stated in the background. Here a first-order oracle call reveals \(\nabla_x\Phi(x,y)\) and/or \(\nabla_y\Phi(x,y)\) at queried \((x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\), along with the ability to compute the required Bregman proximal projections for \(r\) and \(g\).

literature_review.synthesis:
Zhao’s primal-dual smoothing framework targets \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationarity for the composite max-structured weakly convex objective \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under separate smoothness and cross-Lipschitz constants \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy}\), weak convexity \(\gamma\), and non-Euclidean (Bregman) geometry controlled by \(\beta_X\). The algorithmic side is comparatively well developed: Zhao obtains deterministic oracle upper bounds of order \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) (with explicit dependence on \(\gamma,L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\beta_X\)) for primal/dual gradient evaluations by reducing each outer proximal step to a strongly convex–concave saddle-point problem and solving it via a non-Hilbertian inexact accelerated proximal-gradient scheme.

On the lower-bound side, the forward-citation set shows only partial progress, primarily in more restrictive minimax subclasses. The most directly relevant is “The complexity of nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization,” which proves worst-case first-order oracle lower bounds for finding \(\varepsilon\)-stationary points of the primal max function in smooth nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax problems, with complexity \(\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa\,\Delta L}\,\varepsilon^{-2})\) for deterministic linear-span methods. This establishes that nontrivial parameter-dependent lower bounds are possible and that condition-number effects can be inherent, but it does not cover Zhao’s bounded-\(\mathcal Y\) concave (not strongly concave) setting, composite terms \(r,g\), or Bregman-prox near-stationarity.

Other citing works largely advance upper bounds (e.g., single-loop extragradient variants achieving \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) for certain stationarity notions, and proximal/Catalyst frameworks yielding \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) for Moreau-envelope stationarity in nonconvex–concave minimax). These results sharpen the landscape of achievable rates but do not provide matching information-theoretic lower bounds for the full max-structured weakly convex composite class. Consequently, the specific open problem posed by Zhao—deriving worst-case lower bounds with explicit dependence on \(\varepsilon\) and \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma\) (and possibly \(\beta_X\)) for the \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationarity mapping—appears to remain open.

sources.title: The complexity of nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization
sources.theorem_or_result:
For smooth nonconvex–strongly-concave minimax problems \(\min_x\max_y f(x,y)\) with \(f\) jointly \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly concave in \(y\) (condition number \(\kappa=L/\mu\)), the paper proves worst-case first-order oracle lower bounds for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point of the primal function \(\Phi(x)=\max_y f(x,y)\):
- General (single-function) setting: any deterministic linear-span algorithm using the first-order oracle must make \(\Omega\big(\sqrt{\kappa\,\Delta L}\,\varepsilon^{-2}\big)\) gradient evaluations (Theorem 3.1), for suitable regimes of \(\varepsilon\), where \(\Delta=\Phi(x_0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\).
- Finite-sum averaged-smooth setting: any (possibly randomized) linear-span algorithm using an incremental first-order oracle must make \(\Omega\big(n+\sqrt{n\kappa\,\Delta L}\,\varepsilon^{-2}\big)\) oracle calls (Theorem 3.2, under \(L\ge 2n\mu\) and small enough \(\varepsilon\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds on first-order oracle complexity to obtain an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point for max-structured weakly convex objectives \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under Lipschitz and cross-Lipschitz assumptions. This paper provides explicit lower bounds for a closely related subclass: unconstrained smooth minimax with \(r\equiv 0\), \(g\equiv 0\), Euclidean geometry, and *strong concavity* in \(y\) (not merely bounded \(\mathcal Y\)). Their lower bound scales as \(\Omega(\sqrt{\kappa\Delta L}\,\varepsilon^{-2})\), exhibiting a nontrivial dependence on the condition number \(\kappa\). However, it does not cover the full generality of the open problem: it does not address general norm/Bregman geometry (\(\beta_X\)), composite terms \(r,g\), bounded \(\mathcal Y\) without strong concavity, nor the weak-convexity parameter \(\gamma\) and separate constants \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy}\). Thus it constitutes partial progress by establishing lower bounds in an important special case (NC–SC minimax) and offering techniques (zero-chain constructions) potentially adaptable to the broader max-structured setting.

sources.title: A single-loop accelerated extra-gradient difference algorithm with improved complexity bounds for constrained minimax optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For smooth constrained minimax problems \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y} f(x,y)\) with \(X,Y\) closed convex and \(Y\) compact, and \(f\) continuously differentiable with Lipschitz partial gradients (Assumption 1), the proposed single-loop EGDA method outputs an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point of \(f\) (in the projected-gradient-mapping sense \(\|\pi(x,y)\|\le \varepsilon\)) in \(O((G_0-G+2L D_Y^2)/\varepsilon^2)\) iterations/gradient evaluations (Theorem 1). In the nonconvex–concave case, it outputs an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point of the primal function \(\phi(x)=\max_{y\in Y} f(x,y)\) measured via the Moreau envelope gradient \(\|\nabla \phi_{1/(2L)}(x)\|\le \varepsilon\) in \(O(D_Y(G_0-G+2L D_Y^2)/\varepsilon^2)\) gradient evaluations (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds on first-order oracle complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of a max-structured weakly convex objective \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under separate smoothness constants \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy}\) and weak convexity \(\gamma\), with Bregman proximal stationarity. This citing paper provides improved upper bounds (\(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\)) for a related but different model: smooth constrained minimax \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y} f(x,y)\) with Euclidean projections and a stationarity notion for \(f\) (or Moreau-envelope stationarity for \(\phi\) in NC-C). It does not establish any worst-case lower bound, nor does it treat the composite terms \(r,g\), Bregman prox geometry, or parameter dependence in \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma,\beta_X\). Thus it is partial progress only insofar as it tightens achievable upper bounds in a neighboring oracle model, suggesting \(\Omega(\varepsilon^{-2})\) may be the right lower-bound order, but it does not prove such a lower bound for the open-problem class.

sources.title: A stochastic smoothing framework for nonconvex-nonconcave min-sum-max problems with applications to wasserstein distributionally robust optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes SSPG, a stochastic log-sum-exp smoothing proximal-gradient framework for nonconvex–nonconcave min-sum-max problems \(\min_y \phi(y)+\tfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \max_{z\in Z}\Psi(y,z;x_i)\). Under compactness and Lipschitz assumptions, it proves: (i) the primal objective \(g\) is Clarke regular (Lemma 2.3), so Clarke stationarity implies directional stationarity (Corollary 2.1); (ii) the log-sum-exp smoothing \(\Phi_i^e(y,\mu)=\mu\log\mathbb E_{z\sim\zeta}[e^{\Psi(y,z;x_i)/\mu}]\) has \(\nabla_y\Phi_i^e\) Lipschitz with constant \(L_\Psi+2l_\Psi^2/\mu\) (Lemma 2.4); (iii) SSPG outputs an \(\varepsilon\)-scaled Clarke stationary point in expectation in \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) iterations (Corollaries 2.2–2.3), and accumulation points are a.s. directional stationary for the original nonsmooth problem (Theorem 2.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds on first-order oracle complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of a max-structured weakly convex objective \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under smoothness/cross-Lipschitz/weak-convexity assumptions, with oracle access to \(\nabla_x\Phi\) and \(\nabla_y\Phi\). This citing paper does not provide any lower bound. It gives an upper-bound iteration complexity \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) for a different but related class: min-sum-max problems treated via log-sum-exp smoothing, targeting Clarke/directional stationarity (and an \(\varepsilon\)-scaled stationarity notion) rather than the Bregman-prox near-stationarity mapping used in the open problem. Its techniques (smoothing the max, controlling Lipschitz constants as \(\mu\downarrow0\), and stationarity measures) are conceptually related and could inform constructions for lower bounds, but it does not address the oracle lower-bound question nor match parameter dependence \((L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma,\beta_X)\).

sources.title: Efficient search of first-order nash equilibria in nonconvex-concave smooth min-max problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives a first-order method for smooth nonconvex–concave min–max problems \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y} F(x,y)\) (with Lipschitz constants \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy}\), compact \(Y\)) that outputs an \((\varepsilon_x,\varepsilon_y)\)-first-order Nash equilibrium (FNE) under a strong constrained stationarity measure \(S_Z\) in \(\widetilde O(T_x T_y)\) gradient/projection calls, where \(T_x=\tfrac{L_{xx}\Delta}{\varepsilon_x^2}\) and \(T_y=\sqrt{\tfrac{(L_{yy}+L_{xy}^2/L_{xx})R_y}{\varepsilon_y}}\). In particular, choosing \(\varepsilon_y=\Theta(\varepsilon_x^2/(L_{xx}R_y))\) yields \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon_x^{-3})\) complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon_x\)-stationary point of the standard Moreau envelope of the primal function \(\varphi(x)=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds on first-order oracle complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of a max-structured weakly nonconvex objective \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under smoothness/cross-Lipschitz/weak-convexity assumptions. This citing paper provides improved upper bounds (algorithms) for the special case \(r\equiv 0\), \(g\equiv 0\), Euclidean geometry, and concave (not merely general max-structured) dependence in \(y\). It does not prove any worst-case lower bound, nor does it address the full composite/Bregman framework of the open problem. However, its rates \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon_x^{-2}\varepsilon_y^{-1/2})\) and the induced \(\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) Moreau-envelope stationarity rate are natural candidates to be matched by lower bounds, and it discusses (citing Carmon–Duchi–Hinder–Sidford) known lower bounds for smooth nonconvex minimization that may inform the max-structured setting.

sources.title: Near-optimal algorithms for minimax optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives near-optimal first-order upper bounds for smooth minimax problems. In particular, for `-smooth, \(\mu_x\)-strongly-convex–\(\mu_y\)-strongly-concave \(f\), it proves an algorithm (MINIMAX-APPA) that outputs an \(\varepsilon\)-saddle point using \(\tilde O(\sqrt{\kappa_x\kappa_y})\) gradient evaluations, where \(\kappa_x=\ell/\mu_x\), \(\kappa_y=\ell/\mu_y\) (Theorem 9). For nonconvex–(strongly)-concave settings it proves upper bounds such as \(\tilde O(\sqrt{\kappa_y}\,\varepsilon^{-2})\) to find an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point of \(f\) (Theorem 12) and \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) for stationarity of \(\Phi(x)=\max_y f(x,y)\) in the concave (not strongly concave) case (Corollary 21).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds on oracle complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of a max-structured weakly convex objective \(q(x)=\max_{y\in\mathcal Y}\Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under Lipschitz/cross-Lipschitz and weak-convexity assumptions, with an oracle returning \(\nabla_x\Phi,\nabla_y\Phi\). This citing paper does not prove lower bounds for this class. It focuses on designing (near-)optimal algorithms and matching known lower bounds in the strongly-convex–strongly-concave minimax setting, and it explicitly states that lower bounds for nonconvex-(strongly)-concave minimax remain open. Thus it provides context and upper-bound techniques (proximal point + accelerated inner minimax solver) but does not resolve the lower-bound question posed in the max-structured nonconvex framework.

sources.title: A catalyst framework for minimax optimization
sources.theorem_or_result:
For smooth minimax problems with concavity in \(y\) and either strong convexity in \(x\) (SC-C) or nonconvexity in \(x\) (NC-C), the paper proposes a Catalyst (accelerated proximal point) framework that yields oracle complexities:
- SC-C: with extragradient/OGDA as inner solver and \(\tau=\mu\), total gradient evaluations \(\tilde O\big( \ell D_Y/(\sqrt{\mu\,\varepsilon})\,\log(\ell D_Y/(\min\{1,\mu\}\varepsilon))\big)\) to reach primal-dual gap \(\le \varepsilon\).
- NC-C: choosing \(\tau_x=2\ell\), \(\tau_y=\ell\), total gradient evaluations \(\tilde O(\ell^2\,\varepsilon^{-3})\) to find \(\bar x\) with \(\mathbb E\|\nabla \psi_{1/\tau_x}(\bar x)\|\le \varepsilon\) (stationarity via Moreau envelope).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for information-theoretic lower bounds (in \(\varepsilon\) and parameters \(L_{xx},L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma,\beta_X\)) for first-order oracle complexity to find an \(\varepsilon\)-near-stationary point of a max-structured weakly convex objective \(q(x)=\max_y \Phi(x,y)-g(y)+r(x)\) under cross-Lipschitz and smoothness assumptions.

This citing paper is primarily algorithmic and focuses on smooth minimax \(\min_x\max_y f(x,y)\) with Euclidean norms, no nonsmooth \(r,g\), and stationarity measured by the Moreau-envelope gradient of \(g(x)=\max_y f(x,y)\). It cites lower bounds for SC-C duality-gap complexity (e.g., \(\Omega(\ell/(\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}))\) from prior work) but does not derive new lower bounds for the weakly convex max-structured composite setting of the open problem. At best, it provides upper bounds/state-of-the-art rates in related NC-C settings, which may inform what a matching lower bound might look like (e.g., \(\varepsilon^{-3}\) dependence), but it does not address the requested parameterized lower bound in the general framework (including \(L_{xy},L_{yy},\gamma,\beta_X\) and Bregman geometry).

title: Extend robustness and continuity results to degenerate controlled diffusion models
background_latex:
Consider a controlled diffusion process 
\[dX_t = b(X_t,U_t)\,dt + \sigma(X_t)\,dW_t, \qquad X_0=x\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
where \(W\) is a \(d\)-dimensional standard Wiener process, the action space \(U\) is a compact metric space, and \(U_t\) is an admissible (non-anticipative) control. The running cost is a bounded continuous function \(c:\mathbb{R}^d\times U\to\mathbb{R}_+\). For each control policy \(\pi\) (e.g., Markov or stationary Markov controls), one considers standard performance criteria such as:

1) Discounted cost for \(\alpha>0\):
\[J_\alpha^{\pi}(x;c)=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}_x\Big[\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha t} c(X_t,U_t)\,dt\Big],\qquad V_\alpha(x)=\inf_{\pi} J_\alpha^{\pi}(x;c).\]

2) Ergodic (long-run average) cost:
\[\mathcal{E}_x(c,\pi)=\limsup_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\,\mathbb{E}^{\pi}_x\Big[\int_0^T c(X_t,U_t)\,dt\Big],\qquad \mathcal{E}^*(c)=\inf_x\inf_{\pi}\mathcal{E}_x(c,\pi).\]

3) Finite-horizon cost for a horizon \(T>0\) and terminal cost \(H\):
\[J_T^{\pi}(x;c)=\mathbb{E}^{\pi}_x\Big[\int_0^T c(X_t,U_t)\,dt + H(X_T)\Big],\qquad J_T^*(x;c)=\inf_{\pi}J_T^{\pi}(x;c).\]

The paper studies an approximation setting in which a sequence of models \((b_n,\sigma_n,c_n)\) converges to \((b,\sigma,c)\) (in a sense ensuring pointwise convergence in the state and continuous convergence in control actions), with associated state processes
\[dX_t^{(n)} = b_n(X_t^{(n)},U_t)\,dt + \sigma_n(X_t^{(n)})\,dW_t.
\]
For each model one has the corresponding optimal values \(V_{\alpha}^{(n)}\), \(\mathcal{E}^{*(n)}(c_n)\), \(J_{T}^{*(n)}(x;c_n)\), and one may compare the performance of controls optimized for the approximate model when applied to the true model.

A key standing condition used throughout the paper is uniform nondegeneracy (uniform ellipticity) of the diffusion term: letting \(a(x)=\tfrac12\sigma(x)\sigma(x)^\top\), one assumes that for each radius \(R>0\) there exists \(C_R>0\) such that
\[z^\top a(x) z \ge C_R^{-1}\,|z|^2 \qquad \forall x\in B_R,\ \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
(and similarly for \(a_n\)). This nondegeneracy assumption enables strong regularity theory for the associated Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equations and is central to the continuity/robustness proofs in the paper.

A diffusion is called degenerate if the corresponding covariance matrix \(a(x)\) fails to be uniformly positive definite (e.g., is singular in some directions, at some states, or on sets of positive measure).
problem_definition_latex:
Develop an analogue of the paper's continuity and robustness theory for controlled diffusion models when the limiting (true) diffusion is degenerate, i.e., when the uniform nondegeneracy/ellipticity condition on \(a(x)=\tfrac12\sigma(x)\sigma(x)^\top\) is dropped and \(a(x)\) may be singular.

Concretely: under a suitable convergence notion for approximating models \((b_n,\sigma_n,c_n)\to (b,\sigma,c)\), determine conditions under which (for one or more of the criteria discounted, ergodic, finite-horizon, or exit-time) the optimal values of the approximate models converge to the optimal value of the true (degenerate) model, and the performance loss from applying an optimal control of the approximate model to the true model vanishes in the limit.

counterexample_suitability_rationale: The question is broadly about extending positive results to a substantially different analytical regime (loss of uniform ellipticity), rather than a sharp finite-dimensional conjecture. literature_review.synthesis:
Pradhan--Y\"uksel (arXiv:2205.05894v2, 2023) develop a PDE-based continuity/robustness theory for controlled diffusions under discounted, ergodic (near-monotone or Lyapunov), finite-horizon, and exit-time criteria. A central technical pillar is local uniform ellipticity (Assumption (A3)), which yields Sobolev/Schauder regularity for HJB equations, compactness of value-function families in \(W^{2,p}\), and It\^o--Krylov representations enabling both value convergence \(V^n\to V\) and asymptotic optimality transfer when applying \(n\)-optimal controls to the limit model.

Forward-citing work to date provides partial progress but does not remove ellipticity. The regime-switching extension proves analogous continuity/robustness results for weakly coupled HJB systems, again under local uniform ellipticity, and thus mainly maps where ellipticity enters and what would need replacement in a degenerate setting. The rough-path robustness paper proves policy-wise continuity and near-optimality transfer for Lipschitz feedback controls under near-Brownian noise perturbations; while it still assumes uniform nondegeneracy to access classical HJB theory for the idealized model, its rough-path continuity arguments are largely independent of ellipticity and suggest a promising tool for establishing continuity of \(J^\pi\) for fixed (regular) feedbacks even when \(\sigma\) is degenerate.

Overall, the open problem remains to develop a full analogue of Pradhan--Y\"uksel robustness when the limiting diffusion is degenerate: one needs conditions ensuring existence/approximation of optimal controls and convergence of optimal values without relying on uniformly elliptic PDE regularity or strong Feller properties. Promising directions include (i) viscosity-solution stability for degenerate HJB equations combined with measurable selection/relaxed controls, (ii) hypoelliptic regularity under H\"ormander-type conditions when degeneracy is structured, and (iii) probabilistic/MDP discretization approaches (e.g., Wasserstein-regular kernel continuity) that bypass elliptic PDE estimates.

sources.title: Robustness of optimal controlled diffusions with near-brownian noise via rough paths theory
sources.theorem_or_result:
Under assumptions (A1)–(A4), including uniform nondegeneracy (A3), and restricting to Lipschitz Markov (or Lipschitz time-state) controls, the paper proves robustness of optimal control to near-Brownian noise perturbations in rough-path topology: if \(v_\delta\) is a Lipschitz \(\delta\)-optimal control for the Brownian/Stratonovich idealized model, then for sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\) (or large \(n\) in explicit approximations) one has
- Discounted cost: \(J^{v_\delta}_{\alpha,T_\varepsilon}(x,c) \le V^{L T_\varepsilon}_\alpha(x)+2\delta\) (Theorem 5.4 / 5.9).
- Finite horizon: \(J^{v_\delta}_{T,T_\varepsilon}(x,c) \le J^{*}_{T,L T_\varepsilon}(x,c)+2\delta\) (Theorem 5.8 / 5.10).
It also establishes continuity of costs for fixed Lipschitz policies (Proposition 5.1, Lemma 5.5) and convergence of restricted value functions \(V^{L T_\varepsilon}_\alpha\to V^I_\alpha\), \(J^{*}_{T,L T_\varepsilon}\to J^{*}_{T,I}\) up to \(\delta\) (Theorems 5.3, 5.7).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks to extend continuity/robustness results to degenerate controlled diffusions (dropping uniform ellipticity). This citing paper is closely related in spirit—it studies robustness/continuity of optimal control under model mismatch—but it does not remove ellipticity. In fact it explicitly assumes uniform nondegeneracy (A3) and uses classical HJB/PDE regularity (Theorems 2.1–2.2) to justify existence/near-optimality of Lipschitz controls for the idealized diffusion. Rough paths are then used to obtain pathwise continuity of the state trajectory with respect to perturbations of the driving noise (and drift), yielding convergence of costs for fixed Lipschitz policies and near-optimality transfer.

Thus, it does not solve the degenerate-diffusion extension. However, it provides a potentially relevant methodological ingredient for the degenerate setting: the rough-path continuity arguments (Theorem 3.9, Corollary 4.6) are largely independent of ellipticity and could still yield continuity of \(J^\pi\) for fixed Lipschitz feedbacks even when \(\sigma\) is degenerate. What remains open (and is not addressed here) is the control-optimization layer in the degenerate case: existence/approximation of optimal controls and convergence of optimal values without relying on uniformly elliptic HJB regularity/strong Feller properties.

sources.title: Robustness of optimal control for controlled regime-switching diffusions with incorrect models
sources.theorem_or_result: Under local Lipschitz and growth assumptions plus a local uniform ellipticity (nondegeneracy) condition (A3) for both the true and approximating models, the paper proves continuity of optimal value functions and robustness of optimal controls for controlled regime-switching diffusions under four criteria: discounted, ergodic (with a Foster–Lyapunov stability condition (A7)), finite-horizon, and exit-time. Concretely, if \((b_n,\sigma_n,c_n,m_n)\to(b,\sigma,c,m)\) as in (A6), then \(V^n_\alpha(x,i)\to V_\alpha(x,i)\) (Thm 3.3), \(\mathcal E^{n*}(c_n)=\rho_n\to\rho=\mathcal E^*(c)\) (Thm 4.3), \(J^*_{T,n}(x,i;c_n)\to J^*_T(x,i;c)\) (Thm 5.3), and \(\hat J^{*}_{e,n}(x,i)\to \hat J^{*}_e(x,i)\) (Thm 6.3); moreover applying an optimal control from the \(n\)-model to the true model yields asymptotically optimal performance (Thms 3.4, 4.5, 5.4, 6.4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to extend robustness/continuity results to degenerate controlled diffusions where the limiting diffusion matrix \(a(x)=\tfrac12\sigma\sigma^\top\) may be singular (dropping uniform ellipticity). This paper does not address degeneracy: it explicitly assumes local uniform nondegeneracy (A3) for the true regime-switching diffusion and for every approximating model (A6)(iii). The proofs rely on elliptic/parabolic Sobolev estimates, ABP/Harnack-type bounds, and It\^o–Krylov formula for \(W^{2,p}\) solutions of (weakly coupled) HJB systems—tools that typically require (at least local) uniform ellipticity. Thus it does not solve the degenerate-diffusion extension, but it provides a closely related robustness framework (including exit-time and hybrid switching) whose arguments indicate exactly where ellipticity is used and what would need replacement (e.g., hypoelliptic/degenerate PDE regularity or viscosity-solution stability).

sources.title: Robustness to Model Approximation, Model Learning From Data, and Sample Complexity in Wasserstein Regular MDPs
sources.theorem_or_result: For discrete-time MDPs on Polish state spaces with compact action spaces, the paper proves quantitative continuity and robustness bounds for optimal value functions and for the performance loss of applying an optimal policy from an approximate model to the true model, with bounds controlled by \,\(\|c-\hat c\|_\infty\) and a uniform Wasserstein-1 discrepancy \,\(d_{W_1}(T,S)=\sup_{x,u} W_1(T(\cdot\mid x,u),S(\cdot\mid x,u))\). Representative results include: (i) discounted-cost continuity (Theorem 2.4) \(\|J^*_\beta(c,T)-J^*_\beta(\hat c,S)\|_\infty\le \frac{1}{1-\beta}\|c-\hat c\|_\infty+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\,d_{J^*_\beta(c,T)}(T,S)\), and if \(J^*_\beta(c,T)\) is Lipschitz then \(\le \frac{1}{1-\beta}\|c-\hat c\|_\infty+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta}\|J^*_\beta(c,T)\|_{\mathrm{Lip}} d_{W_1}(T,S)\); (ii) discounted robustness error bounds (Theorem 2.7) of order \(\frac{1}{1-\beta}\|c-\hat c\|_\infty+\frac{\beta}{1-\beta} d_{J^*}(T,S)\); (iii) analogous average-cost continuity/robustness bounds under either a minorization condition (Theorems 2.5, 2.8) or a vanishing-discount approach under Wasserstein contraction/Lipschitz assumptions (Theorems 2.6, 2.9).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for robustness/continuity of optimal control for continuous-time controlled diffusions when the limiting diffusion is degenerate (no uniform ellipticity). This paper does not treat continuous-time diffusions or HJB/PDE regularity; it works in discrete time with general MDP kernels and uses Wasserstein-1 regularity/minorization/vanishing-discount arguments. However, its methodology is relevant as a potential alternative route for degenerate diffusions: one could discretize time (Euler–Maruyama) to obtain MDP kernels and then seek Wasserstein-type continuity of those kernels under model approximation without relying on elliptic PDE regularity. The paper thus provides tools/benchmarks for robustness bounds in a setting where nondegeneracy is not assumed, but it does not directly resolve the diffusion-degenerate continuous-time robustness question.

title: Achieve the optimal 1 minus 1 over e competitive ratio in reusable-resource matching
background_latex:
Online bipartite matching with reusable resources (OBMRR) is defined on a bipartite graph \(G=(V,U;E)\), where \(V\) is a set of offline vertices (reusable resources) and \(U\) is a sequence of online vertices (requests) arriving over discrete times \(j=1,2,\dots,|U|\) in an oblivious adversarial order. When request \(j\) arrives, its incident edges \(\{(i,j)\in E: i\in V\}\) are revealed, and an online algorithm must either match \(j\) to an available neighbor \(i\in V\) or leave \(j\) unmatched; decisions are irrevocable.

Reusability is governed by a known deterministic usage duration \(d\in\mathbb{N}\): if resource \(i\) is matched at time \(j\), then \(i\) becomes unavailable for the next \(d-1\) arrivals and becomes available again at time \(j+d\). Equivalently, each resource \(i\) can be matched at most once in any window of \(d\) consecutive times.

In the vertex-weighted version, each resource \(i\in V\) has a nonnegative weight \(r_i\). Each time \(i\) is matched, the algorithm earns reward \(r_i\). The total reward of an algorithm is the sum of rewards over all matches it makes.

Let \(\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)\) denote the (expected) total reward obtained by a (possibly randomized) online algorithm on instance \((G,d)\), where the expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness. Let \(\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)\) denote the maximum total reward achievable by an offline algorithm with full knowledge of the entire arrival sequence and graph, subject to the same reusability constraints.

The competitive ratio of an online algorithm is the largest \(\Gamma\in[0,1]\) such that for all instances \((G,d)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)]\ge \Gamma\,\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)\). For the classic non-reusable online bipartite matching (obtained as a special case when \(d=|U|\)), the optimal competitive ratio is \(1-1/e\) for randomized algorithms, and this value also serves as an upper bound for OBMRR because OBMRR generalizes the non-reusable model (for large \(d\), it reduces to the classic case).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists a randomized online algorithm for vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) that achieves competitive ratio \(\Gamma = 1-1/e\). That is, does there exist an online algorithm such that for every instance \((G=(V,U;E),d,\{r_i\}_{i\in V})\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)] \;\ge\; (1-1/e)\,\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)?
\]
If not, determine the optimal achievable competitive ratio for OBMRR.

Online bipartite matching with reusable resources (OBMRR) is defined on a bipartite graph \(G=(V,U;E)\), where \(V\) is a set of offline vertices (reusable resources) and \(U\) is a sequence of online vertices (requests) arriving over discrete times \(j=1,2,\dots,|U|\) in an oblivious adversarial order. When request \(j\) arrives, its incident edges \(\{(i,j)\in E: i\in V\}\) are revealed, and an online algorithm must either match \(j\) to an available neighbor \(i\in V\) or leave \(j\) unmatched; decisions are irrevocable.

Reusability is governed by a known deterministic usage duration \(d\in\mathbb{N}\): if resource \(i\) is matched at time \(j\), then \(i\) becomes unavailable for the next \(d-1\) arrivals and becomes available again at time \(j+d\). Equivalently, each resource \(i\) can be matched at most once in any window of \(d\) consecutive times.

In the vertex-weighted version, each resource \(i\in V\) has a nonnegative weight \(r_i\). Each time \(i\) is matched, the algorithm earns reward \(r_i\). The total reward of an algorithm is the sum of rewards over all matches it makes.

Let \(\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)\) denote the (expected) total reward obtained by a (possibly randomized) online algorithm on instance \((G,d)\), where the expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness. Let \(\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)\) denote the maximum total reward achievable by an offline algorithm with full knowledge of the entire arrival sequence and graph, subject to the same reusability constraints.

The competitive ratio of an online algorithm is the largest \(\Gamma\in[0,1]\) such that for all instances \((G,d)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)]\ge \Gamma\,\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)\). For the classic non-reusable online bipartite matching (obtained as a special case when \(d=|U|\)), the optimal competitive ratio is \(1-1/e\) for randomized algorithms, and this value also serves as an upper bound for OBMRR because OBMRR generalizes the non-reusable model (for large \(d\), it reduces to the classic case).

Determine whether there exists a randomized online algorithm for vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) that achieves competitive ratio \(\Gamma = 1-1/e\). That is, does there exist an online algorithm such that for every instance \((G=(V,U;E),d,\{r_i\}_{i\in V})\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}(G,d)] \;\ge\; (1-1/e)\,\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)?
\]
If not, determine the optimal achievable competitive ratio for OBMRR.
open_problem_quote: The main problem left unanswered in our paper is whether one can obtain the competitive ratio of \(1 - 1/e\) for OBMRR.
counterexample_suitability_rationale: One can computationally search for hard instances (graphs and arrival orders) and estimate the empirical competitive ratio of candidate algorithms via simulation, but certifying an upper bound against all algorithms or proving tightness is not directly amenable to finite search. Still, automated discovery may uncover candidate lower-bound instances that refute specific algorithmic approaches toward \(1-1/e\).
alphaevolve_suitability_rationale: Candidate online policies can be parameterized (e.g., priority scores, reranking schedules, correlated selection rules) and evaluated on generated adversarial or worst-case-seeking instance distributions using a computable fitness signal such as estimated worst-case competitive ratio over a test suite. An evolutionary loop could iteratively improve algorithm designs or produce informative adversarial families that challenge \(1-1/e\) aspirations.
