literature_review.synthesis:
In Delong et al.'s OBMRR model, each offline vertex (resource) can be matched at most once in any length-\(d\) window, and the objective is vertex-weighted reward \(\sum r_i\) over matches. The paper highlights that the natural LP relaxation is not integral (integrality gap at least \(7/6\) for \(d=3\)), so achieving the classic \(1-1/e\) ratio for integral algorithms is nontrivial even though the fractional/large-capacity regime admits \(1-1/e\) via balance-style methods. Their own contributions (Periodic Reranking at \(\approx 0.589\) and an OCR-based primal-dual algorithm at \(\approx 0.505\)) establish the first guarantees beating the \(1/2\) greedy barrier for unit-inventory reusable matching, but still fall short of \(1-1/e\).

Forward-citing work has largely reinforced \(1-1/e\) as the right asymptotic benchmark while leaving the exact unit-capacity question open. The strongest progress toward \(1-1/e\) comes from large-inventory/large-capacity analyses: "Asymptotically optimal competitive ratio for online allocation of reusable resources" proves realization-independent algorithms with competitive ratio \((1-1/e-\delta)\) where \(\delta\to 0\) as \(c_{\min}\to\infty\), and also shows an asymptotic \(1-1/e\) upper bound, establishing optimality in that limit. Related large-inventory robustness results (Batched Inventory Balancing under inventory shocks) similarly obtain ratios converging to \(1-1/e\) as initial inventory grows, even with adversarial replenishments.

On the algorithmic-tools side, work on k-rental problems develops lossless dependent online rounding for fixed deterministic durations, suggesting a potential pathway: if one can design a strong fractional OBMRR policy (perhaps via the OBMRR LP or a tighter relaxation) whose marginals satisfy appropriate online-rounding conditions, then one might lift near-\(1-1/e\) fractional performance to the integral setting. However, current rounding results either apply to identical-unit feasibility systems (k-rental) or to non-reusable matching (lossless online rounding for classic OBM), and do not yet yield a constant \(1-1/e\) guarantee under the bipartite-compatibility plus sliding-window reuse constraints. Overall, the problem of achieving an exact \(1-1/e\) competitive ratio for vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic duration \(d\) and unit inventory remains open; the best known worst-case ratios for integral algorithms in this model remain below \(1-1/e\), while \(1-1/e\) is achievable only asymptotically in large-capacity regimes.

sources.title: Asymptotically optimal competitive ratio for online allocation of reusable resources
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives a randomized online algorithm for online bipartite matching/allocation with reusable resources and stochastic usage durations that is asymptotically optimal in the large-capacity regime: for OBMR with capacities \,\(c_i\) and known usage distributions \,\(F_i\), there exists a realization-independent algorithm (Sample G-ALG) with competitive ratio \((1-1/e-\delta)\) where \(\delta=O(\sqrt{\log c_{\min}/c_{\min}})\) and \(c_{\min}=\min_i c_i\); hence the ratio tends to \(1-1/e\) as \(c_{\min}\to\infty\). It also proves an upper bound that no online algorithm can beat \(1-1/e\) asymptotically. Additionally, a simpler Rank-Based Allocation (RBA) policy is shown \((1-1/e-\delta)\)-competitive for several distribution families (e.g., IFR, exponential, certain two-point).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) admits a randomized \((1-1/e)\)-competitive algorithm for all instances (no large-capacity assumption). This paper achieves \((1-1/e)\) only asymptotically as capacities \(c_i\) grow, and primarily for stochastic durations; deterministic duration is a special case, but the guarantee still relies on the large-inventory regime (and/or distributional assumptions for the simpler RBA). Thus it does not resolve the open problem in full generality (notably, it does not give a \((1-1/e)\) guarantee for unit capacities / general capacities, which corresponds to the original OBMRR model with one reusable unit per resource). It does, however, establish optimality of \(1-1/e\) as an asymptotic limit and provides algorithmic/analytic tools (LP-free certificate, fluid-guided rounding) relevant to pursuing the full result.

sources.title: Robustness of online inventory balancing to inventory shocks
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper studies online assortment/allocation with reusable inventory (deterministic return durations \(d_i\)) and adversarial nonnegative exogenous replenishments. It proposes Batched Inventory Balancing (BIB) and proves (Theorem 1) that for any concave nondecreasing penalty \(\Psi\) and batch threshold \(\gamma\in[1,c_0]\), BIB is \(\Gamma(\Psi,\gamma)\)-competitive against a clairvoyant benchmark, where \(\Gamma(\Psi,\gamma)=\min\{\Gamma_1(\Psi,\gamma),\Gamma_2(\Psi,\gamma)\}\) with
- \(\Gamma_1(\Psi,\gamma)=\min_{x\in[0,1-1/c_0]}\Big\{1-\frac{x}{1/c_0+(1+\gamma/c_0)(1-\Psi(x))+\int_{x+1/c_0}^1\Psi(y)\,dy}\Big\}\) (as stated in the paper),
- \(\Gamma_2(\Psi,\gamma)=\min_{x\in[0,1-1/\gamma]}\Big\{1-\frac{x}{1/\gamma+1-\Psi(x)+\int_{x+1/\gamma}^1\Psi(y)\,dy}\Big\}\).
In particular, choosing the exponential penalty \(\Psi(x)=\frac{e^{1-x}-e}{1-e}\) and \(\gamma=\Theta(\sqrt{c_0})\) yields a competitive ratio that converges to \(1-1/e\) as the minimum initial inventory \(c_0\to\infty\) (large-inventory/asymptotic regime), even with both endogenous (returns after \(d_i\)) and exogenous shocks.
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) admits a randomized online algorithm achieving the optimal \(1-1/e\) competitive ratio for all instances (no large-inventory assumption). This paper does not resolve that in full generality. Instead, it proves an asymptotically optimal \(1-1/e\) guarantee in a different but related model (online assortment/allocation) with reusable resources and even additional exogenous replenishments, under a large-inventory regime (competitive ratio approaches \(1-1/e\) as \(c_0\to\infty\)). For OBMRR with capacity 1 per offline vertex (the usual matching setting), \(c_0=1\), so the theorem does not yield \(1-1/e\) and does not close the gap. Nonetheless, the algorithmic idea (batching units) and the randomized primal-dual/interval-assignment analysis are relevant tools that might be adaptable to OBMRR or to the multi-unit (\(b\)-matching) generalization of OBMRR.

sources.title: Leveraging reusability: Improved competitive ratio of greedy for reusable resources
sources.theorem_or_result:
In online weighted bipartite matching with reusable resources and random i.i.d. usage durations per resource, the Greedy policy is provably competitive against an optimal clairvoyant benchmark (knows the request sequence but not duration realizations):
- If each resource returns in one step with probability at least \(p=\min_i \Pr(D_i=1)\), then \(\mathrm{Greedy}/\mathrm{OPT}\ge 1/(2-p)\).
- If usage durations are geometric \(D_i\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p_i)\) with \(p=\min_i p_i\), then \(\mathrm{Greedy}/\mathrm{OPT}\ge (1+p)/2\), and this bound is tight (approachable on a 2-step, 2-resource instance).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) admits a randomized online algorithm achieving the optimal \(1-1/e\) competitive ratio (vs the offline optimum under the same deterministic reusability constraint). This paper does not address the deterministic-duration model nor the \(1-1/e\) target. Instead it studies a different OBMRR variant with random usage durations and analyzes the (deterministic) Greedy algorithm against a weaker benchmark (a clairvoyant that knows arrivals but not duration realizations). It shows competitive ratios improving with a reusability parameter \(p\), but the guarantees are of the form \(1/(2-p)\) or \((1+p)/2\), which do not imply \(1-1/e\) in general and are not stated against the full offline optimum for deterministic \(d\). The coupling/lost-match analysis technique may be a related tool for analyzing reusable-resource matching, but it does not resolve the \(1-1/e\) question for deterministic \(d\).

sources.title: Online Rounding and Pricing Schemes for k-Rental Problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies adversarial online allocation with reusable identical units (k-rental). For kRental-Fixed (all rentals have the same deterministic duration d), it gives a relax-and-round algorithm (dop-\(\phi\)-fixed) that computes an online fractional solution via a price function \(\phi\) and then rounds it using a new dependent rounding subroutine (Algorithm 2) that is lossless: for any feasible fractional targets \(\hat x_n\) satisfying \(\hat x_n \le \min\{1,\, k-\sum_{j<n}\hat x_j\mathbf 1\{a_j+d>a_n\}\}\), the rounding allocates with probability exactly \(\hat x_n\) (Theorem 1). Under bounded valuations \(v_n\in[v_{\min},v_{\max}]\), dop-\(\phi\)-fixed achieves competitive ratio \(1+\ln(v_{\max}/v_{\min})\) with \(\phi(y)=v_{\min}\exp((1+\ln(v_{\max}/v_{\min}))y-1)\) (Theorem 2), and no online algorithm can do better than \(1+\ln(v_{\max}/v_{\min})\) in that model (Proposition 3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether vertex-weighted OBMRR with fixed deterministic reuse duration \(d\) admits a \((1-1/e)\)-competitive randomized online algorithm (matching the classic non-reusable optimum) or, failing that, what the optimal ratio is. This paper does not resolve that: it analyzes a different but related model (k identical reusable units with per-request valuations, not a general bipartite graph with heterogeneous vertex weights and adjacency constraints). Its main relevance is methodological: it introduces a lossless online dependent rounding scheme (1-ocr) for fixed-duration reusability, which could be a component in designing improved OBMRR algorithms if one can obtain strong fractional guarantees for the matching LP. However, the competitive ratios proved here for kRental-Fixed are of the form \(1/(1+\ln(v_{\max}/v_{\min}))\) (in their convention) and depend on bounded valuation ranges, rather than achieving a constant \(1-1/e\) independent of value spread. Thus it provides partial progress/related tools but not a \((1-1/e)\) algorithm for vertex-weighted OBMRR.

sources.title: Online Rounding Schemes for -Rental Problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies adversarial online allocation with reusable identical units (k-rental). For kRental-Fixed (all rentals have the same deterministic duration \(d\)), it gives a relax-and-round algorithm (Algorithm 3) that computes an online fractional solution via a pricing function \(\phi\) and then rounds it using a new lossless online rounding scheme (Algorithm 2). The rounding result is: Algorithm 2 is a \(1\)-ocr (Theorem 1), i.e., for any feasible fractional targets \(\hat x_n\) satisfying \(\hat x_n \le \min\{1,\, k-\sum_{j<n}\hat x_j\mathbf 1\{a_j+d>a_n\}\}\), it produces integral allocations with \(\Pr[x_n=1]\ge \hat x_n\) for all \(n\). For kRental-Fixed under bounded valuations \(v_n\in[v_{\min},v_{\max}]\), their pricing+rounding algorithm dop-\(\phi\)-fixed is \((1+\ln(v_{\max}/v_{\min}))\)-competitive (Theorem 2), and no online algorithm can beat this ratio in that model (Proposition 3).

This paper does not address that question in the general OBMRR model: it studies a different special case with \(k\) identical resources (no bipartite graph structure/compatibility constraints) and request-specific valuations, plus an additional bounded-valuation assumption \([v_{\min},v_{\max}]\). sources.title: Online matching: A brief survey
sources.theorem_or_result:
This paper is a survey and does not prove new competitive-ratio theorems for online bipartite matching with reusable resources. It summarizes known results, including that for OBMRR with identical deterministic usage duration \(d\):
- Fractional/divisible relaxation admits an optimal \(1-1/e\) competitive ratio via generalized balance (citing [GIU21, FNS21]).
- Integral (randomized) algorithms achieve competitive ratios \(0.589\) via periodic reranking and \(0.505\) via an OCS-based algorithm (citing [DFN+23]), extending to vertex-weighted settings.
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether vertex-weighted OBMRR with deterministic usage duration \(d\) admits a randomized online algorithm with competitive ratio \(1-1/e\) against \(\mathrm{OPT}(G,d)\), or else what the optimal ratio is. This survey does not resolve that question; it reports that \(1-1/e\) is known for the fractional version, while the best known guarantees for the integral version (even with identical \(d\) across resources) are below \(1-1/e\) (\(0.589\) and \(0.505\)). It also notes that heterogeneous durations \(d_v\) remain open, but that is a different open direction than achieving \(1-1/e\) for the integral identical-\(d\) model.

title: Constant-factor multiplicative violation for cut-constrained spanning trees in laminar families
background_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with nonnegative edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). For a nonempty proper vertex subset \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta(S)\subseteq E\) denote the cut-set, i.e., edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). A family \(\mathcal{L}\subseteq 2^V\setminus\{\emptyset,V\}\) is laminar if for any \(A,B\in\mathcal{L}\), either \(A\subseteq B\), \(B\subseteq A\), or \(A\cap B=\emptyset\). Consider spanning-tree feasibility: a spanning tree is a set \(T\subseteq E\) with \(|T|=|V|-1\) that connects all vertices.

In a laminarly cut-constrained spanning tree problem, one is given upper bounds \(b_S\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) for each \(S\in\mathcal{L}\), and seeks a spanning tree of minimum cost subject to \(|T\cap \delta(S)|\le b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal{L}\). In the special case where \(\mathcal{L}\) is a chain \(\emptyset\subsetneq S_1\subsetneq S_2\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq S_k\subsetneq V\), this becomes the (upper-bounded) minimum chain-constrained spanning tree problem.

A common approximation notion allows multiplicative violation of the cut constraints: for \(\beta\ge 1\), the spanning tree \(T\) is said to have \(\beta\)-multiplicative violation if \(|T\cap \delta(S)|\le \beta\, b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal{L}\). (Cost may be compared to the optimum cost among spanning trees satisfying all constraints exactly.)
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists a constant \(\beta=O(1)\) and a polynomial-time algorithm that, for every instance \((G=(V,E),c,\mathcal{L},(b_S)_{S\in\mathcal{L}})\) with laminar \(\mathcal{L}\), outputs a spanning tree \(T\subseteq E\) such that
\[|T\cap \delta(S)|\le \beta\, b_S \quad\text{for all } S\in\mathcal{L},\]
while having cost
\[c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT}),\]
where \(\mathrm{OPT}\) denotes a minimum-cost spanning tree satisfying \(|\mathrm{OPT}\cap \delta(S)|\le b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal{L}\).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Nägele--Zenklusen’s framework, the laminar cut-constrained spanning tree problem (upper bounds \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le b_S\) for \(S\in\mathcal L\)) is highlighted as a canonical setting where iterative relaxation yields near-optimal additive violations but leaves open whether one can obtain \(O(1)\)-multiplicative violations while preserving optimal cost \(c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\). Their paper achieves a quasi-polynomial-time \((1,1+\varepsilon)\) guarantee for chain constraints and extends to laminar families of bounded width, but the running time is quasi-polynomial in general and does not settle the fully polynomial-time, general-laminar question.

Subsequent work has made substantial progress on the multiplicative-violation side for general laminar families via “laminar thin tree” techniques. In particular, "Thin trees for laminar families" and Klein’s dissertation chapter on laminar crossing spanning trees provide constant-factor bicriteria approximations: they output a spanning tree with \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le \beta b_S\) for a constant \(\beta\), but at the price of a constant-factor increase in cost (e.g. \(c(T)\le O(1)\,c(\mathrm{OPT})\)). These results can be viewed as achieving constant thinness with respect to an explicitly given laminar family, aligning with the thin-tree motivations discussed by Nägele--Zenklusen.

However, the open problem’s stricter requirement \(c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\) (no cost blow-up) remains unmet by the cited forward work: existing constant-\(\beta\) guarantees appear to require relaxing the objective, while exact-cost guarantees are currently known mainly for additive-violation regimes (iterative relaxation) or for restricted laminar structure (chains / bounded width with quasi-polynomial dependence). A promising direction suggested by the trajectory is to combine laminar-aligned rounding/iterative relaxation (to control \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\)) with objective-preserving “alteration” or exchange-based local improvement steps (as in Nägele--Zenklusen) to try to remove the constant cost factor, but no such full resolution is present in the provided citation set.

sources.title: Thin trees for laminar families
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives the first constant-factor approximation for laminar cut-constrained spanning trees relative to the natural LP. In particular (Theorem 2.4), given a feasible LP solution \(x\) to \(\min c^\top x\) s.t. \(x\in P_{st}(G)\) and \(x(\delta(S))\le b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal L\), it outputs in polynomial time a spanning tree \(T\) with \(c(T)\le (2+\sqrt7)c(x)<5c(x)\) and \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le 22\,x(\delta(S))\le 22\,b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal L\). More generally (Theorem 2.5), for any \(\eta>2\) it outputs \(T\) with \(c(T)\le \eta c(x)\) and \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le \frac{(2\eta+3)}{1-2/\eta}\,x(\delta(S))\) for all \(S\in\mathcal L\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time algorithm for laminar families achieving constant multiplicative violation \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le \beta b_S\) while keeping cost \(c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\) (no cost increase). This paper directly addresses the laminar cut-constrained spanning tree setting and achieves a constant \(\beta\) (e.g. \(\beta<22\)) multiplicative violation, but it does so with a constant-factor cost blow-up: \(c(T)\le 5\,c(\mathrm{OPT})\) (since \(c(x)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\)). Thus it makes strong partial progress on the feasibility/violation aspect for general laminar families, but does not meet the open problem’s requirement of preserving optimal cost (factor 1).

Olver), the dissertation proves a constant-factor bicriteria approximation for the laminar crossing spanning tree / laminar thin tree problem: given a weighted graph and a laminar family \(\mathcal L\) with bounds \(b_S\) such that there exists a spanning tree \(T\) with \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal L\), one can find in polynomial time a spanning tree \(T'\) with \(c(T')\le O(1)\,c(T)\) and \(|T'\cap\delta(S)|\le O(1)\,b_S\) for all \(S\in\mathcal L\). The chapter also yields existence/constructive results for laminar-thin trees (thinness w.r.t. a laminar family).

Klein’s dissertation directly addresses the same constraint structure (laminar families of cut upper bounds) and achieves constant-factor multiplicative violation, but it also incurs a constant-factor increase in cost (\(c(T')\le O(1)\,c(\mathrm{OPT})\)), not the exact-cost guarantee \(c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\). Thus it provides strong partial progress (first constant-factor bicriteria approximation) but does not resolve the stricter ‘cost \(\le\) OPT’ requirement of the open problem.

sources.title: Reducing path TSP to TSP
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives a black-box reduction from Path TSP to TSP: given an \(\alpha\)-approximation for TSP, for any \(\varepsilon>0\) it yields an \((\alpha+\varepsilon)\)-approximation for Path TSP (Theorem 1). Technically it introduces \(\Phi\)-TSP (interfaces \(\Phi=(I,T,C)\)) and a “Boosting Theorem” (Theorem 10) that, given an \(\alpha\)-approximation for TSP and a \(\beta\)-approximation for \(\Phi\)-TSP, produces a better \(\Phi\)-TSP approximation with factor \(\max\{(1+\varepsilon)\alpha,\,\beta-\tfrac{\varepsilon}{8}(\beta-1)\}\), using dynamic programming over a laminar family derived from a minimum \(T\)-join dual.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a constant-factor \(\beta\) multiplicative violation algorithm for minimum-cost spanning trees with laminar cut upper bounds \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le b_S\), while preserving optimal cost \(c(T)\le c(\mathrm{OPT})\). This paper is about approximation-preserving reductions for (Path) TSP and a generalized \(\Phi\)-TSP, not about spanning trees with laminar cut upper bounds. It does, however, use a dynamic program that guesses edges across cuts in a laminar family (Section 5, Theorem 17) and explicitly cites N\u00e4gele–Zenklusen (2019) as inspiration for guessing a constant number of edges per cut. Thus it provides technique-level inspiration (DP over laminar families / interfaces), but it does not address feasibility/cost guarantees for laminar cut-constrained spanning trees, nor multiplicative violation bounds.

title: Characterize and compute limits of operator Sinkhorn algorithm for nonscalable operators
background_latex:
Let \(\Phi\) be a completely positive linear operator acting on complex matrices (equivalently, a linear map \(\Phi: \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}\) that maps positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices). Operator scaling asks for invertible matrices \(L,R\) such that the scaled operator \(X\mapsto L\,\Phi(RXR^*)\,L^*\) satisfies prescribed left and right marginals (the operator analogue of making a nonnegative matrix doubly stochastic). The operator Sinkhorn algorithm (also called the Gurvits algorithm) is an iterative normalization procedure that alternately rescales the operator to correct its left and right marginals, generalizing the classical Sinkhorn algorithm for matrix scaling.

In the nonscalable case (i.e., when no choice of \(L,R\) can make \(\Phi\) doubly stochastic, even approximately), an analogue of a Hall-type certificate exists: a nontrivial subspace \(W\subsetneq \mathbb{C}^n\) that is "shrunk" by \(\Phi\) (often called a shrunk subspace). Existence of such a shrunk subspace certifies nonscalability, in the same way that a Hall blocker certifies absence of a perfect matching for bipartite graphs.

The cited paper discusses extending matrix-scaling-based certificate-finding results to operator scaling, and notes that doing so may require understanding the limiting behavior (or limit objects/accumulation structure) of the operator Sinkhorn iterates in the nonscalable case.

literature_review.synthesis:
In the matrix case, Hayashi–Hirai–Sakabe analyze nonscalable Sinkhorn iterates by reinterpreting the algorithm as alternating minimization for KL-divergence between the row- and column-marginal affine slices. When the target marginals are infeasible, the iterates converge to an oscillating pair \((M^*,N^*)\) minimizing the KL objective, and the limit marginals \(p^*=N^*\mathbf 1\) admit an explicit block-constant form governed by a refined Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) decomposition / principal partition of a polymatroid. This yields a concrete “limit object” (a canonical flag/partition) from which Hall blockers can be read off by sorting the limiting marginals.

For operator scaling, the forward-citation literature provides substantial partial progress toward an analogous description, but not a complete characterization of the accumulation set of the standard operator Sinkhorn (Gurvits) iteration in the nonscalable regime. The paper “Gradient descent for unbounded convex functions on Hadamard manifolds and its applications to scaling problems” develops a general recession-function theory for geodesically convex objectives on Hadamard manifolds and applies it to the operator-scaling Kempf–Ness potential. In the nonscalable case, it proves that gradient flow/descent diverges but converges in cone topology to a unique boundary direction characterized by a generalized DM-flag and the minimum-norm point of the moment polytope; this direction canonically encodes shrunk-subspace certificates. Complementarily, “A scaling characterization of nc-rank via unbounded gradient flow” gives a duality between minimal achievable scaling residuals and the recession function \(f^\infty\), identifying \(f^\infty\) with a Lovász-extension-type formula over flags/subspaces, again linking limit directions at infinity to shrunk subspaces.

On the algorithmic side, “Shrunk subspaces via operator Sinkhorn iteration” shows that one can deterministically compute the (unique) minimum shrunk subspace in polynomial time using a Sinkhorn-style iteration for a modified (majorization/perturbed) capacity, together with rounding from approximate independent sets. This effectively computes a canonical certificate associated with nonscalability, but it bypasses a full dynamical description of the original operator Sinkhorn iterates’ accumulation points. Overall, the problem of characterizing and computing the actual limit/accumulation structure of the unmodified operator Sinkhorn algorithm for nonscalable completely positive operators appears to remain open; the most promising direction is to transfer the recession-function/DM-flag machinery from continuous-time gradient flows to the discrete alternating-normalization dynamics, aiming for an operator analogue of the matrix-case oscillatory limit pair and its block-triangular structure.

sources.title: Gradient descent for unbounded convex functions on Hadamard manifolds and its applications to scaling problems
sources.theorem_or_result: For the operator-scaling Kempf–Ness function \(f_A(x,y)=\log\operatorname{tr}\sum_{\ell=1}^N xA_\ell yA_\ell^\dagger\) on the Hadamard manifold \(\mathcal P_n^1\times\mathcal P_m^1\), if \(A\) is not \((1/n,1/m)\)-scalable then gradient descent/flow diverges to infinity but converges in cone topology to the unique minimizer of the recession function \(f_A^\infty\) (Theorems 3.7 and 4.24, Corollary 4.25). The limit direction is explicitly characterized by a generalized Dulmage–Mendelsohn (DM) decomposition: there is a canonical coarse DM-flag \(\mathbb C^n=X_0\supset\cdots\supset X_\theta=\{0\}\), \(\{0\}=Y_0\subset\cdots\subset Y_\theta=\mathbb C^m\) yielding block sizes \((n_\alpha,m_\alpha)\) and a vector \((p^*,q^*)\in\Delta_A\) (minimum-norm point of the moment polytope) given by \(p^*=-\tfrac1n\mathbf 1+\tfrac1{C_A}\sum_{\alpha=1}^\theta \tfrac{m_\alpha}{n_\alpha+m_\alpha}\mathbf 1_{I_\alpha}\), \(q^*=-\tfrac1m\mathbf 1+\tfrac1{C_A}\sum_{\alpha=1}^\theta \tfrac{n_\alpha}{n_\alpha+m_\alpha}\mathbf 1_{J_\alpha}\), with \(C_A=\sum_{\alpha} \tfrac{n_\alpha m_\alpha}{n_\alpha+m_\alpha}\), and the cone-limit equals \((G^*,H^*)/\|(G^*,H^*)\|\) where \(G^*=(\sigma^*)^\dagger\operatorname{diag}(-p^*)\sigma^*\), \(H^*=(\tau^*)^\dagger\operatorname{diag}(-q^*)\tau^*\) (Theorem 4.24).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize and compute limits/accumulation structure of operator Sinkhorn iterates for nonscalable completely positive operators. This paper does not analyze the alternating-normalization (Sinkhorn/Gurvits) iterates directly, but it gives a detailed characterization of the limit at infinity for closely related first-order methods (gradient flow/descent of the operator-scaling Kempf–Ness function on \(\mathcal P_n^1\times\mathcal P_m^1\)). In the nonscalable case it proves cone-topology convergence to a unique boundary point (a canonical destabilizing direction) and identifies it via a generalized DM decomposition, yielding explicit block-triangular structure and a way to extract a shrunk subspace. It further conjectures an analogous oscillatory limit-set description for the operator Sinkhorn algorithm (end of §4.2), suggesting how the Sinkhorn accumulation might relate to the same DM blocks, but stops short of proving it for Sinkhorn itself.

sources.title: Shrunk subspaces via operator Sinkhorn iteration
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives a deterministic polynomial-time Sinkhorn-style method to extract the (unique) minimum shrunk subspace from operator-scaling-type iterations. Concretely, for a CP map \(\Phi\) with Kraus operators spanning a matrix space \(\mathcal A\), it introduces a perturbed/majorization capacity \(\mathrm{cap}_{k,r}(\Phi)=\inf_{X\succeq I,\,Y\succeq I,\,z\ge 0}\big(\mathrm{Tr}(\Phi(X^{-1})Y^{-1}e^{z})+\log\det X+\log\det Y-kz-\tfrac1n\sum_{i=n-r+1}^n\lambda_i(\log X)\big)\) and proves (Theorem 3.10) that \(\mathrm{cap}_{k,r}(\Phi)>-\infty\) iff \((k,r)\le (k^*,r^*)\) in lexicographic order, where \(k^*=\mathrm{nc\text{-}rank}(\mathcal A)\) and \(r^*\) is the minimum \(\dim R\) among maximum independent sets \((L,R)\). It then gives algorithms DecisionSinkhorn/ApproxIndep/RoundSubspaces (Theorems 3.11–3.15) that (i) decide finiteness of \(\mathrm{cap}_{k,r}\), (ii) when \(\mathrm{cap}_{k,r}=-\infty\) output an \(\varepsilon\)-independent set violating \((k,r)\), and (iii) for \((k,r)=(k^*,r^*+1)\) round an exponentially accurate approximate independent set to the exact dominant independent set \((L^*,R^*)\), hence outputting the smallest shrunk subspace \(R^*\), all in deterministic polynomial time over \(\mathbb C\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize and compute the limit/accumulation structure of operator Sinkhorn iterates in the nonscalable case. This paper does not fully characterize all accumulation points of the *standard* operator Sinkhorn (Gurvits) iteration. However, it makes strong algorithmic progress on the core motivation: extracting Hall-type certificates (shrunk subspaces) from Sinkhorn-style iterations when scaling is impossible. It does so by (a) modifying the objective/iteration to a majorization/perturbed capacity whose unboundedness corresponds to existence of a violating independent set/shrunk subspace, and (b) proving that sufficiently long runs yield an approximate shrunk subspace that can be rounded to the exact minimum shrunk subspace. This effectively provides a computable ‘limit object’ (the dominant independent set / minimum shrunk subspace) associated to divergence, even though it bypasses a full dynamical description of accumulation points of the original operator Sinkhorn iterates.

sources.title: A scaling characterization of nc-rank via unbounded gradient flow
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a duality/limit-at-infinity characterization for operator scaling residuals and applies it to nc-rank. In particular, for a matrix tuple \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_m)\) with associated completely positive operator \(T_A(X)=\sum_i A_i X A_i^\dagger\), it shows
- \(n-\mathrm{nc\text{-}rank}(A)=\tfrac12\inf_{g,h\in GL(n,\mathbb C)}\big(\|T_{g^\dagger A h}(I)-I\|_1+\|T^*_{g^\dagger A h}(I)-I\|_1\big)\) (Theorem 1.4).
More generally, for a differentiable geodesically convex \(f\) on \(P_n\) with a \(GL_n\)-invariant Finsler metric induced by a unitarily invariant norm \(\|\cdot\|_v\), it proves
\[\inf_{X\in P_n}\|df(X)\|^*_{v,X}=\sup_{H\in S_n:\ \|H\|_v\le 1}-f^\infty(H),\]
and that along a (metric-space) curve of maximal slope \(X(t)\) one has \(\|df(X(t))\|^*_{v,X(t)}\to\kappa^*\) and any accumulation point of \(H(t):=\log X(t)/d_v(I,X(t))\) attains \(f^\infty(H^*)=-\kappa^*\) (Theorem 3.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize/compute limits or accumulation structure of operator Sinkhorn iterates for nonscalable completely positive operators. This paper does not analyze the discrete operator Sinkhorn (alternating normalization) iterates directly. However, it provides a closely related continuous-time picture: it models operator-scaling residuals as the (dual) norm of the differential of a geodesically convex function \(f\) on \(P_n\), and studies an unbounded gradient-flow/curve-of-maximal-slope \(X(t)\) when \(f\) is unbounded below (the nonscalable regime). It characterizes accumulation points at infinity via the recession function \(f^\infty\), which in the operator-scaling setting is identified with the Lovasz extension of the submodular defect \(U\mapsto \dim(AU)-\dim(U)\) (Lemma 4.4). This gives a structural description of ‘limit directions’ (flags and weights) that correspond to shrunk subspaces/certificates, and a dual optimization problem (Remark 4.6). It is thus partial progress/related framework toward understanding nonscalable limits, but it stops short of proving convergence/accumulation descriptions for the actual operator Sinkhorn iterates or giving an explicit algorithm to compute their limit points.

sources.title: 行列スケーリングから非正曲率空間上の測地的凸最適化へ
sources.theorem_or_result:
This article is an expository survey; it does not prove new theorems about the nonscalable operator Sinkhorn limit. The main formal statements it highlights include Gurvits’ characterization for operator scaling (Theorem 4.1): for a completely positive map 
\[T(X)=\sum_{k=1}^m A_k X A_k^\dagger,\]
approximate doubly-stochastic scalability is equivalent to positivity of the capacity-like infimum 
\[\inf_{X,Y\succ 0}\frac{\big(\sum_k \mathrm{tr}(X A_k Y A_k^\dagger)\big)^n}{\det X\,\det Y}>0,\]
to a Hall-type condition on subspaces \(U,V\) with \(u^\dagger A_k v=0\), and to convergence of operator Sinkhorn when scalable. It also summarizes convex-analytic tools on Hadamard spaces, notably the definition of a recession/‘boundary’ function \(f^\infty\) on the boundary at infinity \(CM_\infty\) (Eq. (5.10)) and the criterion that boundedness of \(f\) implies \(f^\infty\ge 0\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks to characterize/compute limits or accumulation points of operator Sinkhorn iterates in the nonscalable case. This survey explicitly notes that in the matrix case, nonscalable Sinkhorn behavior is tied to recession analysis and references work on the nonconvergent case; for operator scaling it discusses the geodesically convex formulation (objective (4.3) on \(\mathcal P_n\times\mathcal P_n\)) and introduces Hadamard-space convex analysis via boundary-at-infinity/recession functions (Section 5.4). These tools are plausibly relevant to describing divergence directions/limit objects of iterates when the objective is unbounded below (nonscalable case), but the article does not itself analyze the operator Sinkhorn iterates’ accumulation structure or provide an algorithm to compute their limits in the nonscalable regime.

title: Determine diameter of acyclic and preorder preference spaces under top-difference semimetric
background_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite set of alternatives with \(|X|=n\ge 2\). An (acyclic) preference relation in the paper is modeled as an \emph{acyclic order} \(\%\) on \(X\), i.e., a reflexive binary relation whose strict (asymmetric) part \(\succ\) contains no directed cycle: there do not exist pairwise distinct \(z_1,\dots,z_k\in X\) with \(z_1\succ z_2\succ\cdots\succ z_k\succ z_1\).

For any binary relation \(R\) on \(X\) and any nonempty subset \(S\subseteq X\), the set of \(R\)-maximal elements of \(S\) is
\[M(S,R):=\{x\in S: \text{there is no }y\in S\text{ with }y\,R^{>}\,x\},\]
where \(R^{>}\) denotes the asymmetric part of \(R\). For acyclic orders \(\%\), every nonempty finite \(S\) has \(M(S,\%)\neq\varnothing\).

Define the \emph{top-difference semimetric} \(D\) on the set \(A(X)\) of all acyclic orders on \(X\) by
\[D(\%,\mathcal{D}) := \sum_{S\subseteq X} \bigl| M(S,\%)\,\triangle\, M(S,\mathcal{D})\bigr|,\]
where \(\triangle\) is symmetric difference and \(|\cdot|\) is cardinality. (Singleton and empty \(S\) contribute \(0\), but the definition sums over all \(S\subseteq X\).)

For any subset \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq A(X)\), its diameter with respect to \(D\) is
\[\operatorname{diam}_D(\mathcal{C}) := \max\{ D(\%,\mathcal{D}) : \%,\mathcal{D}\in \mathcal{C}\},\]
which is well-defined since \(\mathcal{C}\) is finite when \(X\) is finite.

Let \(P(X)\subseteq A(X)\) denote the set of all preorders on \(X\) (reflexive and transitive relations).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Nishimura–Ok (2022), the top-difference semimetric \(D(\%,\mathcal D)=\sum_{S\subseteq X}|M(S,\%)\triangle M(S,\mathcal D)|\) is introduced on the space \(A(X)\) of acyclic orders, motivated by comparing induced choice correspondences menu-by-menu. The paper provides axiomatic characterizations for \(D\) and its weighted variants \(D_\mu\), and derives alternative formulas (notably a polynomial-time computable expression) that avoid summing over all \(2^n\) subsets directly. In terms of global geometry, it computes the diameter exactly for complete preferences (total preorders) \(P_{\mathrm{total}}(X)\): \(\operatorname{diam}_D(P_{\mathrm{total}}(X)) = n2^{n-1}+2-2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}-2^{\lceil n/2\rceil}\), and also notes \(\operatorname{diam}_D(L(X))=2(2^n-n-1)\) for linear orders.

The open problem is to determine \(\operatorname{diam}_D(P(X))\) and/or \(\operatorname{diam}_D(A(X))\) as functions of \(n\). The source paper establishes only the lower bound \(\operatorname{diam}_D(A(X))\ge \operatorname{diam}_D(P(X))\ge \operatorname{diam}_D(P_{\mathrm{total}}(X))\) and explicitly states that it is unknown whether either inequality is an equality. Among the (few) forward citations provided here, one paper develops a weighted top-difference framework but restricts attention to linear orders, offering reformulations and axioms that could be useful for diameter computations on \(S_n\) yet does not address \(A(X)\) or \(P(X)\). Another citing paper is only tangential, referencing the metric viewpoint without contributing to diameter calculations.

At present, based on the available forward-citation evidence, the diameter of \((A(X),D)\) and \((P(X),D)\) remains open beyond the known exact formulas for \(L(X)\) and \(P_{\mathrm{total}}(X)\). Promising directions include constructing extremal pairs of acyclic orders/preorders that maximize menu-wise maximal-set disagreement, and leveraging the polynomial-time reformulation of \(D\) (in terms of principal ideals and overlap parameters) to turn the diameter problem into a combinatorial optimization over DAGs or transitive relations.

sources.title: On the Weighted Top-Difference Distance: Axioms, Aggregation, and Approximation
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper defines a family of weighted top-difference distances on linear orders (permutations) 
\[d^{\mu}_{\beta}(\sigma,\pi)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n],\ |S|\ge2}\beta_{|S|}\,\mu\bigl(M(S,\sigma)\triangle M(S,\pi)\bigr),\]
with computable reformulation 
\[d^{\mu}_{\beta}(\sigma,\pi)=\sum_{x\in[n]}\bigl(f_{\beta}(|x_{\downarrow,\pi}|)+f_{\beta}(|x_{\downarrow,\sigma}|)-2f_{\beta}(|x_{\downarrow,\sigma}\cap x_{\downarrow,\pi}|)\bigr)\mu(x),\]
where \(f_{\beta}(t)=\sum_{k=2}^n \beta_k\binom{t}{k-1}\). It also gives an axiomatic characterization (Theorem 9) of these distances among semimetrics on \(S_n\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the diameter under the (unweighted) top-difference semimetric \(D\) on the space of acyclic orders \(A(X)\) and/or preorders \(P(X)\). This paper studies a weighted generalization of the same top-difference construction but only on the restricted domain of linear orders \(S_n\) (rankings), not on all acyclic orders or preorders. It does not compute diameters of \((A(X),D)\) or \((P(X),D)\), nor even the diameter on \(S_n\) for the neutral unweighted case. Its main relevance is providing formulas and structural characterizations that could be used to attempt diameter computations in the linear-order subspace.

sources.title: Semantics meets attractiveness: Choice by salience
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces and characterizes a context-dependent choice model (“rationalization by salience”, RS) and a testable special case (“rationalization by linear salience”, RLS). A central characterization (Theorem 3) states that for a choice function on a finite set, being RLS is equivalent to (ii) asymmetry of a revealed-salience relation \((\prec)\) defined from minimal WARP violations, and equivalent to (iii) absence of “conflicting menus”. The paper also proves existence of “moody” choices (Theorem 1) and that the fraction of moody choices tends to 1 as \(|X|\to\infty\) (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the exact diameter of the space of acyclic orders (and of preorders) under the top-difference semimetric \(D(\%,\mathcal D)=\sum_{S\subseteq X}|M(S,\%)\triangle M(S,\mathcal D)|\). This citing paper does not study the semimetric \(D\), does not compute any diameters of \(A(X)\) or \(P(X)\), and does not analyze maximal-element symmetric-difference sums over all subsets. It only cites Nishimura–Ok (2022) in passing (as a possible “metric for preferences”) and develops a different framework about salience-based choice rationalizations. At most, it is tangentially related by pointing to the broader theme of defining meaningful distances/metrics on preference relations (footnote referencing ‘a semantically meaningful notion of metric for preferences’), but it provides no results usable to compute \(\operatorname{diam}_D(A(X))\) or \(\operatorname{diam}_D(P(X))\).

title: Determine the asymptotically tight rainbow cycle number in bounded-partite digraphs
background_latex:
Fix an integer \(d\ge 1\). A directed \(k\)-partite graph is a digraph \(G=(V,E)\) whose vertex set is partitioned into \(k\) (nonempty) parts \(V_1,\dots,V_k\), and edges may go between any ordered pair of vertices (including across parts), with no restriction on directions.

Consider directed \(k\)-partite graphs \(G=(\bigcup_{i=1}^k V_i,E)\) satisfying the following properties:

1) (Bounded part size) \(|V_i|\le d\) for all \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\).

2) (Pairwise in-neighborhood condition) For any two distinct parts \(V_i\) and \(V_j\), every vertex \(v\in V_i\) has an incoming edge from some vertex in \(V_j\), and every vertex \(w\in V_j\) has an incoming edge from some vertex in \(V_i\). Equivalently, for all distinct \(i\neq j\) and every \(v\in V_i\), there exists \(u\in V_j\) with \((u,v)\in E\).

3) (No rainbow cycle) There is no directed cycle \(C\) in \(G\) that intersects each part at most once, i.e., \(|C\cap V_i|\le 1\) for every \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\).

Define the rainbow cycle number \(R(d)\) to be the largest integer \(k\) for which there exists a directed \(k\)-partite graph satisfying properties 1)–3) above.

literature_review.synthesis:
The rainbow cycle number \(R(d)\), introduced by Chaudhury–Garg–Mehlhorn–Mehta–Misra, asks for the largest number of parts \(k\) in a directed \(k\)-partite graph with part sizes \(\le d\) such that (i) for every two distinct parts \(V_i,V_j\), each vertex in \(V_i\) has an in-neighbor in \(V_j\) (and vice versa), yet (ii) there is no directed cycle that uses at most one vertex from each part (a “rainbow” directed cycle). The source paper proves the first general polynomial upper bound \(R(d)\le d^4+d\) via a two-stage construction: first building a cycle that may revisit one special part \(\widetilde V_\ell\), then “bypassing” repeated visits using carefully chosen intermediate parts to obtain a simple rainbow cycle. It also gives a linear lower bound \(R(d)\ge d\), leaving a wide gap and explicitly conjecturing \(R(d)=O(d)\).

Subsequent work cited in the source paper improves the upper bound by refining the bypass construction. In particular, “EFX: A simpler approach and an (almost) optimal guarantee via rainbow cycle number” exploits the observation (also noted in the MOR acknowledgments) that it suffices to prepare bypass parts only for consecutive pairs \((V_i,V_{i+1})\) along the eventual cycle, leading to an improved bound \(R(d)=O(d^3)\). Related cycle/fixed-point techniques in “Fixed-point cycles and approximate EFX allocations” are also referenced as contributing to improved rainbow-cycle-number-driven guarantees. However, none of the available citing works (including the fair-division paper “Almost Envy-Free Allocation,” which only cites \(R(d)\) as background) resolves the main asymptotic question: whether \(R(d)\) is linear in \(d\), or more generally what the tight growth rate is.

At present, the best documented general bounds remain polynomially separated, with \(d\le R(d)\le O(d^3)\) (improving the original \(O(d^4)\) bound) and the central conjecture \(R(d)=O(d)\) still open. Promising directions include sharpening the bypass/representative-set method to reduce the number of auxiliary parts needed, and exploring extremal digraph tools tailored to the strong pairwise in-neighborhood condition (a dense, multipartite analogue of minimum in-degree conditions) to force a transversal directed cycle.

sources.title: Almost Envy-Free Allocation
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves several EFX/approximate-EFX existence results via weighted envy graphs, rank, and virtual value. In particular:
- For (∞,1)-bounded valuations: existence of an EFX allocation discarding at most \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor-1\) goods (Theorem 5.6) and a complete EF2X allocation (Theorem 5.7).
- For restricted additive valuations: existence of a \(\sqrt{2}/2\)-EFX allocation (Theorem 6.1).
- For (∞,1)-bounded subadditive valuations: existence of a \(\sqrt{2}/2\)-EFX allocation (Theorem 7.1).
- For restricted additive and (2,∞)-bounded valuations: existence of a complete EFX allocation (Theorem 8.1).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for asymptotically tight bounds on the rainbow cycle number \(R(d)\) in bounded-partite digraphs (a purely graph-theoretic extremal question motivated by EFX). This citing paper is about fair-division algorithms for special valuation classes and uses envy-graph/rank/virtual-value machinery. In the provided text, it cites work on “rainbow cycle number” as motivation/background (e.g., [25], [2], [37]) but does not analyze \(R(d)\) itself, nor prove new upper/lower bounds for \(R(d)\) as a function of \(d\). Thus it does not resolve whether \(R(d)=O(d)\) or provide asymptotically tight bounds.

At most, the paper’s techniques (rankpaths, virtual values, LP feasibility preventing multiplicative cycles) are conceptually adjacent to the cycle-avoidance phenomena that rainbow-cycle-number arguments exploit, so it could be viewed as providing related tools/insight for EFX proofs, not progress on the extremal digraph parameter \(R(d)\).

title: Determine the MMS guarantee of EFX pure Nash equilibria for two agents
background_latex:
Consider a finite set of indivisible goods \(M\) and two agents \(N=\{1,2\}\). Each agent \(i\) has a nonnegative additive valuation \(v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), i.e., \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)\) for all \(S\subseteq M\).

An allocation is a partition \(A=(A_1,A_2)\) of \(M\). For \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), the allocation is \(\alpha\)-maximin-share fair (\(\alpha\)-MMS) for agent \(i\) if \(v_i(A_i)\ge \alpha\,\mu_i\), where the maximin share is
\[\mu_i = \mu_i(2,M) := \max_{(P_1,P_2)\in \Pi_2(M)} \min\{v_i(P_1),v_i(P_2)\},\]
with \(\Pi_2(M)\) the set of all 2-way partitions of \(M\).

Envy-freeness up to any good (EFX) for two agents means: for each \(i\ne j\), for every good \(g\in A_j\) with \(v_i(g)>0\),
\[ v_i(A_i) \ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\}). \]

A (deterministic, no-money) allocation mechanism \(\mathcal{M}\) maps a bid profile \(b=(b_1,b_2)\), where each \(b_i\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{|M|}\), to an allocation \(\mathcal{M}(b)\). Given true valuations \(v=(v_1,v_2)\), a bid profile \(b\) is a pure Nash equilibrium (PNE) if no agent can increase her true utility \(v_i\big(\mathcal{M}(b)_i\big)\) by unilaterally changing her bid vector.

Say that a mechanism \(\mathcal{M}\) has EFX PNE on all instances if for every pair \((v_1,v_2)\) it admits at least one PNE, and for every PNE \(b\), the induced allocation \(\mathcal{M}(b)\) is EFX with respect to the true valuations \((v_1,v_2)\).
problem_definition_latex:
Find the best universal constant \(\alpha^*\in[0,1]\) such that the following holds:

For every mechanism \(\mathcal{M}\) that, for every additive-valuation instance \((v_1,v_2)\), has at least one pure Nash equilibrium and every pure Nash equilibrium induces an EFX allocation with respect to \((v_1,v_2)\), every such equilibrium allocation \(A=\mathcal{M}(b)\) satisfies
\[ v_i(A_i) \ge \alpha^*\,\mu_i \quad \text{for both } i\in\{1,2\}. \]

Equivalently, determine the tight worst-case MMS approximation guarantee (as a function-free constant) enjoyed by EFX allocations arising at PNE of mechanisms whose PNE always exist and are always EFX. In particular, decide whether one can always take \(\alpha^*=1\) (MMS always), or whether \(\alpha^*<1\), and if so, determine the optimal \(\alpha^*\) (the paper proves existence of some \(\alpha>2/3\)).

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem asks for the tight universal constant \(\alpha^*\) such that, for every two-agent additive instance and every mechanism whose pure Nash equilibria (PNE) always exist and whose every PNE outcome is EFX with respect to the true valuations, every equilibrium allocation is \(\alpha^*\)-MMS for both agents. In the non-strategic setting, EFX alone only implies \(2/3\)-MMS and this is tight (Theorem 2.6 in the source paper, via Amanatidis et al. 2018). The source paper shows that imposing the strategic equilibrium requirement strengthens the MMS guarantee beyond what EFX alone provides.

Concretely, the source paper proves three key partial results. First, for the specific Plaut--Roughgarden Mod-Cut&Choose mechanism, PNE always exist and every PNE outcome is MMS (hence EFX for \(n=2\)) (Theorem 4.3). Second, for the entire class of mechanisms with guaranteed PNE existence and universal EFX-at-PNE, when \(|M|=4\) every PNE outcome must be MMS (Theorem 4.5), already separating equilibrium EFX from arbitrary EFX allocations. Third, for general \(|M|\), every such mechanism guarantees \(\alpha\)-MMS at every PNE for some universal constant \(\alpha>2/3\) (Theorem 4.7), but the proof is non-quantitative about the best possible \(\alpha\) and does not settle whether \(\alpha^*=1\).

The forward-citing literature provided here does not resolve the tight value of \(\alpha^*\). The two surveys ("Fair division of indivisible goods: Recent progress and open questions" and "Algorithmic fair allocation of indivisible items: A survey and new questions") contextualize the question among EFX/MMS and strategic equilibrium research but do not improve bounds. Related incentive frameworks ("Fair shares: Feasibility, domination, and incentives") and work in different strategic models ("Fair Division with Interdependent Values") indicate alternative ways to obtain MMS-like guarantees under incentives, but they do not address the stringent requirement that every PNE be EFX in the independent additive model. Thus, determining whether \(\alpha^*=1\) or finding the optimal \(\alpha^*<1\) remains open; promising directions include constructing explicit counterexamples (mechanisms/instances) that force an EFX PNE below MMS, or strengthening the structural arguments in Theorem 4.7 to yield an explicit tight constant.

sources.theorem_or_result: This paper is a survey and does not prove new theorems about the maximin-share (MMS) guarantee of EFX pure Nash equilibria (PNE) mechanisms for two agents. The only directly relevant content is a summary of prior work: it cites Amanatidis et al. [2021b] on mechanisms with always-existing PNE whose equilibrium outcomes are EF1, and it poses an open question about whether stronger guarantees than EF1 are possible at PNE (Open Problem 10).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the tight worst-case MMS approximation factor \(\alpha^*\) guaranteed at every PNE of any mechanism whose PNE always exist and are always EFX (for two additive agents). This survey does not analyze EFX-at-PNE mechanisms or derive any MMS lower/upper bounds for such equilibria. It only provides background on EFX and MMS notions and briefly discusses strategic agents, noting that equilibrium analysis has been done for Round-Robin (yielding EF1 at equilibrium) and asking whether stronger-than-EF1 equilibrium guarantees exist. Thus it neither resolves nor makes partial progress on determining \(\alpha^*\).

sources.title: Algorithmic fair allocation of indivisible items: A survey and new questions
sources.theorem_or_result: This paper is a survey; it does not prove a new theorem resolving the open problem. It summarizes known results on EFX, MMS, and strategic behavior in allocation mechanisms, including that for two agents Divide-and-Choose returns an allocation that is MMS and EFX (under appropriate tie-breaking/leximin++), and it cites Amanatidis et al. (2021b) for the result that Round-Robin PNE outcomes are EF1 w.r.t. true values.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the tight worst-case MMS approximation \,\(\alpha^*\) guaranteed by EFX allocations that arise as pure Nash equilibria of mechanisms whose PNE always exist and are always EFX. This survey does not analyze MMS guarantees of EFX-PNE mechanisms, nor does it provide bounds or constructions for \,\(\alpha^*\). It only provides context: (i) relationships between EFX and MMS in non-strategic settings (e.g., Divide-and-Choose for two agents yields MMS+EFX), and (ii) mentions a related strategic-PNE fairness line (PNE of Round-Robin are EF1), but not EFX nor MMS-at-PNE guarantees.

sources.title: Fair shares: Feasibility, domination, and incentives
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops a framework of feasible shares and self-maximizing (truthful-in-guarantee) shares for fair division of indivisible goods. For additive valuations it proves (among other results) that there is no SM-dominant feasible share (Theorem 1), and it constructs feasible, self-maximizing, polynomial-time computable shares that approximately dominate MMS: for general n a share that is \(\frac{2n}{3n-1}\)-dominating, for \(n\le 4\) a \(\frac45\)-dominating share, and for two agents a PTAS share that is \((1-\varepsilon)\)-dominating (Theorem 3 / Theorem 5 / Theorem 6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the tight worst-case MMS approximation \(\alpha^*\) guaranteed by EFX allocations that arise as pure Nash equilibria of mechanisms whose PNE always exist and are always EFX (two additive agents). This paper does not study EFX, mechanisms, or Nash equilibria of allocation mechanisms; instead it studies share guarantees (feasible shares, self-maximization) and approximation to MMS. It only mentions that feasible shares imply equilibrium guarantees in a generic sense (Proposition 1), but it does not analyze EFX-PNE allocations nor derive an \(\alpha^*\) bound for them. Hence it does not resolve the EFX-PNE MMS-guarantee question, though it provides related MMS-approximation tools and context.

sources.title: Fair Division with Interdependent Values
sources.theorem_or_result: Theorem 3.1: For two agents with equal entitlements and general monotone interdependent valuations, there exists a (guessing) mechanism such that for every signal vector there exists a PNE whose outcome is MMS and EFX for one agent (the cutter) and EF for the other (the chooser) w.r.t. the true signals. Additionally, Lemma 3.4 shows in that equilibrium the cutter gets at least her MMS and the allocation is EFX for her.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the tight worst-case MMS approximation guarantee \(\alpha^*\) enjoyed by EFX allocations that arise at PNE of mechanisms where (i) a PNE always exists and (ii) every PNE outcome is EFX (w.r.t. true additive values) for two agents. This paper does not study that guarantee. Its main positive result for \(n=2\) gives existence of at least one fair PNE (not that all PNE are fair), and the equilibrium outcome is only partially EFX (EFX for the cutter, merely EF for the chooser). Moreover, the setting is interdependent values and general monotone valuations, not the independent additive setting of the open problem. The paper’s negative results (Theorem 6.1) show impossibility of mechanisms where all equilibria are MMS/EF1-fair in the interdependent model, but do not address mechanisms with all equilibria EFX nor the MMS level of EFX equilibria in the independent additive model.

sources.title: On Truthful Mechanisms without Pareto-efficiency: Characterizations and Fairness
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves a characterization: for any permutations-closed class of strict monotone preferences (including strict additive valuations), a deterministic mechanism that is strategy-proof (truthful in dominant strategies), non-bossy, and neutral is a serial-quota mechanism (agents pick up to fixed quotas in a fixed order), even without Pareto-efficiency and even allowing disposal of goods (Theorem 1 / Application 1).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the MMS guarantee of EFX allocations that arise at pure Nash equilibria of mechanisms whose PNE always exist and are always EFX (two agents, additive valuations). This paper studies a different incentive notion (dominant-strategy truthfulness) and different fairness targets (MMS and EF1), and it does not analyze EFX or pure Nash equilibria. Hence it does not determine the constant \(\alpha^*\) for EFX-PNE mechanisms. Indirectly, it provides structural tools (serial-quota characterization under truthfulness+non-bossy+neutral) and shows strong MMS impossibilities for such truthful mechanisms, which may inform comparisons with equilibrium-based (PNE) approaches.

title: Bound lattice width of lattice-free polytopes using only determinant minor parameter
background_latex:
Let $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}$ have full column rank and let $b\in\mathbb{Z}^m$. Define the (rational) polyhedron
\[
P(A,b):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: Ax\le b\}.
\]
The polyhedron is called lattice-free if $P(A,b)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\emptyset$.

For a nonzero direction $a\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$, define the width of $P(A,b)$ in direction $a$ by
\[
w_a(P(A,b)):=\max_{x\in P(A,b)} a^\top x-\min_{y\in P(A,b)} a^\top y.
\]
The lattice width is
\[
w(P(A,b)):=\min_{a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\setminus\{0\}} w_a(P(A,b)).
\]

For $k\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ define the maximal absolute $k\times k$ minor of $A$ by
\[
\Delta_k(A):=\max\{ |\det M| : M \text{ is a } k\times k \text{ submatrix of } A\}.
\]
In particular, $\Delta_n(A)$ is the maximum absolute determinant of an $n\times n$ submatrix of $A$ (which is nonzero because $A$ has full column rank $n$).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exists a function $f:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ such that for every dimension $n\ge 2$, every full-column-rank matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}$, and every $b\in\mathbb{Z}^m$ for which $P(A,b)$ is a (full-dimensional) lattice-free polyhedron, the lattice width satisfies
\[
w(P(A,b))\le f(\Delta_n(A)).
\]
Equivalently, decide whether the lattice width of lattice-free polytopes can be bounded above by a function depending only on $\Delta_n(A)$ (and not on $n$).

Determine whether there exists a function $f:\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ such that for every dimension $n\ge 2$, every full-column-rank matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}$, and every $b\in\mathbb{Z}^m$ for which $P(A,b)$ is a (full-dimensional) lattice-free polyhedron, the lattice width satisfies
\[
w(P(A,b))\le f(\Delta_n(A)).
\]
Equivalently, decide whether the lattice width of lattice-free polytopes can be bounded above by a function depending only on $\Delta_n(A)$ (and not on $n$).

counterexample_suitability_rationale: One can computationally search for families of lattice-free polytopes with fixed $\Delta_n(A)$ and large lattice width by enumerating small integer matrices and right-hand sides and checking lattice-freeness and width via MILP/LP. However, the search space grows quickly with $n,m$ and certifying worst-case growth may require guided constructions beyond brute force.

The challenge is efficiently enforcing full-dimensional lattice-freeness and exploring high-dimensional instances, but evolutionary search could plausibly discover structured families with large width or suggest sharper conjectured bounds.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Celaya–Kuhlmann–Paat–Weismantel) frames the question of whether the lattice width \(w(P(A,b))\) of a full-dimensional lattice-free polyhedron \(P(A,b)=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) with integral right-hand side can be bounded by a function of \(\Delta_n(A)\) alone, independent of the dimension \(n\). Their main flatness advance is Theorem 4, which shows the existence of a facet normal (a row \(a\) of \(A\)) with facet width \(w_a(P(A,b)) < \frac{4n+2}{9}\,\Delta_n(A)-1\) under mild nonredundancy assumptions. This is obtained by linking flatness to a proximity parameter \(\pi(A)\) and proving refined proximity bounds (Theorem 5) in terms of \(\Delta_\alpha(A)\), using Minkowski’s theorem and a planar polygon area lower bound for sets satisfying \(\tau Q\subseteq Q^\circ\).

Despite these improvements, the bound still scales linearly with \(n\), and the determinant-only (dimension-free) bound remains open in general. The paper identifies regimes where dimension-free behavior does hold: for matrices whose \(n\times n\) minors lie in \(\{0,\pm k,\pm 2k\}\) one gets facet-width \(\le \Delta_n(A)-2\) (Theorem 6), extending earlier results for strictly \(\Delta\)-modular matrices. It also points to classes such as simplices and special pyramids (via prior work) where width can be controlled by \(\Delta_n(A)\).

The forward-citing works provided here are adjacent rather than resolving the width question. They develop determinant-parameterized structure and algorithms for bounded-subdeterminant matrices (e.g., threshold phenomena for \(\ell_\infty\)-SVP and strongly polynomial algorithms for structured totally \(\Delta\)-modular IPs), which may offer tools to control geometric complexity (faces, decompositions) in terms of \(\Delta\). However, none establishes a bound of the form \(w(P(A,b))\le f(\Delta_n(A))\) independent of \(n\), so the problem remains open.

sources.title: Totally -Modular IPs with Two Non-zeros in Most Rows
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves algorithmic tractability for a structured class of totally \(\Delta\)-modular integer programs: if \(M=\begin{bmatrix}A & B\\ W & D\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally \(\Delta\)-modular, \(A\) has at most two nonzeros per row, and the block sizes \(m_2,n_2\le k\) are constant, then Problem 2 (and via reduction Problem 3) can be solved in strongly polynomial time (Theorem 4). A key structural ingredient is that for \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\) with two nonzeros per row viewed as a signed-graph incidence matrix, and a weight vector \(w\), the maximum alternating weight of a tree \(\mathrm{alt}(S,w)\) satisfies \(\mathrm{alt}(S,w)\le \Delta\big(\begin{bmatrix}A\\ w^\top\end{bmatrix}\big)\) (Proposition 11), enabling a bounded-adhesion tree-decomposition when subdeterminants are bounded (Theorem 16).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a dimension-free upper bound on the lattice width \(w(P(A,b))\) of lattice-free polyhedra \(P(A,b)=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) in terms of \(\Delta_n(A)\) only. This paper does not study lattice-free polyhedra or lattice width/flatness bounds directly, nor does it provide a bound of the form \(w(P(A,b))\le f(\Delta_n(A))\). Instead it is algorithmic work on integer programs with bounded subdeterminants, using proximity bounds (Cook–Gerards–Schrijver–Tardos and improvements) and new graph-structural decompositions for matrices with (mostly) two nonzeros per row. These techniques are adjacent to the broader theme of proximity/flatness for bounded-minor matrices, but they do not resolve (or explicitly advance) the specific lattice-width question posed.

sources.title: On matrices over a polynomial ring with restricted subdeterminants
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops structural results for integral/polynomial matrices with restricted subdeterminants. In particular:
- Lemma 2: for finite S \(\subseteq \mathbb Z[x]\), the set \(F(S)\) of determinants of forbidden minors is finite and \(\max_{f\in F(S)}|f|\le 2\,(\max_{s\in S}|s|)^2\).
- Theorem 1 (rank-1 parametric decomposition): if \(M=T+xuv^\top\in\mathbb Z[x]^{m\times n}\) is totally \(S\)-modular, then \(T\) is totally \(S(0)\)-modular.
- Theorems 2–3: for specific finite sets \(S(a)=\pm\{0,1,a,a+1,2a+1\}\) or \(\pm\{0,a,a+1,2a+1\}\), recognition of totally \(S(a)\)-modular matrices and ILP with such constraint matrices are solvable in polynomial time (for all but finitely many exceptional \(a\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a dimension-free bound on lattice width \(w(P(A,b))\) of lattice-free polyhedra in terms of \(\Delta_n(A)\) only. This paper studies matrices with *all* subdeterminants restricted to a finite set \(S\) (or polynomial analogues), yielding finiteness/structure and algorithmic results for such matrix classes. It does not address lattice-free polyhedra widths, flatness constants, or provide bounds of \(w(P(A,b))\) in terms of \(\Delta_n(A)\). At most, it is tangentially related because both lines of work use determinant/minor parameters (\(\Delta\)) to control integer-programming behavior.

sources.title: A Threshold Phenomenon for the Shortest Lattice Vector Problem in the Infinity Norm
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a determinant-parameterized threshold phenomenon for the shortest lattice vector problem in the infinity norm for lattices of the form \(A\mathbb Z^n\) with \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) full column rank and \(\Delta:=\Delta_n(A)\). Defining \(f(\Delta):=\max\{n: \|Az\|_\infty\ge 2\ \forall z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\ \text{for some \(\Delta\)-modular }A\}\), they show \(f(\Delta)\) is finite and satisfy
- \(\Delta-1\le f(\Delta)\le \lfloor(\Delta-1)/2\rfloor(\Delta-1)+\mathbf 1_{2\mathbb Z}(\Delta)\).
Consequently, if \(n\ge \lfloor(\Delta-1)/2\rfloor(\Delta-1)+\mathbf 1_{2\mathbb Z}(\Delta)+1\), then either one can find \(z^*\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \(\|Az^*\|_\infty=1\) or certify \(\Delta_n(A)>\Delta\); this yields an FPT algorithm for \(\min_{z\ne 0}\|Az\|_\infty\) parameterized by \(\Delta\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether the lattice width \(w(P(A,b))\) of a full-dimensional lattice-free polyhedron \(P(A,b)=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) can be bounded by a function of \(\Delta_n(A)\) alone, independent of dimension \(n\). This paper does not address lattice-free polyhedra or lattice width directly, and it does not prove any bound of the form \(w(P(A,b))\le f(\Delta_n(A))\). However, it develops determinant-only structural results for \(\Delta\)-modular matrices and derives polyhedral consequences (e.g., integer-hull vertices lie on faces of dimension \(\le F(\Delta)\)). Such threshold/face-dimension phenomena are conceptually related to flatness/width questions and may provide tools toward bounding geometric complexity of integer-feasible regions in terms of \(\Delta\), but no explicit width bound for lattice-free sets is obtained here.

title: Prove square-root lower bound for LP-compatible policies in degenerate restless bandits
background_latex:
Consider a discrete-time finite-horizon restless bandit with a population of \(N\) statistically identical arms. Each arm has a finite state space \(S=\{1,\dots,d\}\) and two actions \(a\in\{0,1\}\) (passive/active). If an arm is in state \(s\) and action \(a\) is chosen, an immediate reward \(R_s^a\in\mathbb{R}\) is earned and the arm transitions to state \(s'\) with probability \(P^{a}_{s,s'}\). Arms evolve independently conditional on actions.

At each time \(t=0,1,\dots,T-1\), exactly a fraction \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) of arms is activated (with the convention that if \(\alpha N\) is not an integer, the policy randomizes between \(\lfloor \alpha N\rfloor\) and \(\lfloor \alpha N\rfloor+1\) active arms so that the expected number of active arms equals \(\alpha N\)). Let \(M^{(N)}(t)\in\Delta_d\) be the empirical distribution of arm states at time \(t\), where \(M^{(N)}_s(t)\) is the fraction of arms in state \(s\). Let \(Y^{(N)}(t)\in\Delta_{2d}\) be the empirical state-action fractions, where \(Y^{(N)}_{s,a}(t)\) is the fraction of arms in state \(s\) assigned action \(a\) at time \(t\). The per-arm reward of a policy \(\pi\) is
\[V^{(N)}_{\pi}(m(0),T):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}} R_s^a\,Y^{(N)}_{s,a}(t)\Big].\]

The standard LP relaxation replaces the hard per-time activation constraint by an equality constraint on expected activation. Writing \(y_{s,a}(t):=\mathbb{E}[Y^{(N)}_{s,a}(t)]\), the relaxation value \(V_{\mathrm{rel}}(m(0),T)\) is the optimum of
\[\max_{y\ge 0}\ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s,a} R_s^a\,y_{s,a}(t)\]
subject to flow conservation
\[y_{s,0}(t+1)+y_{s,1}(t+1)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}} y_{s',a}(t)P^{a}_{s',s}\quad \forall s,\ t,\]
activation budget
\[\sum_{s\in S} y_{s,1}(t)=\alpha\quad\forall t,\]
and initial condition \(y_{s,0}(0)+y_{s,1}(0)=m_s(0)\).

Call a Markovian admissible policy \(\pi=\{\pi_t\}_{t=0}^{T-1}\) a map \(\pi_t:\Delta_d\to\Delta_{2d}\) that, given state distribution \(m\), prescribes fractions \(y=\pi_t(m)\) satisfying \(y_{s,a}\ge 0\), \(\sum_a y_{s,a}=m_s\) for all \(s\), and \(\sum_s y_{s,1}=\alpha\). A policy is LP-compatible if there exists an optimal LP solution \(\{y^*(t)\}_{t=0}^{T-1}\) such that \(\pi_t(m^*(t))=y^*(t)\) for all \(t\), where \(m^*_s(t)=y^*_{s,0}(t)+y^*_{s,1}(t)\).

Let \(S_0(t):=\{s\in S: y^*_{s,0}(t)>0\text{ and } y^*_{s,1}(t)>0\}\). The model is called degenerate if for every optimal LP solution there exists at least one time \(t\) such that \(|S_0(t)|=0\), i.e., at that time the LP solution activates some states fully and leaves the rest fully passive with no state partially split between actions.

The paper provides an example showing that for some degenerate models, the LP-relaxation gap under any LP-compatible policy cannot decay faster than order \(1/\sqrt{N}\), and formulates a general conjecture that this phenomenon is typical for degenerate models.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Gast--Gaujal--Yan (2023), finite-horizon homogeneous restless bandits are analyzed via the relaxed LP (flow constraints plus per-time expected activation). A key dichotomy is between non-degenerate instances (every optimal LP solution has at least one split state at every time) where locally linear LP-compatible policies exist and yield exponentially small gaps to \(V_{\mathrm{rel}}\), and degenerate instances (some time \(t\) has \(|S_0(t)|=0\)) where the paper gives a concrete example with an unavoidable \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) gap for LP-compatible policies and conjectures this is typical. The open problem asks to prove a universal \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound (and matching \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) upper bound) for the LP-relaxation gap of any LP-compatible policy on essentially all degenerate finite-horizon instances.

Forward citations provide partial evidence but no general resolution. The strongest supporting result is the Gaussian-approximation line of work ("Achieving O (1/N) optimality gap in restless bandits through Gaussian approximation" / "Achieving Optimality Gap in Restless Bandits through Gaussian Approximation"), which proves that for a specific degenerate example, every policy in a broad fluid/LP-tracking class has \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) optimality gap and that the LP upper bound itself can be \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) above the true \(N\)-arm optimum. This bolsters the view that when the optimal LP trajectory lies on a boundary (as in \(|S_0(t)|=0\)), CLT-scale fluctuations in the empirical state can force a square-root loss for policies that track the LP prescription. At the same time, that work also shows that second-order (Gaussian/stochastic-programming) policies can achieve \(\tilde O(1/N)\) gaps to the true optimum under a uniqueness condition, indicating that the \(1/\sqrt N\) obstruction is tied to LP/fluid compatibility rather than to the RMAB itself.

Other forward citations mainly develop complementary upper-bound theories in infinite-horizon average-reward settings (e.g., MPC/LP-update policies with \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) gaps under mixing and exponential gaps under nondegeneracy/stability; focus-set/ID policies with \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) gaps under unichain/aperiodicity), and general convex-optimization sensitivity tools that explain why degeneracy blocks second-order improvements. A few works on weakly coupled multi-action systems claim exponential convergence to relaxed LP values without nondegeneracy under Lipschitz-type conditions, but these conditions plausibly exclude the discontinuities inherent in the degenerate \(|S_0(t)|=0\) regime. Overall, the conjectured universal \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound for all LP-compatible policies across essentially all degenerate finite-horizon instances remains open; existing results establish \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bounds for substantial LP/fluid-tracking policy classes on explicit degenerate examples and suggest that proving universality will require a general argument linking boundary optimal LP solutions to unavoidable CLT-scale rounding/mismatch losses.

sources.title: Achieving O (1/N) optimality gap in restless bandits through Gaussian approximation
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves two main asymptotic statements for finite-horizon homogeneous RMABs. (i) Under Assumption 4.1 (the fluid LP has a unique optimal solution), the proposed Gaussian-approximation stochastic-programming policy \(\tilde\pi_{N,*}\) achieves \(\tilde O(1/N)\) optimality gap to the true \(N\)-system optimum: \(V^{N}_{\mathrm{opt}}(x_{\mathrm{ini}},1)-V^{N}_{\tilde\pi_{N,*}}(x_{\mathrm{ini}},1)=\tilde O(1/N)\) (Theorem 4.1). (ii) There exist degenerate instances for which every ‘fluid/LP-based’ policy \(\pi\) in the class \(\Pi_{\mathrm{fluid}}(y^*)\) has \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) optimality gap, and moreover the fluid LP upper bound itself is loose by \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\): \(V^{LP}(x_{\mathrm{ini}},1)-V^{N}_{\mathrm{opt}}(x_{\mathrm{ini}},1)=\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) (Theorem 4.2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound (and matching \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) upper bound) on the LP-relaxation optimality gap for every LP-compatible policy in degenerate finite-horizon RMABs. This paper does not prove such a universal lower bound. Instead it provides: - Evidence supporting the conjectured phenomenon by proving a \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound for a broad class of LP-based policies \(\Pi_{\mathrm{fluid}}(y^*)\) on a specific degenerate example (Theorem 4.2), and showing the LP bound itself can be \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) away from the true optimum on that example. - A contrasting positive result: for degenerate problems satisfying a uniqueness condition on the fluid LP solution, there exists a non-LP-compatible (SP-based) policy with much smaller gap \(\tilde O(1/N)\) to the true optimum (Theorem 4.1). This does not refute the conjecture as stated (which is about LP-compatible policies), but it shows degeneracy does not inherently force \(1/\sqrt N\) gaps for all computationally efficient policies, and it suggests the obstruction is tied to the fluid/LP approximation rather than the RMAB itself. Overall: partial progress—establishes \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bounds for a large LP-based class on an example, but not for all LP-compatible policies nor for all degenerate instances.

sources.title: Multi-Action Restless Bandits with Weakly Coupled Constraints: Simultaneous Learning and Control
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves exponential-in-system-size performance deviation bounds for a class of linear-programming-based (ALP/OALP) policies for finite-horizon weakly coupled restless bandit/MDP systems, without requiring the non-degeneracy assumptions used in prior LP-based asymptotic optimality results. Concretely, for scaling parameter \(h\) (with \(N_i=hN_i^0\)), it establishes concentration of the empirical state–action occupancy process \(Z^{\varphi,h}(t)\) around a deterministic fluid/averaging trajectory \(z^{\varphi}(t)\): for any fixed \(T<\infty\) and \(\epsilon>0\), there exist \(C,H>0\) such that for all \(h>H\), \[\mathbb P\Big(\max_{t=0,\dots,T}\|Z^{\varphi,h}(t)-z^{\varphi}(t)\|>\epsilon\Big)\le e^{-Ch}.\] Using this, it claims that adapted LP policies \(\psi\) satisfying a Lipschitz-type condition (their (67)) achieve \(\|z^{\psi,h}(t)-z^{\bar\varphi^*,h}(t)\|\le C_1 e^{-C_2 h}+\epsilon\) uniformly over \(t\le T\), where \(\bar\varphi^*\) is induced by an optimal solution of the relaxed LP; hence the per-unit reward gap to the relaxed optimum is \(O(e^{-h})\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound on the LP-relaxation optimality gap for LP-compatible policies in *degenerate* finite-horizon restless bandits (where optimal LP solutions have no partially split states at some time). This paper instead develops a general framework (weakly coupled gangs) and proves/claims *exponentially small* \(O(e^{-h})\) performance deviation for a class of LP-based policies (ALP/OALP) relative to the relaxed LP optimum, explicitly stating that their exponential bound does not rely on non-degeneracy of the LP solution. If correct and applicable to the same model class as Gast–Gaujal–Yan (2023), this would contradict the conjectured \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound—at least for the policies they analyze—because exponential decay is asymptotically much smaller than \(1/\sqrt N\). However, their ALP/OALP policies are not shown (in the provided text) to be "LP-compatible" in the specific sense of the open problem (matching an optimal LP solution \(y^*(t)\) on the fluid trajectory), and their key sufficient condition (67) is a Lipschitz closeness of action fractions to the relaxed policy as a function of state-occupancy \(\Upsilon\), which may fail precisely in degenerate cases where the LP optimizer induces discontinuous/tie-breaking action maps. Thus the paper provides partial progress/related evidence: it suggests exponential gaps can occur even without non-degeneracy assumptions, but it does not directly establish or refute the \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound for *all* LP-compatible policies in degenerate models.

sources.title: Model predictive control is almost optimal for restless bandits
sources.theorem_or_result:
For an infinite-horizon average-reward RMAB with per-period hard budget 
\(\sum_i u_i(t)\le \alpha\) and empirical state dynamics \(x(t+1)=x(t)P^0+u(t)(P^1-P^0)\), the paper analyzes the rolling-horizon LP/MPC policy (LP-update) that at each time solves a \(\tau\)-horizon linear program and applies the first control with randomized rounding. Under a mixing/ergodicity condition (Assumption 1: \(\rho_k>0\) for some \(k\)), it proves an \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) optimality gap for the resulting policy relative to the optimal \(N\)-arm average reward:
- Theorem 4.1: for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\tau(\varepsilon)\) such that
\[V^{(N)}_{\mathrm{LP},\tau(\varepsilon)}(\infty)\ge V^{N}_{\mathrm{opt}}(\infty)-\varepsilon - O(1/N) - O(1/\sqrt N).\]
Under additional nondegeneracy and local stability assumptions (Assumptions 2–4), it strengthens this to exponential closeness:
- Theorem 4.2: if \(\alpha N\in\mathbb{Z}\), then
\[V^{(N)}_{\mathrm{LP},\tau(\varepsilon)}(\infty)\ge V^{N}_{\mathrm{opt}}(\infty)-\varepsilon - C'e^{-C''N}.\]
