The open problem asks for a *lower bound* \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) on the LP-relaxation optimality gap for *LP-compatible* policies in *degenerate finite-horizon* RMABs (where optimal LP solutions have times with no partially split states). This paper does not address that conjecture directly: it studies an *infinite-horizon average-reward* setting and provides *upper bounds* on the suboptimality of a specific rolling-horizon LP/MPC policy relative to the true \(N\)-arm optimum.

Relevance: it supports the broader narrative that \(1/\sqrt N\) is the generic rate without additional stability/nondegeneracy (Theorem 4.1 gives an \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) upper bound “in general”), and it explicitly contrasts this with exponential rates under a *nondegenerate* fixed point (Assumption 2) and stability. However, it neither proves that degeneracy forces a \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) *lower* bound, nor does it analyze the finite-horizon LP-compatibility notion from Gast–Gaujal–Yan (2023b) in the degenerate regime. In fact, its exponential result assumes nondegeneracy, which is essentially the opposite of the degenerate case in the open problem.

sources.title: Achieving exponential asymptotic optimality in average-reward restless bandits without global attractor assumption
sources.theorem_or_result: In the infinite-horizon average-reward restless bandit with homogeneous arms, the paper proves: (i) under Assumptions 1 (aperiodic unichain of the LP-induced single-arm chain), 2 (non-degeneracy: a unique neutral state with both actions used in an optimal LP solution), and 3 (local stability: all eigenvalues of the linearized matrix \(\Phi\) satisfy \(|\lambda(\Phi)|<1\)), the proposed two-set policy \(\pi\) achieves an exponential gap to the LP upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{rel}}\): \(R_{\mathrm{rel}}-R(\pi,S_0)=O(e^{-CN})\) for some \(C>0\) independent of \(N\) (Theorem 1). (ii) For ‘regular unstable’ instances (violating local stability: \(\Phi\) has an eigenvalue with modulus \(>1\), plus mild regularity/noise conditions), every policy \(\pi\) satisfies a CLT-order lower bound \(R_{\mathrm{rel}}-R(\pi,S_0)=\Omega(1/\sqrt{N})\) (Theorem 2).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound on the LP-relaxation optimality gap for LP-compatible policies in *degenerate finite-horizon* restless bandits, where at some time \(t\) the optimal finite-horizon LP has no split states (\(|S_0(t)|=0\)). This paper does not address that finite-horizon degeneracy setting. Instead it studies *infinite-horizon average reward* and assumes *non-degeneracy* (existence of a neutral/split state) to obtain exponential gaps, i.e., it explicitly excludes the degenerate case of interest. It does, however, prove an \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound in a different regime: when local stability fails (a linearized dynamics matrix \(\Phi\) is unstable), then no policy can get closer than order \(1/\sqrt N\) to the LP upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{rel}}\). This provides partial progress/related evidence that CLT-order lower bounds arise from structural obstructions, but it neither proves nor disproves the conjectured \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound for LP-compatible policies in *degenerate* models as defined in the original finite-horizon paper.

sources.title: Unichain and aperiodicity are sufficient for asymptotic optimality of average-reward restless bandits
sources.theorem_or_result: Under Assumption 1 (existence of an optimal LP solution whose induced optimal single-armed policy \(\bar\pi^*\) yields an aperiodic unichain Markov chain), the paper constructs “focus-set” policies (including the set-expansion policy and the ID policy) for the discrete-time infinite-horizon average-reward restless bandit with \(N\) homogeneous arms and exact per-time budget \(\alpha N\), and proves these policies are asymptotically optimal with optimality gap \(R^*(N,S_0)-R(\pi,S_0)=O(1/\sqrt N)\).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns *finite-horizon* restless bandits and asks for a universal \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) *lower bound* on the LP-relaxation gap for any LP-compatible policy in *degenerate* instances (where optimal LP solutions have no partially split states at some time). This citing paper instead studies *infinite-horizon average-reward* RBs and provides *upper bounds* \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) for new policies under an aperiodic-unichain assumption, without analyzing degeneracy-induced lower bounds. It does discuss non-degeneracy assumptions in prior work as enabling exponential gaps, but does not prove that degeneracy forces \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) gaps, nor does it address the finite-horizon LP-compatible class in the conjecture.

sources.title: Certainty equivalence control-based heuristics in multi-stage convex stochastic optimization problems
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops certainty-equivalence-control (CEC) relaxations for multi-stage convex stochastic optimization with hard constraints and proposes two feasible heuristics (update/re-solving and projection) derived from the relaxed convex program. It proves upper bounds on the suboptimality gap: under local Lipschitz regularity of the relevant solution/projection mappings, the gap is bounded by a constant times \(\sqrt{\mathrm{var}[W]}+\sqrt{\mathrm{var}[E]}\); under additional local \(C^2\) smoothness (nondegeneracy/LICQ-type conditions), the bound improves to order \(\mathrm{var}[W]+\mathrm{var}[E]\) (Theorems 1–4). In the Markovian bandit scaling where \(\mathrm{var}[E]=O(1/N)\), this yields an \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) bound in general and an \(O(1/N)\) bound under nondegeneracy.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a universal \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound on the LP-relaxation optimality gap for LP-compatible policies in *degenerate* finite-horizon restless bandits. This paper does not prove any lower bounds in \(N\) for degenerate bandits, nor does it analyze LP-compatible policies in the sense of matching an optimal LP solution along the fluid trajectory. Instead it provides a general framework and *upper* bounds for CEC-based heuristics, and it explicitly links faster \(O(1/N)\) rates to nondegeneracy/smoothness, while noting that degeneracy can prevent second-order improvements (e.g., projection mapping degenerate in their numerics). Thus it supplies sensitivity-analysis tools and a conceptual explanation consistent with the conjecture (degeneracy \(\Rightarrow\) only first-order \(O(1/\sqrt N)\) behavior), but it neither establishes the conjectured \(\Omega(1/\sqrt N)\) lower bound nor the matching \(\Theta(1/\sqrt N)\) characterization for all LP-compatible policies.

title: Lower bounds on acceleration thresholds for stochastic momentum methods under growth condition
background_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously differentiable, $L$-smooth and $m$-strongly convex (with respect to the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|$), with condition number $\kappa:=L/m$, and unique minimizer $x^*\in\arg\min_x f(x)$. A stochastic first-order oracle returns a noisy gradient
\[
 g(x)=\nabla f(x)+\varepsilon(x),
\]
where $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon(x)\mid x]=0$. The noise is assumed to satisfy the growth condition: there exist constants $\delta\ge 0$ and $\sigma^2\ge 0$ such that for all $x$,
\[
\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon(x)\|^2 \le \delta\,\|\nabla f(x)\|^2 + \sigma^2.
\]
Consider the following accelerated stochastic gradient-type methods with (constant) algorithm parameters:
1) Nesterov’s accelerated method (NAM), an iteration that uses a momentum parameter and evaluates stochastic gradients at a momentum-extrapolated point.
2) Robust momentum method (RMM), an iteration that updates a momentum variable and a primary iterate using fixed parameters.
3) Implicit accelerated dual averaging (iDAM+), a dual-averaging-based accelerated scheme.
For each method, one is interested in whether it can achieve an accelerated linear bias decay of the form $\exp(-k/c\sqrt{\kappa})$ (or equivalently a per-iteration contraction factor $1-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\kappa})$) under the growth condition when the multiplicative noise level $\delta$ is not small (e.g., $\delta\ge 1$), compared with the non-accelerated $1-\Theta(1/\kappa)$ rate typical of constant-stepsize SGD.
problem_definition_latex:
For NAM, RMM, and iDAM+ under the growth condition, determine (prove) sharp necessary conditions on the multiplicative noise parameter $\delta$ for acceleration over SGD. In particular, establish a lower bound (impossibility result) showing whether there exists a threshold $\delta_0$ such that for some $\delta\ge \delta_0$ and some $(m,L)$-smooth strongly convex objective $f$ together with an oracle satisfying
\(\mathbb{E}\|\varepsilon(x)\|^2 \le \delta\,\|\nabla f(x)\|^2 + \sigma^2\),
no choice of constant algorithm parameters for these methods can guarantee an accelerated bias decay rate $\exp(-k/c\sqrt{\kappa})$ (equivalently contraction $1-\Theta(1/\sqrt{\kappa})$) uniformly over all such problem instances.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Chen–Na–Kolar, 2023) frames acceleration under the growth condition \(\mathbb E\|\varepsilon(x)\|^2\le \delta\|\nabla f(x)\|^2+\sigma^2\) as a bias–variance tradeoff in a unified recursion of the form \(\mathbb E V_{k+1}\le (1-c_1(\delta)/\sqrt\kappa)\,\mathbb E V_k + c_2(\delta)\sigma^2\). For constant parameters, it proves *sufficient* \(\delta\)-regimes for accelerated linear bias decay: NAM and iDAM+ accelerate only for \(\delta<1\), RMM for \(\delta<1/4\), while DAM+ can be tuned to accelerate for all \(\delta\ge 0\). The paper explicitly notes that these \(\delta\)-restrictions are not known to be necessary and calls for lower-bound/impossibility results.

Among the forward-citing works provided, none resolves the requested sharp necessary conditions. The Markovian-noise paper establishes acceleration and lower bounds in a different model (Markov dependence plus almost-sure strong-growth and batching), while the interpolation/strong-growth estimating-sequences paper is about upper bounds and flags a bug for standard momentum forms. The RAAS work shows acceleration for an adaptive method under bounded-moment oracle assumptions, again not addressing impossibility thresholds for constant-parameter NAM/RMM/iDAM+.

Therefore, based on the supplied forward-citation set, the problem of proving sharp lower bounds on the multiplicative-noise threshold \(\delta\) that precludes accelerated bias decay for NAM, RMM, and iDAM+ under the (in-expectation) growth condition remains open. Promising directions suggested by the source paper’s discussion include constructing hard strongly convex instances (e.g., least-squares-type quadratics with large effective \(\delta\)) and proving that for \(\delta\) above a method-dependent constant, the best achievable uniform contraction reverts to \(1-\Theta(1/\kappa)\) for any fixed-parameter momentum tuning.

sources.theorem_or_result:

\[
\mathbb E\big[\|x_N-x^*\|^2 + \tfrac{6}{\mu}(f(x_N^f)-f(x^*))\big]
\le \exp\Big(-\tfrac{N}{3}\sqrt{p^2\mu\alpha}\Big)\,\mathcal E_0
+ \tfrac{p}{\mu^{3/2}\sqrt{\alpha}}\big(\delta^2\tau b^{-1}+\sigma^2\tau^2 b^{-2}\big),

for suitable constant parameters \(p,\alpha\) and batching parameters \(b,M,B\) (Theorem 1), yielding oracle complexity \(\tilde O\big(\tau[(1+\delta^2)\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon)+\sigma^2/(\mu^2\varepsilon)]\big)\) (Corollary 1). sources.title: Robust Accelerated Adaptive Search: High-Probability Complexity Bounds under Bounded-Moment Stochastic Oracles
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes RAAS, a stochastic accelerated adaptive step-search method using both a stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) and a stochastic zeroth-order oracle (SZO), and proves high-probability stopping-time complexity bounds under finite-moment oracle assumptions. In the strongly convex case (Assumption 6), for any target accuracy 
\(\varepsilon>\varepsilon'_\varphi\), Theorem 2 shows \(\mathbb P\{T_\varepsilon\le t\}\ge 1-\text{(poly/exponential tail)}\) provided 
\[t=O\!\left(\frac{1}{C_\kappa(\hat p-1/2)}\log\frac{\Phi_0}{\varepsilon}\right),\qquad C_\kappa=-\ln\bigl(1-(1-\vartheta)\sqrt{2\theta\mu\bar\gamma}\bigr),\]
with \(\bar\gamma=\Theta(1/L)\) so \(C_\kappa=\Theta(\kappa^{-1/2})\), yielding an accelerated order \(T_\varepsilon=O(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Phi_0/\varepsilon))\) down to a noise-determined floor \(\varepsilon'_\varphi>0\).

This paper does not study the growth-condition model nor the same algorithms: its SFO assumptions bound absolute gradient estimation error moments (e.g., \(\mathbb E_t\|G_t-\nabla\varphi(\hat y_t)\|^2\le \epsilon_g^2\)) and allow bias/heavy tails, and it uses an adaptive step-search with extra SZO queries and tunable momentum intervention \(\vartheta\). title: Determine complexity of minimizing sum of boundary cut sizes in hypergraph k-partitions
background_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a (multi-)hypergraph with vertex set \(V\) of size \(n\) and hyperedge set \(E\). Each hyperedge \(e\in E\) is a subset of \(V\). (The paper primarily discusses the unweighted case, i.e., each hyperedge has unit cost; the objective below is stated for this setting.)

For a nonempty proper subset \(U\subset V\), define the cut-set
\[\delta(U):=\{e\in E: e\cap U\neq\emptyset \text{ and } e\cap (V\setminus U)\neq\emptyset\},\]
and its cut value \(d(U):=|\delta(U)|\).

A \(k\)-partition of \(V\) is an ordered tuple \((V_1,\dots,V_k)\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets whose union is \(V\).

For a \(k\)-partition \((V_1,\dots,V_k)\), the paper considers various objectives based on the boundary sizes \(|\delta(V_i)|\). In particular, the variant highlighted in the conclusion asks to minimize the sum of boundary cut values
\[\sum_{i=1}^k |\delta(V_i)| = \sum_{i=1}^k d(V_i).\]
problem_definition_latex:
Given a hypergraph \(G=(V,E)\) and a fixed integer \(k\ge 5\), determine the computational complexity of the optimization problem
\[\min\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k |\delta(V_i)| : (V_1,\dots,V_k) \text{ is a } k\text{-partition of } V\right\}.\]
In particular, decide whether this problem admits a polynomial-time algorithm for fixed \(k\ge 5\) (or whether it is NP-hard) in the unweighted hypergraph setting.

literature_review.synthesis:
The objective in the open problem is the minsum boundary variant of hypergraph \(k\)-partitioning: minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^k d(V_i)\) where \(d(U)=|\delta(U)|\) is the (unweighted) hypergraph cut function. In the notation of the source paper, this is distinct from Hypergraph-\(k\)-Cut (which minimizes \(|\delta(V_1,\dots,V_k)|\) counting each crossing hyperedge once) and from Minmax-Hypergraph-\(k\)-Partition (which minimizes \(\max_i d(V_i)\)). The source paper develops powerful terminal-cut structural theorems (notably Theorem 1.4) enabling deterministic enumeration for Hypergraph-\(k\)-Cut and Minmax-Hypergraph-\(k\)-Partition for fixed \(k\), but it explicitly notes that analogous structure fails for the minsum boundary objective and leaves its complexity for \(k\ge 5\) open.

Subsequent work on submodular partitioning has made partial progress on the minsum side. The strongest direct advance toward the stated objective is the polynomial-time algorithm for minimum 4-partition of a general submodular function, which implies a polynomial-time algorithm for minimum 5-partition when the function is symmetric submodular; since hypergraph cut functions are symmetric submodular, this yields a polynomial-time algorithm for the hypergraph minsum boundary objective at \(k=5\). However, no general polynomial-time algorithm is known for fixed \(k\ge 6\), and no NP-hardness is established for fixed \(k\ge 5\) in the unweighted hypergraph setting.

On the minmax and standard \(k\)-cut sides, polynomial-time solvability for fixed \(k\) is now well developed: minmax symmetric-submodular partitioning admits an \(n^{O(k^2)}\)-time algorithm, and hypergraph minimum \(k\)-cut admits deterministic enumeration algorithms for fixed \(k\). These results supply techniques (terminal-cut enumeration, contraction/uncrossing structure) that may inform future attacks on the minsum boundary objective, but current literature still treats the fixed-\(k\) minsum symmetric-submodular/hypergraph partition problem beyond \(k=5\) as open.

sources.title: Min–max partitioning of hypergraphs and symmetric submodular functions
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves that Minmax-SymSubmod-\(k\)-Part is solvable in polynomial time for any fixed \(k\): given a symmetric submodular function \(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\) via an evaluation oracle, one can find a \(k\)-partition \((V_1,\dots,V_k)\) minimizing \(\max_i f(V_i)\) in time \(n^{O(k^2)}T\), where \(n=|V|\) and \(T\) is the oracle evaluation time (Theorems 1.2 and 3.1). As a corollary, Minmax-Hypergraph-\(k\)-Part (minimize \(\max_i w(\delta(V_i))\)) has an \(n^{O(k^2)}m\)-time algorithm for fixed \(k\) (Theorem 1.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the complexity of the *minsum* hypergraph \(k\)-partition objective \(\min \sum_{i=1}^k |\delta(V_i)|\) for fixed \(k\ge 5\). This paper primarily resolves the *minmax* variant (minimize \(\max_i |\delta(V_i)|\)) for fixed \(k\) via a structural theorem (Theorem 1.3) and a contraction-based enumeration algorithm. It does not give a polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hardness for the minsum objective on hypergraphs. It does, however, discuss the minsum symmetric-submodular partition problem (Sym-Submod-\(k\)-Part) and proves a structural theorem for minsum (Theorem 4.1) that yields solvability for Sym-Submod-\(k\)-Part up to \(k\le 5\) assuming an algorithm for Submod-\((k-1)\)-Part; but it explicitly states that a general fixed-\(k\) polynomial-time algorithm for the minsum symmetric-submodular/hypergraph partition problem remains open.

sources.title: A polynomial time algorithm for finding a minimum 4-partition of a submodular function
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper gives the first polynomial-time exact algorithm for the minimum 4-partition problem for a general submodular function: given submodular 
\(f:2^V\to\mathbb R\), it computes a 4-partition \(\{V_1,V_2,V_3,V_4\}\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^4 f(V_i)\) in time \(O(n^6\tau(n))\), where \(n=|V|\) and \(\tau(n)\) is the time for submodular function minimization (Theorem 6.1). As a corollary, it computes a minimum 5-partition for symmetric submodular functions in time \(O(n^{14}\tau(n))\) (Corollary 6.2).
sources.connection: For a hypergraph \(G=(V,E)\), the boundary function \(d(U)=|\delta(U)|\) is a symmetric submodular function. The open problem asks for the complexity of minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^k d(V_i)\) over \(k\)-partitions for fixed \(k\ge 5\) (unweighted hypergraphs). This paper advances the general submodular-partition landscape by settling \(k=4\) in polynomial time and giving a polynomial-time algorithm for \(k=5\) only in the symmetric-submodular setting via reduction to the (general) 4-partition algorithm. However, it does not provide a polynomial-time algorithm (nor NP-hardness) for fixed \(k\ge 5\) for hypergraph boundary objectives; it explicitly states the fixed-\(k\) submodular \(k\)-partition problem remains open for \(k\ge 5\), and even shows a compatibility-based approach fails for 5-partitions (Section 7).

This objective is not the standard minimum \(k\)-cut objective (which typically minimizes the number/weight of hyperedges crossing between different parts, counted once per hyperedge). However, algorithms/techniques for hypergraph minimum cut and minimum \(k\)-cut may be relevant as potential subroutines or as a starting point for reductions/complexity comparisons. Based only on the title/abstract, there is no indication the paper studies the “sum of boundary sizes” objective or resolves its complexity for fixed \(k\ge 5\).

sources.title: Deterministic enumeration of all minimum cut-sets and k-cut-sets in hypergraphs for fixed k
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves that for every fixed integer \(k\ge 2\), all minimum \(k\)-cut-sets in a hypergraph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative hyperedge costs can be enumerated in deterministic polynomial time. Concretely (Theorem 1.1 / Theorem 2.1), it gives a deterministic algorithm that enumerates \(n^{O(k)}\) minimum \((S,T)\)-terminal cuts for all \(|S|,|T|\le 2k-1\), forms a candidate family \(\mathcal F\) of \(k\)-cut-sets, and returns exactly the minimum-cost \(k\)-cut-sets; runtime \(O(n^{4k-2})T(n,p)+O(n^{4k^2-2k}p)\), where \(T(n,p)\) is the time for a minimum terminal cut in an \(n\)-vertex hypergraph of size \(p\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the complexity of minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^k |\delta(V_i)|\) over \(k\)-partitions (fixed \(k\ge 5\)). This paper instead studies the standard Hypergraph-\(k\)-Cut objective: minimize the cost of hyperedges crossing the \(k\)-partition, i.e. \(|\delta(V_1,\dots,V_k)|\), equivalently minimum \(k\)-cut-set. It provides deterministic enumeration and structural theorems for minimum \(k\)-cut-sets via small-witness terminal cuts. These techniques may be relevant as tools (terminal-cut based structure/uncrossing) but do not address the different objective \(\sum_i |\delta(V_i)|\), nor prove NP-hardness or a polytime algorithm for that objective.

sources.title: Algorithms for new objectives in graph partitioning and generalizations
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis studies several graph/hypergraph partitioning objectives. Relevant to the open problem, it defines Hypergraph-k-Partition (minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^k w(\delta(V_i))\)) and focuses mainly on (i) Minmax-Hypergraph-k-Partition and Hypergraph-k-Cut (objective \(w(\delta(V_1,\dots,V_k))\)), and (ii) enumeration algorithms for optimum solutions when \(k\) is fixed. It states deterministic polynomial-time enumeration algorithms for fixed \(k\): Enum-Hypergraph-k-Cut in \(O(n^{16k-25}p)\) time and Enum-MinMax-Hypergraph-k-Partition in \(O(k n^{4k^2-2k+1}p)\) time (as summarized in the introduction).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the computational complexity (polytime vs NP-hard) of Hypergraph-k-Partition with the minsum boundary objective \(\min \sum_{i=1}^k |\delta(V_i)|\) for fixed \(k\ge 5\) in unweighted hypergraphs. This thesis explicitly defines that same objective as “Hypergraph-k-Partition” (a symmetric submodular k-partition instance), but the provided excerpt does not contain a hardness proof or a polynomial-time exact algorithm for this objective for fixed \(k\ge 5\). Instead, the thesis discusses: (a) exact/approx/FPT results for graph minmax objectives, (b) hardness/approx for \(\ell_p\)-norm multiway cut, and (c) enumeration algorithms for Hypergraph-k-Cut and Minmax-Hypergraph-k-Partition. Thus it provides context and related techniques (submodular/hypergraph partitioning framework, enumeration/structural results), but does not resolve the stated complexity question for the minsum boundary objective.

title: Certificate for unboundedness of polynomial optimization when moment-ray condition fails
background_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be a basic closed semialgebraic set
\[
K:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: c_i(x)=0\ (i\in E),\ c_j(x)\ge 0\ (j\in I)\},
\]
where \(E,I\) are finite index sets and each \(c_i,c_j\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) is a polynomial. Let \(g\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) be a polynomial of degree \(d\), and consider the polynomial optimization problem
\[
\inf\{g(x): x\in K\}.
\]
Write \(\tilde x:=(x_0,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). The homogenization of a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) of degree \(\deg(p)\) is
\(\tilde p(\tilde x):=x_0^{\deg(p)}p(x/x_0)\), and its highest-degree homogeneous part is \(p_{\mathrm{hom}}(x):=\tilde p(0,x)\).
Define the compact “homogenized” feasible set
\[
\tilde K:=\{\tilde x:\ \tilde c_i(\tilde x)=0\ (i\in E),\ \tilde c_j(\tilde x)\ge 0\ (j\in I),\ \|\tilde x\|_2^2=1,\ x_0\ge 0\},
\]
and the “horizon” (the section \(x_0=0\))
\[
K^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n: c_{i,\mathrm{hom}}(x)=0\ (i\in E),\ c_{j,\mathrm{hom}}(x)\ge 0\ (j\in I),\ \|x\|_2^2=1\}.
\]
A (truncated) moment sequence \(z\) of degree \(d\) supported on \(K^{\circ}\) is an element of the moment cone \(R_d(K^{\circ})\), i.e., there exists a Borel measure \(\mu\) supported on \(K^{\circ}\) such that \(z_\alpha=\int x^\alpha\,d\mu\) for all \(|\alpha|\le d\). For a polynomial \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x]_d\), the pairing is \(\langle p,z\rangle:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le d} p_\alpha z_\alpha\).
The paper discusses a sufficient “decreasing-ray” moment certificate for unboundedness: feasibility of a linear moment system of the form
\[
\langle g_{\mathrm{hom}}, z\rangle=-1,\quad z\in R_d(K^{\circ}).
\]
(Equivalently, the existence of a ray in an appropriate dual moment program.) This condition is sufficient for \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\), but the paper exhibits examples where \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\) while this moment system is infeasible.
problem_definition_latex:
Given polynomials \(g\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) and \(c_i,c_j\in\mathbb{R}[x]\) defining \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) as above, design a computationally convenient certificate (a verifiable condition) that implies
\[
\inf\{g(x):x\in K\}=-\infty,
\]
in the regime where the moment-ray condition
\[
\langle g_{\mathrm{hom}}, z\rangle=-1,\quad z\in R_d(K^{\circ})
\]
is infeasible.

Equivalently: characterize or certify unboundedness of \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)\) by an efficiently checkable condition that applies even when no feasible \(z\in R_d(K^{\circ})\) satisfies \(\langle g_{\mathrm{hom}}, z\rangle=-1\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Nie–Yang, 2023) proposes a sufficient unboundedness certificate for \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\) based on homogenization and a decreasing-ray condition on the horizon section \(K^\circ\): feasibility of \(\langle g_{\mathrm{hom}},z\rangle=-1\) with \(z\in R_d(K^\circ)\). Appendix A shows how this arises as a decreasing ray of the dual of a homogenized conic program and how it can be searched for via a hierarchy of SDP relaxations over moment/localizing matrices on the compact set \(K^\circ\). However, the paper also gives explicit examples where \(\inf_K g=-\infty\) while the horizon moment-ray system is infeasible (e.g., when \(g_{\mathrm{hom}}\ge 0\) on \(K^\circ\) but lower-degree terms drive \(g\to-\infty\) along feasible rays), motivating the open problem.

Among the forward citations provided, none resolves this gap by giving an SDP-style alternative certificate that remains valid when the horizon moment-ray condition fails. The closest conceptual alternative is the tangency/optimality-at-infinity approach of “Optimality Conditions at Infinity in Semialgebraic Vector Optimization”, which characterizes boundedness from below via finitely many asymptotic limits \(\lambda_k\) along components of a tangency variety defined by conditions of the form \(0\in \nabla g(x)+N(x;K)+\mu x\). This suggests a different computational route: certify \(\inf_K g=-\infty\) by exhibiting a tangency-at-infinity branch along which \(g\to-\infty\), potentially reducible to solving polynomial systems/critical point methods at infinity. The other citations contribute tools for handling noncompactness in SOS hierarchies or alternative liftings (e.g., adding redundant constraints like \(c-f\) to enforce bounded sublevel sets, or recession-cone-based tensor/copolytope duality), but they do not provide a general, efficiently checkable unboundedness certificate beyond the horizon moment-ray feasibility.

Overall, the problem remains open: current moment/SOS certificates based purely on \(g_{\mathrm{hom}}\) over \(K^\circ\) are not necessary for unboundedness, and forward-citing work has not yet produced a replacement certificate with comparable computational convenience. Promising directions include (a) certificates that incorporate lower-degree terms through multi-scale homogenization or weighted projective compactifications, and (b) tangency-variety/critical-at-infinity characterizations translated into polynomial-algebraic conditions amenable to SDP or Gröbner/critical-point computation.

sources.title: Optimality Conditions at Infinity in Semialgebraic Vector Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For minimizing a lower semicontinuous semi-algebraic function \(f\) over an unbounded closed semi-algebraic set \(S\), assuming the qualification condition at infinity \((QC)_\infty\), the paper characterizes boundedness from below and the optimal value via the tangency variety \(\Gamma(f,S)=\{x\in \mathrm{dom}f\cap S: \exists\mu\in\mathbb R\text{ with }0\in \partial f(x)+N(x;S)+\mu x\}\). Decomposing \(\Gamma(f,S)\setminus B_R\) into finitely many unbounded connected components \(\Gamma_k\), defining \(f_k(t):=f(x)\) for \(x\in \Gamma_k\cap S_t\) and \(\lambda_k:=\lim_{t\to\infty} f_k(t)\in\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\), they prove: \(f\) is bounded below on \(S\) iff \(\min_k \lambda_k>-\infty\) (Theorem 4.1), and under \((QC)\), \[\inf_{x\in S} f(x)=\min\Big\{\min_{x\in\Sigma(f,S)} f(x),\ \min_k \lambda_k\Big\},\] where \(\Sigma(f,S)=\{x:0\in\partial f(x)+N(x;S)\}\) (Theorem 4.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a computationally convenient certificate of unboundedness \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\) for polynomial optimization when a specific moment-ray certificate on the horizon set \(K^\circ\) is infeasible. This paper does not address moment/SOS certificates, homogenization, or truncated moment cones. However, it provides an alternative geometric/variational characterization of when a semi-algebraic optimization problem is unbounded below: unboundedness corresponds to existence of a tangency component \(\Gamma_k\) along which \(f_k(t)\to -\infty\) (i.e., some \(\lambda_k=-\infty\)). For polynomial \(g\) and basic closed semi-algebraic \(K\), one can take \(f=g\), \(S=K\) (with \((QC)_\infty\) typically holding since polynomials are locally Lipschitz) and obtain a non-moment-based certificate: detect a tangency-at-infinity path satisfying \(0\in \nabla g(x)+N(x;K)+\mu x\) with \(g(x)\to -\infty\). The paper claims these conditions are ‘verifiable’ and gives a ‘computable formula’, but it does not provide an explicit SDP-style certificate comparable to the requested moment-ray alternative.

sources.title: Convergences of Lasserre hierarchy of an SDP relaxation for robust non-convex polynomial optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For a convex polynomial program \(\min\{f(x): g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\dots,m\}\) over a possibly noncompact semialgebraic set, the paper proves: (i) asymptotic convergence of a modified Lasserre SDP hierarchy built from the truncated quadratic module generated by \(c-f\) and \(-g_i\) (Theorem 2.1: \(f_k^*\uparrow f^*\)); (ii) if the Lagrangian \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)\) has a saddle point \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) with \(\nabla^2_{xx}L(x^*,\lambda^*)\succ 0\), then \(f-f(x^*)\in M(-g_1,\dots,-g_m,c-f)\) (Theorem 3.1), implying finite convergence of the hierarchy (Theorem 3.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a computational certificate of unboundedness \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\) when a specific homogenized “moment-ray” condition on the horizon set \(K^\circ\) is infeasible. This citing paper does not study unboundedness certificates or horizon/moment-ray infeasibility. Instead it addresses the opposite regime: convex polynomial programs that are bounded below (so \(\inf> -\infty\)) and establishes SOS/quadratic-module representations and convergence of Lasserre-type SDP relaxations without compactness by adding the redundant constraint \(c-f\) into the quadratic module. While not a direct answer, its technique suggests a general SDP-verifiable approach to handle noncompactness by enforcing bounded sublevel sets (via \(c-f\)) and coercivity; however it does not provide a certificate that \(\inf=-\infty\) when such boundedness fails, nor does it characterize unboundedness beyond the convex/bounded-below setting.

sources.theorem_or_result:
For POPs with linear inequality constraints of the form \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Bx\le b,\ x\ge 0\}\), the paper gives an exact lifting to a convex tensor program and then an equivalent completely positive tensor program (CPTP). Concretely, for a homogeneous objective \(f(x)=\langle A_f^h,M_d(x)\rangle\), under attainment it proves equivalence between \(\min\{f(x):x\in F\}\) and
- \(\min\ \langle A_f^h,X\rangle\) s.t. \(X\in \mathcal{C}^*_{n+1,d},\ \langle X,M_d(a)\rangle=1,\ X\times_1A\times_2A\cdots\times_dA\in \mathcal{C}^*_{m+n+1,d}\) (Theorem 5),
and similarly for inhomogeneous \(f\) an exact CPTP in \(\mathcal{C}^*_{n+2,d}\) with additional linear/tensor constraints (Theorem 6). It also derives dual copositive tensor programs and shows strict feasibility/strong duality for these primal–dual pairs (Section 4.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a computationally convenient certificate of unboundedness \(\inf_{x\in K} g(x)=-\infty\) when a specific moment-ray condition on the horizon set \(K^\circ\) is infeasible. This paper does not address that moment-ray failure regime or propose an alternative unboundedness certificate based on homogenization/moments on \(K^\circ\). Instead, it develops exact completely-positive/copolytope tensor reformulations for POPs with linear inequality feasible sets and analyzes recession cones to build lifted convex models. While recession-cone analysis is conceptually related to detecting directions of unbounded descent, the paper’s main theorems assume attainment of an optimal solution and focus on equivalence/strong duality of CPTP formulations, not on certifying \(-\infty\) optimal value. Thus it provides potentially relevant tools (recession-cone-based lifting; copositive duals) but no direct certificate for unboundedness beyond the moment-ray condition in the open problem.

sources.title: Moment and polynomial optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper solves an infinite-dimensional moment problem for nonnegative measures supported on the unit ball of a Sobolev space (equivalently, a compact ellipsoid of Fourier coefficients) and constructs semidefinite outer/inner approximations of the corresponding moment cone. In particular, for an index set A it defines spectrahedral outer approximations \(C^{\mathrm{out}}_{r,\rho}(A)\) via positivity on a truncated quadratic module \(Q_{r,\rho}\), proves \(C^{\mathrm{out}}_{\infty,\infty}(A)=C(A)\) (and similarly \(C^{\mathrm{inn}}_{\infty,\infty}(A)=C(A)\)), and derives a Hausdorff-distance bound \(d_H(C(A),C^{\mathrm{out}}_{r,\rho_A}(A))\le 9(2\rho_A+1)^n\, r_A^2/r^2\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a computational certificate of unboundedness for a finite-dimensional polynomial optimization \(\inf\{g(x):x\in K\}\) when a specific “moment-ray” certificate on the horizon set \(K^\circ\) is infeasible. This citing paper does not address unboundedness certificates for finite-dimensional POPs or propose an alternative to the failing condition \(\langle g_{\mathrm{hom}},z\rangle=-1,\ z\in R_d(K^\circ)\). Instead, it develops moment/SOS machinery for measures on compact sets in infinite-dimensional Sobolev/Fourier coefficient spaces, including semidefinite approximations of moment cones and Positivstellensatz-based representation results. These techniques are broadly related to moment-SOS methods, but they do not directly yield a new unboundedness certificate in the regime described by the open problem.

Page 15, Section 5 (Concluding Remarks)

Thus, one may ask if it is possible to regulate data marketplaces to avoid such inefficiencies. Unfortunately, our results highlight that typical suggestions, such as avoiding monopolistic platforms, may not be effective. Since our results hold for any fixed participation rate, a platform can exploit information leakage regardless of its market size. Further, differential privacy cannot eliminate the underlying issues in this case, which comes from inter-group and intra-group correlation. Thus, an important problem motivated by our work is: what approaches can be brought to bear to mitigate the impact of information leakage and the privacy paradox in data marketplaces?
title: Design mechanisms to mitigate information leakage and privacy paradox in data marketplaces
background_latex:
Consider a data marketplace (online platform) with a population of agents whose private data may be statistically correlated across agents. When an agent participates and shares data, this can create information leakage about other agents with correlated data, generating privacy externalities.

A platform/analyst designs a data-acquisition mechanism that interacts with agents and may (i) offer payments, (ii) choose which agents' data to acquire, and (iii) influence participation incentives. The platform has an objective related to statistical estimation accuracy (e.g., bias-variance trade-offs) and operates under constraints such as limited budget and incentive compatibility. Agents' utilities incorporate both participation benefits and privacy costs that depend on participation decisions of others due to correlation.

Information leakage and correlation-driven privacy externalities can lead to oversharing (the "privacy paradox") and market inefficiencies, including reduced payments and distorted participation behavior. Standard tools such as increasing competition (avoiding monopoly) or applying differential privacy may not eliminate these correlation-driven externalities.

Let a class of feasible regulatory or market-design interventions be denoted abstractly by \(\mathcal{R}\). An intervention \(R\in\mathcal{R}\) can represent any rule or policy imposed on the marketplace (e.g., restrictions on data use, limits on inference, compensation rules, information disclosure requirements), without committing to a specific model beyond being implementable alongside the marketplace mechanism.
problem_definition_latex: Identify and analyze interventions \(R\in\mathcal{R}\) that mitigate the impact of information leakage due to correlated data and thereby reduce the inefficiencies associated with the privacy paradox in data marketplaces.

Since our results hold for any fixed participation rate, a platform can exploit information leakage regardless of its market size. Further, differential privacy cannot eliminate the underlying issues in this case, which comes from inter-group and intra-group correlation. Thus, an important problem motivated by our work is: what approaches can be brought to bear to mitigate the impact of information leakage and the privacy paradox in data marketplaces?

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Liao–Su–Ziani–Wierman–Huang, 2021) formalizes the privacy paradox in a data-acquisition mechanism with verifiable data and correlation-driven privacy externalities: an agent who does not participate still incurs privacy loss \(g(c,\theta_i;\alpha_i)\) from others’ participation, while a participant incurs \(h(c,\theta_i;\alpha_i)=c\,b(\theta_i;\alpha_i)\). This creates a wedge \(h-g\) that lets the platform induce participation with lower payments and can generate oversharing and inefficiency. The open problem asks for interventions \(R\in\mathcal R\) that mitigate this information leakage (inference about nonparticipants from correlated participants) beyond standard fixes like competition or differential privacy.

Among forward citations, none directly propose or analyze such correlation-targeted regulatory interventions. The closest partial progress comes from differential-privacy-based mechanism design for data acquisition ("Bridging central and local differential privacy in data acquisition mechanisms" and "Optimal and differentially private data acquisition: Central and local mechanisms"), which provide strong tools for incentive-compatible payments and for choosing privacy parameters to trade off estimation error and compensation. However, these works largely assume conditional independence across agents and treat privacy loss as individual (DP/RDP) rather than as an externality induced by correlation \(\alpha\); consequently, they do not address the core channel in the source model where participation of one agent changes others’ utilities via \(g\) and \(h\).

Other citing works study marketplace interventions of a different kind (fairness/balance constraints, demographic secrecy, or user-facing redaction tools). They are useful methodologically: they show how constraints imposed alongside a market mechanism can backfire by preventing market formation, and how costs of interventions can amortize with market growth. Translating these lessons to privacy-externality mitigation suggests that promising directions for \(\mathcal R\) likely require explicit limits on inference about nonparticipants (e.g., correlation-aware privacy constraints, restrictions on cross-agent predictive use, or compensation rules internalizing \(g\)-type externalities), and equilibrium analysis to avoid participation collapse. Based on the provided forward-citation set, the problem remains open.

sources.title: Bridging central and local differential privacy in data acquisition mechanisms
sources.theorem_or_result: For Bayesian data acquisition with users having heterogeneous weights between local and central Rényi differential privacy losses, the optimal incentive-compatible and individually rational mechanism reduces pointwise (for each reported type vector \(c\)) to minimizing \(\gamma\,\mathrm{MSE}(\varepsilon^{(l)},\varepsilon^{(c)},\hat\theta)+\sum_i \psi_i(c_i)\varepsilon^{(l)}_i+\sum_i (1-\psi_i(c_i))\varepsilon^{(c)}_i\) (Theorem 2), where \(\psi_i(c)=c+F_i(c)/f_i(c)\) is the virtual cost. For linear estimators with Gaussian mechanisms, the resulting nonconvex program (7) admits a PTAS: for any \(\delta>0\), Algorithm 1 outputs \((\varepsilon^{(l)},\varepsilon^{(c)},\hat\theta)\) with objective within factor \(1+\delta\) of optimal in time \(\mathrm{poly}(n,1/\delta)\) (Theorem 3). Additionally, in an optimal Gaussian two-part mechanism it is never optimal to add extra central noise (Proposition 1: the optimal central-noise privacy parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon=\infty\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for regulatory/market-design interventions \(R\in\mathcal R\) that mitigate information leakage and correlation-driven privacy externalities in data marketplaces. This paper designs an optimal Bayesian incentive-compatible acquisition mechanism under differential privacy, but it assumes users’ data are independent conditional on \(\theta\) (no cross-agent correlation) and models privacy loss via local/central RDP rather than explicit correlation-driven leakage about nonparticipants. Thus it does not address the core externality mechanism (inference about others from correlated data) nor propose interventions targeted at that externality. However, it provides related mechanism-design tools: (i) a two-part privacy model separating platform access (local DP) from public release (central DP), and (ii) computational/structural results (pointwise reduction, PTAS) that could be components of an intervention class \(\mathcal R\) in settings where DP-style constraints are the regulatory lever.

sources.title: Optimal and differentially private data acquisition: Central and local mechanisms
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper designs Bayesian incentive-compatible, individually rational mechanisms for purchasing verifiable user data under heterogeneous differential privacy costs, and characterizes (near-)optimal estimators and privacy-loss allocations in both central and local DP architectures. Key characterizations: (i) Central DP minimax mean-estimation with heterogeneous privacy losses \(\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_i)\): \(L_c(P^*,\theta,\varepsilon)\ge c\,\max_{k\in\{0,\dots,n\}}\big(\frac{1}{n-k+(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i)^2}\wedge 1\big)\), and a Laplace-noised linear estimator achieves this up to a \(\log(n)\) factor (Theorem 1). (ii) Under regularity (monotone virtual costs \(\psi_i(c)=c+F_i(c)/f_i(c)\)), the optimal central-mechanism privacy losses \(\varepsilon_i^*(c)=y_i^*\) solve the pointwise program \[\min_{y\ge 0}\ \frac{n+1}{(\sum_j y_j)^2}\Big(2+\sum_i y_i^2\,\mathrm{var}\Big)+\sum_i \psi_i(c_i) y_i,\] with estimator weights \(w_i=y_i^*/\sum_j y_j^*\) (Theorem 3). (iii) In the local DP architecture, optimal privacy losses solve \[\min_{y\ge 0}\ \frac{n+1}{\sum_i \frac{1}{\mathrm{var}+2/y_i^2}}+\sum_i \psi_i(c_i) y_i,\] with weights proportional to \(1/(\mathrm{var}+2/y_i^{*2})\) (Theorem 4). Efficient computation: \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm for the central program and a PTAS for the local program (Propositions 3–4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for regulatory/market-design interventions \(R\in\mathcal R\) that mitigate information leakage and correlation-driven privacy externalities (privacy paradox) in data marketplaces with statistically correlated agents. This paper instead studies optimal data acquisition mechanisms under differential privacy when users’ data are modeled as i.i.d. \(X_i=\theta+Z_i\) (independent across users) and privacy costs are heterogeneous but private. It provides mechanism-design and algorithmic tools for choosing personalized DP levels and payments (central vs local DP) to trade off estimation error and compensation. However, it does not model correlation-driven information leakage across agents, nor externalities where one agent’s participation affects others’ privacy costs via correlation, nor does it propose regulatory interventions limiting inference about nonparticipants. Thus it is relevant mainly as a mechanism-design baseline/toolkit for DP-based marketplace design, not as a direct solution to correlation/externality mitigation.

sources.title: Machine-Learning Fairness in Data Markets: Challenges and Opportunities
sources.theorem_or_result: The thesis develops theoretical models of data markets under fairness interventions. Key results include: - In a fair-representation/data-reuse model, demographic secrecy can impose an additional welfare loss beyond the cost of fairness; under a random-functions model, expected cost of demographic secrecy grows as \(\Omega(2^{n/2}\sqrt{|V|})\) while expected cost of fairness is \(\Theta(n\sqrt{|V|})\), and with high probability there exist incentive-compatible (non-demographically-secret) representations achieving the maximum fair welfare \(\beta\) (Theorems 2.5.1–2.5.3). - In a centralized data-market model with endogenous data production, fairness interventions enforcing demographic-balance constraints can backfire (market fails to form) for some market conditions (Theorem 3.5.1), but market growth can mitigate backfire risk and the relative cost of fairness can amortize to 0 as the number of buyers grows under unbounded economic potential (Theorems 3.6.1–3.6.3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for regulatory/market-design interventions \(R\in\mathcal R\) that mitigate information leakage and correlation-driven privacy externalities in data marketplaces. This thesis is not about correlated-data privacy leakage; it focuses on fairness interventions and incentive-compatible information control in data reuse/markets. Still, it is relevant as a mechanism-design template: it studies how constraints on information release (demographic secrecy vs incentive-compatible representations) and marketplace rules (acceptance constraints enforcing demographic balance) change equilibrium participation, welfare, and can cause ‘backfire’/market collapse. These analyses provide tools and cautionary lessons for designing \(R\) in privacy-externality settings: interventions must be market-aware, account for participation incentives, and may need growth/scale conditions to avoid collapse. However, it does not model statistical correlation across agents nor privacy costs/externalities from inference, so it does not directly resolve the leakage-mitigation problem.

sources.title: The Cost of Balanced Training-Data Production in an Online Data Market
sources.theorem_or_result: In a stylized online data-market game (based on Agarwal–Dahleh–Sarkar) with endogenous data production by sellers and a marketplace-imposed demographic-balance constraint (accepting a seller’s dataset iff its group proportions equal a target \(\tau\)), the paper characterizes Nash equilibria and shows: (i) fairness constraints can prevent market formation in small/emerging markets (Theorem 5.1: for any target \(\tau\) there exists a market where baseline forms but intervention does not); (ii) in fully-forming markets, the uniform target \(\tau_g=1/|\mathcal G|\) guarantees formation (Theorem 5.2) but non-uniform targets can still backfire (Theorem 5.3); and (iii) under market growth where some group’s potential economic value \(V_g\to\infty\), the normalized “cost of fairness” amortizes: marketplace and sellers’ utility ratios \(\to 1\) and buyers’ ratios \(\ge 1\) (Theorem 6.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for regulatory/market-design interventions \(R\) that mitigate correlation-driven information leakage and privacy externalities in data marketplaces. This citing paper studies a different ethical intervention—demographic balance/fairness in training-data production—under assumptions that explicitly remove cross-agent/cross-group statistical dependence (samples i.i.d. and independent across groups; “zero inter-group transfer”). It therefore does not model correlated private data, information leakage, or privacy externalities, and does not propose mechanisms to mitigate the privacy paradox. However, it is tangentially relevant as a market-design analysis of an intervention imposed alongside a data-acquisition mechanism, including conditions under which interventions backfire (prevent market formation) and when their welfare cost vanishes with market growth—insights that could inform the feasibility analysis of privacy-mitigating regulations \(R\) in correlated-data settings.

sources.title: Privacy concerns and social desirability bias
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper designs and evaluates post-interview privacy controls for chatbot-based interviews: (i) unguided free editing of the transcript and (ii) AI-aided editing where an LLM flags potential personally identifiable information (PII) and suggests redaction/abstraction (e.g., replacing names with placeholders like \([\mathrm{NAME}1]\) or generalizing “18 years old” to “young adult”). In a between-subjects experiment with \(N=188\), AI-aided editing reduces PII disclosure while maintaining interview data quality and user engagement relative to no-editing and free-editing baselines.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for marketplace/regulatory interventions \(R\in\mathcal R\) that mitigate information leakage and privacy externalities arising from correlated data in data marketplaces, under incentive/budget/estimation objectives. This paper does not model correlated-data externalities, mechanism design, payments, or market equilibrium; it studies an HCI setting (chatbot interviews) where individuals overshare and proposes a user-facing control (post-hoc editing with AI cues) to reduce direct PII leakage while preserving data utility. As such, it is best viewed as a related tool/intervention idea—human-in-the-loop, post-collection sanitization and disclosure control—that could potentially be incorporated as a policy in \(\mathcal R\) (e.g., mandatory review/redaction stage) but it does not analyze the correlation-driven leakage central to the open problem nor provide formal guarantees for marketplace inefficiency mitigation.

sources.title: How differential privacy impacts data elicitation
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives distribution- and privacy-parameter-dependent bounds on how randomized response (RR) (\varepsilon\)-local differential privacy applied to the sensitive attribute in training data changes group-fairness metrics of the resulting classifier. In particular, under their majority-vote-style learning assumption, for each fixed \(x\): if \(\mathrm{CSD}_x\neq 0\) then \(\mathrm{CSD}'_x\) lies between \(\mathrm{CSD}_x\) and \(0\) (Theorem 4.1). If \(X\perp A\), then \(\mathrm{SD}'\) lies between \(\mathrm{SD}\) and \(0\) (Theorem 4.2). If \(X\not\perp A\), then only one-sided inequalities hold (Theorem 4.3) and \(\mathrm{SD}'\) can flip sign. Under a reliability assumption \(Y\perp A\mid X\), \(\mathrm{EOD}'\) lies between \(\mathrm{EOD}\) and \(0\) (Theorem 4.4).

title: Classify the complexity of Nash equilibrium existence in edge-ranking flow games
background_latex:
A flow allocation game is specified by a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), node supplies \((b_v)_{v\in V}\) with \(b_v\ge 0\), and edge capacities \((c_e)_{e\in E}\) with \(c_e\ge 0\). Each node \(v\in V\) is a strategic player.

In an edge-ranking strategy, each player \(v\) chooses a strict total order (a permutation) \(\pi_v\) of its outgoing edges \(E^+(v)=\{(v,w)\in E\}\). Given a profile \(\pi=(\pi_v)_{v\in V}\), a feasible flow is a vector \(f=(f_e)_{e\in E}\) with \(0\le f_e\le c_e\) such that for every node \(v\), if its total available supply is
\[
F_v \,=\, b_v + \sum_{e\in E^-(v)} f_e,
\]
then \(v\) sends flow along outgoing edges greedily according to \(\pi_v\): it fully saturates the highest-ranked outgoing edge until either that edge hits capacity or \(v\) runs out of supply, then proceeds to the next edge, etc. (Equivalently, \(f\) is a fixed point of the induced greedy allocation mapping.)

Among (possibly multiple) feasible flows for a given profile \(\pi\), the model selects the clearing state \(\hat f(\pi)\), defined as the coordinate-wise maximum feasible flow (the supremum in the lattice of feasible flows for monotone strategies). The utility of player \(v\) under \(\pi\) is the total outgoing flow in the clearing state:
\[
u_v(\pi) \,=\, \sum_{e\in E^+(v)} \hat f_e(\pi).
\]

A pure Nash equilibrium is a profile \(\pi\) such that for every player \(v\) and every alternative permutation \(\pi'_v\),
\[
u_v(\pi) \ge \nu_v(\pi'_v,\pi_{-v}).
\]

The decision problem of interest is: given \((G,(b_v),(c_e))\), does there exist a pure Nash equilibrium in edge-ranking strategies? Complexity is measured in the usual Turing model with \(b_v,c_e\) given in binary.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine the exact complexity class of the following decision problem.

Input: an edge-ranking flow allocation game \(\Gamma=(G,(b_v)_{v\in V},(c_e)_{e\in E})\).

Question: does there exist a pure Nash equilibrium profile \(\pi=(\pi_v)_{v\in V}\) of edge-ranking strategies (permutations of \(E^+(v)\)) with utilities \(u_v(\pi)=\sum_{e\in E^+(v)}\hat f_e(\pi)\) defined by the clearing state \(\hat f(\pi)\)?

In particular, decide whether this Nash-existence problem lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\), whether it is \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete, or otherwise characterize its precise complexity.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Flow Allocation Games (Bertschinger–Hoefer–Schmand), edge-ranking strategies (permutations of outgoing edges) induce a monotone allocation map whose feasible flows form a complete lattice; the model selects the clearing state \(\hat f(\pi)\), the coordinate-wise maximum fixed point. Section 5 of the source paper shows that, unlike unit-ranking strategies, edge-ranking games can lack pure Nash equilibria and that deciding existence of a pure Nash equilibrium (and strong equilibrium) is strongly NP-hard (Theorem 20). However, the paper explicitly leaves open the *exact* complexity classification: Remark 21 notes that NP-membership is unclear because verifying best responses can be NP-hard, while membership in \(\Sigma_2^p\) is straightforward.

The forward-citing literature provided does not resolve this gap for the edge-ranking permutation game. Instead, it supplies supporting evidence from closely related clearing-based strategic models in financial networks. In particular, works on strategic debt forgiveness (edge removals) and strategic prepayments establish NP-hardness of pure-strategy Nash equilibrium existence under default costs in proportional-clearing (Rogers–Veraart/Eisenberg–Noe) settings. These results suggest that equilibrium-existence hardness is robust across clearing mechanisms and strategic action spaces, and they offer reduction templates (e.g., from PARTITION) and structural nonexistence/existence phenomena that may be adaptable to the edge-ranking setting.

On the algorithmic side, Computing Tarski Fixed Points in Financial Networks provides strongly polynomial algorithms for computing minimal/maximal clearing fixed points for broad monotone piecewise-linear payment rules, explicitly including edge-ranking. Such results strengthen the toolbox for any attempt to place Nash-existence in NP (via polynomial-time evaluation of \(\hat f(\pi)\) and utilities) or to sharpen upper bounds. Additional related-tool papers on claims trading and debt swapping develop complexity and structural techniques in the same edge-ranking/maximal-clearing framework, but do not address equilibrium existence. Overall, the exact placement of edge-ranking Nash-existence between NP and \(\Sigma_2^p\) (or higher) remains open in the provided citation set.

sources.title: Optimal Bailouts and Strategic Debt Forgiveness in Financial Networks
sources.theorem_or_result:
In the Eisenberg–Noe/Rogers–Veraart proportional-clearing financial network model with strategic debt forgiveness (each bank chooses a subset of its incoming liabilities to delete), the paper proves NP-hardness of equilibrium-related decision problems: in particular, with default costs 
\(\alpha=\beta=1/\sum_i e_i\), deciding whether a pure Nash equilibrium exists is NP-hard (Theorem 15a). It also shows that without default costs and without cash injections, a pure Nash equilibrium always exists (Theorem 7), while with cash injections (even without default costs) a pure Nash equilibrium need not exist (Theorem 9).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the exact complexity of pure Nash equilibrium existence in edge-ranking flow allocation games (players choose permutations of outgoing edges; outcome is the maximal/clearing fixed point of a greedy allocation). This citing paper does not study edge-ranking strategies; instead it studies a different strategic model (edge-removal/forgiveness of incoming debts) under proportional-clearing payments with possible default costs and bailouts. Nevertheless, it is directly relevant in two ways: (i) it provides a concrete NP-hardness result for deciding existence of pure Nash equilibria in a closely related class of financial-network clearing games (Theorem 15a), suggesting that Nash-existence questions in clearing-based flow games can be computationally intractable; (ii) it gives explicit non-existence examples (Theorems 9 and 12) and existence guarantees on restricted topologies (Theorems 7 and 13), which may inform analogous structural/complexity classifications for edge-ranking flow allocation games. It does not resolve whether the edge-ranking Nash-existence problem is in NP, \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete, etc., nor does it provide a reduction tailored to the permutation-strategy edge-ranking model.

sources.title: Optimal bailouts and strategic debt forgiveness in financial networks
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves NP-hardness results for Nash-equilibrium questions in a related financial-network game where players choose sets of incoming debts to forgive (edge removals) and outcomes are maximal clearing payments. In particular (Theorem 15a), in edge-removal games with default costs \(\alpha=\beta<1\), deciding whether a pure Nash equilibrium exists is NP-hard; additionally, verifying a given profile is a PNE is NP-hard (Theorem 15b), computing a best response is NP-hard (Theorem 15c), and computing a welfare-maximizing profile is NP-hard (Theorem 15d).

This citing paper does not analyze edge-ranking strategies; instead it studies a different strategic model (edge-removal/forgiveness of incoming debts) under proportional clearing payments (EisenbergNoe/RogersVeraart) and sometimes cash injections/default costs. Nevertheless, it provides evidence that Nash-existence questions in closely related flow/clearing models can be computationally hard: it shows NP-hardness of deciding PNE existence once default costs are present (Theorem 15a) and gives examples of non-existence even without default costs when cash injections are allowed (Theorem 9). These results do not settle whether edge-ranking Nash existence is in NP vs \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete, but they suggest hardness phenomena and supply reduction templates (from PARTITION) that might inspire reductions for the edge-ranking setting.

sources.title: A strategic analysis of prepayments in financial credit networks
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper defines a different strategic model (prepayment games in Eisenberg–Noe/Rogers–Veraart financial networks) and proves hardness of pure-strategy Nash equilibrium (PSNE) existence in one of its variants: In the total-assets utility setting with default costs \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), deciding whether a PSNE exists is NP-hard (Theorem 6(c)). It also shows nonexistence can occur (Theorem 4) and that in an equity-utility variant PSNE always exist (indeed every profile is a PSNE; Theorem 7).

This citing paper does not resolve that classification. However, it is closely related in spirit: it studies strategic behavior in financial network clearing models and explicitly cites Flow Allocation Games (Bertschinger et al., 2024), which introduced edge-ranking/coin-ranking payment schemes. The paper contributes a separate NP-hardness result for PSNE existence in a different game (strategic prepayments) built on clearing payments with default costs. This provides evidence that Nash-existence questions around clearing-based financial network games can be computationally intractable, but it neither proves NP-membership nor \(\Sigma_2^p\)-hardness/completeness for the edge-ranking flow game, nor does it analyze the permutation-strategy space central to the open problem.

sources.title: Computing Tarski Fixed Points in Financial Networks
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper gives strongly polynomial-time algorithms to compute (i) the minimal Tarski fixed point (minimal clearing state) and (ii) the maximal fixed point for broad financial-network clearing models with monotone, piecewise-linear payment functions (including edge-ranking), and extends to default costs. In particular, Algorithm 1 computes the minimal clearing state in time \(O((n+k)(n^3+m))\) for networks without default cost (Theorem 1), and with default cost in \(O((k+n+m)(n^3+m))\) (Corollary 1). It also shows a polynomial-time reduction from general piecewise-linear payment functions to priority-proportional ones preserving clearing states (Lemma 6), yielding a polynomial-time algorithm for maximal clearing (Corollary 3).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the complexity of *existence of a pure Nash equilibrium* in edge-ranking flow allocation games (players choose permutations; outcome is the coordinate-wise maximal feasible flow/clearing state; utilities are outgoing flow). This paper does not study Nash equilibria or strategic choice of rankings. Instead it studies computation of clearing states (minimal/maximal fixed points) in Eisenberg–Noe-type financial networks with monotone payment functions, explicitly including edge-ranking as a special case. Thus it provides algorithmic tools for computing clearing outcomes for a *given* ranking profile, which is a subroutine potentially relevant to checking best responses or verifying equilibria, but it does not classify the complexity of Nash-existence nor provide NP/\(\Sigma_2^p\) hardness/membership results.

sources.title: Algorithms for claims trading
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies algorithmic and complexity questions for claims trading in Eisenberg–Noe style financial networks with monotone payment functions (including edge-ranking payments). Key results include: - Proposition 9: for edge-ranking payments and a single claims trade, one can compute an optimal creditor-positive haircut rate \(\alpha^*\in[0,1]\) in polynomial time (via a return-network construction and computing a maximal clearing state). - Theorem 15: choosing a subset of incoming claims to trade to make a given creditor bank solvent (IncomingSave-VR) is weakly NP-hard. - Theorem 19: despite NP-hardness, there is a bicriteria FPTAS for incoming-claims multi-trades (allowing haircut rates up to \(1+\varepsilon\)) to achieve assets at least \(A^*-\delta\). - Theorem 22/Corollary 23: for trading outgoing edges under edge-ranking payments, the optimization problem is strongly NP-hard and hard to approximate within \(n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the exact complexity of existence of a pure Nash equilibrium in edge-ranking flow allocation games (players choose permutations of outgoing edges; outcome is the maximal clearing state; utilities are outgoing flow). This paper does not study Nash equilibria or equilibrium existence. It instead analyzes a different strategic/algorithmic intervention problem (claims trading) in financial networks, where payment rules may be edge-ranking and clearing states form a lattice with a maximal element. The main conceptual overlap is the use of edge-ranking payment/flow rules and maximal clearing states under monotone mappings, plus complexity results (NP-hardness/FPTAS) for related combinatorial decision problems. These techniques might be adaptable as tools for reductions or for reasoning about monotonicity/lattice structure in the equilibrium-existence problem, but no direct classification (NP vs \(\Sigma_2^p\), etc.) for Nash existence is provided.

sources.title: Dynamic Debt Swapping in Financial Networks
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies debt-swap dynamics in financial networks under monotone allocation rules, focusing on edge-ranking clearing. Key results include: - Theorem 10: No positive debt swap exists under any monotone allocation rule (i.e., there is no swap where both involved creditors strictly increase total assets). - Theorem 14: A debt swap is semi-positive iff it is Pareto-improving (all banks’ total assets weakly increase and at least one strictly increases). - Theorem 20: For edge-ranking rules, every sequence of v-improving semi-positive swaps has polynomial length; hence SemiSwap(v) can be solved in polynomial time. - Theorem 26/Corollary 27: A local optimum for arbitrary v-improving swaps is PLS-complete to compute; there exist instances where every such improvement path to a local optimum is exponentially long.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the exact complexity of deciding whether a pure Nash equilibrium exists in edge-ranking flow allocation games (players choose permutations of outgoing edges; outcome is the maximal/clearing flow; utility is total outgoing flow). This paper does not analyze Nash equilibrium existence or its complexity. It instead analyzes a different strategic/dynamic model: local graph modifications via debt swaps (swapping creditors of equal-liability edges) and the resulting changes in the clearing state under edge-ranking clearing. While both settings share the same underlying clearing mechanism (maximal fixed point for edge-ranking/monotone allocation), the decision problems differ: swap dynamics/local optima vs. existence of a permutation-profile equilibrium. The paper contributes structural monotonicity and lattice-based arguments (e.g., source–sink equivalency) and complexity results in PLS for local search, which might be useful as techniques or for reductions, but it does not place the Nash-existence problem in NP, ^p, etc., nor does it resolve equilibrium existence.

Assuming homogeneous marginals, does an exchangeable joint mix solve problem (8) for a general convex cost function f? In Theorem 4, we showed that this holds true for quadratic cost. We also know that a joint mix is an optimizer for the general convex cost problem without uncertainty. These observations seem to hint at the possible optimality of some exchangeable joint mix for general convex cost under uncertainty, but we do not have a proof.
title: Extend exchangeable joint-mix optimality for uncertain subsets under general convex costs
background_latex:
Let \(n\ge 2\) and let \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\). Let \(F\) be a univariate probability distribution on \(\mathbb{R}\) with finite second moment, and consider random vectors \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)\) such that \(X_i\sim F\) for all \(i\in[n]\) (identical marginals).

For a subset \(K\subseteq[n]\), define the partial sum \(S_K(X)=\sum_{i\in K} X_i\), with the convention \(S_\varnothing(X)=0\). Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a convex measurable function such that the relevant expectations are finite.

Let \(2^{[n]}\) denote the power set of \([n]\). For a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(2^{[n]}\), define the uncertainty-averaged cost functional
\[
C_f^\mu(X):=\sum_{K\subseteq[n]} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(S_K(X))\bigr]\,\mu(K).
\]
Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be a nonempty set of probability measures on \(2^{[n]}\) (an "uncertainty set"). Call \(\mathcal{M}\) symmetric if for every \(\mu\in\mathcal{M}\) and every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), the permuted measure \(\mu^\pi\) defined by \(\mu^\pi(K)=\mu(\pi(K))\) also lies in \(\mathcal{M}\), where \(\pi(K)=\{\pi(i): i\in K\}\).

The robust multi-marginal transport problem under subset uncertainty is
\[
\inf\Bigl\{\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{M}} C_f^\mu(X):\ X_i\sim F\ \text{for all } i\in[n]\Bigr\}.
\]
A random vector \(X\) is exchangeable if \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\) is distributionally invariant under permutations of coordinates. A joint mix is a vector with \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i=c\) almost surely for some constant \(c\) (for identical marginals this is tied to complete mixability of \(F\)).
problem_definition_latex:
Assume \(F\) is \(n\)-completely mixable (so that at least one joint mix with marginals \(F\) exists) and assume \(\mathcal{M}\) is symmetric.

Determine whether, for every convex measurable \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) (with finite expectations), there exists an exchangeable joint mix \(X\) with marginals \(F\) that attains the optimum of the robust problem
\[
\inf\Bigl\{\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal{M}} \sum_{K\subseteq[n]} \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(S_K(X))\bigr]\,\mu(K):\ X_i\sim F\ \text{for all } i\in[n]\Bigr\}.
\]
Equivalently: characterize conditions under which some exchangeable joint mix solves the above robust optimization for general convex \(f\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The open question posed by Koike, Lin, and Wang asks whether, under symmetric subset uncertainty \(\mathcal M\) and assuming \(F\) is \(n\)-completely mixable, one can always find an exchangeable joint mix that solves the robust multi-marginal transport problem \(\inf_X \sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M} \sum_{K\subseteq[n]} \mathbb E[f(S_K(X))]\,\mu(K)\) for every convex measurable \(f\). The source paper proves this robust optimality for the quadratic cost \(f(x)=x^2\) (Theorem 4) and gives a strong uniqueness statement for max-over-subsets formulations (Theorem 5), showing that the optimizer must be an exchangeable negatively correlated joint mix with equicorrelation matrix \(P_n^*\) in the homogeneous case. However, the extension to general convex \(f\) remains open and is explicitly listed as Open Question 4 in the paper.

Among the forward citations provided, "Extended Convolution Bounds on the Fr\'{e}chet Problem: Robust Risk Aggregation and Risk Sharing" develops sharp bounds for robust aggregation of RVaR/quantile-type functionals over Fr\'{e}chet classes, which is adjacent in spirit to dependence-robust optimization. Nevertheless, it does not treat subset-indexed partial sums \(S_K\), nor the maxmin formulation over an uncertainty set \(\mathcal M\subset \mathcal P(2^{[n]})\), and it does not establish joint-mix or exchangeability optimality for general convex costs. At present, based on the supplied citation set, there is no paper resolving the general-convex-cost robust subset-uncertainty problem; progress appears limited to the quadratic-cost case and related dependence-extremal tools.

sources.title: Extended Convolution Bounds on the Fr\'{e} chet Problem: Robust Risk Aggregation and Risk Sharing
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper derives new sharp extended convolution bounds for robust aggregation of averaged-quantile functionals. In particular, for marginals \(\mu=(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n)\) and \(0\le r<r+s\le 1\), it proves an inequality (Theorem 1) bounding \(R[r,r+s](\nu)\) for any aggregate law \(\nu\in\Lambda(\mu)\) by a linear combination of \(R_I(\mu_i)\) where \(I\) is a union of two intervals, and then optimizes this to obtain an upper bound (Theorem 2)
\[
\sup_{\nu\in\Lambda(\mu)} R[r,r+s](\nu) \le \inf_{\beta\in(1-r)\Delta_n,\ \beta_0\ge 1-r-s}\Big\{\Big(1-\frac{1-r-\beta_0}{s}\Big)\sum_{i=1}^n R[r+\beta_i,r+\beta_i+\beta_0](\mu_i)+\frac{1-r-\beta_0}{s}\sum_{i=1}^n R([r,r+\beta_i]\cup[r+\beta_i+\beta_0,1])(\mu_i)\Big\},
\]
with equality (sharpness) under tail monotonicity conditions (e.g. each \(\mu_i\) has increasing density beyond its \(r\)-quantile). It also gives a corresponding sharp lower bound (Theorem 3) and applies these to sharp bounds for inter-RVaR/quantile differences and to a risk-sharing inf-convolution problem (Theorems 5–6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether, under symmetric subset-uncertainty \(\mathcal M\) and general convex \(f\), an exchangeable joint mix (i.e. \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i=c\) a.s.) is always robust-optimal for \(\inf_X \sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\sum_K \mathbb E[f(S_K(X))]\mu(K)\). This paper does not study subset-indexed partial sums \(S_K\), does not formulate a robust \(\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\) over measures on \(2^{[n]}\), and does not address optimality of joint mixes or exchangeability for such objectives. Instead it treats the classical Fréchet aggregation problem for the full sum \(S=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) and optimizes averaged-quantile functionals \(R[r,r+s]\) (RVaR/ES/VaR-type) over dependence. The techniques (tail-transport inequalities, sharpness via joint-mixability/mutual exclusivity constructions) are conceptually related to dependence extremality and may provide tools/ideas, but they do not resolve the stated robust subset-uncertainty joint-mix optimality question.

title: Large-deviation bounds for stake-volume Markov chain in intermediate deviation regime
background_latex:
Consider the discrete-time, nondecreasing Markov chain \((N_t)_{t\ge 0}\) on \(\{N,N+1,\dots\}\) defined by \(N_0=N\in\mathbb{N}_+\) and the one-step transition
\[
N_{t+1}=\begin{cases}
N_t+1,&\text{with probability }N_t^{-\alpha},\\
N_t,&\text{with probability }1-N_t^{-\alpha},
\end{cases}
\qquad t\ge 0,
\]
where \(\alpha>0\) is fixed. (Equivalently, the increment \(\Delta_t:=N_{t+1}-N_t\in\{0,1\}\) is Bernoulli with parameter \(N_t^{-\alpha}\) conditional on \(N_t\).)

A deterministic growth scale for \(N_t\) is \(t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\), and the paper studies tail probabilities of the form \(\mathbb{P}(N_t\le \lambda t^{1/(1+\alpha)})\) and \(\mathbb{P}(N_t\ge \lambda t^{1/(1+\alpha)})\) as \(t\to\infty\). It introduces the rate function
\[
f_\alpha(\lambda)=(1+\alpha)\lambda\log\lambda-(1+\alpha)\lambda+\lambda^{-\alpha},\qquad \lambda>0.
\]
This function has two positive roots \(\lambda_-(\alpha)<\lambda_+(\alpha)\) and satisfies \(f_\alpha(\lambda)>0\) for \(\lambda\in(0,\lambda_-(\alpha))\cup(\lambda_+(\alpha),\infty)\). The paper proves exponential tail bounds with exponent proportional to \(t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\) in those two outer regimes.

The chain also has a natural “threshold” constant \((1+\alpha)^{1/(1+\alpha)}\) coming from the deterministic fluid-limit scaling \(N_t\approx ((1+\alpha)t)^{1/(1+\alpha)}\), so the intermediate regime \(\lambda\in(\lambda_-(\alpha),\lambda_+(\alpha))\) contains this threshold.
problem_definition_latex:
Prove large-deviation-type exponential bounds for \(N_t\) on the intermediate scale \(t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\) for deviation parameters \(\lambda\in(\lambda_-(\alpha),\lambda_+(\alpha))\). Concretely, establish upper bounds of the form
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(N_t\le \lambda t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\bigr)\le \exp\bigl(-c_-(\lambda)\,t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\bigr),\qquad
\mathbb{P}\bigl(N_t\ge \lambda t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\bigr)\le \exp\bigl(-c_+(\lambda)\,t^{1/(1+\alpha)}\bigr)
\]
for appropriate strictly positive rate functions \(c_-(\lambda),c_+(\lambda)\) throughout \(\lambda\in(\lambda_-(\alpha),\lambda_+(\alpha))\), and in particular up to (or “right off”) the threshold \((1+\alpha)^{1/(1+\alpha)}\).

One limitation of this work is that we focused on the case where least \((a, b)\)-majorized elements exist for each choice of \(a\) and \(b\). Moreover, the definition of these elements requires them to be optimal for any choice of separable convex objective structure. Thus, it is interesting to investigate whether the existence of least \((a, b)\)-majorized elements for specific (sets of) values of \(a\) and \(b\) can be characterized. In particular, an interesting question is whether such a characterization exists for \(b = 0\), i.e., when we only consider scaled objective functions.
title: Characterize least (a,b)-majorized elements for fixed scalings and shifts in feasible sets
background_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and index set \(N:=\{1,\dots,n\}\). For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(S\subseteq N\), write \(x(S):=\sum_{i\in S} x_i\). Fix a scaling vector \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n_{>0}\) and a shift vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

For vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \((a,b)\)-majorization by
\[
 x \prec_{(a,b)} y \quad\text{if}\quad x(N)=y(N)\ \text{and}\ \sum_{i\in N} a_i\,\phi\!\left(\frac{x_i+b_i}{a_i}\right)\le \sum_{i\in N} a_i\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i+b_i}{a_i}\right)\ \text{for all continuous convex }\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}.
\]
Given a feasible set \(C\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), a vector \(x^*\in C\) is called a least \((a,b)\)-majorized element of \(C\) if \(x^*\prec_{(a,b)} y\) for all \(y\in C\). Equivalently, \(x^*\) simultaneously minimizes the family of separable convex objectives
\[
 x\mapsto \sum_{i\in N} a_i\,\phi\!\left(\frac{x_i+b_i}{a_i}\right)
\]
over \(C\), for every choice of continuous convex \(\phi\).

A major theme in the paper is that if one requires existence of least \((a,b)\)-majorized elements for all choices of \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n_{>0}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\) within the class of compact convex sets, then the feasible sets are precisely base polyhedra of submodular functions (and analogous characterizations for weaker notions lead to other polyhedra). The paper explicitly notes a limitation: it treats the case of existence for every \(a,b\), rather than for specific fixed \(a,b\) (or subsets thereof).
problem_definition_latex:
Given a feasible set \(C\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and fixed vectors \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n_{>0}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^n\), characterize (in structural/combinatorial terms) when \(C\) admits a least \((a,b)\)-majorized element, i.e., when there exists \(x^*\in C\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in N} a_i\,\phi\!\left(\frac{x_i^*+b_i}{a_i}\right)\le \sum_{i\in N} a_i\,\phi\!\left(\frac{y_i+b_i}{a_i}\right)\quad\text{for all }y\in C\text{ and all continuous convex }\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R},
\]
(with the implicit requirement \(x^*(N)=y(N)\) for all \(y\in C\) whenever \((a,b)\)-majorization is used).
In particular, investigate whether such a characterization exists in the special case \(b=0\) (scaled objectives only).
