open_problem_quote: One limitation of this work is that we focused on the case where least \((a, b)\)-majorized elements exist for each choice of \(a\) and \(b\). Moreover, the definition of these elements requires them to be optimal for any choice of separable convex objective structure. Thus, it is interesting to investigate whether the existence of least \((a, b)\)-majorized elements for specific (sets of) values of \(a\) and \(b\) can be characterized. In particular, an interesting question is whether such a characterization exists for \(b = 0\), i.e., when we only consider scaled objective functions.

Automated search could generate examples of sets lacking least \((a,b)\)-majorized elements, but that would not directly yield the desired characterization.

literature_review.synthesis:
The 2023 paper by Schoot Uiterkamp characterizes, for compact convex feasible sets, when least \((a,b)\)-majorized elements exist uniformly for all scalings \(a>0\) and shifts \(b\): this happens exactly for base polyhedra of submodular functions (and analogously for weaker majorization notions and other polyhedra). The open problem asks for an analogous characterization when \((a,b)\) is fixed (not universal), especially for the scaled-only case \(b=0\). The source paper explicitly leaves this as a limitation and future direction.

Among the forward citations provided, the INFORMS Journal on Computing article on symmetric separable convex RAPs with disjoint-interval bounds gives partial progress in a different direction: it shows that a least-majorization-type “reduction property” (existence of a single solution optimal for all convex \(\varphi\)) can fail once the feasible region departs from the convex/base-polyhedron setting (here via nonconvex disjoint-interval constraints), while still providing structural monotonicity and exact algorithms for certain structured cases. This supports the view that any fixed-\((a,b)\) characterization will likely need to impose strong structural restrictions on \(C\) (e.g., convexity plus exchange properties) and may bifurcate sharply between convex polymatroidal sets (where least elements are induced by quadratic minimization) and more general/nonconvex RAP feasible regions (where simultaneous optimality can fail).

At present, based on the limited forward-citation evidence supplied, there is no identified paper that resolves the fixed-\((a,b)\) characterization problem. Promising directions suggested by the source paper’s techniques include: (i) specializing the greedy/Edmonds-style arguments used for the universal quantification over \(a,b\) to a single pair \((a,b)\), potentially yielding a characterization in terms of a single submodular function or a single chain of tight inequalities; and (ii) relating fixed-\(a\) (with \(b=0\)) to weighted versions of discrete convexity/M-convexity and to parametric quadratic minimization over candidate polyhedra. Counterexamples from nonconvex RAP variants indicate that convexity (or hole-freeness plus discrete exchange) is likely essential for any clean structural characterization.

sources.title: Symmetric separable convex resource allocation problems with structured disjoint interval bound constraints
sources.theorem_or_result: For the resource allocation problem with symmetric separable convex objective \(\sum_{i\in N}\varphi(x_i+b_i)\) and disjoint interval bound constraints \(x_i\in\bigcup_{j\in M}[l_{i,j},u_{i,j}]\) under four structured cases (F1,L1), (F1,L2), (F2,L1), (F2,L2), the paper proves existence of an optimal solution whose chosen interval indices are monotone (Lemma 2: there exists an optimum \(x^*\) with \(j(x^*,i)\le j(x^*,k)\) for \(i<k\)), and gives an exact algorithm (Algorithm 3) that solves these cases in time \(O\!\left(\binom{n+m-2}{m-2}(n\log n+nF)\right)\), where \(F\) is the cost of evaluating \(\varphi\) (Theorem 1). It also shows by counterexample that the ‘reduction property’ (existence of a single solution optimal for all convex \(\varphi\)) fails for RAP with semi-continuous/disjoint constraints (Section 3 counterexample).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a structural characterization of when a feasible set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) admits a least \((a,b)\)-majorized element for fixed \(a>0\), \(b\) (especially \(b=0\)). This paper studies a different but related setting: feasible sets given by a resource hyperplane \(\sum_i x_i=R\) intersected with nonconvex ‘disjoint interval’ constraints, and objectives \(\sum_i\varphi(x_i+b_i)\) with a common convex \(\varphi\) (i.e., symmetric separable convex). It leverages known results that for simple RAP with box constraints, an optimizer of the quadratic objective is simultaneously optimal for all convex \(\varphi\) (a least-majorization phenomenon), but then proves this simultaneous-optimality fails once the feasible set becomes nonconvex (disjoint intervals). Thus it provides (i) a concrete counterexample showing nonexistence of a least-majorized element in a natural nonconvex class, and (ii) algorithmic/structural monotonicity properties (Lemma 2) for optimal solutions in certain structured nonconvex sets. However, it does not characterize, for fixed \((a,b)\), which general sets \(C\) admit a least \((a,b)\)-majorized element; nor does it treat general scalings \(a\) (weights) in the objective family.

background_latex:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be an atomless probability space and let \(\mathcal X\) be a linear space of real-valued random variables (losses) with \(L^\infty\subseteq \mathcal X\subseteq L^1\). For \(X\in\mathcal X\), write \(F_X\) for its distribution function and \(F_X^{-1}(p)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R: F_X(x)\ge p\}\) for its left-quantile, \(p\in(0,1]\). An \(n\)-allocation of an aggregate loss \(X\) is an \(n\)-tuple \((X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathcal X^n\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i=X\) almost surely.

A (not necessarily cash-additive) risk measure is a map \(\rho:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,\infty]\). Given risk measures \(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_n\), their inf-convolution is
\[\big(\square_{i=1}^n \rho_i\big)(X)=\inf\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^n \rho_i(X_i): (X_1,\dots,X_n)\in\mathcal X^n,\ \sum_{i=1}^n X_i=X\Big\}.\]

Fix a right-continuous function \(\Lambda:\mathbb R\to[0,1]\) that is not identically equal to \(1\). Define the Lambda value-at-risk plus functional by
\[\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+(X)=\sup\{x\in\mathbb R: F_X(x)< 1-\Lambda(x)\},\]
with the conventions \(\sup\emptyset=-\infty\) and \(\inf\emptyset=\infty\) (when needed). For multiple agents, allow \(\Lambda_i\) and corresponding \(\Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\), \(i=1,\dots,n\).

The paper studies risk sharing via inf-convolution for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\) and for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) combined with another risk measure under additional structure, but explicitly states that the case of inf-convolving multiple \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) remains open.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Liu (2023), the inf-convolution problem for multiple agents is solved in considerable generality for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\) (the inf-quantile definition): when the \(\Lambda_i\) are monotone in the same direction and mild boundary/attainability conditions hold, \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}\) admits an explicit characterization as \(\inf_{x_{n-1}} \Lambda^{x_{n-1}}\mathrm{VaR}(X)\), and in favorable cases collapses to a single \(\Lambda^*\mathrm{VaR}(X)\) where \(\Lambda^*(x)=\sup_{\sum y_i=x}(\sum_i \Lambda_i(y_i))\wedge 1\). Optimal allocations can be constructed by partitioning the probability space according to the uniform transform \(U_X\) and assigning tail events to agents, closely paralleling classical VaR risk sharing.

For the plus-variant \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\), Liu (2023) shows that even the two-agent inf-convolution is substantially harder because \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) interacts with dependence/robust aggregation effects; the paper therefore treats \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\square \rho\) only when \(\rho\) is SSD-consistent, yielding an optimization over \((x,y)\) and an optimal allocation of the form \(X_1^*=F^{-1}_{x^*,y^*}(U_X)\), \(X_2^*=X-X_1^*\), which is generally neither comonotone nor a simple tail-event split. Subsequent work on Lambda-VaR under ambiguity and optimal risk sharing for lambda value-at-risk provides strong partial progress in the multi-agent direction, but for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\) (and capacity/robust extensions) rather than \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\): these papers establish closure under inf-convolution and give explicit event/capacity characterizations and tail-splitting optimal allocations when \(\Lambda_i\) are monotone.

At present, there is no paper in the provided forward-citation set that gives a tractable explicit characterization of \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) for general \(n\ge 3\) under a probability measure, nor a general structural theorem for existence and form of optimal allocations. Related advances on nonconvex quantile-based risk sharing (e.g., averaged-quantile inf-convolutions) and on robust \(\Lambda\)-quantiles via extremal distributions suggest that progress will likely require combining (i) tail-splitting/partition constructions with (ii) robust aggregation or extremal-coupling arguments to handle the dependence uncertainty intrinsic to \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\).

sources.title: Optimal risk sharing for lambda value-at-risk
sources.theorem_or_result:
For monotone (in the same direction) Lambda functions, the paper proves closure of the class \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\) under inf-convolution and gives an explicit downset/capacity characterization and optimal allocations. Concretely, if \(\rho_i(X)=\Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^{w_i}(X)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R: w_i(X>x)\le \Lambda_i(x)\}\) with continuous capacities \(w_i\) and \(\Lambda_i\in H_I\) (all increasing) or \(\Lambda_i\in H_D\) (all decreasing), then
- \(\square_{i=1}^n \rho_i(X)=\inf\{x\in\mathbb R: \{X>x\}\in A^{\Lambda,w}_x\}\), where \(A^{\Lambda,w}_x=\{\cup_{i=1}^n A_i: w_i(A_i)\le \Lambda_i(y_i),\ \sum_i y_i=x\}\) (Proposition 8 / Theorem 3).
- Moreover \(\square_{i=1}^n \rho_i\) is itself of the form \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\) for some monotone \(\Lambda\) and capacity \(w\) (Proposition 8).
- If the infimum is attained at \(x^*\), an optimal allocation is \(X_i=(X-x^*)\mathbf 1_{A_i^*}+y_i^*\) with \(\sum_i y_i^*=x^*\) and \(w_i(\{X>x^*\}\cap A_i^*)\le \Lambda_i(y_i^*)\) (Theorem 3 / Proposition 8).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a tractable characterization of \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) (multiple agents) and the structure/existence of optimal allocations. This paper does not directly treat \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) under a probability (it focuses on \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\) and \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) under capacities, but the risk-sharing/inf-convolution results in Section 5 are for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\), not \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^{+,w}\)). However, it makes strong partial progress by:
- Introducing an equivalent representation of \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\) (for monotone \(\Lambda\)) via families of downsets (Theorem 1), and proving that induced risk measures are closed under inf-convolution (Theorem 3).
- Applying this to obtain an explicit event/capacity characterization of \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^{w_i}\) and explicit optimal allocations (Proposition 8).
Thus it essentially resolves the analogous ‘multiple \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\)’ inf-convolution problem (and under ambiguity/capacities), and provides tools likely adaptable to \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\). But it does not claim or show a full characterization for \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) as posed in the original paper, so it is not a complete solution to that open problem.

sources.title: Lambda Value-at-Risk under ambiguity and risk sharing
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a general inf-convolution/optimal-allocation theorem for Lambda-VaR under capacities and monotone Lambda. In particular, for continuous capacities \(w_i\) and \(\Lambda_i\in H_I\) (or all \(\Lambda_i\in H_D\)), it shows
\[
\Big(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^{w_i}\Big)(X)=\inf\{x\in\u211d:{\{X>x\}}\in A^{\Lambda,w}_x\},
\]
where \(A^{\Lambda,w}_x=\{\cup_{i=1}^n A_i: \exists y_1+\cdots+y_n=x\text{ with }w_i(A_i)\le \Lambda_i(y_i)\}\). Moreover, if a minimizer \(x^*\) exists, an optimal allocation is
\[
X_i=(X-x^*)\mathbf 1_{A_i^*}+y_i^*,\quad \sum_i y_i^*=x^*,\quad w_i(\{X>x^*\}\cap A_i^*)\le \Lambda_i(y_i^*).
\]
It further shows closure: if all \(\Lambda_i\) are monotone in the same direction, then \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^{w_i}\) is again of the form \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\) for some capacity \(w\) and some \(\Lambda\in H_I^*\) (resp. \(H_D^*\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an explicit/tractable characterization of \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) (the plus version under a probability) and the structure/existence of optimal allocations. This paper does not directly treat \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) inf-convolution. Instead it develops a parallel theory for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^w\) (the inf version) under capacities and proves a general inf-convolution formula and explicit optimal allocations via families of downsets (Theorem 3, Proposition 8). These results are highly relevant because \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) is the dual/sup-quantile analogue (they define \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^{+,w}\) too), and the open problem concerns the difficulty of handling multiple \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\). The papers downset/partition method and closure-under-inf-convolution results provide strong tools and suggest a route to attack the \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) case, but it does not provide the requested characterization for \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) itself.

sources.title: Risk sharing with Lambda value at risk under heterogeneous beliefs
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper derives semi-explicit characterizations and optimal allocations for inf-convolutions involving Lambda Value-at-Risk under heterogeneous beliefs, and for VaR+ only in the two-agent (or one VaR+ plus a general monotone risk measure) setting. In particular, Theorem 6 shows for \mathrm{VaR}^{+ ,Q_1} and a monotone law-invariant \(\rho^{Q_2}\):
\[\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^{+,Q_1}\square \rho^{Q_2}(X)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\inf_{y\ge x}\inf_{U\sim U[0,1]\text{ under }Q_1}\Big\{x+\rho^{Q_2}\big(X-\Lambda^{-1}_{x,y}(U)\big)\Big\},\]
with an optimal allocation \(X_1^*=\Lambda^{-1}_{x^*,y^*}(U^*),\ X_2^*=X-X_1^*\) when a minimizer exists. Taking \(\rho=\Lambda_2\mathrm{VaR}^{+,Q_2}\) yields an (implicit) formula for the inf-convolution of two \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) and the corresponding optimal allocation.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for an explicit/tractable characterization of \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) and optimal allocations for general \(n\ge2\) on an atomless space. This paper does not provide a full characterization for multiple (\(n\ge3\)) \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) inf-convolution; indeed it states this remains unsolved. However, it makes substantive progress by:
- Providing a general variational representation and optimal allocation structure for \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\square \rho\) (Theorem 6), which includes the special case of two \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) (set \(\rho=\Lambda_2\mathrm{VaR}^+\)).
- Showing the optimal allocation for the two-agent \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) case has a non-comonotone/non-pairwise-countermonotone form \(X_1^*=\Lambda^{-1}_{x^*,y^*}(U^*)\), highlighting structural differences from the \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}\) case.
Thus it partially addresses (i)-(ii) only for \(n=2\) (and more generally \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) with another risk measure), not for general \(n\).

sources.title: Extended Convolution Bounds on the Fr\'{e} chet Problem: Robust Risk Aggregation and Risk Sharing
sources.theorem_or_result:
Theorem 5 (Risk sharing for averaged quantiles). For X\in L^1\) and parameters \(\beta_i\in(0,1)\) with \(\beta:=\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i\in(0,1)\), let \(I_i=[0,\beta_i]\cup[1-\beta+\beta_i,1]\). Then the inf-convolution of the average-quantile risk measures \(R_{I_i}\) satisfies
\[
\square_{i=1}^n R_{I_i}(X)=R_{[0,\beta]}(X).
\]
If \(X\) is bounded above, an optimal allocation exists and can be chosen as
\(X_i=(X-t)\mathbf 1_{A_i}+\frac{X}{n}\mathbf 1_{A^c}+\frac{t}{n-1}\mathbf 1_{A\setminus A_i}\), where \(A=\{U_X\le \beta\}\), \((A_i)\) partitions \(A\) with \(\mathbb P(A_i)=\beta_i\), and \(t\ge (q^-_1(X))^+\). If \(X\) is unbounded above, no optimal allocation attains the infimum (Theorem 6), but a sequence of allocations approaches it.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an explicit characterization of \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) and optimal allocations. This paper does not study \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) or its inf-convolution directly. However, it solves a closely related nonconvex risk-sharing/inf-convolution problem for a class of quantile-based (average-quantile) risk measures \(R_I\) where \(I\) is a union of two tail intervals \([0,\beta_i]\cup[1-\beta+\beta_i,1]\). The resulting inf-convolution collapses to a single lower-tail averaged quantile \(R_{[0,\beta]}(X)\), and the paper gives explicit optimal allocations and an existence criterion (boundedness above). Since \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\) is also defined via distribution/quantile-type constraints, the techniques (new RVaR inequality, tail-splitting allocations, dependence-structure arguments for non-attainment) may be adaptable tools toward characterizing inf-convolutions of multiple \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\), but no direct formula for \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) is provided here.

sources.title: Robust Lambda-quantiles and extreme probabilities
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper’s main result (Theorem 1) shows that robust (worst-/best-case) \(\Lambda\)-quantiles over an uncertainty set \(\mathcal M\) can be computed as \(\Lambda\)-quantiles of the extremal distribution functions \(F^-_{\mathcal M}(x)=\inf_{F\in\mathcal M}F(x)\) and \(F^+_{\mathcal M}(x)=\sup_{F\in\mathcal M}F(x)\), with additional attainability conditions for some of the four \(\Lambda\)-quantile variants. In particular, for the Bellini–Peri variants \(\tilde q^-_\Lambda, q^+_\Lambda\) one always has \(\sup_{F\in\mathcal M}\tilde q^-_\Lambda(F)=\tilde q^-_\Lambda(F^-_{\mathcal M})\) and \(\inf_{F\in\mathcal M} q^+_\Lambda(F)= q^+_\Lambda(F^+_{\mathcal M})\); for the other variants equalities hold under attainability of \(F^-_{\mathcal M}\) or \(F^+_{\mathcal M}\), and simplify when \(\Lambda\) is decreasing.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an explicit characterization of the inf-convolution \(\square_{i=1}^n \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) and optimal allocations. This paper does not study inf-convolution or risk sharing/allocations. It studies distributional robustness of \(\Lambda\)-quantiles (including variants closely related to \(\Lambda\mathrm{VaR}^+\)) and provides extremal-distribution formulas for worst-/best-case \(\Lambda\)-quantiles under moment/Wasserstein/marginal-aggregation uncertainty sets. These extremal-distribution techniques might be tangentially useful if one reformulates inf-convolution problems via distributional bounds or aggregation sets, but no direct results on \(\square_i \Lambda_i\mathrm{VaR}^+\) are given.

title: Verify gamma^{-beta} truncation schedule meets summability condition in policy gradient algorithm
background_latex:
Consider a finite-state Markov chain (or finite MDP under a stationary randomized policy) with state space \(\mathcal X\) and a designated recurrent regeneration state \(x^\ast\in\mathcal X\). A policy is parameterized by \(\theta\in\mathbb R^\ell\), inducing an aperiodic irreducible transition kernel \(P_\theta\) on \(\mathcal X\), and a bounded one-step cost \(C_\theta(x)\). Fix a risk factor \(\alpha>0\).

The risk-sensitive exponential average cost is
\[\Lambda_\theta:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\mathbb E_\theta\Big[\exp\Big(\alpha\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}C_\theta(\Phi_i)\Big)\,\Big|\,\Phi_0=x\Big],\]
which exists and is independent of the initial state \(x\in\mathcal X\) under the stated ergodicity assumptions.

To construct trajectory-based stochastic approximation algorithms, the paper introduces a family of smooth truncations indexed by \(M>1\), yielding an approximating objective \(\Lambda^{(M)}_\theta\) defined implicitly as the unique \(\Lambda\) solving
\[g^{(M)}(\theta,\Lambda)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[ G^{(M)}(\theta,\Lambda)\,\big|\,\Phi_0=x^\ast\big]=1,\]
where \(G^{(M)}(\theta,\Lambda)\) is a smooth, bounded modification of

title: Find stronger closed-form eigenvalue bounds for balanced independent sets in regular bipartite graphs
background_latex:
Let $G=(V_1\cup V_2,E)$ be a bipartite graph. A pair $(A,B)$ with $A\subseteq V_1$ and $B\subseteq V_2$ is a bipartite biindependent pair if there is no edge between $A$ and $B$, i.e., $A\times B\cap E=\emptyset$. Such a pair is balanced if $|A|=|B|$.

Define the balanced independent-set size
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G):=\max\{\,|A|+|B|:\ (A,B)\text{ is a balanced bipartite biindependent pair in }G\,\}.
\]
Equivalently, $\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)=2\max\{|A|:(A,B)\text{ balanced biindependent}\}$.

A basic spectral upper bound for certain biindependent-pair parameters is obtained as follows. Suppose $G$ is $r$-regular with $|V_1|=|V_2|=n$, and let $A_G\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$ be the adjacency matrix of $G$. Let $\lambda_2(A_G)$ denote the second largest eigenvalue of $A_G$ (equivalently, the second largest singular value of the $n\times n$ bipartite adjacency block).

The paper defines an eigenvalue-based bound
\[
\mathrm{b}h(G):=\frac{n\,\lambda_2(A_G)}{2\,(r+\lambda_2(A_G))},
\]
obtained by restricting certain semidefinite relaxations to highly symmetric feasible solutions. For bipartite regular graphs one has an inequality of the form
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)\le 4\,\mathrm{b}h(G)
\]
whenever the relaxation used indeed upper bounds $\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)$ (the paper studies several such balanced SDP relaxations and shows that their natural symmetric specializations collapse to $\mathrm{b}h(G)$).

The motivating issue is that $\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)$ is NP-hard to compute, so efficiently computable closed-form spectral upper bounds (in terms of eigenvalues of standard matrices associated to $G$) are desirable, especially bounds that exploit the balancing constraint $|A|=|B|$ more sharply than existing ones.
problem_definition_latex:
Determine a closed-form eigenvalue-based upper bound on $\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)$ for $r$-regular bipartite graphs $G=(V_1\cup V_2,E)$ (with $|V_1|=|V_2|=n$) that is provably stronger than the bound obtained from $\mathrm{b}h(G)=\frac{n\lambda_2(A_G)}{2(r+\lambda_2(A_G))}$, i.e., a bound that can be strictly smaller than $4\,\mathrm{b}h(G)$ while remaining valid for all such graphs.

Equivalently, find a tractable (spectral, closed-form) bound that better exploits the balancing requirement $|A|=|B|$ than the existing symmetric eigenvalue bound arising from the paper's balanced semidefinite relaxations, which all reduce (up to scaling) to $\mathrm{b}h(G)$ on regular bipartite graphs.

literature_review.synthesis:
The original problem asks for a closed-form spectral upper bound on \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)\) for \(r\)-regular bipartite graphs \(|V_1|=|V_2|=n\) that improves on the Laurent--Polak--Vargas symmetric specialization \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)\le 4\,\mathrm{b}h(G)=\frac{2n\lambda_2}{r+\lambda_2}\). In the source paper, multiple natural balanced SDP relaxations (balanced variants of Lov\'asz-\(\vartheta\) and first-level Lasserre relaxations) are introduced, but their symmetric/closed-form reductions on regular bipartite graphs all collapse back to \(\mathrm{b}h(G)=\frac{n\lambda_2}{2(r+\lambda_2)}\), indicating that new ideas beyond these symmetric SDP templates are needed to get a strictly stronger universal eigenvalue formula.

Among the forward citations provided, the only citing work is an SDP-based extremal paper on cross-intersecting families. While it does not contribute a new bound for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\) in regular bipartite graphs, it exemplifies a successful strategy for obtaining sharp results: constructing explicit dual SDP certificates and verifying PSD constraints via association-scheme diagonalization. This suggests a plausible direction for the open problem: identify additional algebraic structure (e.g., distance-regular/association-scheme settings, or refined block-diagonalizations beyond the \(\{I,J,A_G\}\)-span) where balanced constraints can be enforced in the dual and yield a closed-form expression strictly improving \(\mathrm{b}h(G)\). At present, based on the supplied citation set, no paper resolves the requested stronger universal eigenvalue bound, so the problem remains open.

sources.title: A semidefinite programming approach to cross -intersecting families
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves sharp SDP-based extremal results for cross 2-intersecting families. In particular, for integers \(k\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 3(k-1)\), if \(\mathcal F,\mathcal G\subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}\) are cross 2-intersecting (i.e., \(|F\cap G|\ge 2\) for all \(F\in\mathcal F, G\in\mathcal G\)), then \(|\mathcal F|\,|\mathcal G|\le \binom{n-2}{k-2}^2\), with characterization of equality cases (Theorem 2). It also proves the measure analogue: for \(0<p\le 1/3\), cross 2-intersecting \(\mathcal F,\mathcal G\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) satisfy \(\mu_p(\mathcal F)\mu_p(\mathcal G)\le p^4\), with equality characterization for \(p<1/3\) (Theorem 4).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a stronger closed-form eigenvalue upper bound on the balanced biindependent-pair size \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}(G)\) in \(r\)-regular bipartite graphs, improving on a specific spectral bound \(4\,\mathrm{b}h(G)=\frac{2n\lambda_2}{r+\lambda_2}\). This citing paper does not study \(\alpha_{\mathrm{bal}}\) in regular bipartite graphs nor derive eigenvalue bounds in terms of \(r\) and \(\lambda_2\). Instead it uses semidefinite programming and association-scheme diagonalization (Johnson and Hamming schemes) to solve extremal problems for cross-intersecting set families, formulated as maximum product of sizes/measures of cross-independent sets in a specially constructed bipartite graph. Methodologically, it is related in that it constructs explicit dual SDP certificates using symmetry/eigen-decomposition, similar in spirit to the SDP/spectral techniques in Laurent–Polak–Vargas (the original paper), but it does not provide a new spectral closed-form bound for balanced biindependent pairs in regular bipartite graphs.

title: Characterize when irreducible Steiner-cut facets remain valid for global cut dominants
background_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq V\) be a terminal set with \(|T|\ge 2\). For \(S\subseteq V\), write \(\delta(S)\subseteq E\) for the cut consisting of edges with one endpoint in \(S\) and the other in \(V\setminus S\). A \(T\)-Steiner cut is a cut \(\delta(S)\) such that \(T\cap S\neq\emptyset\) and \(T\setminus S\neq\emptyset\).

Let \(\chi(\delta(S))\in\{0,1\}^E\) denote the incidence vector of \(\delta(S)\). The \(T\)-Steiner cut polytope is
\[\mathrm{CUT}(G,T)=\mathrm{conv}\{\chi(\delta(S)) : \delta(S)\text{ is a }T\text{-Steiner cut}\}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^E.\]
The \(T\)-Steiner cut dominant is the dominant (upper-closed hull)
\[\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T)=\mathrm{CUT}(G,T)+\mathbb{R}^E_{\ge 0} = \{y\in\mathbb{R}^E: \exists x\in \mathrm{CUT}(G,T)\text{ with }y\ge x\}.\]
Similarly, the (global) cut dominant is \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G)=\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,V)\).

Consider a nontrivial valid inequality for \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T)\) of the form
\[c\cdot x \ge \gamma,\]
where \(c\in\mathbb{R}^E_{\ge 0}\) and \(\gamma>0\). Such an inequality is facet-defining for \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T)\) if the face \(\{x\in \mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T): c\cdot x=\gamma\}\) has dimension \(|E|-1\). The paper uses the notion of an irreducible facet inducing Steiner graph \((G,T)\), meaning (i) \(G\) has no cut vertex, and (ii) no nonterminal node \(v\in V\setminus T\) has degree 2. (Equivalently, such a facet is not obtainable from smaller facet-inducing instances by the paper’s subdivision and gluing operations.)

A key monotonicity relation is \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T)\subseteq \mathrm{CUT}^+(G)\) whenever \(T\subseteq V\): any inequality valid for \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G)\) is automatically valid for \(\mathrm{CUT}^+(G,T)\), but the converse may fail. The paper notes explicit examples where enlarging the terminal set (turning a nonterminal into a terminal) can destroy validity of a previously facet-defining Steiner-cut inequality.

title: Prove covariance inequality between number in service and work in M GI n queues
background_latex:
Consider a first-come-first-served (FCFS) many-server queue with Poisson arrivals and general i.i.d. service times.

1) Model. An M/GI/n queue has:
1) arrivals given by a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda>0\);
2) \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) identical servers;
3) i.i.d. service times \(S\) with \(0<E[S]<\infty\) and \(E[S^2]<\infty\);
4) FCFS discipline, no abandonments.

Let \(\mu_S = 1/E[S]\) denote the service rate of a single server, and define the traffic intensity
\[\rho := \frac{\lambda}{n\mu_S} = \frac{\lambda E[S]}{n},\qquad 0<\rho<1.\]
Assume the system is stable and admits a steady state.

2) Steady-state quantities. Let \(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\) be the steady-state number of busy servers (number in service). Let \(\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\) be the steady-state total remaining workload in service, i.e. the sum of the residual service times of all jobs currently in service (with idle servers contributing \(0\)).

Equivalently, if \(R_1(\infty),\dots,R_n(\infty)\) are the (random) residual service times in steady state on each server (with \(R_j(\infty)=0\) when server \(j\) is idle), then
\[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)=\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{R_j(\infty)>0\},\qquad \mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)=\sum_{j=1}^n R_j(\infty).\]

3) Covariance interpretation. The inequality
\[E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)]\,E[\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)] \le E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\,\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)]\]

2) \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) identical servers;
3) i.i.d. service times \(S\) with \(0<E[S]<\infty\) and \(E[S^2]<\infty\);
4) FCFS discipline, no abandonments.

Let \(\mu_S = 1/E[S]\) denote the service rate of a single server, and define the traffic intensity
\[\rho := \frac{\lambda}{n\mu_S} = \frac{\lambda E[S]}{n},\qquad 0<\rho<1.\]
Assume the system is stable and admits a steady state.

2) Steady-state quantities. Let \(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\) be the steady-state number of busy servers (number in service). Equivalently, if \(R_1(\infty),\dots,R_n(\infty)\) are the (random) residual service times in steady state on each server (with \(R_j(\infty)=0\) when server \(j\) is idle), then
\[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)=\sum_{j=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{R_j(\infty)>0\},\qquad \mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)=\sum_{j=1}^n R_j(\infty).\]

\[E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)]\,E[\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)] \le E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\,\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)]\]

open_problem_quote:
Conjecture 1. In any M/G/n queue in which \(E[S^2] < \infty\) and all relevant steady-state distributions exist, it holds that
\[E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)]\times E[\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)] \le E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)\times \mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty)],\]

literature_review.synthesis:
In Li--Goldberg (arXiv:1706.04628v3), the covariance inequality \(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty),\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty))\ge 0\) is posed as Conjecture 1 because it would remove the negative correction term in their drift identity (Theorem 9) and yield the clean bound \(\mathbb E[L(\infty)]\le \tfrac12\mathbb E[(S\mu_S)^2]\,\rho/(1-\rho)\) for \(M/GI/n\). The conjecture concerns the steady-state joint distribution of the vector of residual service times \((R_1(\infty),\dots,R_n(\infty))\), specifically the mixed moment \(\mathbb E[\sum_j \mathbf 1\{R_j>0\}\,\sum_j R_j]\), and asks for a positive-association type statement under FCFS with Poisson arrivals and \(\mathbb E[S^2]<\infty\).

The limited forward-citation evidence provided does not contain a proof or counterexample. The most relevant forward-citing work, “A new -scaling bound for multiserver queues via a leave-one-out technique,” develops a BAR-based decomposition for steady-state means in \(GI/GI/n\) and introduces leave-one-out couplings to control boundary terms that are explicitly interpreted as covariance-like corrections between indicators of boundary events (e.g. emptiness) and residual service quantities. While this does not establish a sign for \(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}},\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}})\), it suggests a plausible strategy: represent \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}\,\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}]\) via a BAR/Poisson equation and attempt to show that the relevant boundary term is nonnegative (or asymptotically negligible) using conditional independence/monotonicity arguments.

“Novel Lower Bounds on M/G/k Scheduling” is methodologically related through its BAR/drift analysis of workload-type processes and explicit moment calculations in surrogate models, but it does not engage with FCFS many-server residual-service vectors or positive correlation properties. Overall, based on the provided citation set, the conjectured covariance inequality appears to remain open; progress seems to be primarily methodological (BAR decompositions and couplings) rather than a direct resolution. Promising directions include exploiting association/positive dependence results for FCFS queues (e.g. via Palm calculus and monotone couplings) to show that conditioning on more busy servers stochastically increases the residual workload in service, or proving the inequality under additional structural assumptions on \(S\) (e.g. decreasing hazard rate, log-convex tails) and then extending by approximation.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves new universal steady-state mean queue-length bounds of order \(O(1/(1-\rho))\) for the FCFS \(GI/GI/n\) queue (via a modified system), e.g. for \(M/GI/n\): \(E_\pi[Q]\le R_s^{\max}/(1-\rho)\) under light-tail/non-lattice/positive Harris recurrence assumptions, using BAR and a leave-one-out coupling to control boundary “covariance” terms.
sources.connection: The open problem asks to prove \(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty),\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty))\ge 0\) in steady state for FCFS \(M/GI/n\). This paper does not study \(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}\) or \(\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}\) directly, nor does it establish a nonnegative covariance between them. It does, however, derive BAR-based decompositions for \(E_\pi[Q]\) involving boundary terms \(\Gamma_{s,j}=E_s[\mathbf 1\{Q=0\}\,\mu R_{s,j}]-(1-\rho)E_\pi[\mu R_{s,j}]\), which it heuristically interprets as covariance-like quantities between \(\mathbf 1\{Q=0\}\) and residual service times, and then bounds them via a leave-one-out asymptotic-independence argument. These techniques may be adaptable to analyze correlations between service occupancy and in-service workload, but no such covariance inequality is proved here.

sources.title: Novel Lower Bounds on M/G/k Scheduling
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces the Increasing Speed Queue (ISQ-k), a single-server variable-speed model, and proves workload/relevant-work lower bounds for M/G/k queues under arbitrary (possibly preemptive) scheduling policies. Key statements include: - Proposition 6.1 / Theorem 4.3: for any arrival/job-size sample path, the total work in any k-server system is lower bounded by the total work in ISQ-k; hence in steady state, for Poisson arrivals, \(\mathbb E[W^{M/G/k}]\ge \mathbb E[W^{ISQ-k}]\). - Theorems 6.26.3: the mean SRPT-relevant work \(\mathbb E[W_x]\) in M/G/k under any policy is lower bounded by that in auxiliary Sep-ISQ-k and (for some recycling stream) Rec-ISQ-k. - Propositions 8.3 and 10.3: explicit formulas for \(\mathbb E[W^{ISQ-2}]\) and \(\mathbb E[W^{ISQ-k}]\) via a BAR/drift method with differential-equation-derived test functions (DiffeDrift).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a nonnegative covariance inequality between the steady-state number in service and the total residual workload in service in an FCFS M/GI/n queue: \(\mathrm{Cov}(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty),\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}(\infty))\ge 0\). This paper does not study FCFS M/GI/n steady-state joint distributions of (busy servers, residual service workload), nor does it address covariance/association properties. Its main objects are (i) mean response time lower bounds under arbitrary scheduling in M/G/k, (ii) SRPT-relevant work integrals (WINE), and (iii) total work in system (sum of remaining job sizes) in a variable-speed single-server surrogate. While it develops BAR/drift techniques for variable-rate workload processes that could be conceptually useful in analyzing moments of workload-like quantities, it provides no result implying \(\mathbb E[\mathrm{Num}]\,\mathbb E[\mathrm{Work}]\le \mathbb E[\mathrm{Num}\cdot\mathrm{Work}]\) for FCFS M/GI/n, and it does not even define \(\mathrm{Num}_{\mathrm{service}}\) and \(\mathrm{Work}_{\mathrm{service}}\) in the many-server FCFS sense.

title: Prove consistency and rates for smoothness-minimizing estimator under variance target
background_latex:
Let \(d\ge 1\) and \([a,b]^d\subset \mathbb{R}^d\) be a compact hyperrectangle. Let \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) satisfy \(2m>d\). Let \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^d\) be a multi-index with order \(|\alpha|=\sum_{j=1}^d \alpha_j\), and let \(D^\alpha\) denote the (weak) partial derivative operator.

Let \(\mathcal{F}_m\) be the space of generalized functions (Schwartz distributions) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) whose weak partial derivatives of order \(m\) are square-integrable, i.e.
\[\mathcal{F}_m:=\Bigl\{f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}: \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (D^\alpha f(x))^2\,dx<\infty\ \text{for all }\alpha\text{ with }|\alpha|=m\Bigr\}.\]
Define the smoothness (roughness) functional
\[J(f):=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} (D^\alpha f(x))^2\,dx,\]
and the empirical squared error for data \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n\) by
\[E_n(f):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i-f(X_i))^2.\]
Assume observations satisfy the regression model \(Y_i=f^*(X_i)+\varepsilon_i\), where \((X_i,\varepsilon_i)\) are i.i.d., \(X_i\in[a,b]^d\) has a positive continuous density on \([a,b]^d\), \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i\mid X_i]=0\), and \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i^2\mid X_i]=\sigma^2<\infty\). Let \(f^*\in\mathcal{F}_m\).

Consider the smoothness-minimizing estimator \(\hat g_n\) defined (for a given tolerance \(S_n\ge 0\)) as any solution of
\[\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}_m} J(f)\quad\text{subject to}\quad E_n(f)\le S_n.\]
This is Problem (B) in the paper. The paper notes that if an additional inequality holds,
\[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat g_n(X_i)-f^*(X_i))^2\le \frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i(\hat g_n(X_i)-f^*(X_i)),\]
then the same optimal rate as for the constrained least-squares estimator \(\hat f_n\) would follow. The dependence of such an inequality on the choice of \(S_n\) is not established in the paper.

title: Equilibrium of refined learning threshold with Coxian service times setting
background_latex:
Consider a system of \(n\) identical server pools, each with infinitely many servers, so that tasks at a given pool are processed in parallel and a task’s service requirement is unaffected by the number of concurrent tasks. Tasks arrive according to a Poisson process of rate \(n\lambda\) (constant in time) and are dispatched immediately upon arrival to one server pool according to a threshold-based rule.

Service times are Coxian (phase-type) with at most \(r\) exponential phases: a task starts in phase \(1\), completes phase \(m\) after an exponential time with mean \(1/\mu_m\), and then either advances to phase \(m+1\) with probability \(p_m\) or departs the system with probability \(1-p_m\), with \(p_r=0\). The mean service time is \(1/\mu\), and the offered load per pool is \(\rho:=\lambda/\mu\).

Let \(x_i(t)\in\mathbb{N}\) be the total number of tasks at pool \(i\) at time \(t\). Define the occupancy tail fractions
\[q_n(t,i):=\frac{1}{n}\#\{\text{pools with at least } i \text{ tasks at time } t\},\qquad i\ge 0,
\]
so \(q_n(t,0)=1\) and \(q_n(t,i)\) is nonincreasing in \(i\). The normalized total number of tasks is
\[u_n(t):=\sum_{i\ge 1} q_n(t,i)=\frac{N_n(t)}{n},\]
where \(N_n(t)\) is the total number of tasks in the system.

Fix an integer parameter \(\Delta\ge 1\). The dispatching rule uses a threshold \(\ell_n(t)\in\{0,\Delta,2\Delta,\dots\}\) and an upper level \(h_n(t)=\ell_n(t)+\Delta\): arrivals are routed uniformly at random to (i) a pool with fewer than \(\ell_n(t)\) tasks if any exist; else (ii) a pool with between \(\ell_n(t)\) and \(h_n(t)-1\) tasks if any exist; else (iii) any pool (all have at least \(h_n(t)\) tasks).

A refined learning scheme updates \(\ell_n(t)\) at certain arrival epochs based on partial occupancy information (fractions of pools above/below threshold). The question concerns whether, under Coxian service times, \(\ell_n(t)\) stabilizes to an equilibrium value (typically \(\lfloor \rho\rfloor_\Delta\), the greatest multiple of \(\Delta\) below \(\rho\)) in large systems.

literature_review.synthesis:
The Coxian-service version of the equilibrium question is essentially resolved in the 2024 paper "Learning and balancing unknown loads in large-scale systems". In the constant-arrival Coxian setting, the authors analyze the threshold-based dispatching rule with a learning outer loop and prove eventual stabilization of the threshold when the threshold is updated via the basic estimator \(\ell_n(t)=\lfloor N_n(t)/n\rfloor_\Delta\). Under the nondegeneracy condition \(\rho\notin\{i\Delta\}\), Theorem 3 yields a pathwise large-\(n\) statement: there exists \(\sigma>0\) such that for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(\ell_n(t)=\ell^*\) for all \(t\ge \sigma\) almost surely, with \(\ell^*=\lfloor\rho\rfloor_\Delta\). The same theorem also quantifies the resulting near-balance of the occupancy tails: \(q_n(t,i)\to 1\) for all \(i\le \ell^*\) and the excess tail mass beyond \(\ell^*+\Delta\) decays at least exponentially fast at rate bounded below by a hazard-rate constant \(\eta\).

Methodologically, the paper avoids a full fluid limit for the detailed Coxian state descriptor \(s_n(j_1,\dots,j_r)\) and instead proves strong approximations and dynamical inequalities for aggregate “mass” functionals (total mass and tail masses). This is crucial because Coxian service induces heterogeneous residual times across phases, making standard low-dimensional fluid closures difficult. The earlier paper "Utility maximizing load balancing policies" provides partial progress in the exponential case for a related self-learning threshold mechanism, establishing convergence of a learned threshold index and global stability of the limiting equilibrium; however it does not treat phase-type service.

A remaining gap relative to the user-stated open problem is the refined learning scheme under Coxian service times (where threshold updates are triggered by partial occupancy fractions rather than by \(N_n(t)\)). The 2024 paper explicitly notes that proving eventual equilibrium for the refined scheme with Coxian service would require additional nontrivial arguments, even though tail-balance bounds analogous to Theorem 3 can be obtained once one has an upper bound \(\ell_n(t)\le \lfloor\rho\rfloor_\Delta\) after some time. Thus, for Coxian service times the equilibrium characterization \(\ell^*=\lfloor\rho\rfloor_\Delta\) is established for the basic learning scheme, while the refined-scheme Coxian stabilization remains an open extension.

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(|V|=n\), \(|E|=m\), and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. An \(M\)-alternating path is a simple path whose edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\). An \(M\)-augmenting path is an alternating path whose endpoints are unmatched vertices (with respect to \(M\)); augmenting along such a path increases \(|M|\) by 1.

The Micali--Vazirani (MV) algorithm finds a maximum-cardinality matching by repeating phases. In one phase it finds a maximal set of vertex-disjoint minimum-length augmenting paths (with respect to the current matching \(M\)) and augments along all of them. A phase uses a graph-search subroutine called double depth-first search (DDFS) to discover either an augmenting path or a certain contracted structure (petal/blossom). During a phase, the algorithm maintains a dynamically changing parent-like map \(\mathrm{bud}:V\to V\) that maps each vertex to the current \"bud\" representing the petal containing it, and the iterated map \(\mathrm{bud}^*(v)\) defined by repeated application of \(\mathrm{bud}\) until reaching a fixed point:
\[
\mathrm{bud}^*(v)=\begin{cases}
 v, & \text{if }\mathrm{bud}(v)=v,\\
 \mathrm{bud}^*(\mathrm{bud}(v)), & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
Computing \(\mathrm{bud}^*\) is implemented via a disjoint-set union (union--find) data structure, where unions correspond to newly formed petals/blossoms and finds return the current representative \(\mathrm{bud}^*(v)\). On a pointer machine model, standard union--find with path compression runs in \(O(\alpha(m,n))\) amortized time per operation, yielding \(O(m\,\alpha(m,n))\) time per phase if there are \(O(m)\) such operations.

The paper proves correctness of MV and shows a per-phase time bound \(O(m)\) on the RAM model and \(O(m\,\alpha(m,n))\) on the pointer model when union--find is used to maintain \(\mathrm{bud}^*\). It states that Micali and Vazirani claimed (without proof) that, due to special blossom structure in MV, path compression alone suffices to make the total time spent in maintaining \(\mathrm{bud}^*\) linear per phase on the pointer model, i.e., eliminating the extra \(\alpha(m,n)\) factor. The paper also poses a related question: whether the union--find based MV implementation already runs in linear time per phase because the number/structure of operations is more restricted than in worst-case union--find analysis.

Page 18, Section 8 (Conclusion)

While we prove positive liquid welfare guarantees under mild learning assumptions, we leave open the problem of whether stronger learning guarantees imply better liquid welfare. For example, can we get better liquid welfare guarantees if the players have high competitive ratio with respect to the best Lipschitz continuous function that maps values to bids? Or if the values are sampled from a distribution instead of being picked adversarially?
title: Design learning guarantees that improve liquid welfare in sequential budgeted auctions
background_latex:
Consider a sequential auction with one item per round over rounds \(t\in[T]=\{1,\dots,T\}\) and players \(i\in[n]\). Player \(i\) has a hard budget \(B_i>0\) and per-round value \(v_{it}\in[0,1]\) for winning the round-\(t\) item. (In the additive-valuation model, the value of a set of won rounds \(S\subseteq[T]\) is \(\sum_{t\in S} v_{it}\).) In each round players submit bids; in a first-price auction the highest bidder wins and pays her bid. Let \(V_i\) and \(P_i\) denote player \(i\)'s total realized value and payment over all rounds, and let the (budgeted quasilinear) utility be \(U_i = V_i-P_i\) if \(P_i\le B_i\) and \(-\infty\) otherwise.

The system performance metric is liquid welfare. Player \(i\)'s liquid welfare contribution is
\[\mathrm{LW}_i := \min\{B_i, V_i\},\qquad \mathrm{LW}:=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathrm{LW}_i.\]
Let \(\mathrm{LW}^*\) denote the maximum liquid welfare over all feasible allocations of items across rounds.

Players are assumed to be learning (not necessarily converging to equilibrium). A baseline behavioral benchmark studied in the paper is comparison to the best fixed multiplicative shading multiplier \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) applied to values each round, subject to not exceeding the remaining budget. More generally, one can consider richer benchmark classes mapping values to bids; e.g., a (scalar) bidding rule \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) that is Lipschitz continuous (with some Lipschitz constant \(L\)) and induces bids \(b_{it}=f(v_{it})\) each round, again subject to the remaining budget. One can also distinguish adversarially chosen value sequences \((v_{it})\) versus values drawn i.i.d. from a distribution (stochastic model).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exist stronger, still natural learning-style performance guarantees on bidders' utilities that imply strictly better worst-case approximation of optimal liquid welfare \(\mathrm{LW}^*\) in sequential budgeted first-price auctions than the bounds obtained under comparison to the best fixed shading multiplier.

In particular, analyze the liquid-welfare price of anarchy achievable when each player attains a small competitive ratio (or no-regret) with respect to richer benchmark classes such as:
1) the best Lipschitz continuous bidding function \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) mapping values to bids, and/or
2) the best fixed shading multiplier when the values \((v_{it})\) are sampled from a distribution rather than chosen adversarially.

The goal is to characterize the best provable factor \(\alpha\) (as a function of the learning guarantee parameters) such that \(\mathrm{LW} \ge \mathrm{LW}^*/\alpha\) (up to lower-order additive terms, if unavoidable) under these stronger learning assumptions.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Fikioris--Tardos) establishes that in sequential budgeted first-price auctions, a per-bidder learning guarantee relative to the best fixed shading multiplier \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) implies a liquid-welfare approximation \(\mathrm{LW} \ge \mathrm{LW}^*/\alpha\) with \(\alpha=\gamma+\tfrac12+O(1/\gamma)\) (additive valuations), and nearly matching lower bounds \(\Omega(\max\{\gamma,2\})\). The open direction is whether strengthening the behavioral benchmark (e.g., to Lipschitz value-to-bid maps) and/or assuming stochastic i.i.d. values can strictly improve worst-case liquid-welfare guarantees, especially in the \(\gamma\approx 1\) regime where the paper’s bounds leave a gap between \(2\) and \(\approx 2.41\).

Forward citations provide partial progress along two axes. On the stochastic side, "Budget pacing in repeated auctions: Regret and efficiency without convergence" proves that gradient-based pacing under i.i.d. value profiles guarantees expected liquid welfare at least half of the optimal ex ante liquid welfare (up to \(\tilde O(n\sqrt{T})\) additive loss) without requiring convergence, matching the familiar factor-2 barrier in expectation. On the richer-benchmark learning side, "No-regret algorithms in non-truthful auctions with budget and roi constraints" shows that in i.i.d. environments one can in fact achieve no-regret (full information) against the best \(L\)-Lipschitz bidding function, substantially strengthening what is algorithmically feasible beyond fixed multipliers; however, it does not connect such guarantees to market-level liquid welfare when all bidders learn.

Several related works reinforce both possibilities and barriers: equilibrium-based analyses in autobidding models with budgets show factor-2-type liquid-welfare guarantees under additional assumptions (e.g., \(v\le B\)) or under pacing-equilibrium abstractions, while other results show large inefficiency is possible in deterministic first-price mechanisms absent such assumptions, and computational hardness suggests that selecting outcomes beating factor \(2-\epsilon\) can be intractable in related settings. Overall, the open problem remains unresolved: existing stochastic-learning results achieve \(1/2\)-optimal expected liquid welfare under pacing, and richer benchmark regret is achievable for single bidders, but a general theorem translating Lipschitz-benchmark no-regret (or i.i.d.-value assumptions) into strictly better worst-case liquid-welfare approximation for sequential budgeted first-price auctions has not yet been established.

sources.title: Budget pacing in repeated auctions: Regret and efficiency without convergence
sources.theorem_or_result:
Main aggregate-efficiency guarantee: when all agents use (generalized) gradient-based pacing (Algorithm 1) in any core auction with i.i.d. value profiles across rounds (allowing arbitrary within-round correlation), the expected liquid welfare of the induced allocation rule x satisfies
\[W(x,F) \ge \tfrac12 W(y,F) - O\big(n v\sqrt{T\log(v n T)}\big)\]
for every single-round allocation rule \(y:[0,v]^n\to X\) (Theorem 3.4), where \(W(\cdot,F)\) is ex ante liquid welfare. In particular, taking y to be an optimal allocation rule yields a \(2\)-approximation to optimal expected liquid welfare up to an additive \(\tilde O(n v\sqrt T)\) term, without requiring convergence of the learning dynamics.
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether stronger learning guarantees (e.g., regret vs richer benchmark classes like Lipschitz bidding functions, or stochastic values) can imply strictly better worst-case approximation of optimal liquid welfare than guarantees obtained when comparing to the best fixed shading multiplier. This paper directly addresses the stochastic-values variant: it assumes values are drawn i.i.d. across rounds and analyzes simultaneous learning via pacing multipliers (a fixed linear shading form). It proves a constant-factor liquid-welfare guarantee (\(\ge 1/2\) of optimal expected liquid welfare, up to \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) additive loss) that holds along the entire learning trajectory (no convergence needed) and for first-price auctions (indeed any core auction). However, it does not improve the approximation factor beyond \(1/2\), nor does it analyze regret against richer benchmark classes such as Lipschitz value-to-bid functions; the individual regret results are primarily against pacing-multiplier benchmarks (best fixed multiplier in stochastic settings; perfect pacing sequence in adversarial settings). Thus it provides substantial progress on part (2) of the open problem (stochastic model) but not on part (1) (richer benchmarks) and not on achieving a strictly better worst-case factor than the fixed-multiplier-based bounds.

sources.title: No-regret algorithms in non-truthful auctions with budget and roi constraints
sources.theorem_or_result:
In a stochastic repeated-auction model with i.i.d. draws \((v_t,d_t)\in[0,1]^2\) (value and highest competing bid), a single budget \(B=\rho T\) and ROI constraint, and first-price or more generally hybrid pricing \(p(b,d)=q b+(1-q)d\) satisfying Assumption 3.1, the paper gives no-regret algorithms against the benchmark OPT defined as the best (possibly randomized) \(L\)-Lipschitz bidding function \(f:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) chosen with knowledge of the distribution. In particular:
- (Full information) Theorem 4.1 (informal Thm 1.1): an algorithm with full-information feedback achieves \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) regret vs OPT while satisfying budget and ROI constraints (ROI exactly via a reduction), with regret scaling as \(\frac{1}{\beta^2\rho}\,O\big(\sqrt{L T\log T}+\sqrt{T\log(1/\delta)}\big)\) under a slack parameter \(\beta>0\) (Eq. (2)).
- (Bandit, first-price) Theorem 5.1: any bandit-feedback algorithm can incur regret \(\Omega(T^{2/3})\) even with constant value \(v_t\equiv 1\) and budget \(\rho=1/4\).
- (Bandit upper bound) Theorem 5.2: a polynomial-time bandit algorithm achieves regret \(\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{\beta\rho}(L^{1/4}T^{3/4}+T^{1/2}L^{1/2})\big)\) (and can be made ROI-exact with extra \(1/\beta\) factor under conditions).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether stronger learning guarantees—especially no-regret vs richer benchmarks like Lipschitz bidding functions and/or in stochastic (i.i.d.) environments—can imply strictly better worst-case liquid-welfare approximation in sequential budgeted first-price auctions than guarantees based only on best fixed shading multipliers.

This paper directly advances the learning side of that question in the stochastic model: it replaces the weak “best constant pacing/shading multiplier” benchmark with the much richer class of \(L\)-Lipschitz value-to-bid maps, and proves near-optimal \(\tilde O(\sqrt T)\) regret (full information) under budget/ROI constraints. Thus it establishes that such stronger learning guarantees are achievable (algorithmically) in first-price/hybrid auctions.

However, it studies a single bidder’s regret relative to OPT and does not analyze multi-bidder equilibrium/price-of-anarchy style implications for liquid welfare \(\mathrm{LW}\) versus \(\mathrm{LW}^*\). In particular, it does not prove a liquid-welfare PoA bound (as a function of the Lipschitz-regret parameters) for sequential first-price auctions when all bidders run these algorithms. Therefore it does not resolve the open problem’s welfare-characterization goal, but provides a key ingredient (no-regret-to-Lipschitz benchmark in the i.i.d. model) that could potentially be plugged into a welfare analysis.

sources.title: Efficiency of non-truthful auctions in auto-bidding with budget constraints
sources.theorem_or_result:
In the auto-bidding model with return-on-spend (ROS) and hard budget constraints, the paper proves price-of-anarchy bounds for several (single-shot, per-query) first-price-style mechanisms with respect to optimal liquid welfare (allowing randomized/fractional allocations). Key theorems include:
- For deterministic first-price auction (FPA), 
  - 
  \[\mathrm{PoA}(\mathrm{FPA}) = n\] 
  in the worst case (Theorems 3.1–3.3), when benchmarking against the optimal randomized allocation.
  - Under the assumption \(v_{i,j}\le B_i\) for all bidders/queries, 
  \[\mathrm{PoA}(\mathrm{FPA})\le 2\] 
  (Theorem 3.10).
- For randomized first-price auction rFPA with two bidders per query, 
  \[\mathrm{PoA}(\mathrm{rFPA})\le 1.8\] 
  for a suitable parameter choice (Theorem 4.3).
- For quasi-proportional (power) first-price allocation, 
  \[\mathrm{PoA}\le 2\] 
  as the power parameter \(\alpha\to\infty\) (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for stronger learning-style utility guarantees (e.g., no-regret vs richer benchmark classes like Lipschitz bidding functions, or stochastic/i.i.d. values) that imply strictly better worst-case approximation to optimal liquid welfare in sequential budgeted first-price auctions than guarantees based on best fixed shading multipliers.

This citing paper does not study sequential no-regret learning or benchmarked regret guarantees. Instead it analyzes equilibrium (pure Nash) efficiency in an auto-bidding model with ROS and budget constraints, measuring liquid-welfare PoA against optimal (possibly randomized) allocations. Nevertheless, it is directly relevant in two ways:
- It provides tight lower/upper bounds showing that deterministic FPA can have \(\mathrm{PoA}=n\) when compared to the optimal randomized allocation, due to an \(n\)-factor gap between optimal fractional and integral liquid welfare (Theorem 3.1). This informs what any learning guarantee could hope to imply if the benchmark is fractional Opt.
- It shows that randomization in the mechanism (rFPA, quasi-proportional FPA) can restore constant PoA (\(\le 1.8\) for two bidders; \(\le 2\) for any \(n\) in quasi-proportional limit), suggesting a different route to improved liquid welfare than strengthening bidders’ learning benchmarks.

However, it does not answer whether no-regret against richer bidding-function classes (e.g., Lipschitz \(f\)) or stochastic-value assumptions improve the liquid-welfare guarantees in the sequential-learning model of Fikioris–Tardos; it operates in a different behavioral model (equilibrium of a one-shot multi-query game) and with value-maximizing (ROS) agents rather than quasilinear utility maximizers with \(-\infty\) budget violations.

sources.title: A field guide for pacing budget and ROS constraints
sources.theorem_or_result:
In a stochastic i.i.d. repeated-auction model with a single value-maximizing bidder facing both a hard budget constraint and a return-on-spend (ROS) constraint, the paper analyzes the decentralized “min pacing” bid rule
- bid each round: \(b_t=\min\{\tfrac{1+\lambda_t}{\lambda_t}v_t,\tfrac{1}{\mu_t}v_t,B_t\}\)
with multiplicative-weights updates \(\lambda_{t+1}=\lambda_t\exp(-\alpha(v_tx_t(b_t)-p_t(b_t)))\), \(\mu_{t+1}=\mu_t\exp(-\eta(\rho-p_t(b_t)))\).
Under single-crossing/Lipschitz/strong-monotonicity assumptions on expected constraint gradients, it proves regret \(\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{OPT}-\mathrm{Alg}]=O(\sqrt{T})\) (Theorem 1) and ex-post ROS violation \(\sum_{t\le T}(p_t(b_t)-v_tx_t(b_t))\le O(\sqrt{T}\log T)\) plus budget depletion within \(O(\sqrt{T})\) rounds of the horizon (Theorem 2). It also shows any sequentially-decoupled architecture can incur \(\Omega(T)\) ROS violation or \(\Omega(T)\) regret (Proposition 3.3).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether stronger learning-style guarantees (e.g., no-regret to richer benchmarks like Lipschitz bidding functions, or stochastic i.i.d. values) can yield strictly better worst-case liquid-welfare approximations in sequential budgeted first-price auctions than guarantees based on best fixed shading multipliers.

This paper does not analyze liquid welfare or multi-bidder sequential first-price auctions. Instead it studies a single bidder’s online optimization (value maximization) with budget and ROS constraints, in an i.i.d. stochastic environment, and proves \(O(\sqrt{T})\) regret/constraint-violation guarantees for a minimally-coupled pacing algorithm. The relevance is indirect: it provides learning guarantees in the stochastic model and discusses (via related work [LPSZ23]) liquid-welfare efficiency when many such autobidders interact, but it does not itself establish improved liquid-welfare price-of-anarchy bounds under richer benchmark classes (e.g., Lipschitz bidding functions) for the sequential budgeted first-price auction setting of the open problem.

sources.title: Robust Temporal Guarantees in Budgeted Sequential Auctions
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper studies sequential first-price (and some results for second-price) auctions with hard budgets where bidders’ objective is to maximize the total number of wins (all items equally valuable). It proposes the Primal Budget Pacing Algorithm with update 
\[b_i^{(t+1)}=b_i^{(t)}+\eta(\rho_i-p_i^{(t)})\]
where bidder i’s total budget is \(\rho_i T\) (budgets normalized so \(\sum_i \rho_i=1\)). Main guarantees include:
- (Robustness vs adversarial opponents) If a learner with budget \(\rho_L T\) uses the algorithm with \(\eta=1/\sqrt{T}\) and initial bid \(b^{(1)}=\rho_L\), then any (possibly colluding) budget-feasible opponent with budget \(\rho_O T\) can win at most \(\frac{\rho_O}{\rho_L+\rho_O}T+3\sqrt{T}\) rounds (Theorem 3.1), hence the learner wins at least \(\frac{\rho_L}{\rho_L+\rho_O}T-3\sqrt{T}\).
- (Temporal/interval guarantees in self-play) When all agents use the algorithm in first-price auctions, after a burn-in of \(O\big(\frac{1}{\rho_{\min}\eta}\log\frac{1}{\eta}\big)\) rounds, each agent i wins approximately its budget share in every interval of length \(\tau=O(\sqrt{T})\): at least \(\rho_i\tau - O\big(\frac{1}{\rho_{\min}}\big)\) wins (Theorem 4.1). For equal budgets, play becomes round-robin after \(O\big(\frac{n^2}{\eta}\log\frac{1}{\eta}\big)\) rounds (Theorem 5.1).

This paper does not analyze liquid welfare, utilities \(V_i-P_i\), or regret/competitive ratio against benchmark bidding functions. sources.title: Tight Inapproximability for Welfare-Maximizing Autobidding Equilibria
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves tight NP-hardness of improving upon the known liquid-welfare/welfare price-of-anarchy threshold in autobidding settings: for any constant \(\epsilon>0\), it is NP-hard to compute a (second-price) autobidding equilibrium whose welfare is within a factor \(2-\epsilon\) of the welfare-optimal equilibrium (Theorem 1.1 / 3.14). It also shows NP-hardness for relaxed outcomes generated by learning dynamics: for any \(\epsilon>0\), it is NP-hard to compute a “responsive learning sequence” whose average welfare approximates the welfare-optimal one within \(\frac{2e}{2e-1}-\epsilon\) (Theorem 1.8 / 4.9).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether stronger learning-style guarantees (e.g., no-regret vs richer benchmark classes like Lipschitz bidding functions, or stochastic values) can yield strictly better worst-case approximation \(\mathrm{LW}\ge \mathrm{LW}^*/\alpha\) in sequential budgeted first-price auctions than guarantees obtained from comparison to a fixed shading multiplier. This paper does not address sequential first-price auctions with hard budgets, nor does it analyze regret to Lipschitz bidding-function benchmarks. Instead it studies (parallel) second-price autobidding with RoS constraints (often with budgets lifted so liquid welfare equals welfare) and proves computational inapproximability of finding equilibria or learning-generated sequences that beat the baseline PoA-type constants (notably the factor 2 barrier). Thus it provides negative evidence in a related but different model: even if better-than-2 outcomes exist, selecting/computing them can be intractable; and for certain relaxed learning notions, achieving approximation better than \(\approx 2e/(2e-1)\) is NP-hard. This informs the open problem by suggesting barriers to improving worst-case welfare guarantees via stronger behavioral assumptions, though it does not resolve the specific sequential-FPA/Lipschitz-benchmark question.

title: Classify stable serial knockout competitions up to equivalence for larger powers of two
background_latex:
Fix an integer \(k\ge 2\) and let \(n=2^k\). A (balanced) single-elimination knockout tournament on a player set \(P\) with \(|P|=n\) is a rooted binary tree with \(n\) leaves labeled bijectively by the players; the tournament has \(k\) rounds, and players \(x,x'\in P\) are said to be able to meet in round \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) if, given the fixed bracket, there is a possible sequence of earlier match outcomes under which they face each other in round \(i\). Formally, for a knockout tournament \(T\) on \(P\), define \(v_T(x,x')=i\) if \(x\) and \(x'\) can meet in round \(i\) in \(T\).

A serial knockout competition (SKC) on \(P\) is a set \(\mathcal{T}\) of \(n-1\) knockout tournaments on the same player set \(P\). For each round \(i\), the SKC \(\mathcal{T}\) is called stable in round \(i\) if there exists a constant \(c_i\) such that for every distinct pair \(x\ne x'\) in \(P\),
\[
\#\{T\in\mathcal{T}: v_T(x,x')=i\}=c_i.
\]
It is stable if it is stable in all rounds \(i=1,\dots,k\). For an SKC with \(|\mathcal{T}|=n-1\), counting implies \(c_i=2^{i-1}\).

Two knockout tournaments \(T,T'\) on player sets \(P,P'\) are considered identical if \(v_T(p,q)=v_{T'}(p,q)\) for all pairs \(p,q\) in the common player set; and two SKCs \(\mathcal{T}\) on \(P\) and \(\mathcal{T}'\) on \(P'\) are called equivalent if there exists a bijection \(s:P\to P'\) such that \(\mathcal{T}'=\{T(s): T\in \mathcal{T}\}\), where \(T(s)\) is obtained from \(T\) by relabeling each player \(p\in P\) as \(s(p)\). The paper constructs, for every \(n=2^k\), a stable SKC via algebraic structure on \(\mathrm{GF}(2^k)\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The defining constraint for a stable SKC on \(n=2^k\) players is that for each round \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\) and each unordered pair \(\{x,x'\}\), the number of brackets \(T\) in the family \(\mathcal T\) with \(v_T(x,x')=i\) is constant (necessarily \(c_i=2^{i-1}\) when \(|\mathcal T|=n-1\)). Lambers–Pendavingh–Spieksma construct such families for all \(2^k\) using algebra over \(\mathrm{GF}(2^k)\), and they prove uniqueness up to relabeling only in the smallest nontrivial case \(n=8\) (via the Fano plane). The open problem asks whether this algebraic construction is essentially the only one for \(n>8\), e.g. \(n=16\), or whether inequivalent stable SKCs exist.

Among the forward citations provided, the only citing work is an operations-research survey that briefly summarizes the existence result and its Galois-field connection but does not contribute new structural, classification, or nonisomorphism results for stable SKCs. Consequently, based on the available forward-citation evidence, the classification/uniqueness question for \(n=2^k>8\) remains open. Promising directions suggested by the original paper’s viewpoint include translating stability into incidence/association-scheme language on pairs of players (where \(v_T\) induces a hierarchy of partitions by “round of possible meeting”), analyzing automorphism groups of the \(\mathrm{GF}(2^k)\)-constructed SKC, and searching for alternative constructions via difference sets, orthogonal arrays, or other finite-geometry designs that could yield inequivalent SKCs for \(n=16\) or prove rigidity.

title: Prove NP-hardness of deciding convexity of coordinate projections of rotation matrices
background_latex:
Let \(n\ge 3\). Let \(\mathrm{SO}(n)=\{X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:X^\top X=I,\ \det(X)=1\}\) denote the special orthogonal group (rotation matrices).

For a set of matrix coordinates \(S\subseteq [n]\times [n]\) (where \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\)), define the coordinate projection map \(\pi_S:\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\to\mathbb{R}^{|S|}\) by
\[
\pi_S(X) := (X_{ij})_{(i,j)\in S},
\]
i.e., \(\pi_S(X)\) records the entries of \(X\) indexed by \(S\) (in some fixed order).

Define the decision problem \(\mathrm{CONVEX}\): the input is \(n\) and a coordinate set \(S\subseteq [n]\times[n]\); the output is \(\mathrm{TRUE}\) if the image set \(\pi_S(\mathrm{SO}(n))\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{|S|}\) is convex, and \(\mathrm{FALSE}\) otherwise.

Convexity here is in the usual Euclidean sense: a set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex if for all \(x,y\in K\) and all \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in K\).
problem_definition_latex: Determine the computational complexity of \(\mathrm{CONVEX}\). In particular, prove (or refute) that \(\mathrm{CONVEX}\) is NP-hard: given \(n\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\times[n]\), decide whether \(\pi_S(\mathrm{SO}(n))\) is convex.

title: Recovery threshold for complete LP relaxation in semi-random rank-one Boolean tensors
background_latex:
Let \(n,m,l\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\) and let \(G\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m\times l}\) be an observed binary tensor. A rank-one binary (Boolean) tensor is a tensor of the form
\[W=x\otimes y\otimes z,\qquad x\in\{0,1\}^n,\ y\in\{0,1\}^m,\ z\in\{0,1\}^l,\]
with entries \(w_{ijk}=x_i y_j z_k\).

Assume a planted (ground-truth) rank-one tensor \(\bar W=\bar x\otimes \bar y\otimes \bar z\in\{0,1\}^{n\times m\times l}\). In the fully-random corruption model with parameter \(p\in[0,1]\), each entry is independently flipped: \(g_{ijk}=\bar w_{ijk}\) with probability \(1-p\) and \(g_{ijk}=1-\bar w_{ijk}\) with probability \(p\). In the associated semi-random corruption model, after the fully-random flips an adversary may apply any sequence of monotone corrections: it may change \(g_{ijk}\) from \(0\) to \(1\) only when \(\bar w_{ijk}=1\), and from \(1\) to \(0\) only when \(\bar w_{ijk}=0\).

An optimization problem is said to recover the ground truth if it has a unique optimal solution and that solution corresponds to \(\bar W\) (equivalently \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\)).

The paper studies linear programming relaxations of rank-one Boolean tensor factorization. The strongest relaxation considered is the \(\textit{complete LP}\), which optimizes the standard linearized objective for rank-one BTF using an extended formulation with auxiliary variables representing all bilinear products and constraints capturing the convex hull of the local multilinear relations.

Concretely, define index sets from the observed tensor \(G\):
\[S_0:=\{(i,j,k): g_{ijk}=0\},\qquad S_1:=\{(i,j,k): g_{ijk}=1\}.\]
Introduce variables \(x\in[0,1]^n\), \(y\in[0,1]^m\), \(z\in[0,1]^l\), and auxiliary variables \(w\in[0,1]^{n\times m\times l}\) as well as bilinear auxiliaries \(w^1\in[0,1]^{n\times m}\), \(w^2\in[0,1]^{n\times l}\), \(w^3\in[0,1]^{m\times l}\). The complete LP minimizes
\[\sum_{(i,j,k)\in S_0} w_{ijk}+\sum_{(i,j,k)\in S_1}(1-w_{ijk}),\]
subject to a system of linear inequalities (given explicitly in the paper) that enforce a tight convex relaxation of
\(w_{ijk}=x_i y_j z_k\) together with \(w^1_{ij}=x_i y_j\), \(w^2_{ik}=x_i z_k\), \(w^3_{jk}=y_j z_k\), in a way implied by level-2 reformulation-linearization but with only \(O(nml)\) constraints.

Let the planted factor densities be
\[r_{\bar x}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \bar x_i,\quad r_{\bar y}:=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^m \bar y_j,\quad r_{\bar z}:=\frac{1}{l}\sum_{k=1}^l \bar z_k,\quad r_{\bar W}:=r_{\bar x} r_{\bar y} r_{\bar z}.\]
The paper establishes high-probability recovery thresholds for weaker LPs (standard LP and flower LP) under the semi-random model, but does not give such a threshold for the complete LP.

More explicitly: characterize, in terms of the corruption probability \(p\) and planted densities \(r_{\bar x},r_{\bar y},r_{\bar z}\) (and asymptotic growth of \(n,m,l\)), conditions under which the complete LP has a unique optimal solution corresponding to the planted tensor \(\bar W=\bar x\otimes \bar y\otimes \bar z\) with probability tending to one as \(n,m,l\to\infty\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem from Del Pia–Khajavirad asks for a high-probability exact-recovery threshold for the strongest LP relaxation they propose for rank-one Boolean tensor factorization, the complete LP, under a semi-random monotone corruption model. In the source paper, recovery thresholds are proved for weaker relaxations (standard LP and flower LP) by constructing explicit dual certificates and then showing that the required deterministic inequalities hold with high probability under the random corruption model; robustness (monotone semi-random corrections) is handled via a general monotonicity argument.

Among the forward citations provided here, the only analyzed citing work is "Linear programming and community detection", which studies a different planted model (stochastic block model on graphs) and a different LP (metric polytope relaxation for minimum bisection). It does not resolve the tensor complete-LP threshold, but it reinforces a general methodological paradigm: (i) derive deterministic necessary/sufficient conditions for LP exact recovery via dual optimality and complementary slackness; (ii) translate these into probabilistic recovery/failure regions under a planted random model. Adapting such a program to the complete LP would likely require identifying the right notion of a dual certificate for the extended formulation variables \(w,w^1,w^2,w^3\) and proving concentration bounds for the resulting (more intricate) inequalities.

Given the limited forward-citation set supplied, there is no evidence that the complete-LP recovery threshold in the semi-random model has been characterized. Thus, based on the available citation analysis, the problem remains open. Promising directions include extending the source paper’s dual-certificate analysis from flower inequalities to the full set of complete-LP constraints (which already imply flower and running-intersection inequalities), and developing sharp probabilistic bounds that capture the empirical improvement observed for the complete LP in the source paper’s experiments.

sources.title: Linear programming and community detection
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper analyzes the metric-polytope LP relaxation (triangle inequalities) for minimum bisection under the 2-community stochastic block model. It proves: - (Recovery, very dense) If edge probabilities are constants with \,0<q<p<1\, and \,p-q>1/2\,, then with high probability the LP uniquely recovers the planted bisection (Theorem 6). - (Non-recovery) In multiple regimes (very dense, dense \,p,q\asymp n^{-\omega}\,, and logarithmic \,p,q\asymp (\log n)/n\,), it gives explicit parameter conditions under which the LP fails w.h.p. (Theorems 7 and 8).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for high-probability recovery thresholds for the *complete LP* relaxation for planted rank-one Boolean tensors under a *semi-random monotone* corruption model. This citing paper instead studies a different problem (graph minimum bisection / community detection) and a different LP (metric relaxation) under the *purely random* SBM model, without semi-random monotone adversarial corrections. It therefore does not provide a recovery guarantee for the tensor complete LP. At best, it offers methodological analogies: (i) deterministic dual-certificate style sufficient conditions for LP recovery; (ii) probabilistic translation of those conditions under a random model; (iii) evidence that weaker LPs can have much worse thresholds than stronger convex relaxations (SDP), which is conceptually relevant when comparing standard/flower/complete LPs in Boolean tensor factorization.

title: Order dependence of sequential issue-by-issue voting without LAMO bases
background_latex:
Let \(d\ge 2\) and let \((\mathbb{R}^d,\|\cdot\|)\) be a finite-dimensional normed vector space.

1) Voters and preferences. There are \(n\ge 3\) voters (with \(n\) odd). Voter \(i\) has an ideal point (peak) \(t_i\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Preferences are induced by the norm distance to the peak: voter \(i\) weakly prefers outcome \(v\) to \(v'\) iff \(\|t_i-v\|\le \|t_i-v'\|\).

2) Issues as a basis. Fix an algebraic basis \(B=\{x_1,\dots,x_d\}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Any \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) can be uniquely written \(v=\sum_{j=1}^d \alpha_j(v) x_j\); here \(\alpha_j(v)\in\mathbb{R}\) is the \(j\)-th coordinate of \(v\) in basis \(B\).

3) Sequential issue-by-issue voting. For a permutation \(\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_d)\) of \(\{1,\dots,d\}\), consider the sequential procedure that determines the coordinate along \(x_{\sigma_1}\) first, then \(x_{\sigma_2}\), etc. At stage \(k\), voters report a real number for the coordinate along \(x_{\sigma_k}\); the stage outcome is the simple majority (one-dimensional) median of reported numbers. Earlier stage outcomes are observed before later-stage reports are chosen. The equilibrium concept is ex-post perfect equilibrium, and the paper focuses on the equilibrium surviving iterative elimination of weakly dominated strategies.

4) Order independence. The family of sequential procedures associated with the fixed basis \(B\) is called order independent if, for every profile \((t_1,\dots,t_n)\), the resulting equilibrium outcome in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is the same for all permutations \(\sigma\).

5) Birkhoff--James orthogonality and LAMO. For vectors \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), \(x\) is Birkhoff--James (BJ) orthogonal to \(y\) (written \(x\dashv y\)) if \(\|x+\lambda y\|\ge \|x\|\) for all \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\). For a basis \(B=\{x_1,\dots,x_d\}\), let \(X_j\) be the subspace spanned by \(B\setminus\{x_j\}\). The basis satisfies left-additive mutual orthogonality (LAMO) if \(X_j\dashv x_j\) for every \(j\) (equivalently, every linear combination of the other basis vectors is BJ-orthogonal to \(x_j\)).
