title: Determine the asymptotic order of maximum independent sets in recursive Markov random graphs
background_latex:
Fix parameters \(p\in(0,1]\) and \(r\in(0,1)\), and write \(\gamma:=1-r\in(0,1)\). Define the random graph \(G^r_{n,p}\) on vertex set \(\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}\) by the following recursive Markov edge-generation rule.

1) For each \(i\in\{2,\dots,n\}\), the edge \((v_1,v_i)\) is present with probability \(p\).

2) For each fixed \(i\in\{3,\dots,n\}\), the edges \((v_j,v_i)\) for \(j=2,3,\dots,i-1\) are generated sequentially as a (non-homogeneous) Markov chain along increasing \(j\): conditional on the previous edge \((v_{j-1},v_i)\),
\[
\mathbb P\big((v_j,v_i)\in E\mid (v_{j-1},v_i)\notin E\big)=\mathbb P\big((v_{j-1},v_i)\in E\big),
\]
\[
\mathbb P\big((v_j,v_i)\in E\mid (v_{j-1},v_i)\in E\big)=r\,\mathbb P\big((v_{j-1},v_i)\in E\big).
\]
Equivalently, if \(X^i_j\in\{0,1\}\) indicates whether \((v_j,v_i)\) is an edge, and \(p^i_j:=\mathbb P(X^i_j=1)\), then \(p^i_1=p\) and for \(2\le j\le i-1\),
\[
 p^i_j = p^i_{j-1}\big(1-\gamma p^i_{j-1}\big).
\]

Let \(\alpha(G)\) denote the stability number (maximum cardinality of an independent set) of a graph \(G\). The asymptotic regime is \(n\to\infty\); “with high probability (w.h.p.)” means with probability tending to 1 as \(n\to\infty\).

title: Derive an exact tractable convex program for robust Markov decision processes
background_latex:
A discounted robust Markov decision process (RMDP) is specified by finite sets of states \(S\) and actions \(A\), nonnegative rewards \(r_{sa}\in\mathbb{R}_+\) for \((s,a)\in S\times A\), a discount factor \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), an initial distribution \(\alpha\in\Delta(S)\), and an uncertainty set \(\mathcal{U}\subseteq (\Delta(S))^{S\times A}\) of plausible transition kernels \(P=(P_{sas'})\). A stationary policy is \(\pi\in\Pi:=(\Delta(A))^S\). For a fixed transition kernel \(P\), the discounted return of \(\pi\) is
\[
R(\pi,P)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi,P}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t\, r_{S_tA_t}\ \Big|\ S_0\sim\alpha\Big].
\]
The RMDP objective is the max–min problem
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \min_{P\in\mathcal{U}}\ R(\pi,P).
\]
A common tractable structure is rectangularity of \(\mathcal{U}\). Under sa-rectangularity one has \(\mathcal{U}=\prod_{(s,a)\in S\times A} \mathcal{U}_{sa}\) with \(\mathcal{U}_{sa}\subseteq\Delta(S)\) convex and compact, and the robust Bellman operator \(T:\mathbb{R}^S\to\mathbb{R}^S\) is
\[
T(v)_s = \max_{a\in A}\ \min_{p\in\mathcal{U}_{sa}}\Big\{ r_{sa}+\gamma\, p^\top v\Big\},\qquad s\in S.
\]
The fixed point \(v^\star\) of \(T\) yields an optimal robust value function and an optimal stationary policy. Unlike the nominal MDP case (where a linear program exists), the maps \(v\mapsto T(v)_s\) need not be convex or concave, so the feasible sets \(\{v\in\mathbb{R}^S: v\ge T(v)\}\) or \(\{v\in\mathbb{R}^S: v\le T(v)\}\) are not known to admit a straightforward convex description in general.
problem_definition_latex:
Find conditions and a polynomial-size convex optimization formulation (e.g., conic, geometric, or other convex program) whose optimal solutions encode an optimal robust stationary policy and the optimal robust value function for the discounted RMDP
\[
\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \min_{P\in\mathcal{U}}\ R(\pi,P),
\]
under classical rectangular uncertainty (in particular sa-rectangular or s-rectangular \(\mathcal{U}\)), without introducing an approximation scheme based on regularization (i.e., an exact convex reformulation of the original RMDP rather than a sequence of convex programs converging to it).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Grand-Cl\'ement–Petrik, 2023) frames a central gap between the nominal discounted MDP case—where the Bellman inequalities \(v\ge T_P(v)\) yield a polynomial-size LP—and the discounted robust case under classical rectangular uncertainty, where the robust Bellman operator \(T(v)_s=\max_a\min_{p\in\mathcal U_{sa}}\{r_{sa}+\gamma p^\top v\}\) is generally neither convex nor concave in \(v\). The paper’s main contribution is therefore approximate: it adds entropic regularization in the maximization over actions and applies an exponential change of variables to obtain a polynomial-size convex (often conic) program whose solutions converge to the robust optimum as the regularization parameter tends to 0. The open problem asks whether one can remove this regularization/limit and obtain an exact polynomial-size convex formulation for the original max–min RMDP.

Among forward citations, no work is identified as giving such an exact convex reformulation in full generality. The closest structural progress is "Tractable robust Markov decision processes", which sharpens the landscape of when Bellman fixed-point dynamic programming is valid: for compact convex uncertainty sets, s-rectangularity and sa-rectangularity are essentially the only models that are tractable for all rewards/policies. This supports focusing on rectangular sets but does not by itself yield an explicit conic/LP description of \(\{v: v\ge T(v)\}\) or a single convex program encoding \(v^\star\) and an optimal robust policy.

Several papers provide partial tools rather than a full convexification. Data-driven distance-based ambiguity-set work (and related \(\kappa\)-rectangular modeling) emphasizes that for many practically used \(\mathcal U_{sa}\) (e.g., norm or divergence balls), the inner minimization \(\min_{p\in\mathcal U_{sa}} p^\top v\) is a convex optimization problem with tractable duals, suggesting that if one could decouple the outer \(\max_a\) and the dependence of \(p\) on \(v\) in a convex way, a conic epigraph might be possible in special cases. Conic-duality approaches in robust constrained MDPs show that even when the inner adversary problem is SOCP-representable, coupling it with policy choice typically introduces bilinearities, pinpointing a key obstruction to a global convex program. Algorithmic works (policy gradients; IWOCS) exploit rectangularity and saddle-point structure for computation but do not provide exact polynomial-size convex formulations. Overall, based on these forward citations, the exact convex-program reformulation for discounted rectangular RMDPs without regularization remains open; promising directions include identifying uncertainty-set classes where \(v\mapsto \min_{p\in\mathcal U_{sa}} p^\top v\) admits a conic epigraph that interacts benignly with the \(\max_a\) (e.g., via extended formulations), or proving impossibility/size lower bounds for general rectangular sets.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves a characterization of when robust MDP policy evaluation admits a dynamic-programming fixed-point formulation via rectangular extensions. For compact convex uncertainty sets \(\mathcal P\subseteq (\Delta(S))^{S\times A}\):
- \(\mathcal P\) is s-tractable (i.e. for all stationary \(\pi\) and all rewards \(r_{sas'}\), \(\min_{P\in\mathcal P}\mu^\top v^{\pi,P}=\mu^\top u^\pi\) where \(u^\pi\) is the fixed point of \(T^\pi(v)_s=\min_{P\in\mathcal P}\sum_a\pi_{sa}P_{sa}^\top(r_{sa}+\gamma v)\)) iff \(\mathcal P\) is s-rectangular: \(\mathcal P=\prod_{s\in S}\mathcal P_s\) (Theorem 2).
- \(\mathcal P\) is sa-tractable (analogous statement with \(\tilde T^\pi(v)_s=\sum_a\pi_{sa}\min_{p\in\mathcal P_{sa}} p^\top(r_{sa}+\gamma v)\)) iff \(\mathcal P\) is sa-rectangular: \(\mathcal P=\prod_{(s,a)}\mathcal P_{sa}\) (Theorem 4).
Under next-state-independent rewards \(r_{sas'}\equiv r_{sa}\), they give a weaker simultaneous-solvability condition (Theorem 5) that holds for r-rectangular and other non-rectangular sets, implying fixed-point solvability and strong duality/stationary optimal policies for convex \(\mathcal P\) (Theorems 6–7).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an exact polynomial-size convex optimization reformulation of discounted robust MDPs under classical rectangular uncertainty (s- or sa-rectangular), avoiding approximation/regularization. This paper does not provide a new explicit conic/LP-size convex program encoding the optimal robust policy/value for general rectangular RMDPs. Instead, it characterizes when dynamic programming (fixed-point Bellman equations) exactly solves policy evaluation and optimization, proving that among compact convex uncertainty sets, only s-rectangular/sa-rectangular sets are tractable in full generality. It also notes a convex program to compute a fixed point of a monotone contraction (Proposition 2), yielding a convex formulation for policy evaluation \(u^\pi\) (and similarly for \(u^\star\)) as \(\max\{\sum_s u_s: u\le T^\pi(u)\}\), but it does not develop this into a full polynomial-size convex program for the original max–min RMDP with explicit constraints for general \(\mathcal U_{sa}\) beyond the DP oracle/minimization. Thus it provides structural/complexity insight and a potential route (via fixed-point-as-convex-program) rather than the requested explicit exact tractable convex reformulation.

In particular (Theorem 4.4): for monotone, law-invariant, non-constant \(\rho\), dynamic programming (Conditions 1–2) forces \(\rho\) to be \(\operatorname{ess\,inf}\) or \(\operatorname{ess\,sup}\) for static kernels, and \(\operatorname{ess\,inf}\), \(\operatorname{ess\,sup}\), or \(\mathbb{E}\) for resampled kernels. Theorem 4.1 then implies existence of optimal stationary policies and validity of value/policy iteration whenever Conditions 1–2 hold.

This paper does not provide such a convex program for robust MDPs; instead it studies a broader ambiguity-averse framework and proves an impossibility/rigidity result: among monotone law-invariant risk measures compatible with state-based dynamic programming, only worst-case (\(\operatorname{ess\,inf}\), i.e., robust), best-case (\(\operatorname{ess\,sup}\)), and (in resampled case) expectation survive. This supports the idea that robust MDPs are essentially the only law-invariant DP-tractable epistemic-uncertainty model, but it does not resolve the convex-formulation question for robust MDPs (e.g., whether \(\{v: v\ge T(v)\}\) admits a polynomial-size conic description under sa-rectangular sets). At most, it provides conceptual constraints and points to an (appendix) convex program for computing \(V_{\nu,\rho}\) under additional convexity assumptions on \(\rho\), which is not the same as an exact convex reformulation of the robust max–min problem.

sources.title: Robust markov decision processes with data-driven, distance-based ambiguity sets
sources.theorem_or_result: The dissertation establishes asymptotic and finite-sample guarantees for data-driven robust MDPs with distance-based ambiguity sets under (s,a)-rectangular and s-rectangular uncertainty. Representative results include: for (s,a)-rectangular discounted RMDPs with ambiguity balls of radius \(\varepsilon_N\to 0\) and a distance satisfying a topology-metrization condition (Assumption 1 / generalized Pinsker inequality), the robust optimal value \(\tilde J^N(\varepsilon_N)\to J^*\) almost surely (Theorems 1,4) and robust-optimal policies are eventually optimal for the true MDP (Theorems 2,5); for finite \(N\), if a concentration inequality holds (Assumption 3), then with probability \(\ge 1-\gamma\), the out-of-sample value of the robust-optimal policy is at least the robust value \(J_P(\hat\pi^N)\ge \tilde J^N(\varepsilon_{N,\beta(\gamma)})\) (Theorems 3,6). For a family of distance-based s-rectangular ambiguity sets \(\mathcal P(\rho,\varepsilon)\), under lower-semicontinuity/convexity of the distance, for any \(\rho<\infty\) there exists \(\varepsilon^*\in[\varepsilon/m^{1/\rho},\varepsilon]\) such that the s-rectangular robust optimal value matches an (s,a)-rectangular one: \(\tilde J_\infty(\varepsilon^*)=\tilde J_\rho(\varepsilon)\) (Theorem 8).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an exact tractable convex optimization formulation (polynomial-size) for discounted robust MDPs under classical rectangular uncertainty, avoiding regularization-based approximations. This dissertation does not provide a new exact convex program for the robust Bellman fixed point or the max–min objective. Instead it (i) analyzes statistical properties of data-driven distance-ball ambiguity sets and (ii) discusses computational solution via robust value iteration, where each Bellman backup requires solving an inner minimization \(\min_{p\in\mathcal U_{sa}}\{r_{sa}+\gamma p^\top v\}\), which is convex for many distances and sometimes reducible to LP/1D concave maximization. These are algorithmic/structural results, not a global convex reformulation of the entire RMDP. Theorem 8 relates s-rectangular and (s,a)-rectangular models via matching robust optimal values by adjusting radii, but again does not yield a single convex program encoding \(v^*\) and an optimal policy for general rectangular \(\mathcal U\). Thus it is partial/indirect progress: it provides related tools (convex inner problems, continuity/compactness arguments) and clarifies tractability for specific ambiguity sets, but does not solve the convex-formulation open problem.

sources.theorem_or_result: From the title/abstract only: the paper introduces a parametric family of \(\kappa\)-rectangular robust MDPs (interpolating between existing rectangularity notions) and provides results comparing their conservativeness plus asymptotic and finite-sample properties of the resulting robust policies/values. sources.source_url: N/A (not provided in citation analysis block)
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper studies a discounted robust constrained MDP with uncertain transition probabilities modeled as \,\(p=\bar p+u\)\, where \,\(u\)\, lies in an s-rectangular uncertainty set \,\(U\)\, defined by polyhedral constraints and second-order-cone constraints (ellipsoidal-type). For a fixed stationary policy \,\(f\), it shows each inner worst-case expectation problem \(\max_{u\in U} (1-\alpha)\gamma^T(I-\alpha P_f(u))^{-1}c_f\) is equivalent to an SOCP via a change of variables (Lemma 1), and by SOCP strong duality derives an equivalent reformulation of the overall robust CMDP as an SOCP with bilinear constraints in the policy and dual variables (Theorem 1; similarly Theorem 2 under an alternative positivity assumption).

This paper does not provide a convex reformulation of the robust MDP objective \(\max_\pi\min_P R(\pi,P)\). Instead it treats a more complex robust CMDP and derives an exact reformulation that remains nonconvex because of bilinear terms coupling the stationary policy \(f\) with variables like \(\bar P_f\) and \(F_f(s)\) in constraints (12b–c,12f–g). The work is relevant in that it uses conic duality for s-rectangular uncertainty sets and produces SOCP representations of the inner minimization/maximization, but it stops short of an exact tractable convex program for the outer robust control problem; indeed it explicitly notes the final formulation is non-convex and solved with global solvers.

sources.title: Policy Gradient Algorithms for Robust MDP with Nonrectangular Uncertainty Sets
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops first-order algorithms (projected Langevin dynamics, Frank–Wolfe, and actor–critic) for robust discounted MDPs with general convex (possibly non-rectangular) uncertainty sets \(\mathcal P\). Key guarantees include:
- Projected Langevin dynamics (Alg. 3.1) returns \(\xi\) with \(\mathbb E[V^{P_\xi}_\pi(s_0)]\ge V^\star_\pi(s_0)-\varepsilon\) after \(M\) iterations with \(M\) exponential in parameter dimension \(q\) (Thm. 3.6).
- A Frank–Wolfe method (Alg. 3.2) terminates in \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) iterations and outputs \(\hat P\) with suboptimality bound \(V^\star_\pi(s_0)-V^{\hat P}_\pi(s_0)\le \delta_d(2\varepsilon+\delta_{\mathcal P})\), where \(\delta_{\mathcal P}=0\) for \(s\)-rectangular sets (Thm. 3.12, Cor. 3.13).
- An actor–critic scheme (Alg. 4.1) finds an \(\epsilon\)-optimal robust policy improvement solution in \(O(1/\epsilon^4)\) iterations given an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate robust evaluation oracle (Thm. 4.5).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an exact polynomial-size convex optimization reformulation of discounted robust MDPs under classical rectangular uncertainty (\(sa\)- or \(s\)-rectangular), without approximation/regularization. This paper does not provide a convex program reformulation of the robust Bellman fixed point or the max–min control problem. Instead it proposes gradient-based algorithms (including for non-rectangular sets) and proves convergence/suboptimality bounds. For rectangular sets, it notes global optimality of its Frank–Wolfe evaluation method (Cor. 3.13), but this is an iterative first-order method, not an exact tractable convex program encoding \(v^\star\) and an optimal stationary policy. Thus it offers algorithmic tools and complexity/comparison results rather than the requested convex formulation.

sources.title: Soft robust mdps and risk-sensitive mdps: Equivalence, policy gradient, and sample complexity
sources.source_url: N/A (not provided in citation analysis block)
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves an equivalence between a class of “soft robust MDPs” with penalty-regularized adversarial transitions and a new formulation of risk-sensitive MDPs based on convex risk measures. In particular, if the penalty function and risk measure are Fenchel conjugates so that
\[D(\hat P_{sa},P_{sa})=\sup_V\big(-\sigma(P_{sa},V)-\mathbb E_{s'\sim \hat P_{sa}}V(s')\big),\]
then the soft robust value functions and Q-functions coincide with the risk-sensitive ones, and an optimal robust policy can be taken stationary deterministic:
- \(V^\star=\tilde V^\star\), \(Q^\star=\tilde Q^\star\)
- \(\pi^\star(s)=\arg\max_a\{r(s,a)-\gamma\sigma(P_{sa},V^\star)\}\).
It also derives a policy-gradient theorem for these objectives and gives global convergence of exact policy gradient under tabular direct parameterization, plus an offline algorithm (RFZI) with sample-complexity bounds for the KL-penalized (entropy-risk) case.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for an exact, polynomial-size tractable convex optimization formulation for the classical discounted rectangular RMDP max–min objective (hard uncertainty set \(\mathcal U=\prod_{sa}\mathcal U_{sa}\)) without approximation/regularization.

This paper does not provide such a convex program. Its main technical development concerns a different objective: a “soft” robust MDP where the adversary is regularized/penalized via \(D\) (e.g., KL), which the open problem explicitly excludes as an approximation scheme. While the authors note that choosing \(D\) as an indicator of a constraint set recovers the standard robust MDP, the paper’s equivalence and algorithms are developed primarily for the penalized formulation and for risk-sensitive Bellman equations, not for deriving an exact convex feasible set/LP/SOCP/SDP for the hard rectangular robust Bellman inequalities.

Nevertheless, the Fenchel-duality viewpoint (risk measure \(\leftrightarrow\) penalty) is a potentially relevant tool: it rewrites inner minimizations over transition kernels as conjugates of convex functionals, which could inspire convex-analytic reformulations in special cases (e.g., KL/\(\phi\)-divergence balls) but does not resolve the general exact-convex-formulation question posed in the original paper.

sources.title: Revisiting the static model in robust reinforcement learning
sources.source_url: N/A (not provided in citation analysis block)
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes the IWOCS meta-algorithm for robust RL under transition uncertainty. Using (i) the equivalence between static and dynamic adversaries for stationary policies under sa-rectangular uncertainty (Iyengar, 2005, Lemma 3.3) and (ii) a saddle-point/no-duality-gap condition (Wiesemann et al., 2013), it motivates solving 
\[\max_{\pi}\min_{T\in\mathcal T} V_T^\pi(s_0)=\min_{T\in\mathcal T} V_T^\*(s_0)\]
by iteratively: (a) solving standard (non-robust) MDPs for a growing finite set \(\mathcal T_i\subset\mathcal T\), (b) defining \(Q_i(s,a)=\min_{T\in\mathcal T_i} Q_T^\*(s,a)\), and (c) selecting a new worst-case model \(T_{i+1}\in\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T} V_T^{\pi_i}(s_0)\). It establishes monotonicity and bounds: 
- \(Q_i(s,a)\ge Q^*_{\tilde{\mathcal T}_i}(s,a)\ge Q^*_{\mathcal T}(s,a)\) where \(\tilde{\mathcal T}_i\) is the sa-rectangular hull of \(\mathcal T_i\).
- \(Q_{i+1}(s,a)\le Q_i(s,a)\) for all \(s,a\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an exact, polynomial-size convex optimization reformulation (e.g., conic/geometric) that encodes the optimal robust stationary policy/value for discounted RMDPs under rectangular uncertainty, without approximation/regularization. This paper does not provide any convex program for the robust Bellman inequalities or the max–min objective. Instead it develops an algorithmic heuristic (IWOCS) that reduces robust optimization to repeated solutions of nominal MDPs plus a worst-case model search (black-box CMA-ES in continuous domains, brute force in a toy discrete example). The method is not an exact convex reformulation; it offers no guarantee of reaching the true robust optimum in general (the authors explicitly note convergence is not necessarily to \(Q^*_{\mathcal T}\)). Thus it does not solve the convex-formulation open problem, but is tangentially related as an alternative computational approach to robust RMDPs and highlights duality/saddle-point structure used in convex-analytic treatments.

title: Equivalence between discount-to-one limit and average optimality in risk-averse MDPs
background_latex:
Consider a discrete-time controlled Markov process with state space \(X\) and action space \(A\), with (possibly randomized) Markov policies \(p=(\pi_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\), where each \(\pi_t(x)\) is a probability measure on \(A\) supported on an admissible set \(A_t(x)\subseteq A\). Let \(P(t,x,a,\cdot)\) be a transition kernel on \(X\), and let \(C_t(x,a,x')\in\mathbb{R}\) be a bounded one-step cost. 

Fix a discount factor \(\gamma\in(0,1)\). A (time- and state-dependent) law-invariant convex risk measure at the distributional level is a functional \(\sigma_{t,x}\) mapping the law \(\mu\) of a bounded real random variable to a value in \(( -\infty,\infty]\), satisfying (i) translation invariance \(\sigma_{t,x}(\mu*\delta_c)=\sigma_{t,x}(\mu)+c\), (ii) monotonicity with respect to first-order stochastic dominance, and (iii) convexity with respect to mixtures (as formalized on probability measures). A dynamic risk measure (DRM) \(\varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C)\) is constructed by nesting/composing the one-step risk mappings \(\sigma_{t,X_t}\) applied to regular conditional distributions of future (discounted) cost streams under a controlled process \((X,A)\).

For each \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), define the infinite-horizon discounted risk-averse performance criterion (value) under an admissible policy (or controlled process) as \(\varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C)\). In classical risk-neutral MDPs with finite state/action spaces, the scaled limit \((1-\gamma)\, \mathbb{E}[\sum_{t\ge 0} \gamma^t C_t]\) as \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) coincides with the optimal long-run average cost under suitable conditions; the paper highlights that an analogous statement for the present risk-averse DRM framework is not established.
problem_definition_latex:
Establish conditions under which the discount-to-one limit of the discounted infinite-horizon distributional dynamic risk measure recovers an average-optimality criterion. Concretely, analyze whether there is an average-cost (or average-risk) optimality notion \(\mathrm{Avg}(C)\) for the risk-averse MDP such that, for appropriate scaling and under suitable assumptions,
\[
\lim_{\gamma\uparrow 1}\, (1-\gamma)\, \inf_{(X,A)\in\Psi}\, \varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C) 
\quad\text{equals}\quad
\inf_{\text{admissible policies}}\, \mathrm{Avg}(C),
\]
or otherwise characterize the limit \(\lim_{\gamma\uparrow 1} \varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C)\) (possibly after scaling) and its relationship to an average optimality objective in this risk-averse setting.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Cheng–Jaimungal) constructs discounted infinite-horizon distributional DRMs \(\varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C)\) by nesting state-dependent law-invariant convex risk measures \(\sigma_{t,x}\) applied to regular conditional laws of \(C_t+\gamma\,\text{future}\). Under weak continuity of the transition kernel and lower semicontinuity/Fatou-type regularity of \(\sigma_{t,x}\), it establishes finite- and infinite-horizon DPPs and existence of optimal Markov policies for each fixed \(\gamma<1\). It also explicitly highlights that, unlike the risk-neutral case, an Abelian/Tauberian link between the \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) discounted problem (possibly scaled by \(1-\gamma\)) and an average-cost/average-risk criterion is not known in this nonlinear, time-consistent risk setting.

Prior work by Ruszczyński provides the canonical recursive risk-averse dynamic programming framework via risk transition mappings, while Bäuerle–Glauner develop related discounted DPP theory for recursive risk measures and conditions for deterministic optimal actions. These works clarify that time consistency alone yields a Bellman recursion but does not supply the linear structure used in classical proofs of discount-to-average equivalence (e.g., additive Poisson equations and affine contraction arguments). On the average-criterion side, Shen–Stannat–Obermayer treat risk-sensitive Markov control processes including average dynamic risk measures under strong regularity (e.g., strong Feller-type) assumptions, thereby offering candidate definitions of \(\mathrm{Avg}(C)\) in a time-consistent risk-averse framework; however, they do not prove that \((1-\gamma)\inf\varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}(C)\) converges to that average criterion as \(\gamma\uparrow 1\), nor do they address the distributional/state-dependent \(\sigma_{t,x}\) formulation.

Recent forward citations focus on robust/time-consistent recursion and finite-horizon robust RL with nested distortion risks; they provide tools for recursion and worst-case quantile calculations but do not engage with infinite-horizon \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) asymptotics. Overall, the discount-to-one versus average-risk equivalence remains open for the distributional DRM setting. Promising directions include: (i) imposing stationarity and ergodicity/unichain conditions plus additional structure on \(\sigma\) (e.g., coherent/spectral forms admitting dual representations) to derive an additive eigenvalue problem \(h+\lambda=\mathcal{T}h\) for a nonlinear Bellman operator \(\mathcal{T}\); (ii) developing nonlinear Tauberian theorems for nested risk operators, possibly via subadditivity/positive homogeneity and span seminorm contractions; and (iii) identifying counterexamples where nonlinearity breaks the Abelian limit, to delineate the sharp assumptions needed.

sources.title: Uncertainty propagation and dynamic robust risk measures
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops a finite-horizon framework of dynamic uncertainty sets \(u=\{u_t\}\) and associated dynamic robust risk measures \(R^{u,\rho}\) defined by one-step robustification \(R^{u,\rho}_{t,s}(X_{t+1:s})=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}\{\rho_t(Y):Y\in u_{t+1}(X_{t+1:s})\}\). Its main structural theorem (Theorem 5) gives a recursive representation: \(R\) is weak recursive iff there exists a static uncertainty set \(u^{\varsigma}\) such that for all \(t\),
\[R_{t,T}(X_{t+1:T})=R^{u^{\varsigma}}_t\bigl(Y_{t+1}+R^{u^{\varsigma}}_{t+1}(Y_{t+2}+\cdots+R^{u^{\varsigma}}_{T-1}(Y_T)\cdots)\bigr),\]
with \(Y_t=X_t-R^{u^{\varsigma}}_t(0)\); and if additionally normalised then this yields strong time-consistency (a robust analogue of the Cheridito–Delbaen–Kupper recursion).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) (discount-to-one) limit of infinite-horizon discounted, distributional, law-invariant convex dynamic risk measures in risk-averse MDPs and its relationship to an average-cost/average-risk criterion. This citing paper is finite-horizon and focuses on axiomatic/time-consistency and recursive representations of robust dynamic risk measures built from uncertainty sets; it does not study Markov decision processes, stationary control, infinite-horizon limits, or any Abelian/Tauberian link between discounted and average criteria. At most, its recursion/time-consistency results could be used as technical tools when defining well-posed dynamic risk criteria under model uncertainty, but it provides no results about \((1-\gamma)\varsigma^{X,\gamma}_{0,\infty}\) as \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) or average optimality.

sources.title: Robust reinforcement learning with dynamic distortion risk measures
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops a finite-horizon (
0T<\infty\)) robust risk-aware RL framework for strongly time-consistent dynamic risk measures built by nesting one-step conditional robust distortion risk measures. Key technical results include explicit characterizations of the worst-case conditional quantile in a conditional 2-Wasserstein ball: for uncertainty set \(\{Z^\varphi: \|\breve F_t-\breve F_{\varphi,t}\|_2\le \epsilon_s\}\), \(\breve F^*_{\varphi,t}(\cdot\mid s,a)=\big(\breve F_{\theta,t}(\cdot\mid s,a)+\gamma_s(\cdot)/(2\lambda^*)\big)^{\uparrow}\) with \(\|\breve F^*_{\varphi,t}-\breve F_{\theta,t}\|_2=\epsilon_s\) (Thm 3.2); and with additional moment constraints (Eq. (2.2b)) an explicit affine-in-\(\breve F_{\theta,t}\) formula for \(\breve F^*_{\varphi,t}\) (Thm 3.5), plus a deterministic policy-gradient formula for the resulting robust dynamic objective (Thm 3.6).
sources.connection: The open problem concerns the \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) discount-to-one limit and its equivalence (after scaling) to an average-cost/average-risk criterion for infinite-horizon risk-averse MDPs under distributional dynamic risk measures. This citing paper does not study infinite-horizon discounted criteria, does not analyze \(\gamma\uparrow 1\) limits, and does not define or relate to an average-risk optimality notion. Its \(\gamma\) denotes a distortion function (not the discount factor), and the setting is episodic finite-horizon RL with nested one-step conditional (robust) distortion risk measures. Thus it does not resolve the discount-to-average equivalence question; at most it provides related methodology (quantile/Wasserstein robustification, time-consistent nesting) that could be ingredients in a future average-risk analysis.

title: Largest achievable domination factor for feasible self-maximizing polynomial-time shares under additivity
background_latex:
Consider fair division of a finite set of indivisible goods \(M\) among \(n\ge 2\) equally entitled agents, with no monetary transfers. Each agent has an additive valuation \(v:2^M\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), meaning there are item values \(v(j)\ge 0\) for \(j\in M\) and \(v(S)=\sum_{j\in S} v(j)\) for all \(S\subseteq M\). An allocation is a partition \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)\) of \(M\) into \(n\) (possibly empty) disjoint bundles.

A (fairness) share is a function \(s\) mapping a valuation \(v\) and an agent count \(n\) to a nonnegative value \(s(v,n)\). A share \(s\) is feasible (for additive valuations) if for every instance \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\) of additive valuations there exists an allocation \(A\) such that \(v_i(A_i)\ge s(v_i,n)\) for all agents \(i\).

Given a share \(s\), define its (worst acceptable-bundle) guarantee \(\hat s(v,n)\) as the minimum value (under \(v\)) among bundles whose value is at least \(s(v,n)\):
\[\hat s(v,n)=\min\{v(S): S\subseteq M,\ v(S)\ge s(v,n)\}.\]
For a true valuation \(v\) and a reported valuation \(v'\), define the implied guarantee
\[\hat s_v(v') = \min\{v(S): S\subseteq M,\ v'(S)\ge s(v',n)\}.\]
The share \(s\) is self-maximizing if truthful reporting maximizes the implied guarantee for every additive \(v\): \(\hat s_v(v)\ge \hat s_v(v')\) for all reports \(v'\).

The maximin share (MMS) for additive \(v\) and \(n\) agents is
\[\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)=\max_{(B_1,\dots,B_n)\text{ partition of }M}\ \min_{j\in[n]} v(B_j).\]
A share \(s\) is \(\rho\)-dominating (for a fixed \(n\), or uniformly over \(n\)) if it guarantees at least a \(\rho\) fraction of the MMS pointwise:
\[ s(v,n)\ \ge\ \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\qquad \text{for all additive } v.\]
(Equivalently, it \(\rho\)-dominates every feasible share, since \(\mathrm{MMS}\) dominates all feasible shares when defined on a fixed \((M,n)\).)

Consider fair division of a finite set of indivisible goods \(M\) among \(n\ge 2\) equally entitled agents, with no monetary transfers. An allocation is a partition \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)\) of \(M\) into \(n\) (possibly empty) disjoint bundles.

A (fairness) share is a function \(s\) mapping a valuation \(v\) and an agent count \(n\) to a nonnegative value \(s(v,n)\). A share \(s\) is feasible (for additive valuations) if for every instance \((v_1,\dots,v_n)\) of additive valuations there exists an allocation \(A\) such that \(v_i(A_i)\ge s(v_i,n)\) for all agents \(i\).

\[\hat s(v,n)=\min\{v(S): S\subseteq M,\ v(S)\ge s(v,n)\}.\]

\[\hat s_v(v') = \min\{v(S): S\subseteq M,\ v'(S)\ge s(v',n)\}.\]

literature_review.synthesis:
The Babaioff--Feige open problem asks for the largest uniform \(\rho^*\) such that there exists a share function \(s(v,n)\) for additive valuations that is simultaneously feasible (there is always an allocation meeting all agents' shares), self-maximizing in the implied-guarantee sense \(\hat s_v(v)\ge \hat s_v(v')\), polynomial-time computable, and pointwise \(\rho\)-dominating the maximin share \(\mathrm{MMS}_n\). In the source paper, Babaioff and Feige introduce the share/contract viewpoint, prove that exact SM-domination is impossible for any class containing additive valuations (via picking-order shares and MMS infeasibility), and then give explicit positive constructions: ordinal maximin shares (self-maximizing by design) and the nested shares \(\mathrm{NS}_{n,3}\), which are feasible, polynomial-time computable, and guarantee \(\frac{2n}{3n-1}\)-MMS for all \(n\), improving to \(4/5\)-MMS for \(n\le 4\); for \(n=2\) they give a PTAS achieving \((1-\varepsilon)\)-MMS.

Subsequent work in the forward-citation set does not determine \(\rho^*\) in this exact framework. Several papers explore adjacent notions of feasible shares: quantile shares and thinned quantile shares establish constant-quantile feasibility (even universal feasibility for all monotone valuations after thinning), and these benchmarks are also (informally) self-maximizing and efficiently approximable by sampling. However, these works do not provide pointwise lower bounds of the form \(s(v,n)\ge \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\) for all additive \(v\), so they do not improve the best known \(\rho\) under the MMS-domination requirement.

On the incentives side, work on truthful(-in-expectation) mechanisms and on characterizations of deterministic truthful mechanisms highlights strong constraints when one insists on dominant-strategy truthfulness of allocation rules; these results yield poor MMS approximations for broad classes of truthful mechanisms. While conceptually related, they do not translate directly to the implied-guarantee self-maximization condition for shares. Overall, the state of the art remains that constant \(\rho\) is achievable (at least \(\approx 2/3\) uniformly in \(n\) via nested shares, and \(4/5\) for \(n\le 4\)), but the optimal uniform \(\rho^*\) for feasible, self-maximizing, polynomial-time shares that dominate \(\mathrm{MMS}_n\) for additive valuations remains open.

sources.title: Fair division via quantile shares
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces the q-quantile share \(\tau_q(v,n)\), defined as the \(q\)-quantile of \(v(X)\) where \(X\) is the random bundle obtained by assigning each item independently to an agent with probability \(1/n\). It proves feasibility results for this share notion: - (Conditional) If a special case of the Rainbow Erd\H{o}s Matching Conjecture holds, then the \(1/(2e)\)-quantile share is universally feasible for all monotone valuations (Theorem 2). - (Unconditional) For additive valuations, the \(q\)-quantile share is feasible for \(q<0.14/e\) asymptotically (Proposition 4). - For unit-demand and matroid-rank valuations, feasibility holds up to \(q\approx 1/e\) (Propositions 5–6), and \(q>1/e\) is infeasible for large \(n\) (via Proposition 3).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the largest \(\rho^*\) such that there exists a share \(s\) that is simultaneously (i) feasible for additive valuations, (ii) self-maximizing in the Babaioff–Feige sense (truthful report maximizes the implied worst acceptable-bundle guarantee \(\hat s_v\)), (iii) polynomial-time computable, and (iv) \(\rho\)-dominates MMS pointwise: \(s(v,n)\ge \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\) for all additive \(v\), uniformly over \(n\).

This paper studies a different share family (quantile shares) and establishes feasibility/universal-feasibility thresholds for \(\tau_q\). It notes that quantile shares are self-maximizing (in an informal sense) and efficiently approximable by sampling, but it does not analyze domination relative to MMS, nor does it optimize \(\rho\) in \(s(v,n)\ge \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\). In fact, quantile shares are not designed to approximate MMS and can be either more or less demanding than MMS fractions depending on the instance (Example 2). Therefore it does not resolve \(\rho^*\) and does not provide a candidate share with a proven constant \(\rho\)-MMS domination guarantee under the self-maximizing + feasibility + polytime constraints.

sources.title: Thinned Quantile Shares are Universally Feasible
sources.theorem_or_result:
Main results (for general monotone valuations):
- There exists a universal constant \(c>0\) such that the \(c\)-thinned \(e^{-c}\)-quantile share \(\tau^{(c)}_{e^{-c}}(v,n)\) is universally feasible (Theorem 1.5 / Theorem 4.2).
- Assuming the rainbow Erdős matching conjecture, the (unthinned) \((1/e)\)-quantile share is universally feasible (Theorem 1.7), and for any \(c\in(0,1]\) the \(c\)-thinned \(q\)-quantile share can be infeasible for any \(q>e^{-c}\) (Proposition 1.8).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the largest \(\rho^*\) such that there exists a share \(s\) for additive valuations that is simultaneously (i) feasible, (ii) self-maximizing in the Babaioff–Feige sense, (iii) polynomial-time computable, and (iv) \(\rho\)-dominates \(\mathrm{MMS}_n\) pointwise.

This paper studies a different share family (quantile shares and their \(c\)-thinned variant) and proves strong feasibility results—indeed universal feasibility for all monotone valuations—for \(\tau^{(c)}_{e^{-c}}\). Quantile shares are known to be self-maximizing (and the paper states this extends to thinned quantile shares), and they are Monte-Carlo approximable.

However, the paper does not analyze domination of \(\mathrm{MMS}\) for additive valuations, nor does it optimize or even provide a constant \(\rho\) such that \(\tau^{(c)}_{e^{-c}}(v,n)\ge \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\) for all additive \(v\). In fact, since Babichenko et al. show no constant fraction of MMS is universally feasible over all monotone valuations, these universally feasible quantile-type shares cannot \(\rho\)-dominate MMS uniformly over all monotone valuations; the open problem is restricted to additive valuations, but this paper does not bridge that gap.

Thus, the connection is mainly methodological/background: it provides a new universally feasible, self-maximizing benchmark share (thinned quantile share) and extremal-set-theory tools, but it does not resolve \(\rho^*\) for additive valuations under the additional MMS-domination requirement.

sources.title: Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanisms for MMS Approximation
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper designs polynomial-time randomized allocation mechanisms for strategic agents with additive valuations that are truthful-in-expectation (TIE) and guarantee ex-post approximations to MMS (and TPS). Main stated guarantees include: - For general n, an ordinal TIE distributional mechanism that is ex-ante proportional and guarantees each agent at least \(\frac{1}{H_{n-1}+2}\)-MMS ex-post (Theorem 1). - With small additional cardinal information and relaxing incentives to \((1-\varepsilon(n))\)-TIE (negligible \(\varepsilon(n)=n^{-\log n}\)), an ex-ante proportional mechanism guaranteeing \(\Omega(1/\log\log n)\)-MMS ex-post (Theorem 2). - For \(n=2\), a TIE distributional mechanism that is ex-ante proportional and \(\frac{2}{3}\)-MMS ex-post (Theorem 3).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the largest domination factor \(\rho^*\) achievable by a share function \(s(v,n)\) that is (i) feasible for all additive instances, (ii) self-maximizing in the sense that truthful reporting maximizes the implied guarantee \(\hat s_v(\cdot)\), (iii) polynomial-time computable, and (iv) pointwise \(\rho\)-dominating MMS: \(s(v,n)\ge \rho\,\mathrm{MMS}_n(v)\) for all additive \(v\), uniformly over \(n\).
This paper does not study shares \(s(v,n)\) with the feasibility/self-maximizing definition from Babaioff–Feige ("Fair Shares"). Instead it studies TIE mechanisms (randomized allocation rules) that approximate MMS/TPS ex-post. TIE is an incentive notion about expected utility, not the paper’s self-maximizing share notion based on worst acceptable bundles \(\hat s\). Likewise, the paper’s guarantees are about existence of a mechanism producing allocations with ex-post MMS approximation, not about a per-agent share function \(s(v,n)\) that is always simultaneously feasible across all agents’ shares.
Nevertheless, the paper is partially relevant: it provides new incentive-compatible (in expectation) constructions and impossibility insights around truthful fair division without payments, and it highlights computable benchmarks (TPS) and approximation factors (e.g., \(1/(H_{n-1}+2)\), \(\Omega(1/\log\log n)\), \(2/3\) for \(n=2\)) that could inform upper/lower bounds for \(\rho^*\) if one attempts to relate self-maximizing shares to implementable truthful mechanisms. But it does not directly bound or determine \(\rho^*\) under the self-maximizing-share framework.

sources.title: Near-Optimal Best-of-Both-Worlds Fairness for Few Agents
sources.theorem_or_result:
For additive valuations with a fixed small number of agents, the paper gives Best-of-Both-Worlds (BoBW) randomized allocation algorithms/distributions with strong ex-ante proportionality/envy-freeness and strong ex-post guarantees. In particular:
- For 2 agents and any \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an FPTAS outputting a distribution over at most two allocations that is ex-ante envy-free (hence proportional), ex-post EFX, and in every realized allocation each agent gets at least \((1-\varepsilon)\,\mathrm{MMS}_2(v_i)\) (Theorem 1.2).
- For 3 agents, there exists an ex-ante proportional distribution supported on at most six allocations such that every realized allocation is EEFX and gives each agent at least \(\tfrac{9}{10}\,\mathrm{MMS}_3(v_i)\), and moreover is IMMX (each agent either gets her MMS or is EFX-satisfied) (Theorem 1.1). Polynomial-time variants via FPTAS achieve ex-ante proportionality with ex-post \((\tfrac{9}{10}-\varepsilon)\)-MMS (Theorem 5.1) or approximate ex-ante proportionality with EEFX retained (Theorem 3.2).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for the maximal domination factor \(\rho^*\) achievable by shares \(s(v,n)\) that are simultaneously (i) feasible for all additive instances, (ii) self-maximizing (truthful reporting maximizes the implied guarantee \(\hat s_v\)), and (iii) polynomial-time computable, while (iv) pointwise \(\rho\)-dominating MMS for all \(n\ge2\).

This paper does not study shares \(s(v,n)\) or the self-maximizing (incentive) constraint; instead it studies randomized allocation algorithms achieving ex-ante/ex-post fairness (BoBW) for \(n=2,3\). Its results are therefore not direct progress on determining \(\rho^*\) under self-maximization.

Indirectly, the paper strengthens what is achievable (algorithmically, and in some cases with FPTAS) in terms of ex-post MMS approximation factors for small \(n\) while also satisfying strong envy-based properties (EFX/EEFX). These constructions might inspire candidate shares or feasibility constructions, but they do not establish any \(\rho\)-dominating self-maximizing polynomial-time share uniformly over all \(n\), nor upper/lower bounds on \(\rho^*\).

sources.title: On Truthful Mechanisms without Pareto-efficiency: Characterizations and Fairness
sources.theorem_or_result: Main characterization (Theorem 1 / Application 1): For any permutations-closed class of strict preferences (or strict valuations) that contains all lexicographic preferences—hence in particular any class containing additive valuations—every deterministic mechanism that is strategy-proof (truthful), non-bossy, and neutral (even without Pareto-efficiency and even allowing disposal) must be a serial-quota mechanism (fixed agent order and fixed quotas; each agent in turn picks her quota-demand from remaining goods). Consequently, for additive valuations, any such truthful mechanism has very poor MMS approximation, at most \(1/\lfloor (m-n+2)/2\rfloor\) (Application 2, via known bounds for serial-quota mechanisms).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for the best domination factor \(\rho^*\) achievable by feasible, self-maximizing, polynomial-time computable shares relative to MMS under additivity. This paper does not study shares, feasibility of shares, or the self-maximizing condition \(\hat s_v(v)\ge \hat s_v(v')\). Instead it characterizes truthful (strategy-proof) allocation mechanisms under neutrality and non-bossiness, and derives impossibility/upper bounds on MMS approximation for such mechanisms. While conceptually related (both restrict incentives and compare to MMS), the incentive notion here (dominant-strategy truthfulness of mechanisms) is different from self-maximizing shares, so the paper does not resolve \(\rho^*\). It may provide techniques/negative intuition suggesting strong limits when incentives are imposed, but it does not translate directly to the share framework.

title: Characterize simultaneous ordered spectral decompositions needed for spectral-function critical cones
background_latex:
Let \(\mathbb{S}^n\) be the space of real \(n\times n\) symmetric matrices. For \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n\), let \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) denote the vector of eigenvalues sorted in nonincreasing order. Write an eigen-decomposition \(X=U\,\mathrm{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^\top\) with \(U\in O_n\). Let \(\mu_1>\cdots>\mu_r\) be the distinct eigenvalues of \(X\), and define index blocks
\[\alpha_m:=\{i\in\{1,\dots,n\}:\lambda_i(X)=\mu_m\},\qquad m=1,\dots,r,\]
so \(\{1,\dots,n\}=\bigcup_{m=1}^r \alpha_m\) is a partition.

A spectral function is a function \(g:\mathbb{S}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) of the form \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\), where \(\theta:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is symmetric (permutation-invariant). Assume \(g\) is convex and lower semicontinuous, and let \(Y\in\partial g(X)\) be a (convex-analytic) subgradient. A known characterization (for convex spectral functions) implies there exists an orthogonal matrix \(U\in O_n(X)\cap O_n(Y)\) such that
\[X=U\,\mathrm{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^\top,\qquad Y=U\,\mathrm{Diag}(\lambda(Y))U^\top,\qquad \lambda(Y)\in\partial\theta(\lambda(X)).\]
For each block \(\alpha_m\), define the corresponding principal submatrices
\[\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}:=\big(\mathrm{Diag}(\lambda(Y))\big)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\in\mathbb{S}^{|\alpha_m|},\qquad H_{m}:=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\in\mathbb{S}^{|\alpha_m|},\]
where \(H\in\mathbb{S}^n\) is a direction and \(U_{\alpha_m}\) denotes the submatrix of \(U\) with columns indexed by \(\alpha_m\).

Two symmetric matrices \(A,B\in\mathbb{S}^k\) are said to have a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition if there exists \(Q\in O_k\) such that \(Q^\top A Q\) and \(Q^\top B Q\) are both diagonal with diagonal entries sorted in nonincreasing order (equivalently, they are simultaneously diagonalizable in a way compatible with the eigenvalue orderings).

Give necessary and sufficient conditions (checkable from spectral data and/or algebraic relations) ensuring that, for a given convex spectral function \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\), a point \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n\), a subgradient \(Y\in\partial g(X)\), and a direction \(H\in\mathbb{S}^n\), the following property holds:

For every block \(m=1,\dots,r\) associated with the distinct eigenvalues of \(X\), the pair of matrices \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\in\mathbb{S}^{|\alpha_m|}\) and \(H_m=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\in\mathbb{S}^{|\alpha_m|}\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Mohammadi–Sarabi (2024), the ordered simultaneous diagonalization condition appears as the key remaining structural ingredient in the critical-cone description for convex spectral functions \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\). Specifically, Proposition 5.4 shows that \(H\in K_g(X,Y)\) is equivalent to (i) the reduced-space condition \(\lambda'(X;H)\in K_\theta(\lambda(X),\lambda(Y))\) and (ii) for each multiplicity block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the pair \((\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m},\,U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m})\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. The paper explicitly notes that giving intrinsic, checkable necessary-and-sufficient conditions for this blockwise ordered simultaneous decomposition is open, and it is precisely this gap that the present problem asks to fill.

Forward-citing work largely treats the ordered simultaneous decomposition requirement as a black-box condition embedded in critical-cone or second-order formulas. The paper “Characterizations of tilt-stable local minimizers of a class of matrix optimization problems” uses the same blockwise ordered simultaneous diagonalization condition to characterize critical directions for polyhedral \(\theta\), and derives concrete block-structure consequences by refining each \(\alpha_m\) according to equal eigenvalues of \(Y\) within the block. “Twice Epi-Differentiability of Spectral Functions and its applications” extends the same critical-cone characterization beyond convexity, again with the ordered simultaneous decomposition as the decisive extra condition. In the singular-value analogue, “Twice epi-differentiability of orthogonally invariant matrix functions and application” provides an iff critical-cone characterization featuring blockwise simultaneous ordered spectral decompositions, typically tied to equality cases in Fan/von Neumann trace inequalities; this strongly suggests that the eigenvalue-only case should admit a similarly checkable characterization, but an explicit standalone criterion for the symmetric-eigenvalue blocks is not provided in the forward-citation summaries.

Overall, the state of the art indicates the problem remains open: existing papers identify where the ordered simultaneous decomposition is needed (critical cones, second subderivatives, tilt stability) and sometimes translate it into block-structural consequences once such a decomposition exists, but none supplies a complete intrinsic characterization (purely in terms of spectral data and algebraic relations of \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m\)) guaranteeing the existence of an ordered common eigenbasis on each \(\alpha_m\). Promising directions include exploiting equality characterizations in Fan’s inequality \(\langle A,B\rangle\le \langle \lambda(A),\lambda(B)\rangle\) on each block, commutator-based criteria for simultaneous diagonalizability (augmented with order-compatibility constraints when eigenvalues repeat), and refining the block partitions induced by ties in \(\lambda(Y)\) to reduce the ordered condition to diagonalizability within smaller invariant subspaces.

sources.title: Characterizations of tilt-stable local minimizers of a class of matrix optimization problems
sources.theorem_or_result:
For convex polyhedral spectral functions of the form \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\) on \(\mathbb S^n\) with \(\theta\) symmetric polyhedral, and for \((X,Y)\in\mathrm{gph}\,\partial g\) satisfying a nonemptiness condition \(K(X,Y)\neq\emptyset\), the paper proves (Remark 4.10(ii) citing/using [30, Prop. 5.4]) that a direction \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) lies in the critical cone \(C_g(X,Y)\) if and only if:
- \(\lambda'(X;H)\in C_\theta(\lambda(X),\lambda(Y))\), and
- for each eigenvalue block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the pair \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(P_{\alpha_m}^\top H P_{\alpha_m}\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition.
In addition, under \(K(X,Y)\neq\emptyset\) it computes a minimal quadratic bundle element
\[q(H)=\Upsilon_{X,Y}(H)+\delta_{\mathrm{aff}\,C_g(X,Y)}(H),\]
where \(\Upsilon_{X,Y}(H)=2\sum_{1\le l<l'\le r}\sum_{i\in\alpha_l,\,j\in\alpha_{l'}}\frac{\lambda_i(Y)-\lambda_j(Y)}{\lambda_i(X)-\lambda_j(X)}(P^\top H P)_{ij}^2\).

The open problem asks for necessary and sufficient, checkable conditions ensuring that for each eigenvalue block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the matrices \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\) admit a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition.

This citing paper does not give a standalone algebraic characterization of simultaneous ordered diagonalizability for arbitrary \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m\). However, it directly uses and highlights an equivalence from the cited work [30] (Parabolic Regularity of Spectral Functions): membership \(H\in C_g(X,Y)\) is equivalent to (i) a condition on \(\lambda'(X;H)\) and (ii) exactly the blockwise simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition property in the open problem (Remark 4.10(ii)). It further reformulates (ii) into an explicit block-structure condition (Remark 4.10(ii)') in terms of the partition \(\gamma_s^l\) induced by equal eigenvalues of \(Y\) within each \(\alpha_l\), i.e., \(P_{\alpha_l}^\top H P_{\alpha_l}\) must be block diagonal along the \(\gamma\)-partition and each block can be orthogonally diagonalized with eigenvalues ordered compatibly across blocks.

Thus the paper provides partial progress: it embeds the desired simultaneous ordered decomposition condition into a full critical-cone characterization for polyhedral spectral functions and gives concrete structural consequences, but it does not fully answer the open problem’s request for intrinsic necessary-and-sufficient conditions purely in terms of spectral/algebraic relations for the pair \((\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m},H_m)\) in complete generality (e.g., without reference to critical cones / \(\theta\)-data, and for general convex spectral functions beyond polyhedral \(\theta\)).

sources.title: Twice epi-differentiability of orthogonally invariant matrix functions and application
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper develops second-order variational analysis for convex orthogonally invariant matrix functions \(F=f\circ\sigma\) (singular-value functions). A key result directly tied to the open problem is Proposition 5.2: for \(Y\in\partial(f\circ\sigma)(X)\), a direction \(H\) lies in the critical cone \(K_{f\circ\sigma}(X,Y)\) iff \(\sigma'(X;H)\in K_f(\sigma(X),\sigma(Y))\) and, for each nonzero singular-value block \(\alpha_i\), the pair \(\Sigma(Y)_{\alpha_i\alpha_i}\) and \(\tfrac12(U_{\alpha_i}^\top H V_{\alpha_i}+V_{\alpha_i}^\top H^\top U_{\alpha_i})\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition, while on the zero block \(\beta\) the pair \(\Sigma(Y)_{\beta\hat\beta}\) and \(U_{\hat\beta}^\top H V_{\beta}\) admits a simultaneous ordered singular value decomposition. The paper also gives exact formulas for second subderivatives under parabolic regularity assumptions (Theorem 5.6) and twice epi-differentiability for the nuclear norm (Corollary 3.6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for necessary and sufficient, checkable conditions ensuring that for each eigenvalue-multiplicity block \(\alpha_m\) of a symmetric matrix \(X\), the pair \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m\) has a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. This paper provides such a condition (via Fan’s inequality equality characterization) but in the singular-value/orthogonally invariant setting: Proposition 5.2 characterizes exactly when the required blockwise simultaneous ordered spectral decompositions occur (they are part of the iff description of the critical cone). Although stated for \(f\circ\sigma\) and blocks of equal singular values, the mechanism is the same as in the symmetric spectral-function case \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\): equality cases in Fan/von Neumann inequalities force simultaneous ordered diagonalizations on multiplicity blocks. Thus it gives a concrete necessary-and-sufficient criterion (commonly checkable as equality in the relevant trace inequality, equivalently existence of a common ordered eigenbasis) for the blockwise property—covering the analogous condition needed in spectral-function critical cones, but not explicitly specialized/proved for the eigenvalue-only (\(\lambda\)) framework in full generality.

sources.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability of Spectral Functions and its applications
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves a critical-cone characterization for (possibly nonconvex) spectral functions and uses it to derive a second-order theory. In particular (Proposition 3.2): under mild regularity (e.g. subdifferential regularity of \(g\) or local Lipschitzness of \(\theta\) with \(Y\in\partial \hat g(X)\)), \(H\in C_g(X,Y)\) iff \(\lambda'(X;H)\in C_\theta(\lambda(X),v)\) and, for each eigenvalue block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the pair \(\mathrm{Diag}(y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition (for \(Y=U\mathrm{Diag}(y)U^\top\)).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for necessary and sufficient, checkable conditions ensuring that for each multiplicity block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the matrices \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\) admit a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. However, it elevates exactly this property to a necessary-and-sufficient condition for membership in the spectral-function critical cone \(C_g(X,Y)\) (Proposition 3.2), extending prior convex results. sources.title: Smoothness of subgradient mappings and its applications in parametric optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: For reliably \(C^2\)-decomposable functions \(g\) (a class including many spectral/eigenvalue functions), strict proto-differentiability of the subgradient mapping is characterized by a relative-interior condition: for \((\bar u,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial g\), \(\partial g\) is strictly proto-differentiable near \((\bar u,\bar y)\) (equivalently, \(g\) is strictly twice epi-differentiable near \((\bar u,\bar y)\)) iff \(\bar y\in\operatorname{ri}\partial g(\bar u)\) (Theorem 5.8). As a concrete spectral-cone instance, for \((X,Y)\in\operatorname{gph}N_{\mathbb S_+^n}\), \(N_{\mathbb S_+^n}\) is strictly proto-differentiable near \((X,Y)\) iff \(Y\in\operatorname{ri}N_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}X+\operatorname{rank}Y=n\) (Corollary 5.10).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for necessary/sufficient conditions ensuring that, on each eigenvalue-multiplicity block \(\alpha_m\) of \(X\), the pair \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) and \(H_m\) admits a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. sources.title: Twice epi-differentiablity and parabolic regularity of a class of non-amenable functions
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops second-order variational analysis (parabolic epi-differentiability, twice epi-differentiability, and parabolic regularity) for composite functions of the form \(f(x)=\vartheta(F(x))\) where \(\vartheta\) is piecewise twice differentiable (PWTD) and \(F\) is parabolically semidifferentiable. Under MSQC and parabolic regularity, it proves proper twice epi-differentiability with formula
\[
 d^2 f(x\mid v)(w)=\begin{cases}
 \min_{z}\{d^2 f(x)(w\mid z)-\langle v,z\rangle\} & w\in C_f(x,v),\\
 \infty & \text{otherwise},
 \end{cases}
\]
and provides sufficient conditions (Theorem 5.1) ensuring parabolic regularity via upper/lower estimates of second subderivatives.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for necessary and sufficient conditions guaranteeing, within each eigenvalue-multiplicity block \(\alpha_m\) of a symmetric matrix \(X\), that the diagonal block \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) (from a subgradient \(Y\in\partial g(X)\)) and the rotated direction block \(H_m=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\) admit a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. This paper does not address that simultaneous ordered diagonalization question directly. However, it is closely related in spirit: it studies parabolic regularity and twice epi-differentiability for non-amenable composites, and it explicitly treats a spectral example (type IV: \(F(X)=\lambda_{\max}(X)\), \(\vartheta=\delta_{\mathbb R_-}\)) and cites work on parabolic regularity of spectral functions. The techniques (parabolic semidifferentiability, second-order tangent/critical cone analysis, and conditions ensuring parabolic regularity) are tools that could be applied to spectral functions \(g=\theta\circ\lambda\), where the need for simultaneous ordered spectral decompositions arises when analyzing second-order objects on eigenvalue-multiplicity blocks.

sources.title: Variational Analysis in Spectral Decomposition Systems
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops an abstract framework of “spectral decomposition systems” \(\mathfrak S=(X,S,\gamma,(\Lambda_a)_{a\in A})\) and proves transfer formulas for generalized normals/subdifferentials of spectral sets/functions. In particular, for an \(S\)-invariant \(\varphi:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(X\in\mathcal H\), it shows
\[\partial^\#(\varphi\circ\gamma)(X)=\{\Lambda_a y: y\in\partial^\#\varphi(\gamma(X)),\ a\in A_X\},\]
for \(\#\in\{F,L\}\) (Theorem 4.1), and gives a Clarke-subdifferential representation (Proposition 4.11) plus a generalized Lidskii-type majorization theorem (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for necessary and sufficient conditions ensuring that, for each repeated-eigenvalue block \(\alpha_m\) of a symmetric matrix \(X\), the pair \(\Lambda(Y)_{\alpha_m\alpha_m}\) (a diagonal matrix of subgradient eigenvalues restricted to the block) and \(H_m=U_{\alpha_m}^\top H U_{\alpha_m}\) admit a simultaneous ordered spectral decomposition. However, it is tangentially relevant as it provides general variational-analysis transfer principles for spectral functions/sets (Fréchet/limiting/Clarke subdifferentials, commutation principles) in a unified framework that includes the symmetric-eigenvalue setting. These tools could be used in future work to re-derive first-order objects appearing in critical-cone descriptions, but they do not resolve the specific ordering/simultaneous-decomposition characterization requested.

title: Enumerate minimal balanced collections on n players in cooperative games
background_latex:
Let \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\). A (transferable-utility) cooperative game is a set function \(v:2^N\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(v(\emptyset)=0\).

A family \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq 2^N\setminus\{\emptyset\}\) of nonempty coalitions is called a balanced collection if there exist strictly positive weights \(\lambda_S>0\) for \(S\in\mathcal{B}\) such that each player is covered with total weight 1:
\[
\sum_{S\in\mathcal{B}:\ i\in S} \lambda_S = 1,\qquad \forall i\in N.
\]
A balanced collection \(\mathcal{B}\) is minimal if it contains no proper subcollection that is balanced. (Equivalently, \(\mathcal{B}\) is inclusion-minimal among balanced collections.)

Write \(\mathcal{B}^*(n)\) for the set of all minimal balanced collections on \(N\) excluding the trivial collection \(\{N\}\). It is known that \(\mathcal{B}^*(n)\) is finite and that any minimal balanced collection has cardinality at most \(n\).
problem_definition_latex: Given \(n\ge 1\), determine (exactly) the set \(\mathcal{B}^*(n)\) of all minimal balanced collections on \(N=\{1,\dots,n\}\), or at least determine \(|\mathcal{B}^*(n)|\) (the number of minimal balanced collections) as an explicit function of \(n\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The paper "On the set of balanced games" (Garcia-Segador–Grabisch–Miranda, 2025) frames minimal balanced collections \(\mathcal B^*(n)\) as the combinatorial objects indexing the facet-defining inequalities in the Bondareva–Shapley characterization of balanced games: for each \(\mathcal B\in\mathcal B^*(n)\) with unique positive balancing weights \((\lambda_S)_{S\in\mathcal B}\), balancedness is equivalent to \(\sum_{S\in\mathcal B}\lambda_S v(S)\le v(N)\). Thus, exact knowledge of \(\mathcal B^*(n)\) or even \(|\mathcal B^*(n)|\) would yield an explicit facet description of the balanced-games cone \(BG(n)\) and its normalized variants \(BG_\alpha(n)\), \(BG^+(n)\), and would directly support algorithmic tasks such as projection onto these polyhedra.

Among the forward-citing works provided, "On the closest balanced game" gives substantial partial progress on the counting aspect by proving sharp asymptotics for \(B_n:=|\mathcal B^*(n)|\). It shows \(B_n\sim 2^{n^2-n+1}/n!\) and that asymptotically almost all minimal balanced collections have maximal cardinality \(n\). Conceptually, this indicates that the facet structure of \(BG(n)\) is overwhelmingly governed (for large \(n\)) by minimal balanced collections of size \(n\), and it links their enumeration to counting certain invertible \(0/1\) matrices with positivity properties of the inverse applied to \(\mathbf 1\).

However, the original open problem asks for exact enumeration (or a closed-form exact formula for \(|\mathcal B^*(n)|\)), and no such exact classification or formula is supplied by the available forward citation. Therefore, based on the provided evidence, the problem remains open; the best progress recorded here is asymptotic enumeration and structural concentration on \(|\mathcal B|=n\) collections.

title: Construct natural valuation counterexamples to envy-free multi-divisions with long knives
background_latex:
A multi-layered cake consists of \(m\) layers, each identified with the unit interval \([0,1]\). A \emph{layered piece} is an \(m\)-tuple \(L=(L_\ell)_{\ell\in[m]}\) where each \(L_\ell\subseteq[0,1]\) is a (finite union of) disjoint closed subintervals in layer \(\ell\). A \emph{multi-division} into \(q\) pieces is a \(q\)-tuple \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_q)\) of layered pieces whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union covers the entire \(m\)-layered cake.

A layered piece \(L\) is \emph{contiguous} if each \(L_\ell\) is a single interval. It is \emph{non-overlapping} if for every two distinct layers \(\ell\neq \ell'\), the interiors of \(L_\ell\) and \(L_{\ell'}\) are disjoint as subsets of \([0,1]\) (equivalently, they intersect only on a finite set of points). A multi-division is \emph{feasible} if each \(A_j\) is non-overlapping, and it is \emph{contiguous} if each \(A_j\) is contiguous.

A common restricted class of feasible contiguous multi-divisions is given by \(q-1\) \emph{long knives}: one chooses cut positions \(0=t_0\le t_1\le\cdots\le t_{q-1}\le t_q=1\) and cuts \emph{every} layer at these positions, producing \(q\) intervals \([t_{r-1},t_r]\) in each layer. A feasible contiguous multi-division using \(q-1\) long knives then assigns to each bundle \(A_j\) exactly one of these \(q\) intervals from each layer, in such a way that within any fixed bundle \(A_j\), the chosen intervals from different layers have disjoint interiors in \([0,1]\).

Each agent \(i\in[n]\) has a \emph{valuation function} \(v_i\) that assigns a real value \(v_i(L)\) to every layered piece \(L\). (The paper discusses both general choice functions and valuations; here we focus on valuations as the paper’s open question does.) Envy-freeness for a multi-division \(A=(A_1,\dots,A_q)\) means there exists a surjective assignment \(\pi:[n]\to[q]\) such that every agent weakly prefers her assigned piece to any other, e.g. under valuations \(v_i(A_{\pi(i)})\ge \max_{j\in[q]} v_i(A_j)\) for all \(i\in[n]\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether there exist \emph{natural} valuation functions \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) (in the sense intended by the paper) for which \emph{no} envy-free multi-division exists that is both feasible and contiguous and is obtained using \(q-1\) long knives; equivalently, either:

1) construct an explicit instance (specified by \(m,n,q\) and valuations \(v_i\)) with this nonexistence property, or

2) prove that no such counterexample exists for a suitably broad and natural class of valuation functions.

The paper does not formalize what counts as “natural”; the task is to resolve existence of such counterexamples under an appropriate natural valuation-function model.

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper proves a strong positive result for the long-knives model under very general (choice-function) preferences: when \(q\) is a prime power and \(m\le q\le n\), there exists an envy-free feasible contiguous multi-division obtainable with \(q-1\) long knives (Theorem 1). The proof encodes long-knife feasible divisions and assignments in the chessboard complex \(\Delta_{2q-1,q}\) and applies Volovikov’s equivariant Borsuk–Ulam type theorem, together with Gale’s averaging trick and a flow/rounding lemma, to force a point where the aggregated preference vector hits the barycenter \((1/q,\dots,1/q)\). For \(m=2,q=3\) the paper also gives an existence theorem with one short and one long knife under monotone/hungry preferences and an FPTAS for \(\varepsilon\)-envy-free solutions under monotone Lipschitz valuations.

The open problem highlighted in the concluding remarks concerns the gap between the choice-function impossibility for non–prime-power \(q\) and the valuation-function setting: known counterexamples for choice functions (when \(q\) is not a prime power) do not automatically yield counterexamples for additive/continuous/Lipschitz valuations. At present, the forward-citation set provided does not contain a paper resolving this gap. Adjacent work on multi-layered cakes establishes proportional (rather than envy-free) feasible contiguous allocations under additive absolutely-continuous valuations, often using cutting primitives beyond long knives (e.g., a pair-of-knives model), suggesting that long-knife restrictions may be the true bottleneck. On the algorithmic side, reductions from approximate envy-free cake cutting with monotone preferences to approximate root-finding for monotone switching functions indicate a possible route to efficient approximation schemes if the multilayer long-knife constraints can be expressed in a suitably monotone fixed-point/root framework.

Overall, with the information available here, the problem remains open: no explicit ‘natural valuation’ counterexample to envy-free long-knife multi-divisions is identified, nor is there a theorem guaranteeing existence for broad valuation classes when \(q\) is not a prime power. Promising directions include (i) attempting to adapt non–prime-power obstruction constructions from choice functions to additive absolutely-continuous valuations while preserving feasibility/non-overlap across layers, and (ii) formulating the long-knife envy-free conditions as a continuous (possibly piecewise-linear) equivariant map problem or as a monotone root-finding instance to leverage algorithmic/topological machinery beyond Volovikov’s prime-power regime.

sources.title: Fair Division of Multi-layered Cakes
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves existence/computation results for feasible contiguous proportional (and in one case exact) multi-allocations under additive absolutely-continuous valuations: - Theorem 1: for any 2-layer cake and 2 agents, there exists an exact complete feasible multi-allocation (not necessarily contiguous). - Theorem 3: for 3 layers and 3 agents, there exists a proportional complete multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous. - Theorem 5: for 3 layers and any number of agents \(n\ge 3\), there exists a proportional complete multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous. - Theorems 7–8: for \(m=2^a\cdot 3\) layers (\(a\in\mathbb Z_+\)) and \(n\ge m\), there exists a proportional complete multi-allocation that is feasible and contiguous, with a recursive procedure based on majority switching points and merging diagonal pieces.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for ‘natural’ valuation counterexamples showing that envy-free feasible contiguous multi-divisions obtained using \(q-1\) long knives may fail to exist (or a proof they always exist) under a natural valuation model. This paper does not study envy-freeness under the long-knives restriction, nor does it construct impossibility instances. Instead it develops algorithms/existence proofs for proportional (and one exact) allocations using diagonal-piece cuts and a new ‘pair of knives’ moving-knife model. These techniques are adjacent to the long-knife framework (the author notes a pair of knives generalizes a long knife when one knife is at an endpoint), but they do not address whether envy-free allocations exist when all layers are cut at common \(t_1,\dots,t_{q-1}\) and bundles pick one interval per layer with non-overlap. Hence it neither resolves nor directly advances the counterexample question, except by providing alternative cutting primitives and existence results in a different fairness notion (proportionality).

sources.title: Computing approximate roots of monotone functions
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves query-complexity bounds for computing an \(\varepsilon\)-root of a Lipschitz, Miranda/positive-switching function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^d\) under monotonicity assumptions. In particular:
- For \(d=2\), if either a single diagonal monotonicity condition holds (e.g. \(f_1\) increasing in \(x_1\)) or a single ex-diagonal condition holds (e.g. \(f_1\) decreasing in \(x_2\)), then an \(\varepsilon\)-root can be found with \(O(\log^2(L/\varepsilon))\) value-oracle evaluations (Theorems 1.3/1.4).
- For fixed \(d\ge 2\), if all \(d^2-d\) ex-diagonal conditions hold (\(f_i\) decreasing in \(x_j\) for all \(i\ne j\)), then an \(\varepsilon\)-root can be found with \(O(\log^{\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil}(L/\varepsilon))\) evaluations (Theorem 1.6).
It also gives lower bounds showing exponential-in-digits behavior without sufficient monotonicity (Propositions 1.2, 1.5, 1.7), and a reduction from approximate group envy-free cake cutting with monotone preferences to approximate root finding (Theorem 1.9).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for natural valuation counterexamples (or impossibility) for envy-free multi-divisions of multi-layered cakes restricted to contiguous feasible allocations produced by \(q-1\) long knives. This paper does not study multi-layered cakes, long-knife feasibility/non-overlap constraints across layers, or existence/nonexistence of exact envy-free allocations under such geometric restrictions. Its cake-cutting application concerns a standard one-layer interval cake and (group) envy-freeness, and only in an approximate sense (\(r\)-near envy-free), via a reduction to finding approximate roots of certain monotone/switching functions. Thus it provides algorithmic/root-finding tools and complexity insights that might be useful if the multilayer-long-knife problem can be encoded as a Miranda-type root problem with suitable monotonicity, but it neither constructs valuation counterexamples nor proves existence for the long-knife multilayer model.

title: Remove the log factor in residual complexity for locally Lipschitz monotone inclusions
background_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a single-valued monotone operator and let \(B:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) be a maximal monotone (set-valued) operator with nonempty domain \(\mathrm{dom}\,B\). Consider the monotone inclusion problem
\[
\text{find }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ such that }0\in (F+B)(x).
\]
Assume a solution exists. For \(x\in \mathrm{dom}\,B\), define the residual of \(F+B\) at \(x\) by
\[
\mathrm{res}_{F+B}(x):=\inf\{\|v\|: v\in (F+B)(x)\}.
\]
A point \(x\in \mathrm{dom}\,B\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-residual solution if \(\mathrm{res}_{F+B}(x)\le \varepsilon\).
Assume further that \(F\) is locally Lipschitz continuous on \(\overline{\mathrm{dom}\,B}\): for every compact \(\Omega\subseteq \overline{\mathrm{dom}\,B}\) there exists \(L_\Omega>0\) such that \(\|F(x)-F(y)\|\le L_\Omega\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\Omega\).
An algorithm is measured in operation complexity by the number of fundamental operations, consisting of evaluations of \(F\) and evaluations of the resolvent \((I+\gamma B)^{-1}\) (assumed exactly computable) for \(\gamma>0\). Under global Lipschitz continuity of \(F\), the optimal complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-residual solution of a monotone (not strongly monotone) inclusion is \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) in this operation model.
problem_definition_latex: Design an algorithm for the above monotone inclusion setting (monotone \(F\), maximal monotone \(B\), and \(F\) locally Lipschitz continuous on \(\overline{\mathrm{dom}\,B}\)) that finds an \(\varepsilon\)-residual solution \(x\in\mathrm{dom}\,B\) with \(\mathrm{res}_{F+B}(x)\le \varepsilon\) using at most \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) evaluations of \(F\) and \((I+\gamma B)^{-1}\), i.e., improve the known \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log \varepsilon^{-1})\) operation complexity to \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) in this local-Lipschitz setting.
