literature_review.synthesis:
The open problem posed by Lu and Mei (2024) asks whether one can improve the \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) operation complexity of their Algorithm 2 (outer regularization + inner primal-dual extrapolation with backtracking) to \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-residual solution of \(0\in(F+B)(x)\) when \(F\) is monotone and only locally Lipschitz on \(\overline{\mathrm{dom}\,B}\). Their current logarithmic overhead comes from solving a sequence of strongly monotone regularized subproblems with geometrically changing regularization/accuracy parameters.

Among the forward-citing works provided, the paper "Parameter-free non-ergodic extragradient algorithms for solving monotone variational inequalities" is conceptually related: it develops backtracking/parameter-free extragradient schemes that work under local Lipschitz continuity without requiring a global Lipschitz constant. However, its last-iterate residual rate is \(o(1/\sqrt{T})\), corresponding to \(T=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) to reach residual \(\le\varepsilon\), and it focuses on VIs of the form \(0\in F(z)+N_Z(z)\) rather than general maximal monotone \(B\). Thus it does not resolve the \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) factor issue in Lu–Mei’s residual complexity, but it suggests that more refined adaptive/backtracking mechanisms might be useful ingredients.

Given the limited citation set supplied here, there is no evidence that the \(O(\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bound has been improved to \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) in the local-Lipschitz setting for general monotone inclusions. The problem therefore appears to remain open, with the main gap being how to avoid multi-stage regularization (or otherwise control local Lipschitz constants) while preserving the \(O(1/T)\)-type residual decay characteristic of globally Lipschitz monotone operator splitting methods.

sources.title: Parameter-free non-ergodic extragradient algorithms for solving monotone variational inequalities
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes parameter-free extragradient algorithms (PF-NE-EG) for monotone variational inequalities on a closed convex set \(Z\) with operator \(F\). Under local Lipschitz continuity (Assumption 2), Algorithm 2 (non-monotone backtracking) generates iterates \(z_t\) such that the last-iterate extragradient residual \(\|F(z_T)+\xi_T\|\) satisfies \(\|F(z_T)+\xi_T\|^2=o(1/T)\) (Proposition 2), where \(\xi_{t+1}:=-(1/\eta_t)[z_{t+1}-(z_t-\eta_t F(w_t))]\in N_Z(z_{t+1})\) and \(w_t=\mathrm{Proj}_Z(z_t-\eta_t F(z_t))\). Moreover \(\|F(z_{t+1})+\xi_{t+1}\|\ge T(z_{t+1})\) (Lemma 3), so the same \(o(1/\sqrt{T})\) last-iterate rate holds for the tangent residual.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for removing a \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) factor in operation complexity for finding an \(\varepsilon\)-residual solution to the monotone inclusion \(0\in (F+B)(x)\) when \(F\) is only locally Lipschitz on \(\overline{\mathrm{dom}\,B}\), aiming for \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) evaluations of \(F\) and the resolvent \((I+\gamma B)^{-1}\). This paper treats monotone VIs (equivalently inclusions of the form \(0\in F(z)+N_Z(z)\)) and gives parameter-free extragradient schemes with backtracking that work under local Lipschitz continuity and achieve a last-iterate residual rate \(\|F(z_T)+\xi_T\|=o(1/\sqrt{T})\), i.e., \(T=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) to reach residual \(\le\varepsilon\). Thus it does not achieve the desired \(O(\varepsilon^{-1})\) residual complexity, nor does it address a general maximal monotone \(B\) beyond normal cones / projections. However, its backtracking ideas and local-Lipschitz handling are conceptually related tools for designing parameter-free methods in locally Lipschitz settings.

title: Achieve faster residual decay for cocoercive-operator Newton-corrected inertial dynamics
background_latex:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with inner product \(\langle \cdot,\cdot\rangle\) and norm \(\|\cdot\|\). Let \(M:H\to H\) be a single-valued \(\rho\)-cocoercive operator for some \(\rho>0\), meaning
\[
\langle M(x)-M(y),x-y\rangle \ge \rho\,\|M(x)-M(y)\|^2\quad\forall x,y\in H.
\]
Assume the set of zeros \(\mathrm{Zer}
M:=\{x\in H: M(x)=0\}\) is nonempty.

For a trajectory \(y:[s_0,\infty)\to H\) with \(s_0>0\), define the (formal) time derivative of \(M(y(s))\) by the chain rule notation
\[
\frac{d}{ds}(M(y(s)))
\]
(when \(M\) is Lipschitz, this can be understood in the a.e. sense along absolutely continuous \(y\)).

Consider the second-order inertial dynamics with vanishing viscous damping and a Newton-correction term
\[
 y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+c(s)\,\frac{d}{ds}(M(y(s)))+M(y(s))=0,\qquad s\ge s_0,
\]
where \(\alpha>1\) and \(c(s)>0\) is a prescribed scalar coefficient. Two specific choices discussed are
1) \(c(s)=\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\), yielding the system
\[
 y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\,\frac{d}{ds}(M(y(s)))+M(y(s))=0,
\]
for which the paper proves \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\).
2) \(c(s)=\frac{2s}{\alpha+1}\), yielding the closely related system
\[
 y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{2s}{\alpha+1}\,\frac{d}{ds}(M(y(s)))+M(y(s))=0,
\]
which another work reports satisfies the sharper decay \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s^2)\) and \(\int_{s_0}^\infty s^3\|M(y(s))\|^2\,ds<\infty\).
problem_definition_latex:
Determine whether the time-scaling and perturbation approach developed for steepest-descent-type systems can be used to obtain the improved convergence rate
\[
\|M(y(s))\|=o\!\left(\frac{1}{s^2}\right)\quad\text{as }s\to\infty
\]
(and/or the corresponding weighted integrability \(\int_{s_0}^\infty s^3\|M(y(s))\|^2\,ds<\infty\)) for the Newton-corrected cocoercive-operator inertial dynamics
\[
 y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\,\frac{d}{ds}(M(y(s)))+M(y(s))=0,
\]
or for an appropriately modified coefficient \(c(s)\) within the same time-scaling/perturbation framework, under the standing assumptions that \(M\) is cocoercive and \(\mathrm{Zer}\,M\neq\emptyset\).

literature_review.synthesis:
In Attouch–Boţ–Nguyen’s time-scaling/averaging program, the cocoercive-operator baseline flow \(z'(t)+M(z(t))=0\) yields only \(\|M(z(t))\|=o(t^{-1/2})\), and after the specific open-loop scaling \(\tau(s)=s^2/(2(\alpha+1))\) one obtains the Newton-corrected inertial dynamics
\[y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\frac{d}{ds}M(y(s))+M(y(s))=0\]
with \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\) and \(\int s\|M(y(s))\|^2ds<\infty\) (Theorem 12 of the source paper). The paper explicitly notes (Remark 8) that a closely related modification with coefficient \(\frac{2s}{\alpha+1}\) in front of \(\frac{d}{ds}M(y(s))\) enjoys the sharper \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s^2)\) and \(\int s^3\|M(y(s))\|^2ds<\infty\) in subsequent work, leaving open whether the original time-scaling/perturbation route can recover this sharper decay for the \(\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\)-coefficient model or via a nearby choice of \(c(s)\).

Among forward citations, the strongest evidence that \(o(1/s^2)\) residual decay is achievable within a Newton-corrected operator framework comes from the continuous/discrete Fast OGDA analysis, which studies a more general vanishing-damping Newton-corrected dynamics with a tunable scaling \(\beta(t)\) and an additional \(V\)-term coefficient tied to \(\beta\). It proves \(\|V(z(t))\|=o(1/(t\beta(t)))\) and \(\int t\beta(t)^2\|V(z(t))\|^2dt<\infty\); taking \(\beta(t)\asymp t\) yields exactly \(\|V(z(t))\|=o(1/t^2)\) and \(\int t^3\|V(z(t))\|^2dt<\infty\). This matches the target rate/integrability but for a dynamics that differs from the open-problem equation by the presence of an extra coefficient multiplying \(V(z(t))\), so it does not directly settle the \(c(s)=s/(\alpha+1)\) case.

Other cited works develop complementary time-rescaling equivalences (Heavy Ball \(\leftrightarrow\) Fast OGDA), stochastic time-scaling/averaging transfers, and anchored/Tikhonov regularization equivalences for operator-derivative systems. Collectively they suggest two plausible routes to \(o(1/s^2)\): (i) modify the Newton-correction model so that the coefficient in front of \(M(y(s))\) is coupled to \(c(s)\) (as in Fast OGDA-type templates), enabling Lyapunov cancellations that yield \(o(1/(s c(s)))\); or (ii) embed the dynamics into an equivalent first-order anchored flow (possibly with Tikhonov regularization) where sharper residual decay can be proved and then transferred back by time rescaling. At present, none of the forward-citing papers provides a proof of \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s^2)\) for the exact equation with \(c(s)=s/(\alpha+1)\) under only cocoercivity, so the problem remains open in the stated form.

sources.title: Fast Optimistic Gradient Descent Ascent (OGDA) method in continuous and discrete time
sources.theorem_or_result:
For a monotone continuous operator \(V:H\to H\) with nonempty zero set \(Z\), the paper studies the second-order Newton-corrected vanishing-damping dynamics
\[
\ddot z(t)+\frac{\alpha}{t}\dot z(t)+\beta(t)\frac{d}{dt}V(z(t)) + \frac12\Big(\dot\beta(t)+\frac{\alpha}{t}\beta(t)\Big)V(z(t))=0,\qquad \alpha>2,
\]
with \(\beta\) nondecreasing and \(\sup_{t\ge t_0} \tfrac{t\dot\beta(t)}{\beta(t)}<\alpha-2\). They prove last-iterate rates
- \(\|V(z(t))\|=o\big(\tfrac{1}{t\,\beta(t)}\big)\) and \(\langle z(t)-z^*,V(z(t))\rangle=o\big(\tfrac{1}{t\,\beta(t)}\big)\) for any \(z^*\in Z\),
- weighted integrability \(\int_{t_0}^\infty t\,\beta(t)^2\,\|V(z(t))\|^2\,dt<\infty\),
and weak convergence \(z(t)\rightharpoonup z^*\in Z\). For polynomial \(\beta(t)=\beta_0 t^\rho\) (\(\rho\ge0\)), this yields \(\|V(z(t))\|=o(1/t^{\rho+1})\) and \(\int t^{2\rho+1}\|V(z(t))\|^2<\infty\).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether time-scaling/perturbation ideas can upgrade the residual decay for the Newton-corrected inertial dynamics
\(y''+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\frac{d}{ds}M(y)+M(y)=0\)
from \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\) (and \(\int s^3\|M(y)\|^2<\infty\)) under cocoercivity.

This paper provides a closely related, more general monotone-operator framework with an explicit time-scaling function \(\beta(t)\) and a derivative correction term \(\beta(t)\tfrac{d}{dt}V(z(t))\), proving \(\|V(z(t))\|=o(1/(t\beta(t)))\) and \(\int t\beta(t)^2\|V(z(t))\|^2<\infty\). By choosing \(\beta(t)\asymp t\), one gets \(\|V(z(t))\|=o(1/t^2)\) and \(\int t^3\|V(z(t))\|^2<\infty\), matching the target rate/integrability.

However, the open problem concerns a *specific* dynamics with fixed coefficient \(c(s)=\tfrac{s}{\alpha+1}\) and only cocoercivity (not general monotonicity plus the extra \(\tfrac12(\dot\beta+\tfrac{\alpha}{t}\beta)V\) term). The paper does not show that the original \(c(s)=\tfrac{s}{\alpha+1}\) system can be transformed into their model, nor does it derive \(o(1/s^2)\) for that exact equation. It instead shows that within a modified time-scaling/Newton-correction framework (with an additional \(V\)-term coefficient tied to \(\beta\)), one can indeed achieve \(o(1/t^2)\) by taking \(\beta(t)\sim t\).

sources.title: Recovering Nesterov accelerated dynamics from Heavy Ball dynamics via time rescaling
sources.theorem_or_result:
For a monotone and continuous (in particular, cocoercive) operator \(V:H\to H\), the paper studies the Heavy-Ball-type Newton-corrected dynamics
\[\ddot y(t)+\lambda \dot y(t)+\mu(t)\tfrac{d}{dt}V(y(t))+\gamma(t)V(y(t))=0\]
under the asymptotic ratio condition \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\gamma(t)/\mu(t)=:L\in(0,\infty)\) and growth bounds (Assumption (4.12)). It proves (Theorem 4.3) that any strong global solution satisfies
- \(\|V(y(t))\|=o(1/\mu(t))\), \(\langle y(t)-x^*,V(y(t))\rangle=o(1/\mu(t))\), and \(\|\dot y(t)\|\to 0\),
- \(y(t)\rightharpoonup \bar y\in\mathrm{Zer}\,V\).
Moreover, via time-rescaling equivalence with Fast OGDA (Proposition 5.1), it recovers for the vanishing-damping system
\[\ddot x(s)+\tfrac{\alpha}{s}\dot x(s)+\tfrac{d}{ds}V(x(s))+\tfrac{\alpha}{2s}V(x(s))=0\]
that \(\|V(x(s))\|=o(1/s)\) (Theorem 5.2).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether a time-scaling/perturbation framework can upgrade the residual decay for the specific Newton-corrected inertial dynamics
\(y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\frac{d}{ds}M(y(s))+M(y(s))=0\)
(from \(o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\)) for a \(\rho\)-cocoercive operator \(M\).

This citing paper develops a closely related time-rescaling program, but for a different family of Newton-corrected operator dynamics: it analyzes a Heavy-Ball-with-constant-friction model with two free scalings \(\mu(t),\gamma(t)\) in front of \(\tfrac{d}{dt}V(y(t))\) and \(V(y(t))\), and then shows it is time-reparametrization equivalent to the Fast OGDA vanishing-damping system with coefficients \(1\) (for \(\tfrac{d}{ds}V\)) and \(\alpha/(2s)\) (for \(V\)). The resulting residual rate is \(\|V(x(s))\|=o(1/s)\), not \(o(1/s^2)\).

Thus it does not solve the stated open problem. However, it is highly relevant because it (i) provides an explicit time-rescaling equivalence for Newton-corrected monotone-operator inertial dynamics, and (ii) gives a general residual estimate \(o(1/\mu(t))\) that suggests how choosing faster-growing \(\mu\) might yield faster residual decay in the constant-friction time variable. What is missing for the open problem is a rescaling/choice of coefficients that maps to the specific \(c(s)=s/(\alpha+1)\) model and yields \(o(1/s^2)\) residual decay in the \(s\)-time variable, as well as the weighted integrability \(\int s^3\|M(y(s))\|^2 ds<\infty\).

sources.title: Stochastic inertial dynamics via time scaling and averaging
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops a time-scaling-and-averaging framework (in a stochastic setting) that transfers convergence properties of first-order stochastic (sub)gradient flows to second-order inertial dynamics with implicit Hessian-driven damping. In particular, for the deterministic/noiseless case and 
- viscous damping \(\gamma(t)=\alpha/t\) with \(\alpha>3\),
- geometric damping \(\beta(t)=t/(\alpha-1)\) (equivalently \(\beta\equiv \Gamma\) for the associated \(\Gamma\)),
under suitable integrability of the diffusion term (or \(\sigma\equiv 0\)), they obtain fast rates for the inertial system
\[\ddot X(t)+\tfrac{\alpha}{t}\dot X(t)+\nabla f\bigl(X(t)+\beta(t)\dot X(t)\bigr)=\text{noise},\]
including \(f(X(t)) - \min f = o(1/t^2)\) a.s. and \(\int_{t_0}^\infty t^3\|\nabla f(X(t)+\beta(t)\dot X(t))\|^2\,dt<\infty\) a.s. (Corollary 3.5).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether the time-scaling/perturbation approach from Attouch–Bot–Nguyen can yield the sharper residual decay \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s^2)\) (and weighted integrability) for the Newton-corrected inertial dynamics with a cocoercive operator term \(c(s)\tfrac{d}{ds}M(y(s))\). This citing paper does not analyze that Newton-corrected cocoercive-operator ODE. Instead it treats (stochastic) inertial dynamics of implicit Hessian-driven type, where the ‘Newton correction’ is implicit: \(\nabla f(x+\beta\dot x)\), not an explicit \(\tfrac{d}{ds}M(y(s))\) term. Nevertheless, it provides strong evidence that time scaling + averaging can upgrade rates from \(o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\) for residual-like quantities in related second-order systems, and it explicitly mentions as a future direction extension to non-potential cocoercive operators. Thus it is partial progress/related methodology rather than a solution: it supplies a transferable technique and achieves the desired \(o(1/t^2)\)-type rate for gradients in the gradient/subgradient setting, but does not establish \(o(1/s^2)\) for \(\|M(y(s))\|\) in the specific Newton-corrected cocoercive-operator dynamics with \(c(s)=s/(\alpha+1)\).

sources.title: Tikhonov regularization of monotone operator flows not only ensures strong convergence of the trajectories but also speeds up the vanishing of the residuals
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proves that adding Tikhonov regularization (and, via time-rescaling/anchoring equivalences, certain first-order flows) yields strong convergence and improved residual/velocity decay. In particular, for the first-order regularized flow \(x'(t)+M(x(t)) + \tfrac{1}{t}x(t)=0\) with monotone continuous \(M\) and \(\mathrm{Zer}
M\neq\emptyset\), it establishes \(\|x'(t)\|=O(1/t)\) and \(\|M(x(t))\|=O(1/t)\) and strong convergence \(x(t)\to P_{\mathrm{Zer}M}(0)\). It also shows an equivalence between a second-order vanishing-damping/derivative-of-operator system \(z''(s)+\tfrac{\alpha}{s}z'(s)+\beta(s)\tfrac{d}{ds}M(z(s))+(\beta'(s)+\tfrac{\beta(s)}{s})M(z(s))=0\) and a first-order anchored system \(z'(s)+\beta(s)M(z(s)) + \tfrac{\alpha-1}{s}(z(s)-v)=0\), yielding residual rates such as \(\|M(z(s))\|=O(1/s^{\alpha})\) when \(\inf_{s\ge s_0} s\beta'(s)/\beta(s) > \alpha-2\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether time-scaling/perturbation methods can upgrade the residual decay for the Newton-corrected inertial dynamics \(y''+\tfrac{\alpha}{s}y' + \tfrac{s}{\alpha+1}\tfrac{d}{ds}M(y)+M(y)=0\) from \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\) (or weighted integrability). This citing paper does not analyze that specific coefficient choice \(c(s)=\tfrac{s}{\alpha+1}\) nor prove \(o(1/s^2)\) for it. However, it develops a time-rescaling framework and, crucially, shows that a related class of second-order dynamics with a \(\tfrac{d}{ds}M\) term (equation (3.1)) is equivalent to a first-order anchored/Tikhonov-regularized flow, from which strong convergence and explicit residual rates follow. These techniques are conceptually close to the open problem’s requested “time-scaling/perturbation framework,” and they provide fast residual decay (e.g., \(O(1/s^{\alpha})\) for suitable \(\beta\)), but they do not directly yield the desired \(o(1/s^2)\) for the particular Newton-corrected system in the problem statement.

sources.title: Long-Time Analysis of Stochastic Heavy Ball Dynamics for Convex Optimization and Monotone Equations
sources.theorem_or_result:
For a monotone and Lipschitz operator \(V:H\to H\) with \(\mathrm{zer}
V\neq\emptyset\), the paper analyzes stochastic Heavy Ball systems with a correction term involving the time derivative of \(V\). Via time-rescaling, it derives fast rates for the stochastic Fast OGDA dynamics
\[z''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}z'(s)+\beta\frac{d}{ds}V(z(s))+\frac{\alpha\beta}{2s}V(z(s))=0\]
(and its SDE version), proving in particular (a.s.) \(\|V(Z(s))\|=o(1/s)\) and \(\langle Z(s)-z^*,V(Z(s))\rangle=o(1/s)\) for \(\alpha>2\), plus corresponding \(O(1/s)\) or \(O(1/s^2)\) bounds in expectation for squared residuals/velocities.

The open problem asks whether the time-scaling/perturbation approach can upgrade the residual decay for the Newton-corrected inertial dynamics
\[y''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}y'(s)+\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\,\frac{d}{ds}M(y(s))+M(y(s))=0\]
from \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\) (or weighted integrability), under cocoercivity.

This citing paper is highly thematically aligned: it explicitly uses time-rescaling to transfer convergence-rate results between heavy-ball-with-friction systems and vanishing-damping systems, and it treats monotone equations with a correction term involving \(\frac{d}{dt}V(y(t))\). However, the specific fast-rate result it transfers for monotone equations is for the Fast OGDA-type dynamics
\[z''(s)+\frac{\alpha}{s}z'(s)+\beta\frac{d}{ds}V(z(s))+\frac{\alpha\beta}{2s}V(z(s))=0,\]
which yields residual \(o(1/s)\), not \(o(1/s^2)\). It does not analyze the Newton-corrected coefficient choice \(c(s)=\frac{s}{\alpha+1}\) (or \(\frac{2s}{\alpha+1}\)) nor does it prove \(o(1/s^2)\) residual decay or \(\int s^3\|M(y(s))\|^2<\infty\) for that system.

So it does not solve the open problem, but it provides partial progress/nearby results and a concrete time-scaling framework in the operator (non-potential) setting that could be adapted when trying to tune coefficients to improve residual decay.

sources.title: Fast Krasnoselskii-Mann Method with Overrelaxation and Preconditioners
sources.theorem_or_result:
For the continuous-time second-order system
\[\ddot x(t)+\frac{\alpha}{t}\dot x(t)+\beta(t)\frac{d}{dt}Q(x(t))+b(t)Q(x(t))=0\]
with monotone Lipschitz operator \(Q\) and \(b(t)=(1-\eta)\dot\beta(t)+\theta\beta(t)/t\) where \(\eta\in(0,1)\) and \(\theta=(1-\eta)+\eta(\alpha-1)\), Theorem 2.2 proves (under growth condition \(0\le \dot\beta(t)t/\beta(t)\le \alpha-2-\varepsilon\)) that
- \(\|Q(x(t))\|=O(1/(t\beta(t)))\), and if \(\alpha>2\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) then \(\|Q(x(t))\|=o(1/(t\beta(t)))\) and \(\int_{t_0}^\infty t\beta(t)^2\|Q(x(t))\|^2dt<\infty\).
In discrete time, Algorithm 1 (generalized fast Krasnosel’skii–Mann) yields for nonexpansive \(T\): \(\|x_k-T(x_k)\|=o(1/k)\) and \(\sum_k k\|x_k-T(x_k)\|^2<\infty\) (Theorem 3.3).

with \(M\) cocoercive from \(\|M(y(s))\|=o(1/s)\) to \(o(1/s^2)\) (and \(\int s^3\|M(y)\|^2<\infty\)).
This citing paper develops Lyapunov/time-scaling analysis for a closely related class
\(\ddot x+\frac{\alpha}{t}\dot x+\beta(t)\frac{d}{dt}Q(x)+b(t)Q(x)=0\)
with monotone Lipschitz \(Q\), proving \(\|Q(x(t))\|=o(1/(t\beta(t)))\) and weighted integrability \(\int t\beta(t)^2\|Q\|^2<\infty\). However, it does not treat the specific coefficient choice \(\beta(t)=t/(\alpha+1)\) (which would violate their growth condition unless \(\alpha\ge 3\) and still gives only \(o(1/t^2)\) at best), nor does it analyze the exact Newton-corrected cocoercive-operator dynamics in the problem statement. title: Convergence of single-valued fixed-point iteration for Gibbs-form equilibrium operators
background_latex:
Consider a discrete-time infinite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) with finite state space \(S=\{1,\dots,d\}\) and compact action space \(U\subset \mathbb{R}^\ell\) with \(0<\mathrm{Leb}(U)<\infty\). A relaxed (randomized) feedback control is a map \(\pi:S\to \mathcal{P}(U)\), where \(\mathcal{P}(U)\) denotes probability measures on \(U\). For \(\lambda>0\), an entropy-regularized objective is used in which the stage payoff includes a Shannon differential entropy term. Under entropy regularization, the equilibrium (in the sense of intra-personal subgame-perfect equilibrium for time-inconsistent discounting) can be characterized as a fixed point of a single-valued operator of Gibbs (softmax) form.

More concretely, for each state \(i\in S\) and vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), define a probability density \(\Gamma_\lambda(y,i)\in \mathcal{D}(U)\) by
\[\Gamma_\lambda(y,i)(u):=\frac{\exp\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}(f(0,i,u)+p_i^u\cdot y)\right)}{\int_U \exp\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}(f(0,i,v)+p_i^v\cdot y)\right)\,dv},\qquad u\in U,\]
where \(f(0,i,u)\) is the one-step reward (at time-difference \(0\)) and \(p_i^u\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is the transition-probability row vector from state \(i\) under action \(u\). Given \(y\), the corresponding relaxed control is \(\Gamma_\lambda(y,\cdot):S\to \mathcal{P}(U)\). Let \(J_\lambda^\pi\) be the entropy-regularized value functional and let \(V_\lambda^\pi\in\mathbb{R}^d\) be the associated continuation-value vector (expected future discounted reward plus discounted entropy starting one step ahead). Define the induced single-valued self-map \(\Psi_\lambda:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) by
\[\Psi_\lambda(y):=V_\lambda^{\Gamma_\lambda(y,\cdot)}.\]
Fixed points \(y^\star\) of \(\Psi_\lambda\) correspond to entropy-regularized relaxed equilibria \(\pi^\star=\Gamma_\lambda(y^\star,\cdot)\).

A natural numerical approach is fixed-point iteration on \(\Psi_\lambda\) (equivalently on the policy operator \(\Phi_\lambda(\pi):=\Gamma_\lambda(V_\lambda^\pi,\cdot)\)), i.e., start from some \(y_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\) (or \(\pi_0\)) and generate \(y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\) (or \(\pi_{n+1}=\Phi_\lambda(\pi_n)\)).
problem_definition_latex:
Give conditions under which the single-valued fixed-point iteration
\[y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\qquad (n\ge 0)
\]
converges (e.g., from arbitrary initialization, or from some specified set of initial points) to a fixed point \(y^\star\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying \(\Psi_\lambda(y^\star)=y^\star\), equivalently producing a regular relaxed equilibrium \(\pi^\star=\Gamma_\lambda(y^\star,\cdot)\) for the entropy-regularized time-inconsistent MDP.

literature_review.synthesis:
In Bayraktar–Huang–Wang–Zhou (2024), entropy regularization turns the equilibrium best-response into a single-valued Gibbs map \(\Gamma_\lambda\), yielding a single-valued equilibrium operator \(\Psi_\lambda(y)=V^{\Gamma_\lambda(y,\cdot)}_\lambda\). Existence of fixed points is obtained via Brouwer after establishing uniform logarithmic entropy bounds (Lemma 2.1) under Lipschitz dependence on actions and a uniform cone condition on \(U\). The paper explicitly leaves open the convergence of the naive fixed-point iteration \(y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\) (Remark 2.6), which would make the approximation-by-regularization approach fully rigorous as a computational method.

Among forward citations, the closest progress on iteration convergence is in “Equilibrium for Time-inconsistent Mean Field Games: A Systematic Analysis by Entropy Regularization”, which proves contraction and convergence of a Gibbs-form policy-iteration map \(\Phi_\lambda\) under restrictive conditions (small horizon and weak terminal interaction) in a continuous-time finite-horizon mean-field setting. This suggests that proving convergence in the discrete-time infinite-horizon finite-state MDP likely requires additional structure ensuring that \(\Psi_\lambda\) (or \(\Phi_\lambda\)) is a contraction or at least has a globally attracting fixed point—e.g., strong discounting/mixing, small effective horizon \(\sum_t \delta(t)\), or quantitative Lipschitz bounds on \(y\mapsto V^{\Gamma_\lambda(y,\cdot)}_\lambda\) combined with the \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz nature of the softmax map.

Other citing works mainly develop existence/approximation theories via entropy regularization and Schauder/Kakutani fixed points (including mean-field stopping and diffusion-control analogues) but do not establish general convergence of the fixed-point iteration for the Gibbs operator. Therefore, based on the provided forward-citation set, the convergence problem for single-valued fixed-point iteration of \(\Psi_\lambda\) in the Bayraktar–Huang–Wang–Zhou discrete-time infinite-horizon setting remains open.

sources.title: Equilibrium for Time-inconsistent Mean Field Games: A Systematic Analysis by Entropy Regularization
sources.theorem_or_result: In a finite-horizon continuous-time time-inconsistent mean field game with compact action set and Shannon entropy regularization, the paper proves: - Existence of a regularized relaxed mean-field equilibrium \((\pi^*_\lambda,m^*_\lambda)\) for all sufficiently small \(\lambda>0\) via a Schauder fixed point for an operator \(\Phi_\lambda\) built from the Gibbs map \(\Gamma_\lambda\) and the induced value/measure flow (Theorem 3.1(ii)). - As \(\lambda\to 0\), along a subsequence \((\pi_{\lambda_n},m_{\lambda_n})\to(\pi^\infty,m^\infty)\) yielding an equilibrium of the unregularized time-inconsistent MFG (Theorem 4.1). - For fixed \(\lambda>0\), a policy-iteration algorithm \((J^{k+1},m^{k+1})=\Phi_\lambda(J^k,m^k)\) converges to the regularized equilibrium provided the horizon \(T\) is small and terminal interaction is weak (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring convergence of the single-valued fixed-point iteration \(y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\) (equivalently policy iteration \(\pi_{n+1}=\Phi_\lambda(\pi_n)\)) for entropy-regularized time-inconsistent MDPs with Gibbs-form equilibrium operator. This paper proves a convergence result for a closely related fixed-point/policy-iteration map \(\Phi_\lambda\) in a different setting: continuous-time finite-horizon time-inconsistent mean field games. Under additional assumptions (notably short time horizon and weak terminal measure dependence), they show \(\Phi_\lambda\) is a strict contraction and policy iteration converges to the unique regularized equilibrium (Theorem 5.1). This provides partial progress and transferable techniques (contraction estimates using Bismut–Elworthy–Li gradient bounds and stability of measure flows), but it does not directly resolve the discrete-time infinite-horizon finite-state MDP iteration convergence question, nor does it give global-from-arbitrary-initialization convergence without small-time/weak-interaction restrictions.

sources.title: Time-inconsistent mean-field stopping problems: a regularised equilibrium approach
sources.theorem_or_result: For a time-inconsistent discrete-time mean-field stopping MDP with entropy regularization, the paper defines a Gibbs/logit best-response operator \(T_1^\lambda\) and a continuation-value operator \(T_2^\lambda\), and proves existence of a regularized equilibrium \(\varphi_\lambda\) as a fixed point \(\varphi_\lambda = T_1^\lambda\circ T_2^\lambda(\varphi_\lambda)\) (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3). It further proves that along a sequence \(\lambda_n\downarrow 0\), \(\varphi_{\lambda_n}\) converges (in a weak-* sense, upgraded after one-step transition) to a relaxed equilibrium \(\varphi_0\) of the unregularized problem (Theorem 3.5).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring convergence of the single-valued fixed-point iteration \(y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\) (or policy iteration \(\pi_{n+1}=\Phi_\lambda(\pi_n)\)) for Gibbs-form equilibrium operators in entropy-regularized time-inconsistent MDPs. This paper also uses entropy regularization to obtain a single-valued Gibbs/logit equilibrium operator and proves existence of fixed points via Schauder, but it does not establish convergence of the naive fixed-point iteration from arbitrary initialization. It proposes a policy-iteration-style numerical scheme (Algorithm 1) for a specific mean-field stopping model and provides illustrative numerical convergence, yet without a general contraction/monotonicity argument guaranteeing convergence of \(\varphi^{(n+1)}=T_1^\lambda\circ T_2^\lambda(\varphi^{(n)})\) or the value-based iteration. Thus it provides related existence/compactness tools and an operator framework closely aligned with the open problem, but not the requested convergence theory for fixed-point iteration.

sources.title: Existence of Markov equilibrium control in discrete time
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves an existence theorem for discrete-time finite-horizon time-inconsistent control: under Assumption 3.3 (nonnegative Borel costs; stage costs inf-compact in controls; monotone l.s.c. nonlinearity; and a strong continuity condition on transition kernels that makes \(u\mapsto\int V(x')P_t(dx'\mid x,u)\) continuous for every bounded Borel \(V\)), there exists a nonrandomized Borel measurable Markov equilibrium policy \(\pi^*=(u_1^*,\dots,u_{T-1}^*)\) (Theorem 3.6).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for conditions ensuring convergence of a single-valued fixed-point iteration \(y_{n+1}=\Psi_\lambda(y_n)\) for an entropy-regularized infinite-horizon MDP, where \(\Psi_\lambda\) is a Gibbs/softmax equilibrium operator. This citing paper does not study entropy regularization, Gibbs-form operators, infinite horizon, or convergence of fixed-point iterations. Its contribution is instead an existence result for finite-horizon equilibria via measurable selection and inf-compactness. Indirectly, it provides background tools (inf-compactness, strong continuity of kernels) that can help establish existence/regularity of equilibrium selectors, which is a prerequisite for analyzing iterative schemes, but it does not provide contraction/monotonicity/nonexpansiveness properties of \(\Psi_\lambda\) or any convergence theorem for iterating it.

title: Prove divergence of last-iterate mixed strategies without monotonicity in 2x2 games
background_latex:
Consider an infinitely repeated two-player \(2\times 2\) stage game with action sets \(\{0,1\}\) for each player and payoff matrices \(G,H\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}\). At each round \(t=1,2,\dots\), player 1 chooses a mixed action \(P_t\in[0,1]\) (probability of playing action 1) and then realizes a pure action \(I_t\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(I_t=1\mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1})=P_t\); similarly player 2 chooses \(Q_t\in[0,1]\) and realizes \(J_t\in\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb{P}(J_t=1\mid \mathcal{F}_{t-1})=Q_t\). Players observe only realized actions (not the opponent's mixtures), so the history up to time \(t-1\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{t-1}:=\sigma\big((I_s,J_s)_{s=1}^{t-1}\big)\).

Define empirical averages of realized actions by
\[\widehat P_t:=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t I_s,\qquad \widehat Q_t:=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t J_s.\]
A (self-agnostic) repeated-game strategy for player 1 is a sequence of measurable maps \(f_t:\{0,1\}^{t-1}\to[0,1]\) so that \(P_t=f_t((J_s)_{s=1}^{t-1})\); analogously player 2 uses maps \(g_t\) with \(Q_t=g_t((I_s)_{s=1}^{t-1})\). A strategy is mean-based if there exist functions (still denoted) \(f_t:[0,1]\to[0,1]\) such that \(P_t=f_t(\widehat Q_{t-1})\), and similarly \(Q_t=g_t(\widehat P_{t-1})\).

Player 1's (external) regret up to time \(T\) against an opponent realization sequence \((J_t)_{t=1}^T\) is
\[\operatorname{Reg}_1(T):=\max_{i\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{t=1}^T G(i,J_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T G(I_t,J_t).\]
A strategy is uniformly no-regret with rate \((r,c)\) if for all \(T\) and all opponent action sequences, \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Reg}_1(T)]\le c\,T^{r}\), where expectation is over the player’s internal randomness (and any randomness in the opponent strategy), and the optimal rate is \(r=1/2\).

Assume the stage game is competitive in the sense that it has a unique completely mixed Nash equilibrium \((p^*,q^*)\in(0,1)^2\).

literature_review.synthesis:
The source paper (Muthukumar–Phade–Sahai, 2022) proves that in competitive 2×2 games with a unique completely mixed Nash equilibrium \((p^*,q^*)\), last-iterate mixed strategies cannot converge almost surely when both players use strategies that are (i) uniformly no-regret with optimal \(O(\sqrt{T})\) rate, (ii) mean-based (depend only on the opponent’s empirical action frequency), and (iii) monotone in that empirical frequency. The core mechanism is a “fluctuation sensitivity” property: any optimal-rate no-regret strategy must react by a constant amount to \(\Theta(t^{-1/2})\) deviations in the opponent’s empirical frequency, and such deviations occur infinitely often due to sampling noise even if the opponent plays the equilibrium mixture i.i.d. This yields persistent oscillations of the last iterate.

The open problem asks whether the monotonicity assumption can be removed while retaining the same conclusion (almost-sure nonconvergence of \((P_t,Q_t)\)). Among the forward citations provided, the closest partial progress is work on last-iterate convergence under uncoupled bandit feedback in zero-sum games, which establishes sharp lower bounds on achievable last-iterate convergence rates and provides matching algorithms. While it does not prove almost-sure divergence for optimal \(\sqrt{T}\)-regret mean-based dynamics, it reinforces the broader message that last-iterate behavior is intrinsically difficult under realization-only feedback. A separate line of work on higher-order uncoupled dynamics shows that local stabilization of completely mixed Nash equilibria is possible in continuous time with auxiliary states, indicating that convergence can be achieved in richer dynamical models, but this does not directly translate to the discrete-time, optimal no-regret, mean-based setting.

Overall, based on the limited forward-citation set provided, there is no definitive resolution of the monotonicity-free conjecture. The main gap remains to either (a) extend the fluctuation-sensitivity/oscillation argument to arbitrary (possibly nonmonotone) mean-based mappings \(f_t,g_t\) with optimal regret, or (b) construct a counterexample: a pair of nonmonotone mean-based optimal no-regret strategies whose last iterates converge almost surely in some competitive 2×2 game. Promising directions include identifying weaker structural properties implied by optimal regret (e.g., sign changes or bounded variation constraints on \(f_t\)) that still force oscillations under \(\Theta(t^{-1/2})\) empirical fluctuations, or leveraging stabilization ideas that require additional state beyond the empirical mean, thereby clarifying whether mean-basedness itself (rather than monotonicity) is the true obstruction.

sources.title: The harder path: Last iterate convergence for uncoupled learning in zero-sum games with bandit feedback
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves lower bounds and gives matching algorithms for last-iterate convergence in uncoupled two-player zero-sum matrix games with bandit feedback. In particular, under the assumption that the opponent’s sampled action is never observed, for any p∈(0,2] no learning sequence can achieve L^p last-iterate convergence rate better than order t^{-1/(2+p)} uniformly over a family of 2×2 Bernoulli games M_ε (Theorem 5.1), and for p>2 it implies no better than order t^{-1/4} (Corollary 5.3). It also provides uncoupled algorithms achieving these rates up to logs: Algorithm 1 achieves L^p rate \(\tilde O(t^{-1/(2+p)})\) (Theorem 6.2), and a regularized mirror-descent/EXP3 variant achieves \(\tilde O(t^{-1/4})\) in L^2 with a doubling-trick meta-procedure (Theorem 8.1).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks whether, in competitive 2×2 games with a unique completely mixed Nash equilibrium, any pair of mean-based strategies with optimal \(\sqrt T\)-regret (rate (1/2,c)) must have almost-sure divergence of the last-iterate mixed strategies (without assuming monotonicity). This paper does not address that question directly: it studies zero-sum games with bandit feedback and focuses on achievable rates of last-iterate convergence in expectation/L^p of exploitability gap, not almost-sure convergence/divergence of the actual mixed strategies \((P_t,Q_t)\) under optimal no-regret learning.

However, it is partially relevant because it (i) explicitly constructs simple 2×2 games where last-iterate convergence is information-theoretically hard under uncoupled/bandit feedback, and (ii) discusses impossibility of almost-sure convergence for some no-regret algorithms (citing Muthukumar et al. 2020). Its lower-bound construction relies on the opponent’s mixed strategy approaching a minimax policy that makes the other player’s actions nearly indistinguishable, which is conceptually related to mechanisms that can prevent stable last-iterate behavior.

Still, it neither proves that last-iterate mixed strategies must diverge a.s. under optimal no-regret mean-based dynamics, nor provides a counterexample of convergent last-iterates with optimal regret in the general competitive 2×2 setting. In fact, it provides algorithms that do converge in last iterate (in L^p exploitability) but at slower rates than \(T^{-1/2}\), so they are not ‘optimal no-regret’ in the sense of the open problem.

sources.title: Higher-Order Uncoupled Learning Dynamics and Nash Equilibrium
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proves local exponential convergence to an isolated completely mixed Nash equilibrium in general finite games using higher-order uncoupled continuous-time dynamics. In particular, for any finite game with an isolated completely mixed-strategy NE \(x^*\) satisfying a nonsingularity/regularity condition (Assumption 2.1), there exist higher-order replicator dynamics of the form (18) (uncoupled, with auxiliary states and a washout filter) such that \((x^*,0,0)\) is locally exponentially stable (Theorem 4.1). More generally, for any standard-order uncoupled dynamics satisfying certain local nonsingularity conditions, there exists a higher-order uncoupled extension making \((x^*,0,0)\) locally exponentially stable (Theorem 5.1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks whether, in repeated \(2\times2\) competitive games with bandit feedback and mean-based (history-through-empirical-mean) strategies achieving optimal \(O(\sqrt{T})\) regret, the last-iterate mixed strategies \((P_t,Q_t)\) must diverge a.s. without assuming monotonicity. This paper studies a different model: continuous-time payoff-based (vector-payoff) uncoupled learning dynamics with auxiliary states, focusing on local stabilization of completely mixed NE. It provides positive convergence constructions (local exponential stability) rather than divergence/impossibility, and it does not analyze no-regret guarantees, discrete-time last-iterate behavior, or mean-based bandit feedback. Thus it neither proves nor refutes the almost-sure divergence claim in the open problem. At most, it offers control-theoretic stabilization techniques suggesting that convergence can be engineered in richer-information or higher-order settings, but these do not directly apply to the mean-based optimal no-regret bandit setting of the open problem.

title: Determine the exact master route ratio for a priori TSP with depot
background_latex:
Let \((V,c)\) be a finite metric space (triangle inequality, symmetry, and \(c(v,v)=0\)) whose points \(V\) are called customers. Each customer \(v\in V\) is active independently with probability \(p(v)\in(0,1]\). A distinguished customer \(d\in V\) is a depot with \(p(d)=1\).

An \emph{a priori TSP tour} is a cyclic ordering (TSP tour) \(T\) visiting all vertices in \(V\), chosen before seeing which customers are active. Given a realized active set \(A\subseteq V\), the realized tour cost is the length of the tour obtained by \emph{skipping} inactive vertices in the order prescribed by \(T\); denote this realized cost by \(c(T[A])\). The objective value of \(T\) is \(\mathbb{E}[c(T[A])]\) where the expectation is over the independent activations.

For a nonempty subset \(S\subseteq V\) with \(d\in S\), a \emph{master route solution} based on \(S\) consists of:
1) a TSP tour on \(S\) of length \(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{tsp}}(S,c)\), and
2) for each \(v\in V\setminus S\), two parallel edges connecting \(v\) to a nearest point in \(S\), where \(c(v,S):=\min\{c(v,s): s\in S\}\).

Under the standard analysis for master route solutions, the expected cost of the master route solution based on \(S\) is
\[\mathrm{MR}(S) := \mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbf{1}_{\{|A|\ge 2\}}\Big(\mathrm{OPT}_{\mathrm{tsp}}(S,c) + 2\sum_{v\in A} c(v,S)\Big)\Big],\]
where \(A\) is the random active set, and the indicator accounts for the convention that if fewer than two customers are active then one may shortcut to cost \(0\).

Let \(\mathrm{OPT}\) denote the minimum possible expected cost \(\min_T \mathbb{E}[c(T[A])]\) over all a priori tours \(T\) for \((V,c,p)\).

The \emph{master route ratio} (with depot) is the worst-case ratio between the best master route solution and the optimal a priori tour, i.e.
\[\rho^* := \sup_{(V,c,p)\,\text{with depot }d} \ \frac{\min\{\mathrm{MR}(S): \varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\}}{\mathrm{OPT}},\]
with the convention \(0/0:=1\) when needed.

\[\rho^* := \sup_{(V,c,p)\,\text{with depot }d} \ \frac{\min\{\mathrm{MR}(S): \varnothing\ne S\subseteq V\}}{\mathrm{OPT}}\]
for the a priori TSP with independent activations and a depot \(d\) satisfying \(p(d)=1\). In particular, decide whether
\[\rho^* = \frac{1}{1-e^{-1/2}}.\]

title: Designing polynomial-time 1/4-competitive secretary matching algorithm under edge arrivals
background_latex:
Consider an undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|E|=m\). Each edge \(e\in E\) has an (adversarial) nonnegative weight \(w_e\in\mathbb{R}\) that is unknown until the edge arrives online. In the edge-arrival secretary model, the edges \(e_1,\dots,e_m\) arrive in a uniformly random order. When edge \(e_t=uv\) arrives at time \(t\), its weight \(w_{e_t}\) is revealed, and the algorithm must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to add \(e_t\) to its matching \(\mu\), subject to feasibility (both endpoints \(u,v\) are currently unmatched).

Let \(\mu^*(E)\) denote a maximum-weight matching in \(G\) (with respect to \(w\)), and let \(\mathrm{OPT}=w(\mu^*(E))=\sum_{e\in\mu^*(E)} w_e\). An online algorithm \(\mathrm{ALG}\) outputs a random matching \(\mu\) and achieves competitive ratio \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) if for every weighted graph instance \((G,w)\),
\[\mathbb{E}[w(\mu)] \ge \alpha\, \mathrm{OPT},\]
where the expectation is over the random arrival order and the algorithm’s internal randomness.

The paper gives an information-theoretic online algorithm for edge arrivals that achieves \(\alpha=1/4\), but whose implementation appears to require estimating certain conditional availability probabilities that the authors do not know how to compute in polynomial time.

where \(\mu\) is the matching output by \(\mathrm{ALG}\), and the expectation is over the uniformly random arrival order of edges and the randomness of \(\mathrm{ALG}\).

title: Polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategies for Pandora problem with budget-additive costs
background_latex:
Pandora's problem has a ground set of boxes \([n]=\{1,\dots,n\}\). Each box \(i\) contains an independent nonnegative random value \(V_i\sim D_i\) with finite expectation. A (possibly adaptive) strategy \(\pi\) sequentially chooses unopened boxes to inspect; inspecting reveals the realized value and contributes to the total inspection cost. After any inspection the strategy may halt and receive reward equal to the maximum realized value among inspected boxes.

A combinatorial inspection cost function is \(c:2^{[n]}\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), assumed normalized and monotone: \(c(\varnothing)=0\) and \(c(S)\le c(T)\) for \(S\subseteq T\). If the strategy inspects exactly the (random) set \(S(\pi)\subseteq [n]\), its expected utility is
\[
 u(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\max_{i\in S(\pi)} V_i\Big]-\mathbb{E}[c(S(\pi))].
\]

A cost function is budget-additive (a.k.a. capped-additive) if there exist nonnegative weights \((w_i)_{i\in [n]}\) and a budget \(B\ge 0\) such that for all \(S\subseteq [n]\),
\[
 c(S)=\min\Big\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\Big\}.
\]
This class is monotone and submodular. The computational model considered in the paper represents \(c\) via oracle access (cost queries): given \(S\), a query returns \(c(S)\).
problem_definition_latex:
Design an algorithm that, given oracle access to a budget-additive cost function \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\) and explicit descriptions of independent value distributions \((D_i)_{i\in[n]}\), computes either:

1) an optimal Pandora strategy \(\pi^*\in\arg\max_{\pi} u(\pi)\), or

2) a strategy \(\pi\) with provable approximation guarantee for \(\max_{\pi} u(\pi)\),

in time polynomial in \(n\) (and the input encoding / desired accuracy), using only polynomially many cost queries.

literature_review.synthesis:
In the source paper (Berger–Ezra–Feldman–Fusco, 2023), Pandora’s problem is extended from additive inspection costs to a general monotone set function \(c:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R_{\ge 0}\). Two key takeaways frame the budget-additive open problem. First, for submodular costs, structural simplicity survives: there exists an optimal strategy with a non-adaptive inspection order (Theorem 4.1), obtained via a reduction to Bernoulli instances and a proof that an optimal policy can be taken to be “impulsive” (open in a fixed order and stop at the first nonzero). Second, computational simplicity fails dramatically in the value-oracle model: even deciding whether \(\max_\pi u(\pi)>0\) requires super-polynomially many cost queries (Theorem 5.2), and hence no polynomial-query approximation is possible for general submodular costs.

Budget-additive costs \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\) form a prominent subclass of submodular functions with additional structure (a single global cap). The cited follow-up/related works largely advance orthogonal directions—correlated values, time/order constraints, and general costly-information acquisition frameworks—typically under additive per-box costs. The most directly relevant progress is indirect: the thesis “Data Driven Search With Costly Information: When to Open Pandora's Box” and “Approximating pandora's box with correlations” develop approximation frameworks and reductions (e.g., to Uniform Decision Tree / Min-Sum Set Cover with Feedback) for correlated Pandora variants, while “Combinatorial selection with costly information” and “Commitment gap via correlation gap” provide composition and ex ante relaxation tools for costly-information MDP models under matroid-type constraints. These techniques suggest possible routes to handle the cap \(B\) by converting it into a coupling/feasibility constraint or by designing surrogate-cost indices, but none yields a polynomial-time (or polynomial-query) algorithm for the oracle-given budget-additive set-cost model.

Consequently, the specific question posed in the source paper’s conclusion—whether budget-additive costs admit polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategies with only polynomially many cost queries—appears to remain open based on the provided forward citations. A central remaining gap is to reconcile the strong oracle lower bounds for general submodular costs with the extra parametric structure of budget-additive functions: either by exploiting that structure algorithmically (e.g., learning \(w\) and \(B\) sufficiently from queries, then optimizing a fixed-order-with-thresholds policy), or by proving matching query lower bounds even for capped-additive costs. Promising directions include: (i) reductions that treat the cap as a knapsack-like resource and apply prophet-inequality/thresholding methods developed for constrained Pandora variants, and (ii) adapting CICS water-filling and ex ante LP approaches to derive efficiently computable indices/thresholds when the only non-additivity is the global cap.

sources.title: Data Driven Search With Costly Information: When to Open Pandora's Box
sources.theorem_or_result: The dissertation develops polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms for Pandora’s Box with correlated values under standard per-box opening costs (additive costs), e.g. a 9.22-approximation against the optimal partially-adaptive benchmark (Theorem 3.5) and improved greedy “generalized Weitzman” algorithms giving 4.428-approximation (Variant 1, Theorem 4.2) and 5.828-approximation (Variant 2, Theorem 4.3). It also gives poly-time \(\tilde O(\log m)\)-approximation against the fully-adaptive optimum via reductions to Uniform Decision Tree (Corollary 5.3/5.5), where \(m\) is the number of scenarios in the explicit support.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for a polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategy for Pandora’s problem when the inspection cost is budget-additive \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\) given by a value oracle. This dissertation’s algorithms and reductions address (i) correlated-value Pandora’s Box with *additive per-box* opening costs (\(\sum_{i\in S} c_i\)), and (ii) extensions to other feasibility constraints (k items, matroids), but it does not treat submodular/budget-additive inspection costs given by oracle. Budget-additive costs couple the decision to open boxes through a global cap \(B\), which is structurally different from the additive-cost model used throughout the thesis. Thus it does not resolve the stated open problem; at best it provides related techniques (LP relaxations/rounding, reductions to set cover/decision trees) that might inspire approaches for oracle-given submodular costs.

sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper develops an amortization-and-composition framework for Costly Information Combinatorial Selection (CICS), modeling each item’s information acquisition as an acyclic MDP under matroid feasibility constraints. Core results include:
- For Markov-chain components, a “water-filling” cost amortization yields surrogate costs and an index policy that is optimal for matroid-min-CICS (Theorem 3.2).
- For general acyclic MDP components, it defines water-filling surrogate costs via optimality curves and proves a Whittle-integral-type lower bound on the optimal adaptive policy: for any matroid-min-CICS instance 
\[\mathrm{OPT}(I) \ge \mathbb{E}\big[\min_{S\in F}\sum_{i\in S} W^*_{M_i}\big].\]
- If each component MDP admits an \(\alpha\)-local approximation commitment \(\pi_i\) (i.e. \(f_{M_i^{\pi_i}}(\alpha y)\le \alpha f_{M_i}(y)\) for all \(y\)), then the resulting committing policy achieves global \(\alpha\)-approximation (Theorem 4.1).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for a polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategy for Pandora’s problem with a budget-additive (capped-additive) *set-dependent* inspection cost \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\) given by oracle queries.

This paper does not study set-dependent inspection costs; instead it studies *per-action/per-item* costs within independent acyclic MDPs, combined with a *feasibility constraint* (primarily matroids) on which items may be ultimately selected. Its approximation guarantees are for CICS objectives of the form “selected values + action costs” (minimization) or “selected values − action costs” (maximization), not for a utility that subtracts a submodular cost \(c(S)\) of the *entire inspected set*.

Nevertheless, the paper is relevant as a tool/framework: it provides (i) surrogate-cost amortization ideas (water filling / Whittle-integral lower bounds) and (ii) composition theorems turning per-item local approximations into global approximations under matroid (and more generally frugal) constraints. These techniques could potentially inspire approaches to budget-additive costs by viewing the cap \(B\) as a global coupling constraint, but the paper does not provide an algorithm or approximation guarantee for oracle-given budget-additive inspection costs in Pandora’s original “max of revealed values minus cost of inspected set” formulation.

sources.title: Pandora's box problem with time constraints
sources.theorem_or_result: They define the very general “Pandora’s Box Over Time” model (time-dependent costs ci(t), time-dependent reward distributions \(D_i^t\), processing times \(p_i\), and post-inspection value discounting \(\bar v_i\)) and give polynomial-time constant-factor approximation algorithms. Main guarantees include: (i) a 21.3-approximation for the general model (Theorem 3.1), obtained via a reduction to maximizing \(f(M)=\mathbb E[\max_{e\in M} Y_e]\) over matchings in a block bipartite hypergraph and a 5.32-approximation for this “Submodular Block Matching” problem (Theorem 3.7); (ii) improved \((4+\varepsilon)\)-approximations when processing times are zero / time-slot availability constraints (Theorems 4.2 and 4.4); and (iii) a 1.37-approximation for “value discounting” with time-independent costs and distributions (Theorem 4.5).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategies for Pandora’s problem with budget-additive (capped-additive) combinatorial inspection costs given by an oracle \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\). This paper does not study combinatorial set costs; its costs are additive across inspected boxes (possibly time-dependent per-box costs \(\bar c_i(t)\)) and feasibility is modeled via time/processing constraints rather than a submodular cost oracle. Thus it does not resolve the budget-additive-cost Pandora open problem. However, it contributes relevant techniques—reductions to constrained Pandora instances, adaptivity-gap arguments, prophet-inequality-based stopping rules, and especially approximation algorithms for maximizing \(\mathbb E[\max_{e\in M} Y_e]\) under structured combinatorial constraints (block bipartite hypergraph matchings). These tools may be adaptable to designing approximation algorithms when the inspection “cost” is submodular/budget-additive, but no such result is claimed here.

sources.title: Commitment gap via correlation gap
sources.theorem_or_result: For Costly Information Combinatorial Selection (CICS) with feasibility constraint \(F\), the paper relates the best achievable performance of committing policies to ex ante free-order prophet inequalities for \(F\). In particular it proves (Corollary 5.5) that for any CICS instance \(I=(F,M)\), the commitment gap satisfies \(\mathrm{ComGap}(I)\ge \alpha_F\), where \(\alpha_F:=\min_D \mathrm{FreeOrder}(F,D)/\mathrm{ExAnte}(F,D)\) (equivalently the frugal correlation gap). It also shows (Lemma 3.1 + Section 6) that the ex ante optimal CICS policy can be computed exactly and efficiently (via an occupation-measure LP) and yields an optimal commitment \(P\) with \(\mathrm{ExAnteOpt}(I)=\mathrm{ExAnteOpt}(I^P)\). For matroid \(F\), this yields an efficient \((1-1/e)\)-approximation by committing policies (Table 1).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for polynomial-time optimal or approximation algorithms for Pandora’s problem with budget-additive (capped-additive) inspection costs given by an oracle. This paper does not study combinatorial inspection cost functions \(c(S)\) of the form \(\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\); instead it studies CICS where costs arise from per-element probing MDPs and feasibility is a downward-closed constraint \(F\) on the finally selected set. Its main contribution is a general approximation framework for CICS via ex ante relaxations, surrogate values, and (ex ante) free-order prophet inequalities, plus exact computation of the ex ante optimum under a separation oracle for \(P(F)\). These techniques may be conceptually relevant if one can reduce budget-additive inspection costs to a CICS/MDP model or otherwise connect the Pandora-with-submodular-cost objective to an ex ante relaxation and prophet-inequality rounding, but the paper does not provide such a reduction or an algorithm for budget-additive cost Pandora directly.

sources.theorem_or_result: The paper introduces Delegated Choice with Inspection Cost (DCIC), a generalization of Pandora’s box with nonobligatory inspection (PNOI), and proves constant-factor approximation mechanisms in several regimes. In particular, for costless delegation (Del=0) it gives a 3-approximation mechanism (Theorem 4.8) and shows this factor is tight for that mechanism (Theorem 4.11). It also extends the 3-approximation analysis to arbitrary monotone set-function inspection costs (Corollary 4.9).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategies for Pandora’s problem with budget-additive (capped-additive) combinatorial costs given by oracle access. This paper does not study that model: its main setting is DCIC with a strategic agent and (mostly) additive per-item inspection costs, with an extension to arbitrary monotone set-function costs in a specific costless-delegation regime. While Corollary 4.9 mentions monotone combinatorial costs, the mechanism there uses at most one inspection and the analysis upper-bounds costs via singleton costs, so it does not yield an approximation algorithm for Pandora’s problem with budget-additive costs (without delegation) nor address oracle-reconstruction of weights/budget. Thus it does not resolve the open problem, but provides related conceptual/technical ideas about handling monotone set-function costs and approximation via simple max-of-two mechanisms.

sources.title: Optimal 4-Approximation for the Correlated Pandora's Problem
sources.theorem_or_result: Main theorem (Theorem 15): For the Correlated Pandora’s Problem in the minimization form (minimize total opening cost plus the minimum revealed volume), the authors give a polynomial-time 4-approximation among partially adaptive policies (fixed opening order, adaptive stopping). The algorithm is Poisson rounding of a convex-program relaxation plus a “Balanced Stopping” rule, achieving expected objective at most \(4\cdot \mathrm{OPT}_{\text{part-adapt}}\).

The open problem asks for polynomial-time optimal or approximate strategies for the *classical* (independent values) Pandora problem with a *budget-additive set function* inspection cost \(c(S)=\min\{B,\sum_{i\in S} w_i\}\) given by oracle, and objective \(\mathbb E[\max V_i]-\mathbb E[c(S)]\) (a maximization with a submodular cost).

This citing paper studies a different model: Correlated Pandora’s Problem with *additive per-box costs* \(c_i\) and a *minimization* objective (cost + min volume), and it restricts to partially adaptive policies. Its 4-approximation does not address budget-additive (capped-additive) *set-function* costs, nor the maximization objective with independent values. However, it contributes relevant techniques—LP/convex relaxations, Poisson rounding, and stopping-rule analysis—that might inspire approximation algorithms for other Pandora variants with non-additive costs.

In particular, it gives a polynomial-time \(\tilde O(\log m)\)-approximation for PB when the joint distribution has explicit support of size \(m\) (Corollary 3.1/3.3), and under a separability condition for a mixture of \(m\) product distributions it gives a constant-factor approximation running in time \(n^{\tilde O(m^2/\varepsilon^2)}\) (Corollary 6.1, via Theorem 6.1 for \(\mathrm{PB}_{\le T}\)).

This citing paper studies a different axis: *correlations* in box values under (mostly) additive per-box opening costs (unit costs, with an extension to non-unit additive costs). It does not model or address submodular/budget-additive set-dependent costs, nor oracle access to \(c\). However, its reductions to decision-tree/cover problems and its thresholding framework for stopping rules could be conceptually useful as tools if one later extends them to combinatorial-cost probing/search settings.

This paper does not address combinatorial costs: it assumes standard additive per-box costs \(\sum_{i\in S} c_i\) and instead adds order constraints (deadlines/time slots). However, its technique—reducing feasibility of inspectable sets to a transversal matroid and then using monotone submodular maximization plus adaptivity-gap and prophet-inequality thresholding—may be conceptually relevant if one can model budget-additive costs or the induced objective within a similar submodular/matroid framework. As written, it neither provides an algorithm nor approximation guarantee for budget-additive cost oracles.

title: Designing ADMM methods for nonsmooth Riemannian optimization without Moreau smoothing
background_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an embedded Riemannian submanifold, and let \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be a given linear map. Consider the composite constrained optimization problem
\[
\min_{x\in \mathcal{M}}\; F(x) := f(x)+ g(Ax),
\]
where:
1) \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is smooth (continuously differentiable) in the ambient Euclidean space (and may be nonconvex).
2) \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex but possibly nonsmooth in the ambient Euclidean space.
A standard variable-splitting reformulation introduces \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and imposes the linear constraint \(Ax-y=0\):
\[
\min_{x\in \mathcal{M},\; y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\; f(x)+g(y)\quad \text{s.t. } Ax-y=0.
\]
An (Euclidean) augmented Lagrangian for this splitting is
\[
\mathcal{L}_\rho(x,y;\lambda)= f(x)+g(y)+\langle \lambda, Ax-y\rangle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|Ax-y\|^2,
\]
with multiplier \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and penalty parameter \(\rho>0\). 

In the paper, the proposed RADMM replaces \(g\) by a smoothed surrogate using the Moreau envelope with parameter \(\gamma>0\):
\[
 g_\gamma(z):= \min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\Big\{g(y)+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\|y-z\|^2\Big\},
\]
and then applies an ADMM-like scheme to the smoothed problem. The open question asks for an ADMM design for the original (unsmoothed) problem above, i.e., without introducing \(g_\gamma\) (or equivalently without the additional quadratic smoothing term used to obtain a smooth surrogate of \(g\)).
problem_definition_latex:
Construct and analyze an ADMM-type algorithm that directly solves
\[
\min_{x\in \mathcal{M}}\; f(x)+g(Ax)
\]
(or equivalently its split form \(\min\{f(x)+g(y): x\in\mathcal{M},\ Ax-y=0\}\)) without replacing \(g\) by its Moreau envelope \(g_\gamma\) or any other smoothing, and establish rigorous convergence guarantees (for example, convergence to an appropriate first-order stationary notion and/or an iteration-complexity bound).

literature_review.synthesis:
Li–Ma–Srivastava (2024) introduced RADMM for the split formulation \(\min\{f(x)+g(y): x\in\mathcal M,\ Ax-y=0\}\) but crucially relied on Moreau-envelope smoothing \(g_\gamma\) to obtain a smooth surrogate and then performed a Riemannian gradient step on the augmented Lagrangian, yielding an \(O(\varepsilon^{-4})\) iteration bound for their \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity notion. The open question in that paper asked whether one can design an ADMM-type method that keeps the original convex nonsmooth \(g\) intact (i.e., uses a genuine proximal \(y\)-update) while still controlling multiplier behavior and tangent-space variation to obtain rigorous convergence guarantees.

This question has been answered affirmatively by the paper "Adaptive Riemannian ADMM for nonsmooth optimization: Optimal complexity without smoothing", which provides an unsmoothed Riemannian ADMM for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) (via splitting \(Ax=y\)) and proves nonasymptotic KKT residual bounds. Its key technical innovation is an adaptive choice of penalty \(\rho_k\) and dual stepsize (together with a decaying primal stepsize) that yields control of \(\|\lambda^{k+1}-\lambda^k\|\) in terms of primal differences and enables a Lyapunov-type descent argument without appealing to the smoothness of \(g_\gamma\). The resulting complexity \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) to reach an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate KKT point matches the natural target for first-order methods in this nonconvex–nonsmooth manifold setting and improves over the \(O(\varepsilon^{-4})\) rate of the smoothed RADMM analysis.

Subsequent and parallel developments broaden the landscape. "A Single-loop Stochastic Riemannian ADMM for Nonsmooth Optimization" extends the unsmoothed ADMM idea to stochastic objectives \(\mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]\), retaining proximal handling of \(g\) and achieving \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) complexity for \(\varepsilon\)-KKT points. On the other hand, augmented-Lagrangian and primal–dual alternatives provide complementary theory: "Oracle Complexities of Augmented Lagrangian Methods for Nonsmooth Composite Optimization on a Compact Submanifold" gives sharp oracle complexities for manifold ALM schemes but still introduces a Moreau envelope implicitly by eliminating the split variable, while "A Riemannian alternating descent ascent algorithmic framework for nonconvex-linear minimax problems on Riemannian manifolds" solves the same composite objective through a Fenchel-type minimax formulation with \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) complexity without smoothing \(g\). Together, these works indicate that the main remaining gaps are relaxing compactness/Lipschitz assumptions (e.g., noncompact \(\mathcal M\), non-Lipschitz \(g\) such as indicators), improving constants and practical adaptivity, and establishing last-iterate guarantees or faster rates under additional geometry (e.g., geodesic convexity, error bounds, or KŁ properties).

sources.title: Adaptive Riemannian ADMM for nonsmooth optimization: Optimal complexity without smoothing
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes an adaptive Riemannian ADMM (ARADMM) for 
\[\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+h(Ax)\]
(with split form \(\min\{f(x)+h(y): x\in\mathcal M,\ Ax=y\}\)) that does not smooth \(h\). Under Assumption 3.1 (compact embedded submanifold \(\mathcal M\); \(f\) \(\ell_{\nabla f}\)-smooth and Lipschitz on \(\mathcal M\); \(h\) proper closed convex and Lipschitz; bounded \(\|A\|_{op}\)), Theorem 3.1 shows that with adaptive penalty \(\rho_k=c_\rho k^{1/3}\), primal stepsize \(\tau_k=c_\tau k^{-1/3}\), and adaptive dual stepsize \(\gamma_k\), for any \(K>2\) there exists \(\kappa\in[\lceil K/2\rceil,K]\) such that the KKT residuals satisfy
- \(\|P_{T_{x_\kappa}\mathcal M}(-A^*\bar\lambda_\kappa)+\operatorname{grad} f(x_\kappa)\|\le O((K+1)^{-1/3})\),
- \(\operatorname{dist}(-\bar\lambda_\kappa,\partial h(y_\kappa))\le O((K+1)^{-1/3})\),
- \(\|Ax_\kappa-y_\kappa\|\le O((K-2)^{-1/3})\),
implying an iteration complexity \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) to reach an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate KKT point (Definition 2.3) for the original nonsmooth problem.
sources.connection: This directly answers the open problem: it designs an ADMM-type method for the original composite nonsmooth Riemannian problem \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) (their \(h\equiv g\)) without replacing \(g\) by a Moreau envelope or any smoothing. The algorithm keeps the nonsmooth term in the \(y\)-update via the exact proximal operator of \(h\) and uses a single Riemannian gradient step for the \(x\)-update. The main technical obstacle noted in the open problem—controlling dual updates when tangent spaces vary and \(h\) is nonsmooth—is handled by an adaptive choice of penalty \(\rho_k\) and dual stepsize \(\gamma_k\), yielding bounds on \(\|\lambda^{k+1}-\lambda^k\|\) in terms of primal differences (Lemma 3.1) and enabling a descent-type potential argument for the augmented Lagrangian. Theorem 3.1 provides rigorous convergence guarantees (to \(\varepsilon\)-KKT points) and an explicit complexity bound \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\), matching the type of guarantee requested.

sources.title: A Single-loop Stochastic Riemannian ADMM for Nonsmooth Optimization
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes MARS-ADMM, a single-loop stochastic Riemannian ADMM for composite problems \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} \mathbb E_\xi[f(x,\xi)] + g(Ax)\) with convex possibly nonsmooth \(g\), and proves that it finds an \(\varepsilon\)-KKT point of the split problem \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M,y}\;F(x)+g(y)\;\text{s.t. }Ax=y\) with oracle/iteration complexity \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) under compactness and Lipschitz/variance assumptions (Theorems 4.10–4.11).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an ADMM-type method on a Riemannian submanifold that handles the original nonsmooth convex \(g\) term without Moreau-envelope smoothing, with convergence guarantees. This paper explicitly updates \(y\) via the proximal operator of \(g\) (no smoothing) and performs a Riemannian gradient step on the augmented Lagrangian in \(x\), with adaptive penalty and dual stepsizes. It provides rigorous convergence to an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary (\(\varepsilon\)-KKT) point and an iteration complexity bound. It therefore addresses the design-and-analysis request, albeit in a stochastic setting and under assumptions like compact \(\mathcal M\) and Lipschitz \(g\).

sources.title: Oracle Complexities of Augmented Lagrangian Methods for Nonsmooth Composite Optimization on a Compact Submanifold
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes manifold inexact augmented Lagrangian methods (ManIAL, StoManIAL) for nonsmooth composite manifold problems \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+h(Ax)\) with \(f\) smooth (possibly nonconvex), \(h\) proper closed convex Lipschitz, \(\mathcal M\) compact embedded. Main deterministic guarantee (Theorem 3.8): with suitable penalty schedule \(\{\sigma_k\}\) and inner Riemannian gradient descent solves of \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} L_{\sigma_k}(x,z^k)\), the method returns an \(\varepsilon\)-KKT point \((x,y,\bar z)\) satisfying \(\|P_{T_x\mathcal M}(\nabla f(x)-A^*\bar z)\|\le\varepsilon\), \(\mathrm{dist}(-\bar z,\partial h(y))\le\varepsilon\), \(\|Ax-y\|\le\varepsilon\) using \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) (Option I) or \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) (Option II) first-order oracle calls (oracle: \(\nabla f\), \(\mathrm{prox}_h\), retraction). Stochastic guarantee (Theorem 4.8): \(\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-3.5})\) stochastic oracle calls to reach an \(\varepsilon\)-KKT point for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} \mathbb E[f(x,\xi)]+h(Ax)\).
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an ADMM-type method that handles the original nonsmooth \(g\) (no Moreau smoothing) for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) with convergence guarantees. This paper does not give a Riemannian ADMM; instead it gives an (inexact) augmented Lagrangian method (ALM) framework for the same composite model with nonsmooth convex \(h\) handled via its proximal operator. However, their ALM eliminates the split variable \(y\) by minimizing over \(y\), yielding an augmented Lagrangian \(L_\sigma(x,z)=f(x)+M_{1/\sigma}h(Ax-z/\sigma)-\|z\|^2/(2\sigma)\), which explicitly uses the Moreau envelope \(M_{1/\sigma}h\). Thus it still relies on Moreau smoothing (though induced by ALM elimination rather than an external smoothing parameter) and does not answer the specific request for an unsmoothed RADMM/ADMM scheme. Nevertheless, it provides strong complexity guarantees for a closely related multiplier-based approach to the same nonsmooth manifold composite problem, and may inform ADMM analysis (penalty schedules, KKT residual measures, inner-solve accuracy control).

sources.title: A Riemannian alternating descent ascent algorithmic framework for nonconvex-linear minimax problems on Riemannian manifolds
sources.theorem_or_result:
The paper proposes a Riemannian alternating descent–ascent (RADA) framework for nonconvex-linear minimax problems on manifolds
\[
\min_{x\in\mathcal M}\max_{y\in E_2}\; f(x)+\langle A(x),y\rangle-h(y),
\]
with convex (possibly nonsmooth) proper closed \(h\) with compact domain and tractable proximal map. With a regularized value function
\(\Phi_k(x)=\max_y\{F(x,y)-\tfrac\lambda2\|y\|^2-\tfrac{\beta_k}2\|y-y_k\|^2\}\), Algorithm 1 (and its instances RADA-PGD/RADA-RGD) returns both an \(\varepsilon\)-Riemannian-game-stationary point \((x_{\hat k},y_{\hat k+1/2})\) and an \(\varepsilon\)-Riemannian-optimization-stationary point \(x_{\hat k}\) within \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) iterations (Theorems 2–4), under standard smoothness/compactness assumptions.
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for an ADMM-type method for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) with convex nonsmooth \(g\), *without* Moreau-envelope smoothing of \(g\), and with convergence guarantees.

This paper does not directly design an unsmoothed Riemannian ADMM for the split form \(\min\{f(x)+g(y):x\in\mathcal M,\ Ax-y=0\}\). Instead it targets the Fenchel-dual minimax form with \(h=g^*\):
\[
\min_{x\in\mathcal M}\max_y\; f(x)+\langle A(x),y\rangle-h(y)=\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+h^*(A(x))=\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(A(x)).
\]
So it provides a *non-ADMM* single-loop primal–dual (descent–ascent) framework that solves the same composite objective without smoothing \(g\) (it only uses proximal steps of \(h=g^*\), not a Moreau envelope of \(g\)). It also explicitly relates its method to augmented-Lagrangian/ADMM variants (Section 5), including an interpretation as a Riemannian symmetric Gauss–Seidel ADMM for a *smoothed* reformulation when \(\lambda>0\). Thus it gives partial progress toward the open question by offering an alternative to Moreau smoothing with rigorous \(O(\varepsilon^{-3})\) complexity, but it does not settle the specific request for a direct unsmoothed RADMM/ADMM scheme on the split constraint \(Ax-y=0\) with convergence analysis.

sources.title: A new inexact manifold proximal linear algorithm with adaptive stopping criteria
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes the inexact manifold proximal linear (IManPL) method for composite problems on an embedded compact submanifold \(\mathcal M\): \(\min_{z\in\mathcal M} F(z)=f(z)+h(c(z))\) with smooth \(f,c\) and convex Lipschitz \(h\). With fixed stepsize \(t_k\equiv t\), Theorem 1 shows IManPL finds an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point (measured by \(\|(z-S_t(z))/t\|\le \varepsilon\)) in \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) outer iterations, and Theorem 2 shows every accumulation point is stationary in the sense \(0\in \mathrm{Proj}_{T_z\mathcal M}(\nabla f(z)+\nabla c(z)^\top \partial h(c(z)))\). When subproblems are solved by an accelerated proximal gradient method on a dual formulation, Theorem 3 gives total first-order oracle complexity \(J(\varepsilon)=O(1/\varepsilon^3)\) for all inner iterations combined.
sources.connection: The open problem asks for an ADMM-type method for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) without Moreau smoothing, with convergence guarantees. This paper does not develop a Riemannian ADMM/augmented-Lagrangian splitting for the constraint \(Ax-y=0\). Instead it gives a (prox-linear) majorization/proximal framework for the unsmoothed composite objective \(f(x)+g(Ax)\) as a special case of \(f(z)+h(c(z))\) by taking \(c(z)=Az\) and \(h=g\). It therefore provides a direct nonsmooth manifold algorithm (no Moreau envelope) with stationarity and complexity guarantees, but it is not an ADMM design and does not address multiplier updates or feasibility of a split formulation.

sources.title: Non-convex Pose Graph Optimization in SLAM via Proximal Linearized Riemannian ADMM: X. Chen et al.
sources.theorem_or_result: The paper proposes PieADMM, a proximal linearized Riemannian ADMM scheme for a nonconvex pose-graph optimization model with unit-quaternion (sphere) manifold constraints and linear coupling constraints, and proves a sublinear iteration complexity bound: under parameter conditions (Theorem 5.2), the algorithm finds an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point in at most \(T=O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) iterations (with stationarity measured by residuals of the first-order optimality system (5.2)).
sources.connection:
The open problem asks for an ADMM-type method on an embedded manifold \(\mathcal M\) for \(\min_{x\in\mathcal M} f(x)+g(Ax)\) with convex possibly nonsmooth \(g\), without Moreau-envelope smoothing, and with convergence guarantees.
- This paper does develop and analyze a Riemannian ADMM variant without Moreau smoothing, and it establishes an \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) iteration complexity to an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary notion.
- However, the objective treated here is a smooth (polynomial/least-squares) pose-graph objective; the nonsmooth convex term \(g\) of the open problem is not present. The only nonsmoothness is the indicator \(\delta_U\) of the sphere constraint, handled by projection.
- The splitting is also not of the composite form \(f(x)+g(Ax)\) with a general linear map \(A\) and a general convex nonsmooth \(g\); instead it is a problem-specific variable-splitting \(p=q\) to multilinearize a quartic objective.
Thus, it provides partial progress/related evidence that unsmoothed Riemannian ADMM with complexity guarantees is feasible, but it does not resolve the general composite nonsmooth problem posed in the open question.
